For years now, Compile Heart and Idea Factory have been visibly personifying video game consoles and companies into their Hyperdimension Neptunia series. The Hyperdimension Neptunia games have been running primarily on Sony platforms as main games would premiere on PS3, then spin-off or be remade for the Vita. They’re a silly, self-aware, and obscure set of games, but offset their humor and art style with dungeon crawling and outlandishly spontaneous boss battles. Hyperdimension Neptunia Re;Birth 1 is a PC port of the Vita version, so PC gamers are finally able to get in on the action as it makes its way to Steam; is this series worth booting up, or left better forgotten?
Hyperdimension Neptunia Re;Birth 1, like all of the Hyperdimension Neptunia games, takes place in the world of Gameindustri. The world is separated into four regions: Planeptune (Sega), Lowee (Nintendo), Lastation (Sony), and Leanbox (Microsoft). Each region has distinctive lands and aesthetics to reflect the individual areas, such as Leanbox has a dungeon called “Halo Mountain”, or Lowee’s “Hyrarule Snowfield”. All of these domains are ruled over by various CPUs (Console Patron Units), AKA our heroines: Neptune, Blanc, Noire, and Vert respectively. Every goddess fights in the Console War (I’m are not making this up) that’s been raging for centuries. Naturally a greater evil is at work behind the scenes, and Vert, Blanc, and Noire effectively remove Neptune from the Console War, and she’s rescued by Compa who nurses her back to health. Assuming the loss of any of her memory is the fault of Amnesia, Neptune and Compa set out to regain her memories and stop the monsters tearing throughout the world. All while making various puns, jokes, and foibles of actual video game lore and history.
It’s this kind of creative humor and writing that tries to carry Hyperdimension Neptunia through its razor-thin plot, but wears out its welcome due to repetitive ideas, setups, and implementations. That’s certainly not to say the writing or plot is bad, but after just 10 hours of gameplay everything just seems to fit a similar, repeated arrangement. There are plenty of gags and jokes that are subtlety slipped into several of voice-acted conversations that merited a chuckle or two, but they were few and far between. The voice acting in-game and cut scenes is adequate; though some of the squeals and noises emitted from the cutesy cast are grating from time to time. You do have the option to switch to Japanese or English voices at any time, but we preferred the English option. On the other end of Hyperdimension Neptuia’s artistic presentation is its undoubtedly “love it or leave it” character designs. Every single female’s characterization is buxom and is not afraid to show it. Their super-powered “HDD” transformation forms are more than likely to ruffle a few feathers, given that their outfits are glorified bikinis straining to stay on their forms.
In the music department, it’s a lesser positive story as every track is about as minimally different from the last, you’re practically listening to one long 40+ hour creation. Hyperdimension Neptunia’s opening track “Miracle Portable Mission” by nao is its most memorable, lingering song, but it’s still high-pitched, lightly-auto tuned J-pop. It’s an absolute shame that the music in Hyperdimension Neptunia is forgettable, because you will be hearing for a long, long time. As a dungeon crawler, you’ll be spelunking through a variety of locales defeating enemies in a familiar “Tales” style battle system, with physical attacks, buffs, magic attack and other usual JRPG fare. Grating more than the repetitive music is the level design and its all too repeated layouts. Every region may have a different look from the outside, but most contain similar dungeons (Ruins, a Tron-esque design scheme, or a basic forest) that are hardly different from the previous iteration(s). Ditto for their inhabitants, as the creatures destined to fall by your blade rarely even get a palette swap to differentiate themselves from their kin. We’re used to seeing JRPGs recycle enemy sprites for years, especially in the earlier generations given limited memory space at the time, but it’s a personal peeve to see it still happening in the modern age.
Luckily the pace is usually slick and progressive while in these areas, but every now and again, the game likes to spike in difficulty and force you to grind and level up to combat a few of the bosses or optional quests battles. You can make through most of the dungeons pretty easily, but occasionally bosses will pounce on you unexpectedly after a long dialog chain; and just as you narrowly defeat them, another arrives giving you no save points or time to recoup your health or magic. It’s not too common, but it does happen early enough that it may be a deal breaker for some and turn them away too prematurely. Stacked, multi-level bosses are typically reserved for end-game, so for them to sporadically appear is frustrating to a gamer of any skill level.
Among other frustrations that encompass Hyperdimension Neptunia: game crashes. It’s rare for a game such as this to crash, and it’s all the more irritating when it does happen, because while save points are rather superfluous, if you’re not too keen on using them rather conservatively, you can lose hours of progress in a moment’s notice. We had plenty of quests and bosses requiring retries and resupplying because the game froze mid-battle or as we earned experience. We eventually learned to save after returning to the over world and as often as possible, but with no auto-save mechanic in place, and random crashes being as prominent as they are, even as a remake and port of an already released game, it’s disparaging to say the least.
By end game, Hyperdimension Neptunia Re;Birth 1 knows it is a niche game for a niche market, and it accepts it and even prods itself with its humor and satirical presentation. Those familiar with comparable games will feel right at home, but newcomers or the unenlightened will be taken aback and not too keen on difficulty spikes, random boss battles, game crashes, and repetitive or “artistically creative” character design. If you’re looking for a an interesting changeup to the JRPG formula, Hyperdimension Neptunia Re;Birth 1 could be just that game to scratch that itch but, buyer beware, what you see is what you get upon loading this game into your life.

If the amount of hours I have played of this game is not evidence enough, I whole heartedly reccomend this game. There are many facets to playing this game - like a rogue-like should - especially with the recent Advanced Edition.
This game appeals to the procedurally generated aspects that so many games on Steam are renowned for while also appealing to fans of space-based games. Aside from 10 vastly different ships and hundreds of combonations of crew, weapons, and augments that affect your gameplay, what keeps me coming back is that there is still stuff to do. There's a great sense of accomplishment and anticipation when you finally unlock a new ship or layout because you know that whether you beat the game this run or die in a flaming metal deathtrap, when you get back, you have all new opportunities at doing better next time.
Also, there is great amusement in having the ability to name your ship and crew and seeing what kind of terrible situations can happen to your personalized crew, whether they're your friends, family, or a crew of celebrity Steves.
I don't want to spoil all the great parts of the game or explain every single aspect of it. Just get it, you'll definitely get your time out of it.

Go forth and enter unholy dungeon. Behold the warped horrors that lie within, in the shadows, waiting for your inevitable doom. Fight your way to the portal as rusted traps and abyssal monsters rend your flesh time and time again. For salvation from this purgatory comes through pain and bloodlust.
Truly an amazing game. Tight gameplay that combines fluctuating unfairness and simplicity to deliver an ever-challenging and evolving experience. The sound is masterfully executed. Exquisitely composed soundtrack coupled with very distinctive sound effects and the most riveting voice-over I have heard in a videogame since Eternal Darkness' autopsies. All bound with an expert use of saturation and lo-bit sinthesizer. The artwork and animations really bring the world come alive with pixelated environments, fluidity and an ochre limited palette that helps focusing on the action while still retaining a solid atmosphere. And, for one, AI is not mind-numbingly stupid. Your "companions" will try to win room after room leaving you unable to catch a breath. Even in their less lucid moments, they feel real due to their movements and decisions.
Now add 4-player local multiplayer. You will never feel the same again.

This is a fun game -- very similar feel to Diablo 2. The main campaign takes about 20 hours and is repeatable through 3 stages (Normal/Veteran, Elite, and Ulltimate). The combat is fast paced and fun, with mechanics mostly based on spamming, dodging, and HP kiting (especially if you're playing a melee character) . The replayability on single characters is pretty decent, since stat checks (you lose % of all resists each time you increase the difficulty level), skills, and 'constellations' (which unlock unique new character traits) make the same fights feel fresh the second time around.
Also, once you make it through one playthrough, the quests are simple enough that you can run through them quickly without thinking. This is sort of a pro and a con -- I can't imagine myself mainlining this game for hours on end, but it definitely pairs well with netflix marathons/hearthstone/anything else that doesn't require your full attention. If you're solo, that is :)

Grim Dawn is utterly amazing.
Pros:
- combat feels more impactful than similar games such as D3 and PoE
-story is far more interesting
-builds can vary greatly
-world is very well designed
-rift system is brilliant
Cons:
-world sometimes feels too big lol
-graphics are good but animations can be lackluster.  Depends on the skills.  Some have good animations, some dont.
Misc:
- I definately would recommend this game.  The pros far outweigh the cons.  The combat may be a little slow at first, but picks up speed about halfway through the main campaign.  Some people on here also mentioned that they dont think melee is viable in this game.  That is actually a misconception.  Melee with tons of active abilities is not that viable. But melee with a few active abilities and tons of passives is amazing.  I have yet to finish the entire game, but I plan on finishing it soon.  I did take a break though for awhile, because of how big the world is.  Im the type of person who has to search every inch of the map, soooo i kinda get worn out every now and then lol.  Nonetheless I think this is a great game.
Comparison:
Diablo 3 vs Grim Dawn vs Path of Exile
-I have played all 3 games and enjoy them all extensively.  I would say Diablo 3 is very fun but feels more casual and fantasy than the other two.  Path of Exile is a good game, but the lack of story depth makes it boring after awhile.  Grim Dawn probably has the most engaging story. (I like Diablo 3's story better, but I feel it is kinda poorly implemented in the game.  Even though Grim Dawn may not have as good of a story, it definately makes you feel like you are an active part of the story.  Hence why I prefer Grim Dawn's story.)  The combat feels more powerful in Grim Dawn.  Path of Exile had good bow mechanics.  Probably the best out of the three.  Diablo 3's combat doesn't quite have the impact that Grim Dawn's combat does, but I can't deny that both Diablo 3 and Path of Exile have wayyyyyyyyy better animations for their combat.
All in all, I love all three games, but if I had to pick one, it would be Grim Dawn.  Grim Dawn makes you want to play for hours on end.  Path of Exile just gets boring after a few hours, and Im not even sure why tbh.  Diablo 3 is really fun only if you are playing with friends.  Sorry about my long post, but anyways...I definately would recommend Grim Dawn.  At least until something better comes out of the Arpg genre.

It's not often I'm getting surprised by the quality of a game, but this exactly what happened to me with The Banner Saga. The reason for this being that this game is a one of a kind.
Surely, the genre of RPG with tactical battles is nothing new, but the developers managed to create an interesting and innovative battle system that gives you quite a lot of possibilities to show off your prowess as a tactician.
But what really makes The Banner Saga a unique experience is its caravan management gameplay that makes you pay heed to every decision you make throughout the game, keep the supplies sufficient and prevent the caravan morale from dropping low.
I must also mention that the difference between the difficulty levels is evident. Given all my previous experience with TRPG I still struggled with some battles on Hard, and the final battle on Hard is really hard, but still possible to win after several tries.
Another aspect of this game that is very important for me personally is the music. I think I haven't listened to such a beautiful and fitting music in quite a long time. One nice bonus is the participation of Malukah in creation of the soundtrack. Her voice adds another dimension to the melodies.
I guess, the only aspect of The Banner Saga I didn't feel completely content with is the character development. Hopefully the developers pay more attention to that in the next game of the series.
My conclusion is that this game is definitely worth to be in a collection of any player that likes tactical RPG, drawn art and Norse mythology.

I had this game on my watch list for some time, but never actually committed to buying it because, although the reviews were quite good, it just seemed too much of an odd-ball game to commit to. Boy was I wrong. Just goes to show you that you don't need graphics card choking high-end visuals and state of the art 3D to make a stellar game. The folks at Stoic have proven that a good epic story, combined with decision making that gives you very unexpected outcomes, and an Archon chess like combat system, (Google it!) can actually be uncannily entertaining. The graphics, although 2D in nature are put to exceptional and very creative use, to give a visually rich playing environment. Music is excellent and ties in well with the mood of the game, although a little more voice acting would have been a nice touch. Play it on normal and you are sure to be challenged, and at times just a bit frustrated, but in a good way. I was able to start playing it on my high end Windows PC, and then finish it on my 4 year old MacBook Air, with no change in look or even performance. Steam’s Cloud synchronization even gave me the ability to just continue playing where I left off. A true gaming outlier that will not disappoint. Enjoy.

I've enjoyed this game, it's very old school style D&D style RPG. The 2 things that just drive me insane about this game:
1- the Rock Paper Scissor 'discussion' with my own party. This is especially annoying when I know I'm selecting the right answer, but yet my partner insists on selecting the wrong answer. 2- combat. There is one thing in combat that makes me so angry. When I'm trying to attack from range (e.g. bow) and the enemy's standing animation shifts, and I click on the floor just behind them. The character will walk to that spot, and I can't stop them (I don't think there is a way) unless I end their turn. The battles are very strategy oriented, and this can ruin the battle. It has honestly made me just quit the game a couple times.
Other than that..I'm really enjoying the game. Some of the puzzles are just ridiculously difficult. There was one that the hint was simply, "Weight of justice" and then there were these pressure plates. I knew I had to put things on them, at different weights, but I didn't get a clue as to how much weight to put on them. Luckily I have google *rolls eyes*
Anyway, overall a very fun game. It can be painful at times with difficult battles and unclear-ish objectives. For the most part it's very fun though.

I thought I'd give it a try for 6 bucks and here's my short review:
Pros:
- fun combat
- good character creation options
- interesting story
- lots of crafting skills
Cons:
- You need energy to chat, yup seriously. And if you talk too much with random folks in general/server chat you can't do any gathering or whatnot because your energy is spent. The whole energy system in Korean mmos like archeage and black desert is fiendishly stupid
- no armor variety unless you shell out $20-$30 for a costume. Anyone who can sit there defending that is seriously a con artist's favorite dupe
- cluttered UI - typical B-class MMO affair, can be fixed but still a deterrant to players new to the MMO genre
- broken quest tracker - gathering missions fail to update and autopath does not lead you back to the NPC quest giver on some missions
If you are new to the MMO genre you might wanna pass on this if you're looking for more story/dungeon type gameplay. I would recommend ESO or FFXIV (my favorite) any day. This game is more interested in charging exorbitant fees in the pearl shop (in-game item shop) than providing a fun experience to players. Don't get me wrong I enjoy things like item shops in guild wars 2 (this game did it right) but at least gw 2 had some seriously cool armors that you could find in game and they made visual customization a synch. I quit the moment I realized chatting used up energy. The energy system isn't too bad but I'm not a hardcore gamer and I often socialize in MMOs. To place a restriction on chatting, a core feature in a genre based on bringing players together, is completely foolish. Had to pass on this one.

I liked it, but I feel it's been overhyped.
The first thing you need to know is that this is essentially Chapter 1 of 3, and the story won't feel complete if you don't play the other chapters (haven't played 2 yet).
Otherwise :
PROS:
Nice caravan system.
Choice and consequence. You do have some control over how your character treats others they encounter along the way, and which characters can stick around with you. Not full control, which means some characters... are better left out. Thankfully, it's not stupidly obvious which ones that is, nor is it unrecoverable or rage-quit inducing if you let them tag along anyways. To get back on topic, this is handled well.
Risk, if you like that sort of thing. It's perfectly possible to lose your best follower to some story event (I did). It's also perfectly possible to still win.
Lore. This is an interesting world with interesting races, characters, etc.
The story, overall. Pretty epic stuff going on there.
Interesting turn-based combat system. Not your typical combat system either. Hps are used for damage, and it works because of the way armor works. Also you have to spread out your damage because each side gets  a turn in which they play a single unit, and you don't want to give high strength or undamaged units more turns (Ie: if you have 4 dudes and so do the ennemy, and you take one out, then each remaining dude plays once every 3 turn instead of once every 4. If you had instead damaged 2 units then they would have been a lot less dangerous each time their turns came up). It's refreshingly different. I wouldn't want this in every turn-based game but in this one it works.
Art style. It's pretty neat.
CONS:
The ending. I won't say more to avoid spoilers. Except no epilogue. WTF.
Managing supplies vs morale vs renown hardly seems to have mattered. Maybe I was just good at it? *shrugs* Didn't feel that way though. Was often in weak morale with no food and no renown (as I purchased a lvl 5 item before i realized how that worked. Protip : don't!).
The story diverges into what I assume is the core of the sequel/trilogy's story quite quickly, which means this chapter's story is not as focused as it could have been. This is probably for the best of the overall trilogy, but it contributes to making the ending suck.
Fairly short. I played about 12 hours.
Overall I recommed this game as it is fairly different, and the story is engaging.

Little Nightmares is a delightful adventure through the maw filled with adorable friends and horrifying monstrosities. You play as Six and you'll know you're a protagonist because unlike the other depressing children, you have a bright yellow rain jacket. For the most part this is a very solid 2.5d platformer and it will take roughly about 2-5 hours for a casual play through. For my general opinions for the games we have
Pros:
-Does a great job of immersing you into the Maw in every aspect
-Six is a fun character and while being a silent protagonist still shows development through the game
-The Gnomes are adorable but not overt
-Enemy design flows very well and is extremely fair
-Puzzles require thought but are not frustrating
-Nothing feels out of place
Cons:
-2.5D graphics can feel clunky at times, there are various sections people will tend to walk off unintended
-AI can be glitchy at times causing unfair deaths, not a major issue but happens occasionally
-Stamina system feels a bit forced and can be inconsistent as well, it is fitting but takes away from the game a bit when Six starts running to a crawl
At this point it would be better to pick it up on sale mainly because it will most likely be more frequent however there is nothing wrong with getting this game at full price. It has plenty of content and replay value with the collectibles in the game and DLC is still being released for the game which adds onto the story. This game is definitely unique and offers an experience that must be had.

Fans of Titan Quest will see many similarities, and if you've played Path of Exile, Torchlight, Diablo, you'll find the same basic cookbook's been used to bake Grim Dawn. The Cthulhu'esque hordes are proliferating, humanity's been oppressed to near extinction, and you will click on thousands of demons and cultists to rectify the situation. One of the best turn based strategy games in existence, hands down. If turned based is your thing and you haven't played this, you are missing out.
It's got a story that keeps you interested and really wanting to push forward. In depth turn based combat that while on harder difficulties will completely change how you approach a fight. Unit, squad, and base advancement that will not only improve its capabilities to push your tech further, but your soldier as well.. physically, genetically, and mentally.
This "World Army" created by corporations, governments, and private investors has its own interesting aspects, especially in the grand scheme of the story. And by far my favorite part is turning on the languages for the different countries for your soldiers, makes the depth of it even better, though I do wish there were more languages.
On the downside, the AI can seemingly get some pretty insane RNG crits on your soldiers even on the easiest difficulties, and the end game is determined pretty heavily on how you play your hand early on. But this is also a good thing if you really like making that choice and sticking to it.
All in all, get it, you wont regret it unless you hate turned based strategy games. And for those who get it and beat it, try downloading and installing "The Long War" mod for the game, it will pretty much triple the amount of play time you get with the game and add a ton of fun new things to it.

Pros:
- The world is beautiful. Enemies are different from your regular MMO.
- The combat system is extremely complexed. You "can" hotbar buttons, however you're handicapping yourself if you don't press them in real actions like Up+F. It's much more fluid if you press action combinations for combos. What makes this the combat different than the others is move canceling. I didn't know this was in this game until I saw another player performing impossible moves.
- The grind actually feels good because you're performing attacks that are beyond that of rinse and repeat. You even feel like an absolute god.
- lots of jobs: crafting, fishing, tanning, etc. You can get lost in them for hours, and there's also a ranking system on it, which is weird but good if you like that kick back experience.
neutral:
- Gender lock, however some classes are just like the other such as Wizard and Witch or Musa and Maehwa.
- confusing minigames and small tutorial in the beginning that won't teach you anymore after the first 10 lvls.
- No fast travel, just your feet or your mount. The mount is an actual being too. Enemies can attack it seperately and kill it.
Cons:
- No endgame anything. Gears is by daily/weekly miniboss challenges in a particular location, which will take you 5-10 minutes on mount.
- No dungeon runs either. Match making isn't in this game. You want to party with people, you do it the old fashion way: by guild or shouting.
- RNG everything. However, this can be fixed with +luck gear. Luck will help increase particular chances but RNG rules most of everything whether farming, damage from particular anything, drops and stats on gear doing particular things.
- A turn-off to newcomers that don't like hard MMOs. The learning curve for this game is pretty high, but if you like a challenge it's rewarding. Those that like just pressing hotbar commands are the first to suffer after reaching lvl 50.
-A Majority of quests (if not life skills) are fetch and kill. Talk to NPC, go kill 30+ enemies, come back. This is what you call a Korean Grinder MMO.
Pay extra portion:
There are key things that make microtransactions somewhat enticing: Pets, value packs, extra inventory and weight limit expansion. Although you can play this game "pay once" like it was intended to be played, however these items make the game much easier PvE. As for PvP, there's nothing that can one up another player PvP other than better gear. Better gear is bought with silver and silver is power. In order to get this sort of silver, there are many ways, and what makes getting silver extremely easier are these items I've listed for microtransactions.
1) Pets w/a max of 4 can pick up items for you and carry on their own. This alleviates some of the stress of picking up items from mobs. Each pet is roughly $8 real money, but if you play the game long enough, 20 days gets you a free penguin (at least for the time being). At lower levels, pets aren't something you'll consider, however in higher levels while you're in a party you'll have that one player with pets, and that player will take everything that's dropped.
2) value packs: you can buy a 30 day value pack for $15, which is basically their version of subscription fee. This can be bought in auction houses with ingame currency, however it's quite hard to get one as it's the highest sought out item in the market and they only release 1-2 every 10-15 minutes. The value pack increase 100 weight limite, 16 inventory slots and 16 storage, and on top of that you get %30 back for auction house sales. What does that mean for sales? W/o it you're typically selling everything for roughtly 60%. That 300k stone sold will only give you back 180k unless you have the value pack in which you'll get back 210k. This actually adds up as you will be selling millions of items in the auction house and a majority of your income is by this.
3) inventory space. In-game there are quests that can increase your inventory space up to 30, or you can pay a premium and increase it even further to around 90, which a lot of life skillers do. If you want to carry a ton of different items, it's almost needed for you to carry so many things at once.
4) weight limit increase. You can grind to increase the strength of your character to carry heavier items, or you can have particular items that already increase your weight limit like the value pack or hercules gear that increase you 150+ weight. However, in higher levels there is gear that is far superior that you'll want to equip, so increasing your strength to carry is something that is either grinded or bought with microtransactions.
There are other items that I didn't list, but that's because they're a want vs need. These 4 that I've listed a borderline "need". All-in-all you can potentially play this game completely "pay-once" as it is intended whether being $6-10, but you will be extremely tempted to purchase one of the 4 items in order to make your life a bit easier in-game. One of the things you'll probably consider is the value pack as it is basically a subscription fee for WoW or FFXIV. Don't let that mentality of trading one MMO for another for its subscription fee sway your wallet. You should only buy this pack if you really do want to invest your time and real money into this game as BDO is multiple games in one. BDO with the core of a MMORPG has many elements that make it multiple games. These other games are called life skils.
1) Fishing: sure, you can fish in any mmo, but can you build a ship go to another island or in the middle of nowhere and fish there? With whatever you've caught you have options of cooking or finding a trader to buy your fish, which becomes an actual job that many players have come to enjoy called AFK fishing.
2) trade empire: I'm new to this concept but you can potentially connect areas through trade routes, process or build trade crates and have them shipped to another area to sell for a profit. You can have works around the world collect and bring back to your storage items in order to process or built crates to trade again making it a trade empire in which you can also haggle prices for these items in a different area.
3) Cooking/alchemy: the most effecient way to cook/alchemy and make money is by having contract NPC workers find resources, bring it back to your storage units in each town where you can make the necessary food or potions and then sell them on the market.
Again, the 4 microtransactions are borderline needs and they're  more purpose for those that are serious about this game and for specific situations. Grinders: pets; traders/fishers: inventory space and weight limit; and alchemy/cooking: value pack. Although you can give your character all of them to make your character more well rounded, they're not much of a need as comparison to these particular key points. I hope this helps, and if you want to know more, leave a comment.

If you are looking for a well-polished, challenging, strategy game with beautiful art and animations, this is the game for you!

Dying light is a unique game for how it manages to walk a fine line of an action, horror, and exploration.  You start out simply enough, learning how to run, jump, and parkour your way around the city while bashing zombies with generic weapons like rusty pipes.  Lending itself to the active running and combat gameplay are the talent trees.  Every time you use a weapon you gain experience toward the power skill tree, and climbing buildings increases your agility skill. This all leads to new abilities that change how you play the game.  Using a skill based leveling system also lends itself to the game's open world design.
In Dying Light you're encouraged to explore by two things, leveling up and random loot.  Similar to games like Diablo and Borderlands, Dying Light utilizes a classic colored random loot system for all the weapons you find in the world.  These weapons however are directly tied to a third skill tree, Survival.  Your Survival skill is what governs the quality of loot you find in the world, and survival points are only acquired by completing quests, helping survivors, or running for airdrops.  This three point system ensures that you're encouraged to explore and complete quests to level up, to get better loot, to kill stronger zombies, to do harder quests, to level up, to get better loot- you get the idea.  Additionally finding powerful weapons is kept in check with item durability, and all weapons need repair but will eventually break completely.   Thus even when you utilizes the games basic crafting system to create an amazing arm, you're encouraged to stay on the lookout for new and equally powerful weapons.
Topping all of this off is a day night cycle that gives the game a risk reward element.  During the day the world is filled with mostly unthreatening shambling zombies, but at night the map is populated with fast running and powerful super zombies called volatiles.  Normally you want to avoid going out at night, but when the real horrors come out the agility and power experience you gain are doubled, giving a sometimes much needed boost to skill leveling.  What's more there are many side quests that require you to run at night and dive head first into dangerous zombie dens, further encouraging you to go out after dark.
All and all Dying light is an amazing although imperfect game that manages to be all about zombies, without being a trite hoard mode survival shooter.  If you like RPGs, exploring, looting, and simple crafting, then Dying Light is for you.

For me, Divinity: Original Sin came out of nowhere. I’d first noticed it during the summer Steam sale but didn’t pay much attention, mainly due to the generic title. After hearing some strong word of mouth from various sources, I thought I’d take a closer look. I was playing through Baldur’s Gate Enhanced Edition at the time so my interest was piqued even more when I realised Divinity was touted as a return to classic PC RPGs.
Developed and published by Larian Studios, Divinity: Original Sin is a turn-based RPG with single-player and coop gameplay. With a particular emphasis on character development and role-playing, you choose two primary characters at the start of a new game. The game defaults to two randomly generated characters, a man and a woman, but you’ve got detailed character customisation options to make these two your own.
There are a number of classes to choose from; much like the classes in Dark Souls these mainly dictate starting skills and gear. You’ve got the freedom later in the game to customise upgrade paths and even re-spec, though I haven’t reached this option yet in my playthrough.
Having two main characters enables the most interesting element in Divinity: Original Sin: both characters have separate personalities and will occasionally disagree over your choices. You can switch between both characters at will, designating one primary and one secondary. Your primary character will lead the party and start most dialogue trees. The secondary character can respond and will sometimes offer an alternate option or behaviour.
If both characters don’t agree on the decision, you’ll move into a rock/paper/scissors mini-game, with each character taking a side in the argument. Whoever wins the mini-game wins the argument and the group goes with their choice. This mini-game also applies when trying to convince an NPC to do something they don’t want to do. The outcome is influenced by your character attributes like reason and charm. This adds a clever extra layer of roleplaying and allows you to play two characters with totally different personalities.
Character and story plays a big part in Divinity. Your choices help to shape your characters and progress the story. This is both a strength and a weakness of the game, as some story options are blocked to you if your characters don’t have certain skills or abilities. For instance, one core quest requires one of your characters to have some thieving skills. If you don’t have the skills, you can’t complete the quest. I would’ve preferred to see multiple ways to proceed rather than being locked into one solution. Of course, I might’ve missed something along the way but that leads into my next point.
Divinity: Original Sin doesn’t hold your hand. There aren’t quest markers or clearly signposted progression paths. I found this both refreshing and frustrating. While it’s a nice break from many mainstream RPGs that make things a bit too easy, a couple times I’ve found myself backtracking and repeatedly speaking to multiple NPCs on the off chance I missed a dialogue option. As for exploring, while you can technically go all over the map you’ll quickly run into groups of high level enemies that’ll destroy your little party. Trial and error plays a big part and this is built into the game, with autosaves common before a dangerous area.
Combat in Divinity is a lot of fun. Rather than using a Baldur’s Gate style pause system, the developers opted for turn-based combat similar to the recent X-Com: Enemy Unknown. You draw from a pool of action points to move, use items, and attack (whether physical or magical). Character abilities have cooldown periods and you need to balance the various actions across your party. The concept of balance is key in Divinity: Original Sin, especially in considering magic and the elements.
Ice is weak against fire. Lightning will elecrify water. You can affect the environment to burn away hazards or create deadly poison clouds. If you’re not careful you’ll end up healing an enemy with your attacks. The depth of the combat system is increased exponentially through this element interaction. You really need to use strategy in every fight; I ran into several situations where I couldn’t do any damage because all my attacks were fire-based and I was fighting fire elementals. I also found that having a magic user is practically essential; you’ll be at a serious disadvantage if you’ve only got melee characters due to the heavy magic use.
Generally Divinity is nicely polished. The graphics are crisp and the music is amazing. There are a few UI issues, however, especially when managing inventories between two characters and manuvering around the map. The developers are still active after the official release and there’s an update every week or so. Modding support is included and it’s still early days but there’s a lot of potential here.
I’ve got a few criticisms, but these are generally minor. The upgrade system isn’t very clear or intuitive. I put several points into Telekinesis before I realised it was used primarily for ranged loot collection. Speaking of loot, sometimes less is more but Divinity employs the Diablo approach of more is more. Eventually I just started trading everything away. Your characters have separate inventories as well, so bear that in mind if you’re trying to complete a quest with a specific item; I had a situation where I needed to move the item from my secondary character to my primary in order to finish the quest.
Divinity does a lot of things right. I love the focus on character and roleplaying, the quirky humour dispersed throughout (like the talking clam and gravestones), and the deep combat system. This is a game that will only improve over time, with UI fixes and mods allowing for new quests. If you can look past the generic title and minor quibbles, Divinity: Original Sin is a worthy successor to classic RPGs and a must play for any fan of the genre.

This is the best game I have ever played.  This is the best game I will ever play.  People owe it to themselves to load up GotW, and I'm a little disappointed Steam/Valve haven't bought it on behalf of every single Steam user.  The game has amazing graphics, fluid animation, wonderful mechanics, the best sound effects money can buy (the 'walking on wood' sound was so good I felt I was walking on water) and an atmospheric, chilling soundtrack.
I play this game every day.  Sometimes I pretend I'm actually the main character in person, skulking around the dark, moody castle (my bathroom), whilst other times I pretend to be Isabella and hide from everybody else, no matter how often they get upset and beg me to come out.
Here's my take on the in-game characters:
Laszlo's sadly dead from the start but that very discovery will make you tear up and suck you into the detailed plot.  Even dead characters here put other games' in the shade.
Filch Hoodwink has the misfortune of looking like a creepy child molester and having a name that people often mistake for 'Filth', which doesn't help matters.  It's a shame, really, as all he wants to do is eat juicy, juicy apples.  I've never met anybody that immediately wants to hold a conversation about them, but this man is positively apple obsessed and brings the subject up several times in the game.  He loves seeds too and will hand them out to anybody and everybody at parties.
Isabella, friendly soul, insists she'll be nearby and yet shows up a total of three times in the adventure (one of which involves being rescued at the end), for a combined screen time of probably a minute.  Curiously, despite the brief encounter(s) she seems to hint of a possible romance between the pair of you; Filch clearly doesn't do much for her and, frankly, who can blame her?
Artemis was born with a permanent Roger Moore-esque raised eyebrow which, I'm sure, led to a great deal of ridicule as a child (but fruitful experiences when he was old enough to discover women).  He has the deepest, villianiest voice I've ever heard which must be annoying when attempting to hide villainy motives.  In any case, I hope his sore throat clears up soon; I recommend Wrigley's 'Lockets' which have a lovely, gooey, honey centre.
The guards are all very helpful and uniform (which guards should be!), greeting you cheerfully and pointing you towards your map.  If I found a real guard like this I would want to shake his hand quite firmly for a minimum of no less than five seconds, or until he asked me to stop.
Kitchen Wench™.  Unknown motive(s); one suspects cooking food.  Prone to panic.  Prone to face collapsing when killed to death.
I refuse to comment on the wolf itself as overexposure will diminish its quite dramatic entrance.  All I can say is this: once you see it, you will never forget.  Isn't that what we all strive for in life?  I know I do.
I'd like to address some laughable 'negative' points I've come across, both here on Steam and elsewhere:
Stealth.  The stealth system is actually nuanced and in-depth.  Each guard has their weapon on display at all times and an unsuccessful pat down of their bottoms will result in a major tongue-lashing.  I can't explain the sheer euphoria I felt when I managed to steal a key to a dungeon; something I can only claim to have done a handful of times before in real life.  The fact this genre-busting mechanic isn't documented anywhere within the game is entirely the point; you have to get into your character and into the mindset.  Don't be lazy; explore, probe, discover, learn.  Fondle.
Now, I'm puzzled by the negativity in regards to the black outlines.  They are perfect.  They are us.  They accurately convey the darkness we all have in our souls which is, presumably, why Filch 'Filth' Hoodwink is completely encased in blackness at one point.  To remove these outlines is to remove a part of ourselves.  Even the scenery needs these lines; nature can be unforgiving and cruel.
Another gripe seems to be in regards to objects, and the fact many can be walked through.  All I can say is this: if you were trying to hide from a werewolf, I think you'd be thankful you could hide inside a large rock or tree!
Overall, you must buy this game.  This is not a request and it makes me weep to know there are genuine, decent people out there deprived of this experience.

A very nice JRPG at the crossroad between a light novel and a true bred JRPG. That's all ! I am really enjoying playing this game, and I hope the next chapter will be available soon on Steam.

First of all, an excellent game developed by Telltale that requires some background story before you play it, but it doesn't ruin your experience if you haven't watched a single minute of HBO's series Game of Thrones, it just make less enjoyable. So I highly recommend you to watch until the end or until the end of the third season. In the beginning you get a little confused by the many characters that's presented to you, but it's a matter of time. The story begins a little chaotic, but it settles down after a while. I have to say that the story is great, it's way better than Tales from Borderlands, well developed characters, great cenarios, diplomatic choices (I'll talk more about the issues with the choices below). The graphics are simply amazing, it looks like that you're looking into a animated paint, you can see the paint-brush trails really well, it's not a current-gen graphic, but is really beautifull. I don't have anything to say about the gameplay, it's just like the other TellTale games, mouse only in most of the time and keyboard usage just to walk and combat. The audio is good and "normal", not too much special and not negative points about it. The "enjoyability" is connected to your choices and if you liked or not the development of the story. The dubbing is good, luckily there are some characters from the HBO's Series that are in the game and they are voiced by the real actors from the show.
The only thing that I've had the problem with in the FIRST and the SECOND episode, was the choices. Choices in this game aren't really choices. Example: you choose to fight with someone before you meet the person, but when you meet you don't fight, you just end up talking to "him". It's not what we expect about a CHOICE GAME, GODDAMMIT. And when you have a real choice to make, is just too simple. Example: You can kill a person in public, so you decide to kill, everyone see, they don't like it and it's just that (This don't occurs in the game). Too simple, no deep consequences, just moral choices that are quickly forgotten by the people. That is just unacceptable for a game that has this phrase in the beggining "your story are tailored by the choices you make", B.U.L.L.S.H.I.T. This first episode is pathetic, it looks like a novel than a game that has a interactive story and important choices to make, unfortunately. But STILL has a great story.
An excellent game developed by Telltale, good graphics, great story, good gameplay. It requires some knowledge about the first to the forth season of HBO's series Game of Thrones to really enjoy the story at its maximum, but you can catch up by playing it. The knowledge it's kinda extra but it's very cool and reccomended. But the game has its flaws like in the first and the second episode, choices are not real choices but that change's a little bit as the episodes goes on.

First, this is really only for a group of people to play. This is strictly a multiplayer game. yeah it has single player and the first 2 or 3 times you go through single it is fun, but it gets old really fast. Like a good board game, the real fun comes from familiarity, mastery and competition. When you first start just the design and idea is pretty cool, but as you play and start to learn what everything does and how it works, there comes a depth of planning when playing against friends. The bore comes from the limited set pieces, levels are randomly generated but have a pretty limited amount of props and hazards, so when you play against the computer it very quickly just feels like "Same old, same old". With friends you never know what the other players might do, the computer has a pretty standard process of playing the game. The weapons, items, bosses and levels are all kind of randomly rolled out, but from a pretty limited stock. There's only 2 or 3 bosses, a handful of weapons and items and as I said pretty limited level sets. What makes all this fun is human players, randomizing how it is used and doing unexpected things with it. The computer fails to really be inventive, duh, it's a computer. SO, if you have a couple friends that are interested, this will be a blast. However, if you're a hermit like me and rarely have company over or just company that isn't into competitive gaming, you might want to set this one out.

Overall, it's a decent, atmospheric puzzle platformer.  But it has lots of issues.
Quick pros and cons
Pros
- great presentation and visuals
- interesting meta story
- some solid timing platforming moments
Cons
- controls
- trial & error puzzles can be unnecessarily frustrating
My biggest gripe is the controls.  5 buttons for a puzzle platformer is a bit much, imo, especially when one (Grab) is unnecessary for some mechanics and sometimes doesn't function as it'd seem anyway.  I.e. you push things automatically, but can only pull by Grabbing.  Makes sense, right?  Well, not in some puzzles where you're limited in certain dimenionsal planes.  But why should you push things automatically but not Grab them?  Also, sometimes when you jump up to boxes, you automatically grab them and pull yourself up.  Other times you don't.  Very counter-intuitive.  There are even times you don't grab on to things just b/c they are about 1mm away from you.  Chalk it up to the 3D aspect.
Also, there are a lot of cheap trial & error puzzles (w/ lots of deaths sandwiched in) and puzzles w/ elements that just come out of nowhere to ruin your trialing.  All of which involve the people you are hiding from.  But still, there are some nice logic puzzles that flow w/ intuition and discovery.
I really wanted to like this game, but I just don't.  I'm sure others will find it great and get over the aforementioned elements.  But the heavy trial & error aspect that lacks any sort of intuition is just bad "puzzle" design.  The bunky controls don't help matters either.
However, I can't give it a "No" on recommendation.  This game has other things about it worthy of checking out.  It's worth a try for anyone who likes puzzle platformers.  Just buyer beware.

Beat Hazard is a top down dual stick arcade shooter similar to the classic game Asteroid, but on neon colored steroids. Its pretty much contained in a single screen and the game throws waves of asteroids, ships and space worms after you. Since its a dual stick shooter, the controls are easy, left stick to move, right stick to fire the direction you're aiming. There are also bombs to clear the screen when it gets completely full of enemies.
Beat Hazard has a major twist. Your rate of fire is controlled by the tempo or beats per minute of the music. Not just your bullets but the enemy speed too. If you don't care for the songs that the game comes with, you can play one of your own .mp3s or listen to Internet radio. The neon laser beams make the game come to life as more than a game. It could be a visualizer for your mp3 playlist.
Every song is a level. When the song ends or your lives run out, you see your high score and the game remembers how far you got and your high score. So you can play it again for a better high score or to go further in the song. I'd much rather have the game go from song to song than force me to start up a new game for the next song. There is a survival mode that will keep going song to song, but its just a single life.
The enemy diversity shines through in the game. There are simple ships that fly in long waves. Larger ships that take more damage. Even larger ships that explode into a hail of homing missiles. Still other ships have dual repulsor beams to push you around. Magnetic ships have dual rays that pull you in. There are segmented space worms, easier to defeat neon worms. It is a varitable feast. Not just that, but diverse bosses. Everything from huge space ships, gigantic worms to star fish that coil up their tentacles for protection. These enemies will fill your screen in no time especially on the upper three difficulties. The game has a way to keep your mind engaged as to how you can survive.
Every score that you have go to your level or rank. The score is like experience. You will rank up and get to unlock a perk. You need to buy the perk once its been unlocked. Not just buy it, but buy multiples of it. Then equip it. There are perks that give you extra lives, extra bombs, and increase score multipliers. Other things that can get unlocked are extra difficulty modes for when 'hardcore' gets too easy for you.
There are other layers of complexity to the Beat Hazard such as a risk reward system. If you don't shoot a set amount of time your score multiplier goes up. If you survive long enough without dying, the multiplier goes up again. Before you know it you're at 45+ of a score multiplier if not 100+ with perks. All the while enemies will drop things for you to pickup such as extra multipliers, money, bombs to use, power ups for your laser and volume increases. Its very risk or reward. Do you leave your safe corner of the screen, navigate through the madness to get your $10?
The game is kind enough that when you die, it litters the area with items to get you back up and competing again. That is a downfall of other games that if you die late into a game, your underpowered ship is useless against the high difficulty enemies.
If you get lonely there is 2 player and online multiplayer where you compete on a single screen against someone. Not just that, but the game will notify you if someone is trying to multiplayer at that time. You can interrupt your own game to play against someone. This ensures there's always someone to play.
I say this game is well worth the $10 asking price.

Faster than Light is a game that could have come out in the eighties or nineties, the premise is that remarkably simple. You have a top-down "cross-section" view of your ship, showing the various compartments and and your men, women and space creatures hard at work. You order your crew around the various compartments to do things like man stations, conduct repairs, and fight boarders, and you act as a kind of "eye-in-the-sky" god.
In combat, you see a top-down view of the enemy ship next to your own, and you use your weapons, drones and boarding parties on their compartments and crew while keeping your own ship together by repelling boarding parties, putting out fires, sealing hull breaches, and managing the ship's power supply and subsystems. Between battles and various encounters, which are handled by RPG-style dialogue boxes, you spend scrap (the game currency) on system upgrades. That's basically it.
So why do I recommend FTL, if this is all you do? Firstly because of the game's atmosphere -- graphics, music, and the overall presentation come together to create a game that's so elegant, so humble, and just feels so "right", right from the beginning at the main menu when the incredible title soundtrack starts to play. In a day an dage with games released full of bugs and imbalances, it's such a good feeling to get to play a game that's so polished and elegant and
.
More importantly, though, FTL is incredibly open-ended, and comes with a huge selection of star ships, alien races, and sci-fi gizmos, and the fact that it's randomized and non-linear means you're constantly being challenged, as you can't simply restart when you die and know exactly what to expect. Dead is dead, and when you die (and you will), the game records your score and achievements and generates a new universe for you. The only linear element of the game is that you have eight "stages", with progressively harder enemies and an incredibly brutal boss to beat at the end. You choose how to navigate the beacons at each stage, and often when you've cleared a sector, the path to the final boss stage forks, letting you choose between easier or tougher encounters.
Beyond that, it's all up to you, and though there is a very large degree of randomness, you eventually discover that success or failure largelly depends on what you do with the freedom the game gives you, both in terms of tactics and strategy. You need to both plan ahead and make the most out of what the game offers you. If you stumble across a space store that sells a crew teleporter, you'll need to consider if your ship and crew is cut out for boarding action. If your ship can fire missiles, you need to think about how best to conserve them so that you don't run out when you really need them. If you come across a burning space station and the game asks you if you want to send crewmen over to try to extinguish the fires or rescue survivors, you know that you could end up with some kind of reward, but also that the rescue operation could go horribly wrong, costing you valuable crew members.
This is the beauty of FTL -- it's all about dilemmas, and having to think carefully about everything you do. It's also about slowly building a small ship with a skeleton crew into a versatile and powerful warship to be reckoned with, as you grow more and more atteched both to vessel and crew. Which makes it all the more painful when things suddenly go belly-up
, and all the more rewarding when finally, after so many attempts, that big rebel flag ship
goes up in flames.

I have to get this out of the way first and foremost - I am a HUGE fan of werewolf fiction. Not Stephenie Meyer's shape-shifting pet poodles, or the wolf anthros that plaster Furaffinity, Tumblr and DeviantART; the horror werewolves that made the werewolf the legendary creature it is today. And I'm sure you are too! But I just can't help but feel that this is a cash-in on one of horror's most venerated creatures.
When I first started Identity of the Canine, it was good enough for an indie game. The atmosphere of some serious faecal matter was about to happen was great and the controls were intuitive enough that I didn't need to reference the controls at all. Then it came to an abrupt halt when I was rudly told at the front gate that I had to look for some special item. Scrounging around the countryside (if it can be called that) of naked trees with a ridiculous cartoony outline for about 45 minutes, I finally found an axe in the least probable area one would expect to find it: Lodged on the opposite area of the map where the logging cabin was! Suffice it to say that it was one of the most jarring treasure-hunts for the most basic item that shattered the suspension of disbelief. But a voice in my head said, "Be nice. It is their first game. They at least took your advice to take out the irrelevant jump-scares."
I was starting to wonder why I listened to that voice in the first place until I saw the highlight of the gaming year so far - a poorly voiced Russian princess (who oddly has a Spanish name and British-American accent) with a shocking taste in clothing and historical accuracy, and a comical outline that gave her the hint of a five o' clock shadow. After I finally stopped laughing if only to save my underpants, I began laughing at the dialogue structure. It's so clichèd with the genre and roles of the characters that I had to step out for five minutes to calm down. It's not totally asinine, though. There is a nichè choice structure that at least changed the next piece of dialogue, but for the sake of the chair and linen - I muted the sound. The magic-man behind bars was a similar story, though his voice acting was at least a cut above the rest. The Count wasn't much better than either, and his lines screamed of his role in the story. Probably the most organic lines came from the guard to the front door, and that was just plain flat. But I calmly reminded myself that Shape of the Lupine was still an indie game.
I know I said the controls were tight and intuitive enough that I didn't need to look up the controls again, but the gameplay itself was like the graphics - patchy, glitchy and unforgiving at best, and nightmarish cluster-bomb on common sense's front doorstep at worst. Getting chased by the hairy attack dog was a nice shot of adrenaline through the game, but its appearances give you no option to escape or hide other than the linear chase prescribed by the developers. One chase even has you charging TOWARD the werewolf when there are no less than three good hiding spots to wait for the hulking mastiff to pass on. And no less than five times did I think, "Hang on. There are windows around with moonlight coming through, and I have an axe which smashes through baricades. Why can't I fight the poodle?" I discovered the answer after being savaged for the umpteenth time: because it's not using your brain. I know that the protagonist is a brainiac in his own little lunch-box, but we, the cruel angels of fate, are not. By this point, I was thoroughly outraged I spent $15 on a game worth about $7 for its cheap laughs and wacky graphics. But brace yourself for a shock, because there are some things that did go right. Just enough to bump its worth up to a possible $8.50.
The fact that you can turn into a werewolf, if only for two minutes and in set checkpoints of moonlight, is really what gives a credible note to the game. It was a nice little feature but it sucks in that the only combat takes place in wolf form. Even then, it's you - the unstoppable pet bulldog of The Hulk - against a scared guardsman just following orders. Horror games like Outlast and Amnesia have little, if any, combat, but it's done well! You can run, you can stun, you can hide, you can be savaged and wait for the beasties to pass on post-mortem - not follow blind instructions to the letter by running down a hall and pressing the "I Won the Race" button. Taking a chunk out of the guards was oddly satisfying in its own demented way, but I soon felt guilty after killing the most human and realistic characters in the game.
I still think it was a damn shame that you couldn't take a chunk out of the characters that mattered to the wearily predictable plot. You have so many stereotypes packed into each character that you can judge their role just by looking at them - the cursed love interest (if you hadn't worked that out within the first ten minutes, you were probably too busy staring at her incredibly well-endowed bosum), the bad guy with a name, the deus ex chamberpot, the bored guard, the scared castle hand, the self-insert know-it-all-but-can't-remember-a-thing protagonist, the.... Oh wait, that's the list. They're so riddled with nits and bullet-holes that it's hard to sympathise with any of the characters. Hard at best and frustratingly difficult at worst, but it is possible. I did find myself at one point going, "A
... Poor Filch." Though it still doesn't excuse the fact that he only shows up once in a while to say a few lines, give you a book and reveal his backstory, only to leave you hanging for the puzzles. The princess is about as useless as you would expect as anything other than the protagonist's love-interest McGuffin, and the Count's plan was sure to backfire from stage one. I'm sure it sounded great to the drunk, semi-literate peasant farmer who the Count discussed the plans with, but he could have at least planned it with someone along the lines of Caesar or Alexander to get the kinks out
For those cheaky strumpets that skipped right to the bottom: A good game this is not. Good and Likeness of the Wild Tundra Dog just don't mix. Not bad for what it's worth, but just not good! This review is being written because this was the only game I nominated in the 2017 awards for which I could write a review that I hadn't.
First I'd recommend this game to fans of "South Park" and I wouldn't to non fans.  It is remarkably true to the spirit of the TV series including its scabrous and scatological humour.  You need to be in the top 40% of least easily offended people on the planet to enjoy this game because at least half the adult planet will hate it.  Also it's not for younger children.  Certainly no-one who isn't at least a teenager and 15+ is preferable.
Secondly I'd very strongly recommend to only get this game if you have a controller.  Some maneouvers are tricky with a controller and probably nigh on impossible with a keyboard and mouse.
So the game itself - basically Cartman and Co are playing a Tolkien themed kid's game and so you have a game which effectively sets the tropes of a FRPG in South Park's suburbia.  Combat is Pokemon style turn based and can be tough at times.  Sometimes you'll need the various health boosts that can be collected and bought in game.
What pushes the game from moderately good/ okish to clearly recommended is the game's sense of humour.  Cartman as usual is the main comic engine of events and both the humour and knowing the characters and places make the game more of a delight.  Somtimes some of the material even I found offensive but I took it on the chin and continued on.
Overall I'd recommend the game as being faithful to the show and a surprisingly strong FRPG in the 2D/ turn based mode.  TV and film tie-ins have a deserved reputation for producing some of the most unbelievably bad games ever made (E.T. destroyed Atari) but without the South Park licence and the humour it would still be a moderately good game.
Here the humour and the South Park theme improve the pleasure in playing the game and on sale it is well worth adding to your games library.
Unless you're more than averagely easily offended.

FTL is basically the child of Star Trek and roguelikes, which basically means the USS Enterprise being piloted by an all-red-shirt crew. You start with a dinky little ship and a bunch of fresh-off-the-academy recruits and you are expected to save the entire Federation from the massive Rebel faction.
Keep in mind that FTL's space combat is more Star Trek than Wing Commander - choose ship components to target, tell your weapons guy to fire, watch the energy inputs of your shields and engine, that sorta thing.
Dying in FTL is a perfectly normal experience, and should not deter you from replaying. No one will also judge you if you play at Easy first.
The free update expands on your options on pretty much everything: new weaponry, a new alien race, new ships, new scenarios, so it really increases the replayability.
So if you're a fan of both space exploration and dying frequently, this game's for you.

This game is worth playing, but be warned -- your choices will hardly effect your outcome. I played the game normally once and ended up with a bad ending, made one small change near the end of the game and ended up with a good ending, and then made all of the opposite choices than my first playthrough (but still the same last choice) and got the same good ending. I may have to consult a walkthrough to get more achievements for this game, or keep clicking random buttons -- thank goodness for the built-in fast-forward feature that knows which options you have already chosen, and lets you speed past text you've already read, I am thankful for that.
All in all -- this game felt a little bit long towards the middle, but quickly got interesting. Seems I was only about 40 minutes from ending the game once I began to feel it was getting long-winded, so that's good. I suppose I'd say it's a decent length then. It took me a little over 4 hours to pass the first time, and about an hour when trying again thanks to the text-skipping (> button).
The in-game character graphics are alright, but the stills are a bit crudely drawn, in a kind of rushed sketch manner. It is this way with the H-scenes too, if you decide to download the patch (which you can find on the game's official website, just save it in the correct folder where the game is). So whether or not those are worth it are up to you. I just did so because I really like trying to pass games as much as I can before tiring of them, and the black screens where the stills are removed were annoying me a bit. Even so, I only saw one side-nipple throughout the entire game .. not sure why Steam keeps trying to censor these things ..
Anyhoo, this game is a good way to kill a couple hours, and it's free. So if you're used to flash games and like mystery-based dating sims or even just .. people sims in general (it is really, really hard to actually get with anyone apparently, soo), this game is worth a read -- although I wish there was a 'meh' button, because I'm a bit of a jerk like that (and have not gotten a truly 'satisfying' ending yet -- good OR bad, hrmm).
Also, as far as I'm aware -- this game isn't really as sad as anyone is saying (unless you get the good ending? even so, it's more .. eh .. stoic or mysterious than sad, really). So if you're the type of person who prides themself on trying to find a really good tearjerker (I know I can be like that sometimes), perhaps this isn't your jam unless you're really sensitive. But I'd still say it's worth a playthrough for the bizarre twist about 2/3rds through. I mean, it's short enough to try.

So I've been playing this game for a while now, and I'm quite shocked I haven't wrote a review for it yet. I originally got this game because it was recommended to me by a friend, and since I wasn't into anything remotely like Civilization V at the time, I was fairly skeptical, having most of the games I had played up to that point being RPG's and FPS games. Civilization V did not fail to impress me, even back then. I will admit I was peeved at times from the difficulty I faced in those early days, but I quickIy began to enjoy the challenge it provided (Even though the AI still remains to be very silly when it comes to what it wants to build, and how it fights at times). Not only do I enjoy the singleplayer experience, but I love to play this game with my friends, save for the odd moments where i feel the wrath of nuclear detonation destroy my capital city. I definitely recommend this game to anyone who is wanting to take their first steps into 4X games, as it is an enjoyable experience, and is found to be a game where you have a hard time putting it down after you start getting into it, until you look at your clock and realize that 7 hours have passed by. The game generates maps at relative randomness, depending on the map settings that you chose, so you'll find a lot of re-playability with this game.
TL;DR
If you want to play a 4X game, this delivers a good product, with a lot of hours that you can sink into it. Seriously recommend it.

I've seen two major complaints;
--------------------------------
One | Too complicated - As far as I can tell, it's a learning process. Everytime a MMO tries to cut away from the norm, I.E WoW, FFXIV, ect, it's deemed too complicated. Coming from EvE Online (Which, maybe that skews my view of "complicated") this feels fresh for the traditional MMO feel. Leveling happens, sure, but you hit a wall where it becomes super slow.
As I've seen it described, it's about lifeskilling. There's a lot to learn, and do. I would describe it as more of a sandbox. Nothing is locked off to you, and everywhere is open. The only instanced thing is houses that you can own, decorate, and invite people in. (As an avid RPer, this game has been a life send, though lacking in more animation emotes, to be fair.)  I've slowly been learning it, and I've talked to others who have played for months and they're only learning.
Do you really want to learn and master a game in a week?
I played EvE Online and it was learning for years.
Have a thirst for socializing, knowledge, and fun, and here's BDO.
----------------------------------------
Two| Busy UI/Messy, Poor Voice Acting(English) and graphical Popin - Okay, Albiet I just clumped some things together as I looked at some other reviews, I'm going to bring up everything that isn't mechanic based.
UI - I would agree that is a littler messier that Western sytled MMO's. Again, coming from EvE, I'm biased. Strangely enough, I read an article about how Asian culture processes information differently, usually looking at one thing at a time. It's VERY customizable, however. Everything can be moved, resized, and you can save three UI layouts.
So, it's not neagtive, in that regard, for me.
Poor Voice Acting - Well. I have to admit, some of these voices made me laugh. One uniquely sounded like a 12 year old trying to put on a fake deep voice and be a soilder. Others are mismatched for the visual, but maybe that's just breaking stereotypes. However, for me, 60-70% actually sounds, well, perfect. So again, it doens't break it for me.
Graphical Pop-in - There's a LOT going on in this game. Maps are open, no loading, no quick travel, and everything near you looks just so damn beautiful. I do agree that they could have done a better job with how it transitions. Things LITTERALLY just pop into existance when you're closer, or change so much that it looks like a tree just got replaced with another tree. I noticed it at first, but after a while it just became part of it. The landscapes are the most beautiful I've seen in a game.
Don't even get me started on the character editor. Thing is a avid Sim players dream with more sliders and modifcation areas that you can shake a mouse at.
------------------------------------
Conclusion
It's different. It's well optimized (still running a stock Nvidia 770, and I can get 60 frames even with some of the nicer settings on), probably due to how they pop things in and out to keep it beautiful. The characters are well animated, and with the creator, given time, you can make yourself look different than anyone else and still look good.

Extremely good game, something I say rarely.  I picked it up with my mate and we started playing, planning to play a couple hours before we went to sleep.  We kept playing until he went to work, and loved every minute of it.
The combat is highly tactical and fairly difficult.  I played a tanky melee and he went pure mage.  We both felt useful, effective, and each had a dicisive effect.  Rarely do I see such a good magic experience that doesn't leave melee lacking, but I felt quite happy with my choice of class, even while he did tactical genius magic.  (And not so genius, my only two deaths were from some friendly-fire issues.)  I spent a lot of time positioning enemies, disabling them, and generally keeping them from doing anything effective until the fire came for them.
I highly reccommend the game as a co-op experience, and I suspect the rpg side is rather impressive as well.  The roleplay between player characters is comedy gold, and leads to a surprising amount of character attachment.  Equally the rest of the game seems solid and sometimes pretty original.  The combat is turn-based, but speaking as someone who normally is annoyed by JRPG style turn-based, this combat system seemed great.  It may be turn-based, but that is because everything you do is worth careful consideration.  This is a good game, get it with your friends.

My fandom of the series started when I located Hyperdimension Neptunia Mk.2 in my local GAME store. Since that day, I have been aiming to get my hands on every HyperNep game available including the Noire Spinoff for Vita. Anyways, I found this version of the game while I was hunting down the Vita version of all 3  Re;Birth games since getting it recently. Upon finding it, It became an Insta-buy. After plaing for hours, and near completing it, I thought I share my thoughts
Story: The game follows the plot of the first game, where the CPUs battle it out, and by the bad guy's words causing the main character to fall from Celestia and become an amnesiac. However, unlike the original story, they added several originally DLC from Victory and added them to the story too. As well as removing several characters as well, including the original DLC characters of the first game. (Namely the optional Nisa and Gust). The story follows the original one very closely however. The main focus of this is the Console War, which reflects how consoles fight in reality as well as each CPU and their Landmasses represent real life game consoles, except for Neptune being based on a console that didn't came to be.
The dialogue is not suppose to be serious in any way, and if you know Neptune who's 100% aware of the 4th wall and smashes it with a sledgehammer (metaphorically), the seriousness will vanish in a second. Each character has different personalities that can cause clashing with others but that's what makes it fun. IF and Noire are considerably serious about things, Most of the seriousness come from these two. Vert is a typical Gamer, choosing games over her work. Blanc is a quiet person but has a short temper and will swear a lot. Then there's Compa who is also kinda silly, She's seen as the cute, innocent nurse character.  A notable thing is that the story is linear and the 2 endings follow the same route with a single difference at the final boss itself if conditions are met, which is a bit disappointing to be honest. Then again, It's not so much like the original where it's linear, but you cannot follow through a whole landmass' story in one go so that's an improvement.
