“Hyperdimension Neptunia Re;Birth” is not only a mouthful of a title, but also a turn-based RPG in the style of older “Final Fantasy” games, even including a turn order for good measure. It’s a PC port of the game which was originally released on the Vita, and is easily one of the most self-referential games we’ve seen in a while. It plays this to its advantage, making a giant parody out of the games industry, and almost never retaining a serious tone, something that can be appreciated if done well, considering how many devs are willing to throw humor to the wind.
First up however is the combat, as it is by far the game’s strongest selling point for fans of older turn-based RPGs. While not having the same depth as some of the titles released on other systems, in terms of having a wide variety of elemental attacks and various abilities to go along with them, it still retains some level of strategy in how the combat plays out. This is largely due to not being as traditional as most turn-based combat systems. Every fight is instanced, meaning they take place in their own area, but the characters retain the 3D movement used to navigate the overworld, and focuses on positioning area-of-effect abilities, as well as the hitbox in front of the character, which determines how many enemies that particular combo hits.
Which brings us to the second part of the combat system, the game has attacks set to be either abilities that use up the SP bar and the EXE drive, or as combos that can be customized to death between a wide-variety of attacks which each have their own characteristics in terms of how much they cost to include in the combo, as well as how much damage they deal. The attacks within combos are split into three parts: Rush for building the EXE drive gauge, which allows the use of special EXE abilities along with finishers at the end of each combo; Power for pure damage output; and Smash for breaking through an enemy's guard gauge.
The guard gauge is especially important, as breaking an enemy’s guard causes them to take increased damage from practically everything. Juggling between healing the party, using various buffs and debuffs, repositioning the characters, and actually dealing out damage can make the combat tense at times, but always enjoyable to go through. If nothing else, the sheer number of options at the players disposable can make even the most lackluster battles at least helpful, if not fun.
The game’s story focuses on the land of Gamesindustri, where four goddesses rule over their own lands, and fight each other in the never-ending “Console War,” with the names of the lands being “Lowee,” “Lastation,” “Leanbox,” and the odd one out, “Planeptune.” The jab at gaming as a whole goes far beyond this reference alone, and the entire game is tech-themed to more or less extents. Special abilities are burned to discs for the goddesses or “CPUs” to use, which have their own swappable processor units, and are even referred to by the people who worship them as CPUs.
So the setting itself is already a good starting point for anyone with a good sense of humor, however the story is a different beast entirely. It’s so self-referential that taking the game seriously is really only done in boss battles, and nowhere else. Not to say that it’s a bad thing -- it isn’t, but for those who like their gaming experiences to be serious affairs, stay away. The character interaction is the highlight of the story here, as a ragtag group originally consisting of a fallen goddess with amnesia, a nurse student, and a wanderer gather more and more people into their party, as well as meeting various characters that come and go throughout the story. It’s hard not to smile at some of the jabs that get traded back and forth. That said, when it comes to the actual story component, the dialog can tend to drag along quite a bit, and the game switches between voice-acted and non-VAed dialog sections, which makes some of the dialog more enjoyable than usual, while the rest can have the player stuck reading blocks of text.
The game’s graphics are not much to speak of, as the in-game models and environments are a bit too low in resolution for something that touts itself as being in 1080p thanks to the power of PC, but the redone sprites and art in general for the game are absolutely fantastic. Clearly quite a bit of effort was put into making the character sprites for dialog look great, regardless of whether it was done for the Vita or PC release, and it definitely helps make use of all the extra pixels on our displays over the Vita’s handheld display.
The game is a good PC port, despite suffering some minor performance issues in the combat. It’s hard to say that the game actually has any standout issues considering the only framerate drops to experience come during turn-based combat. The entire rest of the game is solid at the worst of times, and pretty fun at the best. It’s enjoyable from beginning to end, with so much customization in combat that we can only imagine how many heads it spun. Variety and choice in the combat is reminiscent of older turn-based titles, and that’s definitely a good thing. A solid offering by Compile Heart and Idea Factory, and any fans of this title have a PC port of the next remake to look forward to on June 2nd.

This game was an absolute MESS. After the initial... I hesitate to call it a quest because it wasn't, you'd be forgiven for thinking that the game was broken as the key to moving forward (I hesitate to call it a puzzle) relies on a mechanic that the game never really tells you exists. There aren't really any puzzles, certainly none that couldn't be solved by applying a solitary brain cell to them. The only challenging part to this game is finding all the things necessary to complete missions, and that's not a good kind of challenge. It's one that frustratingly made me stay up until four in the morning playing because I wanted to see if it redeemed itself in the end and I knew I wouldn't have the willpower to start it up again if I shut it off. The combat is wholly unnecessary, as you can quite blithely run straight past the guards who are too slow to swing to really do any damage to you and not only don't chase you, if you transform right in front of their bloody eyes and then leave the room and come back, they have apparently FORGOTTEN that the alchemist they're talking to just transformed into an unholy beast right in front of their eyes, making them utterly superfluous. Not helped is the fact that their dialogue (And pretty much everybody elses) is completely phoned in on the part of the voice actors. There are only four characters in this game, counting yourself, and two of them have a whopping THREE LINES, and yet we're supposed to care about them. Oh, and that monster they're always touting? Seen three times in the game. You see it, it chases you, you hide or cut off its path, and then it just gives up IMMEDIATELY.  I regret this purchase. I sincerely, sincerely regret it.

Let me  start by saying that the developers should be ashamed of themselves for this project. (except the music artists... they did good.)  In no way shape form or fashion at the final stages of development should you all have said, "Yeah, game looks good, ship it out."  Were you rushed?  Were you strapped financially?  Those questions are irrelevant.  After a project like this your company should just fold, hand in the towel, and send its employee's elsewhere to find better career opportunities.  This game is TERRIBLE.
Now to the meat and potatoes, so we can figure out why its bad.  (I am not even going to give a warning for spoilers, because I think everyone who bought this should fight steam and have them refund their purchase.  Anyone who has not bought it.. DON'T!)
I played this game for 2 hours and 54 minutes (approximately) that is from start to finish.  The opening of the game gives you no indicator that the story is even actually happening beyond the main character saying that he needs to go someplace and find someone.  It starts you off in a fashion that someone made a level in unreal tournement where you spawn in a location with no intro.  There should have at least been a cutscene introduction on par with the ending cutscene of the game. (don't get me started on the quality of the ending cutscene, but at least a cutscene to explain what is going on is nessesary!!!)
With no true direction (or clue) to where to find your current target objective (due to a lack in informative begining), you might decide to follow the blood trail to a horse.  Thats it for the clues beyond that. You are then greeted with the option to head for the gates, only to be told that you are missing something.  now with no sense of injury or purpose, you then are left to wander the cold wilderness in an attempt to find the corpse of a character that is literally meaningless to the plot due to no introduction or other such information.
You are then greeted with yet another way the game decides to illustrate story.  By walking up to the gate, it immediately warps you to a bed chamber and a talk to a literal stick of a human being.  The characters that ARE present in the game, are emotionless and look like they are incredibly dated (probably inspired by 2001 time period character models) HELL THATS BEING GENEROUS!
Regardless, the options are bland, they don't have any apparant meaning for either selection of choice, and the voices seem remarkably quiet and uninspired.  And this is constant through the game, when you actually do get choices for dialogue.
The game play is dated, adventure games have come along way since this rustic example of old school room escape games.  (even in those games, the items you used to solve the puzzles disappeared out of your inventory.)  Instead, the items you collect kinda serve to guide you as a gauge for how much longer you have to suffer through the game.
The tutorial consists of a help file that opens from the options, or in the start of the game.  And even that tutorial does not actually explain some of the mechanics of the game (LIKE THE STEALING MECHANIC!)  Its ambiguous, and not intuitive.  There should have been a small, subtle example of each mechanic as the game introduces them to you, but it never does explain anything in the game.  It doesn't even have a story that really truely explains what exactly is going on.
The story is there, but its vague, and rarely seen.  The journal entry literally gives a hint as to your next direction, and that is your only motivation to do much of anything.  Its rediculous.
The stealth mechanics are terrible.  There are two spaces in the game where you are actually supposed to hide from the crappy looking werewolf.  TWO.  And one of the doesn't work.  Those two specific instances don't even really add to the tense atmosphere that was supposed to be there.  one of them was out right  broken, and I ended up solving the area, by grabbing the cog, and dying only to appear back at the ladder with the cog in my inventory.  The stealing in the game is effortless and in general unessesary outside of two times due to the lack of need for anymore than 200 gold pieces.  You only need to steal a minimum of 3 times.  And when you do need to steal, there is no indicator as to where and who you need to steal from.  Good luck guessing on a first playthrough.
There is no sneaking in the game.  There is no descernable combat in the game.  There are very small amounts of platforming, and the puzzles are actually few and far in between.  Its mostly collection oriented situations.  "Man I would like an apple." - go get apple- "Thanks, here is a key to the door to continue the game." - rinse and repeat.
The music, is good.  The music is actually well done, and probably the only thing worth-while in this game. After this dev team is disolved I hope that the music artist will get a job somewhere else.
The end cutscene in the game looks and runs like a damn story board.  The art is half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥because it looks genuinely un finished.  If you ever watch a story boarding session for disney or something, you will see how this cutscene runs.  Its insulting.
I paraphrased alot of what the issues are with the game.  And if you realy want to see how bad it is, then check out my youtube channel for the whole playthrough of the game. In closing, the game is not worth a penny, its clearly an early alpha build at best.  I spent some of my time trying to figure out how to unlock myself from the terrain I clipped through, or figuring out how to get back into the level after moving through it.  Bad game is bad, and this one is just terrible.  Not worth the time, not worth the money, and a disappointing addition to the ever small selection of werewolf titles.
Devs, you asked me to play the demo for you, and you got my hopes up, and you got me excited.  I jumped in to green light this game, I spoke highly of it for you people.  And then you do me this.  I am sorry for sounding brutal, but I am honest.  You mislead anyone that believes your description of the game.  Half of the description for the game in the steam advertisement section, is either pulling for strings in an effort to sell the game to folks, or outright lying.  This game is terrible, and I am not happy that I jumped and spent money on this title.  Anyone that bought it, needs to go and demand steam refund the purchase.
If you are one of the two people (at the time of this review) who gave this game a thumbs up (despite the 4/10 from one of you), you should come chat with me so I can show you some actual good games to play to put this game into some perspective.  That or I would be lead to believe that you were paid to give your shallow praises for the game.
Bad show devs... bad show.  I want my money back.  I would suggest you either take this game off the steam roster, or drop the price to free to play.  This is (at the time of this review) a 15 dollar purchase.  I expect much more from you guys if you are going to charge this much.

FTL is basically the child of Star Trek and roguelikes, which basically means the USS Enterprise being piloted by an all-red-shirt crew. You start with a dinky little ship and a bunch of fresh-off-the-academy recruits and you are expected to save the entire Federation from the massive Rebel faction.
Keep in mind that FTL's space combat is more Star Trek than Wing Commander - choose ship components to target, tell your weapons guy to fire, watch the energy inputs of your shields and engine, that sorta thing.
Dying in FTL is a perfectly normal experience, and should not deter you from replaying. No one will also judge you if you play at Easy first.
The free update expands on your options on pretty much everything: new weaponry, a new alien race, new ships, new scenarios, so it really increases the replayability.
So if you're a fan of both space exploration and dying frequently, this game's for you.

Little Nightmare is an interesting little indie horror / thriller game, similar to LIMBO or INSIDE. The plot is murky and difficult to grasp, which leaves room for imagination in the world of yellow-raincoated Six and the vessel in the sea. The game is very dark and atmospheric and contains (easy-to-solve) little puzzles for the player to try to beat. Visuals are detailed and the art style seems fitting to the mood of the game. Audio and sounds are fun too.
Unfortunately, there were more than a few occasions where keyboard controls proved to be glitchy. This kind of unresponsive and unpredictable behavior caused many deaths, because Six got stuck in objects I didn't point her to move at. Newcomers to genre should be warned, the game is very linear.
Overall, it's a very solid game and an easy recommend for fans of the genre. There is about 5 hours of playtime.

(Safe! No spoilers inside!)
Note: This review was written by the time episode 1 came out. Only the very end of it has short updates about new episodes.
I played through episode one, and I loved it! Having said that, there is criticism about it and I believe it's partly warranted. I don't share that criticism because it relates to something that doesn't personally bother me, but it will bother some people, so can you be disappointed with the purchase?
First, I'll describe the game a bit. Most of the gameplay of this game consists of picking dialog options on a timer; all other gameplay is secondary and forgettable. This system works very well by giving you hard choices in tense scenes, whose consequences feel potentially very impactful. There is some action that requires pressing the right buttons quickly, which I believe is the weakest point of the game. Fortunately they're sparse and easy. I find a particular action scene choreographed rather poorly, almost breaking suspension of disbelief. However, the action that matters in this game happens in the form of dialogue, and that's where it truly shines.
You play three new characters that are not part of the show. They never meet, but even though in different places, they all move the same story forward, and their actions impact the others. The three characters are all related in their origins. The usual flow of the game consists of a brief introduction of the character/scene in a relaxed pace, followed by a rise of tensions up to a climax, at which point the game changes characters giving the player a calm after the storm. Then it introduces the context of the next character only to ramp up tensions towards the end of the scene again. This pattern repeats, and I must say, every time the character changed, it always felt jarring to me. It was always unwelcome. I wanted to keep playing the other character because I was too immersed in that scene that just ended. However, they won me over every single time, quickly making me care by introducing high stakes to some event as the scene unfolded.
There are only a few characters from the show appearing in this episode, but all of them have great performances and behave like you'd expect from any episode from the tv series. I don't think that the game's enjoyment is completely dependent on watching the show, but it will be severely impaired if you haven't. The game's story occurs between two seasons, so if you haven't watched it and plan on watching it, it will contain very heavy spoilers. If you don't plan on watching it, you'll be able to follow the main story line without a problem, but you won't understand many references and, most importantly, you won't feel the same tension on some scenes that you'd feel had you known more about some characters. In some cases, the characters from the show are barely introduced at all.
Now, let's get to the meat of the complaints. I said before that these scenes "feel" very impactful due to the potential consequences of your actions, but many people have criticized the game for not changing much "under the hood" according to your choices, claiming that there's no choice, only the illusion of choice. This criticism comes from the fact that the game's marketing, as is usual with other games from the same developer, repeats the mantra that the game will adapt to your choices. I would say right off the bat that the developer's statement is true, although its vagueness is what creates wild expectations on many consumers. You might expect the story to branch out multiple times and have multiple endings, depending on your choices. The truth is that the choices do matter... a bit. Some people will simply have different expectations about the degree with which the game changes. Choices change content, but they change it in a self-contained way so that they can reduce the extra work-load that it creates, and the main event that ends the episode doesn't change. Now, bear in mind that these choices might have an impact on next episodes (in fact, that's very likely the case), but I'm only addressing criticism of outcomes not changing within the first episode. In the end, the main story arc will be the same (meaning that the episode always starts at point A, event B happens, and ends at C), but process will change slightly (meaning which characters are present in a scene and how they act).
The problem in expectations also results from the definition of a game. I think there could be much to say about this, but to avoid going on a long tangent here, I'll say that I believe this game (to a lesser extent than others, like Dear Esther) challenges that definition. There are failure states, where you have to restart a scene, but only on more physical action sequences. You know, the ones I said were too sparse, easy to get through, forgettable, etc. The core of the game doesn't really have failure states. It's more of an interactive story where your actions dictate how that story is told, but not whether you win or lose. The outcome is already set in stone. You might ask then, why having interactivity in the first place, and I'd say that, beyond the obvious instances where things do change, I believe that the choice of options on a timer during dire situations are a great use of interactivity as a device in story-telling.
To sum it up, I'd say that, with the caveats that 1) I didn't have the expectation of a more ambitious branching story, 2) I knew and loved the tv show, and 3) I was primarily looking for more of the show: the experience was absolutely thrilling and I totally recommend this game.
---
Update on episode 2:
So, episode 2 left me in a less enthusiastic state. I'd describe it in a word as: fine; and even though fine isn't bad, the contrast with episode one makes me feel slightly disappointed with just fine. To sum it up, there's a lot more of action, and a lot less of psychologically tense scenes or shocking twists. The more action-dependent episode doesn't really mesh well with the franchise nor with the strengths of Telltale's storytelling devices, in my opinion. More quick time events, but less of an impact. Even the appearance of a fan-favorite character of the show seemed lackluster due to the circumstances and the lower stakes presented to the player.
But then again, it's fine. I was kept entertained and interested in the story.
---
Update on episode 3:
I literally just finished it... and it's awesome! I was worried after not feeling it with the second, but this one, I'll dare to say it's the best episode yet. It starts slow, but after it picks up it kept my attention all the way through. It's full of difficult decisions to make and I feel like they made a great job in making all of them feel organic and interconnected. The plot advanced at a fast pace, lots of tension and excitement, the main action sequence towards the end was very well done (one of my problems with the first two), so all in all, five stars. Even though the first episode still has the most shocking twist, I'd rank the 3rd on top for its consistency in its quality. I'm very impressed with it.

I had been looking to get some of the Hyperdimension Neptunia games on PS3 for the past few months, as I assumed such a long series meant those games were selling and had to be somehow popular. A faithful viewer from my stream actually gifted me the remake of the first game of the series on Steam, and here I am reviewing it for you.
Just a little bit of background: I'm somehow versed into Japanese culture, I really dig J-RPGs, I don't mind listening to Baby Metal or Hatsune Miku, I watch a decent amount of animes and I can't wait for my next trip to Akihabara.
If you are looking for a difficult and rather serious RPG game, Re;Birth 1 is not for you. The game is good, but it has its limits. The game is all about humor and references to the video game culture/history/industry. All characters are basically a personification of whether a console, a developer, a publisher or even a single game. It's sometimes really hard to guess who is who, especially for non-initiates (I'm not sure Marvelous AQL rings a bell in many Western heads).
The localization of the game left me with a mixed feeling, somehow. I started to play the game in English, but I had to switch the voices back to Japanese very fast, as the English voices felt totally out of place. Maybe this is just due to me being so used to watch animes with the same type of art in original version with subtitles. The texts were actually accurate, with a good use of video-game references. Some sentences were not reflecting the complete Japanese text (a 30 seconds long voice-over in Japanese summed up in 5 words in English), but this is still a job well done.
Regarding the game itself, you should note that there will be a lot of history-related dialogues: Re;Birth 1 seems to have put a massive emphasis on story-telling, but it sometimes feels a bit over the top. I have recordings of me "playing" the game for more than 30 minutes without even pressing a button, just listening/reading dialogues between different characters. You have options to automatically scroll through dialogues or to even skip them in fast forward. I wouldn't recommend skipping on your first playthrough, but don't hesitate to do so on your NG+ run. Some figures to highlight this point: my first/blind playthrough took me between 35 and 40 hours, my NG+ run in fast forward took me less than 10 hours, including some item or boss farming... Even if NG+ is faster as all your progression from your first playthrough carries over, it's still a massive difference.
Re;Birth1 is divided into 8 chapters. Most of them are divided like so: opening dialogue, event, mission, carry the mission in a dungeon, report back to the main city, new dialogue, new mission, boss fight, dialogue to introduce new area/town/dungeon, new chapter. If you are looking for an open-world game which is not a corridor simulator, you might want to look elsewhere, as this game only offers you the possibility to travel through an overhead map, totally static. The areas you get to explore feel really dull: I unlocked 36 dungeons over the course of the game and I think I didn't see more than 7 different area settings. Most of the time, the new dungeon you explore is going to be a copy of a previous setting, with a different spawn point, a different layout with sometimes an extra level, and a different set of monsters.
You'll be most of the time exploring a dungeon to gather items from its fauna, which is a core element of Hyperdimension Neptunia: Re;Birth1's gameplay. The storyline will tell you to explore a bunch of areas, but those are just the tip of the iceberg, as you can unlock many other dungeons through crafting, which requires items gathered while hunting down monsters. In your adventures, you will be unlocking plans, which will allow you to craft new items, new costumes, new armors, new weapons and, somehow, new dungeons. For each dungeon, you will also get the possibility to unlock extra options, like adding more enemies or turning them into super enemies. Who says new enemies means new items, which will help you to craft new recipes. This idea, which might sound extremely silly to many Westerners, is actually like paradise for players used to grind their way through J-RPGs or completionists. You have hundreds of items to create, hundreds of recipes to craft and some of them are extremely tricky, especially the ones connected to the game's DLC.
Items have a massive impact on the gameplay, and can turn an extremely tough fight in a walk in the park. Crafting better weapons or armors for your characters can obviously directly impact a fight, but sometimes, just unlocking a better healing potion can make a difference. As long as you didn't unlock the item through crafting, you can't buy it and the storyline won't unlock it for you. You will have to leave the story aside at times to take the time and farm up ingredients for crafting recipes.
This part of the gameplay is in my view meant to get you to overcome the difference gap between your character level and the difficulty increase in the storyline. A rule of thumb for leveling in the game is that you need to take around 5 levels between every boss you have to fight. The issue lays in the fact that the dungeons are extremely small and that you sometimes need to grind a lot waiting for the monsters to respawn to get your EXP. A good alternative is, as said, to go and explore other dungeons to maybe unlock new recipes in the mean time. It's still a grind, but you add an additional objective to your grind, which will be completed much faster and far less frustrating.
The monsters you'll be facing will, like the dungeons, look a lot a like: the bestiary is very limited and offers mostly recolorations. You'll be facing rad, blue, yellow, orange flowers. You'll slay green, red and blue Mario pipes. You'll tear apart 5 different types of visual-novel games screenshots. But each of them will drop a different item that you might need for a recipe or another. I can only recommend you to check out the guide section connected to this game to get an entire drop list and make your life a lot easier. Combats will most of the time be easy, but necessary.
The combat system itself will leave a different impression depending on the player. Some will find it boring, some others will find it extremely entertaining. I personally really enjoyed the turn-base aspect of it, even if it was sometimes hard to get a grasp of why your opponent would be allowed to get two turns in a row or why specific choices made you fall back a bit further down the "turn to attack" line. You have many options to choose from in combat: the deities can take their HDD forms and improve their statistics and their movesets, all characters can decide whether they want to use skills (heal/buff/debuff/attack/resurrection) or a string of attacks. If you decide to attack with your weapon, you'll be offered the possibility to use three moves in a row, each one can have a different impact on your target. Some skills are meant to reduce your foe's defense, others to directly target your enemies HP bar and the last one will increase your EXE gauge, which will allow you to use super attacks once you get enough energy. The animations for those skills are pretty impressive, and you can even create combination attacks between characters through the friendship system built in the game (Lily ranking). Some will try to fill up their EXE gauge as fast as they can to brainlessly spam super powerful atacks, some will play around buffs and debuffs to weaken their foes. It's all up to you, but don't hesitate to spam the HDD transformations. Because lollies.
All in all, this review can sound a little gloomy, but the game is still worth a try, it will keep you busy for a little over 60 hours if you want to go for all the achievements, it offers a lot of content (even if it's sometimes just duplicated) and you get all the fan service and references an Otaku can dream of.

This game was a bit of a disappointment. When a game implements a certain style and feel it should be done right and with lots of details. This game fails to achieve just that and fails to deliver. It starts with the resolution itself, some weird low-res 1000 x 800, not widescreen but not 4:3 either. The graphics are cell-shaded but done very generic and it looks just bad. The effects for water, fire and particles are dx6 or something.
The sound is also not very good and sound rather cheap. The voices are rather cheesy and lipsinc is not in sync (understatement).  Music is ok but gets annoying quickly.
When you move it feels like you are very small because you are a bit close to the ground. You interact with things when your dot changes to a hand. That's about it what you can do.

It's a Mahjong game. If you've ever played it on previous versions of Windows (when it was also known as Taipei way back when) then you know what this game is. It's a simplistic game and yet I'll probably get a couple paragraphs out of this review because that's how I tend to do things. It's rather annoying but here I go.
Mahjong is played by choosing a tile layout and then clicking similar tiles away until every tile is off the board and you win. There are four different styles of tiles to choose from as well as four different animated backgrounds to choose from. The backgrounds are all very nicely drawn and this game is a rather relaxing time waster as a result. About the only negative is that there is only one music track in the entire game so it can get a bit repetitive after a while, particularly if you're going after all the achievements which you earn simply by beating each of the seventy layouts.
If you're looking for a fun little time waster or an easy way to pad up that perfect game count on your Steam profile, pick this up.

So I've been playing this game for a while now, and I'm quite shocked I haven't wrote a review for it yet. I originally got this game because it was recommended to me by a friend, and since I wasn't into anything remotely like Civilization V at the time, I was fairly skeptical, having most of the games I had played up to that point being RPG's and FPS games. Civilization V did not fail to impress me, even back then. I will admit I was peeved at times from the difficulty I faced in those early days, but I quickIy began to enjoy the challenge it provided (Even though the AI still remains to be very silly when it comes to what it wants to build, and how it fights at times). Not only do I enjoy the singleplayer experience, but I love to play this game with my friends, save for the odd moments where i feel the wrath of nuclear detonation destroy my capital city. I definitely recommend this game to anyone who is wanting to take their first steps into 4X games, as it is an enjoyable experience, and is found to be a game where you have a hard time putting it down after you start getting into it, until you look at your clock and realize that 7 hours have passed by. The game generates maps at relative randomness, depending on the map settings that you chose, so you'll find a lot of re-playability with this game.
TL;DR
If you want to play a 4X game, this delivers a good product, with a lot of hours that you can sink into it. Seriously recommend it.

Matches can drag on and being on a losing team for 45 minutes because people refuse to surrender can become a massive chore if you're only one on your team who is not turtling. Playing with random teammates at worst can be a massive chore, since it's really hard to get anything done by yourself especially considering you need to be point blank range to actually do proper damage to the core, and good luck with that if all your team does is turtle.
On the technical standpoint I didn't see any massively glaring problems and fps stayed good at all times, Characters speaking same one liners all the time does get annoying and frequency should be cut to half.

So I'm raiding this massive ufo, right, and my team gets ambushed: in one room, 3 elite thugs in the balcony corner my sniper and a support, while down the hall a meelee thug that reaction fire wasn't able to kill is about to smash a wounded solder's face in, plus, two other gunmen pop out further across the hall poised to kill, and all this is happening after half my soldiers have already gone through their turns. So I'm thinking, oh crap, I'm about to loose a solder and have to restart the save because I'm a save scum mc bucket, better rescue what I can, so I have my support grenade the 3 elite thugs in the balcony above, doing 5 damage to each one - a pitiful figure considering they each have 14 hp and 1 turn alive is all they need to tear my troops a new buttcheek, so out of desperation I command my sniper to shoot across the hall at the meelee thug and kill it, maybe we can at least give the wounded operative a fighting chance... but then the game notifies me: "In the Zone!"
In the Zone is an ability of snipers in which every shot that kills an alien who is out of cover or flanked will not cost a turn, which is kind of a big deal during a turn based game when you realize your grenade blew the elite thugs's cover, exposing them... with this awesome realization, my sniper picked them off one by one with ease, and then even managed to score a kill on one of the aliens across the hall, doing 5 confirmed kills in a single turn, it was glorious - I don't care I was playing on the easiest difficulty because that level was freaking hard!
Bottom line: fun turn based tactics, although the cartoonish graphics may not be your thing.

We've all done it: played GTA and tried simply to cause as much chaos as possible. Saints Row knows exactly what you want. And so Saints Row is like "Hey dude. Here's a gun that shoots dubstep. Kill as much♥♥♥♥♥♥as you can!" And we love it for that. Saints Row is all about having fun without worrying too much about why. Case in point; this game starts off with you being the President of the United States. "You" being "The Boss" of the Saints, a once-small gang that made it big. Big enough to get elected president. But, as these kinds of things happen, Earth gets invaded by aliens. And it's upto The President and his/her fellow saints to blow stuff up- I mean, save the world.
The gameplay is pretty much the same as SR: The Third, only with the added bonus of having SUPERPOWERZ. Because, hey, why the hell not? Jumping and sprinting over skyscrapers never gets old, and neither does bombing the hell out of stuff, shooting black holes at people or crashing down to the ground with the power of a nuke (I'm not even kidding.) It also pokes fun at other games, not the least of which Mass Effect, what with "Loyalty missions" and the ability to 'romance' your crewmembers on a ship that serves as your base. It is all just so much fun! All the usual bonkers stuff you know and love about SR is in here too, but now with superpowers!
Which brings me to the first negative point about this game. SR3 had many whacky vehicles and the thing is, with having the powers to sprint faster than a bullet and jumping as high as towers, SR4 renders vehicles completely obsolete. Again, it never gets -old-, but I figure part of the fun of these kinds of games is the many many vehicles you can steal. What also bothered me is that the vast majority of the side quests seem to consist of just doing activities that were already open/available anyway, and constantly switching back from Steelport to the ship that serves as your base is kind of annoying. The final thing that bothered me is that this game is pretty heavy on the nostalgia about SR1 and SR2 and, not having played them, I felt like I was kind of missing out a little.
But hey, do you really care about all that stuff? Don't you just want to bomb stuff from high in the air, zoof over buildings,  singing along with "What is love? Baby, don't hurt me!" while punching aliens in the groin? Exactly.
The Good: More Saints Row... with superpowers. Seriously.
The Bad: Copy/paste Steelport from SR3, missions seem less than SR3, little heavy on the nostalgia, and overal just a tad less enjoyable than SR3.

FTL is basically the child of Star Trek and roguelikes, which basically means the USS Enterprise being piloted by an all-red-shirt crew. You start with a dinky little ship and a bunch of fresh-off-the-academy recruits and you are expected to save the entire Federation from the massive Rebel faction.
Keep in mind that FTL's space combat is more Star Trek than Wing Commander - choose ship components to target, tell your weapons guy to fire, watch the energy inputs of your shields and engine, that sorta thing.
Dying in FTL is a perfectly normal experience, and should not deter you from replaying. No one will also judge you if you play at Easy first.
The free update expands on your options on pretty much everything: new weaponry, a new alien race, new ships, new scenarios, so it really increases the replayability.
So if you're a fan of both space exploration and dying frequently, this game's for you.

Tripwire, as a company, has really shown their true marketing colors as of a short while post-KF1 release. How does this tie into Killing Floor 2? I'll show you.
My first talking for this point is the most obvious: Killing Floor 2 is the first game with better graphics and hit detection. That's unavoidable and to be expected. Moving past this, the question of whether or not it's a worthwhile sequel falls on how it's managed to avoid its predecessor's downfalls and improve on the set formula. To be blunt, it's a much better game before the bosses, which are my primary gripe with the game as it is.
Bosses, previously being the Patriarch alone with his machine gun/rocket launcher and cheap instagibs, were just a means of capping off a game so the players felt like they had accomplished something. Despite KF1's engine issues, this played out far better in the first game than the second. Killing Floor 2's bosses are purebred bullet sponges with a much faster flee-and-heal response, and greater speed with this process. Effectively, this means you're going to be dumping rounds into a meatshield for 3-4 cycles as he heals to full over the course of 5-8 seconds over and over. Take it from me, it's a huge break in tempo from tactically prioritizing the most dangerous zeds or delegating target priority to the best-suited class (e.g. shotgun wielding supports vs scrakes) to "everyone throws rounds downrange while the boss occasionally just instagibs people anyway. It takes the depth out of the fight and is not a satisfying end to an otherwise very intense game.
I'll spare nitpicking about the bosses themselves, but the pacing of these fights is poor. Tripwire has had feedback to this effect and has done nothing to rectify the balance or tempo of the endgame fights. Instead, they've focused on Zed rebalances (positive) and dumping tacky cosmetics and gun customizations (disgustingly predictable) into the game. If you played much KF1 before 2's closed alpha release came out, you remember the DLC weaponry that outclassed vanilla pickings and how Tripwire's mentality clearly honed in on microtransactions for their second game with how they handled the first. Companies imitating Valve and their admittedly huge profit margins on cosmetics (especially community-made cosmetics) is a grim sign for the future of any game. What we have here is an inexperienced developer with a decent product choosing quantity over quality on a gross level. My opinion being this way, I'll move onto my last gripe with how Killing Floor 2 was handled.
Triple A/well-known brand games tend to expand on their storylines as to not go stale, right? it's an inevitable way to expand the playerbase and explore the background lore for the content the developers produce. Killing Floor, both as a mod and the standalone, began with the concept of a paramilitary bioweapons company causing disaster in the process of attempting to create frontline super-soldiers. Basic enough, right? Yeah, beyond a few character blurbs the lore was fairly straightforward, sarcastically B-movie type stuff. And that was good: it fit the characters, scenarios and mood of the game.
Killing Floor 2 decided to get up it's own♥♥♥♥♥♥with its lore and add onto the first game's storyline with the concept of Horzine (the company responsible for the Zeds) hiring on randoms and ex-military personnel as mercenaries with the explicit task of ending the zombie/mutant crisis. We go from the stereotypical British characters referring to money as "dosh" to the second game's storyline outright naming the newly-dubbed currency Horzine pays out in as "Dosh". This turns the tone of the game from being a matter of survival/eradication to an almost comedic run'n'gun with its new characters being your typical diversity sequelitis go-to's. The storyline presents less of a clash with the tone than the gameplay does, though, which leads me to my last point.
Killing Floor 2 is actually a quality gore-heavy shooter with monstrously awkward pacing issues. I mean it, the animations on both guns and Zeds is good material, fighting the hordes feels frantic and the (oftentimes forced) darkness in the map makes it difficult to keep /everything/ under control, meaning it's important to keep moving throughout the maps. The jokey revamped storyline and over-commercialized approach to microtransactions drains a lot from the immersiveness and tone of the game, though, as well as the boss battles I mentioned before. You go from an engaging firefight with minion-type Zeds where each class can shine to a boring, horribly executed slugfest against an AI that repeatedly just flees under literal invisibility to go heal to full. Bear in mind, during this endeavor you're still not getting any extra ammo or real progression in the fight.
Lastly, the maps and environments in KF2 are okay. They're nothing exceptional and don't lend particularly well to the formula's mobility trends, but they look nice and don't have glaring issues. I sort of think that the degree to which the ground gets stained with bright red paint, I mean blood, is a little extreme given the fact that anywhere a fight goes down will soon be just a static, consistent red color as opposed to the blood decals being changed up even a bit. This is a minor thing, but it looks weird to be honest. I love gore in zombie shooters, but the texturing job was just lazy this game around.
Buy it if you like-- it's a good shooter with an unforgivably cheap dev team behind it. Given their history, I doubt they'd rework the poor boss battles or do anything besides tweaking weapon numbers (still better than nothing, don't get me wrong,) and adding new DLC crap. Paying Tripwire is bad for the industry, so help us achieve total entropy and make sure bad devs stay flush with cash (sorry, Dosh xDDD) for lazy development so we can all move on past playing video games and get back to being bored adults.
-Your Mike

I have been a Game of Thrones since the very beginning. I read the books and watched the TV show several times over. Yet, my review is written for those who may not know much about game of thrones or haven't quite got into it yet.
The gameplay of this game is fairly standard for a telltale game, there are choices you must make quickly and QTE's when it comes to combat. Yet as supposed to the walking dead or the wolf among us, I found myself using up almost all of the time alloted to me when making decisions. The decisions are never black and white and usually when making a decision the consequences are so high stakes that is agonizing. For example, one choice forces you to decide between saving a close friend or a nobleman and as soon as I decided in favor of the noble a polearm was shoved through the neck of my friend. That is part of the draw of Game of Thrones, nobody is safe and your favorite characters can die at any moment.
Telltale successfully brought this concept to bear throughout the game and after the finale I was staring slackjawed at the screen before bellowing a string of obscenities and swearing vengeance.
The art style is fairly standard for telltale games yet that is part of the charm of this game and makes it truly unique. It can be spectacularly beautiful whether in the sun baked city of Kings Landing or the cold seat of house of Forrster.
It was also nice to see familiar faces from the series and books appear and since telltale got the actual actors to play the parts in the video game it was a nice bit of fan service that is set to include Jon Snow in the next episode and possibly Dany Targaryen.
For fans of the show or books this is a no brainer buy immediately situation.
However if you are a Game of Thrones novice or only managed to scratch the surface I think the choice is equally clear. Telltale Games has delivered an experience that would be familiar to Game of Thrones fanatics or a nice introduction to those who have never heard of it.
My one minor gripe is that after my playthrough was over is that there was precious little action outside of the first chapter. I assume this will be remedied as the first episode is usually to set the stage and the action comes hard and quick for the rest of the series.

Competent, no-frills version of Mahjong Solitaire. 70 advertised layouts but several feel like very close duplicates of each other, and many don't feature the full count of tiles so the difficulty (i.e. how often you have to guess) varies quite a bit. Everything works as advertised, I experienced no real slowdown or crashes. But it has a lot of the hallmarks of a contracted port of a mobile game. The graphics get the job done, the backgrounds are nicely animated and the tiles are attractively rendered. No serious problems, just a long list of relatively minor nitpicks that could be resolved to make this game really shine
Loading times feel longer than they should. From main menu to actually playing a game requires ~12 seconds and this is not a graphically demanding game, nor should the algorithm that places tiles be all that computationally expensive. The options menu can only be accessed by completely exiting to the main menu, some of the sound effects are not properly normalized to the rest of the sfx (the tile clear sound in particular is entirely too loud), there are two music tracks, the menu music and the game music. For some reason no music plays during loading screens. Music and sound effects have on/off toggles but no volume control, so either they're muted or they're on at full volume.
The largest complaints come down to the design and responsiveness of the UI. I just want a 'quick play' button that gives me the traditional layout from a random seed so I can begin playing immediately instead of having to sit through multiple loading screens. There's a short period between matching tiles and the animation of the tiles clearing where you can't click on tiles that are now free and that's kind of frustrating. You have to sit through the leaderboard prompts animating in and out every time you clear a stage; the game should just remember an 'automatically upload my scores to leaderboards' setting. These little details separate what could be a casual relaxing session of solitaire to one that introduces brief periods of irritation while you try to chill.
Simply put, this game has a lot of story and replay value. Defenitly recommend it.

A disappointing poor product clearly rushed out to capitalize on the show's popularity.
I was sceptical for a long while, as one should with licensed games, but then I played the excellent Wolf Among Us and figured that it's still a Telltale product, and thus ought to rise to a certain level of quality. Not so.
First of all, the most important element of any visual novel, the writing, is shoddy, dull, and repetetive. I didn't keep an exact count, but approximately one third of the lines are just variations of "this House is your responsibility now" or "our House is on the line here." Constant flat statements about the core of the story in the manner of a childrens' movie and the main cast of characters are such obvious one-dimensional copies of the Stark family to the point where it's comical. In addition, the dialogue options you're given are often so similar to each other as to feel pointless.
Furthermore, the gameplay, and I use the term in the loosest sense possible, is terribly unengaging. The story is heavily railroaded during the dialogue segments and the actiony bits might as well have done away with the QTE-inputs altogether. Sure, this is how these Telltale games work, but previous titles have managed it much better. In The Walking Dead there were action beats where you could die because you'd forgotten to pick up a shotgun shell in the scene before, and the story progression would take breaks for you scavenge areas for supplies or have conversations with characters that fleshed them out. The Wolf Among Us didn't do much with its action sequences, but there you got to have "detective" scenes where you'd search a place for clues, and future dialogue scenes could change depending on what you found or missed. Game of Thrones does nothing like this. There are two or three scenes where you get to walk around and look at things, but they're frightfully empty of both fluff dialogue and quest objects.
Finally, the graphics are ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, there's no way around it. I'm in no way a graphics ♥♥♥♥♥, but when your game is pretty much a semi-interactive movie, presentation is everything, and Game of Thrones is poorly presented. The models' movements are stilted and awkward, the facial animations of talking characters are badly desynched and characters who aren't talking spend a lot of time staring blankly into space rather than listening to and reacting to what's being said. Worst of all are the textures, which even on High look like they belong in a game from 2004, not 2014. I also found the voice acting to be really hit and miss, which is disappointing considering how on point it was in Wolf Among Us.¨
All in all, I think this is a bad game which reeks of being rushed out to soon. How the negative reviews on here can be outnumbered ten to one by the positive is a mystery.

We'll be going over our opinions on the graphics, music, content, controls, and gameplay of this game.
Graphics:
We believe the graphics are beautiful. Each map is well made and the blocks are related to the scene of the map. Each character we found to be very cute. The game also included filters for each map, which is pretty neat.
Music:
We found the soundtrack very smooth and it fits the scenery of the game. Its something that we found ourselves jamming to here and there. It also wasn't too overpowering.
Content:
We were able to change the time limit to either 3, 5, 7, or 10 minutes, which we found great. There are a couple of different maps, along with the ability to change the filters that we mentioned above in graphics. The variety of scenery is great.
Controls:
Can't really say how it feels when using a keyboard. But using a controller was very simple and easy to learn, which made us have some really competitive games right off the bat.
Gameplay:
This game was very enjoyable and fun. The objective is to build towers and keep them standing while trying to knock down your opponent's towers. The game is pretty fast-paced, but very easy to flow with.
Verdict: TL;DR
This game is fun, simple, and easy to play and the best part of it is that it's FREE! We give this a 9.5 because there was some bug that we ran into, but nothing game breaking. Some people spoke about the fact that there's no online feature, but that's not what we were looking for in the first place.

Little Nightmares is a bit of a survival platformer in the vein of Limbo and INSIDE. You play a little figure in a bright yellow rain slicker trying to escape a dark, scary place. Controls are tight, though it takes some getting used to to platform on the 3D plane, and there are often multiple solutions to clear the area you're in, just be aware that the game is not very long.
I have to set a paragraph aside just for how friggin beautiful this game is. The environments are richly detailed, the lighting effects are wonderful and dramatic, and some of the characters look freakishly real enough it's like you're looking at filmed puppets, not 3D rendered characters. Granted, that's partly because the camera is always a bit pulled out, but still. I was repeatedly awestruck by how good this game looks.
Aside from that, it has beautiful music, and as more often with these kinds of games, it paints a world and story without using words, leaving you to piece it together, and, if you're like me, wishing you could see more of it. When the game's done, there's still the challenge of finding all hidden collectibles to complete. Normally I don't bother, but I think I'll want to go back in just to see everything again.

Grim Dawn is an ARPG game which features complex character development, hundreds of unique items, crafting, quests and lots of point and clicking goodness. It's based on Titan Quest engine and it's one of the better games of its type.
So, Grim Dawn has a story, but I was never interested in stories in ARPGs. The goal is to point at the mob and click to then point at the loot and click again. This clickability, along with interesting character progression and balanced difficulty is what makes an ARPG good for me. And this one hit the mark almost perfectly. With good graphics, interesting classes, excellent character progression and nice loot Grim Dawn is one of the better time sinks out there.
Everyone know what it's competitors are, so to compare I'd say it's almost as good as Diablo and a little bit better than Path of Exile. I don't like PoE much though, too much investment needed. Anyhow, GD looks on par with D3, a little less flashy though, which is good as you can actually see what you're clicking on. The audio on the other hand is horribly terrible, just mute and put on your fav playlist. The character progression is very interesting with the option to go single- or dual-class and lots of active and passive skills to back any way of playing, but it's never ovewhelming. You have option to correct your build at any given moment by refunding points spent in an outpost, so experimentation is welcomed. The game has four difficulty levels, with two unlocked from the start.
Basically it's your ARPG stuff done right. It took me ca. 50hrs to finish on first difficulty level and I played another 50 hrs to almost complete it on the third difficulty level. If you're into these kind of games it should last you for 100s of hours.
I liked:
* nice graphics, very grim
* interesting classes and progression system
* can be played in sessions of 15mins or 5hrs
* leveling alts is fun
I disliked:
* horribad music/audio (thank you for volume slider!)
* after 100hrs it's not that easy to get a new cool shiny
Get this is:
* if you like ARPGs
Don't get this:
* if you need to have your♥♥♥♥♥kicked for 100s of hours before being able to fight back (I'm looking at you PoE)

Dying Light represents a much improved sophomore outing from Techland. Disappointed as I was with the original Dead Island, I did not buy Riptide and I was even turned off of Dying Light initially. Oddly enough, It did actually have a pre-release demo, though it committed the cardinal sin of being of timed duration. Also unfortunately, it prominently displays the game's weakest element- low-level melee combat, before you acquire the various showy moves and weapons that don't amount to more then an actual broken goddamn table leg. 
Combat continues to be a bit of a chore even into the late game, unless you decide to use a gun. There is a particular type of large, muscular zombie called a Demolisher that duffs you over with similar ease to Dead Island's Thug zombies, and its no less irritating each time it happens. Attempting to melee them is suicidal at best, but you could instead just throw a sickle at their face and they go down like any other zombie. Really, there's no balance to be had. Avoiding the zombies is actually more entertaining then fighting them off: with investment in skills, you can learn to ramp up and over a zombie's head, crash through them like a rampaging football player, and execute a flying double kick to their faces. 
Do not play Dying Light alone, at least initially. The early game hell is strong and without a better equipped player backing you up, the experience is much like Dead Island: boring, cheap, and uncompromising. It is a cooperative game and should be played as such, the more the merrier. It actually suffers in one respect as compared to Dead Island, which had four different playable characters with varying abilities, wherein this game everyone plays the same guy, Kyle Crane. Admittedly his skill tree is excellent and you can obtain all abilities available, but he is otherwise generic fuzz-faced white male protagonist #87, and a bit whiny, besides. Roger Craig's Smith work as Chris Redfield is enjoyable primarily because Resident Evil is ♥♥♥♥ing ridiculous and it fits. But Dying Light is ostensibly a serious game, and he comes off as rather forced and unbelievable when Crane is trying to be emotional. The game's writing over all is very weak, offering little narrative payoff and constant depressing disappointment at every turn- as per standard for the zombie survival genre. Crane is a freelance operative employed by the Global Relief Effort, or GRE, to enter the maybe-Turkish city of Harran, which of course overrun by a zombie plague. Your target, an insane, narcissistic, wannabe-social Darwinist ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ by the name of Rais, is in possession of a document of immense value. You insert yourself with a local population of survivors in the hopes of finding Rais and this document, but things go pear-shaped pretty fast as you are in the city mere seconds before you get bit, and the game is pretty much one predtictably horrific ♥♥♥♥♥orm after another.
Most people who play this probably wouldn't give a ♥♥♥♥, but if a game has a plot, I follow that plot. Where Dying Light shines, however, is the much advertised parkour elements. Moving through the urban sprawl of Harran is simple, smooth and enjoyable, unlike, say, Brink. You eventually earn a grappling hook that can be used to pull you directly to ledges and other surfaces, physics be damned, though there is a persistent issue with being able to grapple onto ledges you can't actually grab afterwards, sending you plummeting helplessly to the uncaring ground below. I think I might actually have died more often from falling damage then from any enemies, in spite of a tuck-and-roll maneuver you can use to avoid damage from a long, but non-fatal fall. Too bad most of my falls were longer.
Game flow is open ended, with a generous helping of boxes to open, side quests, challenges, and small dungeons in the form of quarantine zones scattered about the game's two major zones, the slums and old town, with the latter having much taller buildings and things like tall streetlamps and telephone wires to let you flex your parkour skills. The challenges are predictably annoying, proving themselves once more the zit on the face of sandbox action games, with extremely tight time limits and paltry rewards of experience points. There are occasional new blueprints to be had for the game's tastefully simple crafting system from them though, which involves strapping things like nails, electrical wiring and lighters to anything from a fence board to a machete to a medieval warhammer, to make them deadlier. You can make firecrackers, shuriken, medkits, grenades and bunch of other things, besides.
Overall, the game is substantially less dense then Dead Island, but is largely better for it. It plays better and runs better, too. I passed the game up on release a year ago, and picked up the game for $20 at the suggestion of a friend and I was not disappointed, though I can say with certainty that Techland has a long way to go yet. I expect bigger things from them in the future.
Good night, and good luck.

We've all done it: played GTA and tried simply to cause as much chaos as possible. Saints Row knows exactly what you want. And so Saints Row is like "Hey dude. Here's a gun that shoots dubstep. Kill as much♥♥♥♥♥♥as you can!" And we love it for that. Saints Row is all about having fun without worrying too much about why. Case in point; this game starts off with you being the President of the United States. "You" being "The Boss" of the Saints, a once-small gang that made it big. Big enough to get elected president. But, as these kinds of things happen, Earth gets invaded by aliens. And it's upto The President and his/her fellow saints to blow stuff up- I mean, save the world.
The gameplay is pretty much the same as SR: The Third, only with the added bonus of having SUPERPOWERZ. Because, hey, why the hell not? Jumping and sprinting over skyscrapers never gets old, and neither does bombing the hell out of stuff, shooting black holes at people or crashing down to the ground with the power of a nuke (I'm not even kidding.) It also pokes fun at other games, not the least of which Mass Effect, what with "Loyalty missions" and the ability to 'romance' your crewmembers on a ship that serves as your base. It is all just so much fun! All the usual bonkers stuff you know and love about SR is in here too, but now with superpowers!
Which brings me to the first negative point about this game. SR3 had many whacky vehicles and the thing is, with having the powers to sprint faster than a bullet and jumping as high as towers, SR4 renders vehicles completely obsolete. Again, it never gets -old-, but I figure part of the fun of these kinds of games is the many many vehicles you can steal. What also bothered me is that the vast majority of the side quests seem to consist of just doing activities that were already open/available anyway, and constantly switching back from Steelport to the ship that serves as your base is kind of annoying. The final thing that bothered me is that this game is pretty heavy on the nostalgia about SR1 and SR2 and, not having played them, I felt like I was kind of missing out a little.
But hey, do you really care about all that stuff? Don't you just want to bomb stuff from high in the air, zoof over buildings,  singing along with "What is love? Baby, don't hurt me!" while punching aliens in the groin? Exactly.
The Good: More Saints Row... with superpowers. Seriously.
The Bad: Copy/paste Steelport from SR3, missions seem less than SR3, little heavy on the nostalgia, and overal just a tad less enjoyable than SR3.

Often called Mirror's Edge with zombies and weapons, Dying Light is an enjoyable open world first person parkour zombie-fest.
The story sees you playing a secret agent of some generic organization that may not have everyone's best interestes in mind. You're parachuted into a city in qurantine due to a zombie outbreak and you are tasked with infiltrating various groups of survivors to find a man who stole information about your generic spy organization. There are no real choices for the player to make throughout the story, which can be frustrating when you see yourself doing something stupid just because your boss over the phone told you too. Overall it's a fairly dull plot, and my biggest complaint is the ending (which i will spoil and talk about at the very bottom of this review).
Gameplay is a nice mix of free running and combat. Parkour feels just like the aforementioned Mirror's Edge, although with less advance features, like wallrunning. Halfway through the game, you should unlock the grappling hook ability, which basically makes you spiderman.
Any game where you turn into spiderman halfway through is a good game.
Melee weapons in this game have improving stats as you progress in level. basically a hack n slash loot drop system, not unlike borderlands. Guns play an interesting role, as they are few and far between, and, in the early game, extremely powerful. The late game however, they will become almost useless due to the fact that they dont scale in power the way every other weapon does. Nor can you upgrade them with cool abilities like other weapons. An interesting choice on the Dev teams part, and the right one I think. Like Dead Rising and Mirror's Edge, guns aren't the central focus, but they can be a powerful trump card in a pinch.
The multiplayer features the player being able to be a super zombie and even has its own level progression. In a multiplayer game, one player will be the super zombie, tasked with defending egg caches from the players, and killing them 10 times. while 1-4 players will be their normal human characters and have to destroy all the eggs before they run out of lives. That's the only mode, and while it does sound a bit tacked on, it can be a lot of fun. Especially when you have a full game of 5 people. unfortunately, the servers are mostly empty at this point because the multiplayer isn't seperate from the single player. players seeking to be a super zombie will have to invade other people's single player games at night, and most people turn off that online feature. so basically, multiplayer's dead unless you've got 5 people you know.
And speaking of friends, you can have up to 3 people join your game and run around doing stuff with you. It's fun, you should do it.
Overall, the game features addicting gameplay, an average story (for a video game), and lots of developer support post launch in the form of free and paid DLC.
SPOILERS (not that anyone cares)
My biggest complaint about the story is the ending, or lack therefore. The final boss battle takes place in the form of a very dissappointiong quick time event. something this game has been trying to stay away from throughout. once you've defeated the end boss, your character tells his boss over the phone that he quits. and thats just about it...
you're still in the city and all your survivor friends are still not evacuated. If i didnt know any better I'd suspect the real ending is in the DLC you have to pay for... oh wait... who published this game? Warnor Bros?
d**k move, Warner Bros, d**k move. (also f@#*ing fix batman, god!)

Grim Dawn is an arpg from Crate Entertainment, which was formed from the ashes of Iron Lore, the makers of Titan Quest. Of all the arpg's I have played (torchlight 1 and 2, victor vran, diablo 2 and 3, titan quest and the van helsing franchise) I easily enjoy Grim Dawn the most. Let me explain.
Pros:
- Classes. Game right now has 6 classes, of which at level 2 you choose one and at level 10 you can choose another. People who are familiar with Titan Quest know this skill and class system very well. This double class system allow people to create tons of classes and an amazing amount of combos. Chain lightning dual wielder in heavy armour? Why not. Rifle wearing gunslinger with meteor showers? Absolutely. A mage with death rays and bolts of chaos? Sounds like fun.
- Progression and Leveling. The leveling is easily better and more immersive than Diablo 3 for example. You have side quests (granted, most are easy to complete and are easily unlocked progressing), hidden locations where you can't access right away, needind special materials to unlock. There are also devotion shrines around the world which give you devotion points, creating even more class customization.
-Setting. The world of grim dawn is a post apocalyptic world that was destroyed after the event, well, "Grim Dawn" where the aetherials (one of the antagonists of the game) pured from the aether and destroyed the world as we know it. Humanity is trying it's hardest to survive, and the world is depressing in a sense that so much has been destroyed and lost. Many environments, different enemy types, settings (swamps, forests and snowy mountains) and hidden lore notes about the world keep the player immersed in this dark, amazing world.
-Combat. The combat is fluid, fast an interesting. Not as quick as some other arpg's (d3 for example) grim dawn offers more skill options, skills and procs from different items, runes and augments which boost your skills or give you totally new abilities. This creates varied styles of combat from long range casters to melee sword and boarders and all in between.
-Loot. Loot is varied, and the rarities are from white--->yellow--->green--->blue--->purple. White items are regular weapons and armor with almost nothing too special about them. Yellows and greens are magical items with varied stat increases and buffs. Blue items are rares, with a specific name, look and enchantments. Lastly, the purple, or legendary category. Very rare and they drop after you reach level 50. These are like rare items, but with more attention to graphical detail and even more powerful enchantments.
Negative (note. I don't find these points totally negative, but they have negative aspects that might influence your opinion of the game)
-Co-op and online play. The game doesn't haver official servers of it's own, but online play is possible from the game client. While mostly fine, sometimes the online play can stutter, or even crash. Worts I personally have experienced is loot that we can't pick up. I have now played about 200hours of the game in coop, in which we have had this happen about 8 times. Quick relog always fixed this for us.
-End game content. The games had 4 difficulties; normal, veteran, elite (new game plus) and ultimate (new game plus plus). You can also create hardcore character swhich give you a new challenge, since the first death is permanent and your character is lost after this. I have personally never liked hardcore, but it creates the strongest build since people want to get as far as possible without dying. There are also 2 rogue-lite dungeons, which you can't quit until you beat the final boss or die. They are challenging but offer some amazing rewards. But what grim dawn lacks is a proper end game for max level characters other than finding those BiS items, unlike for example D3 which has tons of end game content.
Other things about the game:
-Reputation system. You cain positive reputation for good factions by doing quests, killing bosses or completing their bounties, which are repeatable missions. Negative influence is gained by killing members of evil factions, meaning they get more and stronger enemies, including bosses. The reputation also allows you to buy strong items from faction specific merchants once you are liked enough by them.
All in all, this game is amazing, it just got it's first free content patch, it is updated constantly and both the community and the developers are amazing people. First actual dlc is coming out soon too :)

A fantastic strategy game.  While initially seeming entirely luck based, stick with it and you'll find this has less to do with luck, and more to do with how the player deals with each scenario as it is presented.  Overwhelming odds can seem unfair until the player begins to grow comfortable with the ship's systems and watching carefully for opportunities.  None available?  Fleeing is an option.  The game is about planning and execution, not simply throwing one's arsenal at the enemy.   With a large volume of available system and upgrade types, ships, characters and possible events, all randomized for each play session, the possibilities in play are EXTREMELY varied and it won't be too often that one encounters a similar play through on more than one occasion.
That positive also carries a negative, and one that is only a negative depending upon the player: patience and time is required.  The player will lose often as he/she learns how the game works, and what play style and strategic methods suit him/her most.  For myself, this was a huge part of the draw; but if one is the type of gamer just looking for a quick romp without requiring too much thought then it may be best to stay away from this game.  For those with the time, patience and a strategic mind of any sort, it will be an extremely rewarding experience.

Killing your friends just got inherently more satisfying.
You can be the hero, buy trinkets and weapons to kill the big bad evil guy.
Or you can just kill yourself and become a variety of goons, traps and the big boss itself.
The game can get very hectic at 4 players. I've had trouble trying to discern things on the screen, because there had been so much going on.
As the game starts, you can choose a deity to worship. All of which give bonuses and a little set of 3 different, upgradable monsters, which you'll control when you die.
You get a lot of things to play around with. As the good guy, you get tons of weapons and some spells, each weapon has their own moveset. It's a shame that most weapons look the same, the khopesh doesn't have its sickle shape, it just looks like a straight sword.
Bad guys get to control the various obstacles in the dungeons, this is the part of the game which hooked me. It's like every enemy that recklessly beelined to hurt the immortal hero (you) in other games, suddenly grew a brain and started using actual strategies.
Of course you aren't forced to play with others, you can play alone with bots. The AI, from what I've experienced in hard difficulty, is actually very proficient and ruthless at the game. There are also single-player monster challenges, which are great for learning how to play as the monsters and to squeeze some extra playtime on the game.
It's a good game, you can get it.
