Are you tired of Japanese cultural dominance over the foreign animated market? Sick to death of “waifu’s” being all “kawaii”? Are you ready for a different cultural experience that utilizes the distinct art style pioneered by the Japanese yet takes advantage of a different cultural setting? Well then I have good news for you! With “Everlasting Summer” you shall no longer be forcibly confined to the same banal dialogue consisting mostly of an endless stream of chans, kuns and samas; instead immerse yourself in the glory of the Soviet Union with the Communist simulator 2014!
Okay, okay, I jest, but in all seriousness I’d kinda grown tired with the Japan-centric video game industry and the community. That’s a big reason why “Everlasting Summer,” comes as a breath of fresh air. The simple idea of a Young Pioneer camp is, at this point in time, a momento of a bygone era. Therefore, as an American bred on apple pie, baseball and the free market, the presentation, music and overall style of this game comes across as well…highly exotic. Not that I have any real love-lost with the former U.S.S.R. Yet, the uniforms, the Lenin references, the dialogue, district-centers, and the language all carry a flair and charm that’s just so unlike anything I grew up with. Did you know there was rock and roll in the Soviet Union? I certainly didn’t.
There’s a definite sense of nostalgia for the past here. Yet, at the same time it captures the attitudes of a generation transferring to a different way of life. I believe it was in Ulyanas story line that she suggests our main character that sees himself as a savior for the new generation, or something along those lines. Perhaps it says something about modern Russian society in the post-Soviet era. Most all of the endings have the main character exploring some exciting new career path, basically the visit to the past was the epiphany needed to discover what kind of person he wanted to be in the present.
Russia, it can be said, is a nation founded on the idea of active resistance. Moscow is a city on open plain, a city that is not easily defensible; and as we say in social studies, “geography determines destiny.” Much of Russian history involves expansion, extending the borders to defend the capital. This of course leads to all sorts of interesting stereotypes about the Russian people. The only that exists in the modern American historical school, specifically based off of the studies in the Wisconsin school is that the Russians are highly xenophobic, expand their borders when they’re insecure and that their leaders are generally wary of anything beyond their control. I really feel like this story is a product of that environment. Perhaps, unconsciously the writers have portrayed some aspects of the modern mentality of the Russian people. Unsure, a bit insecure, yet ready to find a new identity, somewhere and somehow.
The game isn’t perfect of course. The dialogue is at time superfluous or grammatically incorrect, but this is to be expected when you have a game in translation like this. There are some plot holes and to my knowledge at least one story is left open ended. At least one doesn’t make sense to me, but again, crazy capitalist ‘Murican here.
All in all this is a good VN. Yes the appeal for most will be the girls (yeah there is actually romance in this game, who woulda thunk it right?), especially with…ahem, well with a certain mod installed, but for those that look for something that goes beyond the superficial nature of most modern VN’s, this one is definitely worth your time.

I never thought a game, or rather a novel, could actually give me such strong emotional reactions over the stuff that happens in it. Everlasting Summer, on the other hand, fixed it.
Everlasting Summer tells a story about a male, Semyon, who gets on a bus and falls asleep. Rather than waking up in the bus or the bus station he wakes up in a pioneer camp not knowing how he got there and why he is there. From this point the story takes a huge leap to more and more absurd things to happen.
I'm not really a heavy reader. I don't read much. But for some reason Everlasting Summer kept me interested, kept me enetertained, kept me wanting to see more. There hasn't been a story that could make me lose my sleep just to see what's next. There hasn't been a story that actually made me focus on it without noticing my surroundings. There hasn't been a story that could actually get heavy emotions out of me.
The visuals, the writing, the soundtrack. Without these three key elements the story wouldn't have been so powerful. All these elements merged into a one epic and unforgettable experience I won't forget in a long time. Everything worked and behaved so well between each other creating even a physical feel at times. Now, I won't spoil anything about the game but there are parts, especially in your first playthrough, which will, or at least I hope, make you feel just like the characters in the story feel at the particular moment. It may be a little bit of cheating adding audio-visual elements in to a written story but because Everlasting Summer is such an absurd tale having you rush through different kinds of emotions you really need to have something to strenghten the emotions, in good and bad.
After completing the main storylines you will be left with unanswered questions (which I talked about behind those spoilers) but there are a couple of more secret storylines to enlighten you about the whole story. As I said, it's more than just a dating simulator. It much more deeper than that. And the (???) ending, Harem ending and a free DLC ending, which can be located from the Options menu scrolling down to the bottom in the Mod section called 'Pioneer's Day', will give you all the answers you need regarding to the story. I strongly recommend playing the DLC
getting all the storyline achievements.
And for all the perverts out there, yes, I tried out the Hentai-patch which, surprisingly, didn't ruin the game. It doesn't really add anything new to the table other than some boobs and a couple of sex scenes but if you truly are playing this game for the story you will not find the scenes sexually appealing in any way.
Everlasting Summer was one of the very few Visual Novels I've played but I still could say Everlasting Summer will end up as one of my favourite games of all time for years to come. Maybe even to the day I die.

is a well written Visual Novel. I find the multiple choice branches to several alternate story lines and interesting endings make it a cut above most VN's.  It has existentialist aspects, bringing to my mind Luigi Pirandello's {1934 Nobel Laureate} play “Six Characters in Search of an Author”. 
The “hidden” stories and screens in the alternate story lines add a lot to the enjoyment of the game and bring many hours of gaming enjoyment.  I have found the game to be quite interesting and, as a ”Free To Play”, it's hard to beat the price. 
:  As the protagonist, you are a 21st Century middle-age man drawn into a strangely inter-time-dimensional mystery.  You are a generally
{fill in a choice for field of endeavor; guitarist, scholar, programmer, on-line consultant, interpersonal relations, etc.}
.  After boarding a bus during a snowy Winter evening in a large Russian city, you fall asleep and awaken to find yourself in an abandoned bus at the gate to some sort of camp bearing the name
{Little Owl}.  And there's a slight catch; it's a bright Summer day and you still are wearing your winter attire and heavy boots!
There you are met by a pretty young girl in a Pioneer uniform who apparently thinks there's nothing strange about you?!  You learn that this is a late Soviet era Pioneer Camp for youths at some indeterminate remote location.  The beautiful young Camp Director has been expecting you and, due to lack of space, she's your roomie!  But that is not enough “strange”.  Before long you have a chance to look in a mirror and see a teenager staring back at you!!  And so it goes. 
WHAT is going on?  Can you figure out how this happened and get back to your “present”?  Do you even WANT to get back or should you try to stay here? 
:  During my first pass through this VN, I found the story to be interesting but could not figure out how to direct the story line to a desirable ending.  Result?  Protagonist
{my personal specialty}!  There are many {have not counted} choices which may provide potential turning points.  There are at least 5 potential love Interests and a missing fellow Pioneer {I almost typed “prisoner”}. 
In bewilderment, I turned to the Community Guides for, what else ... guidance.  While, with a large number of attempts, I might eventually have been able to figure them out, the guides saved what probably would have been months of effort.  The reward has been significantly differing sets of story lines as the {now} young man explores ways to get out and develops relationships with the girls of Sovyonok.  Will there be happy times or more failures and disappointments for the protagonist?
:  Usually when I play a game, the BGM is turned down to a bare minimum so it won't disturb me.  As I played Everlasting Summer, I kept finding myself turning the sound level up so I could enjoy the MUSIC.  The Music selections are very well done.  The BGM changes with the scenes and the characters.  It serves to enhance the mood appropriately as one progresses through this excellent VN.  I particularly liked the guitar riffs.  I had to turn BGM up to maximum for those.

I've been trying to write this review for two days now. I played through the game twice. The first time I played was about a year ago. I'm trying to find some quick snippet I can use to surmise the game but nothing comes forth. So I guess I'll provide some exposition.
Its a turn based, tile based, highly narratively driven up to 5 person party adventure. You make decisions as the leader of a large group of traveling humans and a race-- Well, more of a species called the Varl; which more or less are giants.
You are constantly having to manage resources. Battles earn you renown, which is used as a currency and XP. Renown can buy you items for your characters to wear to increase stats, supplies for travel as well as allow ready candidates to level up. Resources are needed on the road for your traveling companions to survive. As well as keep morale up. Poor morale can effect the abilities of your fighters in the from of losing willpower.
On the road you will run into events that you will have to make decisions about. Including dealing with everything from fights in the caravan to deciding to trust outsiders or not. I never quite pinned down if they are all scripted or procedurally generated. Some but not all seem very timely.
The battle system takes a little time to get used to as its slightly obtuse at first. Each characters health is their strength, what this means is as someone gets hurt they progressively become weaker and their strength is directly blocked by the enemies armor. So you must choose to either attack their health or armor. There are some other variables such as willpower, which allow you to move farther or do extra damage in one turn. Killing enemies earn you a notch on the horn which equates to an extra willpower lying in wait when needed. Some other stats that effect the two main ones are exertion and armor break. Exertion limits how much willpower one can use even if they have more. Armor break allows one to do more damage to armor regardless of other variables. There are of course classes for all the characters which have specific abilities such and Tempest, a sort of whirlwind attack and others like Forge ahead that allow you to choose someone to move up in the turn order. If a character falls in battle they will become injured and need to rest, usually for multiple days. The character can still be used in other battles while injured at the cost of lowered stats typically.
The game does have multiple endings. I am interested to see what happens in the sequel regarding them. I will also say the game does sort of end abruptly. It does come to a climax but to be honest, a lot it seems a bit unresolved.
The game is also, from what I can tell, hand drawn. Characters have very fluid animations when attacking and the overall aesthetic is very pleasing.

I so want to enjoy this game more than I actually do. The combat system is fun, sensible, and deep; the artwork is beyond beautiful; the music is fantastic; and the story is enthralling.
But there's just way too damn much railroading. I don't mean in terms of not having much choice as to where you're going (that part's fine with me). I mean in terms of what happens to people.
The bottom line is that characters don't live or die based on the foreseeable outcomes of your choices. They die based on what whoever wrote the story thought should happen. "If you do X, this person will die five hours later in your game. Period. No, you will not see it coming. No, you will not get to react to it or have any
sort of impact on what happens; you will get a bunch of text that tells you what I have decided will happen." You're left completely powerless and turned into a passive observer.
The loss of control kills the story; it completely ruins your immersion in this rich, deep world, and slams you back on the tracks. Whenever someone's died, I've felt cheated in a way no other game has made me feel. My reaction hasn't been "well, I was hoping for a better outcome than that, but fair's fair. I took some risks, and I can see how that would make sense." Nope. The overwhelming feeling I'm left with is "How the heck was I supposed to know that was going to happen?" I feel like I have to constantly second-guess the game by trying to figure out how the various choices are trying to screw me over, instead of getting into the mindset of the characters and thinking "what makes sense here?"
This is the second time I've tried to play this game through, and I'm genuinely sad that I suspect it'll be the last. With such a linear storyline, it's only got so many playthroughs in it. Which is a shame, because apart from that it really is a terrific game. If you don't think that'll bother you as much as it does me, give it a go.

Writing this review, as I JUST beat the end boss, at an ending character level of 43. Grim Dawn is a very good game in the ARPG genre. I do say though, do not compare it to others in the genre, such as Torchlight II. Instead, play it as well as other games, as this one offers a lot of different features.
The environment is dark, to say the very least. The landscapes and different areas are very different from eachother, making gameplay more interesting. As far as the world, my only complaint is that some of the dungeons are massive, taking  quite a while to clear. Also, I am glad that towards the end of the game, things got a little more liner, just as the massive dungeons were starting to get a tad bit annoying.
One of the key aspects that interested me in this game, is the dual class system, which allows you to pick two classes, one at your first level up, and the second at level 10, to use at the same time. This offers an extremely large amount of customization.
As far as gear and weapons, it's as good as it gets really. Upon reaching level 50, you are able to access legendary items, which are very powerful.
The sound is pretty good, and the soundtrack fits the game very well, mainly composed of a deep and droning distorted guitar.
Though, I do wish I could have had the option to pay a set amount of iron bits (the game's currency) to swap out one of my character's classes. This means you have to KNOW what you want in a character. You are able to buy back skill points, which is good, and saved me as soon as I realized that the "putting skills in class" bit meant putting skills into mastery, and not just the skill tree.
Overall, it is a great game with a large amount of replayability. Not sure if I will do the next difficulty just yet, but I am sure I will in the future.
EDIT: About a year later, I am like a third of they way though on a new character, going everywhere and doing everything I can, IE exploring the entire map, doing all the quests, ect. This game is pretty big, and has a massive map. And with this, I can say that the area surrounding Homestead, being a huge desert / dry farmland area, is very repetitive. Same brown backgrounds for a fair chunk of the game.
I have also purchased the crucible DLC, which holds up well. I say this because the overall gameplay and killing things is very solid. It is a bit grindy though, especially in single player, as you can only get so far without buying beacons, which require points to be grinded. Though, the loot is usually pretty good.

I wasn't holding out much hope for Undead Blackout, but I can say in all honesty that it managed to underwhelm me even beyond those minimal expectations.
Graphically, the game is very dark. It's nearly impossible to see anything, which tells me that the "gimmick" for this game is nothing more than a poorly done game of, "Hide & Seek." While I will admit that it was a bit creepy the first time I enountered a group of zombies standing with their backs to me, that only works once. It ceases to be interesting when it's overdone.
The game starts you off with a limited amount of health and stamina, but neither are enough to accomplish anything.  Your flashlight illuminates a very small area, though you do have the ability to turn 360 degrees to light up your surroundings. The problem is that zombies will often pop up behind you when you're trying to open doors or look inside of a cell to determine if it's worth entering. This concept is also overdone, as there are numerous cells, doors, and rooms, with a huge amount of empty, wasted space. I played for an hour, yet I didn't see anything of value, nothing that would remain with me after the game.
Keys, weapons, ammo, and health packs are few and very far between. This game attempts to create random gameplay and thereby add replay value by these items popping up, or all too often not popping up, in various areas. The floorplan seems to stay the same, and I learned very quickly which handful of areas to check for items, so for me, there is no replay value.
Movement and combat are very inconsistent. At times, I would find that sprinting didn't work, even with plenty of stamina available. I also found that the distance for combat isn't definite or consistent. Sometimes I'd have to be right up on a zombie to do any damage, while at other times, I could stand an entire square away and land a good hit. That kind of inconsistency makes it nearly impossible to safeguard the limited health that's provided for the character.
Overall, I didn't see anything that would make me want to play again, and I have no desire to finish the game at this point. When you can't measure, predict, or repeat gameplay activities consistently, all you're left with is frustration and disgust. You'll absolutely want to pass on Undead Blackout if consistency matters to you as a gamer.
*Please note that I did receive a key for this game in exchange for my honest review.

A diffrent animal indeed when it comes to the standard CRPG.
Divinity adds alot of diffrent effects to the mix of the isometric rpg style, while re-invigorating other older parts that some games have dropped over the years.
These new additions dont always work out in the end, but the result is a much more charming, engaging play then I have had in quite a few years.
-The Good
Solid graphics and sound, with good voice acting and music for the enviorments. (nothing stellar, just well done)
Common sense item crafting. Use every item for exactly whats it for, with a large variety of ingriediants, spells, powers and other effects.
No hand holding or shiney bright pathway trails or fully updated maps showing you where all your quest objects are. Great investigation and exploration immersion.
Tried and true combat style typical of other great CRPGs like Baldurs gate. With a new varity of tacticts introduced through enviorment manipulation, object movement and Turn Based style fighting using "action points" rather then a pause button to stop combat real time system but without the over used "grid" system.
Excellent role playing content for both single and co-op games. Interact with everyone, including party members. Build reputation, and even argue "rock, paper, scissors" style with team mates and npcs to win conversations. (this is a big one for me, so many "RPGs" these days arnt even on the map with role playing.)
-The Bad
Looting and combat can be unrewarding most of the time, with a greater amount of the lootable objects and enviorments typicaly being empty (much like Skyrim) and post battle rewards usually being standard or repetitive items.
I have found stealing and cleaning out the town to be far far more lucrative then dungeon crawling.
Many weapons and armor items found are almost always "Unidentified" meaning you have to spend more time and precious gold just to use them. Half the time to find out they are too high a level for you to use currently.
The envirorment effects are actually the only way to win at most battles, as opposed to being an added stratigic effect. This can get a little cliche after awhile when you find yourself always on the look out for barrels of oil, water or ooze as an indicator a fight is coming.
Many vendors in the finished game do not have a gold stash for you to sell items too, meaning extra time spent hunting for places that will buy your unwanted items.
The absence of a "detect trap skill" (so far in my game anyways), means trap finding is based on perseption and will be invisible if the attribute isnt high enough, and most traps will party wipe you on normal to hard difficulty resulting in a trial an error form of exploration that becomes old and annoying.
The "rock paper scissors" conversation role play gets frustrating with AI npcs as they almost always seem to outwit you simply by choosing the winning choice 4 out of 5 times.
Theres alot of walking around. ALOT. In open world rpgs like skyrim this isnt an issue normaly but with an iso-rpg, it can sometimes develope into a, click on the map and walk away and get a drink for a few minutes after the 100th time.
-Over All
To be honest I really enjoy this game. Because of that the things I dont enjoy about it become really annoying. It could just be me personaly, but I remeber games like this (baldurs gate, Icewindale, Neverwinter) being very generous with things like looting and combat rewards. Because it was hard, the game gave you something for your effort.
Divinity tends to nickle and dime you in the way that MMO's often do, with paying for equipment repaire, identifying almost every decent item you find, and being very scant on the amount of things you find from spending a whole hour going through a dungoen or building looking through all the containers and chests. Gold is often in very short supply unless you are thieving your way through town and then re-selling what you steal.
For me the real annoyance came from the enviorment effects being less of a stratigic option from time to time, and more of a forced victory condition. Had the game used this a bit more sparingly, and allowed you to develope ways to use it for certain situations or to disregard it all together, it would be fine. Yet because its such an essential victory device, the game makes you feel like its more of how you blow up barrels and freeze puddles to win rather then how well built, strong and equiped your characters are.
All things considered though this game is a gem to the tired and thirsy rpg gamer who is worn raw from the mountains of linear, hand holding, diversity lacking games out there that seem to suck up all the press and attention. A real triumph in getting back to the roots of a true role playing style game with enough extra spice and little details to keep it from being just a repeat of past glories.

When Dying Light first came out I kind of dismissed it and after picking it up in the winter sale I have no idea why I pushed it aside so easily. I've been playing through it with a friend and we both agree it's a great game.

Yes there are a few fetch quests but generally the manner in which each quest is set out is different from the last so questing really doesn't feel repetitive.
The NPCs are all pretty good characters with decent voice acting and the open world is great. I love how different the environment is between the Slums and Oldtown and the slight alteration in playstyle required as a result. I enjoy how new enemy types appear as the story develops and how the night time is actually scary. There are plenty of interesting locations dotted about in the world as well and each little discovery is always great. Exploration is often rewarded with an interesting weapon or mod blue print. The weapon crafting is intuitive and interesting and the gore system is wonderful.

After playing Quite a few visual novels, I stumbled across this one, hearing about it as 'the Russian Katawa Shoujo', since the idea also came from forums like ♥♥♥♥♥... except this time it was a Russian forum. This is the first review I have ever done, so bear with me.
The first thing I noticed while opening the game, was how well set out it was: the menu was intriguing and was easy to follow, while still being artistic and not sticking to normal "here are blocks that say start game and load, save etc."
Upon starting a new game, I saw the artwork was quite well-done. The backgrounds were vivid, yet dark, as this was the feel it was trying to give off.
Compared to many of the other Visual novels I have played, such as CLANNAD (and pretty much every other Visual novel by KEY) and Katawa Shoujo, The writing was... more Philosophical, more focused on him and what he was thinking. It was almost like listening to a non-maniacal monologue of the protagonist from Cross Channel, with much discussion on the meaning of existence, etc. Not that it bothered me, since it gives you an idea what kind of person the protagonist is.
While I said the art was good, I did notice what many reviewers before me did: the sprites of the characters and the backgrounds clashed. the sprites were cartoonish, while the backgrounds were very realistic, like in Katawa Shoujo. However, at least in Katawa Shoujo said clashing was not easy to notice, here it was. I got used to it, eventually, and it was never really a problem after playing the visual novel for a few hours.
The next thing I would mention is the characters in the game. They seem underdeveloped, but I can see how it might be hard to fit in that much development of character in such a short time, and at least it wasn't to the point where you asked 'who is she again?'. Many of the epilogues don't really require the protagonist to know them all that well, but I won't spoil that for you.
The music. Was. AWESOME. I mean, it was like a micture of rock and metal in certain parts, while some of it was quiet and reflective piano parts. They never jarred the mood of the scenes, which is strange, because when I first heard the music, I just couldn't believe THAT was the kind of soundtrack they would choose for ANY visual novel. Those crazy Russians!
The plot? Well, it is hard to talk about that in too much detail without spoiling it, but if you have ever played or looked up the plot of Cross Channel... it had that kind of weirdness to it. Not exactly the same plot, but the presentation had similaries - shrouded in mystery and never really mattering until you stumble upon it. To make sure you get the most out of the plot, I would suggest doing the "Seymon" route AFTER all the other main routes, because it leads well into the last, and utterly confusing and heartwrenching, final route.
And finally, I guess I could say what I think about the Visual novel as a whole. Honestly, it isn't the best one in the world. THere are spelling mistakes every once and a while (but I kinda let that slide, given it was originally in Russian), the characters aren't as developed as they could be, and the plot.... well, actually, the plot is what saves it (and the awesome music, of course). After completing the final route, I had the same empty feeling inside me as finishing any Nakige genre Visual novel: I reflected upon my life, thought how the story of this Pioneer camp and the (un)fortunate protagonist has impacted me as a whole. How has it impacted me? I still don't know, but I can feel it. Not to mention how much you wish Seymon found happiness, no matter who he ended up with.
If I had to mark this out of 10, I would say Everlasting Summer is an 8. It is definitely worth a read, and definitely has much to offer in the way of mind-screw and the heartnwrenching emptiness it leaves you with - just what people look for in this genre of Visual novels.
EDIT: I would like to add that there is actually some replay value to this game. after completing all routes, I thought it would be a good idea to replay the game, to make sure I didn't miss anything. Since I knew the twists and main overarching plot, foreshadowing to said twists stood out more, where before it just seemed to be Seymon's sayings were just how he described his situations. They turn out to be more than that...

PROS
[Combat & Gameplay]
- By far the best combat system in any MMO, hands down
- Very interesting skill points system, focusing on killing enemies instead of lvling up
- Amazing graphics, realistic, original
- Excellent world design. All the areas aren't just tiny ''hunting grounds''
- Very generous towards you. Constantly gives you  inventory expansions, gear, and other things you find useful in your journey, making you feel like the Pay2Win claim is quite a bit undermined.
- Classes are variable and changes at lvl 56 with the awakening.
- Armor rental. For the first time ever, i find a game where i actually have great use of renting armor. It's more or less free as well, as you get back the 'contribution points' you spent on renting the armor when returning it. This system is great and beginners like myself should take great advantage of it.
- Extremely complex 'society mechanics' within the game in comparison to other games
- Intriguing storyline. Would recommend skipping everything as we all probably do, but focus on the cutscenes and the shadowy companion. Watching him grow and transform is really exciting, and it makes you want to keep going just to see how far does this little guy really go
[Community & Social aspect]
- Great community in terms of chatting, lots of fun topics and trash talk, discussions, help, and other
- The Marketplace is complex at first, but it's very easy to list your own items and quickly gain currency to buy yourself new equipment
- Items in Markeplace are relatively cheap for starters, while the really good items have their strong values for the hardcore people
- There is enough guilds recruiting the new players and try to bring them in and help them out
[Misc]
- Either the third or fourth most popular MMO out there right now, WoW being first with FFXIV following just after, and then comes either this game or Runescape. Should tell you why so many people play it
- Incredible detail to character customization
- The 'Esc' menu, although can be hard to navigate, has about everything you could need if you can't find something otherwise
CONS
[Combat & Gameplay]
- Combat system is basically Mortal Kombat. Lots of complex combos and patterns to remember. Luckily, you have a hotbar. I recommend learning the basic abilities while putting the more complex-performed abilities on the hotbar, as well as utilities like the horse flute if you've got an explorer's package and health potions.
- Combat is a cakewalk up untill 30, then monsters get progressively tankier up untill 40, where they start to get slightly more difficult. Up at 50 you're likely to die quite a few times if you're not paying attention to your health. Monsters get much tankier and do harsh damage. This is not really a con, but this curve is rather quick and can take you by surprise.
- Game is pretty lonely. Even if you bring a friend with you, it doesn't appear to be much connection in terms of doing activities together. It's focused on yourself and your journey is going the much like a single-player experience, but the world is still filled with life. Guilds and PvP, as well as wars is where the game shines and brings you out of the lonely wandering.
- Guiding system is sometimes missleading and in some cases bugs out.
- Server lag spikes can happen at peak times. In personal experience it's been minor and not a significant issue
- Lots of trees and graphics popping in. Very noticable unless you play on ultra high, which rarely a standard gaming rig can handle
- As any MMO, classes tend to be unbalanced in PvP and 1v1's are rarely a fair matchup.
- Easy to exhaust and burn yourself out. Take a break every now and then
-The complex society mechanics can sometimes feel inefficient, such as your horse is in the stable in the town you left it at, 4000 metres away, or your good weapon you couldn't equip at the time is a 15-minute walk away because you had put it in the storage in some city you probably can't even remember
- Game can be quite daunting. The world is as huge as the elder scrolls universe and it's easy to get side-tracked and get lost
[Community & Social aspect]
- In the European region, there is a lot of non-english speaking people in the global chats. Primarily Germans, Dutch, and Polish, as well as French
- Cost energy points to talk in Roleplay/Server/World chat. This makes sense, avoiding global channels from being spammed, but it can be frustrating because there's lots of great memes and conversations you might want to take part in, but you have to make the decision between chilling over there or saving your energy for lifeskills or conversing with NPCs
- Turn off system notifications or get spammed every 0.5 seconds in the cat with ''X has gotten Y!'' Honestly i have no idea why this is on by default.
- No 1-on-1 trading, most probably due to an attempt to stop global chats from spamming ''WTB/WTS'', although it still happens
- There's something about a trading fee percentage unless you get a Value Pack.
[Misc]
- While the game is generous and gives you lots of stuff through your journey, one thing it gives you early on is a 7-day Value Pack. It's great, really, but the problem is that this is a marketing strategy in order to get you used to having the benefits of the pack straight off the bat, so once it actually depletes you feel like you're playing at a 'disadvantage' when in reality you're playing vanilla. It's an attempt at making you want to subscribe for the value pack. If you can see past this, then it is only more power to you because you get a 7-day Value Pack free! Additionally, it also gives you an idea of what the Value Pack offers.
- Very large file. Somewhere around 49GB, which might be problematic for some
- Gender locked classes. I absolutely hate this. Feels like you're playing as somebody. Somebody not being yourself. It makes it hard for me to get immersed in the world if it becomes more of a movie, because the character i play is not even the same gender so how would i personalize it to my liking to get myself in to the world? I forgot to mention that some classes have a male/female equivalent, such as the Kunoichi being a female version of the Ninja- However Kunoichi still differentiates at lvl 56 with the awakening, getting a chakram instead of a katan and turns more AoE-based and ranged. While most clases have a gender equivalent, they still do differ just a tad bit.
- You really, really do need pets and potentially weight efficiency. People saying you can buy pearls off the market or pets are kind of - kind of not wrong, because the problem isn't that you won't be able to afford it, the problem is that everyone has the money for it, meaning as soon as it shows up on the market, it's gone in an instant, making it very hard to actually buy cash shop items for ingame currency
-Random banter-
I can't talk about lifeskills as i haven't spent enough time on it. All i can say is, the amount of hours-vs-price you'll be paying is highly likely to be worth it. Game is flawed and can feel like it's not a full experience just because of how ridiculously huge it is and all the activities to do- Feels like you're basically never going to finish, as well as the cash shop makes you feel like you miss out and waste time because you're not paying to have efficiency.
Overall this game is surely not like any MMO i've played. It might look generic at first with a desert type theme or a forest theme, but if you pay attention, it really is much more original and not just ''Ugh great, it's that forest area like in all other MMOs''. I usually hate forests in MMOs, they tend to be the most generic and standard template out there, but it really, really feels original here. I can't stress that enough. There is a ton of beautiful areas you can just sit down and breathe in for a bit.

Robot Roller-Derby Disco Dodgeball may seem like a shovelware experience from the outside, but when you put yourself on the droid’s wheel, you’ll find a high-octane and competitive twitch-based shooter that’s guaranteed to shake the most hardcore of gamers. While there are problems in the experience, they’re ones you can expect from a low-budget game. Like Supersonic Acrobatic Rocket-Powered Battle-Cars before Rocket League, I believe Disco Dodgeball is one of those fantastic ideas that just needs a little more polish.
Anyone who enjoys first person shooters should honestly consider. Sadly, there’s not a huge fan base with this game, but the ones that are there are friendly and supportive, and there’s a nice catalogue of guides to help you learn the ropes. It’s non-stop frantic fun that gets more rewarding as you become a stronger droid, and nothing tops the excitement of catching a dodgeball mid-air and taking out an opponent with that same ball. While it may not be ready for primetime, this feel like an exceptional pre-cursor to what could be the next major E-Sport.

The third game in the Grisaia trilogy that concludes the story of Kazami Yuuji and the five girls from Mihama Aademy: Yumiko, Amane, Michiru, Makina, and Sachi. Will Eden be able to live up to the high standards set by the first two games, Fruit and Labyrinth? It obviously depends upon personal tastes, but I would have to say... yes.
Eden picks up immediately after the end of Labyrinth's main storyline, "The Cocoon of Caprice" with its own main storyline, "The Seed of Blanc Aile". Obviously you should not even go near this if you haven't finished the first two games unless you want to be confused and/or massively spoiled. What non-spoilery stuff I can say about Eden's main storyline is that the stakes have been raised considerably. For some, who were in this for the sometimes silly, sometimes serious school drama that Fruit was, Eden might not be what they initially signed on for. But having built up to this dramatic climax over the course of the previous two games... I think it works out well. It certainly concludes everything decisively and in a satisfying way, which is really all you can ask for.
Despite the much more action-oriented story, the silly that can be found throughout the Grisaia series is still very much present in Eden as well. All the guns, explosions, and battles don't change the fact that amidst all of that are characters like Michiru, Sachi, or the "new" character Thanatos - all of whom provide plenty of comedic moments. The cast we have come to know over the past games are all present and remain as enjoyable and interesting as ever. Their interactions and development are what make Eden, and the Grisaia series in general, the adventure that it is.
Oddly, once you have finished the tense drama that is Eden's main storyline "The Seed of Blanc Aile", you actually are not quite done with the game. There is also a "Prologue" storyline told from Yumiko's perspective that tells the story of how the five girls of Mihama Academy met and interacted prior to Yuuji transferring into the school (aka, the first game). After the high-stakes of the main story, this prologue is a return to the sort of story that we started the trilogy with: quirky shenanigans with a small but memorable cast of characters. I had heard that there was also a storyline that took place after the end of Eden's main story, but apparently that either was not true or it got cut from this Steam release. Oh well.
Anyway, you shouldn't even play this game unless you have played the first two games in the Grisaia trilogy already. And if you have... chances are you already know whether or not you would want to play Eden as well.
TL;DR... this whole trilogy is nommers. One of the best VN's I have played in quite a while. :3

Dying Light represents a much improved sophomore outing from Techland. Disappointed as I was with the original Dead Island, I did not buy Riptide and I was even turned off of Dying Light initially. Oddly enough, It did actually have a pre-release demo, though it committed the cardinal sin of being of timed duration. Also unfortunately, it prominently displays the game's weakest element- low-level melee combat, before you acquire the various showy moves and weapons that don't amount to more then an actual broken goddamn table leg. 
Combat continues to be a bit of a chore even into the late game, unless you decide to use a gun. There is a particular type of large, muscular zombie called a Demolisher that duffs you over with similar ease to Dead Island's Thug zombies, and its no less irritating each time it happens. Attempting to melee them is suicidal at best, but you could instead just throw a sickle at their face and they go down like any other zombie. Really, there's no balance to be had. Avoiding the zombies is actually more entertaining then fighting them off: with investment in skills, you can learn to ramp up and over a zombie's head, crash through them like a rampaging football player, and execute a flying double kick to their faces. 
Do not play Dying Light alone, at least initially. The early game hell is strong and without a better equipped player backing you up, the experience is much like Dead Island: boring, cheap, and uncompromising. It is a cooperative game and should be played as such, the more the merrier. It actually suffers in one respect as compared to Dead Island, which had four different playable characters with varying abilities, wherein this game everyone plays the same guy, Kyle Crane. Admittedly his skill tree is excellent and you can obtain all abilities available, but he is otherwise generic fuzz-faced white male protagonist #87, and a bit whiny, besides. Roger Craig's Smith work as Chris Redfield is enjoyable primarily because Resident Evil is ♥♥♥♥ing ridiculous and it fits. But Dying Light is ostensibly a serious game, and he comes off as rather forced and unbelievable when Crane is trying to be emotional. The game's writing over all is very weak, offering little narrative payoff and constant depressing disappointment at every turn- as per standard for the zombie survival genre. Crane is a freelance operative employed by the Global Relief Effort, or GRE, to enter the maybe-Turkish city of Harran, which of course overrun by a zombie plague. Your target, an insane, narcissistic, wannabe-social Darwinist ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ by the name of Rais, is in possession of a document of immense value. You insert yourself with a local population of survivors in the hopes of finding Rais and this document, but things go pear-shaped pretty fast as you are in the city mere seconds before you get bit, and the game is pretty much one predtictably horrific ♥♥♥♥♥orm after another.
Most people who play this probably wouldn't give a ♥♥♥♥, but if a game has a plot, I follow that plot. Where Dying Light shines, however, is the much advertised parkour elements. Moving through the urban sprawl of Harran is simple, smooth and enjoyable, unlike, say, Brink. You eventually earn a grappling hook that can be used to pull you directly to ledges and other surfaces, physics be damned, though there is a persistent issue with being able to grapple onto ledges you can't actually grab afterwards, sending you plummeting helplessly to the uncaring ground below. I think I might actually have died more often from falling damage then from any enemies, in spite of a tuck-and-roll maneuver you can use to avoid damage from a long, but non-fatal fall. Too bad most of my falls were longer.
Game flow is open ended, with a generous helping of boxes to open, side quests, challenges, and small dungeons in the form of quarantine zones scattered about the game's two major zones, the slums and old town, with the latter having much taller buildings and things like tall streetlamps and telephone wires to let you flex your parkour skills. The challenges are predictably annoying, proving themselves once more the zit on the face of sandbox action games, with extremely tight time limits and paltry rewards of experience points. There are occasional new blueprints to be had for the game's tastefully simple crafting system from them though, which involves strapping things like nails, electrical wiring and lighters to anything from a fence board to a machete to a medieval warhammer, to make them deadlier. You can make firecrackers, shuriken, medkits, grenades and bunch of other things, besides.
Overall, the game is substantially less dense then Dead Island, but is largely better for it. It plays better and runs better, too. I passed the game up on release a year ago, and picked up the game for $20 at the suggestion of a friend and I was not disappointed, though I can say with certainty that Techland has a long way to go yet. I expect bigger things from them in the future.
Good night, and good luck.

Entirely stylish and charming, Child of Light is an unexpected favorite.
---
To be honest, Child of Light is a game that was not at all what I was expecting. At first glance, I thought it was a labyrinth-styled action RPG. However, It's actually a linear turn-based RPG. Regardless, the game is entirely compelling, and I was hooked on the gameplay throughout, as the exploration and RPG mechanics work well together. I haven't been as invested in an RPG universe since the classic Final Fantasy games.
The art style is fantastic, like a living painting, and the backgrounds give each environment an incredible feeling of depth. The world of Lemuria is alive and is a joy to experience. Surprisingly, you are given a method of fast traveling very early on in the game, though I didn't feel that it took away from my want to explore the land. Furthermore, this soundtrack is amazing - probably my pick for best of 2014. I actually sought out these songs after I was done playing the game, and continue to listen to albums by the artist, Coeur de Pirate. This music is incredibly touching, with strings that swell and fade wonderfully. It just helps that much more to create a truly rainy day game.
The turn-based combat does contain some real-time mechanics in regards to the Firefly sidekick, which can either help swing the fight very much in your favor, or take things the other way entirely, depending on your resource management. Even on the "easy" setting, I felt as if the enemy encounters were tuned just right, so no particular fight was ever a cakewalk or a wall. The fact that you only have two characters taking actions versus three enemies means that micro-management skills will be needed. However, I felt this game's main strength was in the storytelling aspect anyways.
Though you are given a wide cast of characters, there is perhaps a bit of overkill in the buddy department, as I didn't even use most of the extra help. The sidekicks added flavor to the Wizard of Oz-esque storyline, but they weren't really needed and actually became a bit annoying with how often they needed attention in regards to how fast they would level up and need their skill trees adjusted. Honestly, every fight will result in a handful of characters earning enough experience to gain a level or two, during certain boss fights.
Another negative that needs to be addressed is in regards to the story itself - though it does a well enough job of creating a classical fairy tale vibe, there's also the sense that a big chunk of the game is missing somehow. There are only ten chapters of gameplay, and the first eight will fly by within a few hours. After that, the final two chapters take a good amount of time to tie up dangling threads. I'd be interested to see more of this universe, though.
In all, Child of Light is a game that should not be ignored. Though it has to be launched with the absolutely horrible Uplay program (which completely LOST my save file after a crash, five hours in), the game is worth a try. Highly recommended for RPG fans.

You see a dead body lying on the ground. It's a common sight. It's an aRPG, a game, after all. Just another body, another loot. You click on the body, and some items fall out: a rare amulet, some coins, and some trash common. You continue on your journey, rushing through the woods, eager to level up. A few paces later, a note lies on the ground. You pick it up and read it.
The note was written by someone, you don't know who, you only have a name. The author of the note tells you how he came to be in this place, how he was attacked, and he knew he was not going to survive. He asks why did things turn out this way. Why the world became such a hell hole. He hoped his family was okay.
The body you looted just a few seconds ago. What's his name, you wonder. Was he the one who wrote the note? You hover the cursor over the body to find out, but it only says dead body.
Slow down, adventurer. Take a good look around you. And remember those dead bodies, too, once had a name.

Often called Mirror's Edge with zombies and weapons, Dying Light is an enjoyable open world first person parkour zombie-fest.
The story sees you playing a secret agent of some generic organization that may not have everyone's best interestes in mind. You're parachuted into a city in qurantine due to a zombie outbreak and you are tasked with infiltrating various groups of survivors to find a man who stole information about your generic spy organization. There are no real choices for the player to make throughout the story, which can be frustrating when you see yourself doing something stupid just because your boss over the phone told you too. Overall it's a fairly dull plot, and my biggest complaint is the ending (which i will spoil and talk about at the very bottom of this review).
Gameplay is a nice mix of free running and combat. Parkour feels just like the aforementioned Mirror's Edge, although with less advance features, like wallrunning. Halfway through the game, you should unlock the grappling hook ability, which basically makes you spiderman.
Any game where you turn into spiderman halfway through is a good game.
Melee weapons in this game have improving stats as you progress in level. basically a hack n slash loot drop system, not unlike borderlands. Guns play an interesting role, as they are few and far between, and, in the early game, extremely powerful. The late game however, they will become almost useless due to the fact that they dont scale in power the way every other weapon does. Nor can you upgrade them with cool abilities like other weapons. An interesting choice on the Dev teams part, and the right one I think. Like Dead Rising and Mirror's Edge, guns aren't the central focus, but they can be a powerful trump card in a pinch.
The multiplayer features the player being able to be a super zombie and even has its own level progression. In a multiplayer game, one player will be the super zombie, tasked with defending egg caches from the players, and killing them 10 times. while 1-4 players will be their normal human characters and have to destroy all the eggs before they run out of lives. That's the only mode, and while it does sound a bit tacked on, it can be a lot of fun. Especially when you have a full game of 5 people. unfortunately, the servers are mostly empty at this point because the multiplayer isn't seperate from the single player. players seeking to be a super zombie will have to invade other people's single player games at night, and most people turn off that online feature. so basically, multiplayer's dead unless you've got 5 people you know.
And speaking of friends, you can have up to 3 people join your game and run around doing stuff with you. It's fun, you should do it.
Overall, the game features addicting gameplay, an average story (for a video game), and lots of developer support post launch in the form of free and paid DLC.
SPOILERS (not that anyone cares)
My biggest complaint about the story is the ending, or lack therefore. The final boss battle takes place in the form of a very dissappointiong quick time event. something this game has been trying to stay away from throughout. once you've defeated the end boss, your character tells his boss over the phone that he quits. and thats just about it...
you're still in the city and all your survivor friends are still not evacuated. If i didnt know any better I'd suspect the real ending is in the DLC you have to pay for... oh wait... who published this game? Warnor Bros?

I downloaded the visual novel Everlasting Summer, not expecting much on account of it being free. However it turned out to be an emotional and literary feast - to the extent that I have written my first review on Steam about it. (No spoilers.)
There is little ill I could write about it, in fact. I depended on the English translation - there are a few spelling and grammatical errors and perhaps some unusual word choices here and there, but that is about the only criticism I could make - a rather weak one at that. Generally it reads quite well and the humour is not lost.
I very much enjoyed the artwork - backgrounds and characters - as well as the soundtrack. Regarding the story itself, it has a quite interesting plot tree and, even though I did not grow up in the Eastern bloc, I can appreciate the setting of a Pioneers camp as it is somewhat reminiscent of Scouts. I found myself caring for the fates of both the protagonist and other characters - some parts affecting me quite deeply - which is a suitable indication of the writing quality. Moreover, as all good literary works should do, it imparts much truth by means of fiction, at times pondering darker aspects of human nature and metaphysical questions.
If this team ever comes out with other work, and it is available in English, I would happily purchase it. Excellent work folks! Спасибо.

This really was a epic finish for the series.  Out of every sandbox game out there, this is the only series that seemed more entertaining than a grindfest.
--------------WARNING----THIS REVIEW CONTAINS POTENTIAL SPOILERS---------------
For those of you who played the previous installments, this one does have more of the same.  What it lacks in crib customization and immersion in quasi-realistic ways, it more than makes up for in over-the-top superhero powers and numerous pop culture references that will make you laugh and take you back in time.
Many of the activities from the previous installments made it back (some with super powered twists).  The voice acting is top notch.  With the rush of sandbox games hitting the shelves, it's amazing that they took the time to flesh out the characters to the point that you seem like you know them as you would anyone else in your life.  Parts 1 and 2 from the series did it better IMO, but this one was no slouch.
With the super powers being introduced, you will get a few of those "HELL YEAH!" moments.  The same is true for many of the weapons in the game.  I can see why the devs thought this was going to be a series of DLCs, but I am glad it turned into a full blown game.  There were a few things that I feel could have been left out (FFS...CLUSTERS...you'll know when you get there).  While I do believe some of the immersion was lost by losing the ability to walk into many of the buildings like the previous ones, you may be too busy exploring the world with your powers and causing trouble to really care too much.
I HIGHLY RECOMMEND PLAYING THE PREVIOUS INSTALLMENTS FIRST!!  You may feel left behind in some of the story bits.  Going back without your super powers is one heck of an adjustment as well (and yep...I tried it).  You kind of get that GTA: Vice City nostalgia in parts of the game for those of us old enough to know the songs and stories/movies referenced in here.
Sorry for the somewhat sloppy review, but I had to get it out before having a total brain fart.  I may revisit this review to flesh it out a bit more at a later date (then again I can be a bit lazy....).

I have no earthly idea why Black Desert Online is so popular.  At first glance, it seems like it should have everything.  Dynamic combat, lots of classes, something other to do than murder...and yet everything seems to fall flat.  The combat feels like something out of Dynasty Warriors.  I click buttons and lots of generic fantasy baddies die, but I can't for the life of me tell the difference between all these skills I'm supposedly using.
As for the number of classes, BDO artificially doubles the number of classes by having different classes for each gender, except for some archtypes that are only available to one gender.  Want to play a magical giant sword wielding badass but don't want to feel like a creep because you're a guy and would rather play a male character?  TOO BAD!
As for the non-murder bits...I can't see the point.
Finally, it's worth noting that the graphics are absolute trash.  On a fairly high end system (i7, gtx980), any object that's not right in your face gets garbage low rez textures, and once you get close enough you get about 5 seconds of pop-in while the high rez textures load.  I'm sure there's a way to fix this, but I spent 30 minutes and gave up.

Waking up on an old suitcase with nothing but her raincoat, her lighter, and a vision of a mysterious lady, the little girl named Six begins her journey to escape the strange and terrifying underwater locale known as The Maw. So begins Little Nightmares, a frightfully fun game that I can't help but recommend.
Little Nightmares kept me good and terrified each and every night I played it. The Maw is a wonderful world to explore, and guiding Six through its vast innards is incredibly enchanting, especially thanks to how gorgeous the whole game looks. The residents of this bizarre world are all uniquely grotesque and jarring, and their undaunting persistance in chasing you down will keep you on edge through every new area.
My only major complaint would have to be the game's length; I felt it ended a bit too soon, and was dissapointed I didn't get to see more wonderfully weird glimpses of The Maw. Hopefully, Tarsier Studios will give us more DLC - and perhaps even a sequel? - to tide over my craving for more.
All in all, if you're looking for a short but sweet and spectacular new horror game, then take a dive into Little Nightmares. I'm certain you won't regret it.

Finally, I got to conclude the trilogy that is the main stories of the Grisaia series. And boy, was it a ride.
To understand the series, you have to, obviously, start at the beginning; the Fruit of Grisaia (FoG) and take it from there. Yes, the characters are tropés at first (and stay as such, largely, through all three games), but as soon as you get under the skin of each of the main five girls, you quickly realise that the character writing (as in how the characters are "created") is at a really high level of quality. So high that you start to feel WITH the characters, you groan at Michiru, you sigh with Yumiko or you look at Sachi's twisted principes from the perspective of the potential victims. Even though Yuuji is the protagonist in FoG, you don't really get that much under HIS skin, it is very heavily hinted at that his story, before coming to Mihama Academy, is cause for interest. The classic "harem"-tropé where you don't really know a whole lot about the main character (the "you" in the narrative) is thus in place.
However, Yuuji remains largely untouched in FoG. FoG also provided ten possible endings, which until Labyrinth of Grisaia (LoG) were impossible tell what was cannon and what wasn't. LoG picks off at a slightly odd point; where NONE of the endings are cannon, but all of them (the "good endings" for each girl) have mounts of truth to them. LoG focuses on Yuuji's story, and provides the insight into his mind and sight, also because, as we follow his story, so do the girls he live with at Mihama Academy. LoG also gives a very detailed look into the life of Asako; the first person other than his sister, that Yuuji loves (or even likes), which was very heavily mentioned in FoG in pretty much every single flashback from Yuuji's perspective, so it's really nice to get that information. LoG also provides five AFTER stories, which does the same as the "main" story of LoG; takes of from a point where none of the FoG endings where truth, but still had grains of cannon lore. These stories tell, what I guess, WOULD have been cannon, had Yuuji actually chosen anyone in FoG (you "choose" for him, but as of LoG, it's clear that it is not a choice he'd make on his own). LoG also provides a large amount of small extra stories, typically funny skits and shorts that may/may not have been intended as part of the story, but found unfit when it was put together. Kind of like the bloopers to a Jackie Chan movie. LoG's main story ended abruptly on a cliffhanger, so it was natural for me, that when the final main story branch, Eden of Grisaia (EoG), was published, I was quick to get it.
EoG provides a closure, and it does so with gusto and bravour. Even though shorter than both FoG and LoG (main story), it is the one with most action, often leaving you at the edge of your seat, picking many of the problems from LoG up and dealing with them. However, it also gives Yuuji much more feeling as this gives something that surprises even our all's male tsundere agent. As LoG's main story did not have choices, and FoG gave me roughly 30 HOURS of reading before the first choice, I was geniuely surprised when EoG threw not one but TWO choices in my face. It's an amazing conclusion to this massive triology, that I ended up spending +100 hours in. +100 hours VERY well spent, I might add. EoG also added a prequel; how DID the girls at Mihama Academy meet, what was the school like before Yuuji's arrival in FoG? An amazing little story that fills surprisingly many holes.
If I were to pin the stories, FoG, LoG and EoG up against each other, which I find kind of silly as they really are one long story altogether, I would say that.
Fruit of Grisaia: 9.5/10
Labyrinth of Grisaia: 7/10
Eden of Grisaia: 9/10
My reasoning for this score is that Fruit of Grisaia had so much more "meat" to it's story, it tooks it's time describing details in environments, in characters, in the mood. Especially in Labyrinth, the story felt a bit rushed at times. The fact that it also "denies" the endings of FoG also is a bit of a bitter pill to swallow (though I'll admit it works much better for triology as a whole). Eden of Grisaia is very close to reaching Fruit of Grisaia's level, the action filled adventure is much more intense than Fruit of Grisaia is, and even though it keeps a steady pace in it's story-telling throughout it's entire story, it is still coming up a little short, simply due to it's length.
But I'd actually like for you to ignore the scores for each of them separately, and instead take the triology as a whole, thus I will score it as a whole story.
The Grisaia Series: 10/10
I've already explained pretty much my stance and how much I love this universe and in particular, the characters, so there really is no need for further explanations. If you are into VNs (as I am), The Grisaia Series is excellent in terms of art and Voice Acting, but especially the character writing and the overall writing is amazing. Even if you DON'T fancy VNs, I would still recommend this series to you; it IS a bit heavy to get started with, but pays off in the end.

Video review here:
LIMBO. A fun little puzzle platformer with a creepy vibe and an ambiguous story. So when I first heard about Little Nightmares, I was instantly excited. Little Nightmares is a fun little puzzle platformer with a creepy vibe and an ambiguous story, but in 2.5D and with an almost Tim Burton-esque claymation style. It’s delightfully twisted and nails that atmosphere, but it may show its influences a bit too proudly for its own good.
In this game you play as Six, a little girl who’s awoken by a dream of a masked lady aboard the world’s least fun Disney cruise. You follow her as she attempts to escape the ship and its diabolical inhabitants. Along the way, you’ll uncover some new mysteries of the ship and learn about some of its unsavory secrets.
Right off the bat I want to say how much I love the art style here. It’s dark, creepy, dirty, and just plain insane. The way the ship tilts back and forth throughout the whole game gives everything a sense of unease. The environment is really well done and adds to the vibe, but it’s the character models and animations that really shine here.
The long armed janitor makes for an imposing first villain as his reach always make you feel like you’re in danger even when getting away. The gluttonous chefs and patrons absolutely ooze disgust. And the way everything moves in jerky, twisted motions makes everything even better. I mean, the patrons could have just stood up and chased Six, but the developers were like, “Nah, let’s have them crawl toward the little girl like demons!” Imagine the creepiest scenes from Spirited Away with the dial turned up to eleven.
And the visuals aren’t the end of the line. The audio is a treat as well. Creaking floorboards, cracking bones, and squishy grotesque sounds are all here, complimented by a great soundtrack that’s just as dark and foreboding as the graphics.
The only issue I have with this game is the story. While the visuals and locales give off a mysterious and desolate feeling, the story gives off a feeling of confusion. Now I know a lot of people will say that the story is intentionally ambiguous to add to the atmosphere and mystery, but overall I felt it was a bit weak. Being mysterious is one thing, but all of that ambiguity has to lead to something whether it’s clues to solve the puzzle or hints at what’s going on behind the scenes. Unfortunately I get the feeling that the developers just thought of a bunch of cool scenarios to include without giving much thought to how they all weave together.
While playing Little Nightmares, I got the feeling that the developers saw how LIMBO played and figured they could just make the same game. The controls are tight and simple, although having a button to grab onto ledges is weird, but the game never really takes that simplicity anywhere new. You can run, jump, use a lighter to see around you, and climb all over to traverse the environment and solve puzzles. This is used to great effect, but very rarely does it feel original.
Some puzzles have you pushing around boxes to reach a higher platform, which LIMBO did. Others involve using the environment to defeat a mini boss, which LIMBO did. Another has you sneaking around an environment trying not to get caught, which the same studio did in INSIDE. And the problem isn’t so much with the similar goals of each puzzle, but rather with the similar solutions.
The controls and strategies used to solve puzzles in this game aren’t exact copies of LIMBO and INSIDE, but they’re pretty damn close. They even have the awesomely brutal death animations when you screw up! Even then, this would all be okay if the game introduced anything new to the table, but in that area it’s sorely lacking. The puzzles are fun and the feeling of being chased is heart-pounding, but it never really breaks through to the next level or had anything that made me sit back and remark on how clever a certain puzzle was.
That’s not to say the game is without any originality. The swaying of the ship is an aesthetic element, but also a gameplay one as certain things swing or slide around with the ship, bringing some outside the box thinking to the table. And man, those chase sequences go from tense to absolutely terrifying with each escape bringing with it a sigh of relief and a sense f accomplishment.
Still, little things like jumps that should have been landed missing or surprise deaths by trial and error can be irritating. In a game like this, nearly every death should be avoidable with a bit of foresight due to the game design, but I can guarantee that anyone playing this game for the first time will, at some point, call ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t when they die to some arbitrary jump scare.
Lastly, and this is just a nitpick, but how do the blind janitor’s sense work? It’s implied that he smells your character, but only when you’re out in the open. And even if you say it’s because Six is easier to smell when she’s not under cover, it doesn’t explain how he smells a child in a room full of sleeping children! Again, it’s just a fun nitpick, but a small inconsistency that I noticed.
Little Nightmares isn’t a LIMBO clone. It’s not a carbon copy an it shouldn’t be accused of being anything more than a Playdead-inspired game. Even so, if you’re going to come out with a game this similar to the one that inspired you, you better bring something new to the table. Little Nightmares does this, but still fails to reach the highs of its predecessor. Still, it’s a valiant effort and an experience I’ll remember which is why Little Nightmares on the PC gets an 8 out of 10. It could be a little longer, maybe a bit deeper, but overall I enjoyed the game and look forward to what this studio brings us next.

You see a dead body lying on the ground. It's a common sight. It's an aRPG, a game, after all. Just another body, another loot. You click on the body, and some items fall out: a rare amulet, some coins, and some trash common. You continue on your journey, rushing through the woods, eager to level up. A few paces later, a note lies on the ground. You pick it up and read it.
The note was written by someone, you don't know who, you only have a name. The author of the note tells you how he came to be in this place, how he was attacked, and he knew he was not going to survive. He asks why did things turn out this way. Why the world became such a hell hole. He hoped his family was okay.
The body you looted just a few seconds ago. What's his name, you wonder. Was he the one who wrote the note? You hover the cursor over the body to find out, but it only says dead body.
Slow down, adventurer. Take a good look around you. And remember those dead bodies, too, once had a name.

Child of Light was just a joyful and charming little RPG the whole way through. Set in a fantastical (and at times very dark) world that you're given lots of free reign to explore. At the beginning, the game pulls a bait-and-switch and makes you think you're in for another one of the commonplace artsy-fartsy platformers in the vein of Limbo. Pushing boxes, solving simple environmental puzzles, etc. That ends about 30 minutes into the game when you're given something that really sets Child of Light apart: Flight. No restrictions, no time limit, you're just given the freedom to fly around the world, full stop. From then on out it becomes a party-based RPG where you gather more companions as the main quest progresses, and can use one at a time (with the ability to switch between them in combat).
Combat is a really interesting time-based affair. You can pause the combat at any time to queue up attacks, items, abilities, etc. Each action takes a set amount of time to execute and you can stop your opponents attacks if you manage to interrupt theirs while they're getting ready for them. This adds a really great layer of strategy and makes you switch up your attacks frequently for maximum effect. Sometimes it's better to hit the enemy with a tiny attack that stops them from unleashing a huge one than it is to unleash a huge one of your own. However, it goes both ways. Enemies can (and are smart enough to) interrupt and sabotage your strategy as well.
Each character (the main character and all of her companions) has a skill tree with three main branches to go down. Chances are that before the end of the game, you'll be specced into at least two of those branches. There is a new game+ mode, where you can run through the story again and continue to level up. As far as I'm concerned, new game+ should be an industry standard at this point, and it's welcome in any game.
The story just oozes charm. It gets shockingly dark at times, but still manages to be a fun little romp through a fun little world. Every character in the game speaks in constant rhyme, and they managed to pull that off without it ever getting annoying, which is a miracle. Don't want to get into spoiler territory so that's all I'll go into there. I finished in just under 9 hours for one playthrough, and that seems about average. Although it should be noted that there are tons of collectibles and some optional things to do that I skipped on because I was hooked on the main story.
The world is bright and colorful, and this is quite frankly the best looking game I've ever played. This game is 100% proof positive that an amazing art style is better than high-res textures any day of the week. This little, 2D, budget $15 downloadable title has managed to be far prettier than it has any business being.
Child of Light is just one of those games that makes you smile. It does exactly what it set out to do, and it does it well. Can't ask for any more than that. Everything else that's great about it is just an awesome bonus.

I have waited too long for the conclusion of this Trilogy, so I bought it instantly and completed it overnight. Here are some of my thoughts.
-STORY-
This is the last part of the Grisaia Trilogy, after The Fruit of Grisaia and The Labyrinth of Grisaia, continuing from the end of Cocoon of Caprice arc in Labyrinth. It is the ultimate showdown with all the foreshadowings tied together, as well as containing almost all of the characters appeared previously. Thus, you need to play the first two installments to be able to follow what happens.
The story has almost linear plot with only 2 choices, and the only choice that matters is the last one, which is near the end of the main story. After the main story ends, a special prologue can be unlocked.
The story is truly detailed and captivating. It seems that the story assumed all five main routes in The Fruit of Grisaia happened, which can make the beginning a bit confusing at first. However, the story soon picks up, focus on inner thoughts and emotional processes of the character at first, then filled with twists and actions later on. Characters' quirks and the Trilogy's atmosphere are kept consistent throughout the whole story. The ending, though not something mind-blowning, is satisfying enough.
-COMPARING TO ANIME-
If you have watched the anime, the story in the anime followed the VN quite closely. Of course, the VN is greatly more detailed and consistent. However, there is a huge twist at the end that the anime skipped and there is the special prologue.
-SPECIAL-
As I said, a special prologe will be unlocked after you reached main story's true end.The other end will not unlock it. The prologue was told in Yumiko's perspective, centered around life in Mihama before Yuuji arrived, and covered the arrival of each Mihama girl and until the day before Yuuji transfered in.
-LENGTH-
I am not a fast reader and I always listen to the completed voice before going ahead. Thus, it took me 21 hours in total, 15 hours for the main arc and 6 hours for the prologue. If you are a fast reader, it will probably take around 10 hours, 7-8 for the main arc and 3 for the prologue.
-AUDIO AND VISUAL-
Pretty much the same as the first two installments, you get what you see from the preview, still the same high standard.
-R-RATED STUFFS-
Similar to the previous two, R-rated contents are left out of Steam version. I wrote this right after Eden's Steam release so the R-rated version is not released yet, so take my opinion with a grain of salt. The story of Eden is extremely fast-paced compared to the other two games, so, unlike Labyrinth which has a lot of 18+ contents and was heavy affected by the missing 18+ stuffs, the missing R-rated contents in Eden are probably not a lot and definitely doesn't make the game feel unnatural.
-CONCLUSION-
A satisfying end to a splendid Trilogy. Overall, one of the best Visual Novels in the market. And unlike the Steam version of the second game (The Labyrinth of Grisaia), this one isn't affected too much by the missing R-rated stuffs. Thus, The Eden of Grisaia is definitely worth the money if you are not dead set on buying the R-rated version.
