I'd been playing it off and on for a while now, and figured that with the conclusion of the main story line, it would be appropriate to do a review.  For the short version, it's an excellent game with excellent mechanics.  The story line isn't new or ground breaking, but it's there, and it works.
Anyways, Dying Light is a first person melee/shooting/parkour zombie game.  And, well, frankly, it does all of those really well.  Damn well.  In fact, well enough that I'd put it on the same level as Destiny when it comes to gameplay, and I'm sure by now everyone is aware of how much I love Destiny's gun play.  Let's take melee first though.
I hate first person melee games.  They generally suck as.  All the games like Skyrim have horrible melee combat in my eyes.  Even the Witcher 3's melee was less than satisfying.  But Dying Light gets it right.  Melee feels damn good.  It works.  And most importantly, it's satisfying.  Swinging a weapon out in front of you feels good.  You might only connect with one zombie because you hit them at chest level, but you'll cleave through two heads if you get the angle just right.  And when you connect with a crit, time slows down just enough to give you time to relish in the powerful hit.  And hits feel powerful when you get them right.  Weapons have different feels to them, have different weights, swing differently, and if you are like me, you'll prefer some over others.
And getting melee combat was important, because especially at the beginning of the game, shooting is rare.  And when you finally get a good gun, you still have to ration out your ammo.  So melee combat is your bread and butter.
Simply put: every game that does first person melee combat needs to review what Dying Light did and copy it.  Dying Light's melee combat is on the same level as Destiny's gun play.
Shooting is good as well.  If you hit someone in the head, their head explodes.  It feels good.  Weapons have weight, and they work.  There aren't as many options with guns as with melee weapons, but it works well enough.  You aren't using guns as frequently, but when you have to, it holds its own.  What's nice is that you can tell that they didn't just add guns, they at least made sure guns had weight as well.  That they felt like guns, they worked liked guns should, and made gun play satisfying, despite it being use less frequently.
Now, to parkour.  They got parkour right, they got parkour so damn right.  The game's parkour gameplay is, well, a lot of fun.  First, it just works.
First, the controls are solid.  You jump, and if you want to grab onto something, just keep pressing the space bar.  No convoluted extra button press.  Furthermore, it's fairly liberal about you being able to reach place.  There were many jumps I'm sure were a bit short but the game goes for enjoyment rather than realism.  Realism takes a nose dive when you get the grappling hook later in the game, but frankly, I didn't care.  The grappling hook is so much fun, so each to use, and well, just damn awesome.  It's cooldown means you can't just use it everywhere all the time, but it's a fair cooldown, and gives you freedom and mobility.
Simply put, moving around the city is so much fun.  You never feel restricted or confined.  You feel free.  Just running freely around the city is a lot of fun, even without an objective.  And it helps that the game rewards exploration, with lots of stuff to do.  Side quests aren't a burden, they are additional challenges to overcome, and all fit within the general narrative.  It gets a bit strained later in the story when urgency strikes, but with the game just being fun to play, I wasn't really bothered by it.
Beyond those mechanics, there is a progression system, basic crafting, and a inventory system that doesn't suck.  Weapons and big pieces use up space, but ingredients don't.  This means picking up herbs or string or cloth doesn't eat up space.  To often games become inventory management simulators, and that generally sucks (Looking at you Fallout 4).  This game allows movement and momentum, action and danger to lead the way.  The focus is clearly on having fun and not messing around in your inventory all the time.
It's a fun game, and even with the conclusion of the main story line, the game still lets you go back in and continue questing and doing things, improving your character, which I plan to do.  There are multiplayer and coop elements I didn't explore.
It was a surprise to me that the game was as good as it was.  I left out numerous little things ("talking zombies" for example) that really make the game better, but those are better left for you to discover yourself.
I plan on buying the season pass which gets you the next DLC which doubles the size of the original game.  I know I won't be disappointed.

HOWEEVERRRR: Do one simple thing, right click your game link in the library and reaking BACK UP THE FILE. I do this every/other play session or once every 20 levels or so and after major bosses. And honestly i agree with all the people on forums saying that as much as they were bummed out, this is not a game that is dreadful to replay a second time.
Absolutely STUNNING. Everything from the music, voice acting (narraitor), THE ARTWORK, storyline and plot, game systems and combat/skill tree/equipment systems. Pretty much full marks on everything possible, so i might as well state some things that weren't 110% perfect.
The cast of characters were sometimes a little silly. I like the rhyming scheme, very poetic as the tale and art is similar to a child's fairytale or something you would see in the opening of Shrek. Auroras walking speed before she can get wings and 'dash" is just terrible, i convinced myself that jumping sped things up slightly, however, this is only for first half hour till you get wings.
Some characters weren't as usefull as others. Or should i say...you can only have two party members out at a time (which is enough by the way) but the downside is i only really flipped around between Aurora, Finn and Dude with mask and crazy name. I would have loved to use robert and Gen more, perhaps when I repeat in Newgame+ mode. having more players (even at the cost of more monsters on the field) would have made this a bit better.
Something both amazing and not too bad was the puzzles. They're THE SAME THING, use lights, hit things. IT IS NOT REPETITIVE. Same concept-never boring (somehow, quite brilliant to keep the similar type of puzzle interesting).
Another "controversial" thing is the items. YOU GET SO MANY POTIONS, and rarely need to use them, It's cool that you won't be like "crap....someone died and i have only 2 revives and i'm not to the boss yet" but maybe this isn't a problem in the hard difficulty.
I will admit some characters have some not great stuff, Heal spells (at least in first play easy mode) are used maybe a half dozen times max. The dude with mask and crazy name has a "quake" tree that seems pretty impossible to pull off as it takes two turns to use and he is pretty slow to begin with. (still my favorite character though)
Back to the good stuff. Love the combat system. It's like FF but with more strategy because you can slow your enemies down a little bit with the mouse control npc (using it's energy) and time things so that you interrupt them and control combat in more than a "smash this guy first" style. Also, Bosses aren't immune to status effects. Maybe people like challeges but in other rpg's  in this style when you fight a boss and have an enfeeble/debuff character, they kinda become useless. Some debuffs are pretty powerfull especially with Gen but that's at the cost of expensive mp and casting time.
I like to say the artwork is as if Edgar Allen Poe was a painter. Enough said. Holy crap yes.
Anyways, most people have gotten bored of my mologue here. Easily the best $5 (black friday) i've ever spent on anything ever except maybe a gallon or two of gas when it woulda cost me a tow truck home but that's besides the point. And remember to back up your save file. It CAN crash but you don't HAVE to be miserable, i found out the hard way that steam has it as simple as a "right click on game>backup".

I really like Child of Light because of the way battles work. Though you can use a controller I do not recommend it, as you need to control a little light that can be used to heal your characters or slow down enemies which is easier to do with a mouse. What makes battles additionally interesting is that everyone's actions are based on a time bar for which many abilities affect, as well as hitting enemies at a specific time to interrupt them and bump them back on the time bar. It's also interesting because although you acquire many characters you may have only two out at a time--however any of them can switch out as an action and the new replacement may act at that time, opening up for more strategies.
There is an accessories system called oculi--gems you can combine to make bigger versions and newer types that affect three different slots differently. This reminds of the gem system from Diablo II. This on top of the battle system makes for a large amount of ways you can do things, which is great for an RPG.
Overall, Child of Light is really fun because it is an RPG that rolls a little differently--to the point that gameplay is interesting while keeping it simple.

At the time, HL2 was very innovative and a big leap forward in graphics.
Using physics as the basis for puzzles and platforming was new and exciting! There are games releasing even this year that still don't have advanced physics as ingraved so deeply into the gameplay. We take a lot of these things for granted today, because every game has some of those mechanics. I truly believe there is a little bit of Half-life in every fps that comes out now.
On top of that, the story was tight. The look of a post alien invasion Eastern Europe looked hauntingly believable. The art style drew upon classic sci-fi staples (Tripod Stalkers, Zombies, etc.) and made them each unique.
It was so immersive. All the cutscenes were from the first person perspective. Most single player fps games to date still can't match how easily it felt to be like Gordon Freeman.
Now it is old... But it remains a true masterpiece that set high standards for future games.

This really was a epic finish for the series.  Out of every sandbox game out there, this is the only series that seemed more entertaining than a grindfest.
--------------WARNING----THIS REVIEW CONTAINS POTENTIAL SPOILERS---------------
For those of you who played the previous installments, this one does have more of the same.  What it lacks in crib customization and immersion in quasi-realistic ways, it more than makes up for in over-the-top superhero powers and numerous pop culture references that will make you laugh and take you back in time.
Many of the activities from the previous installments made it back (some with super powered twists).  The voice acting is top notch.  With the rush of sandbox games hitting the shelves, it's amazing that they took the time to flesh out the characters to the point that you seem like you know them as you would anyone else in your life.  Parts 1 and 2 from the series did it better IMO, but this one was no slouch.
With the super powers being introduced, you will get a few of those "HELL YEAH!" moments.  The same is true for many of the weapons in the game.  I can see why the devs thought this was going to be a series of DLCs, but I am glad it turned into a full blown game.  There were a few things that I feel could have been left out (FFS...CLUSTERS...you'll know when you get there).  While I do believe some of the immersion was lost by losing the ability to walk into many of the buildings like the previous ones, you may be too busy exploring the world with your powers and causing trouble to really care too much.
I HIGHLY RECOMMEND PLAYING THE PREVIOUS INSTALLMENTS FIRST!!  You may feel left behind in some of the story bits.  Going back without your super powers is one heck of an adjustment as well (and yep...I tried it).  You kind of get that GTA: Vice City nostalgia in parts of the game for those of us old enough to know the songs and stories/movies referenced in here.
Sorry for the somewhat sloppy review, but I had to get it out before having a total brain fart.  I may revisit this review to flesh it out a bit more at a later date (then again I can be a bit lazy....).

This really is one of the best story based games I have played, rich in story, gut wrenching decisions, highly tactical gameplay and your decisions will haunt you long after you leave the game. The characters are interesting and you will feel a connection to them, the main characters are fully fleshed out, with interesting back stories, and their own morals and personality. Even the side characters you will meet, kill or join on your journey are unforgetable (an all too rare thing in games these days) they themselves are developed well through the game, and appearances aren't everything. I spent a week away from this game and I was still pondering on what has happened, will happen or might happen if I just had made a different decision. As you try to come to terms with the story unravelling around you, the game has breath taking landscapes and locations; you maybe fleeing an enemy warband, you might see them trailing you in the distance, or you notice a dialogue event, and what is related to it may be in the background. The game gets harder, more bizarre as you progress, more tense as you transition from a cheery patrol to ragged survivours seeking sanctuary. All in all one of my favorite games, cannot wait until TBS2.

Every one of my games so far have been very enjoyable. I don't know about other people, but I've encountered very few trollers in-game. All of my teams have been fairly helpful. So far I have not been put into a completely one-sided-beat-down match (after 13.2 hours of playing), and it can actually be pretty difficult to break through a tough defense or stand against a coordinated offense.
That said, teams must cooperate and build on each others' characters' strengths to pick and fill roles such as support, defense, tank, assassin, etc to complete the objectives as efficiently as possible. The game doesn't lag much at all for me (I believe they only have one American server atm, so that might be why people are complaining about lag). Some of the character models do look a little bit awkward but I think that it's excusable since they're trying for a zany/cartoony feel. From my experience thus far, the game is very balanced as well. There is no OP character/structure block. The only change that I feel needed is better mini-map readability/zoom.
I think that this game, as is, (as a game and not a piece of software or anything else, so this rating doesn't account for lag, dense individuals in the community, bugs, etc) well deserves a healthy 9.2/10
(P.S. idk what some of the other comments are saying when they mention P2Win, since only skins are available for purchase outside the base game. Also, the "original" price tag is $33 because it comes with Ace of Spades ($15), early access, and a skin pack (other skins can be EARNED in-game). This is not a game I recommend for the weak of heart (or the salty for that matter).

Back to my original statement; this game will do anything it can to screw you over. You WILL miss important shots, enemies WILL hit dangerous shots, the game WILL introduce enemies at horrible times, it WILL put your best units in the sickbed when you need them. This game loves to taste your salt, be it through tears or ragequits. But beating a mission without anyone dying after the game seemingly did everything in its power to kill them all is really satisfying.
I recommend starting on easy, even if you're familiar with turn-based strategy games. You don't want to be too horribly screwed by the enemies before you know anything about them.
-Good things- Unit classes which are all varied with different skills to bring, really fun to play around with some skill sets and combos. Winning a map can be very satisfying. Bit of base management which is good for relieving the stress combat brings. Solid replayability (coming partly from something I'll get to). You can customize your units' appearance.
-Bad things- The base game has a tendancy to break, at some points the game simply froze with nothing to do but close it and load a save (if available), I have not encountered this (to my memory) with the expansion. When you run out of money or other resources for the base building there's nothing active you can do, all you can do is wait for something to happen. Some enemies can ruin your day by just showing up on the map, being most of the later enemies (Floater being the first to come to mind), this can work to the game's advantage with replayability though: many times that I start a new game is because I miss the pre-Sectopod period.
I also recommend getting Enemy Within: the aliens it adds are a bit weak, but everything else it adds makes it worth every penny.

It's quite amazing how the Saints Row series began as an underwhelming Grand Theft Auto clone. In the course of its 3 sequels, the Third Street Saints have gotten crazier and definitely funnier.
Saints Row IV is as much a parody of action movies as it is of its own series. In the First game you lead the Saints to dominance over the city of Stilwater, in Saints Row 2, you topple the head of of the multinational Ultor corporation. In Saint's Row: The Third, the Saints have become pop-culture icons, and defeat an international crime syndicate and a brutal paramilitary organization.  Saint's Row IV continues the trend of upping the ante.
The game starts where the "good ending" of Saint's Row: The Third left off. Cyrus Temple is on the run, but you've saved Shaundi. The Protaganist, and the two top ranking Saints, Shaundi and Pierce Washington, have been recruited to hunt down the now mad Cyrus Temple, who, after the previous game has turned international terrorist, intent on launching a nuclear missile at Washington DC as payback for firing him.
After a short introductory level where the Protagonist channels his inner Michael Bay (complete with Aerosmith soundtrack) to save the White House, the game proper begins. The Saints used the goodwill and gratitude of the nation to take over the white house. As leader of the Saints, and savior of America, you are naturally the President/Gangsta-in-Chief.
Quickly, Aliens attack, abduct your homies (including Vice President Keith David, voiced by Keith David), and after a short battle with evil Emperor of the Zin Empire, Zinyak the player is deposited in a computer simulation of pleasantville. Taking a page out of the Matrix, you are saved by your tech-homie Kinzie Kensington, and from there you are placed in a more "realistic" simulation of the Steelport of Saints Row: The Third.
The majority of the game takes place in a nearly identical environment as its predecessor, however, since your character is basically Keanu Reeves, you are quickly given access to super powers, such as super-speed, super-jumping, super strength, energy blasts and the like. This is where the game succeeds, and unfortunately falls short.
With few exceptions, the world map is identical to the previous game's. In the preceding Saint's Row games, you could either jog everywhere, or use a multitude of vehicles to get from point A to B. The vehicle customization, much like the character customization, was incredibly well-done. Everything could be customized. However, the early introduction of the super-speed power turns you into the Flash. Cars become useless. And you move so fast, and are so agile, that the map feels much, much smaller. Combine this with your ability to jump or run up skyscrapers, and the effect is compounded.
The strength with this game lies in its combat, where interesting guns like the inflato-ray, the bounce gun, the Rectifier and Dubstep Gun can be used in any number of combinations with your powers. Not only that, but the guns themselves can be "reskinned". If you think regular pistols are boring, swap it out for a Star Trek phaser, or Han Solo's trusty blaster. Upgrades for things like special effects, damage, fire rate, projectile speed can be purchased at the local gun shops.
The writing for this game is brilliant. It's heavy on pop-culture references, but the references are well executed, and well implemented. Elements from the Ghost Busters, They Live, and a plethora of old games (Double Dragon, anyone?) will be sure to make you crack a smile.
The DLC missions "Enter the Dominatrix" and "How the Saints Saved Christmas" are a definite must as well.
However, this game does have a bad case of DLC-itis. There are twenty-somehting costume packs  each for a dollar or two, and no compendium option as of yet. However, the two mission packs and the powers pack are worth the purchase.
Another plus is the voice acting. Featuring the voice talents of Keith David, Daniel Dae Kim, Terry Crews, Nolan North, Neil Patrick Harris, and quite a few others, this game is very well voiced. One thing that character customizers will love is that you can even customize your character's voice/personality. There are three male and female voices, plus a "Nolan North" Voice, which is of course, voiced by Nolan North (quote, "THAT'S HOW NOLAN ROLLS!")
The game has an awesome soundtrack, and gameplay lasts about 25-30 hours, not including multiplayer. There's plenty to do in virtual steelport, and a ranking system akin to Star Wars: Rogue Squadron that will give you perfectionists something to do for a while.
8/10 would buy again.

Child of Light is a tribute to JRPG which has a beautiful presentation, lovely soundtrack but lacks a soul in many other aspects. I really wanted to like this game but the more I played, the more I discovered that something(s) were missing and was left hugely disappointed by the end of the game.
It's not a bad RPG but it's not really a good JRPG as it was initially marketed as, since it has way too many issues that were already sorted out by the greats of the past such as not memorable combat, too situational to near useless classes among others.
The art style is top notch. It's a water coloured story book aesthetic and it's extremely beautiful in motion.
The soundtrack is much like the art style is top notch and sets the mood with its melancholic undertones.
The story, though simple, short and digestible is cheerful and gloomy at times.
The boss battles test how well you understand the combat. If you don't understand it fully you're going to have a rough time.
The game requires Uplay, so if you hate it, you'll still hate it. It causes the game to become unresponsive at times and can lead to crashes.
While the rhyme is charming at first it does get tiresome midway through the game. It's not horrible but it'll grind your gears if you grow tired of it so much so you'd wish they'd stop.
The battle system is just a shallow copy of the Grandia's and can be easily 'cheesed' with little thought for tactics and tends to feel rather repetitive fairly quickly.
Combat as a whole is a mixed bag. It's extremely fun in the early stages of the game but gets extremely repetitive in the latter. Early on, I found myself willing to get into fights as they're fun and challenging however, later on I found myself avoiding it as nothing really changed. Your skills for the most part become and stay stagnant pretty quickly. That's a major red flag for anyone who considers combat to be the main aspect of a JRPG and expects some sort of skill variations.
This is the first time I've ever experienced this in a JRPG but RNG is on the enemy's side. I say this as they get their 'chance' skills in regularity while you seldom get yours. This in turn adds fuel to the fire of combat lacking or feeling repetitive.
The characters 'classes' are too situational or down right useless. When you play a JRPG you expect all classes to be useful in their own way, some may do more damage than others, some may use magic better than other but above all, all are useful and you're willing to use them whenever. However in Child of Light, you'll use a select set of classes no matter what as the most useful characters are Aurora (Light), Rubella (Damage dealer, health mage), Finn (Elemental mage), Trista (Damage dealer, protection mage) everyone else is just not good. Why would I use a 'chance' base class when RNG is on the enemy's side as mentioned above.
The platforming controls aren't that great, running feels clunky and flying feels extremely stiff. It would've been wonderful if players were given the option of controlling Aurora with the dpad rather than the stick as using the stick just feels off for a 2d game with side-scrolling aspects.
Gems/Oculi are not a fully thought out idea, it's like a shallow copy of the Materia system from FF7 just not as good. 3 gems can be socketed into a character for attack, defence and talisman granting some actual or chance bonuses however they don't feel like a necessity or rarely pay off. 3 gems can be combined into one large gem which offers greater benefit but you often don't have enough gems to make large ones as they're hardly given out until near the end of the game.
You Can't reorganise your party line-up outside of combat. If you made a mistake and one of your favoured members dies and had to be swapped out there's no way to re-swap until your next battle...this is downright stupid.
Aurora's model doesn't fit the game at all. While it looks good it just doesn't mesh well with the visuals as it looks too 3d almost as if it was made to stand out from the others and looks odd.
Gems/Oculi and other consumables are rarely given throughout the entirety of the game and only generously dished out towards the end. This problem is very apparent as all consumables are found scattered throughout the world but the rate at which you'll find them are extremely low whereas toward the end you're given large clusters in short periods of time. It almost feels rushed in this aspect as with the oculi distribution.
The party line-up is too limiting, I often found myself repeating the same steps when it came to battles ad-infinitum. 1. Open up with Rubella, followed by Aurora, then stagger with Rubella and finish with Aurora, rinse and repeat or 2. Open up with Rubella, followed by Aurora, then stagger with Rubella, Aurora dies/get criticalled, switch out Rubella for Tristan, Revive or heal Aurora, switch back to Rubella, rinse and repeat. It almost feels like the game is begging for a 3 man line-up to spice things up and reduce the tedium of the constant switcheroo game. As it stands, it's tedious to switch out members because they don't fit the situation.
Although the boss battles test your understanding of the battle system, the boss fights simply are not memorable especially the last boss. They're just tedious for some reason; maybe the lacking memorability is effected by the issues mentioned above i.e. Exploitable Battle System, Lacking Combat, Poor RNG, Situational Classes.
I really thought I would love this game but it feels somewhat soulless. Ubisoft positioned this game as a tribute to JRPG of old but for some reason it doesn't feel like a JRPG to me at all. The combat system is not memorable or engaging, the story while simple doesn't really hold up by the end. Don't get me wrong, it's not a bad game it's just not a good 'JRPG' as aspects which make a good JRPG are under developed or simply missing. Maybe next time...because, well it's Ubisoft, you know a sequel is coming.

Banner Saga
3 / 5
A fun turn based strategy combat game with elements of RPG and resource management that may have spread itself too thin. Once through the first play through though, you're mileage may vary.
The Banner Saga is a turn based strategy combat game that tells the story of a Viking-esque world during a time of climactic change. You play as two different groups leading a caravan of soldiers and townsfolk escaping from an ancient foe and trying to find safety. It is here where the resource management comes in as you need to buy supplies for the journey which slowly deplete depending on caravan size. You also have to watch out for morale as spending too many days on the road reduces morale and causes you to slowly lose both warriors and townsfolk. In general, this gameplay device is simple and requires little micromanagement, but does affect gameplay during big battles, which leads me to...
Combat. As mentioned, combat is centered around a turn based strategy system with each character fitting into a "class" with special abilities and methods of attacks. Spearman can attack on the diagonal, archers from afar, etc. Additional gameplay mechanic are introduced (for example, Giants take up more physical space and thus create lanes where smaller humans can attack / retreat, but the giants cannot) as the game progresses, but in general merely add nuance to the basics of this concept. The combat strategy is increased by introducing a health / damage & armor components. Basically, health and damage are the same number, so the more damage you take, the less damage you do. Additionally, armor mitigates damage and if your enemy has more armor than you have damage the chances of you missing altogether goes up tremendously. This effectively creates interesting gameplay choices where a balance between attacks and movements have fairly large impact in the course of battle. This combat is the core of the game and gladly is the most well rounded and satisfying of the game components.
As for "big battles"...at various points in the game you are approached by large "armies" of enemies. Your ability at resource management determines how "even" the battles are (if you are good, you've built up large numbers of warriors, if not not) and thus permit different forms of battle strategy.  Are you pretty even in terms of strength with the enemy showing signs of fear. Make a heroic charge. Determined enemy and slightly outnumbered? Fight defensively. Overwhelming odds...try to flee. You take control of your characters and engage in the same micro level battles you always engage in, but your success (or failure) determines how many losses you take during the course of battle. In the end, its an interesting way of tying the resource management to combat, but really loses impact at lower difficulty settings and in general feels much like the resource management part of gameplay…something interesting and tied together with other elements well , but not a fully fleshed out mechanic .
The RPG elements come in a couple flavors. First is the character development via combat improvement. Getting kills eventually raises levels for each character which raises ability levels and releases skill points that can be used to increase armor break, health/damage, armor, willpower, etc. Each character has maxes set to each attribute based on their "class" so there are some inherent limitations which provide justification for specialization. One problem with this approach though is while level one characters are still effective in battle at later stages of the game, they do suffer from being under-powered on even the lower difficulties. Thus, it’s easy to fall into the old RPG problem of a core set of characters you're almost forced to use and a group you almost can't.
The other RPG element comes via story line. You can converse with characters and learn their stories / engage in some "Tell Tale Lite" conversation dialogues that impact the course of events. An interesting  addition to the game, but it’s not given enough detail to make the effort seem worthwhile, especially considering the individual stories of the characters aren't overly memorable and these interactions typically just means you lose a character from death / running away. In games which utilize this gameplay component in a more robust fashion, this creates meaningful impact to player choice and a sense of real loss when liked (and powerful) characters are lost. Here, the losses seem almost arbitrary and really only have impact if you just so happened to dump a lot of resources into leveling that particular character.
Storyline is mainly told through written dialogue which you read at the bottom of the screen. In general that works, but every so often a character actually speaks their lines, which is surprisingly jarring. I don't remember the specific instances having any special dramatic effect so if you do it occasionally, why not do it for the entire game? The graphics are similar in that regard in that they are perfectly acceptable to the storyline and world created. The predominance of the game is a 2D picture format with some comic book styled depth accents and I might even go so far as to say they created an art style fairly appropriate to the world. However, combat sequences take on a "Saturday Morning Cartoon" look that isn't unappealing, but does kind of clash with the "grim" nature of the story (end of world) and somehow loses some of the appeal found during the rest of the game.
In any case, I've run through quite a few shortcoming of this game, but I want to stress it really is fun for the 5-10 hours it'll take you to beat it. The question is will you want to go back and play this game again and again? I think the gameplay mechanics and difficulty control (going harder really does make the game more challenging) means there will be a subset of people who will enjoy this game many times over...I'm just only going to do so once.

I will spare you from the storyline. If you have any interest in this game whatsoever, you either already have a general idea of what the game is about, or you can look it up in less than five seconds.
So, a turn based JRPG which draws inspiration from many other video games all while maintaining a steady stream of jokes directed at other works of arts should be a fairly chaotic experience, right? Well, it is. And honestly, this game isn't for anyone. If you don't have any interest in either anime or manga, you might as well turn back now, as you would probably cringe at everything the characters say and do.
That's not to say the game is bad though. While the story is slightly lackluster, it's mainly about the hilarious dialogue. If you don't like characters breaking the fourth wall, trolling around or poking fun at each other, the door is still there for you to leave through. For me, who is studying Japanese, this was both fun and educational at the same time.
The combat is where the game shines though, and it reminded me strongly of games such as Dragon Quest. With three characters on the field at the same, with three more as support, one of the more intriguing parts is where you can decide your own battle strategy. Do you want to go full offense? Go with a group of melee fighters. Do you want to play cautiously? Go with long range fighters. And if you want more support, there is always the option for that too. Whatever your playstyle is, with near 20 different playable characters, there is always one that will fit you.
And there will be at least one character you will like more than the others. Oh, and while I'm at it, play it in Japanese, some scenes aren't translated fully to English so you will be left with a couple of quiet scenes.
In the end, the interactions are hilarious, the combat is addicting, and if you are a collector there are a lot of things for you to find and craft. Don't see this as a hardcore game, come here if you're looking for some relaxing light and easy fun. I can't wait for Re;Birth2!

I finished the main campaign in Dying Light yesterday.  I'd been playing it off and on for a while now, and figured that with the conclusion of the main story line, it would be appropriate to do a review.  For the short version, it's an excellent game with excellent mechanics.  The story line isn't new or ground breaking, but it's there, and it works.
Anyways, Dying Light is a first person melee/shooting/parkour zombie game.  And, well, frankly, it does all of those really well.  Damn well.  In fact, well enough that I'd put it on the same level as Destiny when it comes to gameplay, and I'm sure by now everyone is aware of how much I love Destiny's gun play.  Let's take melee first though.
I hate first person melee games.  They generally suck as.  All the games like Skyrim have horrible melee combat in my eyes.  Even the Witcher 3's melee was less than satisfying.  But Dying Light gets it right.  Melee feels damn good.  It works.  And most importantly, it's satisfying.  Swinging a weapon out in front of you feels good.  You might only connect with one zombie because you hit them at chest level, but you'll cleave through two heads if you get the angle just right.  And when you connect with a crit, time slows down just enough to give you time to relish in the powerful hit.  And hits feel powerful when you get them right.  Weapons have different feels to them, have different weights, swing differently, and if you are like me, you'll prefer some over others.
And getting melee combat was important, because especially at the beginning of the game, shooting is rare.  And when you finally get a good gun, you still have to ration out your ammo.  So melee combat is your bread and butter.
Simply put: every game that does first person melee combat needs to review what Dying Light did and copy it.  Dying Light's melee combat is on the same level as Destiny's gun play.
Shooting is good as well.  If you hit someone in the head, their head explodes.  It feels good.  Weapons have weight, and they work.  There aren't as many options with guns as with melee weapons, but it works well enough.  You aren't using guns as frequently, but when you have to, it holds its own.  What's nice is that you can tell that they didn't just add guns, they at least made sure guns had weight as well.  That they felt like guns, they worked liked guns should, and made gun play satisfying, despite it being use less frequently.
Now, to parkour.  They got parkour right, they got parkour so damn right.  The game's parkour gameplay is, well, a lot of fun.  First, it just works.
First, the controls are solid.  You jump, and if you want to grab onto something, just keep pressing the space bar.  No convoluted extra button press.  Furthermore, it's fairly liberal about you being able to reach place.  There were many jumps I'm sure were a bit short but the game goes for enjoyment rather than realism.  Realism takes a nose dive when you get the grappling hook later in the game, but frankly, I didn't care.  The grappling hook is so much fun, so each to use, and well, just damn awesome.  It's cooldown means you can't just use it everywhere all the time, but it's a fair cooldown, and gives you freedom and mobility.
Simply put, moving around the city is so much fun.  You never feel restricted or confined.  You feel free.  Just running freely around the city is a lot of fun, even without an objective.  And it helps that the game rewards exploration, with lots of stuff to do.  Side quests aren't a burden, they are additional challenges to overcome, and all fit within the general narrative.  It gets a bit strained later in the story when urgency strikes, but with the game just being fun to play, I wasn't really bothered by it.
Beyond those mechanics, there is a progression system, basic crafting, and a inventory system that doesn't suck.  Weapons and big pieces use up space, but ingredients don't.  This means picking up herbs or string or cloth doesn't eat up space.  To often games become inventory management simulators, and that generally sucks (Looking at you Fallout 4).  This game allows movement and momentum, action and danger to lead the way.  The focus is clearly on having fun and not messing around in your inventory all the time.
It's a fun game, and even with the conclusion of the main story line, the game still lets you go back in and continue questing and doing things, improving your character, which I plan to do.  There are multiplayer and coop elements I didn't explore.
It was a surprise to me that the game was as good as it was.  I left out numerous little things ("talking zombies" for example) that really make the game better, but those are better left for you to discover yourself.
I plan on buying the season pass which gets you the next DLC which doubles the size of the original game.  I know I won't be disappointed.

Child of Light is a tribute to JRPG which has a beautiful presentation, lovely soundtrack but lacks a soul in many other aspects. I really wanted to like this game but the more I played, the more I discovered that something(s) were missing and was left hugely disappointed by the end of the game.
It's not a bad RPG but it's not really a good JRPG as it was initially marketed as, since it has way too many issues that were already sorted out by the greats of the past such as not memorable combat, too situational to near useless classes among others.
The art style is top notch. It's a water coloured story book aesthetic and it's extremely beautiful in motion.
The soundtrack is much like the art style is top notch and sets the mood with its melancholic undertones.
The story, though simple, short and digestible is cheerful and gloomy at times.
The boss battles test how well you understand the combat. If you don't understand it fully you're going to have a rough time.
The game requires Uplay, so if you hate it, you'll still hate it. It causes the game to become unresponsive at times and can lead to crashes.
While the rhyme is charming at first it does get tiresome midway through the game. It's not horrible but it'll grind your gears if you grow tired of it so much so you'd wish they'd stop.
The battle system is just a shallow copy of the Grandia's and can be easily 'cheesed' with little thought for tactics and tends to feel rather repetitive fairly quickly.
Combat as a whole is a mixed bag. It's extremely fun in the early stages of the game but gets extremely repetitive in the latter. Early on, I found myself willing to get into fights as they're fun and challenging however, later on I found myself avoiding it as nothing really changed. Your skills for the most part become and stay stagnant pretty quickly. That's a major red flag for anyone who considers combat to be the main aspect of a JRPG and expects some sort of skill variations.
This is the first time I've ever experienced this in a JRPG but RNG is on the enemy's side. I say this as they get their 'chance' skills in regularity while you seldom get yours. This in turn adds fuel to the fire of combat lacking or feeling repetitive.
The characters 'classes' are too situational or down right useless. When you play a JRPG you expect all classes to be useful in their own way, some may do more damage than others, some may use magic better than other but above all, all are useful and you're willing to use them whenever. However in Child of Light, you'll use a select set of classes no matter what as the most useful characters are Aurora (Light), Rubella (Damage dealer, health mage), Finn (Elemental mage), Trista (Damage dealer, protection mage) everyone else is just not good. Why would I use a 'chance' base class when RNG is on the enemy's side as mentioned above.
The platforming controls aren't that great, running feels clunky and flying feels extremely stiff. It would've been wonderful if players were given the option of controlling Aurora with the dpad rather than the stick as using the stick just feels off for a 2d game with side-scrolling aspects.
Gems/Oculi are not a fully thought out idea, it's like a shallow copy of the Materia system from FF7 just not as good. 3 gems can be socketed into a character for attack, defence and talisman granting some actual or chance bonuses however they don't feel like a necessity or rarely pay off. 3 gems can be combined into one large gem which offers greater benefit but you often don't have enough gems to make large ones as they're hardly given out until near the end of the game.
You Can't reorganise your party line-up outside of combat. If you made a mistake and one of your favoured members dies and had to be swapped out there's no way to re-swap until your next battle...this is downright stupid.
Aurora's model doesn't fit the game at all. While it looks good it just doesn't mesh well with the visuals as it looks too 3d almost as if it was made to stand out from the others and looks odd.
Gems/Oculi and other consumables are rarely given throughout the entirety of the game and only generously dished out towards the end. This problem is very apparent as all consumables are found scattered throughout the world but the rate at which you'll find them are extremely low whereas toward the end you're given large clusters in short periods of time. It almost feels rushed in this aspect as with the oculi distribution.
The party line-up is too limiting, I often found myself repeating the same steps when it came to battles ad-infinitum. 1. Open up with Rubella, followed by Aurora, then stagger with Rubella and finish with Aurora, rinse and repeat or 2. Open up with Rubella, followed by Aurora, then stagger with Rubella, Aurora dies/get criticalled, switch out Rubella for Tristan, Revive or heal Aurora, switch back to Rubella, rinse and repeat. It almost feels like the game is begging for a 3 man line-up to spice things up and reduce the tedium of the constant switcheroo game. As it stands, it's tedious to switch out members because they don't fit the situation.
Although the boss battles test your understanding of the battle system, the boss fights simply are not memorable especially the last boss. They're just tedious for some reason; maybe the lacking memorability is effected by the issues mentioned above i.e. Exploitable Battle System, Lacking Combat, Poor RNG, Situational Classes.
I really thought I would love this game but it feels somewhat soulless. Ubisoft positioned this game as a tribute to JRPG of old but for some reason it doesn't feel like a JRPG to me at all. The combat system is not memorable or engaging, the story while simple doesn't really hold up by the end. Don't get me wrong, it's not a bad game it's just not a good 'JRPG' as aspects which make a good JRPG are under developed or simply missing. Maybe next time...because, well it's Ubisoft, you know a sequel is coming.
Recommended for those interested in a simple RPG.
Not recommended for JRPG fans looking for a fresh take.
PS: Steam please give us a neutral recommendation option.

Despite a premise that initially seems like a Russian spin on the least original AU-fanfic idea imaginable, Everlasting Summer delivers on interesting and complex characters and an interesting and complex meta-plot that unlocks after enough play-throughs.
There is a hentai patch available from the game's website. The art in the hentai patch is of lower quality than the art in the game in general, so I don't recommend it -- it's the equivalent of five or six frames of mediocre fanart.
My one problem with this game is the quality of the character art. It's definitely superior to the art in a lot of free-to-play or cheap VNs, and is at about the same level as some older professional VNs like Fate/Stay Night; however, it doesn't hold up to current standards.
While the setting is a soviet summer camp, no knowledge about soviet culture is strictly necessary.

Many NPCs unnecessarily have dialogue, especially market vendors, which began to infuriate me to the point that I wanted to throw my speakers at the person who bought me this game.
I found the gameplay progressed a little too slowly for my liking and although it was good in some aspects that there was limited handholding, I would have appreciated a little bit of direction in the beginning.
The turn-based combat was fun, albeit a little tough to get used to (but as I said I am new to this game style). I did find it annoying that the characters always took the most dangerous path during combat usually walking through fire or acid.
The Co-Op idea is great in theory, not so great in initial practice. I was under the impression it was a drop in/out Co-Op and this is definitely not the case. If you were not the initial host but want to play some more of the game, too bad you get to start all over again, or wait to play with your friend again. Also, if you want to have a specific main character you better get the host to create it how you want otherwise you are stuck with whatever they create. Trying to get a Co-Op game going took me and my playmate over an hour to sort out.
7.5/10 - The Co-Op initial setup soured me on this game so much that my care factor about the story is severely limited. I will keep on playing it, but would be more inclined to replay Diablo 3 over this at this stage.

The words "old school" get used alot these days...usually it just means half-finished, side-scrolling, pixelated crap that looks like it was designed for a Nintendo 64...But this game delivers on every level. Nothing too revolutionary, just good, solid gaming with modern graphics.
It took over 200 hours to finish and that felt like an acceptable length of time for this genre without too much grinding or boredom. The game maintained my interest for over 200 hours...and these days thats impresive. Most big publishing houses  these days semm to rush out big titles attached to short, crappy games to cynically cash in. Same goes for most early access I've seen so far...but these guys must love the genre and made sure they released a finished, polished product.
It has a few quirky missions (as these types of games are known for), and at first I felt ripped off by the fact that the camera only rotates through about 80 degrees! But the camera does zoom in deliciously close so you can see your characters in action in breath-taking clarity. All the graphics and effects are gorgeous to look at, and I soon got used to the limitations of the camera rotation.
If you like genuine "old school", turn-based, sword and sorcery, squad-based games that are re-imagined with modern graphics, and that utalises your pc's power behind the scenes with some pretty rock solid programming - then this is one for your library.

Block N Load is one of the best FPS games I have played, it is better than Paladins/TF2 and cannot be compared to the likes of CS:GO etc.
It has a wide variety of characters with fun abilities, but the main and most attractive aspect of this game is that you can transform the terrain. You can build bases, tunnel underground into the enemy base making sure not to be caught, try to find the most well hidden spots for placing spawn points in enemy bases - all to destroy the objective.
Since this game has so much more than just shooting, unlike most FPS, since there is so much to do within a game (most matches last 40 mins each), a strong teamwork is required. It's competitive.
It's ridiculous that this game does not have a greater playerbase. It does however have roughly 300 players in game these days so it won't be hard to make a match. It's a pity that this is not well-recognized already.

A beautiful tale in a watercolor land,
Written as though from a children author's hand.
Every line of dialogue you'll see will be written in verse,
Unwrapping the tale of a princess and a curse.
For the moon and the sun and the stars are all taken,
Aurora's quest is made clear, the sky she must awaken!
Cleverly written with characters as charming as can be,
If you like RPGs, then I'm sure you'll agree!
In all seriousness though, this game is a nice feel-good RPG, although one I felt to be relatively on the short side as far as RPGs go. The gameplay is turn-based with a gimmick in the form of a "speed" bar that will determine who attacks first, who manages to block or disable another, etc. Buffs and debuffs are available to speed you up, slow down enemies, block enemies from being capable of disarming you, etc. An interesting gimmick and well executed. One thing I found however was that there was a serious lack side quests, adding to the game's shortness (there's perhaps three "main" side quests I counted, all of which can be easily completed within less than ten minutes).
The draw here is definitely how unique it is from a visual and storytelling standpoint. As stated, every single line of dialogue rhymes which I have to commend the writers for. Graphics-wise, the game looks like a beautiful watercolor painting. That said, one criticism I personally have was that with the exception of Aurora and a handful of other characters, all animations looks to be done in flash with serious tweening abuse, which I felt somewhat cheapened the experience (though that's likely my inner art snob talking, so take that with however large a grain of salt you will). It does cause some dissonance beside the rendered model of Aurora as well which was initially difficult to see past. These are minor complaints however. This game is gorgeous, the characters are lively and likable, and the soundtrack is amazing. Definitely worth owning.
I do need to point out one final thing however, as this might be a deal-breaker for some. You WILL be forced to download Uplay. It doesn't matter if you launch the game through Steam, it will still automatically open Uplay. I've yet to encounter any problems other than being annoyed by the extra program running, however it might be worth your time to check out other reviews and the experiences other players have described before you make your final decision. There's been a lot of complaints about problems with save files or the game not launching. You have been warned.

If I had to review the game in one word, that word would be:  Meh.
Graphics:  Not the worst I've seen but not very good for 2014 either.  Zoom in even a little bit and you can easily see the pixels on most of the textures.
Sound:  Music is good and sound effects aren't bad.  Not much stands out though, just sort of... there.
Gameplay: Combat can be fun, but also frustrating.  Trying to click on the constantly moving enemies to attack them often leads to your characters deciding that you meant for them to run all the way around the enemy instead of attacking it... Usually running right though poison or fire in the process while wasting precious action points.
Gameplay outside of combat is horrible though.  Constantly waiting for your characters to run to the location you told them to and dealing with the terrible UI and inventory system is just a nightmare.  Not to mention the "rock, paper, scissors" mechanic for the "arguments" are the worst I have seen in any game, bar none.
Lastly, the whole "freedom" concept the game promotes is just flat out wrong.  It's no more open world than any other RPG because going outside of where you're supposed to be just results in you getting mauled by guys 5 levels higher than you.  The "no handholding' means that quests are designed exactly the same as in other games only less robust and without any useful objectives or waypoints to help you figure out what you're supposed to be doing.  It wouldn't be so bad if the parts the game expected you to figure out was more realistic, but just expecting you to find that one key under the cabinet that opens the locked house upon which you need to scan one particular shelf in order to find the appropriate diary to progress the story...  That's not challenging, it's pure luck and entirely frustrating.  Especially when the bad camera angles (and the stupid idea to restrict those angles) makes it hard to see what you're doing.
Story:  This... Is actually okay.  The writing is decent and the story seems interesting.  That being said, there is WAY too much text for saying what little actually matters.  It's like the writers got paid for how many words they used.
Overall the game is okay, but that's it.  It can be fun at times and for those who can see past the flaws (and there are a lot) it will probably be a blast.  However, I can't honestly recommend it as there are much better RPG's out there who are much more deserving of the attention that this game has gotten.  For me, the poor design decisions outweigh the good ones.

A beautiful tale in a watercolor land,
Written as though from a children author's hand.
Every line of dialogue you'll see will be written in verse,
Unwrapping the tale of a princess and a curse.
For the moon and the sun and the stars are all taken,
Aurora's quest is made clear, the sky she must awaken!
Cleverly written with characters as charming as can be,
If you like RPGs, then I'm sure you'll agree!
In all seriousness though, this game is a nice feel-good RPG, although one I felt to be relatively on the short side as far as RPGs go. The gameplay is turn-based with a gimmick in the form of a "speed" bar that will determine who attacks first, who manages to block or disable another, etc. Buffs and debuffs are available to speed you up, slow down enemies, block enemies from being capable of disarming you, etc. An interesting gimmick and well executed. One thing I found however was that there was a serious lack side quests, adding to the game's shortness (there's perhaps three "main" side quests I counted, all of which can be easily completed within less than ten minutes).
The draw here is definitely how unique it is from a visual and storytelling standpoint. As stated, every single line of dialogue rhymes which I have to commend the writers for. Graphics-wise, the game looks like a beautiful watercolor painting. That said, one criticism I personally have was that with the exception of Aurora and a handful of other characters, all animations looks to be done in flash with serious tweening abuse, which I felt somewhat cheapened the experience (though that's likely my inner art snob talking, so take that with however large a grain of salt you will). It does cause some dissonance beside the rendered model of Aurora as well which was initially difficult to see past. These are minor complaints however. This game is gorgeous, the characters are lively and likable, and the soundtrack is amazing. Definitely worth owning.
I do need to point out one final thing however, as this might be a deal-breaker for some. You WILL be forced to download Uplay. It doesn't matter if you launch the game through Steam, it will still automatically open Uplay. I've yet to encounter any problems other than being annoyed by the extra program running, however it might be worth your time to check out other reviews and the experiences other players have described before you make your final decision. There's been a lot of complaints about problems with save files or the game not launching. You have been warned.

This was a fun, short RPG.
The artwork is amazing!  I'll admit that I spent most of my time going "Ooooh!  Pretty colors!"  And the HAIR.  Something about the way it moves is hypnotizing.
The music is dark and mysterious, but after a while, you notice it's pretty much all a variation of the same tune.
The dialogue is a little off-putting; everything is written in poor verse.  To me, this detracted from any sort of important character development.
The fact that your cursor is actually a character that helps with puzzles and battles is pretty entertaining.
Fighting is very remnicint of early/middle final fantasy games.  Turns are active time, but pause as you select your action.  The main difference is that you can see single enemies (that represent the potential group you'll have to battle) stalking the map, and in most cases, you have the option of avoiding them.
Puzzles were a lot of fun at first, but seem really easy once you got the hang of them.
Overall, this isn't a game you play for plot or character development; it's more of a fun little romp in a fantasy world with VERY pretty art.  Worth your time, just don't expect what you would from a major RPG title.

I'll say this upfront: the English translation is horrendous. Spelling and grammatical errors aside, there are a lot of awkwardly worded phrases (i.e. "You cheated me!" should mean "You tricked me!"), incorrect gender pronoun uses, inconsistent phrasing (Haiyin's catch phrase is translated differently almost every time she says it), and mix ups between Hengyi/Fengyi/Fengxi's names. You will likely need to read sentences multiple times to infer the intended meaning. The overall quality is reminiscent of using a text hooker and dictionary software to auto translate your visual novel.
Now, if you can get overlook the flawed translation, the result is a wild roller coaster of emotions and plot twists and turns that will keep you hooked. You will constantly question the motives of everyone and everything that is happening around you, and just when you think you had things figured out, the game pulls a fast one on you and stabs you cruelly in the heart while opening another can of worms.
The visuals are beautiful and humorous where appropriate, and though a lot of the sound effects are unfitting or weirdly used, the music captures the mood well, and the voice actors do a fantastic job at conveying emotion, alleviating the awkwardness of the translation.
This visual novel is long...VERY long. Honestly, the developer could have shortened a few scenes and cut out some fluff. However, it is very thorough in making sure there are no plot holes or unanswered questions (assuming you see all the good endings), leaving a good feeling in your heart.

My first impressions on this game was thoughts of "This better not be a clone of Titan Quest". Don't get me wrong, TQ wasn't a bad game, but it suffers from unsatisfying loot, long levels of grinding, and although it boasts Mastery Trees and encourages Diversifying skills, it takes a massive investment into the mid game or late game to start being interesting as it's not worth it to spread your skill points but better to focus all points into a few abilites in the beginning parts of the game. I don't think it's good design to have to invest tens and tens of hours just to feel some levels of synergy off your branching skill trees.
So a few hours into game I discovered that it quickly took away my fears that it would play like TQ. Levels come and go rather quickly, which means you obtain points much quicker to allot into abilites. There is also an addition of an NPC that returns skill points for a price very early into the game. These two points combined makes it rather interesting and not as punishing to try out synergies or builds. Weapons also come and go and you're not restricted to what weapons you use. Although as you speciliaze into your skills and devotions your options will get more focused.
I'll give the pros and cons of the game here (Please keep in mind these are my own opinions and I may update them as I play the game more)
Overall, it's a fairly well made game, but it's missing out a lot of finesse. It's like a bowl of well made spaghetti, but they forgot the sauce. I really wish there was a in between option and not thumbs down option, because it definitely isn't a bad game. You will enjoy this game if you like theory crafting, and building your character into a Otherworldly Meatgrinder hellbent on churning the flesh of Aetherians, Chtonians, Humans, and Beasts alike. However, there's not much to sink your teeth into. If you don't mind that and can relax on the shallow waters, then you'd definitely enjoy this game. I was looking for more and I was disappointed is all. This game makes me appreciate the enemy designs and variations in Diablo II so much more.
Tl;dr, Not a bad game, if I could choose a neutral ground, I would. This game suffers from simplistic enemies, shallow quest and faction mechanics. It's strength lies in the character skill building and looting.

The enemies - and your allies, for that matter - would be unable to pass the lowest rungs of elementary school and are constantly blowing each other up with grenades. I'm actually writing this review in-game, and I just won a battle with the CIS on Naboo in Galactic Conquest mode by hijacking an AT-RT with an Engineering Droid's slicing ability and running to a command post with a large amount of Clone Troopers and simply walking around in the sea of enemies. It makes this whole game for me.

This is the first time I've played an RPG with multiple characters where the personality that I want them to have actaully adds to the game's mechanics.  This is more than just adding a skill point to charisma.  Through different dialogue that happens as you adventure, your characters are given the opportunity to discuss different situations they encounter.  Actually having a group with diverse opinions and views creates characters with diverse skills and attributes.  In some situations you're merely reflecting on what you've just experienced, and in others you have the opportunity to hash out what the group as a whole will do next.  The bonuses come in the forms of being more spiritual (immune to fear), more romantic (better chance at finding items), or even becoming more pragmatic (better at crafting).  Even playing by myself, I'm encrouraged to have the main characters argue over group decisions just to see what the outcome will be.  It really adds another layer to character creation that can evolve over time depending on how you want each person to behave in situations.

In a simple world, this would be a good game however this is not a simple world therefor this game is bad, very bad. This review is coming from the beta however I have participated in many beta's and have not had nearly as many issues as I've had with Block N' Load. So for starters the ping spikes are horrendous, the server constantly spikes from a range of 40 to 600ms during combat. I played on a GTX 970 4GB and an AMD FX-8350 so FPS was not a problem for me, or well it shouldn't have been. Due to the ping spikes, the game ran at an avg of 40 to 80 frames with excessive spikes which caused me headaches. The game itself looks alright I guess, though this is certainly a TF2-Minecraft clone.
The stuff that's lacking on the TF2 side of things is proper hit detection for starters, non-split channel team chat, inability to change classes during a game, a very very basic scoreboard, no voice chat, small maps and no satisfaction when winning a game. The game is fun fo about 5 minutes and I'm being generous by giving it 5 minutes because after that it becomes extremely stale, bland and boring. The beta takes up around 2.5GB's and if the full game takes up anymore than that, don't waste the storage space on it. Highly don't recommend this for play ability, I suggest you do play it however so that you can experience the buggy mess for yourself.
If the game ever gets a price tag slapped on it, which I believe it will be $30 USD, don't buy this for your own sake. If this were to remain F2P it still wouldn't be worth it because Jagex is surely going to force a P2W model on the game.

First, let me tell you that most of the complains about this game are perfectly grounded.
-Yes, it is really short for 20$ (3-4 hours if you're straight up going for the 100%, 1h-1h30 if you're going for the speedrun).
-Yes, the aesthetic choice for the camera (everything is seen from a 70°-ish angle) makes evaluating distances extremely tricky at times : many death will ensue during parkour phases.
-Yes, the controls (running, sneaking, sliding) are a bit clunky. This is particularly painful during chases, notably because of that issue with the camera, tricking you into hitting an obstacle. This forces Six (the main character) to do a full stop, ending most of the time in a gruesome and somewhat frustrating death.
-Yes, the game is very linear, with little to no puzzles to slow your progression.
Why in heavens am I recommending Little Nightmares then ? It's because, despite it's flaws, the game remains a masterpiece.
-The atmosphere is overall brilliant : every track of the OST is original and fits perfectly to every situation, to every idead or feeling the game is trying to communicate.
Moreover, I cannot but praise that Tim Burton's vibe the devs went for. It makes the game unique and, once again, fits perfectly with the general ideas : it creates a really particular ambiance for the Maw, both oppressive and alluring. The choice of the Unreal IV engine is justified in that matter. Sure, it is more demanding for your computer, but it allows to create really accurate and coherent physics. Water pouring out of a sponge, a soap sliding on the tiling, dust coming out of a book... all of this gives flesh to the universe of Little Nightmares and gives you the feeling to be fully immersed in that unique world the devs are trying to share with you.
-The lore. I, personnaly, am a fan of visual narratives. I like to explore by myself the symbolic that a game has to offer, to claw my way through its' flesh until I reach the pith. The game exceeded all my expectations. The symbolic is extremely rich. Everything, every speck of dust, every pixel looks like it was thought out. Nothing is given to you, nothing will be explicitely explained. Nevertheless, despite it's 3 hours length, LN is dense enough to let you speak about it for hours and hours ... if you're ready to give to the game, and not only to take from it.
All in all, LN is a complex matter regarding critique. I think that most of the bad reviews made about this game were legitimate. All the good ones were too. Is the pricetag of 20$ justified in my opinion? It really depends on how you define what is "a good game". If gameplay is the most important thing to you, I'll advise to wait for a sale, because, as was said, the game is lacky on that point. Do you held artistic value for more important than mere gameplay ? Can you forgive brevity and clunky controls if you are offered intersting lore, an astonishing soundtrack and an unique and absorbing world, all of this concentrated in 3 hours of gameplay ? If you answer "Yes" to this last question, then I cannot praise Little Nightmares enough. The game, indeed, was a very interesting experience. It all depends on you and on what side of gaming industry you want to sit ! Personnaly, I can fully understand both points of view.

Writing a new review because this game has been updated a lot and is also currently on sale for 2 dollars.
TL;DR
This game is insanely fun, and for 2 dollars (or even 10 dollars) you almost certainly will get your monies worth out of it. It has a few minor problems, but it's extremely well fleshed out and probably one of the best instagib shooters on the market right now. It's also an incredibly unique experience you won't find anywhere else, so I would have trouble not recommending it to anyone who even remotely enjoys FPS games. It has amazing physics/shooting, a fully fleshed out singleplayer and mutliplayer, local co-op (if you're into that), and a great community. It also has trickshots, who doesn't love trickshots?
As you can probably see by my hours I like disco dodgeball. A lot. I got this game a long time ago when a youtube named "AllShamNoWow" made a video on it. The game was in very early stages of development, and was very bare bones in comparison to now. The game was fun but had many problems. It had a mechanic called "blocking" that sounded good on paper but ended up just being annoying. It had very little content, no good single player whatsoever and few maps. It had a lot of weird bugs and annoying physics problems. I can safely say that practically every issue and problem I had with the game is now gone however.
The game overall just feels good, yeah it's graphics aren't great, but the gameplay itself is what matters to me and it does that wonderfully. If you see what the game is intended to be and like the concept, buy it. Because it does everything that it intended to do. Its single player is actually surprisingly in depth and fun, with a full fledged "arcade" mode with power-ups and bosses and waves of enemies. As well as many "challenges" including a hoard survival mode (challenges can also be played with up to 3 other players, which is nice). The game has many maps, around 15 I think at the moment. It has an insanely diverse cast of gamemodes, including my personal favorite "hoops" which consists of teams fighting over a golden ball and trying to score it into the opposing teams hoop to score points, so basically basketball where you can kill eachother. And many other fun modes as well as a large selection of "advanced" modes and modifiers which are basically just ways you can make the game even more ridiculous and crazy than it already is, which can be fun.
Let's get down to the core of the game now. Shooting, physics, and other basic gameplay. Well I can say that it feels very unique and well done. The shooting has an element of satisfaction that I haven't seen from any other insta-gib shooter, which I think mostly comes down to how conservative you must be with your shots and the management of picking up dodgeballs. There's usually only around 10-16 dodgeballs in a map, so you have to make your shots count because without one you are practically defenseless (you can catch balls thrown at you, but it's quite difficult). The physics, like ball physics or movement, also feel very unique and good. Unlike most shooters the player is actually a physical object, so things like going off ramps or bouncing into walls actually affects how you move. This adds an incredible level of depth to the game, things like strafing become more difficult because you can't instantly switch directions like in games like cs:go. The balls being physical objects also allow you to pull creative trickshots like bouncing balls off walls (Also did I mention you get extra points for performing trick shots? Because you do. And it's awesome).
There's many other things I love about this game, but I don't want this to be a massive wall of text. Here's a few other noteworthy things however.
-The community, it's really good and extremely friendly. Far more than any other online game I've ever seen, especially a shooter. I'm a moderator for the game and I've almost never used my mod powers to punish anyone, because I've never needed to.
-The customization/modability, this game has not only an incredible amount of cosmetic customization, but it also has the option to create custom gamemodes, or add your own music/voicepacks to the game (the music also reacts to the in game visualizers!). The gamemodes are especially cool, because it allows you to create hilarious or unique experiences that you otherwise wouldn't have been able to do.
Cons to the game:
For me personally, not many. The most noteworthy one I can think of however is the "netcode" as people might call it. Unfortunately this is unavoidable and will happen in any instagib, but things like kill trading or getting hit by a ball when you think you shouldn't have will happen. They are rather uncommon, but they are there sometimes. And that can be a huge turn off for some people. The game also has in the past had a small community, currently it's quite healthy, hitting about 200 players peak per day, but it could drop again, who knows.
Let me know if you have any questions about the game, I'm sure I missed a lot. I know a tun about it so I should be able to answer anything you might have.

A good JRPG on steam, the story is light hearted and not too deep but the quirky characters keep it interesting.
The combat system is fun and surprisingly deep but poorly balanced; characters are pretty balanced until post-game but rush + exe spamming basically dominates most enemies when you manage to craft a EXE Gauge disc (which is to say, about midgame).
The difficulty is incostant to say the least: the game starts pretty easily, gets harder through the middle game, is really easy near the end and then spikes again in the post-game (if you have the DLC).
A normal playthrough will take about 20-30h, but there is plenty of unlockables for completionists which will need at least 3 playthroughs and many many more hours to 100%.
I didn't find the game to be too much grindy during a normal playthrough (actually, probably a little less than the average JRPG), you will need to grind a bit for the post-game stuff but still less than the average JRPG (I went from level 75 to 999 in about 4hours).
Technically, the game is about average: the graphic is not jaw-dropping but the art is nice, the music is not really memorable but does its job.
My main complaint about it is the fact that many dungeons and enemies are recycled or palette-swapped; it's pretty standard in JRPGs but in Neptunia this feels way worse and makes most dungeons anonymous and bland.
I feel like Neptunia is a nice RPG  definitely not groundbreaking but a solid 7/10 IMHO, maybe a little more if you the fanservice does not bother you, you can overlook the recycled assets and are a JRPG/Japanese culture fan.

Decent platformer.
Definitely this is no Inside despite all the comparisons. Inside is in a class of it's own.
The biggest gripe I think I had with this is that there is less wonder and mystery if I had to compare it to Inside. In Little Nightmares, your constantly moving from point A to B with not much story or idea of why. There is nothing really driving me forward either other than my desire to finish the game.
One of the common annoyances with this game is that when you die, you are typically spawned far enough back before the point of frustration that you can't just immediately get back to your mistake to try again. Thus, you will die again and often and constantly be spawned back enough to annoy you A LOT.  Whether it be jumping mistakes, or the lack of contact made towards an object you were reaching for causing you to die. This isn't due to being too far away from grabbing what you were trying to hold on to, but rather an issue with I believe the collision detection at times. Issues like this also came into play regarding throwing objects and not knowing how far away you might be due to the perspective and not truly getting the right angle at times.
With that said, it has it's moments. Graphically, it's beautiful. Didn't capture me as much as Inside, but still a beaut to look at. UE4 on display. The animation was very solid and looked pixar at times, but then other times, you think the quality dips (talking about our first large  monster encounter). It's rather easy to forgive though and carry on. The hide and seek moments were fun when you were in the kitchen and I thought it was well done when you have them hot on your tail just escaping in the nick of time.
The sound really assists the graphics and immerses you well. The moment a creep spots you, it's yell followed by a loud increase in the sound lets you know it just got serious. I thought it was all extremely done well. No qualms here.
A lot of hate went into the length of the game and I thought it was perfect. I honestly didn't need it to be any longer and for that, I did pick up the first little DLC out of curiousity. Not sure it's totaly worth it but I said why not. Honestly, a lot of other games I've played that were shorter and got less hate so I'm not sure what the deal is here. Definitely worth it for $10 if you find it for that or less.
While there were some things that bothered me, I was able to get by them and say I'd recommend it still. I wouldn't recommend it over Inside by no means, but I'd still recommend it. Decent platformer with a creepy vibe to it.
