The remake of the old wonderful UFO - Enemy Unknown brings with it loads of new features.
A class system for your soldiers that are randomly dealt to them after their first levelup (yes, the new games brings levels with it) is one thing, and as mentioned, levels are another.
It removes the old action points system and gives all of your soldiers 2 actions points.
These changes make the game feel new, and even though I loved the old UFO to bits, I must claim that this might be better  than that.
Of course there are ups and downs with this game aswell. The controls can be a bit funky what with trying to see different levels, and moving your soldiers between them, but you'll get used to that.
The story is mainly the same, with a few slight changes. Same thing with the aliens. They're mostly the same, but with a few new ones.
A downside is that it's a rather short game, but then again, it has alot of replayability what with the Iron Man mode, or unlocking random levelups for your soliders and the likes.
I've only played 4-6 PvP matches so far, but they were really fun aswell. The point system seems to work fine, and the various aliens/soldiers you can outfit each have their own playstyle to them.
If you like strategy and Sci-Fi, this is a game for you.

The Banner Saga is a truly fantastic game. It is a tactical RPG set in fantasy world inspired bu Norse mythology. The first thing that you will notice about this game is its very unique, and beautiful artstyle. The striking artstyle reminds me a lot of classic Disney animated films such as The Black Cauldron, and its the first time I have seen it used for a long time in a video game.
The Banner Saga's grid-based tactical combat is challenging and very enjoyable, but most of the game will be spent in between the combat sections, traveling across the land. During this journey your main concern is keeping your clan alive and well, through conserving supplies, maintaining morale, and making tough decisions that will often have major consequences; good or bad. The strength of the game however, is in its worldbuilding and enthralling story. A huge portion of your time playing the game will be spent reading the brilliantly written dialogue and narration, so expect to be reading a lot.
When you are victorious in battle you will receive 'renown', the game's currency, which you will spend on supplies, making decisions, and equipment that can upgrade your party members. This renown system is very unforgiving however, as you will probably spend it on items, decisions, or  supplies, and then later on realise you needed that renown for a crucial decision that could have dire consequences.
The story is fantastic, but a cliffhanger ending left me feeling slightly unsatisfied, although a good sequel would remedy this. Overall, The Banner Saga has very few flaws at all, and should definitely be experienced, if only for its rich story, and stunning aesthetic.

The Banner Saga is an epic role-playing game inspired by Viking legend. She filled with dead gods, apocalyptic events and somber landscapes juxtaposed with beautiful shots of your caravan, all brought to life by breathtaking art and animations.
The Banner Saga is set in a Nordic fantasy universe where giants (named varls) live alongside humans. The game alternates between two intertwining stories — one starring human archers Rook and his daughter Alette, and the other following a varl consortium led by Hakon.
Renown is hard to come by — only success in battle will net you enough, and it's the only currency you can use to grab supplies and items. These, in turn, are necessary to keep you in fighting shape. It's a tough but fair system.
The Banner Saga wants you to have to fight to stay alive, and I loved it for that. I could not put it down.

NOTE: Don't look at my game time as an indicator of actual game length. I often left the game running while doing other things. This review is based on one playthrough, the Alisa - Bad ending. No more information on that path will be given, to avoid spoilers.
Before I start this review, I'd like to point out that as at the time of my playthrough, the steam version of the game is censored. The game is designed to incorporate adult imagery. For that reason, and my otherwise enjoyment of adult imagery, I'd recommend googling the instructions on how to uncensor the game.
---
Everlasting Summer is a free to play Russian Visual Novel. You play as Semyon, an introverted loner. One winter's night, while riding on a bus in a busy metropolitan area, Semyon falls asleep. When he awakens, he finds he's been mysteriously transported to a remote youth camp and it's now mid-summer. Semyon and the reader are placed abruptly in this new environment and we're both left to ponder what has happened. The journey from this point paints a nice story. A little bit of mystery, a little coming of age. The game sold a nice image of camp life and had me wishing I'd given camp a shot. The story wasn't in any hurry to be told and felt a little lingery in places. This was despite a literal and figurative desire to try and uncover what happened to bring us here. We always seemed too busy "camping" to find out. And as abruptly as we're placed in this setting, so are we abruptly removed from it at the end (at least in the Alisa - Bad ending route), leaving us scratching our heads as to what had transpired.
All in all, it was a nice story, with some degree of decision making on the readers part. However, I did feel that we weren't given enough opportunity to make decisions, especially meaningful ones. This was also the feeling that resulted as we lingered too long and didn't peruse the mystery of our presence here. At the end of the day, I had to remind myself that I was, for the most part, a passenger to this story, not the pilot; this is a Visual Novel, not a RPG/Choose Your Own Adventure.
The game was originally written in Russian, but has since been translated into English. The translations don't appear to be professionally done, with a number of minor translation faults, especially in the latter parts of the game. These small faults don't take away from the game or lead to any confusion in with regards to the story, but I feel it should be pointed out regardless. If anything, the faults add in small part to the charm of the game. At times, when strict translations don't exist, such as for Russian products, dishes or concepts, the game presents a sidebar explaining the terms.
The visuals of this visual novel were a little hit and miss. The environment and setting art was quite pretty and quite effectively sold the setting of the camp. The characters however felt a little less complete. They often came across a little too repetitive and static. Part of the visuals of this style of visual novel should serve to attract and sell the reader on the characters; who we like, who we hate and who we wish to get with. As such, they should have a greater array of visuals with more character and expression. When it's the same pose and default faces every time, you don't get that. Another letdown was the "cut scenes”. They were a little too sketchish and a little less "beauty shot". They came across more like concept art rather than final hero piece.
The music of Everlasting Summer was quite beautiful. I often find the music of games to be annoying when I'm away from the game doing other things, or in cases like this game when there's little other sounds so you're hearing the same songs over and over again. This was not the case in Everlasting Summer. I have actually had gone back to the games website to listen to the soundtrack (available for free). There's the occasional foley sound effect in the game as well, but these are minor.
One downside of the game is the achievements. There are 13 different endings, each having an achievement linked to it. So to unlock all the achievements, you need to complete at least 13 playthroughs to unlock all the paths. This approach encourages researching the right decision combos rather than acquiring them organically.
Overall, Everlasting Summer was quite an enjoyable (and free) Visual Novel. The “dating sim” aspect of the game may not appeal to all readers (it’s less pronounced than in some of its ilk) and the lack of definitive answers, or the lack of pursuit of them, may frustrate some people, but if you can get past that, you should enjoy this read.

Before it’s official launch, Black Desert Online (BDO) by Pearl Abyss was one of the most hyped upcoming Korean MMORPGs around. BDO was released in its home country in 2014 and 2016 for North America and Europe.
The game is free to play in Korea, Japan, and Russia while the English version for North America and Europe is pay to play, or more specifically, “buy to play” (players have to buy the game but there is no subscription fee).
While trying to scratch the MMO itch I had recently, I wanted to find a good, immersive and fun game to keep me occupied for a little while. Black Desert Online seemed to fit the description quite nicely and after playing it for a little while, you will certainly like the fact that it’s a solid, immersive and very enjoyable game.
Gameplay
One of the things you will love about Black Desert Online is that this MMO does take itself quite seriously and that’s a very good thing. The gameplay is immersive and truly solid, the experience is created for both beginners and experts, not to mention that the world is massive. At the time of this writing we already had a large expansion dropped in and another one is coming shortly, so the updates and content are coming very fast.
The game world is amazing and detailed, and there are quite a lot of enemies you can find. Thankfully, the enemy variety is not an issue here and you will actually find that dealing with enemies is quite exciting and immersive as you play. Sure, they will avoid following you after a while if you run from them. But, the combat is interesting and you will always try to find new strategies to tackle them. They don’t have the same attack all the time, and that does make the experience quite unpredictable to be honest.
Most of the world and the experience will remind you of WoW but I find Black Desert Online to be a lot prettier. The world is also realistic and while there are thousands of quests and things to do, many of them have a realistic tone. Of course there are fantasy elements, but BDO stays grounded instead of trying to always immerse yourself into the experience which is what matters the most.
I like the attention to detail that they have here because each of the attacks and the enemies are very detailed and realistic. You will sometimes have to avoid massive enemies or groups because that will indeed cause you harm. It’s not easy to do so honestly but as you play you will certainly have the possibility to do what you want and how you want.
The inventory will expand as you play and while that’s not necessarily a bad thing, it’s bothering you at first. It’s very interesting to try and figure out what each skill does though, especially since there are a few hundred of them scattered throughout the skill map. That’s what really pushes you forward and makes you going because aside from having lots of skills, each one can be upgrading.
BDO review
Leveling is a part of the game but it can be quite grindy and unfortunately this will usually spoil the fun. Trying to get a specific skill locked behind a certain level is not that fun, but it does offer some interesting capabilities.
You can get houses and warehouses in any town then use them as storage or as manufacturing facilities. Thankfully, the world is filled with places and traders where you can sell goods so you can indeed get some good money from that. And rest assured that there are tons of places where you can spend your silver if you want that, all you have to do is to be creative and the results will certainly pay off.
I also like the fact that they added hundreds of side activities. Be it side quests or just activities like fishing, riding your horse and leveling him or just gathering flowers/herbs, it’s just something that you will do often. It will also distract you quite a lot most of the time as you try to play, but it’s nice to have such a thing in there. Many times we do want to stay away from killing and there are certainly lots of things to do in Black Desert Online that will keep you company.
Unfortunately, they don’t really have an endgame honestly and there is no level cap either. But, on the other hand, they do update the game often so they do try to add in more stuff to do for high level players. They might even add a proper endgame but for the time being there isn’t a proper one.
Classes are nice and very detailed, they even integrated a ninja class recently. The issue for some players is that some off these classes are locked behind a specific gender which is certainly something you want to avoid in an MMO. But, on the other hand, most of us will not be bothered by this issue.
Performance is good for Black Desert Online as long as you have a high end PC. You can play it on older systems but in order to do so you will have to remove some of the graphic options. However, I feel that based on the way it looks, the performance for Black Desert Online is decent and it does offer plenty for what it requires.
Black Desert Online screenshot
Graphics
As I said, one of the main strengths for Black Desert Online is coming from its graphics. The game world, animations and characters are stellar. They are looking very well and there weren’t that many graphics glitches in the game either. I liked the variety of each region and you can find just about anything you might expect from a fantasy game here, starting with dungeons and ending with massive plains or huge mountains.
The music here is good albeit a little repetitive and the sounds are realistic, to the point. The voice acting might seem a little strange for European and US players, but it’s ok nonetheless.
Conclusion
Black Desert Online is a fun game that I loved playing. It’s nice to get into and it does offer a multitude of unique ideas. Sure, it doesn’t really integrate all its systems properly and the gender locked classes might not be the best idea in an MMO, but it’s a solid game. Plus, if you have a solid PC you can enjoy maybe the best graphics in an MMO right now!

A good JRPG on steam, the story is light hearted and not too deep but the quirky characters keep it interesting.
The combat system is fun and surprisingly deep but poorly balanced; characters are pretty balanced until post-game but rush + exe spamming basically dominates most enemies when you manage to craft a EXE Gauge disc (which is to say, about midgame).
The difficulty is incostant to say the least: the game starts pretty easily, gets harder through the middle game, is really easy near the end and then spikes again in the post-game (if you have the DLC).
A normal playthrough will take about 20-30h, but there is plenty of unlockables for completionists which will need at least 3 playthroughs and many many more hours to 100%.
I didn't find the game to be too much grindy during a normal playthrough (actually, probably a little less than the average JRPG), you will need to grind a bit for the post-game stuff but still less than the average JRPG (I went from level 75 to 999 in about 4hours).
Technically, the game is about average: the graphic is not jaw-dropping but the art is nice, the music is not really memorable but does its job.
My main complaint about it is the fact that many dungeons and enemies are recycled or palette-swapped; it's pretty standard in JRPGs but in Neptunia this feels way worse and makes most dungeons anonymous and bland.
I feel like Neptunia is a nice RPG  definitely not groundbreaking but a solid 7/10 IMHO, maybe a little more if you the fanservice does not bother you, you can overlook the recycled assets and are a JRPG/Japanese culture fan.

It's a fantastic piece of work that almost seamlessly melds roguelike and strategy that's unforgiving in the hands of a novice but nontetheless rewarding and worth replaying constantly. The Advanced Edition upgrades help mix it up a little and make it just a little less mind-numbing, but it still puts a dent in an otherwise near-perfect title.

Crawl can be a great, even amazing, split-screen local multiplayer game with one caveat: you need the right group of people for it, because Crawl is definitely not for everyone.
It's a fast paced game which could be described as a competitive multiplayer dungeon crawl. One player is the hero, who attempts to kill monsters, get gold, buy items and defeat the boss to escape the dungeons. The other players? They play the monsters. The gimmick is that when one of the monster players kills the adventurer, they swap roles and thus everyone keeps going around in circles until someone is finally strong enough to kill the boss.
In many games this might mean the monsters are just downtime between turns getting to be the hero, but not so in Crawl. The monster gameplay is quite in depth with each player being able to level up their stable of hand picked monsters, activate traps and so on. I personally probably prefer being the monsters to being the adventurer!
Of course not everyone will like this confrontational and increasingly high stress gameplay, and those who don't will probably hate Crawl. Otherwise what you have here is a unique, amazingly good looking and sounding multiplayer game which has tons of content and will keep challening players for ages. Even lonely players can have fun with bots, who are perhaps even a bit too challenging.

My first impressions on this game was thoughts of "This better not be a clone of Titan Quest". Don't get me wrong, TQ wasn't a bad game, but it suffers from unsatisfying loot, long levels of grinding, and although it boasts Mastery Trees and encourages Diversifying skills, it takes a massive investment into the mid game or late game to start being interesting as it's not worth it to spread your skill points but better to focus all points into a few abilites in the beginning parts of the game. I don't think it's good design to have to invest tens and tens of hours just to feel some levels of synergy off your branching skill trees.
So a few hours into game I discovered that it quickly took away my fears that it would play like TQ. Levels come and go rather quickly, which means you obtain points much quicker to allot into abilites. There is also an addition of an NPC that returns skill points for a price very early into the game. These two points combined makes it rather interesting and not as punishing to try out synergies or builds. Weapons also come and go and you're not restricted to what weapons you use. Although as you speciliaze into your skills and devotions your options will get more focused.
I'll give the pros and cons of the game here (Please keep in mind these are my own opinions and I may update them as I play the game more)
Overall, it's a fairly well made game, but it's missing out a lot of finesse. It's like a bowl of well made spaghetti, but they forgot the sauce. I really wish there was a in between option and not thumbs down option, because it definitely isn't a bad game. You will enjoy this game if you like theory crafting, and building your character into a Otherworldly Meatgrinder hellbent on churning the flesh of Aetherians, Chtonians, Humans, and Beasts alike. However, there's not much to sink your teeth into. If you don't mind that and can relax on the shallow waters, then you'd definitely enjoy this game. I was looking for more and I was disappointed is all. This game makes me appreciate the enemy designs and variations in Diablo II so much more.
Tl;dr, Not a bad game, if I could choose a neutral ground, I would. This game suffers from simplistic enemies, shallow quest and faction mechanics. It's strength lies in the character skill building and looting.

These are my thoughts of The Banner Saga after four hours of play. If that amount of time is unacceptable to you, I suggest that you quit reading this review. So, why am I doing the Banner Saga after such a short amount of play? Well, I’ve had a lot of time to think on it. To analyze why this game failed to pull me with its story, mechanics and overall presentation. It’s pretty rare that I’ll keep thinking about a game I quit early on for as long as I have. So when that happens, I write a review. So, let’s dig into The Banner Saga and talk about the issues I had with it.
The Banner Saga is a combination of turn-based grid combat and Oregon Trail mechanics tied into a narratively driven campaign. This campaign follows the journey of two clans as they struggle against an unrelenting foe called the Dredge. The player is tasked with keeping these clans alive as best they can, manage their limited resources and survive. The game is split into three phases: conversing, traveling and combat. Conversations happen when the caravan has stopped at a town or some other special event happens. The player reads the lines and decides what to do next. The conversation system is ok. You do get up to four options to how you respond to decisions or particular situations and sometimes that fourth option isn’t always being silent. When traveling, your caravan in the center of the screen travels slowly to their destination consuming the supplies it has. There’s also a morale indicator to show whether everyone is in high spirits or not. This is affected by your decisions and how you fare in battle. Though I never found out if having low morale was bad but I’m assuming it is. The combat has two phases. The war phase that’s only triggered when fighting large amounts of Dredge and let’s you decide whether to be aggressive, retreat or something in-between. It’s very simple and is pretty much decided by numbers and how you fare in the turn based area. Otherwise, it’s the turn based combat that you’ll spend most of your time. It's held on large grids where your heroes battle it out against often outnumbering foes. There’s a bunch of stats that affect each hero and how they’ll perform but explaining them seems a little pointless when the game tells you straight out. I have a lot of issues with how the combat system in this game works so let’s examine it for a bit.
There’s a lot about the combat system that I do not understand from a design point. I don’t understand why there’s both a health and armor system for all characters. I don’t get why health is tied to power. Why are most of the enemies ranged while most of your heroes are melee? Why do they get so many turns to hit you while you get very few yourself? Why do those same archers have armor as well? Why on earth do AOE attacks also hurt your own guys if they’re in range? I had a lot of these questions while I was playing TBS and I’m pretty sure I forgot some of them. This game seems to be encouraging you to level all of your heroes but then it limits them with both a point system that you have to spend between all of them and requiring each hero to land a certain amount of killing blows. So even if they got the required amount of kills they need to level up, they still might not be able to level up because you had to spend all the points on another more important hero. So, some characters are forever doomed to stay low level and be utterly useless for the rest of the game.
It doesn’t help that heroes will come in and out of the story (or get killed) leaving you without their capabilities. Additionally, there’s an obvious lack of synergy between the heroes. So, they become extremely interchangeable and uninteresting as a result. I found that the longer I played, the more the game just mostly devolves into giant (geddit?) attrition grinds where I watch my heroes get shot again and again and again by so many archers while they slowly move across the grid. With me hoping and praying they’ll survive just a little bit longer. Up until they don’t and the whole battle is completely over because they knocked out your two most powerful heroes. That’s pretty much the entire reason I quit.
While I was playing, I had this constant sense of “is this all that this combat system is? Am I really not missing anything?”. I figured out after four hours that I wasn’t missing anything. It’s just a poor combat system with an uninteresting traveling system. But what about the story? Well, that’s where my personal preference is going to take over for a bit.
The game starts the player out joining a group of Varl, a race of giants, at the end of their journey collecting taxes or gifts for some king. However, the place they’re arrived at is under siege by some enemy force. Who you quickly kill and then move on. Then there’s another plot with a Human father and daughter that discover that an evil force is invading their lands on the other side of the continent. This evil force of “Dredge” is now invading the country in full force. Who I’m supposed to be worried about, I think, except that I keep destroying them into the ground every time I meet up with them. Of course, a lot of their fear is implied through the story but they’re given very little build up so I found myself unable to care about them as a threat. Really, I thought this game would be fine just surviving the wilderness. Adding what appear to be magical zombies isn’t that interesting. So, these two parties flee from the Dredge in a desperate bid to find shelter further inland and the player must use their wits to help them survive.
The pacing of this title is all over the place. You’re introduced to new characters with very little fanfare or explanation about them. And just as soon as I got even a little bit attached to them, they’d get killed off. Or we’d switch gears to the other group of people on the other side of the world.
The Banner Saga feels like a game that doesn’t push it’s mechanics far enough or tries to be something different when it really should have stuck with established norms. It’s a game that was clearly created with a universe and visuals in mind but the rest of it feels incomplete or rushed. Both the combat and the traveling are shallow experiences desperately trying to tie themselves together but almost at odds with each other. The combat is perhaps the biggest sticking point for me. There’s conflicting design which leads to an overall really boring and tiring experience. The artistry of the animated graphics is certainly top notch. It invokes the classic animated style of yesteryear exceptionally well while remaining modern. But that’s clearly where all the effort went. The rest of this game feels like a giant step backwards for its genre. Add on a universe and cast of characters that I didn’t really respond with and I find myself unable to recommend The Banner Saga.

I'll preface this with the fact that I've played the original XCOM: UFO Defense for DOS and absolutely loved it. So some of this review will be from a fanboy perspective, but I'll try to also give some objective feedback.
TLDR;
This is a nice and fun game, but if you don't like strategy, especially turn based, or if you do like strategy and are looking for a deep and realistic simulation of defending the Earth from an alien invasion this isn't for you. If you are a fan of the XCOM series and are ok with a simplification of the tactical and strategical mechanics you should get this.
Now a fanboy rant.
Probably the thing that outrages me the most is how few units you send in for the missions...
Technician: Oh hey Aliens are terrorizing Paris, we're the best defense against them how many troops should we send in?
Commander: 4
Technician: 4? 4 people to take out some force that travelled the stars and has way better technology than us. I know our guys are good, and that craft can definately take 6 people
Commander: 4, one of them has to be promoted to a Captain then we can send 5, then one has to be a Major before we send in 6
Technician:  WHAT?! We're possibly talking about the fate of the world and you want to send at most 6 outgunned people to defend a large city? We could arrange transportation for a dozens to get there in time and possibly with some armored vehicles.
Commander: Send in only 4 people
Overall, even if this wasn't an XCOM game or in the similar vein, this is a fun and very polished game. The story is pretty good (especially for a turn based strategy, the DOS predecessor didn't have much of one). Some game mechanics are very simplified no ammo mangement (though you still have to reload), how many units you control, and the cover system. However, a few things are complex like what actions/abilities can be used and if they consume the turn or limit what else you can do in that turn.
To that effect, this game is not a terrific tactical combat game as it is very simplistic in that regard. You have at most 6 units (unless you manage to do some mind control) to command and they have 2 'actions' per turn. The rules get complicated as some things will consume both actions if used first such as attacking, some require and use both actions meaning the unit cannot have moved this turn. Then there's some abilities/traits on your soldiers that change those rules, like run and gun lets you use both actions and move and then attack, and I believe another allows you to attack twice in a round, or attacking doesn't use up both actions.
Another issue is that at least by default, is that unless you are very much flanking an enemy, like at a right angle or more to their cover your positioning has very little effect on your units accuracy. There is a modifier (which might be available from the start as an advanced option) that is suppose to give penalties and bonuses based on the angle (for both you and the enemy) though I haven't tried this.
I'm assuming because of the small squad size (4-6), that the single player has the enemies lay dormant until you first spot them, or vice versa. When this happens the aliens basically get a free move (even if it was their turn and they spotted you) to get into cover and are then active (will roam the map to look for you if for some reason you leave). You might be lucky if you have already ordered a unit to be in overwatch AND is able to see the alien(s) during this free move to get a shot off on them. Other than that, there isn't really any ambushing the aliens. And while this normally keeps the ratio of active/attacking enemies to your units balanced, you often active another set by accident when trying to manuever against the current one. And then there are roaming patrols, usually on crash sites, that do move around the map but when spotted still get the free move. So you can find yourself activating one set, and while moving to attack them activate another, and then during the alien's turn a roaming patrol comes in and sees you and gets a free move into cover. Good luck taking down a dozen (or more) aliens around your 4-6 soldiers.
When it comes to the Strategic gameplay, between battles, it is also lacking. The major decisions are what to research first, what base modules to build and where (when you have money). Their are UFOs that fly around and can be detected and intercepted but the detection method is weird. You launch satellites to cover a country and somehow the satellite only sees inside the country's political boundaries, not a more sensible geographical area. The satellites are also your main source of funding, a country won't give you money per month unless they have a satellite, oh but each country gives a different amount. Thus a satellite over Japan covers a very small area but one over the USA covers a huge area, including Alaska but is somehow blind to anything in Canada. Each satellite costs the same to make, but you are limited to how many you can have up at once which you can increase by building a module.
Aside from the ocassional UFO spotting, you will get (at times random) missions from command. Some actually develop somewhat of a plot but for the most part provide you with some resources. Also I believe once per month you will have an abduction event in which the aliens  are abducting in 3 different countries and for some reason you can only go for one of them. Each country will give a different resource along with increased standing, assuming you are successful, and will lower relations with the 2 you didn't help. Later on there are terror events but they only occur in one spot but are difficult and have this rescue civilians before aliens kill them mechanic.
Now, sigh, about the soldier class mechanic (which wasn't in the original DOS). I will give some credit for being a bit unique as all but 2 of the level ups require you to make an exclusive choice with no respec option. Meaning that 2 soldiers of the same class and level may have different abilities (if you so choose). The bad part is that what solder class you get is completely random (unless its a reward from a mission you will know the class beforehand). While you can get around this by hiring and firing soldiers, the problem is when you hire them they are Rookies and have to get enough experience to level up before they are assigned a class. Also which class they are usually locks them into a specific type of weapon. The assault class is the only exception which can go back to using assault rifle type weapons.
Continued Fanboy rant
The game does play good homage to the original DOS series, but the detection system is convoluted. It is interesting to note that the original was made in the UK and because your detection in that game was geographical the best place for your first base is in Europe. Because while the US does give you the most funding and would at first seem the most logical to defend, the UK, France, and Germany are just below and in total give way more funding than the US alone. However, the system in this game that is limited to borders, favors starting with the US quite a bit since they give the most money and covers the most territory (I think, if not its a close 2nd). While your first base also gives you the continent bonus, starting in Europe or others is still viable.
There are only so many static maps in this game. I'll grant you they are pretty and quite a number of them, but after several missions you will notice you are playing the same map you played before (though maybe entering from a different point, enemies are different and in different spots). The original DOS version basically had tiles that were put together randomly, for every mission (except base defense and the last 2 levels). The aliens were all active (for the most part, some would stay inside the UFO) moving around the map opening doors and all.
Best game ever. End of.

Banner Saga is a fantastically put together game. Stunning visuals and an emotional intense story make for an experience that is enjoyable start to finish. Gameplay is very fine-tuned (if thinking carefully about strategic battles isn't your thing, look somewhere else) but it's fun to experiment with different abilities. At times the combat can get a little frustrating when one small mistake can cause a total party wipe, but there is almost no randomness to damage or saves, so you never feel like the computer is screwing you over. Battles get a bit repetitive in the middle of the game, but the story is enough to keep you interested.
Where this game really shines though is in the story and lore of the world. Getting invested in each of the characters and having to make difficult choices is gutwrenching every time. Be sure to explore the map and participate in every possible dialogue to get the full experience.
tl;dr Banner Saga is a great game that can be played in around 10 hours, contains lots of strategic thinking, emotional dialogue and decisions, and interesting characters.

The last time I felt this gleeful about the sheer freedom and breadth of possibilities of a game was playing Deus Ex for the first time. Divinity: Original Sin is maximalist game design philosophy at its absolute best in RPG form, even if the individual parts aren’t all top tier. I hadn’t played a proper party based CRPG since KOTOR and NWN back in the day and wasn’t particularly interested in the latest wave of Kickstarter revivals either, but curiosity and its promise of clever turn based tactics got the best of me after noticing D:OS had been the number one seller on Steam for WEEKS after its launch. I checked out a random gameplay vid on Youtube, which ended up being a whole encounter early on, which was enough by itself to immediately sell me on the game. Let’s be perfectly honest here, the battle system is the star here and is by far my favorite RPG combat ever. Seriously, nothing but the most complex SRPGs can even hold a candle to the veritable chemistry set of options available to players here. The encounters, at least in the first act, make excellent use of these systems resulting in around 30 hours of stiffly challenging tactical bliss. Just a few fight highlights just in the first map of the game:
Outside of combat, it’s still pretty damn good except for the overall plot and main story writing. I took a liking to the goofy tone (especially the talking animals, like my boy Unsinkable Sam and the murder victim’s dog, who surprising came into combat to help me fight some recently exhumed corpses), which some regard as out of place in a game like this but to me it makes perfect sense. When your various methods of interactivity are so playful and exuberant, why contradict yourself with the standard dreary dark fantasy self-seriousness? Speaking of playful interactions, there’s plenty of it outside of fighting. Pretty much everything in the world exists as a manipulable object with its own physics properties, health and such… Quests can be solved in a crazy amount of ways, which is necessary given the journal doesn’t give you exact information about the what and where. Investigations actually feel like investigations, not errands as they often do in quest marker oriented games. Anything that reminds me of Morrowind in that regard is a plus in my book.
The difficulty and quality of the encounters take a dive after the Act 1, and to be quite honest I didn’t even finish it. Act 1 is transcendent enough to where that barely matters to me, and could be my GOTY based on it alone. What keeps me excited is the
, building up towards what they call “the very big RPG that will dwarf them all”. They’ve immediately shot up into my pantheon of favorite developers along with FROM, Platinum, and EAD Tokyo and their future looks bright as hell.
Shoutouts to the Kickstarter backers and and their collective milli and early access players for helping to make this happen with the balance and volume of stuff it deserved.

Story of a little girl in yellow surviving in a dark yet wonderful fairy tale of a world. The game is amazing and must-have in my books. Here are my main points as to why, divided into three aspects; Plot, Design and gameplay.
The plot of the game is linear. There are no choices to be made. You go and experience the same story everyone's experiencing. Good foreshadinging of certain key turning points are well noted. Imagery and symbolism in those story beats are worth putting some thought into. When I look at games, I look through a lens that highlights artistic decisions and the plot's got very interesting beats that raise a lot of good questions.
Design of the characters and the world is top notch. Tim Burtonesque style of art, curvy edges with dark shadows and overall dreamy and fairy tale alike design is something to enjoy. The characters are very interesting in the regard that they all seem to be hiding behind something, whether that be a mask or a yellow rain jacket. Some beats in the character arc makes you question what the story is all about. It's very interesting, i have to say. Oh and one thing, the last part of the story reminded me of "Spirited Away" by Hayao Miyazaki. I love it.
When it comes to smaller games, gameplay becomes something of a challange. How do you keep the game enjoyable to play at the same time, keeping things very minimal? It's got everything you'd expect from this genre, but the one things that bothered me was holding onto something when you're climbing or carrying. You have to keep pressing the button. So when you're climbing a rather tall rope, you have to keep your finger on that button the whole time. It's a minor design in the grand scheme of things, but a game with only a few mechanics, it stands out. Another thing, sprinting and sliding is very satisfying but awkwards to do with the defaults keys. Shift to sprint and Ctrl to slide. You get the point.

First of all:
Since you can choose in which way you spend your time in this game (crafting, grinding, PvP, maybe even some RP), the gameplay itself is strictly set like every other MMORPG out there. There is nothing, which makes this game more sandboxlike than all the others.
It is in fact an almost
with
-feature (!) later in the game. And it recently turned out, that
The big points of this game are indeed it's presentation and the battlesystem.
The charactereditor is great and you spend much time just to watch all the players' made presets - or even build your own and share it with the community. Even later on you can adjust your character's look (with a shopwise purchaseable Value Pack though).
The world's background story is not very unique and on top of that even unimportant. Questtexts are not really inspiring, so they cut of very much of immersion. The whole stories aren't really cared about, so you learn just to ignore about them. There are no really epic storylines or impacts. But all those ruins, areas and locations are designed with much of devotion. Some players are just roleplaying in immersion, which is a great bonus for a nowaday MMORPG.
The battlesystem is one of the greatest in terms of MMORPGs. You liked TERA? You will love Black Desert. Hit skills' combos, get into flows and learn rotations depending on which kind of enemy you fight against. Your movement keys and some action keys are about to be triggered in the right time and the right order to get the best skills casted and you don't just tab trough enemys - you have to aim right to be effective.
It sounds and feels like a fighting game.
The socalled "parcours system" instead is a merely joke. It is in fact possible to climb on crates, roofs and rocks, but without really a function or purpose. And on top of that, it isn't functioning properly, which means: not truly implemented.
Actually you can choose between 14 (genderlocked) classes. Some may be similar, but each has it's very own playstyle at least when hit the awakening ground with level 56.
The levelprocess starts very fast, but after lv 56 it will be much slower. Player call this a softcap, which is not, but a diminishing progress.
So here the game shows it's true nature of an asia-grinder with very big content-gaps. Much areas which are literally empty and seemingly unfinished. The great "Black Desert" isn't even a very dark location at all, it is just a hot, debuffing place, with few mobspawns and random occuring entrances to the only two high-level-dungeons underground.
One of the other aspects are the socalled lifeskills, which contain all the kind of crafting and gathering methods. Most of them are done almost afk, while the client has to be online - the true nature of a korean internet-cafe-based-issue.
But it also motivates: Catch you very own wild horse, level it and then breed it to have a chance of a better one (higher tier).
Or trade items between NPCs to improve in trading, which generates more money per trade.
Build ships, weapons, armors.
Craft potions, meals or even own tradeitems.
You can spent socalled "contributions points" (earned through quests or crafting) in explored nodes to let hired npcs gather ressources, while you're doing other stuff. Also to unlock crafting buildings or storageplaces in towns. They work as a kind of action-points on the worldmap to unlock a net of nodes for more profitable trade- oder gather-routes.
There is much to do in Black Desert online, very much to grind your time with.
The community of BDO is one of the harshest ever witnessed before. You have to learn to "git gut" without any help ingame so far.
Also you often have to fight your ground while questing, grinding or even just running by. Fishermen who are fishing afk outside safezones are slaughtered, even if you do nothing but ride your horse.
You have to deal with PKs, trolls, exploiters, griefers and insults very often.
And you have to deal with very much frustrating RNG-factors. On top of it: the enchanting system.

The feature list on the store page should be more than enough to grab your attention, because it doesn't just do each of the things it says it does, it does them all well.  Considering the amount of things you can do and how polished it is, I was always hopeful that this game would feel like a truer spiritual successor to Mabinogi than Vindictus ever was, and boy has it delivered.
Cons:
- Graphical pop-in is a bit aggressive, and even noticable at times in pre-rendered videos where they used the in-game engine
- For an action oriented game, most of the time your attacks don't feel like they have much impact aside from numbers
- Combat classes are locked to character design, making it more like Vindictus than TERA or Phantasy Star Online
- The tutorial is a bit long, but not as painful as it could be
- The english dub consists of a lot of amuteur actors, resulting in a lot of awkardly voiced NPCs and cutscenes
- Not enough variety in races for characters (in a world with giants and Goblins and fox people, why do we only get humands and elves and one giant to play as?)
Pros:
- The world is just the right size that running around on foot is still manageable and fun thanks to the fast and fluid movement of the characters
- Rich character customization and at least 14 characters to choose from now, some which are just gender swaps.
- Housing system that's as functional as it is fun to decorate
- The chat amity system encourages actually talking to NPCs and finding quests instead of just being handed everything like other MMOs do
- Plenty to do other than just combat.
- System reqs aren't that intense, if you can go beyond the game will look absolutely stunning
- Easy to solo, but great with friends
- The cash shop is quite reasonable with mostly quality of life kinds of bonuses for purchase.
- No monthly fees
- plenty of in-game opportunities and mini-games that make it possible to get cash shop or rare items

I'll preface this with the fact that I've played the original XCOM: UFO Defense for DOS and absolutely loved it. So some of this review will be from a fanboy perspective, but I'll try to also give some objective feedback.
TLDR;
This is a nice and fun game, but if you don't like strategy, especially turn based, or if you do like strategy and are looking for a deep and realistic simulation of defending the Earth from an alien invasion this isn't for you. If you are a fan of the XCOM series and are ok with a simplification of the tactical and strategical mechanics you should get this.
Now a fanboy rant.
Probably the thing that outrages me the most is how few units you send in for the missions...
Technician: Oh hey Aliens are terrorizing Paris, we're the best defense against them how many troops should we send in?
Commander: 4
Technician: 4? 4 people to take out some force that travelled the stars and has way better technology than us. I know our guys are good, and that craft can definately take 6 people
Commander: 4, one of them has to be promoted to a Captain then we can send 5, then one has to be a Major before we send in 6
Technician:  WHAT?! We're possibly talking about the fate of the world and you want to send at most 6 outgunned people to defend a large city? We could arrange transportation for a dozens to get there in time and possibly with some armored vehicles.
Commander: Send in only 4 people
Overall, even if this wasn't an XCOM game or in the similar vein, this is a fun and very polished game. The story is pretty good (especially for a turn based strategy, the DOS predecessor didn't have much of one). Some game mechanics are very simplified no ammo mangement (though you still have to reload), how many units you control, and the cover system. However, a few things are complex like what actions/abilities can be used and if they consume the turn or limit what else you can do in that turn.
To that effect, this game is not a terrific tactical combat game as it is very simplistic in that regard. You have at most 6 units (unless you manage to do some mind control) to command and they have 2 'actions' per turn. The rules get complicated as some things will consume both actions if used first such as attacking, some require and use both actions meaning the unit cannot have moved this turn. Then there's some abilities/traits on your soldiers that change those rules, like run and gun lets you use both actions and move and then attack, and I believe another allows you to attack twice in a round, or attacking doesn't use up both actions.
Another issue is that at least by default, is that unless you are very much flanking an enemy, like at a right angle or more to their cover your positioning has very little effect on your units accuracy. There is a modifier (which might be available from the start as an advanced option) that is suppose to give penalties and bonuses based on the angle (for both you and the enemy) though I haven't tried this.
I'm assuming because of the small squad size (4-6), that the single player has the enemies lay dormant until you first spot them, or vice versa. When this happens the aliens basically get a free move (even if it was their turn and they spotted you) to get into cover and are then active (will roam the map to look for you if for some reason you leave). You might be lucky if you have already ordered a unit to be in overwatch AND is able to see the alien(s) during this free move to get a shot off on them. Other than that, there isn't really any ambushing the aliens. And while this normally keeps the ratio of active/attacking enemies to your units balanced, you often active another set by accident when trying to manuever against the current one. And then there are roaming patrols, usually on crash sites, that do move around the map but when spotted still get the free move. So you can find yourself activating one set, and while moving to attack them activate another, and then during the alien's turn a roaming patrol comes in and sees you and gets a free move into cover. Good luck taking down a dozen (or more) aliens around your 4-6 soldiers.
When it comes to the Strategic gameplay, between battles, it is also lacking. The major decisions are what to research first, what base modules to build and where (when you have money). Their are UFOs that fly around and can be detected and intercepted but the detection method is weird. You launch satellites to cover a country and somehow the satellite only sees inside the country's political boundaries, not a more sensible geographical area. The satellites are also your main source of funding, a country won't give you money per month unless they have a satellite, oh but each country gives a different amount. Thus a satellite over Japan covers a very small area but one over the USA covers a huge area, including Alaska but is somehow blind to anything in Canada. Each satellite costs the same to make, but you are limited to how many you can have up at once which you can increase by building a module.
Aside from the ocassional UFO spotting, you will get (at times random) missions from command. Some actually develop somewhat of a plot but for the most part provide you with some resources. Also I believe once per month you will have an abduction event in which the aliens  are abducting in 3 different countries and for some reason you can only go for one of them. Each country will give a different resource along with increased standing, assuming you are successful, and will lower relations with the 2 you didn't help. Later on there are terror events but they only occur in one spot but are difficult and have this rescue civilians before aliens kill them mechanic.
Now, sigh, about the soldier class mechanic (which wasn't in the original DOS). I will give some credit for being a bit unique as all but 2 of the level ups require you to make an exclusive choice with no respec option. Meaning that 2 soldiers of the same class and level may have different abilities (if you so choose). The bad part is that what solder class you get is completely random (unless its a reward from a mission you will know the class beforehand). While you can get around this by hiring and firing soldiers, the problem is when you hire them they are Rookies and have to get enough experience to level up before they are assigned a class. Also which class they are usually locks them into a specific type of weapon. The assault class is the only exception which can go back to using assault rifle type weapons.
Continued Fanboy rant
The game does play good homage to the original DOS series, but the detection system is convoluted. It is interesting to note that the original was made in the UK and because your detection in that game was geographical the best place for your first base is in Europe. Because while the US does give you the most funding and would at first seem the most logical to defend, the UK, France, and Germany are just below and in total give way more funding than the US alone. However, the system in this game that is limited to borders, favors starting with the US quite a bit since they give the most money and covers the most territory (I think, if not its a close 2nd). While your first base also gives you the continent bonus, starting in Europe or others is still viable.
There are only so many static maps in this game. I'll grant you they are pretty and quite a number of them, but after several missions you will notice you are playing the same map you played before (though maybe entering from a different point, enemies are different and in different spots). The original DOS version basically had tiles that were put together randomly, for every mission (except base defense and the last 2 levels). The aliens were all active (for the most part, some would stay inside the UFO) moving around the map opening doors and all.
That game sure if fun, more than minecraft. :D

宇宙人と遠隔兵器で戦うターン制戦略ゲーム。
個人スコア9.5/10；戦略性10/10；中毒度10/10；運ゲー＆所見殺し7/10
ノーマルでEnemyUnknownをクリア後、クラシックでEnemyWithinをクリア。
序盤が難しく、金欠とエイリアンの蹂躙の挙句、徐々に内政や兵器改良が安定して自分の育てたレンジャーで無双していくゲームです。
戦闘面で特徴なのは、命中率とダメージが非常にシビアなところです。ダメージはほぼ相互確定破壊です。大体、序盤は二発で相手が死んで、一発でこっちが死ぬ関係です。難易度クラシックだと命中率８０％でも弾が当たらない時は当たりません。１ターン前で何度セーブ＆ロードしても当たりません。そういう仕様になっています。（だから、クラシックを終えた後は、もうインポッシブルやりたくないです。運ゲーを感じてトラウマになってしまいました。）
兵士は死にやすいですが、基本的に第二波などでモードを変えなければ戦闘中でセーブ＆ロード出来ますので、難易度はシビアでもセーブ＆ロードすれば初心者でも俺戦略ＴＵＥＥＥＥ！な感覚を味わえるゲームです。兵種もスナイパー、ヘビー、サポート、アサルト、サイボーグ（ＤＬＣ）、超能力者など役割が多様で、常に最善の一手を打つ戦略性の強いシステムになっています。
経営の戦略性も大事です。内政面ではどんどん装備を強化しないと、敵もどんどん強くなってこっちが負けて詰みます。また、世界中に評議会あり、その地区のエイリアン侵略を止めないと脱退してお金が入らなくなります。衛星の打ち上げで評議会が安定します。兵隊を強くするか、内政に使うか、効率よく金の使い道を振り分けないと任務が遂行出来なくなったり、資金源が途絶えたりします。「次にこんな部隊を作らないと」「衛星打ち上げないと」というプレッシャーがかかりますので戦略性も中毒性もたまりません。
最終的には「ぼくのかんがえたさいきょうのぶたい」が出来上がりますので、平均的に少年心が強いゲーマー達、買いです。

Short version:
This is the best zombie themed game I've ever played. If you are looking for a good zombie game, stop now and buy this game. Enemy variety, tons of weapons, fantastic platforming, solid combat, great horror elements, at least 50+ hours of content. 9.5/10. Buy this game!
Long Version:
I have to give credit to the developers of Dying Light. In today's era of everyone complaining about nothing being original and developers mainly trying to fulfill these complaints, the developers of DL knew what we REALLY wanted. A solid game that takes the best of many other games and fuses them into one.
The core gameplay is a FPS platformer much like Mirror's Edge, but with a refined system allowing you to climb on basically anything. As a general rule in this game, if you can see it, you can go to it. This alone makes the otherwise normal-sized map MUCH larger than it appears, adding lots of depth to exploration. Later into the game, a grappling hook mechanic is introduced, which will make you feel like Spiderman, zipping around the map with ease.
The combat is extremely solid and mainly revolves around melee. I feel this is a much more accurate representation of a zombie outbreak when compared to titles like Left 4 Dead (no running around with machine guns with near-infinite ammo). Guns are rare but powerful, and handle well in combat. In this sense, the combat resembles Dead Island a lot, but feels more refined to me.
The item system is based off a color-coded rarity mechanic similiar to that found in games like Borderlands, which allows you to know if a weapon/item is worth picking up at a glance. On top of this, weapons can be upgraded and modified, adding an extra layer of depth and customizability. Most weapons fit into 3 groups: One handed, two handed, and guns (guns cannot be modified).
This game also involves heavy RPG elements reminiscent of Tomb Raider, with 3 seperate skill trees devoted to parkour, combat, and quests. Characters won't necessarily be unique, as at the higher levels, all skills can be purchased, but this definitely adds more depth to an already massively deep game.
The story is fairly generic, with nothing really shocking or surprising. This is to be expected though, as the zombie outbreak story can only be done so many ways without becoming ridiculous (looking at you, resident evil). As referenced by the title of the game, the story involves the now-familiar 'zombies are more aggressive at night' idea. In addition, special 'volatile' zombies appear, which are extremely deadly and will chase the player around, adding an element of horror to this. The player is encouraged to brave the night with special bonuses to XP occurring only at night, and certain missions only completable at night.
It goes without saying that the graphics are georgous, as this is definitely a next-gen game in that sense. The visuals are solid and consistant, with a full day/night cycle, weather effects, fancy-but-not-intrusive film and blur effects, etc. The sound is fantastic, adding to the overall theme of the game, and definitely contributing to the horror at night.
The 4-player co-op works great, little to no lag, and is very fun. Only issues I've had are some microphone issues, but are relatively minor. The multiplayer PvP is a little odd but not bad. I don't have much experience with this mode so can't comment much on that.
I was extremely surprised at the level of polish and depth in this game, with only tiny little nitpicks here and there. It is very apparent that the developers looked at successful mechanics in popular games (Mirror's Edge, Borderlands, Tomb Raider, Dead Island, etc) and integrated similiar mechanics into their design, resulting in a game that feels completely rounded. This game flew under my radar when it first released, and I received it as a gift for christmas 2015 and started playing it with no prior knowledge. This game really deserves all the praise I could pour on it, and more people should check this out.

Well here's a mixed bag of treats if I ever saw one.
Long story short: this feels unfinished. I can smell HBO's influence and rushing the devs to get this out a mile away.
Pros:
+ Great story so far. No complaints about that. It's certainly Game of Thrones with people dying all over the place simply for the shock factor.
+ Great voice acting. Props to the cast (and the new characters) for doing such a professional job.
+ For me, I like that there is no hand-holding. The story picks up at the Red Wedding and if you haven't watched the first three seasons/read the first three books, you'll be 110% lost.
+ Feels like I'm watching an interactive movie.
Cons:
- The illusion of choice. Your, erm, "choices", do not change the course of the story. The story is still good, mind you, but it's like trying to change the direction of a train by throwing pebbles at it. The choices you make are more for your satisfaction as a gamer than anything else.
- The art style is cool, I guess? But the animations and graphics in general just feel so unfinished! Especially facial animations (particularly mouths). They're dreadful.
- Can't adjust mouse sensitivity? Controls consequently feel sluggish.
- Feels like I'm watching a movie -- I have no control over how the story progresses or where it goes.
Final recommendation: it is worth picking up....at half price or less. Perhaps with the next episodes the choices will become more meaningful, and it'll be worth picking up at full price.
Let's just say I'm glad I liquified my TF2 inventory to pay for this title.

Send out hapless rookies to shoot aliens. Watch the rookies miss and get cut down in a hail of plasma fire. Send out more hapless rookies to throw grenades at aliens, grenades don't miss. Kill the aliens, take their stuff, reverse-engineer it, build plasma weapons for your rookies and promote the rookies to snipers who can shoot across half the map or rocketeers who unleash massive destruction. Now with psionic powers and nanomachines!
The game is very very streamlined compared to the original X-COM:UFO, sometimes a bit too much. "Reload" is a simple action, no more inventory micromanagement of ammo clips, which is good. But when your medic is critically wounded and bleeding out, it gets annoying to realize that the "use medkit" function doesn't actually involve a medkit item that can be picked up, it involves a special ability of the unconscious medic that nobody else can duplicate.
Overall, a few nits like that and the weird sidestep mechanics when firing from cover are not enough to ruin a nice game of small squad tactics. Make sure to check out the Long War mod for more of everything, too (and experience your troops being cut down in a hail of plasma fire again after Long War turns the difficulty up).
Good luck, Commander.

I have played this game on PS3 (even HDN mk2 and HDN Victory) and I'm so happy which I can play it on PC, this game it's a remake of Hyperdimension Neptunia for PS3, so some stuff it's different (with all the changes seem almost to play a different game, even the story got a lot of changes):
-few DLC,  you can get all for around 6 €, (this it's when i have written this) the original game (the one on PS3) have around 90 DLC and it cost me over 80 euros to get them all....
-the intro movie and song changed (for my tastes i think the song was on the PS3 game was better)
-The combat system is identical to the one found in Victory; this change make the combat more fun, the fight in HDN for PS3 take a lot of time, (more easy you play and more long are the battles) better use of items, you have to use sp to change in HDD mode (on the original game you have to do a combo to transmorm, but the "action point" you use recharge to full every turn), magic require "action point" like any attack (on the PS3 game all the magic got by the CD are orrible).
-you cannot change the difficulty of the game (for my point of view I don't like how was set the difficulty on the game, for what I understand play hard mean monster stronger but with less hp, play easy and you get weaker monster but with a lot of hp and that take to enless battles)
-many graphical changes (the HDD transformation had a movie on the original game, the map you use to move it's different, the NPC are not a black silhouette anymore)
-Dialogue has changed much from the original, with updated references and special events taking place not found in the original game; i think some voice actors changed too (at last I feel the voice of Neptune different).
-The transportation system works the same as in Victory and mk2 (on the first game on PS3 you have some location to select for event or dungeon and to go to other landmasses there is a little dungeon you have to do everytime).
-In-dungeon abilities are identical to Victory; players can jump and the search sphere is back as well.
-Re;Birth 1 gets treated as yet another dimension, as characters from other worlds make an appearance.

宇宙人と遠隔兵器で戦うターン制戦略ゲーム。
個人スコア9.5/10；戦略性10/10；中毒度10/10；運ゲー＆所見殺し7/10
ノーマルでEnemyUnknownをクリア後、クラシックでEnemyWithinをクリア。
序盤が難しく、金欠とエイリアンの蹂躙の挙句、徐々に内政や兵器改良が安定して自分の育てたレンジャーで無双していくゲームです。
戦闘面で特徴なのは、命中率とダメージが非常にシビアなところです。ダメージはほぼ相互確定破壊です。大体、序盤は二発で相手が死んで、一発でこっちが死ぬ関係です。難易度クラシックだと命中率８０％でも弾が当たらない時は当たりません。１ターン前で何度セーブ＆ロードしても当たりません。そういう仕様になっています。（だから、クラシックを終えた後は、もうインポッシブルやりたくないです。運ゲーを感じてトラウマになってしまいました。）
兵士は死にやすいですが、基本的に第二波などでモードを変えなければ戦闘中でセーブ＆ロード出来ますので、難易度はシビアでもセーブ＆ロードすれば初心者でも俺戦略ＴＵＥＥＥＥ！な感覚を味わえるゲームです。兵種もスナイパー、ヘビー、サポート、アサルト、サイボーグ（ＤＬＣ）、超能力者など役割が多様で、常に最善の一手を打つ戦略性の強いシステムになっています。
経営の戦略性も大事です。内政面ではどんどん装備を強化しないと、敵もどんどん強くなってこっちが負けて詰みます。また、世界中に評議会あり、その地区のエイリアン侵略を止めないと脱退してお金が入らなくなります。衛星の打ち上げで評議会が安定します。兵隊を強くするか、内政に使うか、効率よく金の使い道を振り分けないと任務が遂行出来なくなったり、資金源が途絶えたりします。「次にこんな部隊を作らないと」「衛星打ち上げないと」というプレッシャーがかかりますので戦略性も中毒性もたまりません。
最終的には「ぼくのかんがえたさいきょうのぶたい」が出来上がりますので、平均的に少年心が強いゲーマー達、買いです。

This game is amazing fun with friends for its simplicity! Easy to learn, hard to master. Definitely worth a try at least, consider the pros and cons yourself:
Still reading on? Let's look at the components individually then, starting with my most valued three: gameplay, storyline and replayability.
Easy to grasp, hard to master. I play this game to relax for a short while, which is marvelously accommodated by the game's mechanics. There are no extensive skill trees. Skill is something you gain through practice. At first you cannot hit a thing. After a while though you will be able to pull off trick shots. Then comes the art of catching. Only to be crushed by meeting a player who already perfected those skills... So you have to practice more and become pro yourself!
Personally, I did not reach the pro stage yet, but I do love coming back and practicing. ^^
The game does not contain a storyline, period.
Except perhaps for the one offered in arcade mode. Nevertheless, you are sure to gather some memorable moments: The first time you pulled off that elusive trick shot, that on-fire super streak, obliterating the other team in elimination mode and so on.
Why do I not mind the lack of a storyline? Because I simply like to play a little, which might actually be hindered by an in-depth plot.
I want the feeling that I spent my money wisely when purchasing a game. A game can be worth its money if you play it a lot, either by coming back to it several times, or playing it for one longer period of time. For RRDDD, it is a bit of a mix, coming back frequently (daily) for a short time (~10 min).
Let's make a quick calculation:
Purchase €5,-
Hours played: 171
Cost / hour: €5,- / 171 ≈ €0,03
Honestly, there are not many games that make that rate. Not to mention you can actually earn back a little through collecting, crafting and trading. I may rest easily at night again, knowing I did not waste my money on this one.
Flashy! No literally, it is flashing. The lights are synchronous to the music playing currently (covered next). I cannot stress enough how all aspects come together and fit the style of this game perfectly. The vivid colours are just one example.
Of course, do avoid if you're light-sensitive, but there is an option to switch this off.
Sure, the visuals do not consist of graphically astounding realistic scenes, but would you go to a blacklight party to see amazing environmental scenes?
The music is another fine example conveying the disco vibe. The best part is that the lights synchronize with the music playing. You don't like the original tracks included with the game? Just play your own music then! What more could you wish for when it comes to music in a game?
As a matter of fact, when it comes to the OST, it is a habit of mine to include it with any purchase. Contrary to other OST, I actually played these tracks once to get into the feeling this game offers. Certainly a plus for the music.

This game is actually incredibly good, I personally think. The combat system is nice, the travel and dialogue system is also cool. I like the "choices=consequences" sub-genre, and this is a shining example.
Unfortunately, the game suffers from a majority of extremely annoying setbacks, such as practically no background info on the extremely weird world you play in, a tutorial that quite simply DOESN'T explain in detail how to play this game properly and finally that it sort of just ends right when it was getting exciting.
It seems cheap to me, to end the game where it ends. Like they sold me half a game, and now expect me to buy the sequel. Which I probably will, so of course, there is nothing wrong with their marketing tactics...
You're expected to make educated choices without having ANYTHING to base those choices on. You. first of all. do not know anything about this fantasy world, you try to plan trips but you're not really informed how many times you can expect to be able to resupply on your trips.
Someone in your group of people, must necessarily have been somewhere and have a clue that a village is coming up in the next 3 days or something, right? Alas no! Everytime you come to a village, it's like it's the first time that village has ever been discovered, even though you're somehow leading the people along a road you're familiar with.
To get back to what I like about the game, the consequences are severe and brutal. Very harsh. You can, like in Mass Effect 2, essentially get pretty much everyone killed. The story goes on - it just gets sadder.
I really didn't like one of the main characters, so I just sort of.. Got rid of that character. My entire game experience was improved as a result. Win!
All in all - This game is very good, but expect to have to do a test run of the game.
Sit down, play for a full hour and call it a tutorial - Don't ever load/save. Just play. Then, restart the game now that you get it, and have SO much more fun with it, than you otherwise would.
Would recommend!

I want to try and tell to english-speaking audience why I like this game, an why they should (or should not) play it.
First of all - for some people in ex-USSR countries this game is something like half-life 3 for everyone - we waited it long enough to be happy to get it. Even if it's not perfect, it's still what we waited so long.
Well, where to start. Once apon a time in the year of 2007, on anonymous imageboard 2ch.ru (now closed) one of the visitors posted a picture he draw, of a young girl with blonde hair. People liked it, so he draw more pictures of her. Later, he moved to another imageboard, and with other talented people decided to make a game. It should have been an adult game with USSR-attributes, becase many people grown-up while there was USSR, and had a good memories about their youth.
Well, it was easier to decide than to do. They started. And there was a lot of promises. A lot of waiting. A lot of drama. Changes in the team. Leaking of not ready game. A LOT OF EVERYTHING. So, when, after all this years, game was published to steam, a lot of people was like "Wow! They really did it!".
Now, the reason why I writing this review. Should you, or should not, play it? Well, if you wondered what is "imageboard", never leaved in ex-USSR countries or just don't like visual novels - probably not. Not that you can't like it, it's about feelings, that is the same for everyone. Also, you probably should not play it, if you expect just a game with lot of boobs. It has gone far from the original idea of adult game, and even though it has boobs, and you may even find adult-patch in the internet, it's still not the main theme of game.
If you are (or ever was) alone, if you live (or ever lived) in ex-USSR countries, if you ever visited imageboards (or even still do) - you can really enjoy this game, I recommend it to you. Or even if you just curious to see, what non-professional developers can do. And if you waited too long for this game to be made - you probably already played it)
Now, something about this game, not connected to this story.
Graphics has problems. It's not because it's bad, but because many people worked on this game on different time, so you  can see the difference between scenes. Not a big problem, but I needed to say about it to impartial. And the backgrounds is so beautiful, you may play the game just to see it!
I don't afraid to say that soundtrack for this game is brilliant. I just love the main theme, based on soviet pioneer's anthem. I hope you would enjoy it too.
Well, as often in indie projects, it's the weak spot of the game. Nice idea, a lot of good humor (but many of it connected to imageboards, so not everyone would understand it. And I have no idea, how good english translation is), and the target audience would certainly share the feelings of characters. But... holes in the plot, unjustified twists, and other mistakes of a beginning story-teller can spoil you some fun. I still like it, because I somehow belong to the target audience, you know :)
Oh, whatever, just play it already, it's free. Even if you have nothing to do with imageboards, never was neither young nor lonely, and believe russians have a pet-bears and wear hats with ear flaps whole year long - there is still something in the game you may like)

Child of Light is a family-friendly game that is written all in rhyme, designed to be played as 2-players side by side (so parents, maybe this is how you enjoy games with your kids rather than shooing them from the room so you can play Saint's Row - or worse, letting them stay in the room with you and play all your M-rated titles)
At best, CoL is a beautiful combination of painting and poetry, which can teach young players some basic platforming and turn-based RPG elements, with a competent adult actually doing the playing, the little player 2 can enjoy the narrative and do a few things that are much needed, once they are shown the way.
As an adult, playing it by yourself, will you enjoy it as much? Well, probably not, which isn't to say it's a bad game, after all, you will be able to see how much work has gone into making this game, and while it may be simple, well that's all the more credit to it, it's a smart design and it doesn't overcomplicate things.
Just, do not, I repeat, do not, under any circumstances, buy oculi. I bought the entire bundle of them along with all the other micro-transacion DLC, but without really knowing why. I guess it's just something we're used to seeing from AAA game devs, and we've been letting them get away with it. (I bought the game and DLC on sale though, otherwise I wouldn't have had even a passing interest in this based on other peoples' reviews that all gripe about Uplay.)
So what are oculi, then? Well, they are gems, that go into sockets on your weapons and armor, each having a small stat benefit, and they are craftable within 3 tiers. They drop in the game as well, so if you don't buy them, don't worry, you get them included in the game already, and for the price of a couple dollars for 3-4 of them, really, you can't let yourself get ripped off like that. It's not like you have to seek out the hardest difficulty setting, there is a casual mode, and really, that's the only way I think it should be played, so you can enjoy it for what it is, and put the evil "Corporate Commander" EA / Ubisoft, out of your mind.
Pros:
- Painted beautiful artifacts in the game, back to front
- Simple, but logical puzzles and turn-based RPG combat
- Gem crafting is straightforward (It's a good thing to have in the game, not a good thing to be nickle and dimed to death over)
- The game's entirely written in poem, so while cheesy, it can produce entertainment
Cons:
- The Golem and other DLC are BEYOND DOUBT content that was supposed to already be in the game, but was gouged out to make more DLC microtransactions
- Uplay can be invasive, especially if you don't have a bunch of Ubisoft games (I don't) and CoL will not launch from steam, so Uplay has to be running and you have to have an account
- Some people reported bugs and lost save data from Uplay, I have not as yet had it happen to me.
Final Verdict
7/10 - The gameplay is solid, if simple. The creators of the game put a lot of time, effort and talent into producing this game, it's just such a shame that their work is tainted by the greedy actions of corporate cronies pulling at our pursestrings.
