Tl;dr: Parkour with zombies, decent with friends.
Dying Light is a(nother) zombie game, in which you run across rooftops killing zombies in... sorry, can't remember where the game takes place; I think I fell asleep during a cutscene. As the last sentence may have implied, the story is completely unengaging and boring, with horrendous pacing and forgettable (lack of) characters. You play as boring standard Americano short black hair semi-military guy "Crane" and you're a double agent or something. Doesn't matter really, since the game assumes you're not paying attention anyways and puts huge orange beacons at your every objective and destination.
So it's another zombie game. Which implies you kill zombies. Which you do, by the truckload. The game has a... wonderful combat mechanic in which you press one button to smash weapn on zombie until dead. Of course, since this is 2016, there's of course a skill tree which gives you more ways to smash (or drop-kick) zombies later on, but still: you don't sell your game well to people if you introduce one of the main elements, combat, by having the player pressing one button until victory.
But Lying Dight is also a parkour game! You can run across rooftops, make leaps of faith between buildings and jump off huge towers before landing in a pile of trash taking no damage. But since you're playing as Crane, the most out-of-shape special operative on the planet, you climb walls slower than my grandfather (he's actually in pretty good shape so bad comparison) and can barely run 30 meters before stopping to gasp for breath, usually in the middle of a horde of zombies. "But klamrisk, there's a skill tree for parkouring!" Yup, which admitevily does give you cool tricks (that cost more stamina) but does NOT give you long distance running perk until close to max level. Thanks. Overall, the parkouring is slow and requires minimal input and reaction times, which takes away most of the thrill of parkouring. It's almost as if it was made for controller based inputs, like a games console. Speaking of consoles....
The field of view in this game is horrendous. And you can't change it. No, being able to change vertical FOV doesn't count. This is probably because this seems to be a console port, but that doesn't make this any less of a problem; a lot of people feel sick while playing on low FOV, one of my friends being among them, which didn't make for an enjoyable experience when we played together. Furthermore, a low FOV on a PC game makes you see less of the things around you, which is just greeaaat for parkouring. Speaking of not being able to see things, the post-processing in Flying Blight is abysmal, often taking up a huge part of your screen, making you see even less of what's going on around you, which is greeaat in a survival zombie parkour game. I turned off all post-processing the game's lacking options allowed me to and the game became bearable to play. Before that, with motion blur and all that shennanigans on, I might as well have been playing blindfolded.
But Buying♥♥♥♥♥♥♥is a game with multiplayer focus, so maybe the story stuff and fluff can be forgiven (no) and it could be a cool multizedslayerapocalypticon experience? Well, yes, to a degree. The experience is certainly enriched by playing with your friends. Not only do they shout at you for being ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, a lot of the mechanics makes way more sense in multi, such as protecting the guy lockpicking, vaulting over each other's heads, clearing big hordes of zombies more effectively as well as loads and loads of challenges of varying degrees of fun. But the game still insists that all of us are the same boring♥♥♥♥♥Crane guy, we have to be all at the same place on this big open-world map to pick up or progress ANY quest (seriously, wtf?) and there's no customization or personalisation beyond differently coloured T-shirts. I wanted to play as Michelle Obama running around killing zombies looking for revenge for Barrack, just like Fallout 4. No such luck (and it ain't that important really), but whatever, just adds more blandness to this already pretty bland game. I suppose you can invade other people's games as a zombie during night which is pretty cool end-game type of stuff I guess but meh, I'd rather play Left 4 Dead 2 for that kinda stuff.
The music is decent, but there's way to little of it and I've heard it loop around several times already.
Now to end this review with positive things. Looting and scavenging is moderately fun, especially when trying to lockpick a car when surrounded by zeds, and the weapon system is actually decent. You're always scavenging for weapons and parts, 'cause all of your weapons eventually break. Forever. No need to save that delicious orange upgrade for later, try it now! Also, while you're at it, make some burning ninja stars and cryo grenades! It's pretty fun and would have kept you on your toes and made you rethink to maybe opt out of some zombie fights.... if weapons weren't so abundantly prevailent. Seriously, you can find purple-rated weapons literally everywhere, strap burning pants to it and then it's a walk in the park.
Overall, Crying Heights is a pretty casual zombie sandbox, with several bad design desicions, to play with your slightly inebriated friends.

As many people have mentioned, this game only gives you the very false sense of choosing your own path, while forcing you down an extremely linear story line.
I tend to be one of those gamers that normally, when faced with a choice, will save the game and see where each choice leads.  Unfortunately, that is not an option in this type of game.  If you make a choice and do not like the outcome, you are forced to sit through the ENTIRE session of dialogue leading up to that choice, which can range from 5-20 minnutes at times because of the horribly placed autosaves and the fact that you are not allowed to skip dialogue that you've already seen before.
Now the first thing of note IS the fact that you cannot skip dialogue.  If this is supposed to be a choose your own adventure game "where the choices you make matter", most people would play it multiple times through to see what impact the different choices you make have on the story.  But solely by not allowing people to skip the standard boring dialogue scenes greatly dimishes the replay value, because when you are forced to watch the same scene 2-4 times in a row just to choose a different answer makes the game EXTREMELY boring and repetitive.  Even their older games (i.e. Back to the Future) allow you to skip dialogue, so if you have played the game before (or decide to reload because you didn't like your outcome) you could fastfoward through all of the chat screens to speed it up.  This is not the case with Game of Thrones.
Now, on to the fact that the game IS NOT A "CHOOSE YOUR OWN ADVENTURE GAME".  Dealing with reading the same text over and over again COULD be reconciled by the fact that each choice you makes changes the game dramatically.  But honestly, most of the time the choice you pick doesn't have any significance, leading up to your character saying something and the opposing NPC giving you a completely off the wall response out of nowhere.  Or, at their very best, you get 1-2 lines of unique dialogue corresponding to your choice, wherein they proceed to launch down their original path of dialogue with no regards to anything you have said to them before.
Point of fact, as a very particular gamer, anytime I had a dialogue choice and picked a response I did not like, I would reload my game.  And sit through 10 minutes of cutscenes and inane chatter.  Only to lead up to me picking a different response and getting THE EXACT SAME LINE OF DIALOGUE I had gotten with my other choice.  Rinse, repeat.  Same deal.
*Spoilers may follow*  In this episode, there is in fact only one choice that matter.  Who you choose to be your "Sentinel" (basically, the Hand of the "Lord of Ironrath" aka ripoff Hand of the King).  And this really affects nothing other than the very last scene of the episode, determining where you meet Ramsey Bolton (Snow) or who you meet him with.  Granted, there are other choices you can make during the game that MAY affect further episodes down the road, but for a company/game that touts "The choices you make affect your gameplay experience" they are getting extremely lazy in developement.
There are a lot of scenes in this game that while the dialogue was happening, I knew what choice I would pick.  And then you dont get the option.  (Spoiler, if you have a very serious diplomat versus a very serious warrior, why would you alienate one over the other instead of choosing them both to be your advisor?)
This game is an extremely forced and contrived story so far, where you opinion doesn't really mean anything.  Telltale Games is basically just cashing in on franchises now, and pushing out a product that, while overall has very good quality, doesn't even come close to a "Choose your own Adventure" type game, which is their biggest selling point.  What they sell now basically equates to watching a 90 minute cutscene, where they stop to let you choose a response to a question and they either humor you with 1 or 2 lines of dialogue in response, or completely ignore what you've chosen and continue on a pre-determing path of dialogue.
Overall, as a fan of Game of Thrones, I liked the game, honestly.  But I don't like Telltale Games as a company.  They are becoming complete sell-outs with no respect for their original property, where its becoming more important to release and episode quickly than work on quality.  And what that results in is a very Linear story where they can't afford to create different story paths because they are so focused on pushing it out quick.
(Spoilers)
Just in this episode alone:
**I don't even have a number to point out how pointless the QTEs are in this game.  I've played through the prologue multiple times to try and save the Lord and nothing changes.  You can fail half the QTEs and the scenes are basically still the same as if getting them right.  Not to mention the fact that they even throw in some QTEs that you CANNOT win just to try and show off some new button presses and gore. (AKA the soldier choking you out and then you throwing him under the horses, or picking up a sword and getting knocked down like a punk every time)
1. Even in the very beginning prologue, no choice that you make matters.  Talk as much crap to the Lord as you want. Be  a horrible person to the other squire. None of it matters.  The only real choice you can make here is to save the other squire when he refuses to listen to you and spouts the same blatant response of "carry the wine" to you each time.  If you save him, he shows up in further scenes during the prologue (although it CAN be very hard to make him out as of after this point he really doesnt matter).  If you choose to leave him, you still sit around the wine trough and watch him die, the camp goes to hell, and you run through the exact same sequence except the Squire will be replaced by a random NPC and you will receive 1** extra dialogue sequence where they ask what has happened to him.  Because in the midst of the battle, the Lord is more worried about some random squire than all of his other people combined PLUS his eldest son who he was just begging you to look after.... RIGHT...  And considering the dialogue sequence leading up to the wine gathering where he basically promotes you from a squire and asks you to look after his eldest, he REALLY doesn't seem to care that much because the plot REQUIRES him to die.
2, Why is Gared (the first main playable character who is very quickly forgotten about) forced to ride to the wall?  This IS supposed to be a "Choose your own adventure" game, right? I would have had him stay and confront Lord Whitehill, or at the very least have a conversation with Lord Ethan.  But instead you are basically forced to leave the city (in order to further their plot line of the "North Grove cannot be lost").  Even his Uncle is like "You need to leave now, this story can't stand up if you don't leave no matter what."
3.  Your dad dies.  Awesome.  No matter what you decide to do, this entire scene has no purpose other than to progress their story line.  You arrive, 3 people on the farm have murdered your father, and no matter what you do you are forced to kill the first guy (who coincidentally is a Whitehill soldier).  You can choose to spare the next one, but it really doesnt matter at all, you're gone.
4.  Lord Whitehill...  No matter what you say to him, he is an a$$hole and doesn't care about anything you say.  You can't appease him (like your uncle wishes) and you can't stand up to him (like your Man-at-Arms wishes).  You may get a different dialogue line depending on if you lick his boots or not, but it changes nothing for the story.
I won't even name anymore.  You can look at any walkthrough for the game and it will show you the choices that you can make, and then immediately proceed to tell you that said choices do not matter.

A review of this game that I read on another site was remarkably illuminating as to the issue of "do your choices matter", both for this and other Telltale games. The story is going to go in the same general direction and along the same general lines no matter what you do, so you should feel free to make decisions as the character, not for the character.
Ultimately, that should be why you play this game... to determine who the character is, why they do what they do, what's at the core of them. Are they a vengeance-driven warrior or a peaceful and pragmatic soul caught up in violence? Are they a smart and canny politician-to-be or just a desperate and helpless fish cast adrift in a pond full of sharks? Are they a waffling little child shirking their duties or do they take their status as lord of a noble House seriously?
These are all storytelling choices that the game allows you to make, because that's really what this is... an interactive story. The fact that some events are predetermined means that you can focus on characterization rather than what will gain you the most favorable outcome. (C'mon, we've all played an RPG and made choices that didn't fit how the character should be played just because it would get us more gold or avoid an annoying fight or keep a well-liked NPC alive or whatever.)
I mean I'm not saying it's some grand, revolutionary, sweeping idea that every other game should emulate. I just think it works out nicely for what games like this and The Wolf Among Us and so on are. Whether intentional or not, the immutable aspects of the story give you a chance to develop the characters as you think they should be, not the way they have to be to get an achievement or some extra gold or the hidden ultimate weapon the Stick of Truth or whatever. The game is in influencing the characters, not the outcome.
Basically, if you're coming into this with the idea that you want to "win" the game with the choices you make, you're approaching it from the wrong viewpoint. You should play this to experience the story, not to pit yourself against it. It's not an adventure game, it's an interactive television show. That said, they could still work to make your choices branch the storyline more, but I suppose that's the limitation of doing a fully-voiced production... if it was just 3D characters using text they'd probably have a lot more freedom of storytelling, but it also wouldn't be nearly as immersive. (At best, it would wind up like Skyrim or Fallout, where you have plenty of different ways to interact with characters... but all those characters are voiced by like six people, because that's all they could afford at that amount of studio hours.)
Anyway, short version: Not an adventure game, hack-and-slash, or "winnable" game, it's an interactive story. Don't go into it playing to win, go into it to enjoy the story, and you should have a great time.

A remake done right, XCOM: Enemy Unknown is a superb reboot of UFO franchise, boldly combining the traditional approach with modern elements of gameplay.
Organization XCOM is formed by world's leading nations in order to research, investigate, respond to  and exterminate the increased UFO activity around our planet. The story is not as cliché as one might sound, as the feelings of dread and vulnerability are masterfully combined with initiative to protect our home and discover the true meaning behind the intruder's invasion.
As a commander of XCOM, you will not only pull the shots once it comes to finances and research projects, but actually command your troops on field, as they storm downed alien vessels and face the horrors of menacing foreign soldiers which survived the crash. Will you be able to take them out? Research their technologies? Take live prisoners? Strike their weakest links? Or will your favorite soldiers lose their lives and leave you alone with a bunch of inexperienced rookies in base? So many decisions, yet everything is intuitive and reasonable.
Despite being so great, the reboot of the series seems to have the same weakness as the original UFO titles.   It features games of revolutionary quality followed by insultingly shallow entries.  The original UFO: Enemy Unknown  ended up with  XCOM Interceptor. In case of XCOM: Enemy Unknown, we had to endure XCOM:Declassified, a FPS with lame writing and complete lack of understanding of the game's pacing and atmosphere.
Final words? Buy this game, and hope we get a sequel in the next few years!

I received this game as a gift and have not been disappointed!
The Banner Saga has a very Nordic feel to it as well as beautiful animation (reminiscent of the Hobbit movie from the 70's).
The game started out a little slow for me at first. The gods are dead, the sun isn't moving, and everyone is generally uneasy, but the pace picks up quickly snowballing, I often felt, out of my control. But I'm pretty sure that's the way you are supposed to feel while frantically trying to protect your people from the scary invading bad guys. (My friend commented, "You know what these guys need? A wall to the north like Game of Thrones." And it does vaguely have that vibe, except they're relentless armored baddies called dredge instead of relentless icy undead or whatever.)
So between the unique battle system and my tendancy to form attachments to fictional characters, I was soon hooked. I tend to play games for the storyline over the combat, but fortunately The Banner Saga is strong on both. The choices you make affect the storyline, often with surprising repercussions. And there's enough mystery and odd happenings to keep you going. In combat you must always be aware of the relationship of the enemy's armor and strength versus your own. If you don't break down your opponent's armor, you can't take down his strength. If you lose too much strength yourself, you can't hit for any amount of damage. It seems logical and straightforward enough, but knowing when to do damage to armor or strength can really be an art. I found the battles challenging at first, but as gameplay progressed I began to find them quite fulfilling. Fight the dredge! Fight! *ahem* Sorry...
I am very curious to see how they resolve or explain those things such as why everyone hasn't floated off the face of the earth due to lack of gravity because the sun is not moving. Or the gods being dead. But mostly the sun, because I feel like that's pretty important.
All in all I feel this is a pretty balanced and enjoyable RPG and I stronlgly recommend it. Especially if you love Norse mythology and vikings. And giants. Because the giants are baddass.

My first ever game review here; and I will explain shortly why this is the case.
I normally don't bother writing reviews for anything because when I write a review, it is usually serious and well thought-out, and that takes time. A lot of time.
Now why did I bother to write a review this time, for this Free-To-Play (eroge?) game no less? Because the contents of this game totally (and very surprisingly) entertained and amused me for the past few hours I played it from start to finish without so much as a pause.
Now, I don't play eroge games often. In fact, I never played one, until Everlasting Summer that is. I simply played this game because, well, it's free; but also because the other reviews heavily favours its storytelling over the visual aspect of the game. Curiosity got the better of me, so I thought, "Why not? First time for everything, right?" Well, I will tell you readers right now, that my past few hours playing this game was well spent. And so is the time fleshing out this review at the moment...
It isn't just the storytelling of this visual novel that is entertaining. The music is very good given that this is a Free-To-Play, and they really suit the atmosphere of the scenes. The only complaint I have about the music is that sometimes you get electric guitar solos playing durings scenes where the characters appear to be playing an acoustic guitar - totally immersion-breaking. But otherwise, for the majority of the game the music is awesome and very well laid out.
What adds more to the atmosphere is the writing style. If you can turn a blind eye over some grammar/spelling mistakes (which there are very very few considering how much text this game contains), the descriptions of emotions, sceneries, thoughts and atmospheres etc are very detailed and beautiful. Perhaps when coupled with the background music or sound, you really start to feel lost in the story as you dive into it.
Perhaps the only major complaints I have about this game is that it takes at least an hour or two (in your first playthrough) before you really start to get past the "introduction" of the story. During my first two hours, I came real close to stopping for a save and perhaps continue it, maybe 2 months later or something... Because of the slow-paced nature of the story, but also I was getting tired of the narrator describing every single emotion or feeling he feels for every piece of dialogue he is engaged with, whether he's speaking to or listening to someone. In that sense, there is a degree of repetition which can get annoying. I feel that if I get to make more choices rather than make a single choice every 10 minutes of reading, it would make things more interesting at least.
However, if you managed to get past the initial 2 hours or so (depending on how fast a reader you are of course), you will find yourself making decisions that somehow make you wonder if they really make a difference... Which I can assure you that they do. I have only played through this once so far and I happened to get the "good neutral ending" because my decisions were based on what I would actually do if I were to be myself (i.e. I wasn't trying to be a bad Johnson flirting with every chick in the game). In fact, I was actually trying to hook myself up with a specific character but because I made a small blunder trying to get to know the other girls first, I ended up giving up the opportunities to learn more about the one girl I was going for... (And I didn't know the story only lasts for several ingame days rather than weeks...) So all in all, if you're aiming to date one of the girls, shoot for her at every opportunity you can get, because if you miss your chance, you may very well have to restart your game to win her heart.
Long story short, this game is simple in design; perhaps at times too simple, but it mimicks certain aspects of real life (other than you seem to be the magnet of every girl in the game) in a sense that if you lose your opportunity, you might not recover from it at all. And at the same time, the storyline isn't hell-bent on chasing after skirts. Like I said, I ended up with the "good neutral" ending albeit unintentionally. And I won't spoil you, but even the good ending itself contains a plot twist...
In terms of replayability, I would say if you are a completionist or you like choice-based storytelling games, and definitely you aren't foreign to reading tons of texts, then you will certain feel at home with this one. However, give it at least one go if you don't mind the occasional cleavage or panty shot. As for me, I am definitely replaying this. (Not for the cleavage and panty shots, although those can be the icing on the cake, perhaps?) ;)

I have just finished the game and I have to say I am so in ♥♥♥♥ing aw that I have to write this review.
The good:
+ Art style and animations: The game is visually incredible. The hand-drawn animations are splendid in cut scenes, dialogues and combats.
+ The atmosphere: The Banner Saga’s mood is somber overall and it goes perfectly well with the art direction. Also, there is something so captivating about watching tiny people marching through the frozen mountainous land.
+ The soundtrack: Emotionally and eargasm material, the music contributes a great deal to the atmosphere of the game.
+ The characters: Most of the characters in the game are fascinating with compelling background story. Too bad the story is short and some characters don’t stick around long enough for you to know them better.
+ The lore and setting: The developers has established massive and in-depth lore which you can read about or discover as the game proceed. I find the Viking setting of the game quite unique and remarkable.
+ That ♥♥♥♥ing boat scene.
The so-so
+/- Gameplay: The Banner Saga uses a combat system resembles some classic SRPG games with a twist. You use a party of maximum 6 heroes to fight in a gridded, chess-like field. Each characters has 2 main stats: Strenght and Armor. Strength determine an unit’s health and attack, meanwhile armor determines your defense. The more strength an unit has, the harder he hits and vice versa. The more armor you has, the less damage you will take and you can ward off an attack completely if your armor is significantly higher than the attacking unit’s strength. Doing armor damage does not reduce health but it does reduce the enemies’ defenses, thus makes them more vulnerable. In addition of strength and armor, each heroes also has willpower. Willpower can be spent to make an unit move farther, deal more damage or using special ability. You and your opponent take turn to move and take action until there is one last person standing of either side. The less people you has in play, the more actions 1 character can take, so you can use 1 or 2 powerful characters over and over again before the enemy can react. Imho, the turn order is the biggest exploitable flaw in the combat system.
The caravan section demands you to balance between your supply, renown and morale of your clan during your journey. Supply sustain your clanmen and army, the larger your caravan, the more supply is consumed each day. If your supply reaches 0, the number of people in your caravan and your morale will diminish harshly with each day passes. Renown is the only currency in the game, which can be used to upgrade your heroes, buy equipment or buy more supply. Morale determines how well your heroes perform in combat, high morale give you booste in willpower during combat and vice versa. Your morale will slowly recede as your caravan travel but it can be boosted by halt your march and rest (consumes however many days worth of supplies you spend resting). The resources in the game are extremely scarce and play brutally important role on how your game progresses.
+/- Difficulty: The game is hard and unforgiving, even in the beginning.
+/- Story and narrative progression: The campaign is line near, but as the story processes, you will be given various choices, some are petty and insignificant, some are morally difficult and make huge impacts on your journey later on. The game is short and seems a little bit rushed, but the replay value is huge with the variety outcomes of the array of decisions given throughout the game.
+/- No permadeath: You may still lose your heroes outside of combats as a result of a wrong decision.
The bad:
- There are some minor bugs that may occur during combat, which can be irritating at times.
The Banner Saga is one of the best strategy game I have played in recent years. It is an extraordinary visual-audio experience but it could use some improvement in the combat system.
Strongly recommended and looking forward to the sequel

Tl;dr: Parkour with zombies, decent with friends.
Dying Light is a(nother) zombie game, in which you run across rooftops killing zombies in... sorry, can't remember where the game takes place; I think I fell asleep during a cutscene. As the last sentence may have implied, the story is completely unengaging and boring, with horrendous pacing and forgettable (lack of) characters. You play as boring standard Americano short black hair semi-military guy "Crane" and you're a double agent or something. Doesn't matter really, since the game assumes you're not paying attention anyways and puts huge orange beacons at your every objective and destination.
So it's another zombie game. Which implies you kill zombies. Which you do, by the truckload. The game has a... wonderful combat mechanic in which you press one button to smash weapn on zombie until dead. Of course, since this is 2016, there's of course a skill tree which gives you more ways to smash (or drop-kick) zombies later on, but still: you don't sell your game well to people if you introduce one of the main elements, combat, by having the player pressing one button until victory.
But Lying Dight is also a parkour game! You can run across rooftops, make leaps of faith between buildings and jump off huge towers before landing in a pile of trash taking no damage. But since you're playing as Crane, the most out-of-shape special operative on the planet, you climb walls slower than my grandfather (he's actually in pretty good shape so bad comparison) and can barely run 30 meters before stopping to gasp for breath, usually in the middle of a horde of zombies. "But klamrisk, there's a skill tree for parkouring!" Yup, which admitevily does give you cool tricks (that cost more stamina) but does NOT give you long distance running perk until close to max level. Thanks. Overall, the parkouring is slow and requires minimal input and reaction times, which takes away most of the thrill of parkouring. It's almost as if it was made for controller based inputs, like a games console. Speaking of consoles....
The field of view in this game is horrendous. And you can't change it. No, being able to change vertical FOV doesn't count. This is probably because this seems to be a console port, but that doesn't make this any less of a problem; a lot of people feel sick while playing on low FOV, one of my friends being among them, which didn't make for an enjoyable experience when we played together. Furthermore, a low FOV on a PC game makes you see less of the things around you, which is just greeaaat for parkouring. Speaking of not being able to see things, the post-processing in Flying Blight is abysmal, often taking up a huge part of your screen, making you see even less of what's going on around you, which is greeaat in a survival zombie parkour game. I turned off all post-processing the game's lacking options allowed me to and the game became bearable to play. Before that, with motion blur and all that shennanigans on, I might as well have been playing blindfolded.
But Buying♥♥♥♥♥♥♥is a game with multiplayer focus, so maybe the story stuff and fluff can be forgiven (no) and it could be a cool multizedslayerapocalypticon experience? Well, yes, to a degree. The experience is certainly enriched by playing with your friends. Not only do they shout at you for being ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, a lot of the mechanics makes way more sense in multi, such as protecting the guy lockpicking, vaulting over each other's heads, clearing big hordes of zombies more effectively as well as loads and loads of challenges of varying degrees of fun. But the game still insists that all of us are the same boring♥♥♥♥♥Crane guy, we have to be all at the same place on this big open-world map to pick up or progress ANY quest (seriously, wtf?) and there's no customization or personalisation beyond differently coloured T-shirts. I wanted to play as Michelle Obama running around killing zombies looking for revenge for Barrack, just like Fallout 4. No such luck (and it ain't that important really), but whatever, just adds more blandness to this already pretty bland game. I suppose you can invade other people's games as a zombie during night which is pretty cool end-game type of stuff I guess but meh, I'd rather play Left 4 Dead 2 for that kinda stuff.
The music is decent, but there's way to little of it and I've heard it loop around several times already.
Now to end this review with positive things. Looting and scavenging is moderately fun, especially when trying to lockpick a car when surrounded by zeds, and the weapon system is actually decent. You're always scavenging for weapons and parts, 'cause all of your weapons eventually break. Forever. No need to save that delicious orange upgrade for later, try it now! Also, while you're at it, make some burning ninja stars and cryo grenades! It's pretty fun and would have kept you on your toes and made you rethink to maybe opt out of some zombie fights.... if weapons weren't so abundantly prevailent. Seriously, you can find purple-rated weapons literally everywhere, strap burning pants to it and then it's a walk in the park.
Overall, Crying Heights is a pretty casual zombie sandbox, with several bad design desicions, to play with your slightly inebriated friends.

I'm very happy with the overall design of this game.  My favorite features are the large map and lush scenery.  Also, I like how you don't have to keep buying town portal scrolls (like in other games) - you just get to cast a portal for free as part of your basic controls.  The inventory design is a bit retro, with each item consuming a certain size and shape of your pack space.  This adds to the challenge of inventory management.  Another cool aspect is one of the reasons I bought Grim Dawn - the skill tree allows you to combine traits of several character classes instead of being locked into one set of abilities.  For example, I can have close combat abilities from my Nightblade PLUS the option to summon creatures with my Occultist.
The only thing I dislike at this point...is my personal portals disappear when I exit the game.  This means I have to make it a goal to reach one of the preset portals in an area before closing the game down.  Sometimes, it's just not possible - I have to re-clear an area's enemies the next time I boot up the game.  When I have to leave for work, I gotta go!  No time to make it to the nearest area's portal.
I bought this as a huge fan of Torchlight II a similar game which I've put at least 300 hours into) and I'm very satisfied with Grim Dawn so far.  I'll give it a 9/10 with a point off for the inconvenient thing about portals.  I highly recommend Grim Dawn, with highlights for replay value!

Pros:
Beautiful - The lighting and animations gave me a constant eyegasm.
Sound/Music - Original and themed very well, suspensful when it needed to be.
Immersive - The game lives up to it's title.
Cons:
Controls - They were bad, I don't think the interact/push/pull key should be combo'd with catchledge/getonladder key.
Glitches - Many animation glitches.
Camera - The way it autofollows is frustrating. I'll be inbetween doors and the camera will just lock to one side.
Resolution - Minor gripe, but it doesn't actually support true ultra wide (2560x1080), you'll get black bars on the side
Length - I'd have to say it's too short to pay full price for this game, catch it while it's on sale.
Conclusion:
This game grew on me gradually as I progressed through it. There is definitely some deep atmospheric vibes that got my heart pumping and very few of these moments relied upon "jump scare" cheap tactics. There is no talking in the game, so the game does it's best to reveal to you an impartial story of which you'll eventually be left to draw your own conclusions, I don't hate or like this, it's just one of those types of games.
The controls got me irritated more than once, there were many times where control dexterity and timing were important to progress but I felt like the controls weren't polished enough to warrant such mechanics in the game. Perhaps that's part of the charm of the game. The controls weren't so bad that it's unplayable, far from it. But the issues are there.
I experienced quite a few animation glitches as well. I'd say a glitch every 5 scenes/levels. At one point I found myself out in the open and the baddies couldn't grab me despite having full access to me. I've had door closing animations stuck in repeat, which really killed the immersion.
The game is so short, like most of these style of games, I always find that I really start to enjoy them just as they are ending.
Overall, it's worthwhile to play to experience the story, the artwork, the animation and the suspense but has some issues. I'd give it a 7/10.

I found this to be the best game I've come accross in the past few years, definitely worth to get it.
- Excellent Co-op experience
- Great combat system and game mechanics
- Amazing art and music
- Offers challenge to a wide variety of people
- A lot of entertaining quests and conversations
- The possibility to have multiple characters/companions with some rather unique set of skills
- Quite much entertainment for money spent

- If you're not so experienced with similar games, the first 5-6 levels can be a very rough start
- Personally encountered very minor graphical bugs here and there (they might be not as widespread though, my friend doesn't have them)
- Sometimes the controls and positioning can be a bit off (easy to misclick in a combat and waste points on movement instead of attacking, backstabbing position seems weird quite often, relatively hard to see where the environmental effects begin and end)
- While conversations are amusing, some might find there are way too many quests involving jokes and puns.
- Really addictive. When your friend in co-op tells you the second day in row: "Dude, did you realize it's 6 am already?", then you know you spent too much playing the game.
I'd definitely suggest to buy it, but for the maximum level of entertainment you should get a Co-op partner too with voice communications - possibly one that's willing to read through plenty of conversations and play during same hours as you do.
If you're anything like me and not really familiar with games like these, you might want to read up on basic game mechanics - such as sneaking, stealing, pickpocketing, the reactions of elements in combat, weaknesses of different opponents - otherwise it might be a rather tedious start. With a sub-optimal party you might run into trouble in the first couple of levels already.
The game itself offers a wide variety of skills and classes (at least I'd consider it so nowadays) which results in quite good combat scenarios, the only thing that can be a bit of a letdown if the randomness turns against you - but that's part of the game.
Aside from combat, there amount of quests, side-quests and just interesting NPCs is just incredible. Many of them will basically require you to do some sort of investigation based on what you're learned through your conversations, sometimes you might just have to talk with dozens of NPCs to find out who can help you, sometimes it takes several minutes to find that hidden switch or logic to progress to the next part of the quests. Which is really a good experience from the old times, seeing how almost all the new games will save you from using your brain at any cost.
The level of details is very good as well. There're towns with multi-leveled buildings, each of them have dozen of items like tables, chairs, cups, knives, paintings, quill, ink and whatever you can imagine. Some of these you can steal and vendor, others can be used for crafting! You can even move most of these.
The art and voices are pretty good and the music is just perfect. Really the only thing that annoyed me was the sounds of characters speaking in caves, there's a weird echo to it, but it's nothing major.
While the positive things by far outweigh the negative in this game, I do have to mention some of the annoyances - although these might be fixed soon enough.
One of these annoyances are the downtimes between battles and conversations, when you're basically doing nothing but traveling. The default movement speed on your characters are pretty slow, while there're waypoints to help that, often you just have to move back and forth between NPCs to find out what to do. It's the same thing with healing between fights, feels just like a pointless downtime (although I can see how it could be exploited).
Other than that, there're some minor things, such as it's hard to see when are you actually going to step on an environmental effect (you might think your character can pass right near that little blazing grass, but sometimes it'll set you on fire) and there seems to be a little inconsistency between host and a co-op player on where some of the enemies are facing - this and the very small angle at which backstab works can make the life of Scoundrels a nightmare early on.
A friend of mine and me spent almost 30 hours with this game so far and we can't see the end of it yet. We might still create new characters once we finish, as we didn't even get to try crafting properly yet, or the quests where you talk to animals, or a lot of characters, or the steam workshop, or many of the other things this game can offer!

Do I recommend this game?
Well. Yes and No.
Yes.
Because the game is fun. The combat is fun, leveling up is fun, doing quests is fun, finding and completing plans is fun, battling bosses is fun, finding a strategy that works is fun, late-game is fun, doing all that kind of stuff is fun. I can say with confidence that there isn't really a moment in the game where you don't have anything to do. There are always plans to complete, there are always tougher bosses you can try and take down, there are always quests that need doing. And once you've done all that, you make progress in the campaign and suddenly you're flooded with things to do again. So there is a lot a content here, you don't just get a sword, kill the bad guy and woop-dee doo you saved the world. There is a lot more to it than that, which I can say happily, but unfortunately, this is heavily weighed down by other factors, if you'd like to keep reading.
No.
Because of the heavy, and when I say heavy, I mean heavy-as-a-ton-of-bricks rehash of assets.
This includes:
-Monsters
= 9 times out of 10, a new enemy in a new zone will just be the same enemy you've already seen in another zone, just but the colour has been changed, the name has been SLIGHTLY changed and the stats have been increased.
I can not stress enough how annoying this can get at times. So picture this, at the start of the game, you encounter tulips and weird dog things in a park styled zone. Makes sense, right? Those are the sort of things that you can roughly associate with that area. But imagine later on in the game, you go into a tech themed area and you see that SAME plant, just with a different colour and slightly different name. You'd probably be thinking "Oh look. It's that same plant again. Woohoo".
But the worst crime is that this doesn't happen just once, oh no, it happens A LOT. Like, a LOT a lot. Almost every enemy follows this pattern, and it's a darn shame to be honest. When you FINALLY encounter a different enemy, you will be like "Oh game, you're so nice to have treated me with this oh so precious new enemy".
-Zones
= A lot of the zones are just a zone that you have already seen that has either just straight up been copied and pasted or has been changed a SLIGHT bit. In a similar way to the monsters, this can get mighty annoying. Some areas are exact copies of other areas.
Here's another reason for 'No'.
So, you buy this game, have fun, complete the game, and the game says "Hey. You can do a 2nd run. How does that sound?" and you'd probably think "Great! It's a New Game+! I know a bit more about the game now, so this should be more fun" or something along those lines, right?
Oh, and when you think of New Game+, you think of starting the game from the beginning, with most of stuff such as levels and equipment, but the enemies have been buffed so that it's a more tough and grueling game that really challenges you and pushes you to your limit? You might be reminded of something like Borderlands 2, with the True/Ultimate Vault Hunter Mode, right?
Well, unfortunately, that is NOT the case with this game, and that's a big stinking NOT. Tell ya why? Because the 2nd playthrough (not even gonna say New Game+ because it's not really worthy of that title) has you fight the enemies that have NOT been scaled up in difficulty. So, what is the point in letting me restart the game with all my stuff, if you're not gonna make the enemies harder so that I'm not completely OP to the point where I can EASILY kill bosses that are supposed to kill you in order to progress in the campaign? You know those bosses, you lose but you don't actually lose and the campaign continues? Yeah, those ones. I was curious to see what would have happened if you had killed that boss at that point. The game recognised it in the same way as if I were to have lost and continued on with the story anyway. So, yeah.
So, if you're going to go for a second playthrough, implying that you have already done most of the plans and quests on your 1st playthough, you will blaze through it. Which is really sad to be honest.
And another thing. There is a choice, between Japanese and English voice actors. The Japanese voice actors can have you saying "Shut uuuuuup" at times, esspecially Compa. Her VA makes me angry. The VA's for the older characters are good from what I heard at the start. I went with the English voice actors because I felt that they did an overall better job with them, and I could actually understand what they were saying in battle. Oh, but you were thinking that I was gonna end that there on a good note, huh? Well guess what? The English voice actors didn't voice all of the main story, so there will be random segments of the story where it is just silence, unless you want to go with the JVA's, at which point I said to myself "I'll just read the bits that are silent."
Oh and don't get me STARTED on those DLC characters. Jeez. They're just OP. Shamelessly OP. Don't get them. Save your money. They're not only cheap in price, but cheap in pride. Just a big no. Not only are they OP, but they are CPU's and can use HDD, which is sorta like a super mode. So yeah. They play no part in the story at all and they level up faster than the other characters, being a good 5 levels ahead of my other characters by level 20.
Summary:
Get this game IF (and that's NOT a reference to the character IF in this game):
-You've looked at some gameplay and have said "Yeah, it looks fun".
-The game is on sale OR you've got too much money sitting around the place.
-You can look past the OVERWHELMING AMOUNT of repetitiveness of this game, which honestly takes a lot. I managed to look past it at first, but it wittles you down over time.
If not a single one of the following critera are met, do NOT get this game. Otherwise, do. It's a pretty solid and overall decent game, it just could have used some more TLC and a bit more time in the oven.
From a personal stand point, I've given this game a thumbs down. This is because of the reasons above. But I did enjoy myself, but looking back, there are a lot of things that are wrong with this game.
That feels like all, and it feels like a lot off of my chest. Thanks for reading and I hope this has helped.

How RNG works in this game:
- Unless you have a 100% hit rate, it's ALWAYS 50/50: you either hit or miss the shot. Never let those % fool you. Grenade is exception though.
- The above rule applies to enemy shots. But you never have a 100% chance to avoid getting shot by an alien because you cannot see the number.
That explains scenarios I have encountered (these happened more than I can remember):
1. My soliders miss a 96% hit chance shot, or a 90% chance stun.
2. My soliders get a 13% hit chance shot landed and crit an alien.
3. An alien one-shot (with critical) my soilder who is behind a full cover on a higher ground, with smoke grenade covered.
In short, I highly recommend this game because I cannot think of any other cons except the broken RNG system. A MUST PLAY strategy game!
Just try not to let the ridiculous RNG ruins your mood and you will always enjoy the game. And yeah, good luck on Iron-Man mode if you REALLY want to suffer from the RNG god :)

Now that ive actually played quite a few hundred hours i can finally put a realistic perspective about the good and bad things that surround this game.
PROS
Hunting, Gathering, Life skills, all that stuff that other reviewers rave about IS actually kind of neat if you have the patience to actually get into them.
Combat. Probably one of the best combat systems i have ever seen in any mmorpg.
Graphics. Graphics are absolutely stunning and honestly doesnt need an ultra high end PC to run this game fully. However towns get laggy no matter what.
AFK- you can literally afk and make money.
CONS
Marketplace- Honestly, this one is just so toxic. Everything is pre-valuated on the marketplace so that even if you wanted to sell something for cheaper than the other 500 listings of the same product, you are restricted of doing so and must hopelessly list your unsellable item. Basically waste time and money. On top of this, if you are ever planning on buying your armour on the marketplace to get good enough gear for node wars.. etc, GOODLUCK. It is honestly ridiculous, they have a bidding system that is the worst RNG cancer i have ever seen. You will have more lucky getting struck by lightning then getting armour that is viable for node wars through the marketplace. AND FINALLY, the pre-order system is absolutely absurd, You cant see other people's pre orders, so you basically have to guess how much the previous pre orders are and HOPE FOR THE BEST, and on top of that you might not even win the RNG battle because when the item gets registered, it has 50/50 chance to go on marketplace, or to go to hgihest pre-order. People pre-order 3m things for like 80m, its absolutely disgusting.
Grind. - As much as people will defend the fact that this is a grind game and thats just the reality of it, they are right. But this fact alone is sad. It really should not be the case for such a beautiful game. They ruined THAT aspect of it. Grind to be good. Or invest thousands of real life dollars.
Loneliness- I think the combat alone is fun, but gets EXTREMELY repetitive. Unless you got some friends to play with, be prepared to be extremely lonely.
Endgame PVP - Node wars is almost one of the only end game pvp things you can do, which doesnt make sense to me considering this game is so based around being a PVP orientated MMORPG.
Thats it for now, until i continue playing and get better GS i will report back and continue this review.

XCOM's a great example of turn based tactical gameplay done right with a nice selection of difficulty settings and loads of replayability to be found both in the base game, its mutators and the honest to goodness actual expansion pack Enemy Within. Also mods if you are of that persuation ;)
in XCOM you take the role of a commander tasked with organizing earths defense after having been invaded by an at first overbearing alien force. Through the "XCOM project" you will be able to draft the best of the best in the name of Earths defence and slowly beat back and uncover the reasons for the aliens sudden interest in our planet.
But you all kinda knew that already, so what can I tell you that you'd like to go into the game knowing?
The game can be said to be a kind of paradoxical badass-simulator; paradoxical in that you both have been given the most powerful infantry military assets of the world to play around with while you at the same time are expected to blow the aliens to goop in every instance they appear. The keyword here is expected as just a few mistakes during combat can turn not only the specific combat instance very difficult to come out of on top, but can to some extent make the rest of your playthrough difficult by way of both losing important team members or funding nations deeming your abilities lacking. Dying is for real and you will lose people the minute you missplay. Between that and the "kind of" difficult (as in nobody will tell you how to do it effectively leaving you to figure it out as you play) construction and researching meta game, to stay a badass you either will have to load yourself out of unwinnable situations, or actually be a total badass to begin with :P. There is little to no room for error and you WILL have to learn how to play well to make it past both easy and normal difficulty, This is not a bad thing of course. The game makes some effort to teach the players basic tactics during combat and the pacing is such that even if a restart or two is required you'l learn eventually :)
If you have not played the originals, know that they are more fidgety and have an UI that would make DOS blush. Enemy Unknown is streamlined both for better and for worse, with some things like base management being a bit easier, and characters having less options in combat regarding movement. Soldiers have more or less the same stats (without mutators) and level up from killing beasties, giving them perks and stat boosts much like in an rpg. Soldiers have hp, aim and nerve basically and gain some every level based on their class. They get skills to based on class. Medics can heal more often and throw smoke grenades while heavy soldiers carry heavy ordonance to battle. Planning out one or more effective teams is important to beat difficult enemies, and the game allows players to field whatever they think will work best, rather than forcing certain picks out of them becoming very enjoyable once enemy types and class strengths become apparent to the player.
Compared to others in the genre XCOM is both stellar while also being a bit samey. The game relies on its intuitive nature rather than hand holding allowing players to reach proficiency on their own (and in their own way), but what it essentially always comes down to is your ability to kill all the aliens. About 90% of the missions main objective is to go in and shoot all the enemies, and while that is nice, games such as Lotr: The third age (from the time of not bad EA titles) offers more in variance between missions.
That's not to be said missions don't take on different forms. Between defusing bombs, infiltrating downed ships and rescuing civilians there is lots of variety to be had, but all these become sub-objectives to "kill all aliens" in all but the bomb defusing case (there are some levels that differ but they are uniqe and very few).
The reason for this is probably (to some extent at least) that every turn, both you and your enemies are allowed to move every one of your active characters. In your case this means all your soldiers always, but in the enemies case this only means discovered aliens. Aliens not yet discovered will move around a bit but stand idle and uninterested in the fog of war, up until being discovered when they will throw on their most convincing growl, act very surprised and bolt for cover.
This adds one level of tactics for the player to explore while removing another.
To some extent, there is tactics to be thought when both positioning and moving your troops. Preferably you want to flank "activated" enemies while avoiding finding more groups, which can be both fun and tense :)
However, having all aliens standing around in small cliques on the levels makes such senarios as attacking scouting parties or flanking around already heavily defended positions activities that have more to do with imagining what three thin men were doing in a certain position, or how well the surprised group entrench themselves on the fly rather than on carefull planning or recon from the players side. The tactics at this point become more about exploiting the AI than studying the map, but its still good fun and creeping forward is still tactical, just not in the same way.
Bottom line:
i missed covering a lot of stuff, but you get the general idea. Shoot many aliens but be smart about it in a nice entertaining package.
I reccomend this game if you are okay with the slight sameyness and expectation to get progressively better as you go.

I have played numerous of MMORPGs for years now, and I definitely recommened playing this game if you enjoy playing MMORPGs, or if you're not very familiar with this genre but want to get into it. For the price, its worth it or the amount of content of gameplay.
• There are various choices of different classes and builds depending on your playstyle.
• The character creation is very detailed and you can spend a lot of time creating your character if wanted (I spent an hour).
• The combat mechanics look and feel amazing, which is my personal favorite of the game. You do combos by remembering key patterns, but luckily there is also a hotbar to place skills like most games of this genre.
• The overall graphics design is stunning and looks very clean compared to others. Especially the skill animations.
• The story line is interesting, and the main quests and side quests are not ridiculously stressing but more so balanced and rewarding. Some take more time than others. The quests give you equipment, inventory slots, energy, contribution points, and other things to help you with your game progression.
• There are unique features such as having workers, crafting, enchanting, and etc. Skills like gathering, fishing, alchemy, cooking, and etc. Similar to Runescape if you are somewhat familiar with the game.
The game itself at first is fairly easy to begin with, and in time gets a bit more grindy, talkative, and you travel alot (but thats like any other MMORPG). The grinding (PvE) begins to change as you level higher and higher. 1-56 shouldn't be too difficult. 56 and above is when things REALLY begin to change. Exp rate is... depressing. Very grindy. PvP end game gets pretty crazy and you need to be well prepared/geared. Once you hit level 50, PvP is enabled once you leave safe zones. Be ready for random fights over grinding spots or just because people want to fight lol. Doesn't happen too often, but will happen. This game may have situations that will be confusing to understand and get the hang of things, but as you become more familiar, it becomes extremely addicting to play and full of enjoyment. There is alot to do in this game. Actively playing or while you're away and afk. Whether it is doing life skills or grinding or questing or boss faming. The community is awesome, helpful, and you'll see some funny♥♥♥♥♥stuff on the server chat time to time. Don't go on the RP one..

I suppose there are already a lot of reviews for this game that either give it a formal break down or a short affirmative "thumbs up," so I feel the need to add my two cents to the "random but heartfelt thoughts" reviews.
About a year ago, I decided to update my Dad on first person shooters. His only previous fps experience was CoD2 (which he plays about once a year). I wanted to convince him that the fps genre was always evolving in new and interesting ways (and that it was reasonable for me to continue spending ungodly amounts of my time on them :)). Together we explored vast, beautiful worlds and intense plots. I was choking on nostalgia through all these experiences that had once made me feel something worth while... but I don't think that my Dad ever felt like he was having a valuable experience until we visited good old Half-Life 2.
We didn't play for very long. In fact, we stopped playing before we even made it to the manhacks. The writing was much cheesier than I remembered. The dystopian world was stuck in the shadow of the other, more modern worlds we had experienced in our previous play sessions... and yet we were more involved with this world than with the others. I'm not exactly sure how to say what this game does right without describing the same things that make many others games great, but I'll give it a try.
This game makes you feel like a badass. Now, I know that's what most shooters set out to achieve, but Half-life 2 does it really, really well. You still have that traditional-shooter-power-structure-thingy where your metaphorical♥♥♥♥♥♥gets bigger as you progress, but this game also isn't afraid to take the things that you've earned away from you or show you that they can't be used for every situation... and this makes you feel like a bigger badass! The satisfaction of playing a baddass combines with the satisfaction of being a badass combines with the satisfaction of solving a puzzle combines with a reward in the form of a new weapon or suspenful or triumphant story beat... this game doesn't just try to get one moment right, it adds a bunch of other moments to get right at the same time.
Well, that answer felt a bit vague... but at least it was random and heartfelt! In short, my dad and I had a fun afternoon playing Half-life 2. Anticipation can be a double edged sword. You get that stuttering, spine tingling feeling, so excited from the potential of something, but equally fearful because you glimpse something with such promise that you pray for it to live up to it, knowing how many times you’ve been disappointed before. This was the sensation I had when I first heard about Child of Light. Knowing the creators of Far Cry 3 were taking a brief step away from triple-A development to work on a smaller downloadable title sounded improbable, but very exciting.  But once I witnessed the jaw-dropping announcement trailer powered by the same graphical muscle behind the equally gorgeous and flamboyant Rayman Origins and Legends, I was immediately grabbed by the premise. I had my reservations, like my surprise that the publishers of the mega-franchise Assassin’s Creed would green-light this smaller project on a whim and whether the gameplay would eventually be a turn off for me, someone who has played very few JRPG’s. But that’s the incredible thing about Child of Light. It never failed to surprise me.
Like a classic bedtime fairy tale, a calming chime and the voice of a whimsical woman heralds us in the opening moments, telling the story of Lemuria and the fall of this prosperous kingdom. A young girl named Aurora mysteriously falls comatose, causing her father to slip into illness from grief. She awakes in a mysterious land and the story begins, Aurora setting out to reunite with her father.
The story is wrapped around a layer of iambic pentameter, presenting this almost Shakespearean prose with grace and ambience. Never in a game have I seen the writing take such center stage in the presentation. Whether in the several pre-rendered story cutscenes or traveling around Lemuria, you never go long without another sentimental and enjoyable piece of poetic lyric to accompany your journey. As a lover of well written situational poetry, I love how well the lines sync up with what you are doing at that moment, really adding to my enjoyment. The cast of characters may seem like generic fairy-tale characters, but their personalities were interesting companions for Aurora’s coming-of-age story. With a lovesick mouse, a helpless poetically challenged jester, a cowardly dwarf and more, the cast is colorful and varied, really allowing me to lose myself in this fantasy world. The firefly Igniculus isn’t a standout, but on top of serving numerous gameplay purposes, seems to be rather clueless and curious to aspects of the real human world. Aurora herself seems a bit spoiled at first, but quickly grows into the hero of her story. She helps the citizens of Lemuria, but always stays fixed on her goal of reuniting with her father. Her troubles at the end of the game after taking the whole journey with her made me care about her struggle. While it missed several story opportunities, it still provided a compelling reason to push through to the end.
This was where my fears initially began to creep in. As I said, I’m not very familiar with JRPG’s or turn based gameplay in general, but the promise of the game allured me to keep an open mind. Simply put, the gameplay is sublime, simplifying the often-muddled ambiguous speed stats and who attacks first with a simple bar with moving icons on the bottom of the screen. The red end of the bar represents when you can make a move. This bar seamlessly tells you when you can attack and when your opponents can attack, allowing you to make decisions of what action to take. Every action, from using an item to casting spells has a cast time simply laid out from Instant to Very Long. Your opponents speed must be considered with every action, especially since if you are attacked while casting, you are interrupted, canceling your action and sending you further back on the bar. Mix this in with defending, status effects and attacks that hit multiple people at once, and you begin to see how this deceptively simple combat maintains it’s speedy pace and complexity. It’s easy for anyone to pick up, but true masters will learn the speeds of each adversary and know exactly when to interrupt, when to make gutsy plays and when to play it safe. You must always think two steps ahead to maximize your damage and minimize the damage you receive. You can only have two characters out at a time, and while I wished to eventually be allowed to use three, it may have made the game too easy. There are also skill trees and equipable stones to craft and upgrade the abilities of each party member. The skills are pretty varied and useful, but it made me wish for an even greater array of skills to upgrade to, instead of just endlessly upgrading the same abilities.
Other aspects of the genre blend perfectly into the overall formula. The game mixes in puzzling and platforming elements as well between fights. The puzzles are simple fun, but won’t really provide much of a challenge. They also lack variety, with puzzles mostly boiling down to pushing blocks on a switch or casting shadows onto walls to open doors and activate objects. You quickly gain the ability to fly, naturally encouraging exploration for hidden items and chests in the sky and underground. Health is a bit too plentiful, but environmental hazards and hidden enemies keep you on your toes frequently. You also have Igniculus, a firefly companion who proves useful throughout the entire game. In combat he can slow down enemies and heal your allies. During exploration and puzzles he can open distant chests, light dark areas, activate switches, as well as letting you get the jump on unsuspecting enemies, yielding positional advantages on the bar for a Surprise Strike. A second player can control Igniculus, but unless you fully cooperate with your partner to maximize his abilities you may be better off by yourself.
The gameplay rarely is difficult on Normal difficulty, but on Hard mode even a common enemy can inflict greater damage, with boss battles becoming a thrilling challenge. A New Game + option evens the odds, letting you carry over your stats in a second playthrough.
Child of Light is a living, breathing poem and painting, with the soft voice of melancholic, child like wonder bringing you to a different place entirely. The Ubi-Art Framework engine that provided Rayman Legends with such vivid and colorful backgrounds are even more stunning here, with every distant mountaintop, forest, underwater grotto and nightmarish castle painstakingly delivered with a painterly, handcrafted feel.  The beauty and underlying danger around every corner compliments the calm atmosphere of exploring this world. The music is another major highlight, with an orchestral score evoking the mystery and danger of Lemuria, as well as the build-up necessary to show Aurora’s coming of age. There are also some opera-esque pieces for dramatic combat sections, which really give an epic feeling to the boss battles and major fights. It’s one of the most memorable soundtracks for me in recent memory, with numerous tracks coming to mind even after finishing the game.
The measure of a masterpiece does not come from a singular element. It is achieved through the seamless melding of every aspect of the creation into one, cohesive vision that artfully sends the message of the artists. Child of Light is a wonderful and beautiful game, uncompromising in it’s commitment to it’s writing choice. The visuals are gorgeous, with almost every screen could stand alone as a beautiful watercolor painting. The combat is deep and extremely enjoyable, the story an endearing one of a girl facing a new, threatening world. The exploration is ominous and foreboding, but inviting. Every aspect of Child of Light blends into this amazing, central whole, providing an incredibly memorable and personal experience that stands as one of the absolute best games of 2014. I hope this wonderful game eventually cements itself as a classic.

I wanted to love this game, I truly did. And, truth be told, I don't hate it. I've had a decent time with it so far - It doesn't have any noticeable bugs, it runs fine, and all of its systems perform just fine.
Caveat: Just fine. That's how I'd describe the game, and the reason I can't possibly recommend it.
See, Grim Dawn is a spiritual successor to Titan Quest, an ARPG released back in 2006 in the middle of a decade that was mostly dry of any such games. Since the release of Diablo 2 in 2000 and until the release of Torchlight in 2009 the only two RPGs of note were Titan Quest and Sacred 2 - And by when TQ released, even Sacred 2 was still way off. This meant that Titan Quest was basically the first 3D ARPG to actually be worth a damn, it did what it did well, and the setting helped it a lot. It was fun, it was nice, it was all a Diablo 2 fan could have wanted in an era where Blizzard refused to so much as acknowledge the existence of Diablo 3.
Fast forward a full decade and, well, we get Grim Dawn. The ancient mythology has been changed for a custom world because of the impossibility to obtain the rights to the IP, but the game itself is... Well, calling it a spiritual successor to TQ is quite a mouthful. It may as well be a Titan Quest reskin with just a few quality of life improvements and a much blander, generic setting. And that's a problem, because a lot of things have happened since 2006 for ARPGs, and while other games have moved on Grim Dawn feels very much stuck in 2006. It plays just like Titan Quest did back then, with barely any gameplay upgrades (The graphics do look better tho), and with a storyline that, well, I don't give a rat's♥♥♥♥♥about. Now, to make this a bit simpler, I'll explain how I feel about each of the elements in the game:
Graphics/Visual style: They're OK. I like the grim setting, but to be honest the whole thing looks rather generic, and I feel other games - Namely Path of Exile, which is free - have done this better. It's not an ugly game, not at all, but it just doesn't stand out when compared to other games of the same kind. Even Val Hensing's looks stand out, and of course if you're more into cartoonish looks you'll find Torchlight 2 or even Sacred 2 to be way better than this, because absolutely nothing stands out graphically here. Everything looks toned down and samey. Even Titan Quest had more of a characteristic look than this one, which means Grim Dawn is sort of a step backwards on that regard.
Gameplay: Plays exactly like Titan Quest did, down to the ability trees following the same formula. The few things that were added are rather small, like a faith system that gives you small bonuses, and the reputation part of the game was much better done by the Val Hensing series. Honestly, if what you want is a game that you can play in tons of ways where classes feel fully different, you could go with Diablo 3 or Sacred 2. If what you want is customization, then Path of Exile does much better, for free. If what you want is average gameplay, Van Helsing will do it better than this one, with better graphics and storyline.
Storyline/Worldbuilding: May as well not exist. I mean, it IS there but... yeah, no reason to care. Titan Quest had me caring because I knew of the setting beforehand - of course traversing the Styx meant something, because your average player had read about it in myths long before the game came around. The storyline and worldbuilding in Grim Dawn are samey, repetitive, and don't quite stand out. ARPGs aren't known for having deep stories, and some like Diablo 3 have downright terrible ones, but in this one there is just no reason to care. Van Helsing did a great job at giving you a story. Path of Exile gave your character a reason to do what he or she did. Sacred 2 also threw you into a storyline that was easy to understand right away. This one does neither.
But perhaps the worst part in Grim Dawn is that the game simply has no charm at all. There's no identity to be found, where all other exponents of the genre have one. I found myself longing to get the witty comments of my ghost companion from VH while playing this, or hearing snark from the player character like in Sacred 2, or even the horrible one-liners from Diablo 3 that should have seen its writers sent to jail. But I got nothing, nothing at all. There's nothing in place to make the game fun beyond killing monsters in complete silence with a background track and monster sounds. There's no interaction whatsoever, whatever characters there are are paper-thin and the world doesn't really have much that stands out and pikes your curiosity.
So it is based on all these things that I just can't recommend Grim Dawn. I'll keep playing the game, and it is moderately fun, but in the end my review comes down to one thing: Should I recommend this game to people looking for a good ARPG, when there's so much better out there?
The answer is no, I shouldn't. Because the game is at best average and at worst anchored to a decade that's gone. There's better out there, and while I'm sure most will enjoy this, you'll likely enjoy this game's main competitors more - and you can find those at a fraction of the price, or for free, if you know where and when to look for them. Skip this unless you absolutely felt Titan Quest was the epitome of an ARPG and don't want absolutely any changes on the formula, because for all the things this game does reasonably well it just doesn't advance the genre at all, when other titles since 2006 have done so.

This game could be a great storytelling art piece. Although it is more like an action horror paced arcade puzzle game with what I personally call “Mario” gameplay of jumping and doing timed passed objectives. Main character can't grab and pull out objects properly or cannot respond quickly on input commands. Instead, a player is forced to spend nerves on pushing controller buttons in frustration rather than spending nerves on actual atmospheric and spookiness of this great nightmare world.  I thought this is similar to Amnesia games. Where the story is told by exploring and the gameplay spooks and "trolls" the player almost passively. Where a lot of phycological tension going on but yet no fast-paced action. Only a little.
There is no narration and explanation to the works your are in. It might be a good artistic approach for the game to let player figure out what is going on and why. At least there could be a small written texts or notes scattered around puzzle levels to tell the player the story… Or maybe main character thoughts while being in the nightmare…
Puzzles are uninformative, there are no hints where to start unless if you take your time to explore and poke your noise at things to figure out.  That is, actually a good approach” because it forces you to “immerse” into this strange world and explore, look around. Although it does not apply if your character is under threat and a player needs to figure it out  the puzzle very fast. And here come trial and error. Tried once - fail - start over. Fail again, start over from the checkpoint. 2’d and 3rd  try  give you an impulse/motivation to try again, especially in tense spooky situations.  After 10th failing you start to loose that atmospheric roleplay as you go the same thing over again just to be able to move into the next puzzle room.  You take off your high-quality headphones off, pause you immersive felling as it is no longer pleases you, turn off volume and look closely into the monitor with your fingers trying to do Olympic gymnastics to quickly press buttons for your character's movements to do quickly in sequential order as quickly as possible in the only sequence you have to do - there are no alternative routes, no alternative solution to puzzle solving. It is a straight up mono gameplay. At first I love the immersions of this game but out of frustration, gave up on this and have not finished it. Do not want to break "RT" button on the controller nor my mouse.  I genuinely wish I could put a “so-so” recommendation, although this small review looks like a "rage quit" big comment. It is better to watch a good youtube silent lets-play,  should it become a spooky movie. One off game.
