Do I recommend this game?
Well. Yes and No.
Yes.
Because the game is fun. The combat is fun, leveling up is fun, doing quests is fun, finding and completing plans is fun, battling bosses is fun, finding a strategy that works is fun, late-game is fun, doing all that kind of stuff is fun. I can say with confidence that there isn't really a moment in the game where you don't have anything to do. There are always plans to complete, there are always tougher bosses you can try and take down, there are always quests that need doing. And once you've done all that, you make progress in the campaign and suddenly you're flooded with things to do again. So there is a lot a content here, you don't just get a sword, kill the bad guy and woop-dee doo you saved the world. There is a lot more to it than that, which I can say happily, but unfortunately, this is heavily weighed down by other factors, if you'd like to keep reading.
No.
Because of the heavy, and when I say heavy, I mean heavy-as-a-ton-of-bricks rehash of assets.
This includes:
-Monsters
= 9 times out of 10, a new enemy in a new zone will just be the same enemy you've already seen in another zone, just but the colour has been changed, the name has been SLIGHTLY changed and the stats have been increased.
I can not stress enough how annoying this can get at times. So picture this, at the start of the game, you encounter tulips and weird dog things in a park styled zone. Makes sense, right? Those are the sort of things that you can roughly associate with that area. But imagine later on in the game, you go into a tech themed area and you see that SAME plant, just with a different colour and slightly different name. You'd probably be thinking "Oh look. It's that same plant again. Woohoo".
But the worst crime is that this doesn't happen just once, oh no, it happens A LOT. Like, a LOT a lot. Almost every enemy follows this pattern, and it's a darn shame to be honest. When you FINALLY encounter a different enemy, you will be like "Oh game, you're so nice to have treated me with this oh so precious new enemy".
-Zones
= A lot of the zones are just a zone that you have already seen that has either just straight up been copied and pasted or has been changed a SLIGHT bit. In a similar way to the monsters, this can get mighty annoying. Some areas are exact copies of other areas.
Here's another reason for 'No'.
So, you buy this game, have fun, complete the game, and the game says "Hey. You can do a 2nd run. How does that sound?" and you'd probably think "Great! It's a New Game+! I know a bit more about the game now, so this should be more fun" or something along those lines, right?
Oh, and when you think of New Game+, you think of starting the game from the beginning, with most of stuff such as levels and equipment, but the enemies have been buffed so that it's a more tough and grueling game that really challenges you and pushes you to your limit? You might be reminded of something like Borderlands 2, with the True/Ultimate Vault Hunter Mode, right?
Well, unfortunately, that is NOT the case with this game, and that's a big stinking NOT. Tell ya why? Because the 2nd playthrough (not even gonna say New Game+ because it's not really worthy of that title) has you fight the enemies that have NOT been scaled up in difficulty. So, what is the point in letting me restart the game with all my stuff, if you're not gonna make the enemies harder so that I'm not completely OP to the point where I can EASILY kill bosses that are supposed to kill you in order to progress in the campaign? You know those bosses, you lose but you don't actually lose and the campaign continues? Yeah, those ones. I was curious to see what would have happened if you had killed that boss at that point. The game recognised it in the same way as if I were to have lost and continued on with the story anyway. So, yeah.
So, if you're going to go for a second playthrough, implying that you have already done most of the plans and quests on your 1st playthough, you will blaze through it. Which is really sad to be honest.
And another thing. There is a choice, between Japanese and English voice actors. The Japanese voice actors can have you saying "Shut uuuuuup" at times, esspecially Compa. Her VA makes me angry. The VA's for the older characters are good from what I heard at the start. I went with the English voice actors because I felt that they did an overall better job with them, and I could actually understand what they were saying in battle. Oh, but you were thinking that I was gonna end that there on a good note, huh? Well guess what? The English voice actors didn't voice all of the main story, so there will be random segments of the story where it is just silence, unless you want to go with the JVA's, at which point I said to myself "I'll just read the bits that are silent."
Oh and don't get me STARTED on those DLC characters. Jeez. They're just OP. Shamelessly OP. Don't get them. Save your money. They're not only cheap in price, but cheap in pride. Just a big no. Not only are they OP, but they are CPU's and can use HDD, which is sorta like a super mode. So yeah. They play no part in the story at all and they level up faster than the other characters, being a good 5 levels ahead of my other characters by level 20.
Summary:
Get this game IF (and that's NOT a reference to the character IF in this game):
-You've looked at some gameplay and have said "Yeah, it looks fun".
-The game is on sale OR you've got too much money sitting around the place.
-You can look past the OVERWHELMING AMOUNT of repetitiveness of this game, which honestly takes a lot. I managed to look past it at first, but it wittles you down over time.
If not a single one of the following critera are met, do NOT get this game. Otherwise, do. It's a pretty solid and overall decent game, it just could have used some more TLC and a bit more time in the oven.
From a personal stand point, I've given this game a thumbs down. This is because of the reasons above. But I did enjoy myself, but looking back, there are a lot of things that are wrong with this game.
That feels like all, and it feels like a lot off of my chest. Thanks for reading and I hope this has helped.

Being new to the Telltale games I was reluctant to pick this one up. The gameplay from The Walking Dead series seemed boring to me as someone who never enjoyed the series to begin with (I prefer max-brooks zombies to walking dead zombies). Game of Thrones however is a very good program and adaption from ASoIaF, so I was really looking forward to the story telling in this one.
They pulled it off, only one episode in and the story is immersive and engaging. Much like the books and the tv series I'm on my seat waiting for the next episode to arrive, no complaints in the story department.
This is honestly one of the best casual games I've played on PC in a very long time. Not much in the way of graphical quality. I myself had the immursion ruined when running into a couple of familiar faces who looked like they were painted by someone with an impressionism fetish. However, the shaders are nice and you certainly don't need a beast of a machine to run this one on the highest settings.
Gameplay is quite minimal aswell, but it is surprisingly satisfying performing some of the menial tasks the game demands on you while you're trying to go from A to B. QTE events, although comprising most of the "interactive" portions of the game don't feel forced, button mashing is to a minimal and for the most part the system seems quite fluid... Honestly, this game doesn't need to have action or interactivity to be enjoyable. If that were the case then the whole Grand Strategy series would seem pointless, but theres a reason i've sunk hundreds of hours into Crusader Kings, Europa Universalis, and Victoria.
Here's where the problems begin. The game has a sort of timer for deciding what path you want to take, Unlike Bioware titles where you would be given a wide variety of options in a wheel menu this game forces you to pick from 3 rather mundane and sometimes confusing options within a set time limit. this limit also ends in most cases as soon as your counterpart has finished talking, this leaves you a very small window of oportunity to say something. This game definitely fails one of the major problems with a chose your own path RPG, it gives you a set of options, but the character doesn't always represent the option you chose for them well.
"What do you want for dinner tonight?"
You selected A) Lets go out to eat.
"Why do you always expect me to prepare dinner!? ♥♥♥♥ you, I'm going out with my friends."
Frustrating right?
The other problem I faced were the idiotic KBM controlls. This screams of a poorly made PC port when it comes to UI.
I don't recomend picking up this game unless you have a controller to play it on, because it took me about one minute to restart with a Xbone controller plugged in.
In the end, this is a masterfully done representation of the Game of Thrones universe. For now only one episode is out, but 6 have been planned to be released within about a month and a half of each other. Keeping that in mind I hope this awesome story takes us to Essos at some point. If you can put up with the episodic releases ALL PRAISE BE TO GABEN, poor contols, and overall disipointing at times decisions you are given I would absolutely recomend this game to a fan of the series.

I love this game for its' uniqueness in comparison to other zombie games. While the basic formula is there, the Mirrors' Edge-esque gameplay changes the game entirely. Instead of fighting the zombies, you're encouraged to just run and use wits instead of brawn. (Though it's still hella fun to beat the crap out of the z's) Which is, in all honesty, what you *should* do when faced with a hoard of zombies. The agility and speed of the character while climbing makes it absolutely exhilirating to play, which makes it feel very immersive- especially with the first-person perspective. And the transition to dark is just fantastic. It ups the ante and makes it way creepier.
It's a very beautiful game as well, though it's regrettable that it's a port. It suffers what ports usually suffer- lack of attention and love towards the pc. Some of the controls are wack and forgettable, so I often have to go into settings just to figure out what buttons do what. The menus are probably the worst part of this game, though the annoyance is balanced out with how good the rest of the game is. Holding down enter and using odd buttons to navigate is just...ugh. Being a mainly pc gamer, I don't feel the love from the devs on this point. I'm not asking much- I just want them to pay enough attention to how other mainstream pc games handle, and do it that way. Universal buttons and mouse mapping. Please.
And the storyline is....eh. The bosslady is really annoying, and I often ignore her and the main plot, and just cruise around and play like a survival open world game. It's not the voice actors or anything at all- it's the cold, chilliness of this 'government' that you work for. It really doesn't motivate me to finish the story. Might just be me though lol, I don't respond to 'orders' well. Especially douchey ones.
Potentially, you could play this for a long time, since you can get supplies for people or yourself and sell or use. Or just survive. And craft. Which I'm a huge fan of.
Overall, I'd rate an 8 outta 10.

Beat Hazard is the most badass music game around. Remember Asteroids? The space-based shoot em up collision game? This is essentially a present-day version with saturated (and quite often aggressively pyscadelic) visuals, expanded arsenal, and indie attitude. However, the driving force is of course the music. Your music. Absorb your library into Beat Hazard and blow away billions of enemies (at once) to your tunes until the early hours. As is the most common mechanic within music games, Beat Hazard works with the intensity and speed of the audio source to create the level of action and enemies in the game. As your music intensifies to pulse pounding panic, so does your game situation!
The game supports achievements, leaderboards, matchmaking, several different modes, etc, but most importantly multiplayer. Loading up with a friend and experiencing the thrill of space-based destructive mania and survival to any soundtrack at all is something too easy to get used to every night.

I want to devote the time to this review that this game deserves. I really, truly want to. But I cannot. I'm too eager to get back into the game.
Did you enjoy Ultima 7? How about Baldur's Gate? You know, the games that are revered as "classics" of the RPG genre? Well, unless I run into a massive let-down further down the line - this game will be revered just the same.
The feeling of a huge baddie closing in on your archer, who will surely be cut down by him with little effort at all... Then teleporting the baddie 30 feet into the air, to land in a puddle of oil, and subsequently hitting that oil with a fire arrow to engulf the baddie in flames...
The feeling of turning your thief invisible and sneaking behind enemy lines, waiting for the proper moment, and eliminating a full-health enemy single-handedly with backstabs...
The feeling of swiping a chest key from right under the leader of the Legion's nose and sneaking out without him even knowing anyone was there...
That feeling? It's the feeling you get when playing those old-school classics. The same feeling Dvinity: Original Sin delivers - in spades.
The ONLY con I've run across thus far: The crafting system, while VERY well fleshed-out and sensible... Feels clumsy. That's it, that's my only complaint.

XCOM's a great example of turn based tactical gameplay done right with a nice selection of difficulty settings and loads of replayability to be found both in the base game, its mutators and the honest to goodness actual expansion pack Enemy Within. Also mods if you are of that persuation ;)
in XCOM you take the role of a commander tasked with organizing earths defense after having been invaded by an at first overbearing alien force. Through the "XCOM project" you will be able to draft the best of the best in the name of Earths defence and slowly beat back and uncover the reasons for the aliens sudden interest in our planet.
But you all kinda knew that already, so what can I tell you that you'd like to go into the game knowing?
The game can be said to be a kind of paradoxical badass-simulator; paradoxical in that you both have been given the most powerful infantry military assets of the world to play around with while you at the same time are expected to blow the aliens to goop in every instance they appear. The keyword here is expected as just a few mistakes during combat can turn not only the specific combat instance very difficult to come out of on top, but can to some extent make the rest of your playthrough difficult by way of both losing important team members or funding nations deeming your abilities lacking. Dying is for real and you will lose people the minute you missplay. Between that and the "kind of" difficult (as in nobody will tell you how to do it effectively leaving you to figure it out as you play) construction and researching meta game, to stay a badass you either will have to load yourself out of unwinnable situations, or actually be a total badass to begin with :P. There is little to no room for error and you WILL have to learn how to play well to make it past both easy and normal difficulty, This is not a bad thing of course. The game makes some effort to teach the players basic tactics during combat and the pacing is such that even if a restart or two is required you'l learn eventually :)
If you have not played the originals, know that they are more fidgety and have an UI that would make DOS blush. Enemy Unknown is streamlined both for better and for worse, with some things like base management being a bit easier, and characters having less options in combat regarding movement. Soldiers have more or less the same stats (without mutators) and level up from killing beasties, giving them perks and stat boosts much like in an rpg. Soldiers have hp, aim and nerve basically and gain some every level based on their class. They get skills to based on class. Medics can heal more often and throw smoke grenades while heavy soldiers carry heavy ordonance to battle. Planning out one or more effective teams is important to beat difficult enemies, and the game allows players to field whatever they think will work best, rather than forcing certain picks out of them becoming very enjoyable once enemy types and class strengths become apparent to the player.
Compared to others in the genre XCOM is both stellar while also being a bit samey. The game relies on its intuitive nature rather than hand holding allowing players to reach proficiency on their own (and in their own way), but what it essentially always comes down to is your ability to kill all the aliens. About 90% of the missions main objective is to go in and shoot all the enemies, and while that is nice, games such as Lotr: The third age (from the time of not bad EA titles) offers more in variance between missions.
That's not to be said missions don't take on different forms. Between defusing bombs, infiltrating downed ships and rescuing civilians there is lots of variety to be had, but all these become sub-objectives to "kill all aliens" in all but the bomb defusing case (there are some levels that differ but they are uniqe and very few).
The reason for this is probably (to some extent at least) that every turn, both you and your enemies are allowed to move every one of your active characters. In your case this means all your soldiers always, but in the enemies case this only means discovered aliens. Aliens not yet discovered will move around a bit but stand idle and uninterested in the fog of war, up until being discovered when they will throw on their most convincing growl, act very surprised and bolt for cover.
This adds one level of tactics for the player to explore while removing another.
To some extent, there is tactics to be thought when both positioning and moving your troops. Preferably you want to flank "activated" enemies while avoiding finding more groups, which can be both fun and tense :)
However, having all aliens standing around in small cliques on the levels makes such senarios as attacking scouting parties or flanking around already heavily defended positions activities that have more to do with imagining what three thin men were doing in a certain position, or how well the surprised group entrench themselves on the fly rather than on carefull planning or recon from the players side. The tactics at this point become more about exploiting the AI than studying the map, but its still good fun and creeping forward is still tactical, just not in the same way.
Bottom line:
i missed covering a lot of stuff, but you get the general idea. Shoot many aliens but be smart about it in a nice entertaining package.

Now here we are in 2017 and it's all just...over. Hard to believe..

I wanted to love this game, I truly did. And, truth be told, I don't hate it. I've had a decent time with it so far - It doesn't have any noticeable bugs, it runs fine, and all of its systems perform just fine.
Caveat: Just fine. That's how I'd describe the game, and the reason I can't possibly recommend it.
See, Grim Dawn is a spiritual successor to Titan Quest, an ARPG released back in 2006 in the middle of a decade that was mostly dry of any such games. Since the release of Diablo 2 in 2000 and until the release of Torchlight in 2009 the only two RPGs of note were Titan Quest and Sacred 2 - And by when TQ released, even Sacred 2 was still way off. This meant that Titan Quest was basically the first 3D ARPG to actually be worth a damn, it did what it did well, and the setting helped it a lot. It was fun, it was nice, it was all a Diablo 2 fan could have wanted in an era where Blizzard refused to so much as acknowledge the existence of Diablo 3.
Fast forward a full decade and, well, we get Grim Dawn. The ancient mythology has been changed for a custom world because of the impossibility to obtain the rights to the IP, but the game itself is... Well, calling it a spiritual successor to TQ is quite a mouthful. It may as well be a Titan Quest reskin with just a few quality of life improvements and a much blander, generic setting. And that's a problem, because a lot of things have happened since 2006 for ARPGs, and while other games have moved on Grim Dawn feels very much stuck in 2006. It plays just like Titan Quest did back then, with barely any gameplay upgrades (The graphics do look better tho), and with a storyline that, well, I don't give a rat's♥♥♥♥♥about. Now, to make this a bit simpler, I'll explain how I feel about each of the elements in the game:
Graphics/Visual style: They're OK. I like the grim setting, but to be honest the whole thing looks rather generic, and I feel other games - Namely Path of Exile, which is free - have done this better. It's not an ugly game, not at all, but it just doesn't stand out when compared to other games of the same kind. Even Val Hensing's looks stand out, and of course if you're more into cartoonish looks you'll find Torchlight 2 or even Sacred 2 to be way better than this, because absolutely nothing stands out graphically here. Everything looks toned down and samey. Even Titan Quest had more of a characteristic look than this one, which means Grim Dawn is sort of a step backwards on that regard.
Gameplay: Plays exactly like Titan Quest did, down to the ability trees following the same formula. The few things that were added are rather small, like a faith system that gives you small bonuses, and the reputation part of the game was much better done by the Val Hensing series. Honestly, if what you want is a game that you can play in tons of ways where classes feel fully different, you could go with Diablo 3 or Sacred 2. If what you want is customization, then Path of Exile does much better, for free. If what you want is average gameplay, Van Helsing will do it better than this one, with better graphics and storyline.
Storyline/Worldbuilding: May as well not exist. I mean, it IS there but... yeah, no reason to care. Titan Quest had me caring because I knew of the setting beforehand - of course traversing the Styx meant something, because your average player had read about it in myths long before the game came around. The storyline and worldbuilding in Grim Dawn are samey, repetitive, and don't quite stand out. ARPGs aren't known for having deep stories, and some like Diablo 3 have downright terrible ones, but in this one there is just no reason to care. Van Helsing did a great job at giving you a story. Path of Exile gave your character a reason to do what he or she did. Sacred 2 also threw you into a storyline that was easy to understand right away. This one does neither.
But perhaps the worst part in Grim Dawn is that the game simply has no charm at all. There's no identity to be found, where all other exponents of the genre have one. I found myself longing to get the witty comments of my ghost companion from VH while playing this, or hearing snark from the player character like in Sacred 2, or even the horrible one-liners from Diablo 3 that should have seen its writers sent to jail. But I got nothing, nothing at all. There's nothing in place to make the game fun beyond killing monsters in complete silence with a background track and monster sounds. There's no interaction whatsoever, whatever characters there are are paper-thin and the world doesn't really have much that stands out and pikes your curiosity.
So it is based on all these things that I just can't recommend Grim Dawn. I'll keep playing the game, and it is moderately fun, but in the end my review comes down to one thing: Should I recommend this game to people looking for a good ARPG, when there's so much better out there?
The answer is no, I shouldn't. Because the game is at best average and at worst anchored to a decade that's gone. There's better out there, and while I'm sure most will enjoy this, you'll likely enjoy this game's main competitors more - and you can find those at a fraction of the price, or for free, if you know where and when to look for them. Skip this unless you absolutely felt Titan Quest was the epitome of an ARPG and don't want absolutely any changes on the formula, because for all the things this game does reasonably well it just doesn't advance the genre at all, when other titles since 2006 have done so.

With Saint's Row: The Third, the Saint's Row series really came into it's own -- opting for over-the-top action and off-the-wall silliness over the Grand Theft Auto series' more gritty, serious tone. With the fourth installment, Volition continues to carve out it's niche in the open-world crime -- er, puckish rogue -- sandbox genre.
The same basic structure from SR:III carries over; you have a primary storyline, and dozens of activities. A nice improvement is the wrapping the activities into narrated "sidequests" that, while adding nothing to the narrative, do go quite a ways to making the activities less tedious to complete. Plus the rewards are usually interesting.
There's a slight RPG element to the upgrade system that unlocks higher tiers of skills like health and damage resistance or ammo capacity as you earn more EXP, all costing cache. The upgrade system is well-paced, though it is rather difficult to budget between upgrades to the player character or to their guns at first. A few hours in though, you're making enough cache that it's not an isssue.
The super-powers are a fun replacement for the grenades, though I do miss being able to sprint normally in some cases, as the "Super-Sprint" button overrides the "sprint" button (though this may only be an issue for players using a gamepad), and the super-jump's charge is a little unpredictable. I often found myself jumping three feet into the air when I wanted to jump a building, and clearing four stories when I only wanted to hop up the stairs.
All in all, a fun game with great doses of self-referential humor and so much poking fun at other games and genres. I'd say pick it up on sale if you're a fan of the genre or if you enjoy the humor of games like the Borderlands series, and if you've played a Saint's Row game before and enjoyed it, I'd suggest picking this up ASAP.

Saint's Row IV initially had me concerned.
SR3 was bad enough with how far a departure from 1 &2's  gameplay and storyline.  IV is even further detached from the original games.
Yet SRIV is a really entertaining game.
Ironically, this game is chock full of fan-service. Throwbacks to SR1, 2 and 3 are abundant. There are parts where you quite literally fight the default SR protagonists as boss fights. You'll end up fighting the Ronin, Morning Star, Sons of Samedi and other gangs from the previous entries.  Based Johnny Gat makes a return, too.
The superpowers work great.... when they're avaliable. It is frustrating to be progressing and leveling up your powers to have them stripped away constantly by various missions.
Humor is a strong point of this game, too. While it's a bit too referential humor for my taste, there are many lines of dialogue that had me laughing and chuckling.  SRIV is a really self-aware parody of pop culture.
One huge downside is that while the game's full of fan-service, the recycled content can feel grating. The city of Steelport is still a pretty boring place to explore in comparison to Stilwater from SR1+2. There aren't really any building interiors aside from shops, which is another issue with the city feeling bland and uninspired.
Cars are absolutely pointless in this game, you will not use them outside of mandatory mission segments.
All in all, I highly recommend SRIV if you're looking for something that doesn't take itself too seriously.  Though, I can't help but feel this game's just a more fleshed-out expansion to SRIII, which it was originally intended to be.

It is a game of two halves; ground combat and air combat.
Ground combat makes up the bulk of the game and gives you have a choice between six classes (four universal & two unique per side) with several game modes available.
Air combat is rarer and sees you take control of fighters/interceptors/bombers to take on enemy craft. You have the ability to land on the enemy ship as a marine and try to take out vital systems but you CANNOT win solely by using this technique.
However, the game is flawed in many ways. Overall, I would recommend this game but I would warn anyone looking at this game to not expect anything close to a perfect game.

Possibly the best and the most enjoyable non-RPG Star Wars game made. Although mainly a FPS almost identical to the Battlefield series in the terms of the amount of reserves, but in this game there are also dogfight space battles and more, and also a more tactical game mode where you are to conquer the galaxy.
The campaign is of a good length and covers the II-IV parts of the series, however you are able to play on any other planet that was mentioned in the series. The multiplayer is really fun, especially the Mos Eisley map where there is an option that every player is a special character. These include all the famous characters such as jedis, which are more powerful then the ordinary footsoldiers you get to play as in the singleplayer campaign. There are also bunch of other mods for these custom missions. The game is very fun to play with your friends, however the PC version does not include split-screen which is a shame, so you and your friends will have to play it online.
The graphics are still good, although aged, unless you are a whiney Crysis kid who values the game by its visual aspects only. If that is the case then this game might not be for you. However if you are not and decide to get it, you will be suprised that the game still looks nice, but that isn't why you bought it then.
Some people might also find the game hard to play, since it can get pretty difficult, especially in the later levels.
The bad parts of the game is that there are some issues with newer versions of Windows, and that you might wait a couple of days before getting your CD key, since Disney shut down the magnificient LucasArts and we all know what Disney is about now : $$$
The story is linear, and so are the objectives that are mainly to capture an objective or to defend a position while killing the enemy, but the combat is fun and the missions are interesting.
Also the bad part is that there arent plenty of multiplayer servers (currently about 50) so you don't have quite a big choce, and most of them are filled with veterans who will dominate you over and over again, but when you are playing with friends you will probably host the game.
I have played this game since it came out, and I have finished the singleplayer many times. If you have the amount of money it costs and you don't mind slightly outdated graphics, then immediately purchase this game and you won't regret it.

My name is SynificHD and I am a YouTuber who uploads many gameplay content, such as this game.
This review will show my thoughts and opinions towards the game, also including a link to the game for you guys to check out and hopefully enjoy; and give you an insight of the game!
The game "Dying Light" is a first-person survival horror, zombie apocalypse, where you play as a "GRE agent" who is to secure a file that includes secret data towards the outbreak. You uncover survivors who tell their story and have a meaning to their home Harran, and you are to help them by jumping, sliding and doing fancy maneuvers, before their very little lives come to an end.
"Dying Light" would have to be my most favorite Zombie game currently, as it features better movement than most zombie games (Dead Island, Left 4 Dead, DayZ, State of Decay). The parkour system can be a little buggy and annoying sometimes when you go to jump and grab a ledge but it doesnt respond so you fall and damage yourself or fall into a bunch of bitters who are like magnets and cling onto you, but its so far the best working mechanic compared to others. The storyline is somewhat okay, it can be a little cliché but afterall arent we here to kill zombies and chew gum? I would also recommend buying the DLC "The Following" as the driving ability makes the game a little more fun, especially with friends.
I recommend this game TRUELY to people who enjoy the satisfaction of slicing zombies up, running around doing somewhat cool parkour, and having an open-world map to run a muck; uncovering many weapons and mysteries.
This game should be fine for recording, if you're looking to record the campaign you might want to rethink about it though because the campaign is somewhat lengthy and beefy (If you know what I mean). Id give this a 8/10 easy to record.

Alright, serious review time... if that's even possible.
This game cannot really be taken serious.
Each character and some monsters are references to games, consoles and/or companies. You can fight against pipes from SMB, ghosts from Pacman, pixelvaders, and floating screenshots of a visual novel. Yes.
The first companions you meet are Compile Heart and Idea Factory. I mean companies. I mean Compa. And IF.

It's a turn based RPG, but very different to most.
What's typical:
Turn based
attack, skills, guard, items, escape options
get exp, money and items from killing enemies
get money and items from finishing quests
buy equipment and items from the store
some sort of Tech bar (the Exe Drive Gauge)
some sort of ,,Your team was surprised!" system (Symbol attacks)
What's special:
A three-dimensional factor: You can walk around during your turn to, for example, get closer to enemies or to run away, get as many enemies as possible with an attack affecting an area, close a gap between your teammates and select yourself with a heal-environment skill to heal all teammates surrounding you (as well as yourself).
Combos: Once you attack, you can perform 3 additional attacks. There's Rush combos, Power combos and Break combos. Power combos deal the most damage to the health bar, Break combos deal the most damage to the guard bar (once the guard bar's depleted all attacks do more damage to that enemy until it regenerates), and Rush Combos fill your Exe Drive Gauge much quicker than other attacks (You don't need them as long as you haven't unlocked the gauge (by making progress in the story)). You get stronger combos as you level up, you need to choose which combos you want to use in battle yourself. My advice: Just choose strong Rush and Power combos, and leave Break Combos entirely.
Exe Drive Gauge: It's a bar which fills up if you deal damage. If you charged it in one battle, you keep the charge in all other battles in the dungeon until you leave it. You can use it in two different ways:
1. It unlocks the 4th combo attack in battles. Using it does NOT deplete the EDG.
2. It unlocks the ultimate attacks of your characters in battles. Using them DOES deplete the EDG.
Depending on how far you progressed in the story, you can have 0-4 charges. A 4th combo may require 1 charge to work, some 2, some 3. Same goes with ultimates.
Transformations: Goddess characters, or CPUs can transform into HDD (Hard Drive Divinity). Transformations take 20% of your SkillPoints, but the character becomes stronger, the appearance and personality changes (as well as names and descriptions of some skills) and skills don't take as many SP as they did before. You need to unlock HDD  before you can use it, by progressing in the story. (DLC characters and unlockable characters (check guides to see them) start off with unlocked HDD).
Plans: You can customize many things. With plans, you can enable items popping up in the store, you can make enemies stronger or weaker, you can change items and enemies in dungeons to get special loot, you can unlock new dungeons. To get the swimwear I mentioned you gotta unlock many many dungeons, and sometimes you can miss a plan because you progressed too far. So you gotta load an older save (There's 50 slots) or play through the game and start over with your OP characters. With plans you can also unlock special characters, the sisters. If you've watched the anime of HDN or played the second game, you know what I'm talking about.
Symbol attacks: If you run into an enemy, whether the enemy gets the first blow or you do depends on the stats of your characters. If an enemy runs into you, they'll get the first blow. If you press the attack button and hit an enemy before it hits you, you get the first blow (Symbol attack).
There's only 1 fully animated scene, and that is shortly after you start playing. Dialogue happens just like in a visual novel, with 1-3 characters standing infront of you as a spectator. The characters are animated (breathing, mouth movements, random blinking, head movement) which makes it seem sort of 3D. Except for the mouth animations, I find them all really well done. I wish they'd move their arms or something, though. Of course there's a text box containing English subtitles, whether you chose Japanese or English voice acting.
English voice acting is okay I guess, but obviously the Japanese voices fit the characters much better and are less forced. Compa's English VA did a damn good job, though. ¯\_(ツ)_/¯

This is a perfect example of a game that is easy to pick up and extremely difficult to master.
The easiest way to describe it is as a physics-based FPS with THPS-style tricks: You're a robot on wheels. It's dodgeball, only with scores of interesting modes. You can perform silly but incredibly satisfying moves for extra points — like helicopters (turn 360° mid-air) and godlikes (catch an opponent's ball mid-air and hit someone else with it before you land). Perform them in Score Battle mode to win faster. Perform them in regular deathmatch mode for kudos or just to show off.
The one downside with the game is that the online community, while dedicated, is very small. However, I still give it my fullest recommendation because of the decent AI, which is incredibly entertaining to play against.

As an artistic endeavor, Banner Saga's ambition is only outpaced by it's success.
From the outset the writing seizes your emotions and fills you with hope and despair. This is a world and characters so perfectly wrought that I am deeply saddened by it's fatalistic tones.
This is a true triumph of not only gaming but interactive art itself.

Overall I'd give this game a 3/10. It has some good ideas, but it's very poorly executed.

A beautiful, well-crafted game with an interesting story.
Unfortunately, the gameplay is stale and repetitive. Further, the choice system leaves a lot to be desired. You never feel like you are making a hard decision you can weigh but with unclear future pros / cons- in most cases, one is the "right decision" that gets you a new item or men and another is the "wrong decision" that gets a character killed. Games like Mass Effect and the Witcher series do this excellently, where you can weigh decisions and what seemed like a good decision at first may have disastrous consequences down the road. Decisions in the Banner Saga are deeply disappointing - there is no way to weigh the options before making a decision and for the most part the consequences are immediate and black-or-white.
I like the combat system - the idea of armor and health/strength couples with alternating turns is a new and pretty interesting one. However, it's underdeveloped. Abilities feel lacking and characters never feel like they synergize. Combat could be good, but would require significant fleshing out.
I recommend this game if you can get it on sale and want an "Experience", not a good game. It is wonderfully produced, the world is fresh and it feels epic, but the gameplay cripples it.

I really enjoyed The Banner Saga - it has beautiful art, wonderful soundtrack, no bugs to speak of, engaging combat mechanics, and an interestingly branching and fairly systemic narrative. There's really only one thing I didn't like about the game.
As a not-so-great player, I found the final boss fight spiked incredibly in terms of difficulty - so much so that I abandoned the game with just the one more fight to go before the credits rolled. Over a year later I returned, tried a bunch again and kept failing, and finally cheated my way through the final fight, on Easy, because I guess I'm terrible at games. My main problem with the final boss fight was that when it rolled around I didn't have a full roster of max-level, uninjured characters to play with. That wasn't something to be fixed by changing strategy in the final battle - you should really metagame your entire character roster in preparation for this fight, ideally from the start of the campaign.
That boss fight aside, though, this was a fantastic, really enjoyable game. I'd recommend it to anyone who's into turn-based games or great art and music, and I really look forward to the sequel.

I wanted to love this game, I truly did. And, truth be told, I don't hate it. I've had a decent time with it so far - It doesn't have any noticeable bugs, it runs fine, and all of its systems perform just fine.
Caveat: Just fine. That's how I'd describe the game, and the reason I can't possibly recommend it.
See, Grim Dawn is a spiritual successor to Titan Quest, an ARPG released back in 2006 in the middle of a decade that was mostly dry of any such games. Since the release of Diablo 2 in 2000 and until the release of Torchlight in 2009 the only two RPGs of note were Titan Quest and Sacred 2 - And by when TQ released, even Sacred 2 was still way off. This meant that Titan Quest was basically the first 3D ARPG to actually be worth a damn, it did what it did well, and the setting helped it a lot. It was fun, it was nice, it was all a Diablo 2 fan could have wanted in an era where Blizzard refused to so much as acknowledge the existence of Diablo 3.
Fast forward a full decade and, well, we get Grim Dawn. The ancient mythology has been changed for a custom world because of the impossibility to obtain the rights to the IP, but the game itself is... Well, calling it a spiritual successor to TQ is quite a mouthful. It may as well be a Titan Quest reskin with just a few quality of life improvements and a much blander, generic setting. And that's a problem, because a lot of things have happened since 2006 for ARPGs, and while other games have moved on Grim Dawn feels very much stuck in 2006. It plays just like Titan Quest did back then, with barely any gameplay upgrades (The graphics do look better tho), and with a storyline that, well, I don't give a rat's♥♥♥♥♥about. Now, to make this a bit simpler, I'll explain how I feel about each of the elements in the game:
Graphics/Visual style: They're OK. I like the grim setting, but to be honest the whole thing looks rather generic, and I feel other games - Namely Path of Exile, which is free - have done this better. It's not an ugly game, not at all, but it just doesn't stand out when compared to other games of the same kind. Even Val Hensing's looks stand out, and of course if you're more into cartoonish looks you'll find Torchlight 2 or even Sacred 2 to be way better than this, because absolutely nothing stands out graphically here. Everything looks toned down and samey. Even Titan Quest had more of a characteristic look than this one, which means Grim Dawn is sort of a step backwards on that regard.
Gameplay: Plays exactly like Titan Quest did, down to the ability trees following the same formula. The few things that were added are rather small, like a faith system that gives you small bonuses, and the reputation part of the game was much better done by the Val Hensing series. Honestly, if what you want is a game that you can play in tons of ways where classes feel fully different, you could go with Diablo 3 or Sacred 2. If what you want is customization, then Path of Exile does much better, for free. If what you want is average gameplay, Van Helsing will do it better than this one, with better graphics and storyline.
Storyline/Worldbuilding: May as well not exist. I mean, it IS there but... yeah, no reason to care. Titan Quest had me caring because I knew of the setting beforehand - of course traversing the Styx meant something, because your average player had read about it in myths long before the game came around. The storyline and worldbuilding in Grim Dawn are samey, repetitive, and don't quite stand out. ARPGs aren't known for having deep stories, and some like Diablo 3 have downright terrible ones, but in this one there is just no reason to care. Van Helsing did a great job at giving you a story. Path of Exile gave your character a reason to do what he or she did. Sacred 2 also threw you into a storyline that was easy to understand right away. This one does neither.
But perhaps the worst part in Grim Dawn is that the game simply has no charm at all. There's no identity to be found, where all other exponents of the genre have one. I found myself longing to get the witty comments of my ghost companion from VH while playing this, or hearing snark from the player character like in Sacred 2, or even the horrible one-liners from Diablo 3 that should have seen its writers sent to jail. But I got nothing, nothing at all. There's nothing in place to make the game fun beyond killing monsters in complete silence with a background track and monster sounds. There's no interaction whatsoever, whatever characters there are are paper-thin and the world doesn't really have much that stands out and pikes your curiosity.
So it is based on all these things that I just can't recommend Grim Dawn. I'll keep playing the game, and it is moderately fun, but in the end my review comes down to one thing: Should I recommend this game to people looking for a good ARPG, when there's so much better out there?
The answer is no, I shouldn't. Because the game is at best average and at worst anchored to a decade that's gone. There's better out there, and while I'm sure most will enjoy this, you'll likely enjoy this game's main competitors more - and you can find those at a fraction of the price, or for free, if you know where and when to look for them. Skip this unless you absolutely felt Titan Quest was the epitome of an ARPG and don't want absolutely any changes on the formula, because for all the things this game does reasonably well it just doesn't advance the genre at all, when other titles since 2006 have done so.

Grim Dawn, I never knew about this game until my brother persistently convinced me to try it. Reluctently I purchased the game and had little expectations when trying it out. My mind was blown away the first hour I played. Because of this, Grim Dawn has become my most played Steam game ever.
Pros:
- The story is well written and interesting to follow
- Character Customization, the world is yours to be whatever you want to be
- Item skills and Devotions (Not only do you get your typical 'class' skills, you can obtain even more from game items, relics, and devotions!
- The game gives you that Diablo 2 feel
- The developers are involved with the community, speak to the community through their forums and facebook page
- Free content updates (who wouldn't love this)
- Beautiful world
- The game can be modded and the community have already released so many great ideas
Cons:
- Character animations aren't the best, at least with some attack animations they appear odd.
- Not a lot of variety when it comes to story related bosses. There are plenty of Enemy Heroes to kill though
- I enjoy the soundtrack, but some areas could use different music
- Melee heavy builds, I've tried multiple 'specs', but I feel limited with magic caster decisions
- There isn't exactly an 'endgame'. The game does support the idea of having more than one alternate character, but when you do hit max level and finish the game on Ultimate, you're pretty much done and should start a new character.
This game has a bright future ahead of it, and the creators at Crate continue to deliver a promising series. My cons are personally opionated and I recommend trying this game for yourself, especially if you loved Diablo 2. I cannot wait to see more of what the community releases for game changes.

FTL: Faster Than Light is a fun, addictive game at a cheap price.  The game mechanics are simple enough to make it easy to learn how to play.  Learning to play, though, is not quite the same as learning to win.  When it comes to learning to win, the game gets surprisingly complex.
This is my first roguelike game, and adjusting to the roguelike genre was a bit of a frustration to me at first.  There is no option to save a game to replay a bad encounter- when you lose, that is the end of the line, you start a new game.  Sometimes the game seems brutally unfair in throwing a series of hopeless situations at you.
You only learn to win by suffering a series of spectaculuarly unfair deaths, and puzzling through what you could do next time to prevail.  Once you get past the sting of defeat and accept your ship's destruction as a learning opportunity, you discover that no situation is really hopeless, and that with sufficient planning and strategy (and a bit of luck helps), you have an answer for everything that outer space has to throw at you.
FTL has a lot of replay value.  There is a wide assortment of ships you can unlock and play.  Each ship has its quirks; some have serious design flaws.  Each ship gives you the unique challenge of puzzling through using its strengths and mitigating its weaknesses, forcing you to develop different strategies for winning with each.
For me, it has been one of the most bug-free games I have played.  I have run into one crash over several hundred games.  That's it.  I have not seen any unfinished or incomplete content or obvious hole or exploits.  This game seems to have been proofread and playtested better than most games I have played.
FTL has been a lot of fun for just a few dollars.  It is a great value of a game.

Half-life was one of the first games I played which made me love video games beyond just basic entertainment value. The sequel, Half-Life 2, revolutionalized my view on video games entirely. The first time I sat down to play this game, I knew I was going to love it. The graphics were amazing, the game play was excellent, the story line stellar, and the physics really blew me away. This was the first game I ever played that implemented a legitimate physics engine that actually replicated real life (at least to some extent.) I remember the first time I picked up the gravity gun! Who needed other weapons after getting hold of that device?!? Half-Life 2 convinced me to one day pursue a potential career in the gaming industry and specifically orienting my degree towards developing real-time physics calculations.
Although today this game may not be the best graphics, the most realistic physics, the coolest game out there, it was and still is an amazing game worth playing if you haven't before. I also find myself playing the game over again every couple of years. This game definitely deserves awards in nearly every catagory out there, including "Best Game Ever Made!" Do yourself a favor and buy it if you don't already own it!

With the recently released Advanced Edition, there is absolutely no reason why getting FTL would be a bad idea.
This devilishly addictive game has a complexity of elements yet a simplicity of gameplay, and it works really well. Though the average runthrough is one-two hours, and the changes of victory small (especially when the RNG gets involved), when you finally beat the final boss it is one of the most rewarding sensations.
There is a great variety of gameplay (with the AE more so), with many starting ships to unlock, several alien races to add to your crew, and a ton of weapons, drones, augments, special events, and ship systems, this game will always keep you on your toes. You will never know what to encounter and you will almost always have a choice on how to go about the mission. That is what makes FTL a fun game and I highly reccomend it to any fan of rougelikes with quick sessions of gameplay.
With the praise out of the way, let me point out a few drawbacks. For one, the RNG makes everything uncertain and for some players that randomness of outcome might be more frustrating than fun. If you get good at the game the RNG can be overcome, but not many people have the time to get really experienced at FTL.
Unlocking ships is also a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥ Some vessels are easy as cake to unlock and are fun to play. Others are tremenuosly hard to unlock, and really are not worth the trouble (Stealth Cruser Type C... impossible to unlock, and it sucks). Nonetheless there is a large selection of ships to suit your fancy.
There is also room for improvement with the amount of content possible... but as always, there are mods for that.

Hack an enemy's Oxygen and watch their crew slowly suffocate. Blast them to pieces after a jump with rockets and lasers using a preigniter. Destroy their med bay, and teleport on board with giant space insects to butcher their crew. Activate cloaking to avoid a barrage of missiles and lasers. Light their ship on fire with fire bombs and cackle maniacally as they burn.
All things aside, this is a great game to burn a few (hundred) hours on. Buy it. Do it now.

What thats saying is that the story is not what this game is about by any account. That does absolutely nothing to take away from the game though, if anything it makes it better. No need to fuss over alliances or about how amazing your quest is to save the federation! Mostly because you'll be dead soon enough. Very dead very quickly, or slowly dead but still very dead. Sometimes a crew member will get lucky and simply get a laser in the face when you get boarded, instead of slowly dying with your crew because someones hacked your doors and shut down your oxygen. Slowly but surely. Dead.
Okay cool, now lets get to the game itself. The art isn't going to stand out right away, until you notice all the little details and I sometimes find myself staring into the background after a long hard battle, listening to the music, which is also amazing but we'll touch on that in a bit. The missiles look great flying, the lasers look great lasering. Okay, so the music is great, most times you won't notice it as your in the heat of battle, but other times you'll be just listening for a good 20 minutes. The menu music keeps me captivated for at least 5 minutes each time I start up the game. I'm not some kind of artsy super expert or musical genius so we'll move onto gameplay.
At first, even after doing the tutorial you can get a little confused while playing. It's by no means a hard to navigate interface. It's just during a battle you'll have a bunch of things going on, redirecting power, sending crew members to repair a system, or fight off boarders trying to blow said system to bits. If that sounds overwhelming it can be, but thankfully hitting space will pause the action! And it's a much needed feature. Pausing to look over what your enemies have at the beginning of battle, pausing to look at your systems after taking a hit, pausing to rethink your strategy, pausing to decide if you'll run away because those hull points are not going to hold on for more than 2 more missiles, but you need that scrap for upgrades badly and you're so close to winning.Weighing risks is important too, or if you run into someone wanting to trade. Do you buy a drone system, or another weapon, does your ship have room for another system, the power for it? You probably don't have to worry about that so much as if you'll have enough scrap to do everything. Save up, or upgrade your ships basic systems? Decisions, decisions.
Now that you've read this long winded, but comparetively short review, I hope you consider buying this game, full price or on sale. Either way, it's going to be worth your time. Thanks for reading, and I hope you don't die too quickly.

First and foremost, WOW. I was rather skeptical when I got this game, not sure if I will enjoy a turn-based RPG as I normally play action/ FPS. But since this game had Overwhelmingly Positive reviews, and the fact that I could get it cheap, I decided to give it a try.
I was pretty thorough with my play-through and clocked a total of 13.7 hours. And the thing is, I enjoyed every moment of it. I didn't complete it in one sitting (obviously) but I think it was three. I kept playing on and on and I think part of the reason was the battles. As mentioned, it is turn-based RPG with a focus on a timeline (some mentioned that the Final Fantasy series use this mechanic, but I'm new to it). There is no guarantee that you can even cast your spell, and sometimes you even lose the fight having done completely no action. There is some strategy involved and fights can be frustrating especially in Hard mode. It was new for me and I really liked it.
Apart from the battle system, there is also the crafting system worth mentioning. You collect these sorta gems from chests or from battle drops and you can combine them to form more refined versions or hybrid versions. For example, ruby + sapphire + emerald = diamond ; and 3 x ruby = bigger ruby. Equipping these gems in different slots give different stats that can help you in the battle.
The story is fine, nothing spectacular/ mind-blowing like in Bioshock Infinite, but it flows smoothly just like a Disney classic. The artwork is really well done too.
I really enjoyed this game, and I look forward to upcoming games of this genre.

There are 2 things I want to say before getting to the review itself:
1/ I got this game in a bundle (the bundle was cheaper than the only game I wanted in it). I didn't really want to play Sacred Almanac Traces of Greed, mainly because of other players' negative reviews but since I had it I ran through the whole game to get the achievements. That may explain why I did not fully enjoy it.
2/ It's definitely
a H.O. game for there is not one single HO scene ! That's probably another reason to my disappointment
Now, to the point.
Sacred Almanac Traces of Greed is a casual and very easy game. I'd tagged it as a point 'n click adventure game,  mainly intended for beginners, but certainly not aimed at confirmed adventure gamers.
The game and the mini-games (puzzles) are easy, not challenging at all.
I can't say I really recommend it but on the other hand I don't want to put a thumb down to this game since there are no big technical failures and for the fact that the devs fixed an achievement related bug. Maybe that game wasn't for me but it might fit other kind of gamers.
I believe the storyline was fair enough, though not really my style.
Graphs were ok, especially considering the price.
Deceiving facts :
-No effort was put into the soundtrack, it's very very repetitive and hence quickly annoying.
-Too bad there's no map in this game allowing the player to go from one place to another easily without having to visit useless places dozen of times.
-Game lifetime. It's recorded I played 4 hours and a half but truth is I let the game running while I was AFK for at least an hour. My playthrough lasted  3 hours or so.. not much !!
Technical negative features :
-No resolution option, which sometimes resulted in having only half-visible useful stuff placed on sides of the screen.
-Be aware of 2 game UI related glitches :
1/ During cutscenes and video dialogues, the skip button is just above the hint button and the thing is that this skip button is "lazy" (as far as my experience is concerned). I had to click from 2 to 4 times, never knowing if my click was registered, the danger being to click on the UI hint button just under (and in that case having to do the game all over again just to unlock the last achievement involving not using the hint button during the whole game).
2/ It was often painful to succeed in grabing an item from the inventory. For an unknown reason that part of the game UI was there again not very functionnal. Each time I was to take something from the inventory, at the bottom of the screen, the inventory would pop up but immediately disappear, it wouldn't stay in place. I ended clicking very fast randomly in that inventory zone each time i needed something, hoping for grabbing the item i wanted to.. Sometimes I was feeling like using some cheap mug's game machine you can see in carnivals or fairs, where you mainly lose time and money but never obtain the thing you want ! :D
Apart from that I'm sure this game might please many gamers, most probably beginners.

A decent game, but it has several issues that make me not recommend it.
Pros:
- Story is interesting. It starts out as a typical "chase the villain" game but the locations and characters are interesting.
- Beautiful art
- The map is actually pretty (although can be a bit hard to navigate)
Cons:
- The cutscenes and dialog scenes: they are not voice acted, so you just sit there watching the lips of a character move while you've already finished reading the text, and there's no option to just move forward at your own pace. This got really annoying.
- Minor interface annoyances - it's really easy to accidentally click hint when trying to get the map, and lose the achievement. Also, the way you have to click several times each time you pick up an item (then to accept that you picked it up, etc) get annoying fast
- The cane - not sure why it's a mechanic. I kept forgetting about it. It's a tool built into the UI that just helps you reach for stuff, usually stuff that they could have easily just placed in a way that you don't need it.
- The soundtrack is the same 30 or so seconds on repeat for the entire game, cutscenes, gameplay, everything. And it gets annoying very quickly - I ended up turning it off after a few scenes.
If they would just fix a few of these, I would change to recommending, but as of now, I was frustrated more often than I wanted to be, but did stick with it because the story was interesting.

Dying Light is an open-world zombie game from the company that brought us Dead Island. Now, Dead Island was a disapointment. It was was fun, but the story was awful, and hacking through zombies could only be fun for so long. Unfortunatly, Dying Light has the same primary weakness of Dead Island.
The story BLOWS, and it blows hard! You are Crane, a, uh, character? Really, I am not sure if he has any characteristics other than being the protagonist. I mean, he helps peoplea and occasionally gets angry, does that count? Either way, he is in Harran for some document, I think (Honestly, this story is so dull I am having trouble remembering it, and I was just playing it yesterday). Stuff happens, you encounter a laughably cliched Vaas ripoff named Rais (yes, even the name is a rip off) and you kill a bunch of people/zombies. Trust me, you won't remember it either. Every character is either dull or cliched. We have such great characters as, generic love interest, troubled leader, and young, foolish kid. What a cast!
However, you didn't come here looking for the next Mass Effect or Spec Ops the Line. You came here for parkour and zombie carnage, and there is plenty of that. The parkour is fun, simple, and highly effective. You will find yourself running past zombies, over rooftops to get to your objective. This is an improvement as it removes the unecassary slog from the game and is quite fun by its own merits. When you fight, it is similar to Dead Isalnd. You have melee weapons which degrade (far too fast) and later on you get guns to go along with your new skills you pick up by leveling your character. The addition of the day night cycle leads to some intense missions and subsequent chases as you deal with faster, stronger, and more aggressive zombies at night. The game is beautiful, has a great soundtrack, is well-written, has choice and consequence, features incredibly deep and challenging turn based tactical combat, and is epic in its scale (in terms of the story, at least).  Everything about it is really well done, with the exception of a few odd UI issues which are too specific to list in this kind of review.  Character deaths, betrayals, and all sorts of cause and effect.
I must admit that there are two problems; the first is that there are some choices you make which you think will lead to other options, but there are none.  You're confronted with scenarios and choose a few different things, such as "investigate," or to take action.  Sometimes, however, what I think is the same as an "investigate" option actually IS the action I take in response to something, leading me to feel like my character should have been given the chance to do more.  It feels really gamey in these moments because in real life I'd have been able to do what I wanted.
Not giving too much away, there's just parts where you can ask a question of somebody and somehow that is an equivalent response to posting more guards at the supplies based on the game's logic.  That really sucks.
These situations pop up while your caravan crosses the vast world, which you spend most of the time watching them do.  And these situations are based on what you've done before or sometimes just new things entirely.  But the other problem is that you'll often lack context for how you should act based on a lack of information provided.  There are times when you'll be given the option to perform 3 different actions and you're basically just guessing based on nothing, sometimes being rewarded and other times not.  This doesn't always happen, but it does enough that it gets annoying.  And it's fine sometimes for seemingly random things to happen but sometimes you're acting without much info.  I can't get into better detail or else I'd spoil stuff.
Overall this is a great game which you should play in spite of the minor flaws it may have.  It isn't very long, nor is it very replayable in spite of the choices from my understanding, because the consequence I don't think can be widespread enough to actually change things too much.  Or at least enough to warrant a 2nd playthrough.

(Just so that I can be clear about it I originally played this game on the ps4 on a borrowed copy from a friend. So there are more hours put into the game then will probably ever be displayed. For the curious the steam version is the best version to play mostly for the shorter loading screens as long as you have a decent rig. Other then that they are relatively the same.)
A video review for those who might fancy that instead:
(PS4)
(I highly reccomend you play the game. So go play it. The less you know going in the better experience you will have I feel.)
The cloying sense of an unwelcoming world you don’t belong to or wish to be apart of. Relentlessly hostile by nature ready to snatch you up, and devour your valued worth. We plucked you like the ripened fruit that you are. Made you into something that would be desired. And now you will be served to our clientele who’s insatiable hunger has them fit to burst with excess. In the belly of the Maw some children grow up fast in a situation like this having to do some unsavory things to survive. We play that child in Little Nightmare, and her name is Six. With her we must try to escape this prison because there has to be better then this… right?
Saying that Little Nightmare is a horror game is a bit of an overstatement though. Mind you it has that overbearing atmosphere, sense of small helplessness, and some dark imagery to boot, but compared even to it’s closest counterpart, Limbo, it is rather tame in it’s tone. More of a thriller then a chiller. Don’t count it out though as  a contender for eerie atmosphere. It practically oozes with palpable unease using offset camera angles, washed color pallet, and masterful ambient noise to create an immersive experience that will have you glued till the end. Which will run you about 4 hours. Well it won’t have to hold your attention for very long, but trust me when i say that it delivers in spades.
Its a rather unique game in this age of handholding. Instead of forcing you through a typical tutorial to get you familiar with the controls it instead ops for a more subtle method delaying the prompts for only if you ever get stuck in those beginning areas. Its such a small detail, but in those first few crucial minutes of gameplay to opt in for a less intrusive tutorial does such a wonder of sucking you in especially when coupled with no ui of any kind through out your run of the game to break up your vision. It’s all lovingly crafted scenery thorough out with great shot composition. The controls are simple and intuitive, and the game’s engine does a wonderful job helping you through those trickier platforming moments. but it’s not perfect. it doesn’t happen often enough to be a real issue, but the camera isn’t always on its best behavior.  while you are performing your own movie in motion sometimes it just lacks in being able to convey a sense of depth leading to some moments of accidentally careening off high places, and swearing your right where you need to be but being just off center enough for the game to not register you trying to grab onto anything.
By the way this is some of the most organic level design i think i have seen in a long while. Practically everything can be interacted with, and the linear level design isn’t signposted by obvious out of place, or discolored objects in the environment. This design is so natural that it practically adds another layer of atmosphere that sucks you in, and feels as though you are six trying to navigate this overly large world with nothing but your wits and quick judgment calls. So much detail was put into this game that it is a marvel to just watch in motion, and will be relevant in a moment when we get to the story. But man i really feel i need to talk about one of the creatures you encounter, and just so happen to be the first as well. This gangly armed nightmare (also known as The Janitor) was the cause of a lot of my frustration in my play through of the game. His A.I was so finicky that it was hard to pin point just what logic it was running on. Sometimes it would seem like he would instantly know where i was if i set foot out of a safe area. While others he wouldn’t even know i was even standing right next to him. There was even a moment that he noticed me when using a lighter in an entirely different area out of his sight. It practically felt like blind luck on whether or not i could progress. It wasn’t until a later run-through that i noticed that it was the floor boards that were triggering him to chase me. He is blind after all so  just pay attention to the sounds. That and that his behavior is pretty buggy too. Granted it does make him the most frightening to deal with as the other antagonistic things in the game are rather easy to avoid. The last thing would be the signature final chase sequence at the end of the mid chapters. I really wish that they wouldn’t respawn you at the very beginning with very little time to react. If your caught off guard, or distracted by anything when the game loads... thats it. your boned. It leaves a rather sour taste in the mouth when it happens, but it is rather minor in the grand schemes of things.
*spoilers ahead. scroll to last paragraph* So now lets roll onto the story. What exactly is going on in little nightmares? ….. Well here is the thing. Despite that whole shpeel at the beginning of this video it is rather hard to say what the story is about. There is no dialogue in the game or even texts or messages to gleam information from either. Everything is told through the environment in the game which leaves it in the wonder land of vagueness. It is by design as the developers wanted to leave it up to your own interpretation, but there are some leading theories as to just what is going on behind the curtain. First, and probably the most straight forward is that The lady, yes the final bosses name is THE LADY, is six’s mother who is very self councious of her looks, as indicated by all the mirrors broken in her living quarters, is jealous or fears her daughters beauty, and so casts her within the depths of the Maw with all the other children. Thus the story of six climbing all the way back out for revenge(?) against her mother for what she did to her? Now i don’t know about you but this theory is to simple or empty a story with how much detail is packed into the environment and it’s denizens. No there is to much missing from this recount of the story to be satisfying. And so the second theory frames it more as an allegory for child abuse.
Starting the game in a suitcase,  the man you find hanging early on in the game, why so many wear masks, to the little gnomes that run around. The theory covers a lot that you see in the game, and lines up with what the developers say in interviews, that being a child would view things in more extremes or horrific where for adults would seem more normal. I still feel even this doesn’t line up right though. I certainly see it as an allegory, but maybe instead of child abuse perhaps an adoption home? My knowledge on the state of adoption homes is rather lacking and have no idea how i would go about researching this, but for some reason my gut feeling points me into this direction so eeehhh?
lastly the soundtrack is amazing, and does a great job setting the mood using the genres of ambience and industrial has some great pieces that can be listened to separately from the game, but a fair amount of it just isn’t easy to enjoy by itself. One in particular comes to mind called “the way out” when listened to with headphones just builds to a sense scrambling pitch that had me practically clawing the head set to get away from. So if it is your thing then by all means just be wary of that. To come to a conclusion Little nightmares is a game i think every one should play once, single, lonely number of 1 time as it loses all of it’s excitement that only a fresh perspective could enjoy.

Divinity: Original Sin is an attempt to recreate the experience of a true roleplaying game (the ones with pen and paper) onto your desktop. Hailed by some critics as a modern Baldur's Gate (who has attempted this before) it is meant to be the greatest RPG ever.
Now let me tell you, there is no compromising with this game, this in an RPG to the bone. The main example is that there are no quest markers, you are meant to ask people where to find the objective they just told you to go.
Not a bad thing right? Surely in the age of handholding and being pointed instantly to the right direction a bit of refreshment is nice?
Well, for some, maybe. But let me tell you one of my experiences with the game and first I'll tell you how to solve this within the game, and then how to solve it in an equivelant pen and paper scenario.
The Game:
You, for a quest, need to go to the town Inn. Simple enough right
Maybe ask a person where the inn is! Nope, no such luck, it hasn't been programmed in.
Well a guard surely gives directions! Nope, no such luck here either.
Well maybe near one of the entrances to the town there is a merchant selling maps, or there is a map hanging for travellers so they know where to go? Unfortunately no.
Well maybe check you in-game map then to see if you've already discovered it. Unfortunately only some buildings are actually marked, the inn is either not discovered or it isn't one of the marked buildings.
So after running throughout the entire town you eventually find the inn and can continue your quest.
Now, how would this go in a pen and paper campaign?
Step 1: Ask a random citizen where the inn is.
Step 2: Go to the inn.
You see, I don't have any problems with a lack of quest markers as long as I'm given intuitive tools to find it myself. Often you'll find that knowledge you need for a quest should be common to everyone in a town yet only a handful have been programmed in such a way that you can actually ask the question. For me, this is very frustrating.
The idea of a lack of quest marker is that you need to find your own solution to problems, but games inherently can only account for a few of these solutions. This isn't like Half-Life 2 where there only are one or two solutions to a problem. This is a roleplaying game, where there are a billion possible solutions yet only one or two have been programmed in.
At the end of the day you're left with all the disadvantages of a quest marker (liniear gameplay, no ability to use your own wits beyond what the game allows you to) but none of the advantages (the game accounting for the game's lack of ability to account for everything and telling you information you would have been able to pick up easily had you been able to freely ask NPCs questions).
So no, I cannot recommend this game, that one quest with the inn broke everything for me, I was warned about the lack of handholding but in the end, it was more than that, the game didn't give you the tools you would normally have to overcome certain problems.

Half-life was one of the first games I played which made me love video games beyond just basic entertainment value. The sequel, Half-Life 2, revolutionalized my view on video games entirely. The first time I sat down to play this game, I knew I was going to love it. The graphics were amazing, the game play was excellent, the story line stellar, and the physics really blew me away. This was the first game I ever played that implemented a legitimate physics engine that actually replicated real life (at least to some extent.) I remember the first time I picked up the gravity gun! Who needed other weapons after getting hold of that device?!? Half-Life 2 convinced me to one day pursue a potential career in the gaming industry and specifically orienting my degree towards developing real-time physics calculations.
Although today this game may not be the best graphics, the most realistic physics, the coolest game out there, it was and still is an amazing game worth playing if you haven't before. I also find myself playing the game over again every couple of years. This game definitely deserves awards in nearly every catagory out there, including "Best Game Ever Made!" Do yourself a favor and buy it if you don't already own it!
