FTL: Faster Than Light is a fun, addictive game at a cheap price.  The game mechanics are simple enough to make it easy to learn how to play.  Learning to play, though, is not quite the same as learning to win.  When it comes to learning to win, the game gets surprisingly complex.
This is my first roguelike game, and adjusting to the roguelike genre was a bit of a frustration to me at first.  There is no option to save a game to replay a bad encounter- when you lose, that is the end of the line, you start a new game.  Sometimes the game seems brutally unfair in throwing a series of hopeless situations at you.
You only learn to win by suffering a series of spectaculuarly unfair deaths, and puzzling through what you could do next time to prevail.  Once you get past the sting of defeat and accept your ship's destruction as a learning opportunity, you discover that no situation is really hopeless, and that with sufficient planning and strategy (and a bit of luck helps), you have an answer for everything that outer space has to throw at you.
FTL has a lot of replay value.  There is a wide assortment of ships you can unlock and play.  Each ship has its quirks; some have serious design flaws.  Each ship gives you the unique challenge of puzzling through using its strengths and mitigating its weaknesses, forcing you to develop different strategies for winning with each.
For me, it has been one of the most bug-free games I have played.  I have run into one crash over several hundred games.  That's it.  I have not seen any unfinished or incomplete content or obvious hole or exploits.  This game seems to have been proofread and playtested better than most games I have played.
FTL has been a lot of fun for just a few dollars.  It is a great value of a game.
Deserves a sequel.

With the recently released Advanced Edition, there is absolutely no reason why getting FTL would be a bad idea.
This devilishly addictive game has a complexity of elements yet a simplicity of gameplay, and it works really well. Though the average runthrough is one-two hours, and the changes of victory small (especially when the RNG gets involved), when you finally beat the final boss it is one of the most rewarding sensations.
There is a great variety of gameplay (with the AE more so), with many starting ships to unlock, several alien races to add to your crew, and a ton of weapons, drones, augments, special events, and ship systems, this game will always keep you on your toes. You will never know what to encounter and you will almost always have a choice on how to go about the mission. That is what makes FTL a fun game and I highly reccomend it to any fan of rougelikes with quick sessions of gameplay.
With the praise out of the way, let me point out a few drawbacks. For one, the RNG makes everything uncertain and for some players that randomness of outcome might be more frustrating than fun. If you get good at the game the RNG can be overcome, but not many people have the time to get really experienced at FTL.
Unlocking ships is also a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥ Some vessels are easy as cake to unlock and are fun to play. Others are tremenuosly hard to unlock, and really are not worth the trouble (Stealth Cruser Type C... impossible to unlock, and it sucks). Nonetheless there is a large selection of ships to suit your fancy.
There is also room for improvement with the amount of content possible... but as always, there are mods for that.

FTL is a game I've been pretty interested in since I first saw it. I love making up my own story up for how and why the rebels fought back against the federation and a whole bunch of other things. What thats saying is that the story is not what this game is about by any account. That does absolutely nothing to take away from the game though, if anything it makes it better. No need to fuss over alliances or about how amazing your quest is to save the federation! Mostly because you'll be dead soon enough. Very dead very quickly, or slowly dead but still very dead. Sometimes a crew member will get lucky and simply get a laser in the face when you get boarded, instead of slowly dying with your crew because someones hacked your doors and shut down your oxygen. Slowly but surely. Dead.
Okay cool, now lets get to the game itself. The art isn't going to stand out right away, until you notice all the little details and I sometimes find myself staring into the background after a long hard battle, listening to the music, which is also amazing but we'll touch on that in a bit. The missiles look great flying, the lasers look great lasering. Okay, so the music is great, most times you won't notice it as your in the heat of battle, but other times you'll be just listening for a good 20 minutes. The menu music keeps me captivated for at least 5 minutes each time I start up the game. I'm not some kind of artsy super expert or musical genius so we'll move onto gameplay.
At first, even after doing the tutorial you can get a little confused while playing. It's by no means a hard to navigate interface. It's just during a battle you'll have a bunch of things going on, redirecting power, sending crew members to repair a system, or fight off boarders trying to blow said system to bits. If that sounds overwhelming it can be, but thankfully hitting space will pause the action! And it's a much needed feature. Pausing to look over what your enemies have at the beginning of battle, pausing to look at your systems after taking a hit, pausing to rethink your strategy, pausing to decide if you'll run away because those hull points are not going to hold on for more than 2 more missiles, but you need that scrap for upgrades badly and you're so close to winning.Weighing risks is important too, or if you run into someone wanting to trade. Do you buy a drone system, or another weapon, does your ship have room for another system, the power for it? You probably don't have to worry about that so much as if you'll have enough scrap to do everything. Save up, or upgrade your ships basic systems? Decisions, decisions.
Now that you've read this long winded, but comparetively short review, I hope you consider buying this game, full price or on sale. Either way, it's going to be worth your time. Thanks for reading, and I hope you don't die too quickly.

-No spoilers are in this review-
warning: If you haven't finished reading A Storm of Swords, or finished Season 3 of HBO's Game of Thrones this game will have spoilers.
During the game you control several main characters, much like POV characters in the books. Considering the limited amount of time you get with each character, they do a great job of quickly introducing and getting you invested in them.
The storytelling just FEELS like Thrones. They did a great job injecting their characters into existing plots. It will be very interesting to see how the telltale and official storylines intertwine with future episodes.
My only gripe is that so far many of the choices don't have any real impact on the story (As of episode 1 at least, though I'm sure many of the subtle choices will effect later episodes.)
When Telltale first announced they'd be doing a Game of Thrones game, the thrones nerd in me was really hoping for something on a grander scale. Playing through as POV characters, making choices that differed from the books to see what may have been. However, a game like that would be very difficult to do well, and my dream game probably sounds better in my head than it would turn out in reality.
Overall I'm very satisfied with the first episode, can't wait for more.

In a word: TERRIBLE.
As usually, first the good things:
The idea is really good, the graphical style is wonderful, the voice acting at a very professional level.
Now, the review:
The game it's one of the worst I've ever played. I can see a lot of good intentions in it, but the final result gives the same feeling as spending time hammering your own fingers.
It says to mix RPG, turn based combat and choice driven plot. What you get, instead...
Dumb RPG system
All characters have a predefined class, each class has a starting set of attributes, but they all are already well defined and EVERY attribute has a maximum value that it's nearly reached just as you start playing.
For example, you may have a PC of class "really good with shields":
This PC could begin with Armour 12 out of 16, Strenght 8 out of 10, and other few useless stats. You will be allowed to choose on out of one active ability, and one out of one passive ability (just joking, you can't choose anything, each PC has predefined abilities)
So in the end you will get all predefined PC with NO SPACE for any personalization apart from maybe buying an item for them.
Honestly, this game is labeled RPG, but it has nothing to do with it. Instead, you are given a set of PC you have to use your better for...
Untactical unstrategic turn based combat
I can resume everything with just one sentence: you archers have 4 meters' range.
That is, they need to stay so close to the enemy to shoot him, that the enemy can reach them next turn with its basic movement. Really. And enemy has slinger with the same range, too: yes, a slinger with the same range of an archer.
But if this is not enough...
- Movement is not quantified. You need to click on a PC to see where he can go.
- You can move JUST ONE TIME. It doesn't matter how far you can reach, you can move only once. Now, it could be understandable to stop moving after attacking, but...you can't spend freely your movements and you have to move all at once? Foolishness.
- Your archers has meaningless range, so you protect them with another PC. And because scale with archer has always been a problem in RPG and tactical games, every game has opportunity attacks. This one? Guess what...it has not. So you have your archer right in range of the enemy movement (otherwise he can't shoot him), another PC protecting him, and the enemy just going 'round the defensive PC without any proble,
- The game can't do math. According to game's rules, damage is strenght minus armour, so e.g. a strenght of 10 vs an armour of 5 makes 5 damage.
Usually.
Sometimes is 6 damage.
Sometimes is 3.
And sometime 4 of strenght vs 4 of armour is 2 damage.
And so on...
- Combat is a classic interleaved turn based system: one of your PC, then one of the enemy, then one of your PC, etc. etc.
So, special abilities aside, there is no "retaliation phase": you move your PC next to the enemy, attack, he gets the damage and do not reply; when its turn come, he attack your PC and your PC do not reply.
Usually. When the enemy do not decide to reply to your attack, it goes the way above.
Well, I wrote "special abilities aside", after all, right? Yeah. But the enemy has not that special ability listed O_o
- You can't die during combat. No, really.
Honestly, the combat phase is really terrible. Having played lots of tactical games (and lot of boardgames), The Banner Saga falls so short that it's embarassing. Because at least Farmville is just a casual game, while this one does everything to looks like a tactical game, and fail miserably.
But...as the not-so-present RPG system is just a fake to bridge the game to strategy combat, maybe the the horrible and failed combat system is just put there for something else? Yeah, enter the...
On rails blind-choice driven missing plot
The title pretty sums everything, and sincerly I'm a bit tired typing.
The story proceeds on rails; I went trough half of the game before giving up after getting tired to not be able to decide any real direction. The plot is frozen, the path is carved in the rock, you just stand sit waiting for the game to show you a written dialogue, and asking you to choose if you want a battle or not. Just that, there is a map, there are two parties, and all you do is waiting for a dialogue, clicking on the next button after each sentence, then decide what to do.
Most of the coices are "do you want to battle or not?"; this in reality translate in "do you want an easy battle now and an easy next, or do you skip this and get an hardest next?"
Other choices are really...well, believe me, the entire system it's a mess. You are requested to choose without knowing what is going on, or without the minimum idea of what will come next. Most outcomes are not, in any way, linked to your choices, and you miss a lot of information too. And as a result of this, your PCs die in what often seems a random way (war council after a battle; you ask your allies what they think; you take a decision in disagreement with the young prince; for this he takes his few men and goes dumbly to battle against 820 fully armoured giants; you can stop him BEFORE he show signs of what he is going to do, or when he is already on the field; he dies)
In the end, just a couple of last things:
- I wrote "you just stand sit waiting "...well, that's not entirely true: as the game depict the travel of a caravan accross a land, I actually spent part of the afternoon cleaning my room while the caravan was moving on the screen.
- The game claim to have a beautiful soundtrack. Well, that's just the biggest scam ever; game's sound is a collection of unremarkable background music and a bunch of sound effects thrown here and there.
Personally, I love parkour. That is the reason I like the game. I LOVE PARKOUR! If you guys like to parkour and run from cops, well, here you have it. An AMAZINGLY well built parkour game.

A brief exit from the norm. Not too far off not to be a first person zombie game, but with just enough new in it to keep you locked to playing it until the game has laid its entire story out for you.
Dying Light was a pleasant surprise to me that came across as one of the few "Promise" games that delivered on many of it's statements. Yes, you are mostly a running man with naught but a pipe and brawn to beat your way through the zombie hoards. The game has a arbitrarily ranked RPG system that determines how this one sharp object is somehow twice as deadly as this other sharp object, but overall it doesn't take away from the feeling one gets from slowly working one's way from the literal bottom up of the zombie apocolypse.
Parkour is solid, while not being invasive to one's personal tread into the world. If you've had problems with parkour game's being to "clingy" or "sticky", this one is just the right amount of freedom of movement combined with "Your character grabs the ledge because death sucks" mechanics. It makes sense much of the time.
The story is mildly forgettable, especially if compared to any of the high and mighty titans of Zombie Apocolypse story-telling. (ex. Walking Dead, Last of Us, etc, etc) It tries to surprise us by beginning you in the game with a SECRET AGENT SHOOSH SHOOSH story, but doesn't really care about it enough to flesh it out beyond basic "Do as you're told" pitter patter on a walkie talkie. The characters are fairly human enough, but their deaths (Oh sorry if that's a spoiler, there will be people who say words to you and perhaps die shortly after) leave little to my tear ducts and seem more foreign to me. Improvements could be made, but they're not terrible so I consider that a positive as some of these zombie games can OVERDO it and make things awkward and cliche.
To shorten this: If you need your zombie fix and have done most the super big titles, this is your next best bet. (Although the DLC was pretty weak. PRETTY weak.)

hard.
Enemy AI is extremely simplistic, you can exploit their stupidity easily to force them into killing grounds that any decent AI would adapt to and avoid - they have only one way to handle situations, "attack."
The entire game treats you like you are in multiplayer.  Whereas most good single player experiences let you save progress when you stop playing, Grim Dawn will have you start an entirely new instance if you resume playing later.  This means if you have to spend an hour to get to a boss but don't have the time to finish the dungeon run you are stuck either leaving the game running until you come back to it or starting the entire hour long push through the dungeon over again, hope you have enough time the second go.
And there is the problem of economy, you get next to no money for selling anything and buying anything (including health potions) can become painfully expensive early on.
It lets you make all kinds of characters: tank, glass cannon, pet master, trap layer...  But if you encounter a boss alone it is always a case of dancing around your foe while you heal. Boss' powers aside those fights almost all end up with you running in a circle at one point or another.

Sets, sounds, and textures are all cohesive and enjoyable, they make for a very Diablo 2-esque vibe of dark and fearful, almost sorrowful at times.
The setting is gritty and dark, you get the sense of the horrors both human and otherworldly.
There is a double edged knife in the component and augmentation system, which is used to improve your gear - you have a god damned bajillion options.  It can become rather difficult to figure out exactly what you should be aiming for at times with the system because of that vast array of potential tweaks to your items.
Gear too is interesting and flawed, but drops are almost all useless.  I don't mean some, I don't mean a few...  I mean a vast majority of drops are entirely useless.  The quality system means you will only ever use normal items during your first thirty minutes with a character, and from then on will only use Magic items.  The variety for Magic, Epic and other loot is great though, if you want to specialize into a specific type of damag you can do so with the help of the right gear, and finding some to match your build is not too difficult.
Stats, oh Lord the stats - you have huge variety in damage types, resistances, and effects.  It can seem overwhelming trying to figure out what is going on.
The map is designed...  it is not a random or procedurally generated one.  It has elements which change between sessions, but these are largely pointless and do nothing to enhance the playthrough.

Crawl is a local multiplayer dungeon crawler where it is a race against your friends to be the ultimate hero. Crawl has been in early access for a few years and it might be one of the shining gems to come out of the Early Access void.
Crawl is supposed to be a party game where you or one of your friends control the hero and wanders the dungeon alone while the others try to control one of the monsters and try to kill you and halt your progress as the hero so that they can take your place and vice versa.
From the start Crawl puts your friends and you in a gladiatorial arena battle where you hammer each other to death before one of you emerges from the rubble caused by the commotion to wander into the dungeons. The other people then become ghosts who can control monsters of varying powers and try to kill the hero at every step he takes. Even here it is a race to get the last hit on the hero so that you can become the hero.
It is very frustrating to reduce a hero down to low health by yourself only to see someone else come and take the kill. It does put a lot of pressure on the monsters and they have to be on their guard at every given moment to check out their surroundings.  The other players do not need to become a monster to harm the hero as they can possess things like traps and spring them up at the exact moment to get the kill or throw random objects to hurt the hero.
Crawl also gives the player who has been the hero the least times the most powerful monsters to control so the game never feels unfair most of the time unless someone from your party of your monsters take the kill and it is a rage fest all over again. When a hero reaches Level 10, they can activate a sacrificial portal which allows them to face Giant Boss creatures in a bid to escape his fate and the cursed dungeon.
The other players control the Boss’s different organs in an almost Power Rangers Megazord kind of way. This great loop of gameplay of Crawl where you keep dying and coming back as the hero makes Crawl one of the best couch co op games in recent memory.
As the hero Crawl feels like a typical dungeon crawler RPG where you hack, slash, loot, dodge and earn XP to level up. There are a variety of weapons and spells for the player to use as the Hero and while there are you usual inane weapons which don’t feel anywhere close to some others, there is quite some interesting loot present in Crawl. The game as the hero plays like you would expect but it is the great unknown of the pleothera of monsters waiting behind the next door that is the great draw of Crawl.
As the ghost you have a lot of options to choose from a variety of monsters who have different tiers which require Wraith to unlock more powerful monsters. The monsters are quite obviously different from each other in very unique ways and while it might seem unfair, it gives the lowliest of players the strongest of monsters to have his own time in the glory.
The AI for solo play in Crawl is competent but nowhere near as fun as you will have with your friends. It is completely worth a try for its single play but do make a reminder to invite your friends over later for this one. There is no online play to speak of and considering the gameplay, it is probably for the best too. Crawl feels incredibly polished and the game runs really smooth at any given instance of time.
As far as pixelated art goes, Crawl takes the cake. It has a gorgeous art style which somehow makes even the blood and gore on the screen pretty neat. This is a game famous for spawning countless GIF’s and there are more to come from here. Some of the monster designs are truly incredible and some of them never fail to make you laugh. The game looks incredibly good and there is nothing quite like it.
Crawl has an incredible sound design which compliments its gameplay and visual aesthetics really well. The sound effects are solid and set the mood perfectly. There is little voice acting from the narrator but whatever there is, it is done really well.
Crawl is one of the best couch co op game to have ever graced my screen and there is no two way about it. It is one of the best examples of early access being done right and there is nothing quite like a Crawl party when it really gets going, Crawl works completely fine as a single player game too and there is a lot of content here to justify the price tag but you should definitely get Crawl if you want a solid game to enjoy with your friends.

A fairly flawed game, though very high production values.
First, some of the good points... The VN-style cutscenes are very well done with facial animations and some slight body animations. The characters are pretty fairly interesting, even if they are a bit airheaded. The gameplay is functional. The combat is standard turn-based RPG stuff but it's all 3D and there are no random encounters. It's the sort of game where you hit an enemy on the map and then enter an encounter. Overall the aesthetic, design and world are very well conceived and interesting, however...
There are a number of faults I have with this game and most of them I was willing to look past to be able to enjoy the story. The biggest one that changed that was when I got to the third dungeon (the first one in Lastation) and the difficulty spiked. This is a standard RPG. You get stronger by either leveling up or equipping your heroes. After the second dungeon I had a ton of money and got all the new equipment I could (which wasn't much, a new weapon for my main char and a couple "game discs" which function basically like a necklace/brooch slot in a traditional RPG and that was it) but I still ended up getting wrecked in the third dungeon of the game. The Escape mechanic in battle is broken. Once I tried in vain to flee like 12 turns in a row failing every single time. So basically they want you to go back to the first dungeons and grind just to compete in the third dungeon. Oh, and did I mention there are no revive items available for purchase before this dungeon? You do revive between battles but then you have to actually survive said battle for that to happen. I think I'm going to drop this game just for that since I can't be bothered to grind.
Other issues I had that I was willing to look past include:
-THE AUDIO OPTIONS DON'T SAVE... So annoying. I have to go into the audio options and reset all my audio sliders and change the dialog to Japanese every single time I play. All the other options save but not the audio options.
-The story itself starts out kind of dull. They intoduce you to this interesting world and it's characters in the middle of a war and then have the main character immediately lose her memory and end up slogging around doing mundane quests and such trying to get it back.  I can imagine it gets better as the story progresses but initially it felts like you're being given the backseat to a much more interesting story.
-No skills outside of battle which means you can only heal with *items* between battles.
-The targetting is a little wonky in battle. You have to move your char and then slowly rotate them to line up an attack. You can double-tap left and right to auto-target but then you can miss multi-target attacks so manual is almost always the way to go.
-The camera in battle always resets to pointing at the characters' faces when it's thier turn so you have to turn the camera every time you want to see where you're going. Having to fiddle with the camera occurs a lot on the map, too, but it's not as bad.
-You cannot equip things in a store or even in a city so you have to buy new items, leave the store, leave the city to the overworld map, equip your items, enter the city, enter the store and then sell your old gear... What the why?
-The English text is sometimes way off from the Japanese dialog. It probably matches the English dialog but that just means the English dialog is way off from the original script.
It's very hard for me to click "No" for this review and I wanted to like it but between the difficulty wall on the third dungeon and all the other minor points I mentioned, I just have to. If they smoothed out the grinding I could probably give this a 7 or 8 out of 10 and I could look past the other issues but as it is, I'd have to say 5/10. The production values are good, there are just too many speedbumps holding the game back.

Well guys, it's 97% positive, so I'm just another small voice in a huge choir of praises, but here goes:
Crawl is a peculiar game. It recently left early access, entering the fully released stage. The game’s idea is really original: four players (either bots or humans) are playing at the same time. One of them gets the role of dungeon explorer, going through the dungeon. Other take the roles of ghosts, who can spawn monsters or possess the traps across the rooms. If someone manages to kill the dungeon explorer, he takes his role, while recently deceased player becomes a ghost. The player who manages to get level 10 and kill the dungeon boss wins.
•	Really innovative and fun gameplay: there’s also no downtime for anyone, because all players influence the game in a way. It’s like telling a story from two different points of view
•	Lots of content and variety: different bosses, monsters, weapons and items. As you play more games, you get more unlocks, diversifying the randomized gameplay even further
•	AI is really good
•	The game has its own style: the pixel art is well aligned and fits the theme well
•	A bit of a snowballing tend to happen. If one player levels up while playing explorer, other players (ghosts) are getting stronger monsters. Technically, that tends to even out the disadvantages (weaker players have stronger monsters -> statistically they tend to kill explorer more and take its role) as the game progresses. But if weaker player gets the role of explorer – he still has to fight the strong monsters of at least two other ghosts which often won’t be in his favor. During the midgame this gap is felt the most, but then it evens out if the game drags on a bit. That’s really the only drawback I can name.
•	No online multiplayer: the game could really benefit from it.
•	Also, minor thing, but I could not switch active display on my machine (could not move the game to second screen). The option to do this is there, but it did not work if I changed it.
The game is good in singleplayer, because AI can use the surroundings well and both control and combat the monsters skillfully. However, Crawl shines brightest when played with friends: the hot-cold relationship that turns upside down when someone takes control of the explorer (and the old foe, in turn, becomes somewhat your friend) makes up for a lot of funny and exciting moments. I hate
. I hate it and I have to question whether or not it was either DICE or EA's meddling that, in my opinion, destroyed was initially a promising and unique concept or was it simply ruined from its conception?
portrays itself as a fast-paced action platformer with a parkour influenced movement system. The design of the game itself is very crisp, brightly lit, and presents a wonderful colour palette tastefully accentuated by the use of pastels. Whilst the sound design is sensibly sparse for its locations, the soundtrack is filled with synths and electronic beats befitting of the adrenaline fuelled gameplay. I also have to praise the way falling to my death from a great height has been designed as it elicits an utterly dreadful sensation of anxiety within me that I have not felt with any other game.
What I don't understand is why
fails so hard at its movement system and at providing any logical visual cues that don't suspend my disbelief and immersion of the world. Playing for the first time, I'm finding it incredibly difficult to know where I should be going. There is a "look at objective" button but it's not helpful when my destination is located across several rooftops, with a number of elevator rides along the way, as the button generally won't direct me towards these midpoints in the level. Sometimes I'll risk jumping across an impossibly wide gap that the game points towards, trusting in the almighty button of guidance, only to fall to my death. Then there are the environmental objects that have been tinted red, letting players know these items definitely make up the correct path that will take them to their goal. Why are these two features the only way I would ever know that the correct path is behind a pane of glass if it weren't for the out of place red wall? I imagine that, during playtesting, DICE was presented with an issue where players were having trouble navigating the unnecessarily semi-open levels of
and rather than make the rational decision to remodel the levels into a linear state they instead painted specific items red.
For a game that places so much emphasis on fluid and speedy movement
often feels sluggish, difficult to manoeuvre, and slippery. My character, Faith Connors, disobeys a lot of my intentions and will inexplicably travel in the wrong direction, decide not to grab ledges and pipes, and slide right off the edges of platforms after landing a solid jump or making a sharp turn while strafing. It is especially frustrating to have this happen when the threat of gunfire is raining down upon me, making the decision of where to go and what to grab that much more frantic. I often find myself failing and being reset back to the last checkpoint which can rewind several minutes of progress only to see myself fail again due to Faith not grabbing hold of that red pipe because I wasn't aiming at the correct angle this time.
When I mention of EA's meddling I'm asking if they had something to do with how the design and story of
tends to clash with itself. For instance, the main protagonist, Faith, and her occupation as a highly agile, martial arts trained courier - who has a somewhat merciful and pacifistic outlook of the world - seemingly has no qualms disarming military personnel and instantly blasting holes through their chest with their own firearms. The player has a choice in the matter, of course, to engage and use these weapons but the fact that there are forced combat segment which allow the player to contradict Faith's beliefs and training is yet another betrayal of the game's internal logic and my immersion that is now threadbare.
There's also the matter of the inconsistently styled cutscenes. Whereas the playable areas of
are focused on bright whites and pastel primary colours, the cutscenes themselves are incredibly dark in colour, the characters have tonnes of shading, and it's all 2D animated. It's very jarring to break through a vivid red door as a three dimensional Faith only to lead into a cartoony, shadow-filled cutscene that exits to yet another red door, slammed open into an extremely bright and sunburned environment.
I understand that the general consensus of the gaming community is that
is a really great game and that EA took a chance on a new formula but it just seems off to me, as if either EA or DICE had to implement certain mechanics because of the whole "we need to include this too" mentality and lack of restraint they have with all their games. I do enjoy watching speedruns of players who know what they're doing but as someone who's experiencing this game for the first time it's just too unpredictable, sloppy, and illogical for me to begin enjoying.

Breathtakingly gorgeous game. The art is wonderful to look at and vibrantly colourful, allowing characters to stand out against the often snowy backdrops.
The story and soundtrack are both exceptional, and do an amazing job of drawing the player into the frigid environments of the game, and the desperate struggle for survival.
The world map contains a great amount of lore on every location, even those which are nowhere near the events of the game. This makes the world feel like it has history, helping fit the game's narrative into a larger tapestry. Characters are well-written, but could have used even more dialogue to flesh them out even further.
Combat is tense, and the battle system has a few unique quirks. First, strength is based on a unit's health. Second, turn order alternates between allied and enemy units in a set order. The combat classes are well-balanced and there are interesting synergies when using special skills in tandem. Battles are tense, especially when outnumbered and surrounded. Units level up based on how many kills they get, which can cause a snowball effect and leave many of your units underleveled.
Out of combat, there is light resource management in the form of supplies for your caravan. There are also many decisions to be made, some more difficult than others. Also, your party members can die permanently based on your decisions in these events. On one hand, this feels a bit cheap, since these deaths are unpreventable. On the other hand, this ensures that decisions feel weighty and meaningful, and does not allow choices to be made without care.
Unit upgrades and purchasing supplies and items are handled with the same currency: "renown". This is earned by killing enemies, winning battles, and sometimes through other choices. This resource can get very tight, leading to even more tough decisions.
Overall, an outstanding game that I would recommend to anyone who likes strategy.

Grim Dawn is equivalent to being a direct successor to the Titan Quest series. For the uninitiated, Grim Dawn is developed by Crate Entertainment, of which was what that rose from the ashes of Iron Lore's (Titan Quest's developer) THQ-related demise.
So why mention it?
TQ's strongest selling point back then was it's dual-class system. Pick two different classes to make your own class. Or choose not to and specialise in only a single class. The choice was yours, and quite frankly the choices were nearly unlimited too. GD in being a successor to TQ brings back the dual-classing system, with an additional twist: Devotion skills. The Devotion skills system adds an additional layer of character customisation, which made what was nearly an overwhelming amount of build choices even more overwhelming.
To keep this review brief, to me that is the best selling point about this game: endless build choices. Crate has successfully brought back a personally missed feature in many ARPGs to date, and made it even better. I foresee myself returning back to GD time and again whenever my life permits and never finding myself bored of the game.

Although the much-needed Brave New World expansion took its time to arrive, there's no doubting that Civilization V carved out its own identity on the series. The absence of the 'stack of doom' alone makes it worthy of appraisal by old-timers. Newcomers will be pleasantly surprised at the game's eloquent and all-embracing overview of mankind's history, which to this day sets Civ apart from pretty much any other large scale franchise.
There's no denying that V is somewhat dumbed-down compared to III and IV, but you can adjust your difficulty setting to compensate. In IV I preferred Prince; in V I go for Emperor. As with IV before it, I prefer the Ancient and Medieval as a battling period, simply as you need to make every unit count and haven't the sheer power that arrives in the late game. Of course there's plenty of room to play non-hostile too; the game is very accommodating to players yearning to win without war.
Overall, Sid Meier's Civilization® V is a superb title worthy of spending just...one...more...turn on.

It's like crime how Child of Light can rob you of your time.
The combination of side-scrolling exploration, challenging turn-based tactical gameplay, amusing rhyming dialogues and a wonderful art style makes Child of Light an unusual but enjoyable gem.
You'll quickly fall in love with the beatifully drawn landscapes of Lemuria as you travel through its dark forests, mountains and even under the sea. They are typically riddled with secret areas you can sniff out for treasure, puzzles or hidden bosses. Often there'll be more than one path to your destination, making exploration more interesting.
During your travels, you'll meet many fun characters who'll give your quests, join you in your adventure, or both. My favourite was a female jester who couldn't do the dialogues in a proper rhyming fashion, allowing the other characters to jump in and correct her. Her healing abilities were also very welcome in a fight, making her one of my most used characters during combat.
The combat is turn-based but has a real-time element that lets you delay enemies' turn or slightly heal your party out of turn. Timing this ability is important to winning encounters, as it lets you better use or avoid being the victim of the interrupt mechanic. Interrupting means hitting a character trying to perform an action, resulting in his turn being delayed. If you don't go for the easy difficulty, combat offers good and rewarding challenge that makes you invest time into considering how to specialise your characters.
Each character has a network of specialisation trees, offering abilities unique to him while giving you a choice between the different paths. For example, there's a wizard who can specialise in lightning, water or fire, allowing him to excel against certain creature types vulnerable to his focused element. Another character can choose between improving his defense, his offense or his ability to direct enemy attacks against him.
A problem that grows as the size of your party increases, is the frequency of level ups. Very quickly you'll be looking at one or multiple level ups after pretty much every battle as your characters gain levels and extra skill points to spend. It becomes tedious looking at the skill tree menu this often.
Another part of character customisation is the Oculi system. Oculi are gems you gather and can use kind of like equipment items such as swords and armor in other games. They offer different bonuses depending on color and slot used, and can be combined to form more powerful gems. Oculi juggling gets a little cumbersome, but is nonetheless an important strategic element as you want to equip the right damage and resistance types depending on the opposition of your current area.
Apart from having trouble with Steam starting the game through Uplay for some reason initially, the only bug I noticed in the actual game was that sometimes when entering combat, Aurora's (the main character) usually flowing hair wasn't drawn.
If you're not playing on Easy difficulty and like to explore and look for secrets, you should expect around 20 hours of gameplay from Child of Light.
TIP: While Child of Light offers controller support, I really must recommend using mouse and keyboard. You will need the precision to properly manage the real-time element of the otherwise turn-based combat.
TIP: If, like me, you have trouble starting the game through Steam, try launching Uplay directly and start the game from there. After doing that, it's been working for me no problem.

I'm not going to go into a big review of all the features, since others have already done so, and in a better fashion than I probably would have. :-)  What I will say is that having never played a JRPG game before, I'm having a great time with this game.  I agree with other reviewer who say that there's a lot of grinding needed in order to get to a level where you can handle the harder monsters.  I explored a dungeon that I haven't been able to complete yet - having encountered a "dangerous" level creature (not even a boss), and repeatedly got my rear-end handed to me several times, even in transformed/Goddess mode. lol  Ok, live and learn - I'm going to have to spend some time  in the other dungeons building up strength and levels.  Fair enough.
Maybe I'm weird, but I've actually enjoyed the English dub for the dialog, although there are places where all you get is text with no voiceover.  Another reviewer here said that if the Japanese language is is selected, those "silent" areas will have dialog.  I'll give that a try.  I don't find the lack of voiceover as annoying as some do, though.
I love the puns, references to other games, and the fourth-wall breaking that goes on.  I find it very amusing. :-)
One thing I will strongly suggest here:  USE A GAME PAD CONTROLLER. :-)  The game is playable with keyboard/mouse, but I found it to be extremely frustrating trying to do so (and I typically play all my games with keyboard and mouse).  This game is a port of a console game, and it really shows in the controller area.  Amazon has the Logitech F310 Gamepad available for $15 (as of this writing), so you don't need to spend a lot to get a good solid usable controller.  I purchased this controller specifically because of this game, and haven't regretted it for a minute.  And the nice thing is that I'll still have the controller should I ever encounter another game where a gamepad would be more convenient.
All in all, I'm having a very enjoyable time with this game, even though I've just barely started it as of this writing.  I really hope that PC sales of this game are strong enough that they choose to bring the other Hyperdimension Neptunia games to the PC.  The trailer at NIS America for Hyperdimension Neptunia mk2 looks really good. :-)
To sum it up:  As others have said here, if you like Anime and/or JRPGs and can be tolerant of the need for some grinding to get to a level where you can play parts of the game, I think you're going to like this.  I sure do. :-)

So, as a preface, despite my 0 hours on Steam, I have around 100 hours on this game outside of it.
This game isn't a bad game - it just labels itself as the wrong genre. Black Desert Online is essentially nothing worth mentioning other than its character creation, so for all intents and purposes, consider this game truly belonging in the Fashion/Dress-em-up genre. Nothing else it offers is valuable enough to even consider it as anything else.
Why, you ask? Well, I'll tell you.
The combat in BDO is action-based, and you'll likely find it fairly fun for the first 20 minutes of the game. However, it lacks depth. It's extremely simple, mindlessly pressing your silly little action combos which are always the same with no strategy needed whatsoever. I know you may think I'm exaggerating, but this game genuinely doesn't require any strategy at all in any of the situations you'll be using the combat system. There's typically one better combo you should just always use, streamlining the game to the extent that Club Penguin snowball fights had more strategy involved, at least you had to aim there.
A lot of BDO's players hail its skill system, for giving you 'so much to do', and they're right! You can watch so many shows and play actually good games while participating in the ever exciting gameplay of leaving your character AFK fishing in order to make money. Literally AFK. It requires NO input whatsoever. Sounds amazing, right?
Granted, some of the skills do actually require input rarely, but unless you find pressing a single button fun, there likely won't be much in the game for you. Fact is, that BDO's skill system is done better in every way by other MMOs, such as Final Fantasy XIV with its extensive crafting and gathering system, Runescape with its huge amount of skills and ways to level up on. Even Guild Wars 2 has more depth to its skill systems.
In summary, BDO's skills are just brainless, boring affairs that often have you leaving your game open AFK in order to achieve them.
BDO's PVP is okay. That's about it. You can go and fight other guilds and war them and stuff. However, due to the game's lackluster combat and P2W elements, it will require hundreds of hours of grinding to even get good enough gear (gear is all that matters in this game) to be able to compete in PVP effectively. Or of course, you could just go buy money and items from the cash shop. Some may claim this isn't P2W at all and is just pay for convenience, and I can understand the point, but claiming something you can buy at the click of the button compared to a 400 hour grind isn't even slightly P2W is just delusional.
If you want a game with good PVP, go check out Guild Wars 2, ESO, or WoW. All three of these do pvp content FAR better than BDO does, and have more to do in combat than mindlessly using the same combo over and over.
Nope. Just world bosses that are glorified training dummies with no strategy required. Think GW2's ones, but worse in every way.
BDO's economy tries to be in depth and fun by copying Archeage, and then adding artificial difficulty on top. Oh, you also need to level up multiple alt accounts in order to even try and compete/earn money a decent amount of money within the economy. Of course, you can also just bypass the economy with your wallet, making the system meaningless anyway.
One thing that IS neat about it, is that you can go be a pirate on a boat and steal people's stuff. Like in Archeage.
Easily would be the best thing about this game if it didn't have a whole host of technical issues, such as major pop-in issues that make you feel like you're playing Fallout 4 on an Xbox. The pop-in issues really do ruin this game's otherwise impressive graphics, as it removes any immersion in the world entirely, when you see a tree suddenly pop up right in front of you out of nowhere.
Of course, the game's graphics are best in case on the characters. This game features a highly in depth character creation system, easily the best of any 'MMO' out there, which allow you to make your virtual waifus to your hearts content. As for dressing them, however, you better be ready to grind hundreds of hours for the outfits, or just buy them from the cash shop at around £20 an outfit! Amazing deal, right? - this game NEVER adds outfits that you don't have to buy from the cash shop or from someone who bought them from the cash shop for silly amounts of money. Ever.
Even as a dress your waifu simulator, it falls short due to this. You're much better off making a catgirl in Final Fantasy XIV, which has hundreds of outfits and actual art direction, which this game lacks. And while it is subscription based, a years subscription costs about as much as 2-3 outfits in Black Desert.
There's a story? Maybeeee? I personally couldn't tell.
What's that? Ask the developers of Black Desert, Pearl Abyss.
The only 'endgame' that exists in BDO is dressing your waifu up in new ways. Which overexposing, totally protective piece of armour will you buy next? Will you make her thighs, or butt bigger? The choices are endless!
If for some reason you actually want to participate in the intended endgame of BDO, prepare yourself for the adventure of a lifetime. Thousands of hours doing literally nothing but grinding to level up, make gold, and get new gear. This is a korean MMO at its very core, for those who love nothing more than having a job outside of your job, this is the game for you.
The bulk of BDO's new content is new outfits you can buy for your waifu from the cash shop. Occasionally, they add a new class which is usually gender-locked as they're too lazy to design gear for both genders, since they'd have to give the starter gear away for free instead of put it on the cash shop. Don't expect anything interesting from these classes other than looking cool when you stand around AFK fishing, however.
Black Desert Online is a decent fashion simulator. If you have money to burn, you should go make your new virtual girlfriend or boyfriend right away, and spend hundreds on the illusive array of clothing available to you, featuring unique designs, such as a maid outfit, a cat outfit, and that one armor piece from TERA that the lolis wear.
If you're looking for a good MMO, this isn't the place for you. Everything this game does is done better by another MMO.
Combat? Head for WoW, FFXIV, or GW2.
Skilling? Runescape, FFXIV, GW2.
Fashion? FFXIV, TERA.
Graphics?  Yup, this will suit you.  Beware the ninja pop-in trees. However, you should just go mod single-player Skyrim and make that your fashion simulator instead, it's a lot cheaper, and the outfits don't cost the same as it does to eat for two weeks, they're free.
Raiding? WoW, FFXIV.
There's nothing this game truly excels at other than its character creation, which is shamefully put to waste by the rest of the game. Again, single-player skyrim is better for this, unless you want to ERP, which a large portion of this game's community spends its time doing. Wow, they actually managed to make this game good enough to be called XCOM! In some aspects this game even surpasses the original X-Com: UFO Defense. They altered combat game-play by simplifying the original "time-units" but they have done it very well and kept the game turn based. Soldiers now have classes, it makes them limited to what they can equip but the game adds special abilities to these classes that actually really work.
I dislike the fact that only one base can be chosen but Enemy Unknown counters this with the deployment of satellites and interceptors all over the world and these can be chosen by the player. Superhuman Antarctica challenges will not be possible though ;). Despite that they have created lot of game-play and choices by adding mechanical suits and/or implantation that alter the combat game-play significantly. A brute force player would choose these mechanical suits, run into combat and deploy a flamethrower on multiple enemies. A more subtle player would adopt implants to make soldiers more stealthy and enhances maneuverability. The added features have let the tech tree grow significantly and thus more choices are available to the player.
Combat itself gained a good boost as well, no more counting time-units while the game-play is still in tact. You basically have 2 moves with an upgraded soldier that just leaves a couple of choices: Shoot, walk + shoot, walk + walk and run. This really does not hurt the time-unit game-play of the originals at all. Besides this they added cover. Cover is a important aspect to the game and grants additional defense to your units.  You can find partial cover behind small objects like crates and full cover behind things like walls or big cars. When an enemy flanks you, or the other way around the defense bonus is subtracted and the flanker has a much higher accuracy. This flanking plays a huge part in combat. Besides flanking there is always the option to just blow up enemy cover with a diverse explosive arsenal.
They kept true to the original game-play and everything they altered just works. I usually hate it when they simplify my childhood games but they really did a good job on this one. Everybody should have this game in there collection!

- Excellent strategic turn-based strategy.
- With a wide variety of customisation options you can really make your squad your own.
- You can mix up the gameplay with extra options like randomised class progression and higher damage range

Cons:
- All english language nations have American accents. Localised accents would really have helped immersion.
-Would have liked more story missions.
- Later missions can feel like a grind.

KF 1 was good, creepy, hard, kinda "edgy", and awesome.
KF 2 is mostly terrible in comparison.
Cons:
-KF2 has gone main stream. It feels really "consoleized".  Creepy stalker ladies no longer show boobs. The trader lady doesn't hit on your and make inuendoes.  The funny british slang and swearing is all gone.
There is a run button rather than pulling out your knife. You can't pull out your welder anymore, you just have to try to make the context sensitive weld interface work(which it doesn't). All kinds of nonsence like emote dances, skins and other assorted crap. All the "Character" from the first one is gone in this game.
This feels like the abomination that Payday2 became after they reset all the skill trees and added crates and nonsence.
-KF2 ruined all the level strategy.  Monsters appear from literally everywhere and evey wave is total madness. There is no "lets pick a hall or a few to cover and close and weld doors" strategy.  There is almost no reason to weld doors KF2 and each wave is mosly just people running around like crazy and almost no teamwork happends. Definatly no strategy.
-Somehow the game lost all sence of creepyness.  The graphics are updated and there is blood and guts everywhere, but as you play its all just nonscence and not creepy or scary.
-The Difficulty isn't right.  KF1 had a particular brutalness to it, where you really couldn't let the specimens reach you at all, but you quickly learn to keep moving and shooting and covering your team.  The new one you have lots of life and are attacked all the time and helping your friends just doensn't matter too much other than maybe healing or giving ammo.
-KF2 doesn't have the story mode levels anymore.  There were only a handfull of KF1 story mode levels, but they usually were part of a holiday update and were always a good reason to get back into the game.
Pros:
Almost nothin. I think I actually like the old graphics better.
The only pro I can think of is that I think I finally played so much KF1 that I was kinda bored with the KF1 levels and patriarch and even though there were many user created maps that I did and didn't try, I think I did want some new stuff.
I'm glad there are new boss fights.  Thats about it.

I'm not going to go into a big review of all the features, since others have already done so, and in a better fashion than I probably would have. :-)  What I will say is that having never played a JRPG game before, I'm having a great time with this game.  I agree with other reviewer who say that there's a lot of grinding needed in order to get to a level where you can handle the harder monsters.  I explored a dungeon that I haven't been able to complete yet - having encountered a "dangerous" level creature (not even a boss), and repeatedly got my rear-end handed to me several times, even in transformed/Goddess mode. lol  Ok, live and learn - I'm going to have to spend some time  in the other dungeons building up strength and levels.  Fair enough.
Maybe I'm weird, but I've actually enjoyed the English dub for the dialog, although there are places where all you get is text with no voiceover.  Another reviewer here said that if the Japanese language is is selected, those "silent" areas will have dialog.  I'll give that a try.  I don't find the lack of voiceover as annoying as some do, though.
I love the puns, references to other games, and the fourth-wall breaking that goes on.  I find it very amusing. :-)
One thing I will strongly suggest here:  USE A GAME PAD CONTROLLER. :-)  The game is playable with keyboard/mouse, but I found it to be extremely frustrating trying to do so (and I typically play all my games with keyboard and mouse).  This game is a port of a console game, and it really shows in the controller area.  Amazon has the Logitech F310 Gamepad available for $15 (as of this writing), so you don't need to spend a lot to get a good solid usable controller.  I purchased this controller specifically because of this game, and haven't regretted it for a minute.  And the nice thing is that I'll still have the controller should I ever encounter another game where a gamepad would be more convenient.
All in all, I'm having a very enjoyable time with this game, even though I've just barely started it as of this writing.  I really hope that PC sales of this game are strong enough that they choose to bring the other Hyperdimension Neptunia games to the PC.  The trailer at NIS America for Hyperdimension Neptunia mk2 looks really good. :-)
To sum it up:  As others have said here, if you like Anime and/or JRPGs and can be tolerant of the need for some grinding to get to a level where you can play parts of the game, I think you're going to like this.  I sure do. :-)

The Banner Saga is, quite frankly, a tour-de-force in storytelling. It uses a very simplistic style and point of view for cutscenes, but that is in no way a knock against it. The game manages to bring life to still images, by simply adding a little animation to them, such as the wind blowing on a character's hair and beard or someone's eye twitching.
Even with 2D graphics, the techniques mentioned up add more depths and character to the setting. In addition, the impressive landscapes and the immeasurable scale of all the vestiges of an old civilzation where Gods walked the earth, makes the world simply breathtaking to look at. Combined with the outstanding soundtrack by Austin Wintory, you'll almost feel like the snow is falling on your head, that your feet are soaked from walking in the forest, and sometimes you'll even feel, much like the characters, that all hope is lost.
The game has a pervasive sense of dread to it, as you are just a ragtag crew of norsemen and women, trying to beat seemingly insurmountable odds. Even on Easy, I found the game quite difficult, but it could be just me making bad tactical decisions. The game is very punishing and the AI, a lot of times will take advantage of errors in your tactics. While it can be a little frustrating, I found this dynamic to be quite enjoyable and it kept me coming back for more.
The story is by the numbers, but the gameplay is fantastic. I love the running, jumping and exploration in this game. It is one of the must have games of 2015 IMO.

Grim Dawn is an ARPG. Popular games to compare it to are the Diablo series and Path of Exile (PoE). I usually played Grim Dawn with a friend of mine with either of us hosting and played almost exclusively hardcore mode. Hardcore mode is a character specific difficulty setting that will render your character unplayable if they die. One death and you need to make a new character.
Hardcore vs Non-hardcore; the differences: Asides from the permadeath aspect, the only difference between hardcore and non-hardcore is that these two character types and all their gear can NEVER be mixed and matched. A hardcore player can never join a non-hardcore player's match and vice-versa. Each account has two of its own shared stashes that is shared between all your characters. One of those stashes is for your hardcore characters while the other is for non-hardcore characters. Some special crafting items cannot be put into your shared stash as well as money. Each character has a single page for its own storage; anything can be put in here. In your character select screen, a hardcore character has a distinct yellow aura around them.
In regards to gameplay, Hardcore players need to build extremely carefully as a single mistake can easily lead to death. Many times, in hardcore, my character has been practically instant-killed, almost always due to me either zoning out or thinking my character was immortal; I was swiftly proved wrong.
Classes: You get to choose two classes (In this game, classes are called Masteries); you can choose your initial mastery at level 2 (when you get your first points) and your second mastery at level 10. You are not forced to pick a second mastery at all and can very easily complete the game as one of the basic masteries with a bit of effort. Your choice in mastery is permanent and once you choose one, you are stuck with it as soon as you invest points into it. Each mastery (both your first and second mastery you choose) have something called Mastery Points. Each point in each respective mastery gives you bonus stats and approximately every 5 points unlocks more abilities and passives all the way up to a maximum of 50 mastery points. All masteries have a variety of options at your disposal, meaning there is no set build for any two class combinations. You could easily play as a tanky sword-and-board Blademaster (Nightblade & Soldier) that focuses on bleed damage. Or you can just as easily build a dual wielding blademaster that throws tankiness into the wind to go for massive damage.
There are many options in regards to classes and damage types; from cold to vitality damage, there's a build for practically every single damage type you can imagine. The only limit is your inventory.
Gear Dependence: In regards to true lategame, gear starts to become extremely relevant. The moment you hit Ultimate, enemies become significantly more lethal and its where your build truly starts to be tested. As you make your way through the game, there might be points where you just hit a wall (figuratively) and attempting to progress leads to many deaths. Many times, it just involves a bit of tweaking or adding components to your gear.
(Note: All gear has essentially a single socket. You can add a single component to each piece of gear and many components can only be put into certain gear pieces. You cannot remove a component from an item without destroying either the item or the component.)
Gear is certainly relevant in Grim Dawn, but it doesn't start to become extremely relevant until the hardest difficulty of Ultimate. Until then, you can easily live with what you find on the ground to keep you living.
Online Capability, Netcode & Associated Issues: Many people, like myself, tend to play Grim Dawn over the internet. There are no servers so all connections must be either through LAN, simulated LAN, or local hosting with forwarded ports. Some players have no issue hosting at all, while me and my friend, due to having strange network setups, use an ancient version of Hamachi to connect to one another. Many players use either Hamachi or Tungle if they are having issues with connecting to one another.
Once connected, there are a few issues at times. For the host, there is never an issue; no lag, no delay, as to be expected. For the person connected, there are occasional desync issues, from an item that cannot be picked up (since the host has already picked it up), to a monster that seems to be attacking the host from 30 feet away despite using melee attacks. One of the worst issues me and my friend have had a few times is an extremely lethal DoT applied in an aura to one of us. The other player has some sort of aura around them that will kill other players despite there being no PVP and no way to purge this. I have nearly been killed a few times on my hardcore character by this. Restarting the server is a guaranteed fix.
Graphics & Framerate: The game itself is presented quite well, looking and sounding quite nice. At times it's a bit hard to sift through all the junk on the screen, but I manage quite easily. With many monsters on the screen, at times, the framerate will dip pretty significantly. Asides from this, the game runs at a constant 120+ fps for myself on a fairly powerful rig. On my laptop I occasionally play the game on though, every time my character picks up an item I get a massive stutter/lag spike lasting 0.25 seconds. If you purchase the game, I would recommend checking to see if you have this issue as it can very easily make the game almost unplayable.
Overall, the game is a fun experience, especially with friends. It has a great deal of replayability with a significant amount of variety between the masteries. While it has a few issues, those can be overlooked easily.

Killing Floor 2 is Tripwire Interative's debut in the gaming industry. The original game was first released in 1998 as a total-conversion mod for Half-Life 2. Over the last decade, they have continued to polish and work on the game, and they finally released it last year. While this review might be a little late, I can still say for certain that Killing Floor 2 is one of the best open-world RTS games that I have played this decade.
Killing Floor 2 is a co-op RPG survival game, with many elements of rogue-likes. Death is permenant in this game, and if you die in the game, you die in real life. You team up with 7 friends (or random people!) to kill Zeds, gross monstrosities from the planet Neptune. All of the Zeds have great design, and you can tell that TWI had worked really hard on them. Killing Zeds lets you imbue their strength into your weapons, making them more powerful. I find this to be a very fun mechanic, as people who kill many Zeds are rewarded with very powerful weapons. Prior to the start of the game, you can choose a class. You have the heavy, the demoman, pyro, and Bill. Each class has their own special abilities (the heavy can double jump, and Bill can sprint much faster than the others) which makes them feel very unique. They also start with their own unique weapons, which can be upgraded by killing Zeds, as I mentioned earlier. You play through 25 waves of stronger and stronger Zeds, eventually meeting a boss alien at the end. The mechanics in this game are very unique and the movement controls are amazingly tight (the grappling hook makes this game 10/10 on its own!).
Other people might tell you to buy the sequels like KF: Origins or KF: Brotherhood instead, but KF2 is the original and arguably the best one (definitely don't buy KF though, it's complete garbage and you can read my review to see why). It still has a huge playerbase, so you will have no problem finding a match. Also, it's free, so what do you have to lose by playing this game?

Despite all of the lavish praise this game received, I can't recommend it.
I played the original XCOM on a 486dx33 (yes a 33mhz processor) and loved it.  I will go right to the heart of my grudge against XCOM: Enemy Unknown.  Enemies drop into your battles at random locations, including behind your squad's positions.  This wrecks use of cover.  It wrecks tactical positioning.  It wrecks immersion.  It might be okay if this were a rare thing that happened with certain enemies, but it is a central part of the system.  In my mind, nothing they do right could make up for such a terribly lazy implementation that substitutes randomness for a smart ai and well designed maps.
For example, you are cautiously advancing your squad down a linear hallway deeper into the enemy base.  You are careful to keep them always behind cover for the direction you are advancing.  Maybe you also try to ensure that each squad member is appropriately positioned to use their weapon to full advantage.  You open a door, ready for your doorkicker assault members to burst in and scan for targets.  Suddenly a giant and very strong UFO shaped enemy drops immediately behind you in the hallway that you just cleared!  It takes its turn immediately and blasts your weakly armored sniper that you had left towards the rear.  They are now dead.
Where did this UFO thing come from?  How can it just fall out of the sky?  What is the point of moving as a team if enemies simply drop in anywhere?  How can you use cover if enemies drop immediately behind your cover with no rhyme or reason?  This is terrible game design!  There would be nothing at all wrong with randomly spawning enemies at the start of the battle, but randomly dropping them into the fight is bad design.
Other things missing that the original XCOM (1994) had: fully destructible terrain, fires, a beautiful and working light system (light grenades, fires cast light, etc) that made night missions terrifying, an alien rocket launcher with projectiles that could fly waypoints, freely flying armor, multiple troop carriers to research and build, the ability to set up multiple bases strategically around the globe, potentially catastrophic invasions of your bases, interceptor flight tracking, squad inventory management, etc etc etc.  Also, your characters weren't locked into any specific class nor did they have a radically dumbed-down and simplistic choose-one-of-two skill system.
I remember all of these things even though I haven't played the game in many years because it was the little things like that combined with the awesome tactical combat that made XCOM so memorable and made for the sort of nostalgia that a cheap rip-off like this exploits to sell copies.  Few will remember this game in a few years, but the memory of the original X-COM remains.
For a game that lacks so much of whats it's predecessors had, and messes up the core tactical combat, it is amazing to me that it has received such praise.

Flawed, but a gem in the rough.
Little Nightmares is a surprisingly refreshing game in the sense that it doesn't hold your hand, doesn't tell you what to do, and asks the player to fill in the blanks. There isn't much of a story to go on: you play as a nameless kid in a yellow poncho who awakens on a nightmarish ship where almost everything is out to snatch you up. Your objective, presumably, is to survive and escape.
For being such a stark environment and with a neat title for a game, the graphics certainly do not disappoint. In a way, it reminds me of a Henry Selick flick meeting a Sylvain Chomet film - a tidy fusion of the atmosphere of "The Nightmare before Christmas" with the weird, grotesque aesthetics of The "Triplets of Belleville", to name something more specific. For those who might not cotton to the analogy, Little Nightmares rides a fine line between the cute, the disgusting, and the unnerving. Enemies with long, gangly arms or fat, pudgy bodies look to snatch you up as either pest or as part of their dish. The rooms and hallways are never repetitive, each one has something new to survey and look at, usually with new puzzles or gimmicks along the way to keep it refreshing. To those who are seeking to be scared out of their wits, be forewarned. This is not a true horror game in the sense that it will not scare you every step of the way. It's actually fairly tame and aims for more of a suspense / thriller adventure that's rooted in an ominous environment where you can bite the dust at any given moment in time.
Combined with the dreary ambience and the clattering and creaking of metal at every corner, this sounds like a perfect game. Except there's one problem.
As a game, Little Nightmares is flawed and mediocre. The most frustrating parts about the game are the stiff, clunky controls and the overall lack of polish that comes with it. For those who only have a keyboard and mouse, I would recommend you stay away as even with a gamepad, general movement is stiff and somewhat annoying to navigate around with. The game follows pseudo-tank controls which is okay, but the fixed camera angle from room-to-room makes discerning depth between background, foreground or even what may lie ahead in the next room frustrating since props or even pits can be obscured by the camera. Thankfully, the camera never obnoxiously changes angles on you mid-room, it's always focused on you at any given point and moves along with you.
On top of this, the game relies heavily on making most objects in the environment interactable or at the very least, look the part. Sometimes, you can make a jump onto a ledge stick on pretty well, sometimes, well, you just slide right off, miss the jump, and either game over and/or lose progress. This would be a minor issue but only if the game could do this automatically. You have to hold down a specific button that acts as not only a grab button, but also an interact button, (in my case, RT on the 360 controller) for the vast majority of the game. Coupled with the fact that you have to run, sneak, turn on your lighter and jump at any given moment makes it really awkward to play for longer periods of time because you have to have that button held down along with another button held down (run / sneak) and with an additional button press on top of that. The biggest improvement to cut back on this would just have an automatic ledge-grab and reduce the amount of focus given to that one button. Even letting go of it will make your characters fall off ladders, drop from ledges, or drop what they're carrying at any given time. It seems like a minor complaint, but it cripples the gameplay a lot, especially when your movement speed is fairly slow and can't necessarily turn on a dime or react quick enough to certain hazards.
It's a tough recommendation, because as an adventure, Little Nightmares is an enjoyable experience, if a bit on the short side. (~3-5 hours without the DLC.) But when you boil it down to its most basic gameplay, it needs a lot more fine-tuning and polish to make it work. That portion honestly feels a bit more like an afterthought, like the developers designed the level concepts first, the setpieces second, and then remembered that they were making a game at the last possible moment. The game can be absolutely brutal, especially if you're on the run and you get stuck on a random piece of clutter or the action key decided to fail on you at a crucial point because your character wasn't in the right position.
7/10. I can't really justify buying Little Nightmares at the $20 base price (or the expansion pass either) for the flaws it has and short overall length. That being said, if you are willing to overlook these nitpicks and wait for a sale, I'd say it's definitely worth your time, if for the fact that it's still a very novel and unique game by itself.

I'm not really into the Olympics and knew nothing about the topic. I mostly watched this because the tight formation of 3 bikes looked like a crazy sport and I was curious how it worked. This ended up being an extremely engaging and inspiring documentary.
First, some faults. The performance tracking technology using was interesting, but sometimes it felt like an ad for that stuff. My gut kept telling me this coverage was funded by the celebrity scientists that want to sell those products. I also found it difficult to follow the story of the 3rd and 4th team mates. They keep making a big deal about one getting cut, but never fully explain what that means or when it happened. They also do very little show their personalities outside of their athletic history and strengths/weaknesses. I want to know more about them and feel like there was nothing to grab on to except that they have great relationships with their husbands.
The strongest point is how they set up the premise very early: they have a completely impossible task and no funding to solve it. The only thing that will take them to victory is creative technology and hardcore training. They really showcase the small breakthroughs and stress as they struggle to keep up with their goals. You can see the pain involved and any gamer or dev can recognize it from completing difficult game to shipping a game. And watching 3 bikes in formation was as strange and fascinating as I'd hoped. I learned a bunch and that's always the mark of a good doc.
The female angle is there and awkward at times, but for the most part it just focuses on how to tune the human body in to a superhuman machine. Cool stuff and I think it's worth watching to see how hard Olympians train.
