A long time ago I played parts of this game on release at a friends house. I thought it was interesting. In 2014 I found the game in a steam sale for 2 euros and said why not give it a try.
Three years later I actually installed the game. I remembered nothing about the story from back then, but a fair bit about the gameplay. For good reasons. The story is one of  the worst I have ever seen. Going from terribly boring, to so bad its almost comedic. I did not realize back then, I just shrugged and ignored it.  But looking at it now... Wow! Spoilers further down.
Anyway:
The Good:
Great concept. First person parkour in a sleek and modernistic city was a breath of fresh air and it popularized ideas that spread to other future games.
Great art direction. Despite the unfixable screen tearing and PhysX not working properly this game was a wonder to behold. Not because of pretty graphics. Its a game from 2009 after all. But the design is a work of art and you often stop and stare at the beautiful vistas.
Several levels of the game are better the second time around due to you knowing how they and the mechanics work. You get a much better flow and that's mostly what brings entertainment in this game.
The Bad:
Finky controls that only sometimes worked. Example: Faith (The player character) can fail to jump to a ledge from a pipe because you are too far up and instead of jumping she just let go of the pipe and plummet to her death. A lot of times you had to solve odd behaviours with trial and error.
Immersion: It gets kind of broken when she can jump and climb death defying areas in one moment and then get stopped by obstacles that I could easily climb in real life because there happen to be no context prompt for those thing.
The combat: It is really terrible. Because of that I chose to play a pacifist character that just ignored enemies to the extent possible. It also seemed like the thematic thing to do, being a runner and all. Your health regenerates fully within 6-8 seconds or so, so getting shot on occasion is no worry. 80-90% of bullets that cops shoot at you seem to be duds or something because they visibly do not leave the barrels and do no damage even if they shoot you from point blank range. Might be that I played on easy combat but whatever.
However, the combat is often mandatory. Many times you cant leave an area until you have killed or “pacified” all the cops in it. Which is awful. In the early game its not so big a problem as you can just single out the cops and deal with them once they are alone. But in the last couple of areas I had to actually use weapons taken from the enemies as the cops were always moving in groups and they have no qualms of shooting straight through their own allies in order to hit you.
But even if you are a better man than I and manage to get through all of that wothout violence you cant actually play a pacifist character. Because Faith kills people in cut-scenes.
And yea, let me tell you a bit about the cut-scenes. There is one scene where Faith talks to a female assassin that is holding a gun. Suddenly 5 cops armed with machine guns with laser sights burst in through a door 10 meters away from them and starts shooting. Faith stares at them for a couple of seconds while they shoot then she moves over to the assassin, takes the gun from her and then use the gun to shoot at an exploding barrel next to the cops which kills all five of them. All while the five of them have been firing hundreds of bullets from relatively close range with laser sights over the course of about 5 seconds and apparently missed every single shot... Yea...
Another cut-scene have 3 machine gun cops standing behind Faith before she jumps on a helicopter. She kicks a guy out of the helicopter and rescues her sister. It randomly caches fire and start to crash for seemingly no reason and both of them escapes by jumping back to the building. Once there, roll end credits with them both hugging and staring out over the city. The three cops that was shooting at them 30 seconds ago disappeared in to thin air!
I gave it a thumbs down because while I liked some things I cant recommend a game that I had to force myself to finish. Dont play the game. Go google the concept art instead. Great stuff.

There are few games that after a few hours of painstakingly doing everything to succeed, only to horribly die anyway, you think to yourself you cannot wait to do it all again. FTL is one of those games.
Overall, the game is not difficult. Overall, the concept of it is rather simple. Captain your ship from A to B, and do not die in the process. However, the choices you make as a new player will most likely kill your crew. Then, as you learn what is and is not a good idea, you get a little farther. Finally, once you think you have it all down, you get over confident and get your ship blown up anyhow. To add to it all, every playthrough is random (Rogue-like) so you cannot learn a pattern to "win".
In addtion to that replay value, you can get different ships that are unlocked through various methods, which do not necessarily make the game any easier or harder, but rather fit a certain playstyle better. Now, you could upgrade any ship to do any of these specializations (or all), but each ship also gets different crewmembers (each race has their own abilities) and layouts.
tl;dr Do yourself a favor and get this game!

(Here I am again, trying to review a game without knowing what to say about it.)
FTL is one great game of it's kind.
The fundamentals of the game are deeply simple.
You are a ship and you have to travel through 8 sectors and slay a boss to win the game.
But on your way, you will struggle to fight other ships, buy new upgrades and win random encounters.
The fights are also damn simple. You have guys that gives you bonuses in certain rooms ( driving, weapons, shields) and you must aim your weapons to the other ship to destroy it. Targeting specific rooms can disable some of the opponent's systems.
And the encounters are even easier. They are 100% made of text and scripted choices (often with random results). The first times, you'll fall into traps and learn what you should avoid. And there is the blue options, specific to a race or system you have. Those options have unique results and are always positives.
But, this game is amazing because you can do a lot with little. You will play a funny few game, probably on easy, to learn how to play but the real fun begins when you tell yourself: "This time, I'll beat this game!"
Then, every simple detail become a strategic decision. "Should-I shoot ASAP or wait for my weapons to shoot at the same time?" "Should-I cloak now to have it off-cooldown sooner or wait to dodge an ennemy fire with it?" "Should left my weapon operator at his position or send him to help defending from the hijackers?" "Should-I take his shield down and kill him quick or take his weapons down to be safer?" "Should-I take some power from my shields to shoot with a third weapon?"
Nine ships (each with three versions), seven races, dozens of systems, weapons and drones and countless encounters and ships to fight gives this game an insane replayability.
It was already nice before, it's even better with the (free) Advanced Edition.
Randomness, strategy, spaceships, simple.
That's a yes for me!

Saints Row IV is an interesting game. At its heart, the devs at Volition are hard set at turning the franchise into an over-the-top superhero open world game ala Crackdown/Prototype/Infamous/Hulk Ultimate Destruction...but at the same time they want to assure old fans that this is a Saints Row game *somewhat* (by giving nods to Saints Row's historical past; in particular SR1 & especially SR2 locales & characters).
Saints Row 3 was a slightly above average third person action game in an open world, but a TERRIBLE Saints Row game. Saints Row IV tries to rectify the last game by retconning most of the idiotic decisons in the mythos (killing characters off), expanding on the amount of tiny game content found in SR3, and building the game around a more cohesive plot & meaninful antagonist.
SRIV achieves most of these, but clings to dear life on SR3's worst aspects; bad enemy AI, very boring campaign missions [turret sections galore with no enemies to shoot], writing that has improved ...but still very bad (90% or so of the jokes/parodies fall flat), terrible activities are mostly taken from SR3 (billion variations of Mayhem or the modified lightcycle races now called 'Burst Races'), and all the more emphasis on SR3's terrible new additions to the Saints gang.
Saints Row IV as a superhero open world game is definately fun (especially in coop...though calling it coop is a stretch with both players seperating constantly doing their own thing) and is definately inspired by Crackdown. Using elemental projectiles, telekenesis, and gliding through the air to collect their equivalent to Crackdown's orbs is very fun. To top it off, Saints Row IV has one of the best licensed soundtracks available in recent memory (EMF, Outcast, Montell Jordan, Haddaway, The Romantics, Blur, and Robert Palmer) which you can play out of vehicle now ala Saints Row 1.
As a Saints Row game, SRIV is most certainly better than SR3, but the days of the franchise of being a open world crime game are over. A good superhero game and decent sorta-Saints Row game. True Saints Row fans will still look toward SR2 for their fix, but Saints Row IV isn't a bad distraction for the PC gamer wanting a fun superhero game without having to deal with a bad superhero game port from the consoles (SRIV console version has a ton of performance issues/glitches/bugs).

For $3.29, you could do worse. Kung Fury is an excellent little movie and this game does it a lot of justice.
It plays exactly like the awesome stick figure brawler 'One Finger Death Punch', in that the game only runs on two buttons. Enemies will approach from the left and the right, and you press the corresponding buttons to attack. There are several enemies, which take anywhere from one hit up to five hits to defeat, with a couple of them teleporting from side to side. The game throws them at you in different groups so you're always on your toes.
There are two modes to this game, the first one being story. This involves you fighting waves of enemies as each of the games characters in four chapters, with a special boss fight at the end of each chapter where you actually get to move around normally. Each of the battles is different and escalates in difficulty with the boss adapting new moves each time. The story mode also features short dialogue scenes containing the actual voice actors from the flim, which is enjoyable but there isn't as much dialogue as there could've been.
Endless Mode is the second one on offer, and is basically just what it says; an endless wave of enemies for you to fight against until you die, fighting for a high score all the while. Depending on how much you enjoy the game will determine your mileage on this.
What is different from the aforementioned title this borrows from, is the fact that each character is different.
**You have KUNG FURY of course, who plays rather ordinary with some flashy kung-fu moves, and three health. No fancy mechanics to him oddly enough.
**Then you have BARBARIANNA, who attacks normally with her axe and blasts everything on one side with her gatling gun every fifth hit, and only two health for some reason.
**Next up is HACKERMAN, who has to attack or 'hack' four times to charge up his attack, at which point he can actually destroy every enemy on the screen with one hit each as long as you keep attacking to keep it charged.
**Lastly is TRICERACOP, who fights similarily to Kung Fury but with guns, and in the process actually shifts backwards on each attack so you can get all the enemies on one side or the other, and he has five health altogether.
Each one of these characters plays differently enough to keep the game interesting. For the cost of the game you can get your money's worth. So get this game, go hack and beat up some Nazis and have a nostalgia filled good time.

Tl;dr:  Come for the art and combat, stay for the story and amazing realized fantasy world!
Finally got around to playing this over the holidays.  I got this game expecting some fun strategic combat and cool art, but I was immediately captured by the world in Banner.  Every time I played it I got lost in this beautifully realized world.  I'm a big fantasy buff, and there are some very strong influences visible in Banner (namely LOTR).  Just look at the world map and you'll see what I mean.  But I mean... LOOK at that world map!  There's so much detail, so much unique history creating a world backdrop that I wanted to move into and never leave.  With such a fully realized world, Banner never feels like a copycat or knockoff of other fantasy properties.  It felt like getting to discover something with the depth of Middle Earth again for the second time.
And the music just ratchets up the whole experience.  Amazing orchestral and vocal arrangements really elevate the experience to another level.  A feast for the ears as much as the eyes.  Speaking of the art did not disappoint.  The beautiful hand-drawn art perfectly captures the world and characters in Banner.  A perfect blend of world, visuals and audio will suck you in and make you forget the hours passing in the real world.
There's also a ton of non-combat gameplay that I wasn't expecting.  The story events and decision making feels as rewarding as any other game I've played (Mass Effect series etc.)  The repurcussions of your decisions feel like they have real weight, with sometimes immediate (and sometimes delayed) effects.  The actual combat gameplay (maybe the second reason I bought the game, besides the art) is spot on.  It's easy to pick up, but I feel like I was really only mastering by the end of the campaign (which is fairly short.)  I had some great moments, like getting down to just one of my main characters while the enemy had 2 left and still squeaking out a win.  Experimenting with the different classes of fighters and special moves brought a lot of depth.  So much so, I started a second play through right away just so I could keep playing.  That says something on it's own, as I RARELY ever play a game twice.  As a gamer-dad, time is too precious!
Love this game.  Cannot say enough good things about it.  Already hyped for the sequel, which is good timing that it comes out so soon.

Despite all of the lavish praise this game received, I can't recommend it.
I played the original XCOM on a 486dx33 (yes a 33mhz processor) and loved it.  I will go right to the heart of my grudge against XCOM: Enemy Unknown.  Enemies drop into your battles at random locations, including behind your squad's positions.  This wrecks use of cover.  It wrecks tactical positioning.  It wrecks immersion.  It might be okay if this were a rare thing that happened with certain enemies, but it is a central part of the system.  In my mind, nothing they do right could make up for such a terribly lazy implementation that substitutes randomness for a smart ai and well designed maps.
For example, you are cautiously advancing your squad down a linear hallway deeper into the enemy base.  You are careful to keep them always behind cover for the direction you are advancing.  Maybe you also try to ensure that each squad member is appropriately positioned to use their weapon to full advantage.  You open a door, ready for your doorkicker assault members to burst in and scan for targets.  Suddenly a giant and very strong UFO shaped enemy drops immediately behind you in the hallway that you just cleared!  It takes its turn immediately and blasts your weakly armored sniper that you had left towards the rear.  They are now dead.
Where did this UFO thing come from?  How can it just fall out of the sky?  What is the point of moving as a team if enemies simply drop in anywhere?  How can you use cover if enemies drop immediately behind your cover with no rhyme or reason?  This is terrible game design!  There would be nothing at all wrong with randomly spawning enemies at the start of the battle, but randomly dropping them into the fight is bad design.
Other things missing that the original XCOM (1994) had: fully destructible terrain, fires, a beautiful and working light system (light grenades, fires cast light, etc) that made night missions terrifying, an alien rocket launcher with projectiles that could fly waypoints, freely flying armor, multiple troop carriers to research and build, the ability to set up multiple bases strategically around the globe, potentially catastrophic invasions of your bases, interceptor flight tracking, squad inventory management, etc etc etc.  Also, your characters weren't locked into any specific class nor did they have a radically dumbed-down and simplistic choose-one-of-two skill system.
I remember all of these things even though I haven't played the game in many years because it was the little things like that combined with the awesome tactical combat that made XCOM so memorable and made for the sort of nostalgia that a cheap rip-off like this exploits to sell copies.  Few will remember this game in a few years, but the memory of the original X-COM remains.
For a game that lacks so much of whats it's predecessors had, and messes up the core tactical combat, it is amazing to me that it has received such praise.

Gameplay: Gameplay in Half Life 2 is absolutely perfect. Each weapon is extremely fun to use, and offers different playstyles. You can be a long range sniper with the crossbow, an up close and personal monster with the shotgun, an explosive deviant with the Rocket Launcher or Grenades, or you can just walk up and smash a Combine Soldier's head in with a crowbar. Gameplay is smooth, flawless, and the power of the Source Engine makes it feel like a real battle. Easy mode is easy, Hard mode is hard. Then, Valve does what revolutionized gaming back during Half Life 1, with a perfect blend between story and gameplay, OBLITERATING the use of Cinematic cut-scenes as they mold them into the game itself. Verdict: 10/10
Story: Half Life 2's Story, is VERY good. You wake up, twenty years after the Black Mesa Incident, and the entire world is taken over. Wait, what? You beat the Nihilanth, you SAVED Earth, what happened? Don't fret, Half Life 2 brings a PERFECT reasoning for it. You walk out of the train station, after witnessing the brutality of the Civil Protection that inhabit it, only to come face to face, with the monolithic Citadel, the symbol of the Combine's power. It stands far up in the sky, and you can see it from most out door areas in the game too! The story puts in a sense of urgency as you have to do the impossible, defeat the Combine Empire. Verdict: 10/10
Music: Music in Half Life 2 is phenomonal. You see, a problem in a lot of games is that they try to be TOO good with their music. They make the music so independent of the game, that it almost seems like a different part of it, a droning tune in the background while you slaughter demons or conquer a City. Half Life 2, on the other hand, perfects it. Ambience is a HUGE part of the soundtrack. The music isn't just music, it's the game itself. For instance, there comes a point where you must traverse under a huge bridge, trains roaming over head. With each train comes the rattling of the metal supports you climb over, a tense moment, and then the ambience kicks in, a slow overtone as it heightens your senses, making you pray that you don't fall to your death. But of course, ambience isn't the only part. There come plenty of moments where the music is active, action packed, and with high intensity as you fight off Headcrab Zombies, or mow down Overwatch Soldiers. Verdict: 10/10
Bugs/Glitches: Bugs, are always existent in games. Some games have more than others, and some are harder to find, or may require exploitation to discover. Half Life 2, like all games, has its bugs and glitches. However, you can go throughout the entire game without experiencing a single bug. Now, there is only ONE bug that can be quite a problem, and that is simply because the game is not exactly optimized for modern software, which includes a graphical error which removes a lot of lighting details. This is easily fixable. Verdict: 9/10
Graphics: This game was made in 2004, and yet, at the Highest Setting, this game still looks VERY nice for 2016. It has aged very well, and it has good graphics in the first place! While they aren't phenomonal compared to now, they are certainly good for their time. Verdict: 8/10
Summary:
This has to be one of, if not, THE BEST game I have ever played. It revolutionized the FPS genre and DESTROYED the challenge of being a worthy sequel.
Final Verdict: 10/10

There are four of types or RPG games.  There's the casual, fun-to-play ones that anyone can dive in to, like the most recent Diablo's.  There are the slightly more complex ones where you can craft items that will alter the gameplay, like better weapons, add enchantments, healing potions, the like. I think the more recent Elder Scrolls, Oblivion and Skyrim, fall into this category.  Delightlful, you'll notice I've played an insane amount of Skyrim, and plan to play more again in the future, with different modsets. Divinity:Original Sin falls into what I consider the third category: the things you choose actually matter.  Where you put your points, what answers you choose, which quests you do to advance, they all affect how other characters in the game world view you, and how you'll advance. It's deep, and interesting, but it requires a time and mental commitment to invest in the world.   If you're ready for that, this game is TONS of fun and is a delightful experience.  The fourth level of RPG complexity is something I've only ever gotten from tabletop gameplay with other human players and Game master.
On the whole, I recommend this game to someone who wants to commit a lot of mental effort and thought into the world, character, and system.   It's a lot of fun!

For a game nearly devoid of meaningful plot, characterisation and dialogue; it certainly has a way of wrenching your heart strings every time a squad member has a brush with mortality.
Let's assume you've been sleeping under a rock and have just noticed this gem on a steam sale - XCom: Enemy Unknown is a reboot/remake of a 90s classic tactical turn-based, squad-based shooter.
The core gameplay is centred on your select cohort of highly trained multinational supersoldiers, with the general hope to rid earth of a multiracial group of alien baddies. XCom itself is the title of a highly advanced international military cell tasked with the defence of its constituent nations from an unknown threat. You play the part of its commander, and you answer to a Council of the world's constituent nations.
So far so good? Game on.
This defending of nations business comes about by completing global missions for various nations with differing objectives; taking your soldier's differing abilities into account as you shift, turn by turn, into nail-biting trades of gunfire with whichever variant of alien crusader you're pitted against. As you complete missions, you earn the means to research your increasingly diverse foes; with incrementally more valuable and powerful rewards as you reverse-engineer the enemy's technology to suit your own purposes.
Missions are received as a result of successfully intercepting invading craft (provided you've managed your infrastructure of defensive satellites and aircraft over the world's nations), defending nations as abductions and alien terrorism takes place, or on a particular assignment (story-specific mission) from the "Council" itself. These missions develop nicely in both complexity and variety as the game goes on.
The challenge, and the game itself, lies in the brutally indifferent nature of the random number generator. It decides whether your "95%" aim chance will actually connect, or whether you'll be left watching your precious soldier being blasted into meat paste by plasma fire. Your soldier's innate class abilities offer a rewarding approach to tactical thought as you mitigate the random nature of the gunfights with careful squad placement and movement.
The classes are the centrepiece of your progression throughout the game. As you inevitably settle down on a chosen few soldiers to take on the majority of missions, they gain experience and additional abilities according to their class. These will be pretty familiar to any players of traditional squad-based shooters: long-range, high damage snipers; exceptionally mobile assault units; versatile support units; and high impact heavy units. Each class features an ability tree that provides each soldier with an increasing number of tactical perks to better your chances against ET nasties. Such a careful progression of a chose few individuals make the high-risk gameplay all the more immersive as you will literally cry out with the untimely demise of a hardened veteran. Though the game is ingenious in its ability to never leave you feeling cheated: it is always your mistake.
As mentioned, the other aspect of game progression is presented in technological research. As you encounter more advanced and lethal enemies, you gain more opportunities to better equip your soldiers with advanced weapons, armour and useable items. This is also linked to another mechanic of base-building, where you progressively advance your homebase with laboratories and workshops as you gain the reward of additional staff from nations you've successfully defended.
Whilst so many facets of a game may sound fractured and confusing, the mechanics tie together in a very satisfying manner. Your gametime takes you from an initial desperate scrabble - barely managing from mission-to-mission as soldiers die to superior enemies and countries drop out of the XCom program as you fail to defend them - to a final plateau where you task your honed team of veterans to finish off the alien menace, once and for all.
The game offers a few twists and turns with story missions that allude to a central plot line, though the real enjoyment is testing your favourite soldiers against whatever challenge the game throws at you. There is a genuine satisfaction to be had in having soldiers become ridiculously powerful in terms of combat ability, purely as a result of surviving high odds through your initial struggles.
The Enemy Within DLC presents a new twist to the campaign story with new enemy variants and mission types, as well as sprucing up the soldier classes with the moral quandary that is alien augmentation. You can either opt to hone your soldiers with genetic modification, with more options provided as you discover new aliens from which to splice genes; or do away with their limbs entirely and give them a massively powerful mechanised suit.
The game underlies this newfound power nicely with thoughtful quips from your research staff questioning the intrinsic trade-off of humanity for alien power as you further meddle with your soldiers.
Philosophical tangents aside, the DLC brings enjoyable variety to an already feature-packed game.
Made it thus far? Now the not-so-good. There are some incredible bugs to be found, even at this stage in post-game patching. I’ve been forced to alt-F4 essential story missions as a result of hitches in gameplay with little motivation to continue from where I left off. There are well documented bugs in final-stage missions, especially poor considering the amount of player investment to get to these points.
I’d recommend saving often, if only so you don’t have to trudge dutifully through already-played sections to reach critical points.

I've just finished this game, and most truthful would be that I neither recommend or not recommend this game, but I decided to go with not recommending for various reasons.
First of all, the concept is awesome and the characters are good. I liked the smooth parkour movement a lot, and seeing the rooftops was very nice. However, especially with the pipes and bars, getting to and away from them was clumsy.
Aside from good movement, there is less to tell. While the story is fine, it's very short. You just run from place to place, avoid being killed and watch the cutscenes. I was shocked to see the credits roll when I reached the end without knowing it was the final chapter. I felt that the story was just cut without telling where it was going next. In addition, the lack of Runner characters felt bad; it seemed like there was no connection from Merc's gang to any other Runners, as if they were the only ones, although it turns out there is. This made the story lack depth. The only reason why I kept playing the game after numerous moments of pure rage and ragequitting, even considering refunding and just going to play Mirror's Edge: Catalyst, which I bought on Origin at the same time as I bought this here on sale, was the story, and it's left me disappointed.
On the other hand, the game has left me screaming internally in rage way too many times. While the movement is smooth, sometimes certain jumps just don't seem to get right no matter how often you try. You just end up falling down and trying again, sometimes from further away than you'd like to.
The combat is a thing on its own: highly imbalanced and the biggest cause of rage. You are outnumbered and heavily outgunned. While ALL the enemies have a gun of some sort, you have to rely on melee, get close and beat the enemies you have to beat to get through - and die a dozen times trying to take on the enemies one by one, and die nearly as much every time you have to run away from the enemies who can gun you down. While there is a strategy for defeating the obligatory gunmen, it's still hard to do and you keep dying and respawning. You can take the guns of the defeated enemies but as the guns run out of ammo when you have them, you'll have to toss each of them away soon as useless. If I downright hate anything about this game, it's the combat.
Oh, and another thing. At least the Steam version suffers from the same issue as Batman: Arkham Asylum GOTY's Steam version: the use of PhysX screws the FPS up no matter how overkill your GPU is for the game, so don't turn it on if you want to survive the areas with breaking glass. It's absolutely not worth it. I know that when installed from a disc, Arkham Asylum doesn't have this issue, but I have yet to confirm if it's the same case for Mirror's Edge as well.
All in all, there's good in this game, but then there is the rage-pouring part. In the end, I'm glad that I bought this on sale for 2,49 €.
Pros:
+Smooth movement
+Runs well
+Good interaction between the characters
+The story, albeit short, was ok
Cons:
-The story is short and thus disappointing
-Lack of characters decreases the depth of the world
-Highly imbalanced combat
-Clumsy movement between bars and pipes
-The PhysX-caused severe FPS drop when there is breaking glass

Child of Light is what many call a AAA indie game. It's an hybrid between a JRPG and a (light) platformer, from Jeffrey Yohalem, best known for Far Cry 3.
It's quite the leap, from one game to another!
The team who made this game was far smaller, but more focused as a result. It comes from a place of fairy-tales and fantasy worlds, as form of escapism. It's definitely different from what we
see in videogames, especially from big companies.
Its art caught my eye a while ago, and since it was on sale, I decided to finally try it! Unfortunately, due to university, I couldn't play it all in a few days, having to play it sparingly, in the span of 2 weeks instead.
It took mee a little over 15hours to beat, with every sidequest done, on "Expert" difficulty.
As I said, its
were the first aspect of this game to catch my attention. It instantly reminded me of
's work (who is rather well known for his Swedish Folktale illustrations -- Paradox's Runemaster was mainly inspired by his art as well!), which was a nice surprise. Later on, as I played, I dug a bit deeper and discovered that it was indeed inspired by not only his artwork, but all of the Golden Age of Illustration, which I didn't know about. Look it up, it's great!
The whole game is
, with the addition of some 3D animation as well as lighting effects. Comparisons with pop-up books aren't unfounded either, as the game has lots of different layers of textures in the backgrounds, making the game feel very organic.
The art in general is
, almost looking like a
, but I feel that was intentional. All in all, the game looks great, and certainly unique (!), but I would have liked to see a more detailed version of this style.
Again, when I looked the Golden Age of Illustration up, I was amazed with the detailed drawings. Of course, it's very different to make 10-20 drawings than it is to make probably hundreds, for a complete videogame. Still, since it's Ubisoft we're talking about, maybe the idea will be pursued further!
The
also has some really nice details to it! Not unlike Disney or Ghibli's movies, the best part of it is how they animate the little details and creatures that populate the universe.
Unfortunately, the enemies weren't nearly as fluid and charismatic. Not sure if it was to reinforce the
feeling of the game or not, but it would have been better to flesh those out a bit more.
The backgrounds, though, are full of live, with little creatures constantly popping up. Very nice art direction, overall!
The
was mostly awesome! Honestly, it evoked similar feelings as Brothers: A Tale of Two Sons did. It has calm moments, composed only with a cello and a piano or a flute, on top of the ambience sounds, and it's great! Besides, there are some musician characters around the world, who play their instruments in tune with the background music -- which I always love!
Even the main character plays a flute, at times, making some of the melodies very memorable!
The biggest problem, for me, is how
ideas always seem to fall into the same pit: orchestrating their music. Seriously, it happens way to many times.
Instead of the very organic and personal music with just a couple of instruments, the game sometimes feels the need to orchestrate everything. While it gives it a more "epic" feel, it's much more impersonal and generic, to me.
This happens mostly in the battle tracks, but it was still rather underwhelming, to me.
The soundtrack was composed by Coeur de Pirate. I didn't know of her music, and still don't like it very much. Regardless, she has done a brilliant job in here!
The sound-effects didn't catch my attention. I'll take that as a positive, since I can be easily annoyed by them!
The game has 2 main components: 2D platforming, where you explore the world and meet NPCs, and then the JRPG combat system.
Neither of them are really noteworthy on their own, but everything in the games comes together rather well, creating a very solid overall experience.
The game only has an overworld map, with the ability to fast-travel to previously seen locations.
The adventure/exploration aspect of the game is mainly tied to exploring the landscape, finding Coffers with consumables, Attribute bonuses, and Confessions (which I'll explain later on).
You get the ability to fly very early on, so platforming, per-se, isn't an issue, here.
The maps are fairly open, with lots of (slightly) hidden areas for you to explore. However, the game's RPG side is
stream-lined, making most of the exploration pointless, most of the time. I still did explore, but the payout was very little, because of the combat.
The encounters aren't random, as you can see every enemy. You can also avoid them, if you will. I'm assuming this could be fine if you were playing on Casual Mode ("For those in it just for the story"), but on Expert, you will need to fight the monsters to level up and face the Boss fights. There's no need to grind, and fighting the monsters you encounter normally should suffice.
This is a good way of doing things, although Yahtzee has a good point:
Why is the combat streamlined? Well, for example, there's no equipment. Instead, each character has 3 Occuli slots, which are crystals that you can craft, each with a different effect. The 3 slots loosely stand for Weapon, Armor and Trinket. The crystal's effect in every character is the same, when used in the same slot.
It's actually quite complicated to explain. And even more to discover their uses, since the interface for it is rather clunky. It was clearly made with a controller in mind, and is missing a lot of keyboard+mouse funcionalities.
Each character has a "talent tree" with 3 branches, that give them access to different types of skills. You get skill points from leveling up. There's no re-specializing whatsoever, which can be annoying. If you get another character with the same skills you've already chosen in another character, it can be annoying to be stuck with a bunch of useless skills.
Overall, though, it didn't prove to be a real issue.
For example, you have access to several potions, with stat changing effects (for X turns, in combat). These do exactly the same as characters' skills. So... why use potions? There's almost no reason to! With the exception of H/MP potions.
Then, there's the fact that there's a "progress" bar, influenced by speed. When you reach the "Casting" part of the bar, you're set back, and your spell canceled, if you're hit. This adds strategy to the game, but you're often outnumbered (you have 2 characters, vs. 3 enemies). This gets you interrupt all the time, during Bosses. And it simply feels unfair! It's infuriating, at times, as you almost rendered useless.
...
Then, there's also the fact that buffs don't last long at all, and with only 2 characters, you have to cumbersomely change between characters... it's effective, but very counter-intuitive, and makes the combat less enjoyable than it could have been.
I'm already out of words. I didn't like the combat.
However, I thoroughly enjoyed the overall experience! I think it dragged on a bit, especially with the sub-par combat. And for each of its faults, the game also had some nice little detail to make up for it!
I enjoyed the world and the dialogue (which is all in rhyme -- didn't annoy me at all, I actually found it a nice little effort).
It's a very nicely crafted experience, give it a go!

So, I bought this game on a whim one day, and it took me a little while to actually sit down and play it.
I wasn't expecting much to be honest, just a nice little game to pass the time.
The little expectations I had got blown out of the water entirely.
TL;DR: :
1.You have to download a third party program to play, but it's not very intrusive, so I barely noticed it.
2. THE GAME IS AMAZING AND BEAUTIFUL AND BEAUTIFUL AND BEAUTIFUL, BUY IT RIGHT NOW. 11/10
Every part of this game comes together as a perfect package with a clear theme, it all fits so incredibly well!
The voice acting for our storyteller is soothing, beautiful and grabs your attention. The dialogue for her (and everyone else really) is simple yet poetic and I really appreciate the rhymes and such which increases the feeling of immersion into this bedtime story world.
The visuals are absolutely stunning, and if you spend enough time in areas and/or are observant enough, you will see background animations that are equally engrossing even though they're just there for exactly that; background that you're not necessarily expected to notice.
The story itself is simple, beautiful and a little "scary" at times, just like a good bedtime story should be.
And the music is perfect for this game, I know I keep using the word beautiful, but that's what this game is, so I'll repeat it; The music is BEAUTIFUL. I also really appreciated the sound effects, like the oddly pleasing sound of our main characters bare feet tapping against the ground when you walk.
Personally, I love turn-based combat which this game uses, I also liked the added "realtime" component of using a helper to slow down/heal which makes you have to strategize quickly about what you want to do.
You can to a certain degree choose how you want to evolve your character(s), do you want to be mage-y or fighter-y?
Choose between playing defensive and offensive, will you focus on boosting your team or jinxing your enemy? Or maybe you'll go all out offensive and choose only fighters and have them use items for HP and boosts when needed? It's up to  you.
Not sure I appreciated using the "2 player" mode all the time, (you move one character with the keyboard and a helper with your mouse) but it didn't annoy me either, so it's neither a plus nor a minus.
It IS a minus though that they present it as a 2 player mode kind of thing, it would be incredibly boring for the person playing the helper unless they were usually the kind who preferred watching others play.
Lovely little quest-system, with some optional side-quests that you can do for items.
Crafting of oculi - Meh, felt kind of tiresome and chaotic at times, but at least it's made sort of useful after a while.
All in all the most important part of this game is the story and you really feel like you're in one when you play, and it's a story you're going to want to hear/play again and again for many nights to come.
Also! Plus for awesome female protagonist that's not sexualised in any way but simply amazing.
If you have friends and you have a home, get those friends to come to your home and play Crawl.

Crawl is a game developed and published by Powerhoof
Crawl is an excellent couch co-op game which encourages you to work together as a team to end the hero's life, then take their place and fight your way to salvation by besting the cthulhian horror that resides at the end of it all... or die and have your humanity stolen, only to be cursed to rot forever amidst your wrath in the infinite tombs of Crawl
Monsters scale well over time, going from murderous nuisances to outright tough-as-nails murderbeasts whereas hero weapons and abilities are interesting and varied
Buffs and debuffs provide an additional strategic layer which raises the game from simply "good" to "great". There's a heavy cyber-lovecraftian theme which elevates the mood. It's immersive and tense, appealing to that intrinsic desire to survive which exists within every human
It doesn't have online multi-player, but that's a small concession for what is such a tight and cohesive array of elements that come together and create an experience that'll have you sweating from the sheer intensity
Even if you don't have enough people nearby who can slum it on your couch to gather up 4 players, Crawl provides a powerful AI that will keep you on your toes

Wondering if you should buy this game? Let me answer that for you: yes. At the time of writting this review, I'm at 25 hours of game time according to steam, only just completed chapter 3. There is at least 8 (according to the achievements). Bought the game 2-3 days ago. I have not been this addicted to a game in years.
Pros:
- Great visuals.
- Battle system. Bigger sword should mean more reach, right? Now it does. If you stand right beside the character that gets stomped on by a dragon, you should be too, right? Unfortunately, it does too.
- Humour. I do not think there is a single dialogue where there isn't a joke up to this point. 4th wall keeps being broken, but in such a normal and casual way it feels normal.
- Great music.
- Dungeons are NOT adapted to your level. I learned this one fast. Clear a dungeon by one-rounding all enemies, enter another dungeon I just unlocked, get myself killed in a single hit. For the entire group.
- No grinding. Altough sometimes you will need to kill some specific enemies repetitively in order to get that required item, it is quite rare. For the XP, it's only a matter of finding an enemy easy for you to kill, which gives a lot of XP. Won't be giving spoilers :P
Cons:
- Few bugs/annoyances. Some settings will not be remembered when you next start the game, but this only takes a few seconds, so not very major. Had another bug that prevented the game from running. Running as admin fixed it.
- Redundancy of dungeons/monsters. When reaching higher levels, you will notice a lot more of this: same enemy, different color or same dungeon, with small added part. At least, for the enemy part, it doesn't always mean same attack pattern.
Also, a negative/positive point (depends on point of view): Fan service, as seen in the screenshots. Although most of the time it's purely for fan service (as seen with Verte, 3rd screenshot starting from the right), it is sometimes approched in such an humoristic way, and the characters tend to point out how ridiculous it can be, that I believe that even someone who doesn't like this will still love the game.
Finally, and I simply cannot pass by this point, all the references to popular culture, more specifically video games. Zelda, Mario, Metal Gear, you name it! There is more video game allusions than I can name. For instance, you are in the world of Gamindustri (obivous one), and the 4 goddesses of this world are in war. The Console war. The video game refferences are way too long to start stating, from the goddesses names, their appearance, their cities, etc.

The Good: Lets you use your own music, creates a great game based off of the music, tons of fun perks to unlock, a good amount of modes to play
The Bad: Not many power-ups, lacking visually, not a game for everyone
Being able to play a game using your own music isn’t new, but being a good one is hard. Beat Hazard lets you select your own music and then uses the tempo to create difficulty spikes and flow of enemies. The beat of the song is scene in the bullets you shoot as well as the crazy explosions one screen that can give you a seizure. When you select your music you get to decide the difficulty. Pick a heavy and fast metal song and you’ll be lucky if you get through the whole thing. Pick a normal soft rock song and the difficulty is very gradual.
When you actually start shooting there are several power-ups that range from increasing the volume, shot power, money, and bombs. If you die you can collect the stuff your dropped, but if you keep collecting the stuff you get more and more powerful. You can use the money to buy perks that range from power-ups when you start, extra lives, and other various perks. There’s a good amount and it’s worth playing just to unlock them all. However, the game doesn’t have much depth so this is a 30 minutes-at-a-time game or you will get bored. The visuals are decent, but the special effects that flash around remind me of Geometry Wars on crack.
So this is once again a game that makes you the decider of how fun of an experience you get. The engine underneath does a good job using the songs to great a fun space shooter, but I would liked to have seen more power-ups or maybe something more 3D. If you don’t like 2D space shooters you won’t like this even if you get to use your own music. The game can get really hard quick and can be a bit confusing at first until you get the hang of it. There are quite a few modes such as multiplayer, boss rush, and endless mode so there is some variety there. For the low price you can’t really go wrong so pick it up and enjoy the craziness!

Grim Dawn is a loot-driven ARPG in vein of Titan Quest or Diablo (and it's more Diablo/Diablo 2 than Diablo 3 ;). Set in a bleak and desolate world (fantastic Victorian feel, btw), just after the apocalypse, caused by an invasion of otherworldy malevolent spirits called the Aetherials and just before another apocalypse, planned by another faction of mass murdering worshippers of a cosmic horror called Cthon.
The player character has just recovered from the possession by an Aetherial and is set upon the task of regrouping the remnants of humanity and rebuilding the civilization. All in all, the lore is interesting and immersive, so it's worth reading the quest texts, dialogues and lore notes found through the entire game.
The recent expansion, called Ashes of Malmouth added two new classes: Inquisitor (dual pistols/rifle elemental caster and Necromancer, the pet master.
The player can choose 2 from 8 masteries, to create a character best suited for his/her playstyle: melee, ranged, spellcaster, pet master, assassin, whatever you want.
1. Soldier (heavy armor, shield, melee spec, physical damage)
2. Nightblade (dual wielding rogue archetype)
3. Arcanist (a ranged spellcaster, specializing in elemental and aether magic)
4. Shaman (lightning spells, minions, few sweet support buffs)
5. Occultist (a dark mage specializing in curses, minions, acid attacks and more)
6. Demolitionist (fire themed ranged/melee class, specializing in traps and explosives).
7. Inquisitor (a ranged class, dual wielding pistols or rifles, focusing on elemental/piercing damage)
8. Necromancer (a minion master with many life draining skills).
The classes and skills are mostly well balanced, so almost any class combination is playable.  You can further customize your playstyle with Devotion system, by earning skill points that are used to gain passive bonuses or even new and powerful skills.
If by any chance you either screw up the character build or just decide you want to change your playstyle, it is possible to refund the skill points, devotions and attribute points. That way you don't need to create another character.
The game isn't stingy with loot, you can find it off the many and varied monsters, chests, hidden caches, you can craft your own items with the help of your local blacksmith, buy them from the factions vendors (yes, there are factions you can earn reputation with and it's not as tedious as in, let's say WoW) whatever suits you. In addition to weapons, armor and trinkets you can find components that can further enhance your gear.
Did I mention Grim Dawn has tons of replayability value and three "new game+" modes? It also has modding tools and regular free content updates. The game doesn't have many bugs, during 320+ hours of playtime I haven't encountered any. The devs are friendly and in touch with the community, which is also quite friendly and helpful.
I can absolutely recommend this game for all the loot-lovers, especially those turned off by syrupy sweetness of Diablo 3. 10/10

For a game nearly devoid of meaningful plot, characterisation and dialogue; it certainly has a way of wrenching your heart strings every time a squad member has a brush with mortality.
Let's assume you've been sleeping under a rock and have just noticed this gem on a steam sale - XCom: Enemy Unknown is a reboot/remake of a 90s classic tactical turn-based, squad-based shooter.
The core gameplay is centred on your select cohort of highly trained multinational supersoldiers, with the general hope to rid earth of a multiracial group of alien baddies. XCom itself is the title of a highly advanced international military cell tasked with the defence of its constituent nations from an unknown threat. You play the part of its commander, and you answer to a Council of the world's constituent nations.
So far so good? Game on.
This defending of nations business comes about by completing global missions for various nations with differing objectives; taking your soldier's differing abilities into account as you shift, turn by turn, into nail-biting trades of gunfire with whichever variant of alien crusader you're pitted against. As you complete missions, you earn the means to research your increasingly diverse foes; with incrementally more valuable and powerful rewards as you reverse-engineer the enemy's technology to suit your own purposes.
Missions are received as a result of successfully intercepting invading craft (provided you've managed your infrastructure of defensive satellites and aircraft over the world's nations), defending nations as abductions and alien terrorism takes place, or on a particular assignment (story-specific mission) from the "Council" itself. These missions develop nicely in both complexity and variety as the game goes on.
The challenge, and the game itself, lies in the brutally indifferent nature of the random number generator. It decides whether your "95%" aim chance will actually connect, or whether you'll be left watching your precious soldier being blasted into meat paste by plasma fire. Your soldier's innate class abilities offer a rewarding approach to tactical thought as you mitigate the random nature of the gunfights with careful squad placement and movement.
The classes are the centrepiece of your progression throughout the game. As you inevitably settle down on a chosen few soldiers to take on the majority of missions, they gain experience and additional abilities according to their class. These will be pretty familiar to any players of traditional squad-based shooters: long-range, high damage snipers; exceptionally mobile assault units; versatile support units; and high impact heavy units. Each class features an ability tree that provides each soldier with an increasing number of tactical perks to better your chances against ET nasties. Such a careful progression of a chose few individuals make the high-risk gameplay all the more immersive as you will literally cry out with the untimely demise of a hardened veteran. Though the game is ingenious in its ability to never leave you feeling cheated: it is always your mistake.
As mentioned, the other aspect of game progression is presented in technological research. As you encounter more advanced and lethal enemies, you gain more opportunities to better equip your soldiers with advanced weapons, armour and useable items. This is also linked to another mechanic of base-building, where you progressively advance your homebase with laboratories and workshops as you gain the reward of additional staff from nations you've successfully defended.
Whilst so many facets of a game may sound fractured and confusing, the mechanics tie together in a very satisfying manner. Your gametime takes you from an initial desperate scrabble - barely managing from mission-to-mission as soldiers die to superior enemies and countries drop out of the XCom program as you fail to defend them - to a final plateau where you task your honed team of veterans to finish off the alien menace, once and for all.
The game offers a few twists and turns with story missions that allude to a central plot line, though the real enjoyment is testing your favourite soldiers against whatever challenge the game throws at you. There is a genuine satisfaction to be had in having soldiers become ridiculously powerful in terms of combat ability, purely as a result of surviving high odds through your initial struggles.
The Enemy Within DLC presents a new twist to the campaign story with new enemy variants and mission types, as well as sprucing up the soldier classes with the moral quandary that is alien augmentation. You can either opt to hone your soldiers with genetic modification, with more options provided as you discover new aliens from which to splice genes; or do away with their limbs entirely and give them a massively powerful mechanised suit.
The game underlies this newfound power nicely with thoughtful quips from your research staff questioning the intrinsic trade-off of humanity for alien power as you further meddle with your soldiers.
Philosophical tangents aside, the DLC brings enjoyable variety to an already feature-packed game.
Made it thus far? Now the not-so-good. There are some incredible bugs to be found, even at this stage in post-game patching. I’ve been forced to alt-F4 essential story missions as a result of hitches in gameplay with little motivation to continue from where I left off. There are well documented bugs in final-stage missions, especially poor considering the amount of player investment to get to these points.
I’d recommend saving often, if only so you don’t have to trudge dutifully through already-played sections to reach critical points.

I originally played a trial version of this game when it came out, but I wasn't particularly amazed by it. I had wanted to try it out again, and the Steam release seemed like the perfect time to be a new player. I have absolutely changed my mind thus far.
I really enjoy the combat (playing as a Dark Knight). The game is definitely a little overwhelming for a brand new player, but I think it does a better job than many MMORPGs at trying to introduce how things work. I also know that I still have a ton to learn, but the game is fun enough that I don't mind knowing that I have a lot of learning to do.
One thing that I am not sure about yet is RP, which is one reason why I'm interested in playing BDO, but I have seen recruiting RP guilds, so I don't think this is going to be an issue.

Divinity: Original Sin is a great entry in a genre that has long been thought pretty much dead and which is now experiencing some new bloom thanks to several kickstarted games. It is also the best game Larian has made so far simply because they have finally nailed the fun part in actual gameplay with this one while also keeping their Discworld-esque colourful world and writing.
The combat and tactics were easily the highlight of the game for me even though once you find how things work you can pretty much follow that strategy to the end of the game while also constantly gaining new toys. In the end you can pretty much set the course to win every battle right at the start with a quick buff and AoE spell, which is your choice to do of course.
Main quest felt a bit lacking compared to the side quests, even a bit annoying in a way that someone had to constantly pop up in a predictable way to chatter up a bunch of meh like an information force feed. It even reminded me of vanilla Diablo 3 villain banter and that's as a harsh an insult I'll give to any game. Side quests and lore is good however. Talking to animals is also one of the best things in the game. Only thing missing is the mind reading ability from Divinity 2.
Companions were also lacking despite having fine personal quests. The main problem in the launch period of the game was that the game only offered 2 companions or a choice of hiring a blank mercenary tool, which is really no choice at all in an RPG. It has since been addressed and there are now more companions to choose from. One would think the coming Enhanced edition adds even more choice.
So now for the real issues in the game. Pixel hunting. Some puzzles require you to do this and it's not fun at all. Seems like a dead end? Nope. There is a pixel size button somewhere that lets you progress.
Pre-determined way to approach the game map. The first city makes this pretty clear as it gives you the option of leaving from several gates, but it's no true option at all as if you leave from the "wrong" gate, you will most likely get wrecked or have a very hard time. This continues to the end of the game with the intended way being always most closest to your level. I guess this could also be a positive if you get your kicks out of clearing harder areas first, but in the end it leaves you overleveled for the intended path.
Random loot. I'm starting to forget the pain with this, but sometimes you end up not getting what you need at all. In short, more handplaced loot would have been better to me. Going for merchants to get what you need is not what I want to do.
tl;dr version since whatever  why not.
+ Combat and tactics
+ World and sidequests
+ Music
+ Talking to animals
+ Larian making their best game yet
+/- Pre-determined way to approach the map
+/- Companion choice at launch
- Main Quest annoying info dumps
- Random loot
- Pixel hunting
- 2-3 battles in the game are quite the difficulty spike

So, I bought this game on a whim one day, and it took me a little while to actually sit down and play it.
I wasn't expecting much to be honest, just a nice little game to pass the time.
The little expectations I had got blown out of the water entirely.
TL;DR: :
1.You have to download a third party program to play, but it's not very intrusive, so I barely noticed it.
2. THE GAME IS AMAZING AND BEAUTIFUL AND BEAUTIFUL AND BEAUTIFUL, BUY IT RIGHT NOW. 11/10
Every part of this game comes together as a perfect package with a clear theme, it all fits so incredibly well!
The voice acting for our storyteller is soothing, beautiful and grabs your attention. The dialogue for her (and everyone else really) is simple yet poetic and I really appreciate the rhymes and such which increases the feeling of immersion into this bedtime story world.
The visuals are absolutely stunning, and if you spend enough time in areas and/or are observant enough, you will see background animations that are equally engrossing even though they're just there for exactly that; background that you're not necessarily expected to notice.
The story itself is simple, beautiful and a little "scary" at times, just like a good bedtime story should be.
And the music is perfect for this game, I know I keep using the word beautiful, but that's what this game is, so I'll repeat it; The music is BEAUTIFUL. I also really appreciated the sound effects, like the oddly pleasing sound of our main characters bare feet tapping against the ground when you walk.
Personally, I love turn-based combat which this game uses, I also liked the added "realtime" component of using a helper to slow down/heal which makes you have to strategize quickly about what you want to do.
You can to a certain degree choose how you want to evolve your character(s), do you want to be mage-y or fighter-y?
Choose between playing defensive and offensive, will you focus on boosting your team or jinxing your enemy? Or maybe you'll go all out offensive and choose only fighters and have them use items for HP and boosts when needed? It's up to  you.
Not sure I appreciated using the "2 player" mode all the time, (you move one character with the keyboard and a helper with your mouse) but it didn't annoy me either, so it's neither a plus nor a minus.
It IS a minus though that they present it as a 2 player mode kind of thing, it would be incredibly boring for the person playing the helper unless they were usually the kind who preferred watching others play.
Lovely little quest-system, with some optional side-quests that you can do for items.
Crafting of oculi - Meh, felt kind of tiresome and chaotic at times, but at least it's made sort of useful after a while.
All in all the most important part of this game is the story and you really feel like you're in one when you play, and it's a story you're going to want to hear/play again and again for many nights to come.
Also! Plus for awesome female protagonist that's not sexualised in any way but simply amazing.

WARNING! This is the first review from a novice gamer with only 22 hours in the game. If that turns you off, then don't read this. Please excuse me for any errors I may make in this review. Any suggestions for improvement would be welcomed. Now let me get a few things straight. This review is for those who: have never played Saint's Row before, are Saint's Row haters, are tired of GTA and want something new, are just so damn bored you feel obliged to even read this review. I feel Saint's Row is NOT a GTA clone. Is it open-world? Yes. Can you steal vehicles? Yes. Can you shoot or kill anybody you want? Yes. Is there heat in this game? Yes. And THAT'S as far as similarities go. Here are things you can't do in GTA: customize cars, customize yourself, collect  weapons and vehicles, the ability to gain superpowers and abilities, level-up, a game with far more humor than you'd ever expect, and being able to complete missions together nearly seamlessly with a friend online or LAN (with exception to lag issues) and yes that includes story missions as well. There's alot more differences in the game that I haven't mentioned but these I feel highlight alot of what makes Saint's Row IV unique. Once I complete this game with my friends, I'll give a more detailed review on anything I may have missed. Have you ever wanted to captain your own star ship and fly through the strange and dangerous depths of space? Well now is your chance but it is not for the faint of heart.
In short get this, it is an awesome rogue-like space simulator and you will not regret it. Also buy the soundtrack too, it’s very catchy.
This game is great fun. The ascetics are very retro and remind me of games from yesteryear. The gameplay itself is fun, challenging and highly addictive, you will want to play it through time and again. Even when the odds are against you, and they often are, you will want to fight on and try to be the hero despite your impending doom.
The in game universe is already vast and highly diverse, you never know whether the next warp will be to a friendly planet, devastated space station or rebel ambush. The whole game is more or less procedurally generated so you never have the same experience twice, which keeps it fresh each time you retry.
As the captain you manage what systems you have installed in your ship, what weapons you have equipped, even which crew members fly with you. There is even a basic rpg system for each crew member, so if they do die you feel a sense of lost. I remember getting very attached to the little guys.
This game will kick your butt and laugh at you whilst doing it yet that is a price that is very easily paid considering how enjoyment you’ll get. This is a 100% recommend even at full price, on sale you would be crazy not to get this. And due to a recent update it’s even better. There are also mods that can be applied for an even better experience, I recommend the Captain’s edition
Have fun ^_^

This is not a really fun game. Some of that is by design: you are trying to survive and take care of your people against overwhelming odds, making tough decisions one after another. The dread that your characters feel gets to you.
Sadly, its too much. After being blindsided by some terrible consequences (some from decisions made 45 minutes into the game; others product of a lot of walking around without being able to judge distances/food), you start to feel the game is a chore. For me it was a chore to get to the finish line. Once again, some of that is intentional, but if the game doesn't leave you with a good taste in your mouth, its because it went too far.
Obviously that is a very personal issue with the game; a more general issue will be its combat system. I love turn-based games, but some decisions made here opened the combat to be way too exploitable.
The rest of The Banner Saga goes from average (the lore "borrows" from new places, but is not unique enough) to very good (the ilustrations are amazing, although way too stiff during dialogues).
This has been an enjoyable experience for many (rating "very positive" no?), supporting the developers decisions for some of the choices made here. Sadly, I cannot agree with them enough to give it a thumbs up.

I already have the PS Vita version of this game (and played it a lot) so I picked this up on sale, along with the DLC.  I've only played a bit on PC port, mostly offline.
Hyperdimension Neptunia Re;Birth1 is a really fun game, one of the few JRPGs which I've been able to get into - something about the satisfying combat, sense of humour and videogame references.  It also has a fairly satisfying number of game systems to get into, both in terms of combat, and terms of crafting items which not only affect your characters' stats and outfits but also affect the rules of the world.  I'd strongly recommend it to anyone.
PC Port specific:
Good:
1) The graphics are much improved on the PC port and the game looks gorgeous.
2) Mouse interaction works well.
Bad:
1) I had to install new graphics drivers to get the game to work properly on the laptop I'm playing on at the moment.
2) Steam achievement popping is buggy.  For example, I got the achievement for starting the game, the SECOND time I started a new game, after I got other achievements, which looks weird on my achievements.  But whatever, I don't really care about achievements.  If you do, that could irritate you.
Overall, it's a really great game, the port is pretty good, some normal PC issues aside and you should certainly pick this up, even if you have the Vita version already.

The game itself is awesome. I like the "no fast-travel" thing - there's auto-navigation, and on longer journeys, you can make yourself a coffee or have a smoke or something... The combat is incredible - although there is a quickbar, it's mostly used for items. Almost all the skills are used by some combination of keys, or after/during another skill. I've never got past the levelling phase, so I didn't have a taste of that end-game PvP and Node Wars I hear so much about, but I love taking things slow, and this is just a game for that. No mood for brainless mashing through hordes of enemies? Take your fishing rod and go fish. (And if you think it's boring, just read the chat - it's quite entertaining, even if it sometimes resembles Barrens Chat of distant past.) Order your workers around, and if they're behaving, give them a beer or five. Go tame a wild horse, I dare you.
It can be off-putting for new players because of the possibilities. And of the endless "Is this game P2W?" discussions. But if you can get past this, arm yourself with Google and enjoy your fantasy sandbox. For 6€! (And, let's be honest, 10€ ain't all that much too, in comparison with other titles.) The fun is there, you just have to want to find it. It's a sandbox, for crying out loud.
Feeding the P2W debate: I'm probably not late enough in the game to compare the comfort provided by money-bought convenience stuff. But that's all it seems like - convenience. And cosmetics. Pay for it if you want. Don't, if you don't want to. But don't bash the game because you don't want to spend money on something you don't need to have to enjoy it..
But I guess I'm just a fanboy. (I don't think so, but hell, who knows)

Although the much-needed Brave New World expansion took its time to arrive, there's no doubting that Civilization V carved out its own identity on the series. The absence of the 'stack of doom' alone makes it worthy of appraisal by old-timers. Newcomers will be pleasantly surprised at the game's eloquent and all-embracing overview of mankind's history, which to this day sets Civ apart from pretty much any other large scale franchise.
There's no denying that V is somewhat dumbed-down compared to III and IV, but you can adjust your difficulty setting to compensate. In IV I preferred Prince; in V I go for Emperor. As with IV before it, I prefer the Ancient and Medieval as a battling period, simply as you need to make every unit count and haven't the sheer power that arrives in the late game. Of course there's plenty of room to play non-hostile too; the game is very accommodating to players yearning to win without war.
Overall, Sid Meier's Civilization® V is a superb title worthy of spending just...one...more...turn on.

I'm a bit iffy on whether or not I take a game's price point into account when I review a game. I either enjoy a game or I didn't. That said, when the price point is as low as FEMINAZI: The Triggering, I cannot help but lower the standards for how I would rate the game. If this was priced at $59.99, I would be writing a positively eviscerating review of the game. Instead, the game is priced at $0.99 and goes on sale for less than that. I got it at $0.49 on a Steam sale, and simply have to take that into account. This game is super cheap, and with that in mind, I shall continue.
FEMINAZI: The Triggering is a political satire of the third wave feminist movement; specifically its most vocal and outspoken members, who seem like they wander around just looking to find anything they can deem sexist and/or politically incorrect, freaking out and screaming with the biggest outrage response possible. In this game, that is quite literally what you do. You run around a tiny section of streets, a beach, and a small wooded area, finding white males who haven't conformed to feminist values to scream things like "Bigot!" at. Additionally, you can find women pushing strollers look happy to be moms, and can shout "TRAITOR!" at them. You score points for doing this and build up your triggering meter.
However, two things are required to justify your existence: triggering, and tolerance. To display to the world how tolerant you are, you run around finding anyone with brown skin and say things like "Sorry!" to them. What was weird for me at first was that I couldn't tell who to scream at, who to ignore, and who to be nice to, so I kept losing within about a minute of starting the game. You see, like an idiot, I hadn't read the instructions, and didn't realize what I was supposed to do. I quickly caught on, and was shouting at white males and women with children, and praising anyone with brown skin. Then I could stay "alive"/active, running about doing as I pleased. There are also several minigames to help you get fatter, help police shoot only white criminals, throw male babies in the trash while sparing female babies, and a few others. The minigames are simple and not all that great, but they do add to the game.
When I was running up to white males and shouting at them, I initially believed that the game was portraying them all as good guys, and feminists as the villains. For a political satire, I get that, and it's fine, but what troubled me was that I started to notice the things the white males were saying. Some were saying things like "I like your hair" and other tame statements, while others were shouting positive things about white supremacy and angrily shouting racial slurs in public. I then asked myself "Oh, are the devs supporting white supremacy and racism because the 'good guys' are saying these things?"
Then it hit me: the white males in the game aren't all being portrayed as good guys. I believe the intent here was to show that people all say a broad spectrum of things; some good, some bad, some in between, and the over-the-top feminist player character screams and spazzes out
when dealing with every white male who hasn't conformed to being some sort of metrosexual- or emo-looking fellow, regardless of what he has to say. You can find Adolf Hitler in the game, and she reacts to him exactly the same as she does with a guy making pleasant conversation ten feet away. So when someone is saying something tame, she screams at him, but when someone else is saying something pretty awful, she does the same thing at the same volume. On those rare moments when she might actually be justified in calling someone out and getting upset, everyone is just going to be sick and tired of what she has to say, and simply ignore her. It's "The Boy Who Cried Wolf," except here I suppose it would be "The Feminist Who Cried Sexist."
So with that said, I found that aspect of the game pretty enlightening. I'd considered it with other matters going on in the world right now, but not with folks getting triggered. If you're a Leftist (not a liberal or anyone on the Right), I can't imagine that this game would appeal to you. Folks on the U.S. political Right and Liberals who are fed up with people getting triggered without any sort of provocation can probably find a few smiles with this game for a dollar or less, though it's not amazing fun and doesn't have a ton to do, with a rather tiny map. Given the price point and some well-delivered, albeit brutal satire, though, I certainly recommend it.

Killing Floor 1 was the reason I even got Steam after watching some out of the way video of dudes playing West London and having a hell of a time doing so. Fast forward to 2017 when I actually have money to spend on games and KF2 is out of EA, I HAD to snag the Deluxe Edition.
This game honestly improves on the original in almost every way with a few tradeoffs (more on that later). The movement system is vastly improved; sprinting in all directions without needing to have your knife out, kiting is much more doable, etcc. The weapons feel meaty, satisfying and substantial to hold. You can take a double-barrel and literally blow a zed away by unloading both barrels at once. Automatic weapons have recoil and am audible report that gives the weapon life as it takes it away. You also have more perks to play as.
The enemy AI seems smarter in a way. You'll have zeds juking your shots more and more as your difficulty climbs. Speaking of difficulty: this game seems to have a much better curve that the first one. Going from Normal to Hard in KF1 is like going from Normal to Suicidal on here. Hell on Earth is unforgivingly difficult assuming you have a full team of 6 people (excluding custom servers), so that's a plus.
I'm not usually one to just focus on graphics too much, but god damn, does this game look beautiful for a UE3 game. Its optimization is definitely up there, too. You can gib zeds in multiple ways to the point where it stays consistently satisfying without wearing you out, and the game can really put on a gloomy yet lively atmosphere in the official maps. Community maps for the game are also top-notch 95% of the time as well. Honestly, some of the content creators are at the level Tripwire is bringing for maps.
As for updates, they're a little sparse in the way of significant updates which only happen every few months or so, but the content you do get is absolutely top-notch. The Summer Sideshow, Halloween event, and now the Krampus Event are all superb and breathe new life into the game, whether it be new weapons or new bosses. The dosh vault (FREE CRATES WITH NO KEYS NEEDED), weekly events, and daily challenges all give you reasons to come back and keep playing.
Speaking of bosses: you now have four. Patriarch, Hans Volter, King Fleshfound, and Krampus (Abomination/King Bloat). Each has their own strategy to be beaten with, along with the additions of new zeds in comparison to KF1.
Few cons to list: the game doesn't have the rough and gritty characteristics of the first, imo. The characters in the first seemed like they had more to them in the ways they reacted to zeds, the environment, and with each other rather than KF2. Also, some of the community maps can be really hit-or-miss, but that just adds to the challenge sometimes. Also, some of the weapons from the first game haven't made it to this game yet, so you can fall into a set upgrade pattern for weapons really quickly depending on your class.  These are pretty nitpicky, though, and I can legitimately recommend this game if you want to kill♥♥♥♥♥♥first and ask questions later.
