Friends. Family, Hope. Find all of these things in the game and disregard the real-life counterparts. Withdraw from all social events involving your friends and family. Procrastinate even more skilfully and deftly with this charming and deceptively strategic RPG. And, if you're a student like me, disappoint your parents even further by spending an embarrassingly large amount of time before the screen, watching little animals violently flog one another to death.
Because my goodness is this game glorious.
This game has it all : storyline engineered to make you cry, beautiful watercolour artwork, simple yet strategic gameplay, treasure hunting, side quests, crafting, levelling up (with the possibility of grinding if you're into that), hauntingly heartbreaking music and sexy rats in finery and merpeople (again if you're into that). The world and gameplay are utterly absorbing, such that 7pm quickly becomes 10pm and you give up on doing your essay and instead consign yourself to playing for another couple of hours because it's already late and you're kinda tired and what can you do.
I'll speak on the strongest part of the game (and arguably the most important part) : gameplay.
So the game incorporates the Active Battle System (Active Time Battle ? Active Battle Time ?) seen in early Final Fantasy games - in other words, the player and the enemy each have a bar that charges up, and when it is full they may "cast", or complete an action, be it attacking, defending, taunting or buffing allies up with freakish dancing. An interesting component (or two) included in this game is the ability to interrupt an action by hitting the character in mid-"cast", causing the interrupted to have to refill their charge bar. Time it right and the enemy will never land a hit on you, whereupon the aforementioned flogging takes place. Alternatively, panic as you yourself are trapped in such a vicious cycle of flogging and swear under your breath because the enemy is too many and too fast, and you are too slow and weak and pitiful or both. You also have the ability to manually slow down the enemy (or heal yourself) by clicking and holding the mouse (although it's a firefly in the game) over the characters, allowing you to turn the tide of battle or at least give yourself a bit more breathing room if you're getting absolutely pummelled.
There is nothing more satisfying than defeating a boss that you have branded as being "cheap" and "too fast" in the first minute of battle, nothing more elating than having your frustrated despair abruptly change to malicious glee as you discover the proper strategy required to take them out, and there is absolutely nothing that trumps the feeling of having successfully carried out your petty vengeance by dealing an inordinately and unnecessarily large amount of damage to an enemy barely clinging on to life. Eat it !
So concludes the more positive part of the review.
The negative part is a lot smaller and miniscule in importance.
Essentially, if rhymed poetry is not your friend, or if rhyming in general just gets on your nerves, watch out. The entire game is composed of rhymes, and some of them wholly repetitive. There's only so many words you can rhyme with "bye" or "me" (actually that's a lie, there's a huge amount that rhymes with those two words, but in the context of a video game, let alone a conversation in a video game ? I think not). You can also collect collectibles in the form of "confessions" (essentially background history) which is also completely composed of rhyme. And this time the language is a lot more sophisticated. So if you're lazy, a bad reader (which means you should've stopped reading this review a good 5 paragraphs back), a second language speaker (I joke) or simply rhymephobic, avoid at all costs. But because this game is a combat game and not a reading poetry game, I'd have to say that its impact on the game is fairly minimum.
Anyway. Buy it. Play it. Love it. Finish it. Then don't touch it again until nostalgia brings it to the forefront of your mind.

Crawl is an excellent couch co-op game which encourages you to work together as a team to end the hero's life, then take their place and fight your way to salvation by besting the cthulhian horror that resides at the end of it all... or die and have your humanity stolen, only to be cursed to rot forever amidst your wrath in the infinite tombs of Crawl.
Crawl hits all the right notes:
Monsters scale well over time, going from murderous nuisances to outright tough-as-nails murderbeasts
Hero weapons and abilities are interesting and varied
Buffs and debuffs provide an additional strategic layer which raises the game from simply "good" to "great"
There's a heavy cyber-lovecraftian theme which elevates the mood. It's immersive and tense, appealing to that intrinsic desire to survive which exists within every human.
I love the fact that your scorecard is saved between runs. I also laughed out loud when the game told me that my hero had been "lost forever" because we ran out of attempts against the boss (and then it deleted my scorecard, a really nice touch).
I never felt like any of my deaths were unfair, or that any of the monsters in particular didn't come with their own weakness to exploit. Your decisions really shape your hero and you'd do well to expect your enemies to exploit gaps in your defense.
It doesn't have online multi-player, but that's a small concession for what is such a tight and cohesive array of elements that come together and create an experience that'll have you sweating from the sheer intensity. Even if you don't have enough people nearby who can slum it on your couch to gather up 4 players, Crawl provides a powerful AI that will keep you on your toes. I especially thought it was a nice touch when the AI even goes through the human motions in shops and goes through upgrade menus like a regular player - its an oddly salient touch that I didn't know I wanted until I saw it.

is a Viking-themed epic fantasy RPG featuring tactical, turn-based combat, where each of the many (
) decisions that the player makes throughout the course of the game directly affects the unfolding of the story.
Based on that description, this game could have been custom-crafted for me personally. I should have
this game. I really, really wanted to. Unfortunately, the implementation just doesn't do the concept justice.
Let's begin with the good: the art and music are far and away the best things about The Banner Saga - they're beautiful, immersive, and thematically styled. The graphics have a great hand-drawn feel, and the scenes nicely impart the vastness and desolation of the pseudoNorse landscape.
Technically, the game functioned decently on Ubuntu 15.10 (
).
The narrative, despite the fact that the game continually bombards the player with choices and their consequences, felt very linear and driven.
The writers failed to motivate me to care about any of the characters, their plights, or their fates, which made managing them even more of a drudge - I didn't care which ones lived and which ones died, beyond their limited differences in utility, but I was still forced to go through the motions of doing so. All characters have the same handful of statistics, and leveling up just involves spending reputation to increase one or two of them. There's essentially zero potential for exploration: towns and camps are each represented by a handful of clickable icons that spawn conversations or shops, and the areas between are linear, Oregon Trail-esque sequences of traveling intermittently interrupted by seemingly random events. I have no doubt that if I had continued longer, someone in my party would eventually have died of dysentery.
Finally, I found the combat dull and uninspired. There's not much variety in how the characters behave during battle, there's little opportunity for tactical creativity, and the whole mess devolves into a slog to keep one or two characters alive so that you can get the party back to camp and rest up for the next combat.
There are plenty of great RPGs on Steam - I recommend choosing one of them instead of embarking on The Banner Saga.

I'm one of the people owning vanilla as well, but I had no problem paying 6€ to be able to have it here. I have accumulated something about a hundred hours on vanilla, quarter of these being AFK fishing, so I had no problem starting again. Ok, maybe one small problem - them names. I used all my last good ones on vanilla, and even though this game has Family Names, Character Names have to be unique as well... Well, what can you do.
The game itself is awesome. I like the "no fast-travel" thing - there's auto-navigation, and on longer journeys, you can make yourself a coffee or have a smoke or something... The combat is incredible - although there is a quickbar, it's mostly used for items. Almost all the skills are used by some combination of keys, or after/during another skill. I've never got past the levelling phase, so I didn't have a taste of that end-game PvP and Node Wars I hear so much about, but I love taking things slow, and this is just a game for that. No mood for brainless mashing through hordes of enemies? Take your fishing rod and go fish. (And if you think it's boring, just read the chat - it's quite entertaining, even if it sometimes resembles Barrens Chat of distant past.) Order your workers around, and if they're behaving, give them a beer or five. Go tame a wild horse, I dare you.
It can be off-putting for new players because of the possibilities. And of the endless "Is this game P2W?" discussions. But if you can get past this, arm yourself with Google and enjoy your fantasy sandbox. For 6€! (And, let's be honest, 10€ ain't all that much too, in comparison with other titles.) The fun is there, you just have to want to find it. It's a sandbox, for crying out loud.
Feeding the P2W debate: I'm probably not late enough in the game to compare the comfort provided by money-bought convenience stuff. But that's all it seems like - convenience. And cosmetics. Pay for it if you want. Don't, if you don't want to. But don't bash the game because you don't want to spend money on something you don't need to have to enjoy it..
But I guess I'm just a fanboy. (I don't think so, but hell, who knows)

Since early access it's become a truly great game, and just like KF1 it's well maintained with regular updates & new content.  It's easily worth full price but if you catch it on sale, so much the better.  This is my favorite game.
For the best experience this game can offer, you'll want a 144+Hz monitor and a PC that can maintain >100fps at your panel's resolution.  Obviously it takes a less powerful system to get this done at 1080p than 1440p+.  For the graphics settings, don't hesitate to move down to medium or even low settings if necessary on your system.  I'm playing at medium and the loss of graphical fidelity is really nothing compared to the benefit of maintaining a good frame rate.  For reference my system is: i5-3570k@4.2GHz, 16GB DDR3-1866, RX480 8GB.
If your GPU has a healthy amount of VRAM (like 6GB+) then I'd also recommend trying the startup parameter "-notexturestreaming", which tells the game to load all textures into VRAM up-front instead of streaming them in as you play and move around the map.
Especially on the harder difficulties, some real teamwork is required.  For example if you see a team mate is about to get killed by a flesh pounder, maybe you can heroically take the hit for them?  Instead of healing yourself, heal a team mate if you can.  If your team mates stay alive, your own life expectancy is greatly improved anyway.  Splitting up is usually a terrible idea ; you can't help team mates (or be helped by them) if you're off by yourself somewhere.  It's a co-op game, so cooperate :)

Having just finished my first playthrough, I have to say that I'm ashamed that I didn't pick this game up earlier.  It's an utter masterpiece in the CRPG genre, bringing back very fond memories of the Baldur's Gate series, Fallout series, and even a little of PlaneScape: Torment.  If you're a fan of any of those games, do yourself a favor and pick this game up, especially if it's on sale.
The combat is great, and the classes/abilities are excellent, but the true gem of this game is the story.  There are plenty of side quests packed into the environments if you look for them, and none of them feel cheap or thrown in.  Each contributes in its own way to the main story, with a few that span multiple arcs and were so well done that I wasn't sure which was the main story quest at some points.
The only real complaints I have about the game were related to weapons breaking very quickly (especially for rogue characters), and some design issues related to the last boss (he will auto-target and kill a crucial NPC in the first round of combat if you don't set the fight up correctly).  Other than those two minor gripes, the game is a sparkling gem in a sea of absolutely horrible RPGs.

Crawl is amazing. It's a very unique and exciting local multiplayer game to play with friends. In short, one player is the hero and all other players (human or AI players) control the dungeon's traps and its monsters. Whichever of those gets the killing blow against the hero becomes the hero, and the dungeon crawl continues.
There are really good self-balancing systems built into the game that helps players who are "behind" to have a lot of fun and catch up, and there's a lot of variety between all the creatures, weapons, abilities, procedural level generation, and end bosses so that replayability is very high.
The only real drawback in Crawl is that the multiplayer is limited to local only. To that end I recommend playing with a controller, and if possible, treat it as a console game and play it on a big screen like a TV.
The art is incredible, the music is awesome, and atmosphere is wicked and the game's mechanics are really damn cool. I love this game, I'd give it a solid Spinal Tap 11/10 if I could.

Faith might be too floaty for your preferences, but since this is a platformer with a focus on fluid movement, that is something you would want in a game like this. Mirror's Edge, as a game, fills an interesting niche. It's a first-person shooter, but with the "shooter" heavily de-emphasized. Instead, movement and momentum are the core gameplay elements, utilized through the constant freerunning you'll be performing to both solve its puzzles and defend yourself in combat.
However, Mirror's Edge is far from a perfect game. There are occasional moments where the "grab" detection just doesn't seem to kick in, and you'll find yourself falling to your death even after coming into contact with a pipe or ledge. Combat feels a bit awkward at moments, specifically when disarming enemies or the barebones gunplay. Inputs sometimes feel delayed depending on recent actions, as if there was a half second in between quicker movements. The writing feels a bit shallow and lacks a certain significance other than, "Defeat the baddies, save your sister." Replayability suffers somewhat, since the game, with its linear level design and only a handful of stages, can easily be completed in a single semi-long sitting of possibly 6 hours, the only replay values being collecting a few hidden briefcases or speedrunning due to no custom levels.
Despite this, I always come back to Mirror's Edge. It could easily be placed as one of my all-time favorite games.
Why?
Simply put, the art direction.
Mirror's Edge heavily stylizes itself within a well-polished, vaguely futuristic, and minimalist setting. Expansive, towering cityscapes to interior office rooms are brushed over with a small, but highly contrasting palette of either pure white or a single solid color, intertwined with an extensive use of glass surfaces and very bright lighting. This not only serves to provide a feeling of solidarity, simplicity, and an almost alien feel of the city, but also to act as a clean-cut direction to the player, where most obstacles that allow you to advance in your path are often highlighted in a bright red.
The amount of detail (especially with Nvidia PhysX turned on, you do
want that off) in Mirror's Edge can rival or even surpass AAA titles of today. Glass windows shatter into hundreds of crystals and stays on the floor. Fabrics and plastic sheets tear and leave holes where you collide and even shoot at. The entirety of Mirror's Edge's environment simply feels alive and responsive to the player's actions.
To top it off, the soundtrack for the game is probably one of the best I've heard. The music in Mirror's Edge is what I can only describe as a highly "light" atmospheric electronic ambience, providing a sense of both freedom and a (seemingly) high-tech utopian environment.
In spite of Mirror's Edge's multiple, but not severe, flaws, I feel that the artstyle and soundtrack by itself is enough to make this game worthy of experiencing.

**Note : This is going to a very detailed and lenghty review , so I will put a TLDR at the end of this review.
Grim Dawn is an isometric ARPG made by Crate. I first bought this game on my other account back in 2015 while it was still in closed beta. From all the ARPGs I have played, mainly D2 & 3, Van Hellsing, TL2, Grim Dawn stood out as one of the best ARPGs I have played in my entire life.
Grim Dawn offers a dark atmospheric world where iron bits are worth more than gold, which is why that is the main currency here. The graphics are amazing. Dead bodies hanging from trees? Checked. Blood and gore? Check. Amazing spells? Checked.
Here are the pros and cons I feel about this game.
Pros : - Items have skills that can be utilised all the way to late game.
- Awesome soundtrack. Really fits the dark and grimy atmosphere.
- Amazing art and graphics.
- Build optimization. You can build your character revolving around your skills, certain items or your devotion
system. ( A special system where you unlock by slowly restoring shrines in the world. )
- Devotion system actually have interesting concepts. Much like the skill tree of Path of Exile, but instead of
adding stats, there are skills and passive skills you can unlock.
- Dedicated developers. They delivered as promised during their kickstarter journey and made every cent
worthwhile.
- Incredible storyline. Amazing nuff said. Scattered around the world are mysterious journal and notes where you
can collect and gain insight and deepen the lore and plot of the game.
- Did I mention dual class systems?
-♥♥♥♥♥♥ton of secret areas. Omg.
Alright, before ya'll get your pickforks and start calling me out for giving only positive reviews, here are some cons I felt the game had.
Cons : - Confusing for new players. There are many aspects in the game that require attention to. Physical damage,
pierce damage etc. There are too many elements and might be confusing for starter players.
- Voice acting. There are only few voice dialogues in the game. Actually understandable because the Crate team
isn't huge and implementing voice dialogues might be a little too taxing and delay updates.
- New content. They recently released a new content which is great, however new content can be a little slow as
mentioned, they lack manpower.
-Character customization. You can't customers your characters face etc.
All in all, this game is amazing. I bought one during early access and bought another one for my girlfriend to play. This game does not provide DLCs so the only way I feel I could contribute back to the developers is to get more copies.
In all seriousness, this game is amazing. Get it if you haven't already.
TLDR; get the game. It will make you understand the spirit of ARPG.

TLDR; If you like ARPG's (diablo, baldurs gate, champions series, path of exile, dungeon siege etc) this is absolutely worth the money.
Truly a hidden gem, Grim Dawn is a dystopian-esque ARPG, with a nice plot, great graphics, great gameplay and very high replayability value. Its online community is very active, allowing you to freely host or join games with other people, the difficulty being adjusted to match for every player. If multiplayer with strangers isn't your thing; you can put a password on your game so that only friends may join, or you can just play single player.
I will say that character customisation is rather limited (on the aesthetic side of things), however, class customisation goes rather deep in Grim Dawn, you can really make a class of your very own by combining abilities from various other classes and with the devotion tree system. Wanna be a gunslinging mage? go ahead, nothing is stopping you. A frontline sword fighter with pets as backup, why not?
The main quest in the game spans through many fairly large maps with tons of hidden side areas and side-quests, mini bosses, rare monsters, hidden lore and so on. There are multitudes of weapons and armour, and ways to tweak them through the use of other items to make them suit your needs even further. There are no parts of the game that particularly demand you to play multiplayer, though it would make them slightly easier.
Overall the game is very good, it is not without its faults, some crashing issues - particularly where multiplayer is involved, though they are not gamebreaking and not particularly frequent. This game is certainly worth the money and at the very least, worth a try.

Little Nightmares manages to be a dark, eerie, and creepy game, but still have that exploration and adventurous charm I love in games. I'm a HUGE fan of horror games, and I try to seek for the best. I originally encountered Little Nightmares the day it came out, and it looked pretty interesting, however the idea seemed strange and like it wouldn't feel spoopy enough to me, so I didn't pick it up. About 3 months later I found the game again when ProdCharles (a YouTuber I like) played it. I watched the first 2 epidodes and just wasn't interested. Then JT Machinima made a rap called Hungry For Another One, and I suddenly gained interest in the game I had not had originally, so I picked it up. I originally got it on PC, however due to certaint issues with the game I ended up refunding it and getting it on Xbox, which was a good choice. The controls are VERY smooth, but a bit touchy, which I got used too by the second chapter. Now, on to the game: When I first started the first chapter, I was surprised at how open the game was. I could go in so many places that I wouldn't be able to in other games, and I really liked that. The beginning of the game was perfect, it already had that element of mystery I wanted. Due to the fact that I watched the videos by Charles I aready knew all of the first chapter, but I still enjoyed it. The second chapter was my favorie in the game. It really captured that mystery and dificulty I wanted, It had a lot more secrets, and it really put your stealth skills to the test. The third chapter was pretty good to, but it wasn't the best. It was very compelling and fun, but the mood felt sorta off, it just wasn't what I liked. The forth chapter was VERY good, and it reached my second favorite part of the game. It was very difficult and compelling, although pretty short. And it explained a lot of stuff. The fith and final chapter was probably my least favorite. It was still fun as always but the boss fight just felt too easy. The ending was... interesting to say the least. I won't spoil anything, but it was very confusing. Overall I give this game a 9/10. It was very creepy, compelling, and fun, but some parts just wern't as good as others. I definatly recomend this game, it was VERY fun and challenging, and wasn't too scary, so I think it would fit for 10+. Anyway, I hope you liked my long review, and have a nice day :)

tl;dr Gorgeous, eerie and a joy to behold, but be prepared to wrestle with dodgy controls and the timeless problem of platforming in 3d at forced angles.
Visually, a triumph. It's clear that time and love went into this world and these characters. The world is creepy and strangely real, evocative of Tim Burton and David Firth while building an aesthetic that still seems unique.
Regrettably, the technical side doesn't hold up its end of the deal. I'm not sure if it was intentional, or why it would be, but the controls were the most difficult part of the game. Now, I'm all up for a challenge, but it should be surmountable; given the time and effort I should be able to overcome the challenge and, most importantly, I should bloody well want to. Between the strange bloom that obfuscates the edges of the screen and the camera doubling as an antagonist, everytime I failed a task it was due entirely to the blurred low resolution robbing me of depth perception. Again, I liked the visuals, that was what attracted me to the game and kept me playing for as long as I did, but the decision to warp and occlude parts of the screen either by angle or fuzziness had me ready to give up fairly early on. I couldn't see a real reason to rob the player of their all too important senses; it wasn't building suspense, it wasn't actually raising difficulty, it usually just had me wasting time. Beyond that, I got a few bugs that involved monsters reaching through walls when they normally would not be able to and falling deaths after merely jumping on a level plane and, of course, they only occured when the checkpoint was far enough back to make me want to put the game down. So I did.
Gameplay 1.5/5 Frustrating
Visuals 5/5 Achieves the atmosphere and more
Sound 3/5 Perfunctory
Value: ~5$

TL:DR: A free visual novel game, writing is pretty good. Definitely feels like they put a lot of love into it. Art is hit or miss, with some of the creepier scenes being the best drawn.
Long story: The game is ostensibly a good visual novel. While its not the best free one (Katawa Shoujo claims that), its definitely way better than most things you would actually purchase. It is hard to talk about the best parts without getting too spoilery, as some of my favorite scenes are sharp twists...in fact one of the best storylines is a hard 180 from the rest of the game.
The art style for the characters themselves is fairly consistent, but the CGs is not. It is clear a few different artists worked on this, as the light hearted CGs, the horror parts, and the paperdolls (how the characters look in conversations) all have different art styles. None of it is bad though, they don't tend to clash too hard.
The gameplay itself is pretty simple, and probably the most bland, as it has the typical 'main' part of the story where you make choices which follow along the same path, then the 'ending' where you get whichever ending you were going for. The four main stories all follow this format, with good/band endings for it. After the first two good endings, you kinda know where the last two are going in general. There is one bad end that is a rather sharp turn from the rest, but otherwise its all fairly standard. The game does its best job when it is dealing with the outliers, the paths you unlock later, where you rather quickly skip to the 'ending' and the game does a fairly good job of talking about all the wierdness the other scenarios kind of gloss over. One of the paths is full fledged horror, and is very well done, and is worth installing the game alone for.
Overall, you can 100% this game in two evenings, and its worth the time spent.

Divinity: Original Sin is in my opinion the best RPG I've played since Skyrim. It's a tactical, turn based RPG that allows you to command a party of 4 with their individual skills and equipment. The amount of variety and depth when building your characters truly gives you the feeling that you can tailor your party to how you want to play. This also remains the same for combat; there a hundred ways to approach each fight, one of them would be to sneak around and avoid it all together. The environment plays a huge roll in combat as shooting an arrow at an oil barrel and lighting the oil spill on fire creates an inferno. If your mage were to cast a Rain spell that makes everyone wet on the battlefield and then your archer shot a freezing arrow at an enemy, the enemy would be frozen and unable to do anything for a few turns. This is what makes the combat interesting and stops you to take in account all your options before making a move.
***PROS***
Very lengthy, main campaign is long and sidequests are plentiful
Deep character customization
Random dialogue choices between party members determines alignment
Hard mode offers a challenging but rewarding experience
Enemies are varied and AI is intelligent
Loot is varied and drops frequently
High replayability
**CONS***
Crafting system is sub-par; not well explained in the tutorial and isn't rewarding late-game
NPC dialogue becomes repetitive and annoying
Experience is limited; neglecting quests can leave you crippled later in the game

Summary: This game reeks of quality. Play it with a friend. Take your time: combat is tactical, and the story asks you listen rather than giving you a quest marker to rush at.
What this game does well, it does with gusto; its imperfections are few in number and mostly unimpactful.
This game starts by telling you: "Hey, you. Yeah, you. I ain't gonna make this easy, so you'd better remember the rules of real life while you're playing me."
Early in the game, the player is given multiple chances to be reminded that his choices are important and his options are limitless, showing him that he has to be precise and cautious about his decisions; something as simple as running past a guard can start a fight.
This is the defining factor of the game, and if it is one you can appreciate, you'd be cheating yourself of an experience by not playing this game. But there is something even more important than the incredible freedom that the game gives you to choose: choosing how--and with whom--to experience the game.
This game was built with co-op in mind--or, rather, it seems to have been built on the assumption that most of the game's playtime would be with a partner. That's the second most prominent attribute of this game; it is an incredible co-operative journey, and it can serve to "strengthen" and "renew" friendships as it provides countless hours of silly barrel-smashing, boss-exploding, ally-teleporting goodness. I was lucky to have someone amazing to experience it with, and I know it wouldn't have been the same without him.
Ultimately, it's a classic-style RPG, infused with more modern elements of graphical splendor, flashy abilities, biting humor, and highly interactive environments that make combat highly tactical. New skills allow you to manipulate the environments in new and exciting ways, making your character actually feel more impactful as you gain experience. It comes highly recommended to those with the patience and the mind for tactical combat, a zeal for character design and party building, the taste for quest backstory, and a friend who shares all of the above.

Crawl is one of the most fun local multiplayer games I have ever played, with a unique mechanic whereby players take control of the dungeon and become the hero by killing him. The hero is more powerful than the monsters, so the non-hero players are forced to co-operate to whittle down his health, but once he's at low health that spirit of co-operation goes out the window and everyone is trying to land the final blow for themselves. This game's balance is extremely tight, barring a few exceptions (bows are the worst starting weapon in the game by far) and it's always a blast to play since the games aren't too long.
The mid-game is where Crawl truly shines, as the monster players have gained enough power to defeat the hero and he has yet to gain the powerful late-game equipment that would allow him to defeat such threats. At this point the game becomes a race, where you want to grab enough upgrades to be able to take on the bosses, but not spend so much time in the dungeon that you die and lose your spot as hero.
My only real complaint about Crawl is that I wish there were just a couple more bosses, as for most of the early access period there were only two, and now they have come to full release adding on just one last boss. The boss fights are fun, but with such a limited pool they get old fast, with optimal attack patterns that are easy to counter as the hero.
The game has an interesting story, but I don't recommend it for PC as it's available on IPAD for $5, whereas here it was over $20

The Banner Saga has a great story and art. Unfortunately it also has terrible gameplay, and the story choices seem to have been designed to frustate you during battles as much as humanly possible. This is a great story game, and a terrible strategy game. Play this on easy if it's your first time, and get ready to savescum or pull up a choice guide for the harder difficulties.
Now as to why Banner Saga has such horrible gameplay mechanics:
1. The combat is unintuitive, it's better to just weaken enemies to the point where they can't do anything than to kill them outright. This would be acceptable if it didn't turn every fight into a slog, where you can't kill anyone until the very end of the battle, and all your enemies just move around, attacking ineffectualy.
2. The choices you make have predetermined results, which often reward bad or random decisions. This would be okay if the game was balanced for this, or allowed you some way to recover from a bad choice i.e. hunting/ scavenging for supplies like in Oregon Trail. Instead you may as well just find a guide on all the choices you can make, so you can be sure to make the right ones. You don't need to do this on easy, but you can very easily make choices that make the end game near impossible on higher difficulties. I'm talking specifically about decisions that will permanently kill key party members, which may cripple your combat power.
3. The game forces you to kill a certain number of enemies with a character before they can level. This is obviously a problem when you have to use bad tactics, just to farm kills with support heroes.
4. Characters die/ dissapear regardless of the choice you make. Even if you make all the "right" choices, the game still kills off characters you possibly invested xp/ money in. It even destroys gear the character was holding when it gets rid of them. Why the ♥♥♥♥ would you have something like this in a strategy game? Especially on the harder difficulties when every choice could result in a dead end for the player.
Do not buy this game if you want to play a strategy/ tactics game.

TLDR; If you like ARPG's (diablo, baldurs gate, champions series, path of exile, dungeon siege etc) this is absolutely worth the money.
Truly a hidden gem, Grim Dawn is a dystopian-esque ARPG, with a nice plot, great graphics, great gameplay and very high replayability value. Its online community is very active, allowing you to freely host or join games with other people, the difficulty being adjusted to match for every player. If multiplayer with strangers isn't your thing; you can put a password on your game so that only friends may join, or you can just play single player.
I will say that character customisation is rather limited (on the aesthetic side of things), however, class customisation goes rather deep in Grim Dawn, you can really make a class of your very own by combining abilities from various other classes and with the devotion tree system. Wanna be a gunslinging mage? go ahead, nothing is stopping you. A frontline sword fighter with pets as backup, why not?
The main quest in the game spans through many fairly large maps with tons of hidden side areas and side-quests, mini bosses, rare monsters, hidden lore and so on. There are multitudes of weapons and armour, and ways to tweak them through the use of other items to make them suit your needs even further. There are no parts of the game that particularly demand you to play multiplayer, though it would make them slightly easier.
Overall the game is very good, it is not without its faults, some crashing issues - particularly where multiplayer is involved, though they are not gamebreaking and not particularly frequent. This game is certainly worth the money and at the very least, worth a try.

Dying Light, a zombie game at the forefront of a million zombie games... but how do YOU decide? The answer is usually tricky... watching gameplay videos, reading reviews and talking with your mates... then you have make up your own mind!
I'll make this easy to understand... killing zombies any way you want!! ...and there are alot of them!! You get to make your own unique weapon that to use to cleave, shock, beat, blugeon, dismember... and burn! Not to mention, crush, when you jump from a building after you have performed a speedy parqour ballet on the rooftops on the entire map. Which is enormous also! Oh yeah, then there's guns! Did I mention the Quarantine Zones? These are usually tight, dark, and very hard!! The zones are filled to the brim, with zombies. Co-op up and it just gets harder. Every noise you make draws the rest of their zombie buddies closer! Awesome sunrises and worldly effects during the day cycle lead you into the terrifying and alarming night. The whole game changes! It is truely bone chilling. The only thing that warms you are flaming zombies... and your trusty torch. Skill trees provide yet another list of zombie killing methods with little videos that show you what they do! In the zombie apocalypse, who do you trust? The humans that are left and desperate and cutthroat, but you are there to observe, undermine and redeem there lives. Or just loot your way through the world.
The gruesome reality of this games means that even you are sometimes mortified at your own methods of zombie killing. But everytime you just have to kill another! Now it's time for you to decide they die, ENJOY!

The first Half-Life is an undisputed classic, and I know many people will say it's better than Half-Life 2. For me, I came along late to the party, and much of HL's innovations were common now. So while I enjoyed it, HL2 was really the first single player game for me that made me go "whoa."
From the opening ride on the train, to leading an assault on Nova Prospekt with antlions, to battling up the Combine Citadel with a super powered gravity gun, there are so many moments that stand out to me. Some of my favorite parts of the game though are when things have quieted down and I'm exploring old buildings and abandonded outposts. These are the parts where there is no explicit story but you put together the events in your head, allowing you to become more fully immersed in the world.
Half-Life 2 will always hold a special place in my heart as one of the games that really became a piece of art and changed my idea of what games could do.
Just. One. More. Turn.

There is something great about this game. There is also something pretty awful. On the surface, it looks similar to "Inside", but once you start playing it becomes apparent this game is nowhere near as good. Whereas "Inside" only allows left/right this game allows "forwards/backwards or up/down" too. There's a problem right there. Is it forwards/backwards or is it up/down - well that's context sensitive, which means it often doesn't do exactly what you might expect. The next problem with this is that it can make judging a jump difficult - the number of times I timed a jump beautifully, got the distance just finnicky nit-picky perfect only to see the jump sail in front of the object I intended to land on, because I was just slightly too far forward - I maybe didn't explain that very well, but trust me, this has the most infuriating jump mechanic I have ever played. And I've played Eugene's Lair.
But what makes it even more annoying is, fail to judge the jump, guess the depth, time the swing, just perfectly and you fall. And fall. And fall and fall. Flailing gracefully past all the other beautifully timed jumps it took to get there. Down and down, passing downwards in seconds, what took minutes to climb up. Then you get to do it all over again. All of it.
This is a shame because it has promise, it could have been great. But, if "Inside" is a dimly lit, smoky, sultry Audrey Hepburn of a game, then "Little Nightmares" is Miss Piggy in an aubern wig. Another game Kermy? - Ah, no thanks.

Did you grow up on Diablo and Diablo II, but were disappointed with Diablo III?  If so, I believe this game might be the right one for you.  I don't think I've ever written a review for a game here on Steam; however, after just playing a short amount of time I felt compelled to do so.
This game has a dark and gritty feel, rewarding combat system, deep levels of customization, etc.  I hope this game gets more attention, because it truly deserves it.  I'm amazed at what this development team has done with this game.  I think this game really underscores what a tragedy it was that Blizzard closed down the North campus.  I've been waiting for a game like this for at least a decade.
I'm not one who purchases many games, but I bought this game after watching just a short demo on YouTube.  After seeing the game play, and briefly reading about the game on the official web page, I knew this was a game I could gladly support.
The icing on the cake is the ability to mod, lack of DRM, LAN play, and no required internet connection.  Everything you hated about D3 is gone in this game, and almost everything you love from D1 and D2 is here.  The only thing I miss is my necro, but I hope it will be added later, or through modification.
Again -- Dev team, what an amazing job you have done here.  You've won a fan for life.  Thank you for all of the hard work you put into making this outstanding game, and thank you to all who risked financial difficulties to further pioneer this genre.

An RPG that reminds you of the older RPGs where you were not handheld and not all enemies were dead in a few strikes.
Divinity: Original Sin is a game where you are given the basics of how the game works and you need to figure out the rest while going in your adventure. Many choices you make actually change the world around you and the the way the NPCs regard you.
But what is the game about? Well, you play as a source hunter called, along with another source hunter, to solve a mystery and uncover even greater mysteries that lead you on a quest to save the world. There are 2 main characters, so you can co-op with a friend, or, if you want, play solo like myself as you are not punished for that. You also get 4 unique companions which have their own personalities and stories though you can have at most 2 come with you, one for each main character (you can have even less if you use a special talent that boosts your power but the character can't have a follower, but I wouldn't recommend it, if nothing else, at least for the comments your companions make). If you don't like the unique companions you can get random mercenary companions a bit later.
Now, the world itself is quite big and there is no handholding so you need to figure out some things on your own. While the world itself is real time, the battles are turn based, each of your characters and enemies acting in a queue according to how many action points they posess (this can be changed through stats).
One thing to keep in mind is that this is a game where you need to be attentive everywhere as there can be hidden treasures everywhere (and if not, worthless items to sell at least) or traps that can instant-kill some of your party members. You can sneak to have surprise attacks, you can pickpocket npcs and sometimes you have this rock-paper-scissors games to convince others that your point is the right one(you can skip it if you dislike it).
The game provides interesting challenges and puzzles (like knowing what item goes where, what spell you can use to unlock an item or destroy it etc) which could be challenging to some but that you can even skip if you read all books and papers you encounter as the rules are sometimes explained there. Or, alternatively, you can try to use brute force! You want what's in the chest but don't want to guess how to go through the lava to the key? Smash it with a club and get the contents! Or use your lockpicking to open it instead. Use magic to open it. In general the game gives you multiple choices for different problems you may encounter.
As for battles, enemies are non-respawning, so each you kill brings you closer to the end, and each encounter is unique, some group may use poison then set everything on fire, while another will appeal only to brute force. Sometimes the enemy tries to use tanky characters, sometimes they send 20 bomb bots at you. Each battle is unique, and this makes some harded and some easier depening on your preffered playstyle, it makes you organize and think of the best way. Save often though, you will need it.
That being said, you need to remember, this is a long story, and there will be lots to read. You will sit reading stuff for a long, long time and you better remember the things as... well, no handholding, so not everything is remembered in your quest log.
Graphics - 9.5/10 - really good graphics yet you can see in general the limitations of what they did (for example you can't rotate the map 360%, I belive the rotating angle is more around 90% so you may have problems talking to rats hiding under rocks.
Audio - 9/10 - Awesome music, most NPCs have flavour text that is both written and audio and in general really simulates the town and other area life quite well.
Gameplay - 9.5/10 - As I said, much reading, turn based battle system but open world exploration, quite a few talents, attributes, companions etc.
There are however some negative aspects as well:
1. You need a mage-type character - doesn't matter if it's a companion or main hero(you find companions early on) but you really need a mage as you can't pass some puzzles without the skills that a mage employs.
2. The crafting system is a bit weird. To give you an example, you want to craft a belt, you need 4 wool which you split in 2 stacks of 2, combine them and make 2 yarn, split them, combine them and make a rope. You then get a sharp claw, you get some star flowers which you grind to make stardust, you take a skull or a bone, you grind and make bonedust, You combine the dusts to make 1 pixie dust. You combine pixie dust with claw and make a magical claw. You combine magical claw with rope and you have a lovely +1 strengh belt... a bit dismantling to say the least. Well, this is quite realistic, yet also quite time-consuming and makes you feel like you haven't achieved much. Not all combinations are clear (you can combine a glass of milk with a jar of honey, a bucket of water with flour, yet not a bucket of milk with a jar of honey for whatever reason) so you may need guides on net on how you craft most things.
3. Crafting is not very useful. Sure, you can make potions, that's awesome... but the gear you make is not very good compared to gear you find. In general, the gear you make is common but with some stats and while it can be good if you have no item at all equipped or haven't found an item for that slot for 5+ levels (if this happens, you haven't visisted vendors enough), in general those items are only good for one thing, and that is selling them.
4. The rock-paper-scissors system can be annoying at times, thankfully it is skippable.
Overall though I will say this game is amazing. While it has its issues, these seem to pale in the light of the general feel of the world, the way the mechanics work, the story and the relation between the characters, the dungeons, puzzles, looks and music and this makes it a must have for any older RPG fan. And remember, there won't be much handholding ;)

-Well-designed nightmarish enemies with interesting mechanics and 'fights'.

-Audio design second-to-none. Subtle music and atmospheric effects that build and subside in response to gameplay.
-Whilst not a 'story' as such, the plight of the character and development of the protagonist pulls you in constantly.
Cons:
-Due to the game design it can be a little hard to judge the depth of your character on-screen at times, but never caused any huge issues.
-A little short, if I'm honest. Finished up the main game in 3 + 1/2 hours. However the level of enjoyment for those hours diminshes the short playtime.
As a final thought, I was getting a really strong Spirited Away vibe mid-late game; whether intentional or not I loved the nod toward the Spirited Away universe.
Very much recommended game! Show the devs some love, they very clearly showed their game a lot of love.

Following in the Russian literary tradition of existentialist works, Everlasting Summer is a multi-faceted triumph of art and entertainment.  Originating from IIchan, Everlasting Summer manages to avoid inauthenticity and pretentiousness that is inherent in image board culture to deliver a visual novel that is truly heartfelt and contains a tone and spirit unlike any other VN currently released.  The plot and themes of the game are relatable to anybody, regardless of age or ethnic background, even if one’s experience is the mirror image or exact opposite of the events within the game.  In a genius move, the division of two realities allows anybody to experience the VN while also engaging in a perspective that differs from their own.  Both existential dramedy and meta commentary on life and entertainment in the post-internet age, Everlasting Summer avoids the cynicism and post-post-post-modern irony found in similar releases of its kind.  While it lacks the biting and irreverent satire of a certain Krautchan VN, it more than eclipses the former with beautiful visuals, an effective multi-genre soundtrack and a genuine sincerity that, combined with the tantalizingly gripping writing style, coalesces into an unforgettable experience that unequivocally stands as the best visual novel released in years.  A flawless English translation means that this hidden gem can be experienced by many, many more people.  Play this as soon as you can; time is precious, as Everlasting Summer eventually makes very clear, and you will certainly not waste or regret any time spent with this.

You could probably write several pages about Killing Floor 2 and only scratch the surface. I've put so many hours into this game because of friends and leveling, but I ultimately hate this game. I've peeled away the vibrant and intriguing surface only to find an unfufilling waste of time underneath. People have written exhaustive guides on how "good" and "bad" Killing Floor 2 is, breaking it down bit by bit. I'm not going to do that here.
If you don't know what Killing Floor 2 is, or you are looking at buying Killing Floor 2, let this next part be the important takeaway.
IF you are looking for a game that involves killing hordes of zombies while trying to survive by managing resources and gaining ground, go play
.
IF you are looking for a game that is all about teamwork and using skills and abilities to keep the hordes at bay, all the while working towards some concrete objective, go play
.
IF you are looking for a mildly interesting team game, I'd consider this only if you've run out of better options. There isn't enough staying power here to warrant a full price purchase. It's a bloated mess that looks pretty, but has so many design flaws that it ends up being an unrewarding experience overall.
First, I have to get this out of the way. The game has style. Its artistic, animation, and sound department are top notch. There is an incredible amount of creativity and skill here. All the details in the guns, the maps, the enemies. It's AAA by all standards. My hat is off to those amazing members of the development team who create these incredible assets.
However, Killing Floor 2 is lacking in the game design department. Killing Floor 2 samples from seemingly every item on the game design buffet. It is riddled with too many ideas and mechanics. It's an issue of too many cooks, or not enough. It lacks a cohesive vision of what it wants to be.
It has multiple-personality disorder, but in game form. It wants to be an gorey zombie shooter... or maybe a team shooter... or there is a leveling system? Oh, don't forget about the MOBA aspects of building up your character from the bottom at the beginning of a match. Oh, there are collectibles? All the enemy types have different resistances for some reason? This guy is resistant to explosives for some reason? and this guy is weak to them? How would you know this without reading the wiki?
Every time I play, I just end up asking myself, "Why?". Why do I need to run around the level to buy guns between waves, only to return to same location I was entrenched in previously? Why is this intermission segment timed, leaving me with only a minute to run to the store, buy my guns, and run back, and not a "Ready Up" system instead? Why even buy guns from a specific location, and instead just open up a buy menu wherever I am at? Why even buy guns at all? Why is there a leveling system that takes 30 hours to hit cap on one perk? Why are there 10 perks with overlapping roles? Why is this a TEAM shooter if we're all competing for kills? Why is there bullet-time? Why are there boss battles?
Why this? Why that? Why?
It's a trap, as I see it. The game takes about 20-30 hours before those questions start to creep in. You won't notice it at first, because you'll be swept away by the pure spectacle of all the gore and violence, and the laborous leveling system gives the illusion that you are making progress. Eventually, though, the gnawing questions of poor game design will sneak up on you, and you'll start to see how contrived and disjointed the game really is. Many of the features are just there because... well... they are there. It's feature creep at its finest.
The game's playerbase is divided heavily by the game's convoluted layers of mechanics. You have your low skill or new players wallowing at the bottom in the normal or hard levels of difficulty, playing it like it's a deathmatch game with no sense of teamwork. At high level play, you've got people who have dissected the game down to specific sets of meta, and not knowing that meta will get you crucified. To make matters worse, the game never explicitly teaches you how to play beyond entry level. The developer just expects the high level players to teach the lowbies. Low level players grind out the ridiculous amounts of experience needed to hit cap, and then hop into high level games with no idea how to play. Good luck with this system, Tripwire, because it isn't working, and it is only frustrating everyone involved.
Killing Floor 2 has so much potential, but much of it is dashed against the rocks by poor developer oversight. A lot of the ideas here could be channeled into something profound, or even brilliant. However, it just retreads the same ground that Killing Floor 1 did, and brings little more to the table then updated graphics, an in-game store, and a skinner box drop system. Combine that with a hostile fanbase with stockholm syndrome, and you've got yourself a game that's not really worth the average gamer's time. I could write so much more, but I think that's enough for now.

Well..First of all I would like to say that Grim Dawn (for the price) is actually a very decent game. There are lots of areas to explore and many way of improving and leveling up your character. But unfortunatly (in my opion) falls short on basic RPG principles..Firstly there are not enough save areas in the game when you die all too many times you have to triverse the same area you have already gone through kill the same enemies (which also drains much needed health) just to begin where you left off. It's 2016 there are many other rpg's that have remedied this it's not that difficult to include multiple save points on a a quest that will allow the player to continue the campaign without becoming bored. Even though by reengaging enimies you will continue to  collect experience points to level up your character but it's just to repetitive.
This Is a huge game and you what to explore more.. not doubling back to you previous grave to get back the experience you have lost by getting killed hiking up the same path you where just killed to get there to begin with.  Also bossess respawn what the hell is that about!?  If i'm going back to an area to get some loot I left on the ground how the heck are these guys coming back? You know how..lazy programming. Guys be fair it took a long♥♥♥♥♥time to kill a boss let em die for pete's sake your're not adding any value to the game by not doing that, just additional fustration.
One other thing the map system is VAGUE! Consisdering how large this game is should be a lot more discriptive. Quest should be more clearly marked this would definately help with the overall flow of the game. Lastly with these gripes in mind would I recommend this game the answer is YES..If you have the patience to deal with these issues leveling up and becoming stronger with magic or might is a very cool and rewarding experience. Very few games in a decade have an original personality to them.  Divinity: Original Sin does.  It has humor, puzzles, and complex features that are not seen so artfully done in other games.  Also, for those who have played Dvinity: Dragon Knight Saga, this game is nothing like that.  But that's pretty obvious for anyone who has played any measure of western RPGs.
So, okay, what's great about it?  The art style, the atmosphere, the music, the idle banter with townsfolk, and the dungeons.  And the quests.  Let's compare this to another game that came out recently.  Dragon Age: Inquisition.  DAI has what could be considered MMO-caliber quests in a single-player existence.  D:OS goes the other way, making each quest interactive, unique, and enjoyable.  And no, the game is not easy.  Was Baldur's Gate or Icewind Dale easy?  No.  Were Divine Divinity and Beyond Divinity easy?  No.  So why should you expect this one to be any different.  Dragon Age Inquisition could be seen as easy, with a side of complexity.  Divinity: Original Sin is complex, difficult, and utterly without regret about that point.  It's not Dark Souls 1 or 2, obviously, but it's still pretty difficult.
A game being difficult isn't inherently bad, but it will turn off some players who are afraid to fail.  You will fail in D:OS.  Simply making characters in the beginning is an involved process that can cause you enormous amounts of trouble throughout the game.  I had the ill fortune of my first two characters being made in the exact image of the first (and at the time, only) voiced companions.  So my warrior and mage were entirely the same as the warrior and mage that joined my party.  In say....World of Warcraft, five moonkin druids in an arena match have a change to starfire an enemy to death.  It might work.  But in Divinity, having characters with the same spells and abilities is just...crippling.
The game revolves around a complex and interstellar story that weaves the four great elements together with much finesse.  Fire, ice/water, air,  poison/earth.  There are variations to each element, and each one cancels out another.  Having a party that can effectively control all four elements will make life soooooo much easier for everyone involved.  There are puzzles everywhere, and dungeons require cunning and manipulation of these elements.
If you like JRPGs or Bioware RPGs, you may not like this game.  It has everything that an avid Role Playing Game enthusiest would love, but it's just not built in a way that casual gamers would enjoy.  I mention JRPGs because they're built in an entirely different way.  Sure, they're both turn-based, but JRPGs represent items, damage, and instant encounters so much differently.
In D:OS there ARE NO RANDOM ENCOUNTERS.  You fight the enemies that exist in the world, and once you do, they're dead.  No grinding.  No wasting time.  To compensation for this, each enemy has its own particular brand of evil to employ.  And it's all trial and error.  Sure, you may win a battle against some orcs, but I guarantee to you that the next band of orcs will be entirely different.  They will employ shamans and rogues and all manner of foul magics to make your life hell.
Dvinity: Original Sin is one of the most interesting games I've played, yet it's not something I can play repeatedly.  It's not a Skyrim/Oblivion/Morrowind or a Dragon Age Origion/2/Inquisition.  This game requires you to think.  And when you think, you will succeed.  And when you succeed, you will feel good about it.  That's it.

If you enjoy turn based games and you enjoyed old school Xcom, this is good.
The game itself can be rushed through and finished quickly if wanted. There are moments when it feels like the game is completely against you as well. And some days when you think your people are invincible. Which... against sectiods, they just might be.
Old vs New
Graphics +
They def. went up. Explosions, ships, people.  All of it. But that should be expected.
Teams: Mix
Mixed? Well, you have a bit more control on some things, but you can only get a limited amount of people in your group. Unlike the first one that could have up to 12 or even 15 depending on your craft(and tanks you brought along), this one is limited to six. And you have to buy for those two slots.
Not saying that it's actually a bad thing.. just another use of resources you have to take into account.
Ships: -
You only get a few different ones here. In the original you had your first two, but you could build multiple types, not just attack but also transport, and eventually one (the Firestorm) that did both attack and transport. So you troops were immediately on the scene of the downed craft.
Which leads us too...
Crash sites: Mix
There isn't to much to complain about here, it's about the same. The sooner you get troops on the ground after a crash, the more disoriented the enemy is. The only difference I've seen is, from the old, you crash a UFO in the ocean, you didn't have to go after it. Sometimes that was a plan, down the ship just to keep it from spreading influence but down it in the water because your troop count was bad/injured. Not so lucky now.
Research/Construction: +
I think that's a bonus, just over all. I think the new system they did, did credit to how it used to be.
Base: +
It's def. a nice change. A little skeptical at first at how it would all work, but I like it. Again, a tax of resources, so something to keep in mind, but if you set your base up right, it can pay off well.
Also, either I didn't let the baddies do it, or they just don't in this version, in the old game they could actually attack your base and now you're moving your own troops through home territory. It was kinda cool to see how the game made it look from the combat side.
TDL: I could go on with the different aspects(And I may as I get more hours in) but I've enjoyed the changes they produced and felt it a worthy purchase. Now to go on playing the expansion.

Killing Floor 2 is one of the best first person shooter zombie games I have ever played. The game takes out the open world survival aspect for the most part and just focuses on having satisfying fun killing zombies. While it is true the zombie theme can be a bit overused, I still have fond memories of killing floor 2.
However this game is not a masterpiece by any means. While it is so fun and satisfying to kill zombies there are some shortcomings with the game. The biggest shortcoming in my opinion is the lack of boss fight variety. On the boss wave there is only 2 bosses you can possibly fight. The Patriarch is one, with his summoning of minions and devastating mini gun. And Dr. Hans Volter, who has gas grenades and the ability to drain life from players. After the first few matches it can get boring fighting the same boss as both are easy to pick up their patterns after some experience with the game.
I would personally love to see some DLC for this game that adds new bosses and enemy types. Some extra gear choices and classes would be welcome as well. I find that this game thrives on its variety of class selection, abilities within each class, and basic wave enemy types.
So yes I would overall give killing floor 2 an 8/10

You know, normally I'd write a long winded essay of a review, but I'll keep it short.
Pros: Fun
Cons:
In all seriousness though, if you like games that require a little strategy to play but a LOT of strategy to win, then buy this game. This game will challenge you to think outside the box and sometimes you will only escape with a dented tin can of a spaceship, but when you finally beat the final boss it actually feels as if you accomplished something. Sometimes you may have to teleport a bomb into your own spaceship to kill an enemy boarding team...or maybe just open the air locks and wait for them to suffocate. Maybe you want to brute force your way through the enemy shields and annihilate them with sheer firepower, or you could use ion bombs to disable their weapons and oxygen systems and watch as they slowly suffocate without any way to retaliate. Will you hire a full crew, or only enough to keep your ship running and buy some repair drones to fix your ship systems for you? What will you do if your drone systems lose power and your pilot has to repair them, leaving your ship unable to evade incoming enemy fire? WHAT WILL YOU DO? TELL ME!
Obviously there is a little more to the game than just the numerous ways you can cut off the enemy's oxygen supply, but that's how I like to play. Does that make me a cruel person? NO! It doesnt. I swear.

Its rare when a computer game is able to convey the feelings and connection to a story that normally only a book can. Banner Saga is much a case. The game is predominantly its story and its unfolding through your own actions.
I wont go into the details of the story, because it would be a shame to spoil any of it. Suffice to say that it is heavily influenced by Northern European Mythology and that it takes place in a similarly cold and "bleak" setting.
The game inter-mixes tactical strategy with graphic adventure elements very well, even if the combat and character traits are somewhat simplistic. At the end of the day it doesn't really matter cause once again its all about the story. A story that is most of all, well told.
It is this point that makes the game great, as the developers have managed to convey the story and a multitude of emotions that manage (in a very short time span) to tie you (emotionally) to many of the characters and their situations.
Don't expect action sequences or cinematic or anything of the sort, the graphics are reminiscent of hand drawn Disney classics and the accompanying music is superb.
While there are alternative paths to the end (and different endings apparently), I believe that the average person will not bother to go through a second play-through, if nothing else mostly because they will be satisfied with it enough to not want to spoil it.
So at the end of the day if you like story driven games (and can enjoy a fantasy setting), don't miss this game, it is quite the experience.

Long story short, Black Desert is going to provide you with a decent amount of entertainment with its captivating world and action packed combat. Advice about the game, do not try to compete with top players or keep up with the rest. Play it at your own pace, and experience what you find the most fun.
Black Desert Online has flat out the best world I have seen in an MMORPG and one of the best I have experienced in gaming overall. Its massive, filled to the seems with content and on top of that it's beautifully crafted. Exploration is a big part of the game, and a lot of it's systems depend on it. Through exploration you gain knowledge of each place you visit, each person you talk to, and each enemy you kill. This knowledge can be used to unlock special items and stores from merchants, getting new quests from some NPCs, and increasing your energy pool (more about that later).
On top of the gameplay incentives however, the world is masterfully crafted and it is clear effort was put into it's design. It might not be as fantastical as you'd want (although more regions are coming) but it is detailed and most importantly, it feels alive. With NPCs walking around the roads, workers working at the different nodes, and characters just having casual chatter around the place the place is definitely worth exploring.
A big part of the world in Black Desert is the Node system, which is the integral component for a lot of gameplay in the game. The world is made out of multiple nodes of different types. Firstly, there are settlement nodes, which allow you to purchase housing to use for both personal use, as well as for multiple crafting workshops and warehouses. The second node type you will need to care about is resource nodes, which are where workers can be sent to gather a resource. In order to send a worker to a node, you need to invest into each node connecting the settlement node with the resource node. The worker will then have to walk from the settlement to the resource node, spend some time gathering and return before you receive any resources.
In addition to gathering and crafting, nodes are also used to trade. Trading involved buying resources from one node, and selling them at another, trying to maximise your time traveled with the profit. You can also craft items to trade.
This is an interesting one, as I personally find the world of Black Desert to be captivating, and the lore to be quite interesting. That being said, the english translation is sub-par at best. I would not be able to tell you how the script is in the Korean version, but in the English its filled with awkward dialougue and pretty bad voice acting. However, if you can get past the less than ideal translation, the story of Black Desert is one that is definitely worth a follow.
I like to divide the gameplay in Black Desert into 3 distinct categories:
Early on, what you are most likely doing is questing, which involves talking to a bunch of NPCs and grinding the enemies they tell you to grind until an objective is crossed off. For most, this will probably be where most of the time is spent, killing enemies to level. Up until level 50, you will be guided by quests, after which you will be given a more free reign of where to go and how to level (technically you can do that from the start, but you need to do a story quest to be able to get to 50). After you reach 50 is where the game properly begins. You will probably want to find a party in order to be able to abuse high level grind spots without being killed on sight. In addition to grinding trash mobs scattered across the world, you will also be able to grind bosses from scrolls and the variety of open world bosses living in the world. Those will drop armour, and resources used to progress through the game.
As a reward for your time spent grinding, you will be able to take part in open world PvP (starting at level 45). The open world PvP system, in my opinion, is nothing but a method for making the life of other's around you a pain. There is no penalty for dying in open world PvP, and nothing you really gain from killing someone. (What I believe to be) The main use of open world PvP in Black Desert is to take dominance over other players who might want to grind in the area and scare them off. In addition to open world PvP however, there are a few structured PvP types in the game. Node Wars, Guild Wars, Castle Sieges, and the Red Battlefield. Those are incredibly fun (while kinda meaningless) activities you can partake in. Firstly, the Red Battlefield, which is your standard red vs blue PvP arena where you try to kill as much enemy units as possible, and get rewarded quite well for being successful at it. The other 3 are all part of guild activities, which is where the gameplay meat of the game lies. Guilds can compete over nodes and castles to take control of the territory. After they do so, the guild will receive tax income from the region and their guild banner will be displayed across the node affected.
Lastly, Life Skilling is your main meat of PvE in the game. This includes everything from gathering to trading. The game offers a variety of life skills which can be levelled by taking part in activies bound to the skill. And here is where the knowledge gained via exploration comes into play. For each knowldge group you complete, you gain extra max energy, and energy is used to do most life skill actvities. These activities are closely related to the node system and will let you craft a variety of items.
The main issue I have with the game lies here. All of this is great, however player interaction is heavily limited. You are not allowed to trade items with other players and only specific items can be sold on the marketplace. In addition to that, there is little impact players can have on the world, which might be alright to some, makes the game stale to others. Especially when the game has so much potential for emegence but is limited beyond what is necessary. For example, items sold on the marketplace HAVE to be sold within a certain price range determined by an algorithm.
The progression in the game mostly involves RNG. Your main means of progression will be grinding for black stones and putting it into best in slot gear in hopes the gear will level. There is some nuance to this, like fail stacks (where each failure increases the chance of success) but it is ultimately RNG.
This is a weird one, quests in this game feel mostly uninspired, however I am not against them. The thing I hate most about MMOs is making quests completely unrelated to the game's mechanics. For example, making your game filled with quests about interacting with contexual prompts that only exist for that quest, and that quest alone. This game does not do that. Each quest will have you abuse one of the game mechanics, whether its crafting, gathering, trading or killing enemies. Quests also do not give you XP, instead they give contribution points which are used to invest into nodes and rentable items from certain NPCs. Personally, I like the questing here. After level 50 they are not required to play, but provide incentives of their own which is nice.
Yes, the game does have Pay to Win elements, anybody saying otherwise is either too busy fanboying or has a warped definition of what Pay to Win is. There are items on the cash shop that are pretty much necessary to play. You can definitely do without them, but the boosts they provide are so big that not getting them will probably leave you behind. It's stuff like underwear to raise luck, or pets that pick up drops, or extra character slots that can add to your passive daily silver gain. Do they stop your enjoyment of the game? No, but they are incredibly helpful items.

First things first, while there's this thing with Steam Awards voting going on, nominate this as custom category "Most in Need of a Sequel", or something like that. :) It's not likely Valve will actually make a sequel even if all HL fans out there whine for another 10 years, but it's worth it just for a good laugh's sake.
Now to the actual review. If you are going to read this, keep in mind that this is not an objective description, it's a love note.
The most stunning thing about HL2, to me, is that there is so much story and action in it at the same time. And most of the story is told through player's experiences: visual, audial, emotional. An FPS that makes you feel things, how about that.
As a shooter this game can be quite intense. Not impossible, just pleasantly challenging. I can say that this was one of the few games that actually made me use different kinds of weapons for different situations even on normal. That feels nice if you like to do a little fast thinking and planning.
This is a very atmospheric game. The use of color and light not only makes each location unique and memorable, it amplifies the emotional impact on the player. That is, you are going to be scared ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ when game developers want you to be. And you are bound to sigh and think &quot♥♥♥♥♥♥ there's still beauty even in this world" in other moments.
Last but not least, characters. All non-player characters have enough personality to actually make you want to aid them or bash their teeth in. And I've never seen a better companion character than Alyx Vance in a video game (Elizabeth from Bioshock Infinite is a close second, but Alyx was my first love).
