Dying Light is an open world adventure horror game, developed by Techland and published by Warner Brothers, releasing in January 2015 for PC, PS4 and Xbox One. This game sort of came out of nowhere, it didn’t have very much hype behind it prior to release and it came as a welcome surprise to a usually quite month of the year for big game releases.
The game play in Dying Light reminded me so closely of Dead Island. You play in first person view as you explore the world. Of course, the world has been overrun by zombies. One of the changes to the “Dead Island” gameplay style is the parkour system. We have seen parkour systems used in games such as Assassins Creed and Shadow of Mordor, but Dying Light’s version knocks them all out of the park. A third of the gameplay is based around the running and jumping across the landscape – you are able to hide from the zombies when you are jumping rooftop-to-rooftop so it is really in your interest to get to grasp with it as soon as possible. There are times when you will be thrown into the combat situations; this is where the Dead Island mechanics come in – melee weapons are going to be your primary source of damage and they work exactly the same as DI. Your weapons take durability damage each time you hit, but you can repair them on the fly with the required parts. Once you get your hands on a gun, the odds swing dramatically in your favour, but you do get the downside of the noise it creates, and it possibly attracting even more zombies to your location.
One of my favourite mechanics Dying Light introduced though would be the dynamic day and night cycle. During the day time, zombies will act in their usual manner, whilst they are still a danger, they can definitely be managed fairly easily. Once it is night time though; boy oh boy, you better have your running shoes on! The zombies transform into a much more dangerous form, they can sprint, and see a lot further away, as well as their heightened sense of hearing – meaning you will find it very hard to by-pass them.  The day night cycle lasts for about 70 minutes in total, about one hour in daylight, and 10 minutes at night.
Graphically, I am very happy with the quality of graphics on show. I was nowhere near able to push out the game on 4k, even on the menu screen my frame rate plummeted, and I even struggled on 1440p, so I had to make do with just 1080p with all of the settings ramped up.  The lighting effects, explosions, and scenery all look absolutely stunning. Textures are all high resolution and the animations of everything in the game are faultless. Whilst there is a lot of animations that can be annoying after the first few times, such as when you open a chest, you have to wait 2-3 seconds whilst the animation plays out of you opening it; personally I would have liked this to be skippable but it is a really minor issue.
Dying Light starts out in a very easy fashion, allowing you to get to grips with the game mechanics, and the tutorial at the start of the game introduces you to the game very well too. The parkour mechanic can take a little while to get used to as sometimes you will probably fall whilst climbing buildings because you aren’t used to the way it works and feels, but it just takes practice. The only time I had real issues with the combat difficulty would be the later stages in the game, when you are just getting hammered by hordes of zombies over and over again. Little tip; conserve your ammo!!!
The vast open world you are playing in very rarely leaves you with nothing to do; there are tons of side missions, collectables and loot to find. There are over 100 different melee weapons, and they can be modified in different combinations (over 1000 of them!). The side missions do seem a little but samey after a while. I completed about 13 or so out of the 44 before I finished the main story and this was because they are very repetitive. A few other optional objectives consist of finding relief packages which is where you race the opposite faction to get a supply drop, saving survivors from the opposite faction’s men attacking them, and the same for zombies. You can also go out of your way to find collectable items such as trophy’s and notes around the world.
Completing the main story and about a ¼ of the side missions has taken me just over ten hours. Right now I don’t have a dying urge to go back in and complete the rest of the missions, purely because of the repetitive factor, but I will be keeping Dying Light installed so that I can in the future as well as the anticipated DLC which will be releasing soon. The devs have reports that with all of the current content in the game, you should be able to push 50 hours. I struggle to believe that, I would say you can get about 20 hours out of Dying Light at the time of writing this.
I didn’t have any technical issues. The game ran very well at 1080p at a steady 60 fps, the only time it dropped sub 60 was in extremely hectic scenes with hundreds of zombies and lots of explosions but that is to be expected. I played the game with keyboard and mouse, and should be strongly recommended you do not attempt to play with a controller.
To sum up, Dying Light is a really nicely done zombie adventure game. Personally I feel it is a much more rounded off game compared to the Dead Island series, and adds plenty of depth to the genre rather than re-hashing content that’s already been done before. The main story and core gameplay mechanics make’s Dying Light one of the standout games to be released in 2015 and I would strongly recommend this game to any open world genre fans out there.

It is traditional and honest RPG that uses mechanisms of classic RPG's. In an enchanting isometric world, however, it perfectly connects to the sophisticated, detailed and perfectly functional whole, which makes the RPG genre honor and entertain on a truly regal account.
I don't belong to the players who'd constantly extolled the beauty of isometric games, and not even Original Sin is completely excellent in terms of graphics. But to the hell with all the effects if the game offers a varied, vibrant and glamorous world that overpowers you. The result is a fantasy world that has something to say. It also reacts to your every move, and most objects are not only interactive but mainly actively usable in combat.
Divinity: Original Sin is isometric game with simple models and textures, and the plot is a fantasy cliché of the highest caliber. The experience of playing cannot make it worse, because the complexity always go hand-in-hand and drawbacks - they are minor in contrast of charming Rivellon, wonderful turn-based fights, cute detail.

If you enjoy turn based games and you enjoyed old school Xcom, this is good.
The game itself can be rushed through and finished quickly if wanted. There are moments when it feels like the game is completely against you as well. And some days when you think your people are invincible. Which... against sectiods, they just might be.
Old vs New
Graphics +
They def. went up. Explosions, ships, people.  All of it. But that should be expected.
Teams: Mix
Mixed? Well, you have a bit more control on some things, but you can only get a limited amount of people in your group. Unlike the first one that could have up to 12 or even 15 depending on your craft(and tanks you brought along), this one is limited to six. And you have to buy for those two slots.
Not saying that it's actually a bad thing.. just another use of resources you have to take into account.
Ships: -
You only get a few different ones here. In the original you had your first two, but you could build multiple types, not just attack but also transport, and eventually one (the Firestorm) that did both attack and transport. So you troops were immediately on the scene of the downed craft.
Which leads us too...
Crash sites: Mix
There isn't to much to complain about here, it's about the same. The sooner you get troops on the ground after a crash, the more disoriented the enemy is. The only difference I've seen is, from the old, you crash a UFO in the ocean, you didn't have to go after it. Sometimes that was a plan, down the ship just to keep it from spreading influence but down it in the water because your troop count was bad/injured. Not so lucky now.
Research/Construction: +
I think that's a bonus, just over all. I think the new system they did, did credit to how it used to be.
Base: +
It's def. a nice change. A little skeptical at first at how it would all work, but I like it. Again, a tax of resources, so something to keep in mind, but if you set your base up right, it can pay off well.
Also, either I didn't let the baddies do it, or they just don't in this version, in the old game they could actually attack your base and now you're moving your own troops through home territory. It was kinda cool to see how the game made it look from the combat side.
TDL: I could go on with the different aspects(And I may as I get more hours in) but I've enjoyed the changes they produced and felt it a worthy purchase. Now to go on playing the expansion.

When I played ANOTHER WORLD in 1991 I thought to myself "Now this is how you make a computer game!". The combination of the immersive world, and the cinematic feel, combined with platforming, action and puzzles was exactly what I had been looking for in a gaming experience.
Fast forward 25 years and playing LIMBO felt like a sort of spiritual successor to ANOTHER WORLD, though admittedly with a macabre twist! After that we got INSIDE, which scratched my ANOTHER WORLD itch even better than its predecessor. After INSIDE ended (what a trip!) I immediately hunted through Steam for something similar. There were some pale imitations, but nothing on the level of what 'Playdead' studio had done ... that is until LITTLE NIGHTMARES came out.
This is another stunning puzzle / platformer with top-notch production standards and an incredible atmosphere.
Set aside an evening. Put on some headphones. Turn out the lights. And let your own little nightmare begin...

I've been playing for a week and haven't even hit lvl 25 so obviously I have no clue what the end game is like. People told me you can get to lvl 50 in 3 days if you try though.
However what has made me not rush in this game is a multitude of things. The first is probably that I spent a while fishing but it wasn't that lucrative this early on and without it being profitable to run it over night yet and boring to run in the background during the day, I dropped it. What I have been doing is some quests here and there for the fun of it and with the rewards from these quests I invested in nodes. Nodes let you connect cities, towns, farms and more together. Think of it as a route/path between the different places that gives a bonus for every point along the route that you invested in. With this I've traded and made millions. It's been rather fun to watch my knowledge grow, trade routes get bigger and my wagon become more fancy than the day before.
I believe this is a game where you can be what you want and do what you want. I don't feel like I need to level up at all to enjoy the gameplay of BDO and that is fantastic. I'm having fun and making bank just as it is right now and that's what counts.
Onto the negative side of things:
The game crashes a few times a day.
There are some minor performance issues here and there, but it's random and not frequent.
The cash shop is expensive for some items, but luckily you don't need anything from it.
Onto the positive side of things:
You can own a donkey, horse, boat, home, wagon, camel, dog, cat, bird, hawk, desert rat and much more.
There are many professions.
Cash shop items can be bought with silver on the market place from other players.
It's fun.
You get to do what you want pretty much within 20 hours of playing.
You don't feel rushed to do quests.
You get starting funds that help set you up for the job you want.
The bittersweet:
The game is not p2w but pay to save time. In some games the time saving becomes such an advantage that it's essentially winning, but in this game it actually is not so bad that it becomes p2w. Other games just let you flash $$$ to win but not this game.

Yes I'm way more of a Diablo II guy versus a DIablo III guy. I suppose as such, this game was bound to appeal to me.
And appeal it has. What has been most appealing is that the more modern trending of "meta", or essentially being a single build you should play for each "class", is really only applicable to Hardcore, and maybe not even then. Your only limitation is the number of mastery points you have.
-Want to play the game as a true summoner character with a Storm Raven, Hell Hound, Briarthorn, and Primal Beast? Not a problem.
-Want to play a class that focuses nearly entirely on lighting? Go for it.
- Want to really only use a single class, and not mess with a dual class? it's doable.
The Character classs customization is just so awesome.
Othewr positives.
- A real nice spin on a crafting system, nearly the antithesis of D3. You have to actually find the recipes, then search for the right ingredients.
- The devotion system adds some real flavor to the game.
- The game feels much larger than just about any current ARPG, unless you count the MMOARPG's like Path of Exile.
- Varied vistas, and really great graphics considering the budget,
-Responsive Development team that seems to actual play the game they make.
- INnteresting skill tress, where very few if any skills are truly wasted.
-Reasonable frequent patches to address issues.
About the only Con(s) I can think of is that some of the animations are meh, and they resuse a lot of monster models, but that is nit picking when you consider the budget this game was made on.
If you like ARPG's you owe it to yourself to ge thtis game.
Oh and I will address the whole PoE vs Grim Dawn sillyness, if you are interested in an MMO, then get PoE. If ytou want a great single player experience that has old school Multiplayer, then get Grim Dawn.

As an avid fan of the ARPG genre, Grim Dawn gets a very glowing recommendation from me. What sets it apart from other games in the same genre is the amount of freedom and customization you have in regards to your character. The skill trees, like in Titan Quest, offer a lot of skills and ways to customize said skills. You put points into the tree and unlock different tiers of powers. Additionally, at level 10 you can pick a second skill tree which opens things up even more. If that wasn't enough, you find shrines throughout the game you can give offerings to in order to cleanse it. Once that's done, you can put a point into one of a TON of different constellations under what's called the "devotion" panel. They offer different bonuses to even further enhance your character. Other than that, it's an ARPG. There's not much more to be said. The thing is, Crate Entertainment got it absolutely right. It's a wonderfully fun, lengthy romp in a beautifully desecrated land. I love this game and hope others will feel the same way about it. An absolute blast!

Before you read this, remind yourself that this is
, it's my view and my perspective. It's not a definitive thing. It's not the Be All End All review of this game. We all like and prefer different things. Perhaps some of these cons appeal to you. Clearly it appeals to some. But not to me, and this is my review.
.
Pros:
-Visually very appealing.
-Great character creator, so great I might have a crush on my hot character now.
-Some good convenience things like auto-moving to locations or even auto-gathering.
Cons:
-That same convenience is because this game EMBRACES the grind. It's the epitome of Asian MMO's with tedious, overly complicated systems that stops feeling like a game and more like you're organizing a spreadsheet for your boss.
-The story is completely forgettable.
-The localization is at parts nonsensical and in parts plain incomprehensible. Lots of things have been lost in translation and the sentances often don't make any sense.
-Voice acting is equally terrible and the voice lines often don't correspond to the subtitle text. Such as the voice of an NPC saying "There's 3 goblin leaders" but the subtitle read "There's 3 goblin bosss". Yes, they added a third S.
-Gender-locked classes. Why Asia? WHY?
- No race selection
- Once more I will tell you, this game is designed around the grind and going AFK. For example, you can auto-fish and then just minimize the game. You can do this for other things too. Going AFK and just playing it like it's some X4 game is what you're gonna be doing. ANd that's boring, very boring.
-But probably most annoying of all:
- Relies heavily on the use of alts for the grind in lots of ways. To maximize your burdgeoning spreadsheet empire you will need alts that do different things. A single character will not be enough for you if you want to do well as you craft and trade.
This is EVE Online in a fantasy setting, without the fun player interactions, the gigantic battles worth hundreds of thousands of real money or the cool space ships.

For me, the best RPG since Knights of the Old Republic and Dragon Age: Origins.
I just finished it reaching about level 22.5 with my gang of Two-Handed-Warrior, Pyro/Geomancer with a bit witchcraft, rogue and Hydromancer/Aerotheurge. On second replay, I'd take a party consisting of one Two-Handed-Warrior, one rogue, one ranger and one witchy/hydromancing mage, that should work like a breeze.
There is lots and lots of good to tell about this (for example the turn-based combat works perfectly and is very funny without being frustrating... the character development might not be the most complex of all RPGs but is very much enough for me), but there are also some minor things that should be tweaked via patch, for example that most of the items you find are strength-based and as such only usable on warriors... that magic starts strong but get outclassed by bow and melee damage after about character level 10... that the first 7 or so levels are slow because you just don't get enough skill points per level for my taste (you begin with one per level, later two, later three. You should start at two imo).
To sum it all up: nearly a must-have for every RPG fan.

Remember when RPGs were about carefully lain plans and their epic executions? Neither do I. Seems to me it was always grind for XP and snag the biggest loots. All of the important bits in RPG tactical gameplay, D:OS gets right. Magic is a touch overpowering, but other builds work well enough; there is a whole world of skills that can be explored at your leisure. Favorite bit? Surfaces and clouds. These make control zones that can completely decimate enemies by the handfuls. Loads of poison in the air? Light it up and watch them dance.
On the downside, the quest system feels clunky and almost broken. It's super easy to get lost trying to do something, without any idea as to what the next step is or where you should be looking. While the actual character writing is, for the most part, a mostly comical and very spot-on style, the story feels like some perfect linearity shoe-horned into a free-roaming world.
Moreover, and my favorite pet peeve, the monsters don't respawn. You're the greatest adventurers alive. So powerful, that even after a week of napping, not a single bandit, pirate, orc or vengeful dead is going to try again on the roads you've walked. While not entirely unacceptable, thanks to a passable fast-travel system, it makes the world quickly start to feel empty. I don't think even the reagents and crafting materials respawn, making them highly limited.
The final word is, this is a great game, with a very good atmosphere, that manages to display the power of retro styles without trying to actually be a retro game. While it leaves some few things to be desired, it can quickly draw you in and having you hankering for that next fight, or looking for ways to solve the next puzzle.

I paid about 5 dollars for both Xcom and the expansion (Steam sales and a GMG coupon) but honestly I would have gladly done full price.
It's fun, I haven't really had a chance to play a solid tactical game in a while that didn't take me 2-3 hours just to get through the tutorial. That was my favorite part about this game. It really has a good amount of depth between research and foundry upgrades, how you manage your economy and barracks, and even just the general combat of it. Still, with all that in there it does it really good job of slowly introducing you into it. Once you begin to understand how to manage keep countries funding you and the best upgrade routes to take the game really starts to take off (Even moreso if you play it a second time).
The other end of that stick is that about half way through the game you start to trivialize a lot of the mechanics because of upgrades. Granted, this is the pit that most tactical RPG type games fall into. The soldiers you manage to keep with you long enough eventually just have such substantial abilities and equipment that a lot of missions in the end I could have done with only 2-3 of my 6 man party. On top of that it leads to a bit of imbalance, I couldn't really find a time I wanted to use a Heavy over an assault. My end party was three snipers, a mech-soldier, an assault and a support. Even then, the support and the assault I could have easily replaced with more snipers.
Still between the storyline and the overall amount of time I got to sink into it (With other bonuses like great controller support etc) I was really happy with this game. It's especially rare to find a good tactical game, one that is a triple A title none the less.

for those of you who haven't played this game (and you know who you are), Battlefront 2 is one of the greatest Star Wars games ever made. its ridiculous how many hours i have pumped into this game on my Playstation2, my original Xbox and now on PC as well. aside from being from what is most likely the most successful franchise to date when you strip this game down to its bare bones, core mechanics, gameplay, design and the entertainment value are astonishing ... now this game is not without its flaws im not saying that ... it is just that there are not that many flaws in the game which is astonishing.
getting down to business though the game is played through the eyes of a clone trooper serving in the various conflicts of the star wars universe and across both the original and new trilogy stories, in the campaign you play as a clone trooper/ storm trooper from the infamous 501st legion of the clone/imperial army under the command of Anakin Skywalker (clone wars) and then the mighty sith lord Darth Vader (rebellion against the empire) that is more affectionately known as Vaders fist fighting in various battles from the star wars timeline.the game itself can be played either as 3rd person shooter or an FPS either way still works just as well as the other. the core mechanics are the standard for a game like this. you run, jump, roll and shoot anything that moves that is not on your side. you start the game at the outbreak of the clone wars at the battle for Geonosis .. where the game soon gives you what its predecessor was lacking .. A STORY! (and in my opinion a damn good one).. this adds to the game greatly giving you a sense of progression in more than just advancing to the next battle and the abillity to hear the opinions of the soldiers on the war). the story allows the player to see the insight of the clones as they progress through the timeline of the star wars universe but also giving some back story to aspects of the films that the player previously did not get. but back to the campaign, the game plays very well with easy to understand controls and simple but very addictive gameplay, the Geonosis mission is your basic training mission allowing the player to grasp the core concepts of the game but after that the player is pretty much given free reign of the battlefield in future missions. the player must still complete objectives assigned in the missions but they have free reign to do so as they wish. for example during a mission you are ordered to assault and defend a downed tank. now there are several ways this can be done, you can use a standard trooper and just shoot it out, you could use a jet trooper and defend from atop the tank, each different trooper allows for a different approach and with the ability to swap to a different trooper at your command points it makes it so easy to meet any threat you might face upon the battlefield. the command interface for getting your AI troops to follow your orders is also much improved with the ability to command more troopers and with the new AI intelligence they are smarter too, no more of the original games AI antics of trying to stare down a tank with a rifle. your allies will now more effectively make use of grenades, rockets and turrets to combat threats on the field of battle. the campaign in its entirety is solid with superb gameplay and mechanics, a strong story and a very good sense of progression (something i feel is lacking from the modern game)
but on to the biggest part, the multiplayer experience ... you haven't played this game until you are knee deep in a battle against an army of human players. the campaign AI is amazing don't get me wrong but online is a completely different experience.. a small band of human players can be as deadly as an army of AI with the ability to sway the tide of a battle with a single manouver. i was once ina match where my side was dominating the enemy to the point where we were on the verge of victory and then i dont know what happened im guessing the stopped playing with their feet and suddenly i was in a world of hurt getting harrased by snipers and rockets with infantry that played like commandos. the experience is so competitive and immersing its ridiculous. you get a blood lust almost to turn clone troopers and droids into tiny little pieces. the maps are very well designed with varying terrains that can hinder and help the varying styles of play the game allows for but nothing prepares you for the addition of BATTLES IN SPACE!! this was so badly missed from the original game even though fighters were available during ground missions its just not the same xD , the space battles following in suit of the core multiplayer can play out in various ways. you have your standard attrition of just trying to kill all the enemies troops, or you can destroy the key functions of the enemy cruiser both from the outside and from within .. yes .. you can fly into the enemy cruisers hangar and mess up their day with a rocket or two. galactic conquest mode is greatly improved with the space battles extending a game for hours longer. now as i have stated the game is not without its flaws .. for me this comes in the form of the jedi/sith/heroes ... now a lot of people will dislike the point in about to make but it just bugs me a little .. now we had jedi in the first game in galactic conquest mode as a playable bonus in which an INVINCIBLE hero from the star wars universe would take to the battlefield for your faction and annihalate your enemies ( an issue i voiced openly playing the first game). in this game however they have fixed this issue and the heroes are finally able to be slayed upon the field of battle .. but for me the ability to play as the jedi always seemed kind of pointless in a game that was entirely about seeing the conflicts of the star wars universe through the eyes of the soldiers who fought them. don't get me wrong the heroes are a great laugh to play as with very stylish move sets and abilities and even getting their own multiplayer map for playing matches as only the heroes but in the core game i just don't see the point, the jedi in the multiplayer at least make some kind of sense allowing a side that is losing to change the tide of the battle but in the campaign i just feel it takes away from the game. as i said this point is not shared by everybody and i have had many a debate on the matter so i guess its a matter of preference for the player
in conclusion this game is a MUST play for any star wars fan and i guarantee long hours of enjoyment from it. not much else i can really say except BUY THIS GAME :D

Killing Floor 2 (KF2) is a co-op wave-based game where players kill the infected (Referred to as "zed's ingame) to get money to buy at the trader, there are multiple difficultys, classes, and maps to choose from, along with the modding community. The game has multiple boss fights for single-player and multiplayer, and there are a wide variety of enemys and ways they will fight you. It is developed by Tripwire Interactive and published by Deep Silver, and is the successor to 2009's Killing Floor, made by the same company.
The gameplay is very fun, fluid and feels alive compared to the first game. The graphics are greatly improved and so are the animations. The sound effects, gore and graphics defenitly will keep you hooked for hours. The main objective is the game is to stay alive as long as possible until the 4th, 7th, or 10th wave depending on what length you play on. When you reach the 4th, 7th, or 10th wave you will encounter a boss fight, and the whole team will have to stick together to take it down.
There are waaaay more classes to pick from compared to the first game, from a gunslinger to a SWAT officer. There are returning classes like the Beserker, Commando, Field Medic, etc. Each class is unique in it's own way, the Berserker skill tree /class giving you more health and making you do more damage with melee weapons, while the firebug focuses on burning weapons, and the field medic is all about keeping your team alive. There's defenitly a class for everyone.
You can spend hours killing time on the game due to the amount of difficulty levels, servers, and classes. There's tons of mods for the game, too. The playerbase is very active and multiple servers are still being played today.
The game looks and runs great, even on the lowest settings. It's not hard to stay at 30 FPS on this game, and the levels awalys look amazing and bright (or dark.), even on low.
The animations are great as well, when aiming your arms move like you would real life, not just infinte spinning like in Left 4 Dead or the first game. Your arms swing if you spin too fast, and pressing R makes you inspect your weapon if it isn't loaded, and the detail is great as well. If you press R while your melee is bloody you'll throw the blood off of it onto the ground. When being grabbed by a clot the screen shakes violenty and you can hear your character screaming until you bash the clot off.
The detail like I said is amazing. If you bash a clot they can do a full 180 and smash onto the ground, then get up and get angry. If you swing your melee upwards in the air with a katana and cut a crawler in-half you can see the bones, and you can cut them up on the ground.
There's a wide variety of characters to choose from, and unlike the first installment in the series, each character has their own unqiue voice. This actually adds a personaillity to each character, and each character has their own attitude and story. Mr. Foster will cuss out the zeds while others will be more calm. There's also a large amount of customazion you can do with your character, adding different masks, SWAT outfits, Horizon Secuirty outfits, other cosmetics. All of the characters are great and you will defenitly find your favorite.
My least favorite part about the characters is the fact they only have one returning character from the first installment in the KF series, which would be Mr. Foster. Where's DJ Skully, Mrs. Foster, Ash Harding?
This is simillar to the gameplay section, but a bit different. There are multiple difficulty levels, and each one is made for a different perk rank.
Normal is basically "easy" labled as "normal" so you don't feel like a weak noob for playing it. It's hiliariously easy and nearly impossible to lose on, even as a level 0.
Hard is basically normal. Although what's interesting is the higher the difficulty goes, the smarter the zeds become. They'll circle you or block off entrances, forcing you to be cornered and fight them off or run up a set of stairs where you can't escape. On difficultys like Suicidal they will purposely push you into a fleshpound or scrake and then beat on you as you try to fight them. The AI is defenitly very smart and unique, and something that other developers should follow on in their games.
The interesting part about this game is unlike the first installment, there's zero DLC needed to play the game. You can experience the full game without spending a dime. All characters, weapons, classes. However Tripwire still needs to make money, therefore they bassicaly implented a CS:GO skin system, which is something I frown upon personally. There's crates, keys, weapon skins, armor skins, bassicaly what you'd expect from a skin system, but it's defenitly better then having to pay for DLC. I would say it's defenitly a change for the better from KF1.

This game doesn't actually give any choices which make a significant difference.  They just seem to alter the dialogue immediately following what you say.  The game intimidates you into thinking that the choices you make are siginificant with a "They willll remember that" text appearing in the corner.  But this was soon proved to be a fallacy when after a choice you made you were informed the man 'Will remmeber that'.  Indeed they did.  For the next 2 minutes of the game, till they were stabbed in the face.  These choices, which don't really seem to affect anything except dialogue is, in the words of fanboys on the Telltale forum, an 'illusion of choice' (their words, not mine).  Apparently 'everyone knows this'.
I did not know this.  I bought into the marketing hype, where you are told that 'choices matter'.  I regret buying this game.  Recently I've been playing Ys Memories of Celceta.  In that game you can choose what to say.  Then the person you're talking to reacts based upon that, but then after the first couple of dialgoue pieces, carry on in their programmed way with the story.  This game is no different.  It's just like any other rpg which gives choices but those choices don't make any significant difference, which is a little disapointing from a fan of KotOR, or somone brought up on games like Baldur's Gate or Torment.
What makes this game worse is that it is not an rpg.  You don't develop your character.  You don't really get equipment.  Nothing really happens in this game except dialogue.  Dialogue which doesn't actually change anything.
If you are a fan of Telltale then you will obviously know what to expect, as I was repeatedly told on their and other forums.  All Telltale games are like this, something which 'everyone' knows apparently.  This short review is therefore for the people who aren't fans of Telltale: Don't buy into the hype. Your choices don't make any significant difference.  You can play through silently and it doesn't change anything, accept create funny dialogues as you see how the writers try and deal with a mute protagonist.  Spoiler alert: They fail.
Added to this are bad graphics and sound.  Huge clipping issues and sound which jumps in volume as you move between scenes.
This game is just a story book.  If you're a fan of GoT you may like it.  If you're a fan of Telltale you'll probably love it.  If you're just curious, I really wouldn't bother.  Wait till it's much cheaper.  It's a waste of money right now imo.

Yes I'm way more of a Diablo II guy versus a DIablo III guy. I suppose as such, this game was bound to appeal to me.
And appeal it has. What has been most appealing is that the more modern trending of "meta", or essentially being a single build you should play for each "class", is really only applicable to Hardcore, and maybe not even then. Your only limitation is the number of mastery points you have.
-Want to play the game as a true summoner character with a Storm Raven, Hell Hound, Briarthorn, and Primal Beast? Not a problem.
-Want to play a class that focuses nearly entirely on lighting? Go for it.
- Want to really only use a single class, and not mess with a dual class? it's doable.
The Character classs customization is just so awesome.
Othewr positives.
- A real nice spin on a crafting system, nearly the antithesis of D3. You have to actually find the recipes, then search for the right ingredients.
- The devotion system adds some real flavor to the game.
- The game feels much larger than just about any current ARPG, unless you count the MMOARPG's like Path of Exile.
- Varied vistas, and really great graphics considering the budget,
-Responsive Development team that seems to actual play the game they make.
- INnteresting skill tress, where very few if any skills are truly wasted.
-Reasonable frequent patches to address issues.
About the only Con(s) I can think of is that some of the animations are meh, and they resuse a lot of monster models, but that is nit picking when you consider the budget this game was made on.
If you like ARPG's you owe it to yourself to ge thtis game.
Oh and I will address the whole PoE vs Grim Dawn sillyness, if you are interested in an MMO, then get PoE. If ytou want a great single player experience that has old school Multiplayer, then get Grim Dawn.

I've been looking forward to playing an oldschool strategy game, but sadly The Banner Saga turned out to be an utter disappointment. I truly wanted to like the game, with its lovable art design and its interesting setting.
Unfortunately, the game clearly shows that it was designed not for PC but as an app for mobile devices: the controls are cumbersome, and many features are overly simplistic. It also must be mentioned that the game is rather short, in particular when factoring in that about 50% of your gaming experience consist of reading conversations between characters with the occasional making of choices, and watching your clan of tiny pixels wander through pretty landscapes without any real means of interaction.
The other 50% is combat, and this is where The Banner Saga fails rather hard.
For starters, the enemies you encounter throughout the game are incredibly repetitive. Most of the time, you will be fighting "dredge", dark-armored giants which lay waste to the lands. Sadly, most of them look identical to a point that fighting them gets boring very quickly - even the final boss is just a recolored version of common enemies (!).
Another thing that utterly annoyed me are the basic combat dynamics. In The Banner Saga, your characters' HP is also their Strength, which equals how much damage they deal in combat; an injured character is therefore of little use, as he loses his ability to inflict damage.
What looks like a fresh and interesting idea at first turns out to be complete ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ in the context of the fact that in The Banner Saga your characters and enemies will always move in turns - meaning that if you kill an enemy, its turn will not be "lost", but instead the next foe will just take its place. This is beyond stupid for a number of reasons - for starters, it means that killing enemies actually makes a battle harder. An enemy force of two combatants in good condition may easily wreck your six injured warriors, as they are no longer able to inflict significant damage - and each enemy will gain three turns for one of your allies' turns. This means that you have to try and NOT kill enemies in order to win, but instead leave them on the battlefield as weak as possible. In addition, you are basically punished for saving your own characters - if you pull back an injured ally, it means that you will waste turns on a useless character, as Strength cannot be regenerated.
All in all, Stoic has created a combat system that is very counter-intuitive, and quite frankly, stupid.
Another issue I have is that the battles are not only repetitive because of the enemies, but also because of the battlefield itself. The game will exchange the backgrounds, but for the most part, you will be fighting in a square of some sort; I can remember only one map which had some kind of natural obstacles. The only variety the game offers is the positions of your enemies and allies, and as a result, battles become boring very fast.
Perhaps the most ridiculous missing feature of The Banner Saga is the lack of a saving function (!)  - the game only creates automatic savestates, manual saving simply doesn't exist. As a result, you will often have to rewatch tedious cutscenes/dialogues in order to redo a battle, and even then you will sometimes not be able to go back to its beginning (and will instead have to redo the one before it, as no savestate was created in between). What the developers had in mind here was clearly to prevent players from changing the outcome of the decisions you make throughout the journey (which is often harsh - characters dying, for example), as the game *always* saves after having made such a decision. However, why the game does not just simply saves before battles as well is beyond me, as the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ battle system will definitely have you playing some battles more than once. In particular "second battles" - oftentimes the game will allow you to take an additional battle after you have won one. Problem: your characters' strength will not be replenished, making the second one usually much more difficult, and making it much more likely that you will want to try again - have fun doing the first battle again, as of course the game last saved half an hour ago.
The Banner Saga has a ton of other flaws, such as being unable to correct a false command in battle (accidentally moving one tile short of being able to attack your enemy - too bad, you can't go back to the "move"-command, even though the tile easily is within your character's movement radius), a lack of information (the game allows you to chose the position of your characters on the battlefield - however, it neither tells you which foe will move first, nor can you assess your enemies' movement radius) or that the music is sometimes outright annoying (in particular during battles).
On the plus side, the animations and the general art design are really nice, and the story is interesting enough to keep you playing (although in the end there are many loose strings, and The Banner Saga feels like but a setup for its successor).
In conclusion, I would still not recommend buying the game unless you are really, really craving a turn-based fantasy adventure. If you do, The Banner Saga might be worth buying at the current price of 75% off - but you better be prepared to be disappointed.

I highly recommend trying the demo. I thoroughly enjoyed the demo and have not regretted the purchase (though the physics in the demo are slightly different than the full game, and the maps from the demo have been enlarged). Compared to the demo, the full game has more AI difficulties (though 'Easy' is plenty hard for many people), more maps, and a bunch more neat modes. Further, you can even make your own modes (by adjusting preprogrammed variables, such as the number of balls that spawn at the beginning of the game. I highly recommend adjusting this number to the maximum, 24, use the "Fast Respawn" modifier, and play on a medium or small map - this way you spend much less time looking for a ball and much more time aiming/throwing it.)
There is a great variety of modes - from doing trick shots, racing around the map, elimination modes, shooting the "super ball" through one or more hoops (kind of like basketball), and a variety of combinations of these.
Though I have encountered several minor bugs since I purchased the game, the developer has consistently responded to my reports and fixed the bugs.
The multiplayer isn't massively popular, but along with the AIs, it can be fun even when there's no one else on (and depending on when you go online, there may be 10s of people on). It's a drop in/out style; you needn't stay for a whole game or anything. You can even use custom game modes that you've designed if you "host"/create the game, or else become the host (because the previous host left). The multiplayer is generally smooth (though those with higher pings might jump around a bit, which can make aiming at them harder). If you can forgive it a bit of temporary inconsistency, it can be pretty fun. (ex if two people move close to a ball, they both might see themselves picking it up. The server will then have to decide who picked it up first, and the other guy will see his ball disappear. On the plus side, this doesn't happen often, and I am sure that this implementation is why the multiplayer is as smooth as it is.)
Overall, the game does have room for improvement, but it's still great fun and I highly recommend trying it out.

I'm a huge fan of indie games and when I found out that Banner Saga was on sale I had to buy it and finally try it out.  After finishing the game, I'm not really sure how to feel about it.  I guess I had fun?
This game is EXTREMELY story driven.  Which is great!  I love a good story.  However, there was one component missing: ME, the player, actually caring.  I had a really hard time caring for the world, the backstory itself seems like it could be its own game. In fact, I found the backstory far more intriguing and I would've love to play that game instead of what I was currently playing (god war, constant sun, ect). Irritatingly, the game falsely gives you an impression that you'll be exploring the world with limited supplies. Instead you'll be exploring the world on a set path with limited supplies.  The game assigns a main character instead of switching off parties like it seems to do at the beginning of the story.
Speaking of characters, I really had a hard time caring for the characters themselves. Most of the game choices made seem to revolve around "do this so X doesn't die" or “do X and fight more monsters or do X, make someone mad and don’t fight monsters”.  Which would be heart wrenching and hard, if, again, I actually cared about the characters. At the end of the game, you're given a 'major decision' and instead I had to ask myself “who do I care less about in my party?”  I ended up saving all my characters out of more political/gameplay reasons (ie spending a lot of renown leveling up that character that WOULD'VE died). Side note, the developers really hate Egil.
On the topic of renown, I thought it was silly having it do two things: leveling up your characters and buying supplies.  Maybe a gold/EXP system would make more sense, but I suppose it adds a layer of unnecessary difficulty (not letting people in your caravan starve or leveling up your characters to make fights easier and make renown easier to earn)
The combat system is fun I guess.  Frustrating though, having your characters rely on their HP to do damage is infuriating when the opposing mooks decided to gang up on your hard hitter tank, and then suddenly when it’s his next turn (men are apparently only allowed to hold melee weapons) hits like paper.
The graphics are cute, very cartoony. I really appreciated that.  However, the intro teased me by having a fully animated scene, which I expected more of.  Nope, that’s the only animated scene in the whole game is at the beginning.
I think this game suffered from some deadline issues, I feel great chunk of the story gameplay has been removed or modified just to make Kickstarter backers happy.
Overall, this game is alright.  I recommend buying it on sale because it does have some rather interesting gaming elements and a mildly interesting story, however don’t expect it to blow you away.

As an avid fan of the ARPG genre, Grim Dawn gets a very glowing recommendation from me. What sets it apart from other games in the same genre is the amount of freedom and customization you have in regards to your character. The skill trees, like in Titan Quest, offer a lot of skills and ways to customize said skills. You put points into the tree and unlock different tiers of powers. Additionally, at level 10 you can pick a second skill tree which opens things up even more. If that wasn't enough, you find shrines throughout the game you can give offerings to in order to cleanse it. Once that's done, you can put a point into one of a TON of different constellations under what's called the "devotion" panel. They offer different bonuses to even further enhance your character. Other than that, it's an ARPG. There's not much more to be said. The thing is, Crate Entertainment got it absolutely right. It's a wonderfully fun, lengthy romp in a beautifully desecrated land. I love this game and hope others will feel the same way about it. An absolute blast!

Before you read this, remind yourself that this is
, it's my view and my perspective. It's not a definitive thing. It's not the Be All End All review of this game. We all like and prefer different things. Perhaps some of these cons appeal to you. Clearly it appeals to some. But not to me, and this is my review.
.
Pros:
-Visually very appealing.
-Great character creator, so great I might have a crush on my hot character now.
-Some good convenience things like auto-moving to locations or even auto-gathering.
Cons:
-That same convenience is because this game EMBRACES the grind. It's the epitome of Asian MMO's with tedious, overly complicated systems that stops feeling like a game and more like you're organizing a spreadsheet for your boss.
-The story is completely forgettable.
-The localization is at parts nonsensical and in parts plain incomprehensible. Lots of things have been lost in translation and the sentances often don't make any sense.
-Voice acting is equally terrible and the voice lines often don't correspond to the subtitle text. Such as the voice of an NPC saying "There's 3 goblin leaders" but the subtitle read "There's 3 goblin bosss". Yes, they added a third S.
-Gender-locked classes. Why Asia? WHY?
- No race selection
- Once more I will tell you, this game is designed around the grind and going AFK. For example, you can auto-fish and then just minimize the game. You can do this for other things too. Going AFK and just playing it like it's some X4 game is what you're gonna be doing. ANd that's boring, very boring.
-But probably most annoying of all:
- Relies heavily on the use of alts for the grind in lots of ways. To maximize your burdgeoning spreadsheet empire you will need alts that do different things. A single character will not be enough for you if you want to do well as you craft and trade.

Every single game mechanic is designed around wasting your time and trying to force you to spend money to fix the game. For example, this game uses a inventory slot system AND a weight limit system. Items (and even money) will often max out your weight before you even come close to filling slots. Money is also designed so millions of silver is literally nothing so if you wish to carry around enough to even buy a single item, you will fill your weight limit with silver alone. They allow you to put the money in storage banks, but these banks only apply to the town you are in. This forces you to travel to your home town to deposit money (lest you forget which town it was put into and lose it all) and to focus on only storing items in a single town. There is no fast travel so you are forced to run every single time you reach your inventory weight limit. Of course they sell weight increases to fix this problem, but if you refuse to spend money you will literally spend around a quarter of your time in game simply running back and forth to your hometown so you can continue grinding.
Progression is really only achieved by grinding enemies. Up to level 50 this is not much of a problem, you can find a big group of enemies and level from 35 to 36 in a matter of minutes with some fun combat. The real issue pops up once you hit lv 50 and the progression grinds to a halt. You go from getting around .5-1% of a level per kill to around .0012% per kill. It takes literal hours of doing nothing but grinding. This becomes even more of an issue if you refuse to pay for pets which auto loot for you, otherwise you will spend a minute or two looting each and every individual body after every single pull, futher slowing down your progression. I cant think of a single mechanic in this game that is not designed specifically to impede progress and make a microtransaction item more appealing. They are in such high demand because they all comes with stat bonus and buffs they instantly sell, so unless you are sitting at the AH spamming the refresh key and happen to be quick enough to buy the items you will NEVER get a single one of them without spending real cash, so do not listen to fanboys who say you can buy all the items in the auction house. Sure you CAN, just like I can do alot of things, doesnt mean they are even remotly feasible options.
Overall this game is one of the weirdest MMOs I have ever seen in my life. Its designed from the ground up to force you into the microtransaction store, but you also need to buy the game upfront. Generally these sorts of tactics are reserved for F2P games, but with BDO you need to buy the game then continue to spend money to get an even remotly enjoyable experience unless you find spending most of your time in game autorunning between banks and leveling zones, looting dozens of corpses one by one after each pull, or quite literally never being able to compete with players at the highest level.

Absolutely, without a doubt, one of the best couch multiplayer games I have ever played. In fact, just plain one of the best games I have ever played!
The gameplay is fantastic, tight and thrilling. You are one of four adventurers before you turn on one another in a quick and visceral opening scene. Once only one of you is left alive the rest of you take control of your spirits with the options to control monsters, traps and debris in each room as the remaining human player tries to progress. This creates a tense experience as you are always either fighting for your life, just trying to scrape through, or fighting for the chance to regain your humanity - if you kill the human you can restore your humanity and take control of your human body again.
As excellent as the core gameplay is, it is the underlying systems that raise the standard to magnificent. The human needs to reach level 10, gaining levels by defeating monsters, then enter the boss room and defeat the boss to win the game. However, every time the player gains a level, making them stronger, the other players gain "wrath", a currency they can use to upgrade one of their three possible monsters. Each upgrade tier has two choices, offering a wealth of diversity, and indeed mayhem when all of the effects start flying. With the wrath mechanic those who are not playing as the human get progressively more powerful until they have a good chance of getting the kill and reclaiming their humanity once more.
The mechanics of play are simple to understand; one button attacks and another uses your "special", a choice of whatever spell that you choose to buy from the blacksmith, gold permitting.  We had two regular gamers and two non regular gamers and everyone was able to compete out fo the gate. Tutorialising is extremely clever in Crawl, other than the buttons you are introduced to each of the ideas of the game through play; for example one of the bosses offers the chance to utilise a healer mid battle so before you enter the boss room he appears and gives you a glimpse of how it works. It is an extremely clever and intuitive process. Similarly, when you enter a new room items that you can interact with flash.
The meta game is really quite engaging, too. At the start of each run you choose a deity to worship; this determines the three monsters you are able to use during the run and also a passive bonus. After each run you unlock new deities to worship, new weapons and spells to buy from the blacksmith, new monsters to play as and even new traps to utilise in the dungeons. All of this is to say that as you play more, the options increase and the game becomes even more varied on each play through.
In summary, I can't praise Crawl enough. I thoroughly enjoyed every tantalising moment of play, every death throe and every victory. For anyone that enjoys gathering some friends and playing together, both in competition and in co-operation, you can't do any better than Crawl.

Lastly, a few ideas we had...

Thank you again, for the wonderful Crawl.

Mirror's Edge has a small collection of quality of life issues, but overall the game is spectacular.  While I'd hesitate to call the cutscenes themselves "pretty," the use of color in the game itself adds and incredible vibrancy and visibility to the environments that really make the levels pop in a good way.   The combat is challenging, which gave me some "Beyond Good and Evil" vibes in more ways than one.  And the gameplay itself is fun, which is always a bonus.
I only really have a few complaints to make, and these are fairly minor issues in the grand scheme of things.  First, I think the ability to restart from a checkpoint from the pause menu (or any menu) would help expediate parts of the game, especially in areas where you can manage to fall down the level and undo some of your progress.  Not a significant problem, but one that I noticed while playing.
Likewise, I almost feel like too much of the game is spent inside of buildings and warehouses instead of running across rooftops, which is where I had the most fun.  Fairly often (don't quote me on statistics) the game becomes more of a "Prince of Persia" esque platformer, rather than a racing sort of speedrunning simulator.  Not a bad thing necessarily, but not exactly what I expected.
Other than that, nothing really to say.  I do feel like, going back to the "Beyond Good and Evil" analogy, the combat is almost too easy in certain aspects.  Discovering that I could pick guns up off the ground using RMB was a significant game changer for a lot of the dramatically more challening enemy encounters in the last few levels of the game.  The game teases a sort of stealth mechanic, with the ability to disarm enemies immediately from behind, but I never really found any use for this beyond one psuedo boss fight, and I can't help but wonder if maybe the development team intended for that to be a bigger part of gameplay.
I can't really say one way or the other whether it would make the game better or not, but it's easy to imagine a Mirror's Edge where the game is mostly about staying as a far away from enemies and trying to navigate the environment around them, rather than just running straight through them and/or killing them outright, like it is now.
Dunno.  Like I said, small problems.  I really enjoyed playing Mirror's Edge.  I think, if you buy it, you won't be dissappointed.  It can be appropriately challenging in some parts, but never enough to be truly frustrating, in my opinion.  And when it really does get going fast, it's a lot of fun to fly over rooftops, even if it is a bit rare.
Also, some of the collectibles are surprisingly sneaky.

Child of Light follows a young girl named Aurora as she travels in the fantasy world of Lemuria. It's a 2D rpg/puzzle game and if only described with one word, BEAUTIFUL! Beautiful writing, visuals and music.
Child of Light has paintbrushed look and that fits really well with the story and especially the dialogue which is almost all done with rhyming. So as already stated the art in this game is wonderful on so many levels. For the most part there isn't any voice acting, only in few small narration parts.
You start the game alone, but some companions will pop up to join your journey. All of these followers have their own talent trees you can customize. Though these trees are quite restricted and you have to follow just a few branches. You can only have 2 characters active during battle, but you can swap them around freely.
Combat is done with Active Time Battle system, familiar from some of Final Fantasy games. You can buff your team to perform faster or debuff your enemies to be slower on the timeline which determines the turns of characters.
It's not very complex or deep RPG, but well worth the low price!

Completely surprised by how incredibly fun this is! If you like local multiplayer games, this is pretty much a must!
At first glance, this looked like a funny concept that would be amusing for a game or two. Little did I realize how addicting this game can be!
Pros:
+Very simple controls (only two buttons)
+Tons of unlocks and reasons to grind. There's a very large amount of content to unlock through continued gameplay, and what feels like virtually unlimited, Mugen-esque mod potential.
+ AI bots - you can play this alone with AI bots tagging in for other players. No need for friends to enjoy it!
+ Excellent balance system - Your hero levels up by killing monsters, and your monsters level up by other players' heroes leveling up... meaning in one player is dominating, everyone else gets stronger monsters to try and beat them back down
+ Out-of-game challenges - Practice with monsters between games and see what you've unlocked
+ Large variety of spells and equipment - Get awesome powers and cool weapons with both magic abilities and even cursed gear
+ Cool boss battle concept - Try to win the game with 1vAll boss fights
Cons (with suggestions):
- The game has the potential to drag - With random gear in the shop, a hero can get powerful quickly or struggle to survive a few rooms in a row. Bosses can be rough without good gear, so there's no easy way to predict if a single playthrough will last 30 minutes or 90. There could probably be some sort of adjustable gold/XP/item-power/wrath settings that would allow players to customize for faster or slower playthroughs.
- Only two buttons - Your ghosts have an Inhabit/Attack button, and a Special Attack/Exit button. Many a fight has been thrown at a critical moment by checking for a special attack only to basically forfeit the fight by leaving a monster/object. Just adding a third button for Inhabit/Exit would solve this
- No online play - I really, really hope this is something they look into. I would buy a half dozen copies of this in a heartbeat if they added this feature.
- Endgame item shopping is often a buyout - As you get to deeper levels, gold accumulates quickly and being the character alive when you enter the item shop usually turns into a shopping spree as you buyout most of the floor. It can be rough to keep your hero alive in endgame without proper gear. The game has a great mechanic of letting a new player teleport to the item shop after reviving his hero AND clearing the room, but that often doesn't help much if you're the second or third person to get to the shop that floor. And if you're undergeared, you probably won't live to the next floor/shop. I should stress, though... while this is an annoyance, it IS NOT game-breakingly bad by any means. This could be fixed with some sort of minimum item system per-player per-floor.
Neutral notes:
o The game is 1-4 players, and the mood of it changes a lot based on how many there are. 1v1 is a game of slow whittling and constant annoyance. Monster fights are sniping and kiting and trying to break them down over the course of rooms. 4-player games are basically royal rumbles every-other room, and the hero is swarmed with monsters, dies, is replaced by another player's hero who now still has to deal with the leftovers. Control often changes hands twice in a single room. 3-players is my favorite balance so far. Some sort of optional monster handicap setting could add more variety (option to boost in 1v1 for easier turnover, option to weaken in 4-player to make surviving longer easier)

XCOM—Enemy Unknown is the best turn-based game about immigration. How should we treat the immigrants? Should we kill them?
Your immediate response may be: “We should not kill all the immigrants.” Understandable pity. But what if the immigrants are destroying our cities via their plasma weapons?

This game, XCOM: Enemy Unknown, answers that question; in such a case, we must create a multi-national, multi-gender special forces group with which to kill the disgusting invaders.
You see, in the game the aliens enter our atmosphere--UNINVITED--and start stealing our women and shooting our men. And for this reason, the commando organization is made--XCOM. XCOM’s elite soldiers fly to the gas stations and grocery stores and office buildings of our pure Earth, in their jet-version of the V-22 osprey, and shoot the aliens. It is..beautiful. Like Mozart.
I love how the game slows down whilst you see an alien take its final bullet, no longer able to withstand human fire. Do you know the film The Matrix? Of course you do. Imagine, though, that instead of Neo dodging bullets, it is outer space foreigners slowly getting torn to pieces by our Made on Earth bullets; the yellow, green blood spewing from the bodies.

Cross over the ozone layer without a valid passport now, alien! Oh! You can't? Why? Is it because you are dead?
But it doesn’t stop with bullets. XCOM eventually gives your troops laser and plasma weaponry, which replace your metal rounds. And they are worth it, so worth it. The laser and plasma are red, green, and bright. They make the killings like Christmas Eve at night. I actually get the shivers thinking about it. Mmmm, yes. I have..so many memories of the glow, bursting through immigrant bodies. I love to just...close my eyes, and conjure up memories from this game. They are so beautiful.
I almost forgot the explosives. Grenades and rockets fling the xenos’ bodies like rag dolls. Unfortunately, though, the game doesn’t slow down and focus the camera on their flying corpses.
You can also capture the aliens alive. Three times you HAVE to do this. I didn't like those parts.
If you decide to get this game, you should do so right before a vacation begins. I couldn’t stop..hunting after it began. ALSO, you should get the Enemy Within DLC with the base game. Doing so will let you turn your troops into large, mutilated, killer robots. They lose their humanity, yes, but that’s okay; it helps you kill aliens at a faster rate, and with greater force.
If XCOM’s aliens came in peace, then I guess it would be okay not to kill them all. But as the game shows, the aliens do not come in peace.
When the real aliens land on our planet and start taking away our jobs, we should follow XCOM's example.

***SPOILERS REVIEW**
1st off I was a beta tester to this game and I did not see a few of the key parts that I enjoyed so much in the beta in this final version. The 2 things I enjoyed most during beta was the ability to create your own team in the barracks and the ability to pvp with other players. Perhaps these functions were only created to aid in class balancing but when I started playing this game and seen those 2 functions gone I was severely disappointed.
Next, Great story! Every choice you make has ramifications that domino deeper into the rest of the gameplay outcome.
Be VERY careful who you let into your caravans because they may very well backstab you and cause great damage for your story outcome. Also when a dispute happens and someone leaves or dies ytou also loose any equipment that person had currently equiped on them. This is a very costly outcome when reknown is what is used to upgrade your team, buy equipment for your team and buy food for your caravan.
I got through the first playthrough in about 18 hrs. I took my time, read everything and even player a few points twice because I was devistated by the previous chapaters outcome.
I plan to play through it all again and this time be far more slective as to who I let into my caravans and also I plan to see what happens if I just let them caravan people die out because I don't compromise on who gets leveled up and gets gear vs buying food.
Also, I would have liked the ability to explore/adventure around the open world map by my own choices, kinda like an endless oregon trail mode and decide to get back to the story at my leisure. Its a huge world that we only get to see a very small portion of it through the storyline.
Lastly, I beleieve every time you enter camp while on the road, I think the game autosaves. Sooo.... camp ALOT top create save points that you can go back to in the event that a fight or discussion goes south.
Pros: Good story, unique fun combat, great art, ability to change the outcome of your story by your own choices.
Cons: extremely limited team customization, very limited gear customization, no pvp, no world explore/adventure option. You may love a specific character for his or her story but hate their class specialization (Alette for me). It would have been better that every time you introduce a new character that you allow the player to slect that character's specialization within the hardcoded base class. For example. Alette  is an archer base class, with an eagle eye specialization. I hate eagle eyes. I never used her because of this. It would have been awesome to be able to slect her as a bow master instead!
3 out of 5 stars is what Id give this title.  It's a great start to something amazing IF the developers continue to mature and expand on what is already here. I hope that is what is in BS2.

Let me start off by saying I was very surprised and impressed with this game.  If I had known how good it was I probably would have never played Diablo and just played this.  Diablo/Torchlight/Grim Dawn are all the same sort of game, if you're looking for a general description.  There's lots of reviews and hardly anything hasn't been said, but I highly recommend this game to anyone looking for a fun ARPG/Hack'n'Slash.
PROS:
-LOTS of loot, and I mean tons
-LOTS of character customization, you pick a main class, and at 10 you pick a Secondary to combine with the first.  If you want to be a elemental-wielding mage that's also a wicked good warrior, you can do it.
-The Devotion system (sort of like an alternate skill tree, in addition to the traditional one) is massive, with lots of options to choose from
-Combat is simple, and fun
-Spells are satisfying
-You can open a rift anytime you need to teleport to larger rifts you've discovered to travel quickly
-The story is decent, imo, even though I'm not too far into it
-Very atmospheric and dark, reminds me of Darkest Dungeon
-Voiced characters in the main storyline
-Relatively good inventory management for a loot-grinding game
CONS:
-I wish there was more graphics settings options
-A couple small bugs, nothing game-breaking, like corpses (talking to you, harpies) getting stuck after you kill them, they stand there like ghosts of your previous slaughters
-More classes would be nice
OVERALL:
I would highly recommend this game.  Originally I was apprehensive about buying it for $25, and thought I'd wait for the Summer Sale, but it was totally worth the money.  This was just as enjoyable if not moreso than Torchlight 2/Diablo 3.  I really enjoy playing it, and there's LOTS of grinding and slaughtering to be had.
9/10

Combat's fantastic. Best character creator to-date. And a ton of content for no subscription fee, and a really low price (at launch).
One of the best aspects of the combat is that it can be largely played without using any hotkeys like a traditional MMO. You have the option to use the 1-9 numberbar you usually use, but you're better off using the button combos the game suggests. This game's combat is largely centered around combos. All the attacks are really cool to watch, and they only get better as you progress.
If you bought one of the packs, you've gotta press ESC while in-game, and click the redeem button. Should open up Steam Overlay, and you can acquire all your stuff from there. They'll send it all to you in the mail after you've done that.
Game's also got a lot of dumb features turned on by default. I recommend going into Settings->Game->Turn Off System Notifications, and ticking everything but Combat/Safe Zone and Ability Increased. That will get rid of all the annoying marketplace and guild banners in the top middle of the screen.
I also recommend pressing CTRL to activate your cursor, clicking the gear in the top left of the chat box, and turning off System on the right portion of this screen.

I currently have 4 characters above 57, and have been playing since launch. Black Desert Online is the game I keep coming back to, because there’s so much you can do. I really feel as it’s the pre-WoW mmo everyone always asks for. One that doesn’t hold your hand, one that has mechanics that aren’t well known even with the internet, and one that heavily rewards players for the time they spend in it.

Arguably, the main end game is PVP via node wars, and getting into PVP will take a lot of your time to learn it, to become decent at it, and to competitive in it. It also, can take a lot of your money if you let it. There is no traditional subscription, but the cash shop is pricey. You can buy some of the cash shop items in the marketplace, but you’ll rarely find any, because it isn’t worth it as far as how much progress you can get from the amount of real money you can spend. The game isn’t pay to win.

There is a lot of content for those of you who don’t like PVP as well, creating a trade empire that consists of workers whom you pay in beer, and you can fish, cook, do alchemy, train and breed horses, and farm. All of which, also take a lot of time and dedication to become good at, and some of it you can do afk. you can also own almost any of the buildings as homes and furnish them as if it were some The Sims mmo.

It’s also huge plus that the game is extremely beautiful, though expect a lot of texture pop-in.

It’s a good game, the combat is flashy and fast paced, there’s a lot to do, and the world is huge. For a more in-depth review, take a look at my video.

So my friend and I were debating on whether or not to buy this game. I mean, yeah it's only $8 but we were a little strapped at the time. It looked fun, though, which is why we were hesitant.
My friend decided to bite the bullet--he is the one with the better job, after all. I had to go handle my dog, so I was gone for the moment he downloaded it, but I saw the result. It was like nothing I'd ever seen before in my life.
He used to be a fairly heavyset guy with pimples all over his face and an awkward demeanor; not unlike myself, though more so I suppose. The man I walked into that day was different. I saw a 6'3'' bronzed warrior with perfect facial hair and a gleam in his eye that could make any lady drop at his feet. His phone immediately started going wild with notifications about the millions being depositied into his brand-new Cayman Island account. At that moment, I knew what I had to do.
I powered up my crappy laptop, barely even meeting the specs, and told Steam to install this game.
At once I could feel my crotch bulging as I grew three whole feet in as many seconds. The scruffy excuse I had for a beard was replaced with a layer of hair so glorious Zeus himself was jealous as I also grew six inches taller. I wasn't a large man before, but any semblance of being out of shape melted away from my frame like butter in an oven and my muscles gained glory I'd only dreamed of before. Even my dog, who'd only been a pug before, now stood proudly by my side as a German Shepard-Husky mix while a beautiful woman appeared in my arms, who is now my wife. Behind my friend, I saw the ghost of Genghis Khan nod in approval.
We played for a little afterward for giggles. That was fun too.

Picked this up on sale for the potential cringe factor after being egged-on by friends. Turns out I actually enjoy it a lot. The english VA I could take or leave, except for the sheer amount of character VA's that I recognize from games I used to play or shows I used to watch. The premise of the game and the references that it makes to video games in general, along with popular cultural references from my youth, are perfect for my era and generation. The combat is satisfying enough for a person like myself who has always taken interest in the unique storytelling elements provided by JRPG's, and why I ever thought I might not like this game I don't know. The transformation techniques are so reminiscent of The Legend of Dragoon- it does my soul good. I could recommend this game to anyone who can get over the embarrassment that seems to accrue when mixing anime-styled games with T-for-Teen rated storytelling (not that there isn't a few clever adult references in tow, which is no different than children's cartoons today). The ability to enhance the difficulty of dungeons as you play is refreshing, as it adds a bit of tailoring towards those seeking a combat challenge. The story is solid enough, which is surprising given the crazy premise that it is based upon. If you like JRPG's and games that can make fun of themselves (and an all-Female cast), pick this up.

I'll try and make this as short and to the point as possible, as reading endless paragraphs about a game isn't exactly stimulating:
Divinty: Original Sin is an absolutely fantastic classic style RPG. The turn based combat system and vibrant world was a much needed breath of fresh air for 2014 and it's constant disappointing releases. Combat is varied and fun, no matter what skills and abilities you choose. Every combat situation requires strategy and thought to beat, not doing so will often mean you're easily put down. This gives combat a great sense of challenge, and beating a tough group of enemies or a boss is incredibly satisfying. The best part about this is that it can all be done with a friend. The co-op is a brilliant addition that you really should try. Although if you don't have any friends at all, playing it on your own is still a lot of fun.
