Recommended, but not for 40 euros.
+  120 hours to casually work my way through the entire story and nearly all of the side-quests.
+  Tons of magic and combat skills to choose from, with nothing tied to any particular "class".  Build whatever character you like.
+  Story was fun and funny at times, sad and dark at others.  I enjoyed most of the voice characterizations.
+  A ton of inventory.
+  2-player co-op, easily modded to a workable 4-player co-op.
+  Workshop
-  A ton of inventory, with a pretty horrible set of options for dealing with it.  You can sort your main inventory by weight, by gold value, etc., but you can't do the same with your backpack.  Whatever you stuff in there stays in the slot it lands in forever, unless you drag it to a new slot.  There's no option to sort backpacks at all, and since there was sooo much stuff to deal with I'd naturally split it up into various backpacks pretty early on.  I had a food backpack, a crafting ingredients backpack, and so on, but by the end of the game it was so tedious to deal with it all or find anything that I often didn't bother.
-  Which leads to negative #2:  A ton of food, which I barely ate.  I'd be surprised if I ate something half a dozen times throughout the entire game.  Food just wasn't a necessity at all, and was actually pretty much a liability in terms of weight.  Between spells and potions there was no need to eat anything during combat, ever, and since a healing spell outside of combat is free to use there was no reason to eat food outside combat, either.  I ended the game with a massive sack full of pies and juices and assorted goodies, feeling almost like I'd done something wrong by not eating it all.
-  A few broken/bug-prone areas.  Twice I experienced a bug where a character's weapons and/or armor would disappear, during combat.  Despite being able to easily repeat the bug in both locations, and sending in a report, Support says they couldn't duplicate it, so no help there.  All I can say is save very often, and get in the habit of checking each character's inventory often.  It makes everything more tedious, but I guess it's better than realizing too late that some precious bow has been gone for who knows how long.
The game's a ton of fun, but the 40 euro price is a bit steep for something with a pretty clunky way of dealing with the huge amount of stuff you'll be dealing with, and a few potentially game-breaking bugs like disappearing weapons that are still occuring, years after development started.  And the extra 8 euros for the "collectors edition" is a crime for what's included.

Having an incredibly fun time playing through this with my brother - he has fond memories of the original Fallout games, I loved Baldur's Gate.  Here is a game that combines the two, adds its own flair, and provides a massive world to fiddle around in with spell combos, crafting, and the like.
Teleport alone has made for some hilarious times...

FIRST IMPRESSIONS:
Nearly all of the game's dialogue (which is primarily text-only, with spoken narration for cutscenes) is in a poetic rhyming format. Personally, I find this quite annoying, and it distracts me from the text's actual content. However, I did find a character (party member, even) that goes out of her way to use a word that does NOT rhyme, when there's a better-fitting word that DOES rhyme, after which another character corrects them. I find this somewhat amusing.
The combat, however, piques my interest. First off, it uses a "turn-time" system, whereby faster units take more turns than slower ones, as opposed to Pokemon (for example) where speed only determines who moves first in a turn, yet everyone still gets the same number of turns. However, this game takes it a step farther; each unit's turn is split into a wait period and a cast period. Once a unit's wait period finishes, they select an action and proceed to the cast period. Once the cast period is done, the action occurs. However, an action can be interrupted if the unit is hit while in their cast period. This results in a lot of strategy in manipulating the timers, especially given the fact that you can pick an enemy and slow them down nearly any time.
I read a lot of reviews that mentioned having problems with Uplay, be it the inabilty to play or having saves erased. I haven't had these issues. I also read that you should use Uplay in offline mode, which I've done thus far.
SECOND IMPRESSIONS:
Now that I have more than two party members, I now see how party swapping works. It's kind of wierd. At first, I thought it was the same as FF10; on a player unit's turn, you can swap him/her out for any other player unit not already active, and this is completely seamless and takes no time. But there's another option. Lets say you have three party members, named A, B, and C. A is picking an action. B is on the field, but waiting to act. C is off the field. You can use A's action to swap C in for B, and this will cause A's turn to be spent, but C is now immediately ready to act. Confusing? Yeah, I thought so too. As a result, I only use the swap-for-self method that FF10 uses.
I'd also like to comment on the art style. It has its own unique fantasy charm. I like to describe it as the developer being on
the right amount of drugs.
THIRD IMPRESSIONS:
Dang, the game is getting
There's two difficulty levels, Casual and Expert. I picked Expert. The difficulty was high, but managable until recently. It's getting quite brutal at this point. I'm managing, but only barely.

I've played a lot of games from a bunch of genres and a number of platforms over a long time.
Now that my Steam Awards tasks call for it, I will stand up and argue a point I've been saying for years:
Half-Life 2 is the single greatest video game ever made.
Most fundamentally, it is a truly excellent FPS:
-The weapons available are varied and all 'feel right', without being redundant.
-New weapons appear at very welcome intervals, according to gameplay demands.
-The local environments, although linear, are also varied and well-designed both visually and for gameplay.
-The levels change significantly, not only in appearance, but in gameplay requirements.
-The gameplay progression is smooth, includes abundant 'instruction', and is rarely unintuitive.
-The enemies are varied, and not only require various strategies to defeat, but can each be defeated in a variety of ways.
Over and above its qualities as a robust FPS in its own right, I would make two more points that push this game over the top as far as my point is concerned...
The first of these regards the Gravity Gun. I had never seen anything quite like it before, and haven't since. I like to imagine that a large part of the difficulty Valve is having in making Half-Life 3 is because this game included something so revolutionary as the Gravity Gun, and then the Portal Gun, which would have been just as revolutionary in a third iteration (and was hinted-at, in any case), had its novelty spent in its own eponymous series.
In the meantime, however, after a couple hours traversing a usual (if very-well-crafted) FPS environment, one is gifted the "Zero Point Energy Field Manipulator," which starts as a gimmick and a toy used for training, and then almost immediately becomes a core mechanic of the game. Although it is perhaps not desirable, it is both plausible and entertaining that the entire rest of the game can be completed with no other weapon. Furthermore, the Gravity Gun allows for a scale of interaction with the environment that was never before seen, nor since quite repeated.
I have seen games that cross genres, strongly influence genres, strongly influence other genres, and seemingly revolutionize genres by repetition of their qualities. The Gravity Gun by itself introduced something else entirely into a game of a defined genre, and not only did it multiply the diversity of gameplay available, but by the end of the game, it managed to become *better* and *more interesting.*
This game also includes pheropods, which are also made of awesome, but are only briefly useful. By contrast, the Gravity Gun is just the best, forever.
The second regards the story. This was my first Half-Life game, and was more than sufficient to explain itself. There is a good deal of storytelling, but it's set into the FPS game rather than cutscenes, and allows you to become miles-deep immersed even as you have the opportunity to climb the furniture and throw garbage at people's heads.
The voice acting and attending animations are very well-done in this game. Moreover, the time you are stuck in exposition allows for further exploration and gleaning of details that deepen an understanding of the plot.
The story truly goes deeper than this, though... Back in high school English class, I was often told that better stories are told by 'showing, not telling'. This game tells you a lot of its own story, but the amount that it *shows* will fill many more than one playthrough. There are details set into every environment, well above and beyond and beneath and around the glaring enigma that is the G-man.
Who are CPs? What are Overwatch soldiers? What are Stalkers? What are Synths? What has the Combine done to Earth? How have people been living in the meantime?
How are you the "One Free Man," when your actions seem so destined?
That last quastion isn't nearly answered yet [makes imploring face at Valve... HL3? Plz?], but it does add to the air of epic storytelling that makes this game both eminently replayable and somehow still wanting for more of itself.
This might not be my absolute favorite game ever, nor the one I've played the most, but for the aforementioned reasons, I still believe that it is the best.

Reviewing method
Fun: 3 points of 10
Game Balance: 1 points of 10
Game Mechanics: 2 points of 10
Exceptional: 0 point of 10
Score 3/1/2/0 = 6/10
PROS
The game is incredibly good fun and a Must Buy for that, tho make sure it's on offer.
It has a good amount of strategy and tactics and you cannot win without using both.
Much of the fun is watching your overall strategy having an impact on individual battles.
Both Fun and Mechanics are very strong in this game and it must be said that it is hugely addictive.
CONS
The sniper class feels very wrong and lost the game a whole point on the mechanics rating. There  does seem to be greater range of fire but the to hit chance seems through the floor for a precision related class. I found myself frequently swearing at how often snipers missed the shot, ie just as often of more often than the other classes. This also lost the game a point on game balance, since 25% of your basic arsenal is defective.
My major gripe with this game, and it is extremely annoying, is that, even as you begin to know and understand the game, your strategic play is rendered irrelevant.
Fight a battle and lose it. Fine this happens. Then you regear your soldiers in better kit and redo the same battle. You should do better? Not a chance, the game throws harder enemies at you that are matched your better gear.
This leaves you feeling that your strategy, your intelligence and the leeway you leave yourself for contingency plans are a complete waste of time.
Finally. I am on my fifth game at the moment, yet to have won. I don't mind the steep learning curve but after five playthroughs I have noticed that the game basically plays the same every time.
You do get a little extra edge with knowledge of the game structure but you immediately lose almost all of that when the game kits out your enemy on the battlefield to match your gear.
This eventually leaves you feeling that you are in a lose/lose situation.
CONCLUSION
This game is definitely worth playing but you may well end up feeling that you hate how long it takes to learn and the growing feelig that your greater knowledge is worthless anyway.

A frustratingly hard game at times, FTL will challenge you to make smart decisions, conserve precious resources like scrap and missiles, and keep you on your toes while battling enemy ships.  One of my favorite aspects is the variety and balance of the set ups for your spacecraft. While some ships are better suited for different tasks, all have enough versatility to run a different layout. I have played through this game many times, and I play it differently every time. Sometimes I use my crew as a boarding party, sometimes I focus on maximizing the effect of a powerful beam weapon, and then sometimes I utilize drones to do most of my combat for me.
If you buy this game and run through it once and get too frustrated- just try it again. This is definitely a game where you need to find out what works by trial and error, and it is more fun once you've played through a few times.
The new Advanced Edition content is great and provides even more choices and systems to upgrade. Hacking, mind control, and a handful of new ship layouts and a new race are just some of the new content that AE provides (for free!).  Lastly, the soundtrack in this game is amazing. I bought the soundtrack with the game and enjoy listening to it when I'm not playing the game.

In most cases, you want someone who has a large number of hours playing a game to give a review. In the case of this game, that isn't needed. WIthing 10 hours, everybody knows if they like this game or not. Except that EVERYBODY loves this game. Play it once and you'll be addicted as you zoom around, dodging balls, making awesome throws, rocking out to music, and so much more. But after a few games, you run into a problem-- very few people play this game as a whole, and they are further divided by location around the world. While this can put a damper on some round, when everybody leaves and you're stuck with some OP bots, it has its upsides. As you get to play more, you see certain players more often and start to build teams with random people and even learn play style. So, even with its faults, it is an amazing game, everyone should play at least once.
--Edit--
At just under 100 hours and climbing past level 78, I have seen the many changes of this game. The game itself is under constant renovation and is always adapting and evolving to meet the needs of its community. I am happy to sit for hours with my friends and play this amazingly simple game. Good evening.
How great it is to be with you tonight.
Let me begin by thanking the hundreds of thousands of Americans who actively participated in our campaign as volunteers. Let me thank the 2 1/2 million Americans who helped fund our campaign with an unprecedented 8 million individual campaign contributions – averaging $27 a piece. Let me thank the 13 million Americans who voted for the political revolution, giving us the 1,846 pledged delegates here tonight – 46 percent of the total. And delegates: Thank you for being here, and for all the work you’ve done. I look forward to your votes during the roll call on Tuesday night.
And let me offer a special thanks to the people of my own state of Vermont who have sustained me and supported me as a mayor, congressman, senator and presidential candidate. And to my family – my wife Jane, four kids and seven grandchildren –thank you very much for your love and hard work on this campaign.
I understand that many people here in this convention hall and around the country are disappointed about the final results of the nominating process. I think it’s fair to say that no one is more disappointed than I am. But to all of our supporters – here and around the country – I hope you take enormous pride in the historical accomplishments we have achieved.
Together, my friends, we have begun a political revolution to transform America and that revolution – Our Revolution – continues. Election days come and go. But the struggle of the people to create a government which represents all of us and not just the 1 percent – a government based on the principles of economic, social, racial and environmental justice – that struggle continues. And I look forward to being part of that struggle with you.
Let me be as clear as I can be. This election is not about, and has never been about, Hillary Clinton, or Donald Trump, or Bernie Sanders or any of the other candidates who sought the presidency. This election is not about political gossip. It’s not about polls. It’s not about campaign strategy. It’s not about fundraising. It’s not about all the things the media spends so much time discussing.
This election is about – and must be about – the needs of the American people and the kind of future we create for our children and grandchildren.
This election is about ending the 40-year decline of our middle class the reality that 47 million men, women and children live in poverty. It is about understanding that if we do not transform our economy, our younger generation will likely have a lower standard of living then their parents.
This election is about ending the grotesque level of income and wealth inequality that we currently experience, the worst it has been since 1928. It is not moral, not acceptable and not sustainable that the top one-tenth of one percent now own almost as much wealth as the bottom 90 percent, or that the top 1 percent in recent years has earned 85 percent of all new income. That is unacceptable. That must change.
This election is about remembering where we were 7 1/2 years ago when President Obama came into office after eight years of Republican trickle-down economics.
The Republicans want us to forget that as a result of the greed, recklessness and illegal behavior on Wall Street, our economy was in the worst economic downturn since the Great Depression. Some 800,000 people a month were losing their jobs. We were running up a record-breaking deficit of $1.4 trillion and the world’s financial system was on the verge of collapse.
We have come a long way in the last 7 1/2 years, and I thank President Obama and Vice President Biden for their leadership in pulling us out of that terrible recession.
Yes, we have made progress, but I think we can all agree that much, much more needs to be done.
This election is about which candidate understands the real problems facing this country and has offered real solutions – not just bombast, fear-mongering, name-calling and divisiveness.
We need leadership in this country which will improve the lives of working families, the children, the elderly, the sick and the poor. We need leadership which brings our people together and makes us stronger – not leadership which insults Latinos, Muslims, women, African-Americans and veterans – and divides us up.
By these measures, any objective observer will conclude that – based on her ideas and her leadership – Hillary Clinton must become the next president of the United States. The choice is not even close.
This election is about a single mom I saw in Nevada who, with tears in her eyes, told me that she was scared to death about the future because she and her young daughter were not making it on the $10.45 an hour she was earning. This election is about that woman and the millions of other workers in this country who are struggling to survive on totally inadequate wages.
Hillary Clinton understands that if someone in America works 40 hours a week, that person should not be living in poverty. She understands that we must raise the minimum wage to a living wage. And she is determined to create millions of new jobs by rebuilding our crumbling infrastructure – our roads, bridges, water systems and wastewater plants.
But her opponent – Donald Trump – well, he has a very different view. He does not support raising the federal minimum wage of $7.25 an hour – a starvation wage. While Donald Trump believes in huge tax breaks for billionaires, he believes that states should actually have the right to lower the minimum wage below $7.25. What an outrage!
This election is about overturning Citizens United, one of the worst Supreme Court decisions in the history of our country. That decision allows the wealthiest people in America, like the billionaire Koch brothers, to spend hundreds of millions of dollars buying elections and, in the process, undermine American democracy.
Hillary Clinton will nominate justices to the Supreme Court who are prepared to overturn Citizens United and end the movement toward oligarchy in this country. Her Supreme Court appointments will also defend a woman’s right to choose, workers’ rights, the rights of the LGBT community, the needs of minorities and immigrants and the government’s ability to protect the environment.
If you don’t believe this election is important, if you think you can sit it out, take a moment to think about the Supreme Court justices that Donald Trump would nominate and what that would mean to civil liberties, equal rights and the future of our country.
This election is about the thousands of young people I have met who have left college deeply in debt, and the many others who cannot afford to go to college. During the primary campaign, Secretary Clinton and I both focused on this issue but with different approaches. Recently, however, we have come together on a proposal that will revolutionize higher education in America. It will guarantee that the children of any family this country with an annual income of $125,000 a year or less – 83 percent of our population – will be able to go to a public college or university tuition free. That proposal also substantially reduces student debt.
This election is about climate change, the greatest environmental crisis facing our planet, and the need to leave this world in a way that is healthy and habitable for our kids and future generations. Hillary Clinton is listening to the scientists who tell us that – unless we act boldly and transform our energy system in the very near future – there will be more drought, more floods, more acidification of the oceans, more rising sea levels. She understands that when we do that we can create hundreds of thousands of good-paying jobs.

The Banner Saga... Where to begin? I've made many choices,lived and survived to regret it...yet....it had to be done... The game has such a great story and great atmosphere. Decisions you make in the game are crucial and may haunt you or bite you in the back later. I was playing the good guy.... Accepted or helped as many people as I could along the way. I let people join my caravan, assisted those who stayed behind. Until.... Someone turned traitor after a long while. Perhaps it was due to the low morale from our dwindling food supplies... or was it my leadership? I was accused of letting anybody from the road join the caravan. There was mistrust and there was alot of squabbling amongst the clansmen.
My logic was this: The common enemy was the dredge. No point fighting amongst ourselves.
And that was how i rolled throughout the whole game. Pretty much like Game of Throne's Nights Watch style. I'd willingly accept anyone whose willing to join and help those that decide to stay, despite their lost cause. I've made a few good friends that way, lost a few too.
The ending...I think I made the right choice. Though sad, but I felt that whatever that had happened, the great journey, was all just to get that 1 character to the end. Bittersweet indeed.
TLDR:  I felt like Ned Stark in Game of Thrones. Sometimes the best decisions aren't always the morally righteous ones. The game really shines in this part as well. The fighting is similar to XCOM styled games....its decent. You really have to decide your hero placements tactically and their moves too. One wrong move could cost the whole battle.

.

Completely surprised by how incredibly fun this is! If you like local multiplayer games, this is pretty much a must!
At first glance, this looked like a funny concept that would be amusing for a game or two. Little did I realize how addicting this game can be!
Pros:
+Very simple controls (only two buttons)
+Tons of unlocks and reasons to grind. There's a very large amount of content to unlock through continued gameplay, and what feels like virtually unlimited, Mugen-esque mod potential.
+ AI bots - you can play this alone with AI bots tagging in for other players. No need for friends to enjoy it!
+ Excellent balance system - Your hero levels up by killing monsters, and your monsters level up by other players' heroes leveling up... meaning in one player is dominating, everyone else gets stronger monsters to try and beat them back down
+ Out-of-game challenges - Practice with monsters between games and see what you've unlocked
+ Large variety of spells and equipment - Get awesome powers and cool weapons with both magic abilities and even cursed gear
+ Cool boss battle concept - Try to win the game with 1vAll boss fights
Cons (with suggestions):
- The game has the potential to drag - With random gear in the shop, a hero can get powerful quickly or struggle to survive a few rooms in a row. Bosses can be rough without good gear, so there's no easy way to predict if a single playthrough will last 30 minutes or 90. There could probably be some sort of adjustable gold/XP/item-power/wrath settings that would allow players to customize for faster or slower playthroughs.
- Only two buttons - Your ghosts have an Inhabit/Attack button, and a Special Attack/Exit button. Many a fight has been thrown at a critical moment by checking for a special attack only to basically forfeit the fight by leaving a monster/object. Just adding a third button for Inhabit/Exit would solve this
- No online play - I really, really hope this is something they look into. I would buy a half dozen copies of this in a heartbeat if they added this feature.
- Endgame item shopping is often a buyout - As you get to deeper levels, gold accumulates quickly and being the character alive when you enter the item shop usually turns into a shopping spree as you buyout most of the floor. It can be rough to keep your hero alive in endgame without proper gear. The game has a great mechanic of letting a new player teleport to the item shop after reviving his hero AND clearing the room, but that often doesn't help much if you're the second or third person to get to the shop that floor. And if you're undergeared, you probably won't live to the next floor/shop. I should stress, though... while this is an annoyance, it IS NOT game-breakingly bad by any means. This could be fixed with some sort of minimum item system per-player per-floor.
Neutral notes:
o The game is 1-4 players, and the mood of it changes a lot based on how many there are. 1v1 is a game of slow whittling and constant annoyance. Monster fights are sniping and kiting and trying to break them down over the course of rooms. 4-player games are basically royal rumbles every-other room, and the hero is swarmed with monsters, dies, is replaced by another player's hero who now still has to deal with the leftovers. Control often changes hands twice in a single room. 3-players is my favorite balance so far. Some sort of optional monster handicap setting could add more variety (option to boost in 1v1 for easier turnover, option to weaken in 4-player to make surviving longer easier)

This is the best couch game out of all possible couch games.
For context: I play a great deal of couch games with a great variety of people, and what I've learned is that it can be a *challenge* to keep everybody having fun throughout the night. It's one thing to play games with a bunch of Melee pros, or a gaggle of drunk newbies, but what happens when you put them together? Either you play gang beasts, and the tryhards are bored to death, or you put on Samurai Gunn and the poor boy/girlfriend who got roped in gets their♥♥♥♥♥handed to them for the rest of the night. It seems like there's always someone who isn't having fun.
But not with Crawl.
The terrific basis of Crawl is that losing is *fun*. And the worse you are, the more fun it is. The more the tryhard in your group levels up, the bigger, uglier and more powerful your monsters are. Getting stomped for the first half hour? That's ok, now you have a *giant chicken ogre* to stomp that ****er with. It also serves as an auto-balancing system, so that even the worst player in the group has a chance for an epic comeback.
But on the tryhard side, there's a host of options and optimization to sink your teeth into, as well as plenty of things you can pick up to make things more interesting. When one of our guys felt he was rampaging a little too hard, he got the item that gave him massively discounted items in exchange for randomly being turned into a frog - and spent the remainder of the game alternating between a raging fireball of spells and getting pulverized as a helpless amphibian. Taunt the gods to make your victory even sweeter through self-imposed hard-mode. It's a blast.
Plus, the art's great. The gameplay is great. The variety and depth of content is great. The replayability is great. The dramatic lovecraft voiceovers at the start of every game are really, really great.
There are a lot of good couch games this competes with. Duck game, towerfall, Gang beasts, speed runners... but crawl will always stay at the top of our list. If you've got that hard-to-please varied group of gaming friends who can't ever seem to have fun for a whole evening straight, this is the title for you.

As many other reviews state, you'll have a better understanding of what is going on after completing all 13 endings. You'll miss out on a lot if you only do one ending and uninstall.
However, after finishing all the endings, I still do not understand how the situation came to be or how it is hapenning. I may be daft or perhaps I missed something, but it is never explained. The story would have been that much better if everything was explained. Now this doesn't make Everlasting Summer a terrible novel. I still enjoyed the experience.

There are some lovable characters in this game. You may or may not get attached to some of the characters. I, personally, liked most of them quite a bit. I was never bored with the pioneers or staff. There is slight character development with some of the girls.

The writing was well written. It kept me on the edge of my seat as well as in tears. The English is great by the way. They obviously didn't use Google Translate.

The setting is interesting considering the situation the main character is in. I suppose it has to do with the developer, but nonetheless still interesting. Does it contribute to the story? Not really.

The music, to me, is an important part of a visual novel. Most of the music is great for setting the mood. Gets the tears flowing, know what I'm sayin'?

It was good, but not the best. I would still recommend it. Don't let this be your first visual novel though.

The most enjoyable RPG I've played in a long time. Its mechanics are solid, easy to pick up and play, and never seem to leave me bored like so many other RPGs. Its a little on the light-weight side, but its design is very intuitive and to the point, but still presenting a challenge. It has checks and balances against "min-maxing", but that's often done simply. The progression system is also simple compared to older RPGs and some modern one (though much more advanced than, say, games like Final Fantasy 13 or World of Warcraft).
The story is very nice and inspiring, very melancholy and darkly beautiful. Its like looking through the eyes of an innocent child at a destitute world; that's pretty much the theme throughout. Its more than the sum of its parts in the emotions which it evokes.
Its a long-run RPG but ends abruptly, however it still manages to wrap things up nicely. As far as I can tell, there are no end-game quests, no "ultimate weapons" to be had, which I find somewhat disapointing. I know there's some things I haven't completed, but I'm not holding my breath for anything like, say Final Fantasy 8's endgame.
All in all its a great game, and one of the best of its generation of games (Xbox 360 era till now).

Reviewing method
Fun: 3 points of 10
Game Balance: 1 points of 10
Game Mechanics: 2 points of 10
Exceptional: 0 point of 10
Score 3/1/2/0 = 6/10
PROS
The game is incredibly good fun and a Must Buy for that, tho make sure it's on offer.
It has a good amount of strategy and tactics and you cannot win without using both.
Much of the fun is watching your overall strategy having an impact on individual battles.
Both Fun and Mechanics are very strong in this game and it must be said that it is hugely addictive.
CONS
The sniper class feels very wrong and lost the game a whole point on the mechanics rating. There  does seem to be greater range of fire but the to hit chance seems through the floor for a precision related class. I found myself frequently swearing at how often snipers missed the shot, ie just as often of more often than the other classes. This also lost the game a point on game balance, since 25% of your basic arsenal is defective.
My major gripe with this game, and it is extremely annoying, is that, even as you begin to know and understand the game, your strategic play is rendered irrelevant.
Fight a battle and lose it. Fine this happens. Then you regear your soldiers in better kit and redo the same battle. You should do better? Not a chance, the game throws harder enemies at you that are matched your better gear.
This leaves you feeling that your strategy, your intelligence and the leeway you leave yourself for contingency plans are a complete waste of time.
Finally. I am on my fifth game at the moment, yet to have won. I don't mind the steep learning curve but after five playthroughs I have noticed that the game basically plays the same every time.
You do get a little extra edge with knowledge of the game structure but you immediately lose almost all of that when the game kits out your enemy on the battlefield to match your gear.
This eventually leaves you feeling that you are in a lose/lose situation.
CONCLUSION
This game is definitely worth playing but you may well end up feeling that you hate how long it takes to learn and the growing feelig that your greater knowledge is worthless anyway.

I'm a fan of GOT, and was on the fence about this game, but after playing the first episode, I'm totally sold.
People will question the extent to which your choices matter. Only time will tell the impact of some choices, and others seem to have preordained outcomes. The important distinction is that you feel like you're flailing against an unfair world, and not against an unfair game, and in that sense, it is extremely satisfying as a Game of Thrones experience. I do hope that things get less hopeless eventually, though.
Other things:
-The art is pretty. The filter they use for edges and distant objects can be noticeable at times, but overall the aesthetic works well, is fitting, and looks quite nice.
-The likenesses of characters from the show are impressive. They're immediately recognizable, and still fit with the rest of the visuals.
-All the voice acting is good. Characters from the show use the same actors, which is always a risk when you have screen actors do voice acting, but they all did great.
-The first episode was longer than I expected. Not that long, mind you, but there were multiple times where I assumed it was going to end on a cliffhanger, but it continued on to end on a different cliffhanger.
-I did not like that sometimes I felt like I had too much information, on account of knowing the show and the books. The characters I'm playing as shouldn't be quite so omniscient. But to the game's credit, they put thought into structuring things so that most of relevant the information I have would be knowable to the characters, narratively.
Overall: If you like Game of Thrones at all, this is totally worth taking the plunge on.

As its name suggests, Robot Roller-Derby Disco Dodgeball (what a descriptive title!) is a game where you control robots playing dodgeball in a disco nightclub. What's not to love?
This game is fun, fast-paced, and skill-based. You WILL have a blast rolling around the disco while trying to nail your opponents with the ball and dodging their throws. Perhaps most impressive for this sort of game is that there truly is enough content to justify the game's price. There are multiple singleplayer modes, including the addicting arcade mode that pits you against wave after wave of opponents. However, the game was designed first and foremost as a multiplayer "shooter," and the multiplayer is a blast. The game's community is relatively small, but it's large enough that I never have any trouble finding several games going on in my region (East Coast USA).
Overall, this is simple, silly fun, but there's certainly more than enough variety, challenge, and depth to justify paying the full price. I got this in a Humble Bundle and didn't expect much, but Robot Roller-Derby Disco Dodgeball is a diamond in the rough.

This game is 50% fun, fast-paced freerunning through a beautiful sunny city, and 50% trying to figure out where you're supposed to go and how to get there while being shot at by 6 cops in riot gear and dying, then trying again 4 times before getting frustrated and looking up a walkthrough on YouTube.
Especially in the later levels this gets really annoying and obnoxious. But when you do know what to do, the game is so fun that it compensates for all the frustration. Also, first-person freerunning works surprisingly well, and really helps with the immersion. It really feels fast and fluent, and few things feel as cathartic as sliding down a sloped window onto a cop, disarming him like you're Bruce Lee, shooting his friend and then fleeing the scene by somersaulting through a window onto a passing train. Despite it being somewhat frustrating, I'll still recommend it.

The Good:
Mirror's Edge is one of my favorite games. It has really fun first person parkor gameplay. The movement is smooth and during combat you can use takedowns and slow motion (reaction time) this makes combat feel very fluid and intense. You (or your enemy) can use the environment to get an advantage or find different routes on the map. Mirror's Edge has beautiful stylized graphics and environments along with a great soundtrack. You also are discouraged from using guns so no reloading, crosshair, etc, which gives unique and different experience.
The Bad:
The storyline is just ok. There are some frusturating boss fights and puzzles. The guns and gunplay feels basic sometimes. Game lasts only about 6-7 hours which limits replayablity (there are collectables and speedrun options though).
Overall:

I love BDO and truly believe that it's the best MMORPG of the decade - I originally brought this game before it was available on Steam and have clocked at least 1000hrs+, yet I feelt I have only scraped the surface of the game content.
BDO is an entirely openworld map which offers numerous quests, varying in complexity, logevity and numerous other things. Most of the time each quest relating into the somewhat detailed Lore of the game... At times the quests can become tiresome and long winded as most are repetitive and mindless, however this is a MMORPG and such repetetiveness is to be expected.
For those that do not prefer combatant based gameplay, there are plenty of other options for progression - Fishing, Horse riding and breeding, trading on the market
There is also a massively detailed charecter based levelling tree system, which, as players progress, said players can choose their characters innate abilities.
Another mentionable point of the game is the amazing detail the graphical side of the game has to offer, everything is presented in a beautiful package and if your PC can handle it, you'll find no other MMORPG that can match the level of detail
this game has to offer.
My above review until now has in essence only spoken of the best the game has to offer, however there are also a number of negatives to be spoken:- Primarily the intense grind that players will be faced with, a grind that will literally turn people away from the game in the long-run, leaving only the more hardcore members left
.
Something else to note which has become ever increasingly annoying is the latency that the servers have come to suffer due to the influx of players that have joined after the Steam release. Whilst additional "channels" where added into the game, the quality of said channels are horrible causing excessive lag, this means during peak hours the game is barely playable, with NPC talking upto 3 minutes to present a dialong, PVP combat increasingly harder and PvE content not worth the risk as regen potions may take 'x' amount of time before they will be consumed
and in the process the crystals you attached to your equipment lost!
Finally, the biggest negative of all is whilst BDO promotes AFK'ing, it does require your PC to remain on and a connection to the server to be active - Once you disconnect from the game everything basically comes to a hault.
Black Desert Online is awesome and has plenty to offer for people to burn at least 1k/hr+, but be prepared for the grind... Alot of it! Oh yeah and if you plan on using the AFK system - Spending a♥♥♥♥♥♥tonne on your electricity bills.

I meerly wanted to support the game more in my own fashion - However I think it would be advisable for the intergration of pre-steam players to be able to login using the Steam variation or at least link their pre-existing account!
Because of the nature of the family-name system, even providing an account merger for a temporary period of time would be nice to see? Having the ability for pre-steam accounts to override the steam made ones to retain our IGN's/progress etc.

To be honest, I have mixed feelings about this game.
On one hand, the backgrounds are gorgeous, and the 13 separate endings leave for a lot of gameplay. Some of the endings are definitely intruiging, and there's enough realism in most of the endings to seem like it's something that could happen to just anyone, making it somewhat easier to connect with the MC.
However, it's difficult for me to get past the endless pedobear references, panty shots, and generally exhausting personality of the MC enough to have a good time. I know I shouldn't expect much from an otome game, especially from one made primarily by people from 2ch, but the game came so highly rated as something better than most otome that I let myself believe it would rise above things like that.
Still, it's free and it gives enough gameplay to be worth an afternoon or two going through the endings, the girl in the True Ending is a national treasure, and it gives a depiction of being a teen in Soviet Russia that I've never seen before. Did I mention the backgrounds are incredible? Please look at them.
Anyways, if you have it in you to roll your eyes and move past the pedophilia and misogyny (granted, to a degree that's on par with the genre), and can dredge through endless internet nerd references, you'll probably have an OK time playing, especially for the price.

Two-button side-scrolling combat game here.  Press one button to attack an enemy on your left, press the other button to attack to the right.  That's it.
Simple?  Yep.
Easy?  Nope.
The whole point is to build up your combo attack chain as high as possible to get the high score and clear the level.  If you miss, your combo chain resets to zero AND you leave yourself open to an attack.  If you get hit, you lose health and your combo chain resets to zero.  You need Jedi-like reflexes to do well with this game.  I can't even get past the second set of levels (where you play as the bad♥♥♥♥♥Viking babe).  You will automatically switch characters every few levels.  Each character has slightly different attack animations, but the gameplay remains the same throughout.
Character and level design are based on the short film "Kung Fury" which I highly suggest you watch.  You don't need to know the story to play this game, but the movie is a really funny spoof that pokes fun at everything from the 1980's.

What a pleasant surprise this game was!
The art style and atmosphere are captivating and suit the theme of the game perfectly.
The gameplay revolves around puzzle solving, stealth and platforming while trying to avoid being eaten by large monsters. While it's not particularly difficult, it was interesting enough to keep my attention until the end. The end does come fairly soon (3-4h), but I don't consider it a negative. It gave me an unforgettable experience and at its price point, I felt like I got my money's worth. It never became a slog just to beat it, like many longer games.
The one negative thing I can say is that the camera is slightly flawed. Enemies can see you from off-screen while you can't see them, and while it adds to the suspension, it also feel a bit unfair. Also, it messes a bit with your depth perception, which made me miss a jump several times, which got a little frustrating. Luckily, this is rarely an issue.
The scares depend mostly on atmosphere and creepy enemies, but there are a few jump scares. I would recommend this to anyone who wants to frighten their kids, but not necessarily give them PTSD for life.

Imagine finding someone on a cold concrete floor, the room devoid of any windows or open doors.  As he struggles to his feet he notices three of his best friends making the same discovery in the room.  Suddenly, as if a product of his own confusion, a voice shouts in from above telling him that only one of them will survive.  Scrambling to find something useful on the ground, he realized they must have heard that same voice!  Brought back to his feet by the safety of a knife, he notices there is only one left and his back is turned.  The knife is plunged into his back and he immediately falls to his knees with him in dismay.  Regretful thoughts and sobbing are interrupted by the voice again, “Get up, death is no means to an end in this vile place,” and to his uneasy comfort, his friends were floating above him in spirit.
The mechanics of this game have created an incredibly balanced gameplay that is easy for anyone to get into, built on top of a wonderfully themed visual and auditory experience.  Now begins the intrepid narrative through the ever-changing procedural dungeons of Crawl.  This unique four-player split-screen game by the Australian studio Powerhoof starts you off against all your friends (or surprisingly intelligent AI) in a one-hit-to-kill brawl to decide who the hero will be first.  When you are not the hero, you are a ghost that may float around the map getting into whatever he or she may like.  They could inhabit furniture and throw it, they could command traps to aim and activate, they could interact with pictures and holes in the walls, and of course, summon and inhabit upgradable monsters on pentagrams.  Once a monster, or even a trap or furniture kills the hero, that ghost will take his place leading the exploration.  The goal in this game is to reach level 10 and challenge the player-controlled boss.
The cohesive design of the auditory and visual aspects of this game are really the biggest things that set it apart from others.  They had decided on a very low-resolution pixel art type of sprite style, which being paired with the chip-tune style of music creates a beautiful modern take on this classic style.  The title screen and name screen even say “Insert Coin” instead of “Press Start” and only allow you to enter three-character names like an old arcade box.  Many tiny details have been added to the game, proving how much time and dedication it must have taken to build such a piece.  From random seeming pixel glitches on the menu screen paired with auditory glitches, to rich item descriptions, to screen shake.  There is even a narrator at the beginning of rounds that tells the story slightly different every time.  If you are the type of person that is overwhelmed by this art style, which I will admit is pretty common when you first start playing, I urge you to play for a while and really give the game a good shot.
Everyone I have showed this game to seems a little overwhelmed and intimidated at first, just due to the amount of things happening on screen at all times.  The presumption that you will not be good at this game at first, however, is one that could not be further from the truth.  Even if you cannot kill the hero and lead the charge, your monsters will continue to level up as the current hero does.  Inversely, if you are very good at this game and spend the whole time playing as the hero you may have good weapons, but your monsters will be weak and it will be significantly harder to become the hero again.
Given the multiplayer mechanics, the balancing aspects of this game seemed to have just come together inherently.  It feels so very natural to play, and often times, will create some very unexpected outcomes.  The bosses require the ghost players to work together and coordinate their attacks; otherwise it will be all too easy for the hero.
*********************Warning: Spoilers*************************
One boss has an arm that fires sludge that will slow down and damage the hero.  The other arm fires bubbles that will trap the hero and make the final boss weapon much easier to hit.  The last weapon is an enormous eye laser that moves very slowly, but if the other teammates have done their jobs correctly, it will make short work of any level hero.  The other boss is a three-headed elemental dragon that has somewhat similar mechanics, but requires a different strategy.  There is an NPC in this boss fight that heals the player, which means the dragons best bet is to stay between the hero and the health.  As interesting and fun as these bosses are, more bosses would add a lot more variety to each dungeon adding much more replay value to this game.
********************End Spoilers**************************

What do i think to Dying Light? thats a tough one, Dying light suffers from doing certain things great and others not so. Firstly the weapon selection is pretty broad giving a good variety of options each with there own distinct advantages and disadvantages allowing you to adapt you own tactics. On the other hand later on in the game these weapons become incredibly overpowered allowing you to decapitate most zombies in one blow which in my opinion removes the survival aspect from a survival horror game due to you being able to smackdown a large group of zombies easily enough.
Another problem is the storyline it's not easy to be able to create a story for a zombie game but this one is incredibly cliche especially the ending which looked like something from a James Bond movie this ties in with the boss battles none of these battles are particularly tricky
i like to be challenged in a boss fight and genuinely worried about my character dying in them not just a few well placed attacks and then over with.
The night is probably one of the better parts of this game as you geniunely feel like your the prey and being hunted you have to carefully plan moves and avoid contact with zombies in order to stay alive until later on in the game you genuinely struggle to escape from the volatiles and if you do escape you are often wounded. The parkour offers an interesting experience at first allowing for some thrilling chase scenes however it quickly becomes tiresome especially towards end game and due to the fact that running on streets is usally not possible making for a slow travelling experience.

Here's a quick, little platform-puzzle game somewhat in the same vein as "Limbo" and "Inside".
As a whole, I really liked this game... much like I enjoyed playing Limbo and Inside. Simple, platform-driven puzzles. Challenges that are compartmentalized from room to room. Relatively short game (my playtime was probably around the 2-hour marker). And a story thats isn't spoon fed to your, but gradually -- and mysteriously -- unravels through the gameplay.
If I had to rank this game against the other two ("Limbo" and "Inside"), I think it just ekes out the competition. In fairness, they probably stand neck-and-neck in terms of challenge and overall fun, but what I really appreciated about "Little Nightmares" was the environment and character design.♥♥♥♥♥♥s just so creepy, yet so beautiful. Probably helps the game is running on Unreal 4 game engine, but god-damn is it gorgeous.
While this is not going to be my top game of 2017, it will rank high. And I would certainly recommend playing it if you're into puzzle platformers. Now, whether it's worth $20... that's debatable.

Have you been waiting for a successor to Baldur's gate 1 and 2? Well... this is not it. Don't get me wrong; this is a great game, but it is more Icewind Dale than Baldur's Gate. Let me explain: Icewind Dale (2000) versus Baldur's gate 1 (1998) and Baldur's Gate 2 (1999) was all about character. They all played exactly the same: same engine, action, controls, graphics etc., but the Baldur's Gate series had storylines where you really cared for the characters you controlled. Remember these characters from the Baldur's Gate series? Imoen? Aerie? Minsc? Jaheera? Edwin? Yoshimo? How many characters do you remember from Icewind Dale? (if you played it of course). I can't name any because they had no, or a limited backstory. I didn't care for the controllable NPC's in Icewind Dale, just like I don't care for the controllable NPC's in Divinity: Original Sin. Just don't expect this game to give you the same emotional involvement you had with Baldur's Gate 1 and 2 (the funny banter, fleshed out intricate romantic storylines, betrayal etc.) and you will be just fine and thoroughly enjoying this game, just like i am doing right now. If Baldur's Gate 2 was a 10/10, Baldur's Gate 1 was a 9.5/10 and the Icewind Dale series was an 8/10. This game would be  8.5/10.

If your looking for a review on this game you've come to the wrong place, but if your looking for an outstanding pie recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients:
1. 6 tablespoons unsalted butter
2. 1/2 cup white sugar
3. 1/2 cup brown sugar
4. 1/4 cup water
5. 1/4 teaspoon cinnamon
6. 1 pinch salt
7. 5 apples - peeled, cored and sliced
8. 1 pastry for double-crust pie
Directions:
1. Preheat oven to 425 degrees F (220 degrees C).
2. Combine butter, white sugar, brown sugar, water, cinnamon, and salt in a saucepan over medium heat. Bring to a boil, remove from heat and set aside.
3. Roll out half the pastry to fit a 9-inch pie plate. Place bottom crust in pie plate; pour in apple slices.
4. Roll out top crust into a 10-inch circle. Cut into 8 (1-inch) wide strips with a sharp paring knife or pastry wheel. Weave the pastry strips, one at a time, into a lattice pattern. Fold the ends of the lattice strips under the edge of the bottom crust and crimp to seal.
5. Pour butter-sugar mixture over top of pie, coating the lattice, and allowing any remaining sauce to drizzle through the crust.
6. Bake in the preheated oven for 15 minutes. Reduce heat to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C), and bake until the crust is golden brown, the caramel on the top crust is set, and the apple filling is bubbling, 35 to 40 more minutes. Allow to cool completely before slicing.

A challenging RPG that has a lot going for it. Divinity doesn't hold your hand to help you learn more about itself, and at times that can become frustrating for getting ahold of some of the game's mechanics, namely crafting and knowing where to go to progress quests. That being said, I really do enjoy this game for its interesting and challenging combat, and how it lets you play the game the way you want to play. If you want to rob every person you see, Divinity doesn't care, go ahead; you want to be the benevolent paladin who smites all evil, "good for you" says Divinity as it patiently waits.
I think the best way to describe Divinity is to compare it to tabletop RPGs, Divinity is the gamemaster who has created a beautifully in depth world for its players to muck about in, and it's because of this similarity that really draws me to it. Like most tabletop RPGs, I do find that this game really shines when played co-operatively, because at the start of the game, you start with two characters to create, and one of the ways Divinity tries to immerse its players is by giving the players chances to roleplay these characters in sets of scripted dialogue, and I find it hard to immerse myself while trying to roleplay both of these characters at the same time.
All in all, this game works best co-operatively, and, while difficult to get the hang of, is a brilliant RPG for hardcore RPG fans.

Definitely one of the best indie games I've ever played.
First up: The artwork - Wow. Just wow. The animation doesn't need to be complex for the actual appearance of this game to be incredible.
Furthermore, the game has an enjoyable story (including a dialogue that always rhymes, except with one character who is a bit...challenged in this regard).
Now as for the actual gameplay mechanics, this game has one of the best turn-based combat systems for an immersive Pokemon/Final Fantasy style of fighting. Yet at the same time it's different, because whoever is playing as Igniculus the Firefly has a completely different type of support element to play that can completely change the casting/waiting aspect of the combat and can allow for some seriously tactical team-playing to occur. Everybody moves along the timeline at different speeds, and every power has a different casting speed for the pre-set casting zone of the timeline. If you hit or get hit while in the casting zone your spell or attack is interrupted and you're knocked back on the timeline. Your little firefly bro can also turn the tides because he can slow the rate of casting and timeline movement of your enemies, or heal you, all at the cost of Light (effectively his health bar).
Pros:
Incredible artwork
Enjoyable storyline
Can be enjoyed either casually or on a much more intense difficulty level
PC specs don't really matter too much
Very original and ingenious tactical turn-based combat system
Plenty of hidden collectibles to find
Local Co-op (yay!), provided somebody doesn't mind playing as a firefly
8 or 9 different playable characters, all with completely different skills at your disposal (don't underestimate the support characters!)
A very useful crafting system
Cons:
Playing as the firefly might get boring if you don't enjoy working together (often rather humourously with running commentary) with your player 1
The game only takes about 12-15 hours to complete (although there is a new game+ mode)
If you don't like cinematics, your patience will definitely be tested. Think Kingdom Hearts.
You have to use Uplay
Overall: I'd suggest buying this game if you want a light-hearted, genuinely fun game to play. A solid 8.5/10

It’s been a long road for Grim Dawn in its travels to full release from its Kickstarter debut nearly four years ago and my, has it been enjoyable. Looking at my Steam account, I have just a hair under 50 hours clocked since buying it.
Grim Dawn is the first game to come from Crate Entertainment, but make no mistake, this is not some amateur dev team. Founded by Arthur Bruno (the mastermind behind Titan Quest) and created from the ashes of Iron Lore Entertainment, Crate have taken the Titan Quest formula, updated it for 2016, prayed heavily to the Old Gods for influence, and delivered a Lovecraft-themed ARPG that’s of a calibre that we simply don’t see anymore. Make no mistake; Grim Dawn is a game, not a theorycrafting playground as so many ARPGs seem to be as of late. There is a beginning and an end; and that’s a good thing.
It’s no surprise, really, that we’d get a new-age game with a decidedly old-school feel. Crate’s roster reads as a sort of who’s who of classic ARPG and Dungeon Crawler devs. Only, here, there’s an overwhelming wealth of story that’s been written into the game—an unusual addition for a lootgrind kind of game. And this, I feel, is what allows Grim Dawn to truly shine. Unlike so many other ARPGS, which focus on creating a playground for character builds, rather than an adventure for a player, Grim Dawn focuses heavily on its bleak and beautifully crafted world. With the story taking place shortly after the start of the apocalypse brought on by the crazies (Aetherial possessions) and the summoning of hordes of Ch’Thonian demons by end-times cultists who serve the game’s equivalent of The Great Old Ones, Grim Dawn drops the player into a world that is already beyond saving.
Even the player character starts the game in the gallows with the folks of Devil’s Crossing (a makeshift shelter in a prison), attempting to destroy the Aetherial that has possessed him or her (Spoiler Alert: Being Aethertouched makes you awesome). So begins your desperate struggle to make the lives of those around you but a little more bearable, while attempting to piece together what actually happened to the world of Cairn. Interestingly, though, this story isn’t forced on the player and is instead told primarily through notes and books that must be sought out, meaning players that want to just get on with the ham-smashing can do so in peace.
And when it comes to smiting the wicked, the game has done an excellent job of providing options without muddying up the experience. Each of the classes: Soldier, Nightblade, Shaman, Demolitionist, Arcanist, and Ocultist, can be mixed with any one other to provide a wealth of cross-class opportunities, and unlike other games to do this (including Titan Quest, from which the idea was borrowed), there’s an incredible amount of support for the various builds through the game’s itemization. Beyond this, the game’s Devotion system, which allows points earned from restoring sacred shrines to be invested in star sign constellations, allows for further character development, specialization, and stop-gappage in struggling character builds.
There’s a huge amount of attention that’s been paid to giving players control over their characters and creating a genuine sense of cause and effect in the game’s decisions. Sometimes it can mean the death of innocents, or a betrayal from within, or even a quicker route through the game’s story, but choices always have an impact.
This notion of cause and effect is perhaps best represented through the game’s reputation system. Positive reputation with factions unlocks increasingly more powerful loot and item modifications from vendors, in addition to the usual shop discounts. Negative reputation on the other hand, increases enemy spawns, hero spawns, and eventually causes the dreaded Nemesis spawns—one of Grim Dawn’s forms of endgame content. Oh, and some of the factions are mutually exclusive, so choose wisely.
The inclusion of a Veteran Mode for advanced players adds more challenge and life for those of us seeking more of a tactile and tactical experience beyond the mindless smashing and slashing. Of course, Hardcore Mode is also on offer, changing the focus of the game from hack ‘n’ slash into a more methodical, defensively-minded experience—just ask my lvl 84 Blademaster, the 17th of his line.
With the recent update of many of the game’s visuals to even further sell the story through the environment, and a bewitchingly fitting soundtrack, Grim Dawn is one of the easiest ARPGs to recommend in recent years. It’s every bit as beautiful to behold and fun to play as it is sombre and brutally difficult. If it weren’t for the occasional desync issues in multiplayer (an issue I expect will get some love post-launch), Grim Dawn, with all its story and diversity of supported playstyles (in addition to its full mod support) would be just about the perfect A-to-B ARPG.

I used to play a free South Park dress up game when I was a little kid (yes I was one of those kids allowed to watch South Park and other "adult" cartoons), so I got all nosalgic when I got to dress up and create my own South Park character. Unlike the flash game I played way back in 2000, this game has way more outfits and colours for your character and their clothing.
This game has that charming "these are 8/9 yearolds playing pretend in their backyards" feel to it, that had me going "awe, that's so cute!" or "Poor [character name]!" everytime I was reminded that the South Park kids are just that, kids. The plot and other parts of this game is very South Park, as their is a lot of events that seem a bit outlandish for the real world to happen and are beyond the kids' control, due to the adults being stupid, the Visitors making their presence known, or Gnomes (who are one of my favorite characters in the show) stealing your underwear at night.
Though the problems I have with this game is:
1) The "adult/real world" plot overshadows the fantasy game the kids are playing very quickly:
You don't get to spend much time learning about their fictional imagined world of "Zaron", aside from the 2 factions Humans and Elves, and their "Kings" don't like eachother.
You very quickly are no longer playing against either the Humans or Elves, no matter what side you take, as the adult plot adds enimies you fight instead. (I chose to side with Kyle, only beacuse I like him more than Cartman orignally, but was disappointed that I couldn't fight Humans like Tweek or Scott as the orignal fantasy plot ends too soon. Though I was happy to at least face Craig.)
Finally, in my honest opinon the "adult/real world" plot sucks. I'm not very interested in Nazi Zombies or the goverment's stupidity over dealing with the outbreak. It only distracts you from your role as a innocent little kid playing a fantasy game with your new friends. It breaks the "role playing" part of the RPG you originally are playing and shoves you into an entirely different role, with little warning that it was going to happen. Although hinted at by your parents you have a bigger stake in the world of South Park proper, the storyline dosen't allow time for you to adjust or balance out from playing pretend to real life.
Which leads me to:
2) The game is too short.
This game had a lot of potential to be longer and more thought out, than it was. It feels like lots of content was cut out, incomplete, or even missed. Even though this game was delayed and what not during production for reasons, it was obvious that story and quests wasn't one of these reasons. It felt more like I was watching a interactive movie rather than playing a RPG, lenght only being found in hopes the puzzles were too unclear or extreamly easy fights would last longer. (I found myself just punching Elves and Zombies, just to add more playtime.)
There are over 150 weapons and outfits for your character to use and wear. None of these outfits or weapons are locked by your character class, so you can just choose what is the strongest (or simply your favorite look). Unfortunately do the length of the game, you recive the collectable equipment (the equipment you do not buy from the shops) too quickly to be of any use for any lenght of time. Just got all the pecies of Squire or Durid costume? Well here is your upgraded Theif's gear Commander! Along with a new weapon to relace th cool one you just picked up!
It feels like this game could have spent more time in "Zaron", before the Visitors show up to start the Nazi Zombie out break.
Also the plot with the girls joining the boys in their game, they could have been a little more involved with the boys' RPG than just
Generally the fact that you are just a kid trying to have fun and make friends, could have been explored a bit more than it was.
The adult/real workd plot" also could have been expanded on. Even though I'm not a big fan of the inclusion of the Zombies or who they were being delt with, the game could have explored this concept a bit more than it was. Of couse, bing a kid, your not supposed to know all the details of this plotline, as your not supposed to be important to it. But, you do see cut-scenes and things that, you as the main character, would have no ability to know about. Which is why this game is more like a movie than an RPG.
You do not learn these details organicly or by serching yourself. Instead it's directly presented to you as if your character was present/easdropping. From a movie/TV show stand point, this makes sense, but from a gaming stand point it's a bit unrealistic for you to know about these events in the way they were presented to you. (Of course there are RPGs that do present you with infomation that your character couldn't have possibly witnessed, to forward the plot, But, usually this is done because their was no other possible way for you as a player to learn of these details otherwise. In this game theri felt like their was no need for these details to be done as such. Visually their are parts where you as a player would immedately reconize what is happening.)
Basically the problem is, the transiton and flow of the two plotlines, feels choppily placed and as if it was designed for a movie, rather than a game. Events happen too quickly, the plot moves too fast for a game, and the worlds are not fleahed out as they should have for an RPG. The game relys too heavily on you being a fan of South Park or at least being familluar with most of the shows episodes to understand who the characters are, what their universe is like, and why all of this is apparently normal for them (ie, why the adults are such idiots).
This game relys too much on the charm and tropes South Park has created over the years, which it would make players unfamilluar with South Park TV series, a bit confused or lost. The characters might just appear to be rude and boring, filled with tastless fart jokes and swearing. (This is at least according to my brother who has barely started the game, thought.) Without the exensive knowlage of South Park beyond seasons 1 and 2, this game also might just be ignored, as the tone of South Park has change greatly after the 4th season and this game takes a lot of cues and content from the show post 4th season.
In conclusion, well I personally enjoyed the costomization do to childhood nostalgia and being able to play with most of the South Park cast I love. The game is too short and abrupt in plot for the concept it was built on, and felt too much like I was just watching another episode of the show rather than playing a part in it. The story is also so dependant on prior knowlegde of South Park as a TV show, it's hard of this game to stand out as a seprate peice of content, which would make first time players who have not watched the show, confused and lost. Even though I know this is more of a promotional game for the South Park TV show, the game does not have much to offer in inspireing new consumers to go watch the show it's based on. In fact, it feels more like extra bonus content for people already fans of the show.

NOTE: a review copy was provided for this game, but as any good journalist says, that has not influenced my opinion of the game in any way.
Probably the most complex hack and slash aRPG I've ever played.  It layers on its systems in an easy-to-grasp way but contains unbelievable depth.  Master a single class or combine 2 different ones and you have a ridiculous number of builds to work with, helped along by skill trees with drastically varying kings of player abilities.  Graphically, it resembles what Diablo 2 might look like had it been made in 2015: very dark, both in tone and themes, with lots of grotesque enemies to kill.
The game is also paced a bit more slowly than other similar games, like Torchlight 1&2 and Diablo 3.  I've spent about 40 hours on my main character's campaign, yet I'm only in the second of three difficulties.  This is because the world is huge and the game is LONG.  The fact that the world isn't 100% random does a lot for allowing a gigantic world that has interesting secrets tucked away, rather than random events that don't always hit the mark or long stretches of terrain with nothing interesting.  Each player's world will be slightly different, but the overall layout remains the same, and I love the way this system has been implemented.  It's the kind of thing that couldn't easily be done with completely random generation: you'll find packs of friendly NPCs out in the overworld, certain side quests back into corners, and much more.
There is a potential downside to all the depth: while there is always lots to do with countless goals of varying sizes, you might find yourself overwhelmed.  All items can be improved with random drop items called components, and there are nearly 100 of them to find.  While this means that you can always use a component suitable to your build and needs, you may be at a loss if you need to find a specific component.  Sometimes you must find the blueprint to craft that component, while other times they drop from certain types of enemies (but WHICH enemies is information not found in the game).  The best advice I can give is to be liberal with your use of the Grim Dawn Wiki, which has tons of information that makes understanding the game much more manageable.
In a nutshell, there are tons of complex systems at work:
--extensive crafting system with random drop blueprints
--components and augments to add new stats to equipment
--factions you can align with or fight, which will open new quests and vendors, but also spawn more bosses of the enemy faction in the game world
--Skill trees with lots of different abilities to consider (but you can respec these points quite easily and cheaply, no limit)
--"Devotion" system, another layer of character progression, adds stats and abilities that any class can use (based on a gigantic constellation chart that you fill in as you play)
--8 different kinds of damage (so you can either build into a certain type or get wrecked by an enemy using damage that you have very low resistance for)
--3 different difficulties for a very long and detailed campaign mode
--Endgame randomized dungeons
In short, you will feel like you have absolute freedom to build your character the way you want.  You will get lost in the game world, the deep mechanics, and the interesting cause-and-effect relationships they have.  You will be addicted even as you get smashed into a pulp over and over.
You will love it.

The Banner Saga... Where to begin? I've made many choices,lived and survived to regret it...yet....it had to be done... The game has such a great story and great atmosphere. Decisions you make in the game are crucial and may haunt you or bite you in the back later. I was playing the good guy.... Accepted or helped as many people as I could along the way. Perhaps it was due to the low morale from our dwindling food supplies... or was it my leadership? I was accused of letting anybody from the road join the caravan. There was mistrust and there was alot of squabbling amongst the clansmen.
My logic was this: The common enemy was the dredge. No point fighting amongst ourselves.
And that was how i rolled throughout the whole game. Pretty much like Game of Throne's Nights Watch style. I'd willingly accept anyone whose willing to join and help those that decide to stay, despite their lost cause. I've made a few good friends that way, lost a few too.
The ending...I think I made the right choice. Though sad, but I felt that whatever that had happened, the great journey, was all just to get that 1 character to the end. Bittersweet indeed.

I've sunk 117 hours into this game. It's a ten buck indie game, I know what you're thinking. But FTL simply has so much to offer I don't even know how to describe it.
The game gives you a good challenge, which you can tone down with the 3 difficulty levels. The recent update has added new races to the already diverse set as well as adding a new ship and a new ship layout for *all 9 other ships*, totalling 10 ships each with 3 significantly different layouts.
The combat is fun, the choices make you feel like there's risk and weight behind every click, and beating the final boss instills a feeling of glory and accomplishment no matter how many times you get there. Because in FTL, the feeling of success doesn't come from having said, "I played for 8 hours and beat the campaign! Cool!" but instead from, "Well, I tried 5 times but I finally got my strategy down, got some lucky events, and won! Let's try out this ship..."
One other note is the fantastic music score by Ben Prunty - it's worth listening to again and again and its clever presentation (the background music grows violent and tense seamlessly as soon as you engage in combat) make the music all the more enjoyable. Seriously, it got nominated for best music of the year, it's pretty damn nice.
The visuals aren't exactly Crysis, but the cool ship models, laser cannons, and background planets all add a sense of immersion along with the game's hud, flashing as the shields fall or as the FTL drive is ready to make your escape.
If anything, I would highly recommend this game. It's simply a fantastic game and deserves to be recognized. This game is so good I'd want to gift it over and over to everyone that I can simply because it's an incredible experience. Go ahead, get this one. You won't be disappointed.

The positive reviews of the game before 2016 are no longer accurate, because it isn't the same game.  The original game was a beautiful classic, a perfectly oiled machine.  That game isn't available anymore.  The best way I could describe it is, originally you had a PC game, and they replaced it with a mobile port version of the game.  How else can you explain the game running worse than it used to?   And I'm not talking about fps, I mean the game feels inferior while playing it.
The character you control doesn't handle as well as it once did, the game is not as fluid and responsive as it once was.  The character's perfect responsiveness to your button pressing was the whole point, and that was ruined.  These issues were really really bad when their big update first arrived and people reported and a lot of people including myself noted that we were unable to achieve scores even a quarter as high as we usually did due to poor control responsiveness and other odd shifts to gameplay.  The developers have been slowly trying to fix these issues piecemeal, but so far I still don't feel they have managed to completly repair what they broke.
There were a lot of calls for bringing back the original game, at least as a classic mode.  I notice that those forum posts appear to all be gone, though I don't know if they were deleted or simply are no longer accessible from being a couple months old.  Needless to say, all cries for a classic mode were ignored, and the developer passed out some free keys to some smartphone port game in hopes of silencing things.
I paid money for a game and felt I had gotten more than my money's worth.  Then the developers took that game away and replaced it with something inferior, and while it's close, it's still deep in the uncanny valley.  I can't recommend to anyone what is still just a pale imitation of what was once here.
