One Sentence Review:  Hey look, someone made a bad rip off of a Silver Dollar Game.
Three Sentence Review:  One Finger Death Punch is an excellent game.  You should buy that instead.  It has better mechanics and less bugs.
More In-Depth Review
Take One-Finger Death Punch.  Now remove about 75% of it, and replace stick-men with sprites that have 3-4 attacks in total each.  What you've got left is Kung Fury: Street Rage.  It's not even really graphically superior because of that broken old arcade-machine look they implemented, which gives me more eyestrain than nostalgia.
One Finger Death Punch lets you configure your fighter by selecting 3 skills from a large selection and they all impact the game significantly.  There are also a variety of enemies with different abilities.
Kung Fury: Street Rage has 4 characters.  One standard (no abilities but is the best because said abilities are janky), and then three others with two things that set them apart.  So already a lot less selection than OFDP in terms of variety.  For the most part, you're going to want to stick with the standard as the other three have either crippled health, mechanics that can throw off your rhythm, or both.  Your enemy selection is down to 5 types - standard 1 hit, standard 2 hit, 3-hit dodger, stanard 4 hit, and one guy that takes 5 with a different pattern.  Compare to OFDP which also has a 4-hit dodger, 4 hit standard, brawler, type-switching boss, wackloads of special moves, and a  variety of distinct styles of play.
OFDP has helpful guides and information on its screen.  Kung Fury does not.
OFDP has some really nice musical tracks.  Kung Fury does not.
The only thing that Kung Fury has that OFDP doesn't is a unique boss mode, and that's implemented so poorly it's not a positive thing.  While the core of OFDP is about elminiating positioning and button mashing in favour of precise timing, the boss mode suddenly has you moving about and mashing buttons to survive... but the collisions aren't handled well at all (which is terrible considering the whole 2-button game play is about precision) and the last boss fight was prone to bugging out.
All this could be forgiven if it weren't for the fact that OFDP is already a bargain at full price and offers a lot more game.  By itself it isn't terrible, but considering there's already a game out there that does everything this one except it does it better, bigger and came out first... just get OFDP.  Street Rage won't offer any new experiences.
Fun battle system that keeps you on your toes along with a sweet story and likable characters.  Thumbs up.

[My 14 hours represents approximately 8 for the main campaign and 6 for a conquest campaign. I feel this to be representative of the gameplay available, as multiplayer has become defunct.]
SWB2 rather compellingly puts the player in the shoes of the clone soldiers who served first the Republic in a series of battles with the droid-fielding Trade Federation and later fought against the rebels under service to the Emperor. This story is presented well in a series of pre-mission briefings narrated capably by Temuera Morrison (Jango Fett/[questionably] Boba Fett). There is little moralising in the tale, which pits the clones♥♥♥♥♥Stormtroopers as forces of order against forces of chaos and criminality.
Rather than present the player with a conflict in story, the ambition of SWB2 is to present the famous (and often mentioned only in passing) battles in Imperial history in more or less realistic scale, with dozens of NPCs in constant combat with one another around the player at all times. This ambition is partially, but never fully, realised.
The successes of the gameplay are few, but strong. Playing as Darth Vader aboard the Tantive IV, guiding an AT-AT across the icy fields of Hoth, and destroying a Victory frigate (at least the first time) are tremendously fun experiences. While in canon, Leia was stunned by a stormtrooper without much of a fight, in SWB2, I had Darth Vader fly in from fifty paces away and bisect her with his lightsaber (she got better, apparently.) My AT-AT guidance was no less fine than that of General Veers himself, and I was surprised (and pleased) to see a clip from SW:ESB showing the destruction of the shield generator on Hoth when I finally took it out- although this was not a matter of 'Target: Maximum Firepower'. Flying through space (rather strangely, in a transport vehicle with an open-to-the-atmosphere design) and destroying the shields and laughably slim defenses of an Imperial Star Destroyer was diverting during the Rebel campaign.
But the failures and omissions are more, and they grow more glaring with time. Narrative gaps aside- this is the campy Sci Fi-that-is-really-Fantasy of Star Wars, after all- what SWB2 most strongly lacks in consistently engaging combat. Much, if not most, of this issue is a direct symptom of age. The engine cannot support enough intelligent enemies (and, more glaringly at times, allies) to provide an experience in line with its ambitions. While there may be a half-dozen enemy troops in front of the player, they will seldom do anything more than approach head-on and submit to a spray of rapid laser blasts. Meanwhile, enemies rather cheaply respawn immediately in front of the player at times, while allies seldom follow effectively as the player moves to take objectives, which frequently forces the player to go it alone and strafe madly in an effort to survive long enough (as the last trooper alive) to reach the next reinforcement checkpoint.
I seldom felt as though I was one soldier among many fighting on the same side. More often, I was THE soldier, like Rambo, responsible for killing 90% or more of the enemy force and completing all of the objectives alone. At no point did it seem like  I could rely on my fellows for anything besides meat shielding, if that.
Further, I found myself relying on the Engineer class for most of my play, as it is the only class that can heal itself away from a medical droid. While other classes were not useless, their damage dealing potential seemed about the same across the board, which meant that the Engineer had a permanent edge. This balancing issue meant that the already slim number of game mechanics became slimmer in practical gameplay.
In all, I can't recommend SWB2. It fails to provide more than a couple hours of fun gaming, and these are interspersed with a great deal of tedium. The four special galactic campaigns are dramatically more tedius than the regular story campaign, with frequently repeated battles on worlds like Dagobah and Kashyyk that are interesting the first time and unchanged (and boring) each time afterward.

I feel Mirrors Edge is a classic in its own self. Albeit the game came out not too long ago back in 2008. But a sequel came out just last year and thats one of the reasons i'm writing this review, but im pretty late to the party. Now, people consider this as an FPS game, but I really don't feel it is. You use guns, you shoot things, but not always. I consider it as a platformer, as thats the most you do. I love games where you are immensely capable of anything, and Mirror's edge is just that. You can wallride, climb, fight, do absolutely anything. And a high quality game such as this is rare for EA. It's a must have gem for me. I honestly do feel better that the game would be significantly better if it were an open world. They went through all this trouble to plan an elaborate city, yet they only use probably a third of it. Say you were on your way to the Callaghan office, and you had to take the sewers as a shortcut like in the Jacknife level. That kind of gameplay of just exploring the large city and avoiding the cops would be amazing. But the current gameplay is good as it is. And I feel they made it a campaign because they had to set the runners vision. The characters and story is amazing, One of the rare games that I actually watched and enjoyed the cutscenes. Typically, I don't do that. I really liked the transfer between the game and the very uniquely done 2D animations. It made it feel like movie. Speaking about movies, the animation in this is... (and all caps is coming here) PHENOMENAL. An first person game is supposed to be just that. First person. Therefore, you have to see through their eyes and etcetera. Most games you only see the gun and arms. However, this one gets the headbobs down, you can see your body if you look down far enough, and it really feels like a real thing. If a Mirrors Edge VR were made, I would buy it and play it until my eyes bleed. It was what you really desired to see in a first person game. Aside from that, I just have little tidbits to note about. I do feel that more settings were neccessary, as the FOV of the game was a bit iffy. It hurt my eyes a little bit and set me off. And maybe more display settings would be helpful, because the city is white, but its... Too white. Even at any brightness it would come off as too bright or immensely dark. I don't know if this effect is because of the FOV, but still. But aside from that, the game is fabulous.
8.5/10

PREFACE: I would consider myself a "casual" gamer, usually only having 2-3 hours a week to give to playing games. I admittedly have not played a Western RPG since Diablo 2.  It seems to me that there are a lot of modern gameplay tropes that the player is expected to be familiar within order to fully enjoy Divinity: Original Sin.
I had a very difficult time understanding what to do. There are an incredibly large number of people/places/things to interact within the first hour of the game. There are also many gameplay features (recipes, repairing equipment, skills, etc.) all given to the player at once. These CAN be strengths, but I found myself overwhelmed with the options and did not have a clear direction towards "what I'm supposed to do". I'm sure these features can make a very engaging experience when the player understands them well, but I did not. After a few hours of play I eventually gave up.
On the positive side, I found the writing and voice acting very impressive. All of the dialogue is well thought out - even among the most insignificant townsfolk.
This game may be great for you if you are willing to invest the time and you are familiar with this flavor of RPG. However, if you are a casual gamer such as myself you may have a difficult time getting into it.

It is the DLC and so I don't really think it impacts the main game but thought I'd mention it. There is an update in one month so this is written in January 2016. This is currently my favorite offline game. Anytime my usual addictions are unavailable, I always head straight for FTL and tackle another playthrough. This game is easily worth the $10 USD price tag, if not more. The recent expansion pack only adds to this value, and I almost feel guilty for not paying for so much content. It could have easily been a $5 DLC.
FTL is a roguelite space simulation game developed by Subset Games. It features perma-death, realtime strategy with the ability to pause and give orders, randomized level design, and nearly endless replay value.
Starting off with the tutorial, you'll get a quick briefing of the plot and objective, followed by a rundown of the UI. After jumping to the next location, you'll find your first battle which offers some helpful tips like using missiles to take out enemy shield systems. After combat, upgrade your ships reactor and weapon system and you're all set. The whole tutorial takes about 5 minutes. If you can't be bothered with 5 minutes, skip it. You can mouse-over just about everything for detailed tooltips at any point in the game.
My biggest, and only notable, gripe with this game is that it doesn't support Steam Achievements. I find this very odd since it has it's own in-game achievements not recognized by Steam.

South Park meets Skyrim in a flamboyant fashion and holds up well in 2017.
Almost every aspect of Stick of Truth is unique to this game, no quest is like another and never did I worry about doing the same thing over and over, there are no classic fetch-and-run-quests either and the game does a good job providing you reason to complete a specific task.
As a tie-in to the (in)famous TV series every chapter is filled with insider jokes and characters you will have at least heard of at some point in your life and even if you aren't a die-hard South Park fan there will be plenty of content to amuse yourself on. Even the censoring of Swastika and certain Nazi-handsigns in the European version only adds to the Charme of Matt & Tray saying "Eff you, ESRB" though I would have preferred to make my own choice about the censoring but luckily there is unofficial patches available should the need arise.
The story is linear (2-3 hours) but through the open-world factor and the amount of unique quests the playtime extends to at least another 20 hours. I myself took 25 hours to complete the Storyquest, the second time around I went for some achievements I had missed and noticed I could simply complete the Mainstory and did so in a short Marathon. I will be giving the new South Park game a shot too.

One thing I really like in ARPGs is when you could play a "Pet Master" - simply summoning and directing your own wild bunch to take care of business while enjoying the scenery and hunting treasures. Grim Dawn is no stranger to that and it's a blast.
I got the game in early access, so I had plenty of time to try out the classes, their flavor and several mix of them (a nice reminder of Titan Quest, that is still one of my favorite game).
And once the game was finally released, it came with a new class, the Shaman, that just perfectly complement the Occultist to suit my shameless laid-back * style of play.
So, if you want to give it a try, here are the foundations : start with the Occultist and develop the Familiar and Hellhound branches ; when you reach level 10, jump to the Shaman and go for the Briarthorn branch. You can complement these three with one or two other skills you might find useful or enjoyable. For the devotions, start with Shepherd's Crook.
The balance between "class" and "skill" levels is up to you. On my own, I usually spend 2 points in the Class (for character stats) and 1 point a Skill ; and sometimes saving points for later. But with the Spirit Guide that can help you re-spec your skills, you can do as you please.
What you will do most of the time is send your creatures to scout places and eventually attract or attack foes. So bind a key with Pet Attack and be sure that at least Hellhound then Briarthorn are set to Aggressive. What you choose to do with you character (close combat, ranged combat...) is up to you since it matters only 5 to 10% of the time ; you really can experiment here with any combination of weapons, armors and components.
Nevertheless, since no "build" is made perfect, you might encounter some resistance with "infuriated" enemies than can steal a percentage of your pets' health (thus creating a stasis in combat) ; and of course, champions and bosses - not mentioning, champions that can summon infuriated creatures.
* Some might say that this style of play is not very ARPG-y since you don't have to frantically click your mouse to hit enemies like in the good old days, but merely give orders to your faithful minions to carry on the good word. Well, since I've been playing ARPGs since Diablo, I consider this style of play a well deserved treat.

[My 14 hours represents approximately 8 for the main campaign and 6 for a conquest campaign. I feel this to be representative of the gameplay available, as multiplayer has become defunct.]
SWB2 rather compellingly puts the player in the shoes of the clone soldiers who served first the Republic in a series of battles with the droid-fielding Trade Federation and later fought against the rebels under service to the Emperor. This story is presented well in a series of pre-mission briefings narrated capably by Temuera Morrison (Jango Fett/[questionably] Boba Fett). There is little moralising in the tale, which pits the clones♥♥♥♥♥Stormtroopers as forces of order against forces of chaos and criminality.
Rather than present the player with a conflict in story, the ambition of SWB2 is to present the famous (and often mentioned only in passing) battles in Imperial history in more or less realistic scale, with dozens of NPCs in constant combat with one another around the player at all times. This ambition is partially, but never fully, realised.
The successes of the gameplay are few, but strong. Playing as Darth Vader aboard the Tantive IV, guiding an AT-AT across the icy fields of Hoth, and destroying a Victory frigate (at least the first time) are tremendously fun experiences. While in canon, Leia was stunned by a stormtrooper without much of a fight, in SWB2, I had Darth Vader fly in from fifty paces away and bisect her with his lightsaber (she got better, apparently.) My AT-AT guidance was no less fine than that of General Veers himself, and I was surprised (and pleased) to see a clip from SW:ESB showing the destruction of the shield generator on Hoth when I finally took it out- although this was not a matter of 'Target: Maximum Firepower'. Flying through space (rather strangely, in a transport vehicle with an open-to-the-atmosphere design) and destroying the shields and laughably slim defenses of an Imperial Star Destroyer was diverting during the Rebel campaign.
But the failures and omissions are more, and they grow more glaring with time. Narrative gaps aside- this is the campy Sci Fi-that-is-really-Fantasy of Star Wars, after all- what SWB2 most strongly lacks in consistently engaging combat. Much, if not most, of this issue is a direct symptom of age. The engine cannot support enough intelligent enemies (and, more glaringly at times, allies) to provide an experience in line with its ambitions. While there may be a half-dozen enemy troops in front of the player, they will seldom do anything more than approach head-on and submit to a spray of rapid laser blasts. Meanwhile, enemies rather cheaply respawn immediately in front of the player at times, while allies seldom follow effectively as the player moves to take objectives, which frequently forces the player to go it alone and strafe madly in an effort to survive long enough (as the last trooper alive) to reach the next reinforcement checkpoint.
I seldom felt as though I was one soldier among many fighting on the same side. More often, I was THE soldier, like Rambo, responsible for killing 90% or more of the enemy force and completing all of the objectives alone. At no point did it seem like  I could rely on my fellows for anything besides meat shielding, if that.
Further, I found myself relying on the Engineer class for most of my play, as it is the only class that can heal itself away from a medical droid. While other classes were not useless, their damage dealing potential seemed about the same across the board, which meant that the Engineer had a permanent edge. This balancing issue meant that the already slim number of game mechanics became slimmer in practical gameplay.
In all, I can't recommend SWB2. It fails to provide more than a couple hours of fun gaming, and these are interspersed with a great deal of tedium. The four special galactic campaigns are dramatically more tedius than the regular story campaign, with frequently repeated battles on worlds like Dagobah and Kashyyk that are interesting the first time and unchanged (and boring) each time afterward.

Either way, Little Nightmares! To the bad parts. The controls are really bad at times. The depth perception is off and sometimes you die because of this. Especially in the areas when you are being hunted by something and need to do precision jumping. Rendering in really annoying deaths. Also the stealth mechanic is rather shallow compared to other titles. By that I mean other stealth titles which can be very high budget. So take it with a pinch of "well its not a tripple A game" excuse.
The price is bit steep considering how short it is but this is one of those games that gives you double the time of a movie and do not cost much more. It is very cinematic in how it looks, the grim enviroments and the sad story behind it all which is a bit, to me, covered in a heavy mist. But what one understand is that this place is bad and I had a genuine hope for the protagonist to be able to survive and get out.
The game looks fantastic, the sound is okay and I think it is well worth buying on a sale or if you are really into this kind of light stealth, light puzzle kind of games with a pretty interesting style to it with really morbid enviroments and grotesque "monsters" hunting you. I would call it a stealth-puzzle horror game which focus on enviromental storytelling and creating a feeling of dread and "wtf is going on here?".
Even if I did not enjoy the controls always and found the stealth mechanic to be pretty simplistic, "Walk in the open, get seen always, hide under table, be not seen" kind of depth to it, I still enjoyed the game. I am not sure I would have endured a 20 hour game like this either way so the 4 hours I got out of it was okay, perhaps bit to short for some. I heard it can be finished under 1,5 hour.
I still recommend it for those who enjoy this kind of game. The odd look of the game is what pulled me in.

The game has two modes:  Endless and Storyline.  Endless allows you to pick any of the playable characters and go into a series of wave after wave of mobs against you until you die.  Storyline has a little more meat to it with a certain number of waves needed to be completed before facing off against the end boss of that stage.  It also only allows you to play the character for that particular chapter in the storyline.

I recommend this game to anyone that likes a good action arcade style game.  At times I almost felt like I needed to slide another quarter into a slot when I died.  However, the gameplay can become repititive and I recommend playing this game in short bursts.  In the end, the game is definitely worth the price and an immediate pickup if discounted.

FTL is a roguelite space simulation game developed by Subset Games. It features perma-death, realtime strategy with the ability to pause and give orders, randomized level design, and nearly endless replay value.
Starting off with the tutorial, you'll get a quick briefing of the plot and objective, followed by a rundown of the UI. After jumping to the next location, you'll find your first battle which offers some helpful tips like using missiles to take out enemy shield systems. After combat, upgrade your ships reactor and weapon system and you're all set. The whole tutorial takes about 5 minutes. If you can't be bothered with 5 minutes, skip it. You can mouse-over just about everything for detailed tooltips at any point in the game.
My biggest, and only notable, gripe with this game is that it doesn't support Steam Achievements. I find this very odd since it has it's own in-game achievements not recognized by Steam.

In addition, the control system is really buggy and clunky. I've stolen things numerous times without meaning to (could we move this action to another button combination like ALT + Click or something to prevent this from happening?) and my NPCs have started fights by wandering where they should not. It's like playing GTA with cheats turned on, except it doesn't get boring after 2 minutes because the "cheats" are part of the game.

Slightly more polished Titan Quest. Good game for 100 hours gameplay, Past that mark you will either have to fall in love with the game or you will stop playing.
I find problematic the fact of fixed layout for zones with randomly placed road blocks which makes you choose other path from time to time. But otherwise it's still the same. Going trhough 3 dificulties becomes kinda borring. I guess it is a price for more polished graphics and posibility to rotate camera.
Another thing i don't like is the itemization. Probably too many stats to my taste (was also in TQ). Charbound / soulbound items and crafting mats is also pretty annoying, which made me give up on re-leveling new char again, because of reputation reset and crafting mats reset.
Also i don't like speed cap and mob lvl scaling.
But there is hope, because mods can actually fix a lot of things i don't like. Except the necesity to go through game 2 times to unlock ultimate. Useless skills will get eventually modified which will increase limited build variety. But it will require quite a lot of time and active modding scene. So far it is 2 weeks since release of the toolkit, there are already some decent mods outhere, but there is potential for bigger overhaul.
Summary
Pros
- great graphics
- different game pace compared to some other ARPGs on the market
- 1st playthough (50-100 hours)
- modding scene
Cons
- fixed layouts
- 3 difficulties you have to go though
- soulbound items and crafting mats
- many "useless" skills and stats with weird itemization and invisible effect
Despite the many things i don't like, i find Grim Dawn to be a great game for 25€. After some time there might be even bigger reason to pick up Grim Dawn because of the modding comunity.

Disclaimer: This is my first visual novel experience so some of my opinions below may be standards in the genre that I'm not familiar with.
This "game"? has sucked me in more than I thought it would. I'm not even sure how I ended up with it in my library to be honest. But one day I decided to load it up and the next thing I know, I was transported into the world of Sovionok. I made it through the first playthrough and the mystery of how I got there and what was happening was intriguing. I made it through Alisa's ending and then played through Alisa's good ending. Ok, a slight change of ending, I'll get through the rest of the endings quickly.
I swapped then to Lena's ending and saw a completely different ending. Wow. Ok. So, what else is there? How does the bad ending differ for Lena? Woah, that took a turn. I was amazed at how much things change based on the storyline of the character I was following. I started to learn more about each person and why they acted the way they do in other storylines. And then, I did the Miku storyline. Without spoiling anything too much, I don't think I've felt that way in a very long time.
Finally making it through the last two storylines, I look at my played time and it's at 15 hours. Wow. I've been reading and getting immersed in this novel for 15 hours. I think I'm addicted now. This game was amazing. Reading through, following characters, learning about them. The visuals are a plus, but get a bit repetitious over time. The music is amazing. You have the stereotypical anime girls with the usual personalities.
I'm sad my time at Sovionok is over. I feel an emptiness, the same as when I finish a long and fulfilling book. I will say that if you hate reading, you will not like this game. But if you do, you'll find an amazing journey in Sovionok and be unable to put it down for a long time.

I have become a big fan of Telltale's interactive story format, but this is the first time they have made a game in a franchise that I am already invested in. And it makes a world of difference. Even though
tells the story of a relatively minor house that has not appeared directly in the books or television show, I am already well acquainted with other characters and the politics of the world. This gives me a framework from which to base my interactions with these characters. Even if you are new to the series, they do a good job introducing characters with really obvious clues about their true nature. But really, you should read the books up through
or watch the show up through Season 3. Speaking of which, they have all the same actors voicing their characters from the show.
Now let's talk about the characters they have created specifically for the game. House Forrester seems to have been written very similarly to House Stark. They are from the north, they are honorable, and their members have been flung all over the world. It is obvious why they did this: everyone likes the Starks, and Telltale wants the player to like the people they are playing as. I'm a little disappointed that they couldn't find a better way to do that than to follow an established formula. Much like in the books, there are multiple characters whom the player controls. This is where having the characters flung across the world comes into play. As in the books or the show, there are quite a few characters to keep track of, so I recommend going into the game's codex before you start playing so you aren't totally lost.
While reading
, I had gotten so used to George RR Martin's tendency to pull the rug out from under the reader that I could predict when bad things or good things would happen. Thankfully the writers at Telltale didn't follow that formula, so I was legitimately surprised a few times throughout the episode.
The art style is gorgeous to behold. I was expecting it to be cel-shaded like their last four games, but instead everything looks as if it could be straight out of an oil painting. Objects in the background become slightly blurred, and characters' faces have a curious texture. The border between foreground and background objects had a strange shimmer where the blurring ended, which was a little distracting. But does it look good in screenshots or what? By far
is the best looking Telltale game to date.
The gameplay has moved farther away from puzzles and action sequences than even
. Carefully choosing dialogue options is the only meaningful action the player makes. If you do the wrong thing during one of the few action sequences, it is simply game over. It is quite difficult to fail that way.
I don't remember caring this much about the characters' lives I am affecting, even in
. I was so conflicted during dialogue that I sometimes let the time run out accidentally. If Telltale can keep up this level of quality,
will easily be my favorite game of theirs, and probably my favorite game of 2015. Iron from Ice!

The Banner Saga is an adventure game featuring basic RPG elements and a Norse/Viking theme, where the player leads a caravan of civilians and warriors across a wilderness while trying to escape constant attacks by a race of metallic creatures called Dredge.
There's an enjoyable turn based combat system that has some tactical depth. Battles take place on a square grid, and the player has a party of up to 6 warriors. You'll often start the fight outnumbered, but the movement order is similar to chess where the player moves one unit, then the AI moves one unit, and so on, which means having less units isn't necessarily a disadvantage.
Each warrior has two main characteristics - strength and armour. Strength represents both the amount of damage inflicted by a successful attack, and the health of the warrior. When strength reaches zero the warrior is knocked out of the fight, but it also means a warrior who is close to death will do less damage. Armour indicates how difficult it is to successfully damage a unit's strength - if their armour is higher than your strength, you probably won't hit, so sometimes you need to weaken the enemy's armour first before you can actually hurt them.
Positioning is also important. Varl (giants) take up 4 grid spaces instead of 1 and can easily block the movement of both friendly and enemy warriors. Archers have weaker armour so its a good idea to keep them behind melee units. My one complaint about the combat is the lack of variety. Pretty much every unit for both your side and the Dredge, is either melee or archer. There's hardly any offensive magic, and no healing, so most fights play out the same way from a tactical point of view.
Outside of combat you'll have choices to make when certain events happen. Most choices have consequences, which could be good or bad. For example you might encounter another group of people on the road who want to join you, and you can accept or refuse. If you accept, you might gain warriors, or they might steal some of your food. If you refuse, they might leave peacefully or they might just attack you.
The story is okay. It starts slow but gets better after a couple of hours. I never really cared about any of the Varl characters, their personalities didn't develop beyond "I'm a warrior and want to kill stuff", but I did like the main two Humans, Rook and Alette. Their father/daughter relationship at least gave me a reason to care about keeping them alive.
However, the game loses points for presentation. There are lots of nicely animated cutscenes of people walking in a straight line through the snow, but unfortunately as soon as any action happens, its either described by a wall of text, or through dialogue scenes between motionless character portraits - the majority of which has no voice acting.
Overall The Banner Saga is a decent game, but I wouldn't class it as a "must play". If you enjoy turn based combat it should entertain you for the 10 hours needed to finish the campaign, but you might want to wait for a sale.

An action-packed, indie, first-person parkour game that follows the tale of Faith Conners, a runner in Glass City.
The basic story that is told in-game is that the player is Faith Conners, the daughter of two known protestors in Glass City--a colorless metropolis possibly ruled by an oppressive system--and the sister to a blue, Kate Conners. Running around at a young age, Faith encountered Mercury, whom identified as a runner and trained her before she was able to join other runners that operate under his superiority.
In the game, Faith and Kate learn of the murder of a politican and family-friend Robert Pope. Despite not being the one to do it, Kate is eventually framed for the killing, the supposed suspect or suspects using the firearm of a blue to do the bidding. Determined to clear her name, the player must find leads and investigate deeper into the case. You have to scape throughout the urban landscape and use many of the props around the environments to push through and get to the bottom of the conspiracy.
Colorless as the scenes may be, the use of color in certain sections of the world shine brightly and help support the idea of Glass City being something transparent yet dull and restrictive. The characters Faith and Kate are somewhat interesting, and the parkour is pretty awesome.
Without the use of achievements, certain elements of the game, such as the search for the yellow bags runners are commonly tasked to obtain, prove pointless to collect. The few actions scenes against the blues are not always worth going through despite their challenges, and the limited methods of fighting them off sometimes feel useless. A couple of the chapters have the issue of being disorientating, scaling some areas without some form of signal can leave the player astray.
A short, linear story, Mirror's Edge is one of the few unique things that come across the web and am happy to have it and play it all the way through. Alongside the concepts here and there, the game is also open for a player's interpretation on how and where things are in terms of backstory of Glass City.

* Review based upon Season 1/ Episode 1 "Iron from Ice"
Fans of the novels, and/or the HBO series should not pass this one up, however the game is a spin off of the HBO series. Episode 1 "Iron from Ice" begins near the end of Season 3 in the timeline for the show, so if you haven't at least finished Season 3 yet, this game will spoil things for you besides probably also leaving you confused. As the player, you'll take turns throughout the episode playing as different members of House Forrester, a noble house from the North, who are bannermen to House Stark.
The story is well written, and feels right at home to sit alongside anything that the HBO series has put out to date. The familiar faces of a handful of major characters from the show appear in the game with excellent likeness and are also fully voiced by their respective actors. The world feels dangerous, and authentic when you're forced to make quick decisions, and say just the right things to the right people to accommodate your agenda. Telltale Games knocks another one out of the park right on the heels of their ongoing, and wildly successful Walking Dead series.

I have played many RPG's before, both turn-based and hack and slash, and I can say without any doubt that this game is easily one of the best i've ever played.  If you like strategically planning out your attacks and getting into cool battles with nasty enemies in a great turn-based adventure than this is the game for you.  IT EVEN HAS COOP! AND MODS! +50 awesome.  Seriously, how many games these days still have campaign coop?  Not as many as there should be...
From what i know about the origins of this game, this is the product of not having a producer, and such, not having said producers breathing down the developers neck forcing them to change things, and it worked (producers such as EA).
Of course without a producer, its more likely that the game will have some bugs, but lets be honest, most games these days have some really annoying bugs even with a producer.
The story is actually interesting, for a dungeon crawling RPG, you actually somewhat give a damn, its not utterly fantastic, but interesting.  Which is rare, because, I dont know about most people, but in other dungeon crawllers, i dont really care too much about the story and care was more about the loot and killing stuff.
The whole story is set in the land of Rivellon, where you and a friend/partner (if you aren't a lone wolf) are Source Hunters, Source is a kind of really powerful magic that has been corrupted over time to become accursed and dark magic, its kind of a corny name.  And you and your partner are sent to Cyseal (the first town) to investigate a murder that took place and apparently Source being involved.   I will say, the beginning to the game is a little slow, no arguing that, but if you scrounge around, you can get some decent equipment.  A little tip I learned, there is no moral setback for stealing and it can be quite profitable and you can get some good stuff, but DONT get caught, if you do, reload your last save, trust me when i say that.
You are usually with your other half, and the main two starting characters make up your primary team, and you can recruit two more people to help you.  You usually find the main helpers to be Jahan and Madora, pretty early in the game.  Later in the game, but not too much later, you'll get access to an area called the Hall of Heroes where you can recruit new team members for some gold.  This is cool except for some dumb reason the hirlings start off at level 1.  Say you want to change up your team, and you are like level 15 with level 15 gear.  You recruit a new guy from the hall of Heroes, and now your team is crippled and useless since enemies dont respawn, theres no real way to get the new guy up to speed.  Thats a just a dumb mistake and hopefully an easy fix, not a big deal.
Being an RPG, you have choices you can make in the game to determine how people react to you, and how soem quests are completed and things like that, there is a moral system and a personality sorter.  Theres sorters for your two main characters on the lines of altruistic/egotistcal, forgiving/heartless, blunt/considerate, and many others than give bonuses to your character(s) based on what they are which can lead to interesting modifiers of your character based on their personality.
Another intersting mechanic that I like, and have to say is quite unique is the rock, paper, scissors mechanic (at least I've never played another game that has it).  Say some NPC tells your characters to do something, and one character says sure while the other says no, you then have a rock,paper scissors match to determine whose idea wins.  This also happens as the form of reason/charm/intimidate checks with NPCs so you can talk your way out of situations.
The combat system, and this is where I get a bit biased, is turn based, meaning you use a number of Action Points a turn to attack, move, use potions, whatever, and then you turn is over.  A lot of people i know, dislike turn-based combat saying its "boring" or "lame", i disagree, i think planning your moves and thinking and getting a cool kill, is way cooler than mindlessly pressing "X" or whatever.  Thats just my opinion however, if you dont like turn-based combat or are bored easily, you wont like this game.  However, the combat itself, is creative, its very similar to DnD (Dungeons and Dragons), if you can think up a way to kill an enemy or gain an advantage, you can do it (within reason).  For example, if you use fire on a puddle of acid or the game calls "ooze" you get a large explosion or in reverse, you get a ooze cloud.  If you have a couple of enemies in a puddle, hit the puddle with a lightning bolt for large damage and stunning.  If you have a big fire pit in your way, toss a barrel of water or use the Rain spell to douse your friends (and enemis) that are on fire and pretty much anything else you can think up.
My only couple of complaints about the combat is archers and fire.  Archers, specifically enemy archers, are kinda broken, they defintely have more actionpoints than you have, regardless of difficulty and can DEFINTELY hit you when you cant, its kinda lame.  My other complaint which can be hindered by the awesomeness that is the Rain spell, if fire, not fire damage like fireballs so much as firepits.  The damage from those, even with high fire resist its ridiculous, just ridiculous.  Always have someone on your team that knows Rain, trust me, its saved my hide more times than I care to remember.    But those arent my biggest problems with the game, those are just smaller problems that are relativly easy to fix, I would think.
My only real complaint about the game is lack of direction, and no I dont mean make the game linear as hell and spoon feed me, but give me some semblance of a glint of a hint of an idea of where I should go next, without forcing me to use an online guide.  I dont mind wandering around occassionaly to find where to go, but the world is quite large and I dont always want to have to resort to a guide to help me out.   Throw me a bone occassionally.
Also, you can, for some stupidass reason, drop quest items. DONT! EVER DROP QUEST ITEMS!  I dont know why they thought that was a good idea, but DONT DROP ANYTHING THAT HAS "QUEST ITEM" IN YELLOW LETTERS, JUST DONT!
DONT DROP QUEST ITEMS,  YOU WILL REGRET IT!!!!!!!
I really really cannot stress that enough, it kinda screwed up my first playthough because I dropped stuff that i didnt think was important anymore...turns out it was...
One last thing then I will wrap it up, if you are one of those people that saves over one slot every time you save, DONT, make lots of save points, be freaking generous.   I dont honestly understand why people still do that (make one save slot).  Your game screws up, and you have only one save slot, too bad you are done.  Just trust me when I say to have more than one slot.   Also, quicksave, F5, one of the many perks of being on PC, you can use it in battle and pretty much anywhere and have up to four quicksave slots as well as four autosave slots, use that♥♥♥♥♥♥

Multiplayer is basically the game plus one and has no negative effect. Even at max level I joined others just to run around and provide cover fire, just because I can. I'll add a little more negative here but  it isn't really that important. There is barely anybody online anymore because there isn't that much replayability. The DLCs aren't worth it at the moment. Everything spawns a certain way and you have to do everything in the same order exactly rthe same way to win. It is fun sure but I do NOT feel like practising that much for a bow. A bow I technically paid for with a DLC that I can't acess, because I don't feel like memorizing the pattern. It is the DLC and so I don't really think it impacts the main game but thought I'd mention it. There is an update in one month so this is written in January 2016. All in all this is fun, get it with a friend and it is even better. I think there is a hard mode if you want to play well harder but it caters to all. This is the kind of RPG that I've been waiting for.
The battle system is really complex and is really unique compared to other RPGs.  You might also find it to be pretty difficult on normal.  You have to really choose your battles in the beginning and think your strategies out carefully, using the environment and a huge array of skills to your advantage.  It's turn-based combat but with little gems thrown in, such as putting one character in the combat to distract the enemies while you select other party members outside of the skirmish who can then flank the enemies.  If you want to win the battles efficiently, you really have to plan your attacks.
You're also not locked in with the class you choose from when you create your character.  You can level up and put skillpoints wherever you want, so you can be as stealthy/mighty/magic-y as you want to be.
I was really amazed at the level of thought put into every single detail of this game.  You can have one character talk to an NPC, and while he/she is in dialogue, you can control another character to go behind their back to steal their belongings/pickpocket them.  And there's so much loot to be had!  From expensive paintings to rare equipment, you'll want to take everything in sight so that you can afford expensive skillbooks later on.
There are also lots of quests of really in-depth questlines, a lot of which you can complete within the first town (and will want to since battles are really difficult in the beginning!).  However, the game is very old-school and doesn't have any sort of quest markers, forcing you to have to read through your quest logs and figure your way through completing them.  While this might bother a lot of casual gamers, I think it can be appreciated by many who liked games such as Baldur's Gate or other old PC RPGs.
The game's beautiful, everything's 3D modeled, and it'd be pretty easy for a sub-par computer to run it.  The water effects look great, like actual drinkeable water, and a lot of the skill effects are pretty. (Fortify looks awesome, as it encapsules a friend/foe in magic stone armor.)
I haven't yet played any sort of multiplayer co-op or any player-made campaigns, so I will probably edit this review once I do so.  However those are features that I'm really looking forward to, and I can't imagine there being any problems with the multiplayer experience.  Everything is so smooth and fleshed out in this game, it's near perfect.

Aurora, a small child, wakes up in a strange land.  But she was with her father wasn't she?  So where is she now?  She needs to get back to him....
While the story itself isn't all that complicated, and has been done before, the way it is executed here is quite charming and magical.  Characters all have their unique quirks, but for better or worse everyone speaks in rhymes, meaning you can't just blaze through and read the text quickly else you'll most likely miss important key notes or clues.  Some people might get super annoyed by it, personally I felt it made the game much more whimsical and only wish the characters outside of Aurora were more developed.  The game also feels a bit short, completing all the sidequests and most of the treasures and hidden notes you can easily beat this in 10 hours or so.
The game is marvelous to look at.  It feels like you're almost reading through an old text book, with lovely textures and animated sprites.  They even went so far as to have Ignis, the little sprite you control effect things when he bumps into them (Aurora's hair, lamps hanging from the ceiling ect.).  I did find a weird bug when spawning in a battle, sometimes Aurora's hair won't spawn leading to a silly mess.  I'm not sure what creates this but it happened 4 times during my play through and switching her in battle does not fix it.
As far as exploring goes, this game is a blast if a bit too simple and easy to get ganked later on if you choose to ignore enemies.  One of your abilities is moving Ignis over to an enemy to stun it, thereby letting to walk by and pass them with no issue.  The problem is it is incredibly easy to skip enemies altogether and making later boss fights near impossible if you are unfamiliar with RPGs.  Treasure hunting is much the same way, and I wonder why they even put an enemy in front of the chest to begin with (with some chests letting you open them from afar using Ignis).  The actual battle tactics remind me a bit of Grandia back in the day where they use a wait/action bar on the bottom right of the screen dictating when your character is about to be ready for a command imput, and then having a casting period before actually initiating the attack though it is extremely simplified and can get cheap in some scenerios.  When fighting one enemy, it is extremelly easy, two enemies is a decent and level playing field, however when it gets to 3, prepare for a 30min battle or more and that is no exaggeration.  For 80% of the game you really have no area spells or slow/haste abilities outside of one character and some items (and said character is situational anyways) but at about 1/4 through the enemies are doing mass haste casts on themselves.  For people wondering why that is a big issue, it's just making them faster, the problem is that during the casting period of even a basic attack, if the enemy is faster then you and hits you during that phase it will stun you and cancel the command.  Mind you I'm just speaking about basic enemies, nevermind the bosses later on which employ some dasterdly things when you're eternally scrambling around to get an upper hand.  I also want to add on that there is no currency in the game, in fact your equipment are these Occuli gem things that you craft and make together and put in 3 possible slots for each character and each slot can effect the same gem differently depending on where you put it.   But wait, no currency?  What about items?  This is where the game can be rather mean if you let it.  The only way to acquire items is by hunting a limited amount of treasures located in the world you explore.  You run out of those?  Well tough luck and pray.  The game does compensate for this by adding in little "heal" zones in the form of sparkling bushes, but it doesn't account or help if you're in a long grueling boss fight and you could've used that last potion you ended up using 40min ago.  The battle system also allows you to control Ignis on top of the 2 characters you can switch in and out of (but only in the actual fight, not in the menu sadly) to which Ignis can slow an enemy down using his light or heal you slowly but it ends up being a wash as stated above with 3 enemies using haste.  The game itself I don't find to be hard, just really annoying situations can make it a headache.
Playing this both on keyboard/mouse and controller, I can say each has a different strength depending on if you're in battle or exploring.
For exploring purposes, I found the mouse and keyboard to be much more fluid, and Ignis doesn't move slower then molassas then he does when using the controller analog stick which can be problematic when doing time based puzzles and you need him to quickly trip a switch.
However in battle I found the controller shined a bit better, with going through the command menu interface much smoother (though controlling Ignis is still a chore with the controller, it isn't quite as much of a pain).
Also going into the main menu was a bit smoother in controller, but felt mouse/keyboard was way easier when messing around the crafting submenu as I've accidentally put in or confirmed things on accident with a controller.  So honestly it's up to preference but the game can be played with both, though I do recommend a controller for the battle sections.
The reason this game probably has such a high score is the music in all seriousness.  This music is by far almost too good for the game, and sounds positively glorious.  Even the simple battle theme sounds like an ending boss battle.  I do wish the overworld theme was a bit more consistant in not playing the new track for about 5min before switching back over to Aurora's main theme (though that in itself is pretty, you don't get to explore much else of the soundtrack sadly).
Ultimately the game is an experience, and I enjoyed my time with it albiet short though it was.  One other big negative that isn't really the game itself but the fact you need a Uplay account on top of Steam to play this.  And while Steam doesn't have so much as trading cards or achievements, Uplay actually has achievements for the game so it's up to personal preference if you wish to deal with Uplay.  I urge people to try it regardless, and I've not had any Uplay issues that have been reported by other reviewers so I'm not sure what thats all about or if it's been fixed (something about save issues and crashing).

Child of Light is an RPG with a sidescrolling overworld.
Gameplay
+ Skilltrees and party members help you form the team how you want it. For all playstyles there's something.
+ There're no random encounters. Exploring the overworld doesn't feel like a chore because of it. Hunt for treasure is fun.
+/- Interupt battle system. Although interesting, makes some battles feel like a chore or luck-involving. It's unique though. Stepping out of comfort zone should never be frowned upon.
- Difficulty is either too easy or too hard.
- All enemies can be stunlocked, this includes bosses. The biggest threat in boss fights are the side enemies interupting you with the interupt system.
Atmosphere
+ The world feels alive. I'm sure the graphics is a selling point for the majority of people.
Audio
+/- There are a few amazing pieces. Soft slow music is hard to master though. Slow songs can be ''easy'' or ''dull''   While the majority of songs feel alive and are simply easy on the ears. Sometimes I felt like the music was simply boring piano. (Maybe I'm being too hard though. There are some great pieces in here.)
Writing
+ Speech is done with rhymes. This makes every NPC interesting. Reading in this game is a lotta fun!
+/-  Didn't care much for the story. It's not bad but... it felt... like it was just kinda there.

Firstly, I must say I backed this on kickstarter so I naturally may have some biases towards my love of this game.
Grim Dawn is likely one of the best aRPG games I have played in recent years. To explore this I think I will break it down into several areas- World, Loot, Usablity and Progression.
World wise, the game runs a single continous map which only has loading screens when you either warp far away or enter a dungeon. Besides that you could technically run through every map- to every town- in one swoop. It feels very similar to Diablo 2 or Torchlight 2- but with the middle travel sections cut out. Each act has a significantly different terrain to explore with different colours and props. You move from a swamp, to a desert, to a farmland, to a ice world, to a cthulia-esque demon area, to a almost C&C tiberium style crystal world. Each section of the world seems fresh, vibrant and interesting because of this. There is a massive variety of monsters and some which are reused for good story reasons... There is just so much to love about this world. But one thing stands out most of all to me. It isn't always dark. With a game with a title like "Grim Dawn" I was expecting a ton of grim darkness- and while that certainly resonates in the theme and props of the world, the game sports a full day-night cycle which basically just makes the colours of the world come alive. I appreciate that SO much it isn't funny.
Loot wise... It has a nice progression, it has loot colour filters and it has a lot of different rarities. While the loot you receive may not be as crazy as say, torchlight 2, it is really smart about how it does the loot. Legendary items are always exciting to get- and they actually allow you to find "empowered" versions of the epics you found at lower levels. While there may not be as much variety as some games in the genre- they seem to constantly add more and use what they do have very competently.
Usability- this is where the game SHINES. Just when I thought the pet system of torchlight 2 couldn't be beaten- here comes grim dawn. In grim dawn you can freely make portals anywhere, any time. You are mid dungeon run? Teleport back to town and empty out- need to get from one town to another? Use a portal. Too lazy to warp back to the main portal to portal to another portal? Use a portal. They require no mana, no items, they just.. work. I couldn't have imagined just how valuable this ability was until I had a chance to experience it. But besides that there are so many other little features we have found that just make playing grim dawn a pleasure. Loot filters, point by point respec, massive expandable inventory and shared stash, likely many other things I have taken for granted and forgotten. Either way it plays really well.
Finally, Progression. Each level you gain stat and skill points- standard affair- up to level 85. Stat points are as you would expect, they provide broad boosts to various areas while also providing you with the points required to equip better and better items- cool. Skills- interesting. Because you can combo two of any class it is up to you to decide what you prefer. Do you like to summon creatures? Perhaps go for Occultist/Shaman? Want a bit more magical oomph? Try throwing an archanist in there instead. Each class has a sprinkling of both passive and active skills and toggle skills all of which may be upgraded over time. This allows people to really play how they want- when I as an occultist/shaman looked at my Nightblade/Solider friend we were shocked to see the differences. His tree was filled with passives and lots of active abilities- while mine had no passives, only a few actives and a massive amount of points to upgrade existing skills. Add in the "devotion" system you gain points for by fixing shrines and you have a lot of variety in what you can do. Even loot has intersting levels of progression, it often becomes a choice between higher stat boosts/other interesting effects and higher skills. It just requires a lot of tweaking and playing with, but you can really construct a nice character.
There is one more final point I wish to touch on here. Okay so when the game was "content complete" me and a friend powered through 50 hours of this game together and in doing so only reached around act 3? Months later we came back together and decided to keep on playing. Now, a lot had changed, but we were still able to pick up exactly where we left off and keep playing. It took us less then half an hour to get our bearings and come back to playing it. This may not sound like much, but honestly the ability to quickly start playing again is something which I really loved about the game. When we went to play torchlight 2 again for example, we kept starting new characters- it just- didn't work nearly as well for the runback. It may not be much, but I really feel that this trait is a very positive one.
Overall, I really loved this game. It is by far one of the best kickstarters I have EVER backed and I look forward to seeing what they do with it next. Promised free content upgrade in june sounds good- I know at least one paid expansion pack will be in the works thanks to my kickstarter pledge- but overall I really hope this game gets improved upon for years to come.

Grim Dawn is one of best ARPG with most various build choices.
In any APRG games, making a build is extremely important.
They represent you as a player, your style and personality.
Grim Dawn gives you 4 choices to complete the build
1. Class choice : You can choose A class or two
2. Skill choice : You can choose any of skills the way YOU want
3. Gear choice : There are so many variety of items from epic/empowered epic/legendary with many different purpose.
4. Constellation choice : You can choose constellation with 50 points of affinities to acquire special skills/passives/stats.
4 choices but within them, there are so many possible combinations that you will always find a way to make a build you want. You want to cast meteor shower, wielding duel sword, while having 2~3 pets? It is possible!
There are 4 difficulties for the game. Normal Veteran Elite and Ultimate.
Things will get harder at elite and deadly at Ultimate.
So for the end game, it boils down to the "Ultimate Build".
Can you beat Ultimate Loghorrean the Final Boss?!? Can you clear Ultimate Bastion of Chaos the Final Dungeon?
You are required to make a BUILD that can accomplish these to truely "beat the game".
I recommend this game for who loves to theory craft builds and loves to stand out among the others with unique build of your own.

I bought this game back when it first came out, hit level 35 (or whatever the level cap was then), and took about a year or so long break. I told myself I'd be back when they added multiplayer and increased the level cap, and well.. here I am, working on a Stormcaller and an Albrecht's Aether Ray build, and loving every second of it (the AAR grind is killing me softly).
In a lot of ways, it reminds me of Diablo 2, but I find the system they've implemented for character skills (being able to combine two character classes, and the importance of understanding how to proc abilities) differs greatly and actually makes the game more interesting. It also ups the replayability with all the different combinations, which is a plus in my books.
The only critique I can give is that unless you go looking for and read every single note, you'll probably end up missing out on some aspects of the story or the history of Cairn itself. If they'd expanded on some things - be it in conversations with NPCs or maybe even adding cutscenes similar to the opening one - it would have made following the story not only easier, but more enjoyable in my opinion.

Oh, sorry. Didn't see you there misceallenous reader! I was too busy playing one of the best Star Wars games of all time. Battlefront 2 is just a classic? Why? Don't ask questions; it just is. The original game was pretty spectacular, and the sequel adds in some nice little extras; such as Hero/Jedi Playing, dogfighting maps, SPRINTING (yes, you couldn't sprint in the original), and a proper campaign of a decent length as you go from Clone to Empire trooper. Whilst the game has some flaws and bugs, it's also just incredibly fun.
Okay, Battlefront 2 you should get for these reasons; First and foremost is Galactic Conquest. This is where you start of with 3 or so planets, and, as your desired faction go about conquering the galaxy, unlocking units, building fleets and buying bonuses. It's wonderful gameplay, solo or cooperatively. Next up is the campaign. I had a lot of fun running through it back in the day, and will be doing so again promptly. Whilst it can be annoying in certain situations where it's your measily 10 against unlimited enemies, that in itself is fun, and it allows you to relive some of the toughest battles of the film which in some cases were glossed over (Jedi Temple *cough*). Thirdly; MODS. There's a HUGE community out there and thousands of maps, skins, patches, you name it. In addition you can download your own MOD making kit released by Lucasarts themselves to make your own. Good fun if you want to start doing that sort of thing. Finally it features a decent 'instant action' mode where you can try alternative gameplay options such as 'Hunt' (fuuuun), 'Hero Assault' (lots of Saber Bashing) and Capture the Flag (is okay).
The game, being a Star Wars one, features impressive sounds and nostalgic visuals. This release occasionally stutters in audio, however, which is nothing major but a little bit distracting nonetheless. These sounds elevate being a hero from the standard into the extrodinary. You'll get a rush as you leap into a group of Clone Troopers as Darth Maul to Dual of the Fates and cut them all down, or hearing the Imperial March as Boba Fett. Destroying countless enemies is just fun, and what the Force Unleashed compromised with it's enemy types, Battlefront leaves as a massacre. Tanks destroy everything. Rockets send people flying. The Emperor sends people flying with his jump smash. Flying is fun. Also the medal and AWARD system for profiles is nice, unlocking AWARD weapons and bonuses is...well...rewarding...funny that.
But, yes, as great as it is, it is not without drawbacks. The AI can be stupid or predictable. I've found myself getting over 90 kills (out of 150 in a conquest map) with a single death and having my team still lose (shakes fist at Geonosis) due to balancing issues. AI don't play as Heroes which is annoying, as rocket launching Vader into oblivion is somewhat of a console favourite moment of mine. They also seem temperamental at CTF. There's some bugs with weapons; the AWARD Sniper Rifle occasionally goes through things heads (in turrets) without hurting them. This can be gotten around by just destroying them through the chest because it's OP anyway. There's bits and pieces around you'll find, but, for the most part they either don't detract much or, alternatively, just add to the fun!
-Really fun gameplay. Seriously. It just is.

All in all it's a great game, well worth the price and the fact that it no longer needs 4 Discs to install like it did when it came out.

The gods are dead. The sun never leaves the horizon, shining on boundless wastes of tundra. The land is torn between men, giants known as varl and armored creatures known as dredge, neither carry any reason to trust each other. A new day dawns, and the world is at the brink of turmoil, weary of old wars, always anticipating new wars; nearly void of hope. In such a time, you take the role of leading a caravan across frozen wastes to its destiny.
You play the parts of many characters, make their choices and endure the consequences while discovering the beautifully weaved tale of the realm. Each and every character that you lead tell a story of their own in this Nordic, war-thorn saga. Each choice that you make affects your chances of survival, and makes you approach one step closer to your destination. The setting is incredibly rich, expected from any proper RPG game. Every road, landmark, settlement, mountain or forest; every region depicted on the map contains its own local history. The lore is complete and refreshing.
To begin with, the game contains a diverse gameplay, bringing together elements of adventure, role-playing and strategy games. The adventure elements are directly affecting the story, and the outcome of your choices twist and turn to present you alternative destinies. Combats are turn-based in isometric maps, and gameplay is fairly easy to grasp. Yet 'fairly easy to grasp' quickly turns into 'hard to master'. You are able to level up your characters with renown, a kind of currency that you may gain through heroism either in adventure choices or by slaying your adversaries in battle field. Alongside leveling, you are capable of gathering minor and major items to enhance your heroes furthermore.
The Banner Saga presents a direct example for my reason to become a gamer: a story to be told. The game satisfied all my expectations thoroughly. I do not wish to present any spoilers, but it is safe to declare that the story of the realm is not finished in this game. Good news is that The Banner Saga 2 is in development. Cheers!

A fun turn base squad game with some annoyingly text adventure elements in its meta game.
The Banner Saga plays like two games in one, first there is the part where you manage your army in the meta game on the world map, and second is the part where you controls units in turn base squad combat.  This format isn't new, and in fact it has been done repeatedly in recent years by games like X-Com and Xenonauts to name two.  While the game's format isn't new, it does a few things differently, which works some times, and doesn't other times.
Am not going to go into too much detail about how the game plays, since the format is well known, instead am going to focus on what it does differently (for better or worst). To start off, in the TBS section of the game, your units have a default willpower value that increase as they level up.  They can use their willpower to move further, use an ability, or just do more damage. Willpower is finite resource as your units do not generate it during combat. Instead you get 1 willpower, which you can give to any of your units, for every enemy you defeat.  This extra resource management add a layer to the combat section of the game that it needs. The combat overall is decent, but without this extra element it would be unremarkable in any way.
The other two elements that The Banner Saga does differently happen in its meta portion of the game.  First, there is a supply, i.e. rations. During most of the game, you are leading your caravan across the map from point A to B.  And during this time you have to keep your caravan feed, otherwise you'll start to lose troops and your morale will drop. And the bigger your caravan, the more supply you'll need to feed it on a daily bases. So having more troops for war, isn't always a good thing, especially if you don't have the supply to feed them.  This resource management makes sense and actually is kind of fun to deal with. The second thing, however, is rather annoying. Normally text adventure elements are fun. But not in this case, since there are quite a few choices that will results in a unit dying or leaving your group. This wouldn't be so bad, except that for the most part, it seems totally arbitrary. I remember a section of the game where I told one of my units to start a fire, in order to create a distraction, and after it was done, that named character vanished. No real reason was given, and the only thing that was certain, was that they were gone.  And this is nearly game breaking since you spend a large portion of the game leveling up these characters, so to lose one in what feels like random chance is infuriating.
Overall, the game is fun. It does a few cools things, and one really annoying thing. But in the end, I would still recommend it to other people.

I loved the first Neverwinter Nights and the expansions. I loved Fallout 2. I loved the Ultima series, and Nethack, obviously. The developers apparently loved and studied them, too. Divinity: Original Sin is a well thought-out product, and very intuitive to interact with, if you are a fan of the genre. You can come up with imaginative solutions in the game world, e.g.. put out a fire with water, or add nails to a branch to make a crude weapon. The game world is very responsive, easy and fun to approach.
Coop multiplayer takes the cake, though. Alone the game is fun, but playing it together with my wife, it's easily the best coop we've had played Neverwinter Nights. Inventory interaction is made easy, and there are dual conversations with NPCs and each other, in which both players get to speak their mind. These discussions define the characters personality (and gives beneficial traits), and can sometimes turn into an argument. Arguments are decided with rock-paper-scissors matches, and the winner gets her way.
Biggest downside is that there is so much you can do, so it takes a while to get acquintanted with everything. That's why after five hours we're not far in the story, but so far it seems to be at least okay. Maybe I'll update on this later.
Another aspect I like is that it's light enough to run on most modernish computers. We have a Macbook Pro 15" and a 2009 built PC, and it runs fine (not nearly maxed, but not lowest neither) on both. Mac/PC is no problem, even the save games are reliable. No crashing once on either computer, either.
There are some minor issues, as with every game. But they are too minor to mention, and the developers will release more patches. Mods can be loaded, so that's an infinite supply of adventures. Haven't looked too much into that yet, but appears similar to the NWN community from my day.
All in all, a magnificent game. Recommened to all who enjoyed the games mentioned.

An interesting multiplayer take on the RPG genre that works character interaction into the game.
This review was taken after playing several classes 4+ hours into the game.
Pros
- Lots of room for customization of classes using a skill system.  You can create a wizard who fights with weapons, a cleric who picks pockets, or a rogue with healing magic should it please you
- Multiplayer dialogue can make for some funny interactions, especially if the two characters are continually arguing with each other
- Fights are challenging, but beatable if you are using tactics and elements correctly.  In fact, if you get better at the system, you can take on groups of creatures several levels higher easily
- Every decision in combat is important, one mis-step could cost you a battle
- Lots of things to find and do in town
- The quest system is very old-school, in that it gives you the names of people and places without putting a marker on the map.  In other words, you have to do some exploring
- There are a lot of cool elemental combination and weaknesses you can learn and use to give yourself an edge in combat
- Lots of cool items to find
- You can move most things within the game.  In fact, if you're strong enough, you could put a bunch of items in a barrel then carry that barrel around in your inventory.
Cons

Little Nightmares is all about atmosphere, and there are not a lot of games who manage to keep theirs as thick as this game does. There is not a single room that does not feel unsettleing or wrong on at least some level.
The characterdesign goes from cute little Nomes to grotesque and repulsive Guests to a downright creepy drowned Granny (DLC). In terms of gameplay Little Nightmares is pretty simple,
but makes it work brilliantly: Its puzzles might be more on the easy side, but they always fit the narrative and activley make you help build up the atmosphere, while engaging you in the dreadful situations your character is facing. In this way the game reminds me a lot of "Brothers - A Tale of Two Sons", which has been quite similar in its melding of gameplay, narrative and atmosphere. As a small negative I want to mention that the controls are sometimes a bit dodgy, but since you do not face any serious platforming or something of the like this is not a big issue.
For those of you that are usually put off by horror games I can assure you, Little Nightmares will throw neither jump scares nor blood-drenched gore in your face. This game prefers being creepy over actually scaring you to your death. Someone might be watching, maybe even waiting behind the next corner. Did you leave the window open? You were sure you closed it. That kind of thing. The game feels a lot more like Limbo or Inside than Outlast or RE7.
Despite its rather short playtime (3-4hrs) the asking price of 19.99€ is fair in exchange for the unique experience Little Nightmares provides. In fact I'm going to do a rare thing and recommend getting the Complete Edition, which includes the Season Pass for The Depths and the upcoming two DLCs. You will keep wanting more after the main game and The Depths already delivered one of my favourite chapters via DLC.

This is one of the most fantastic RPG games I've ever played, and will appeal to both RPG and fans of the JRPG subgenre. With beautiful art work, character development, an immersive story, and humour, people will find themselves lost in this game, and coming to love the main character, perhaps without even realizing it.
In addition to the art work, the battle system is active and rewarding. The game augments the traditonal turn based combat system of the turn based RPG, by creating the 'action bar', which is a time based system that shows how close a character is to being able to act, and the time it will take to complete an action. With the help of Igniculus, a character you meet right at the start of the game, you are able to influence the time it will take enemies to act, and if you're clever, you can interrupt an opponent in the middle of an action, potentially eliminating their ability to do anything throughout a battle. Beware though, because the same weakness applies to you!
So with the fantastic and beautiful story, and simplistic but innovative battle system, the reasons to love this game are many, and even if it's something totally new to a would be buyer, it's something I recommend to everyone.
*** I see a lot of concern over 'Uplay'. This is my only game I use through Uplay (and steam), and I can attest that Uplay isn't hard to use at all. You just start this game via steam, and it'll open through Uplay, it's not annoying at all (though I would add that you want Uplay to remember your log in information if you want to skip the several seconds it takes to log in!).

FTL: Faster Than Light is a gem of a game.
I've played it for many hours and plan to play many more, because this game is so brilliant. You make FTL jumps between beacons to explore a randomly generated sector in space. When you arrive at beacons so many randomly generated events can occur: there can be distress beacons for ships that may need help or are wishing to lure an easy target, there could be shops selling ship systems, drones, weapons, crew and more.
Every action you make has consequences that echo through your journey until the very end. The unforgiving difficulty of the game makes every positive thing that happens a victory, reducing you to tears of joy, while every negative thing that happens is a disaster. When your ship is destroyed, so is your journey across a randomly-generated galaxy. The feeling you get when you find that weapon in a store you were looking for, or when you can afford a cloaking system, is euphoric.
Interestingly, FTL: Faster Than Light is also a game about moral choices. It's a harsh place out there, and sometimes you just can't risk helping a ship. The game then tells you that the ship in need suddenly becomes quiet, gving you a moment to feel bad before you continue on your journey. On the other hand, if you decide to help the ship, a disaster could occur, or it could be a trap, making you regret your decision. I personally always "Attack the slaver scum!", but usually only because I'll get bribed a free slave. Sometimes I'll make the decision that I must steal supplies from civilians because if I don't, I'll be left without the essentials, but of course it's wrong to steal from innocent civilians when there are ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ rebels out there for my crew's blood.
