This side scrolling RPG game is full of gorgeous art, tells a heartfelt story and has classic turnbased gameplay. It just has a little problem with details.
POSITIVES -
And honestly if that's what you want in a game, Child of Light is completely for you. Its gameplay is very simple, a little repetitive and not complicated, like the usual RPG. It'll throw in stat boosts, debuffs and a rock paper scissors formula as the game goes on, but nothing that's too difficult or new. So if you're fine with that old school feel, you'll be impressed with the game.
The art is painted, water colored and ... well, amazing. The music ranges from soft and to intense; the developer really knew what she was doing. The atmosphere is also done so well, from the dark and moody beginning, to the huge and open bright fields after you've gained your new powers.
And really the feel of this game is what helps the story. You play as a young girl named Aurora who's been thrown down the rabbit hole, everything straight out of an old child book. And it really works. This coming-of-age tale is detailed and imaginative, but still very simple. It's a tale of good vs. evil, growing up and even tragedy. Running through a lonely and dark forest in the beginning of the game, only to shout a cheer when you gain your wings and sword, it just feels triumphant. Our main protagonist goes from being a slightly selfish princess and child, to someone who takes on responsibility, even if it means making tough decisions and charging into a dark world that isn't so different from our own.
NEGATIVES -
The few problems of Child of Light are mainly its tedious puzzles, lack of development in its side cast and rushed ending.
I had no problem with the old feel of gameplay or skill set, like some people do. But after hours of playing the game, even in its last dungeon, you'll be maneuvering around the same spikes, pushing boxes and following clues you've seen before. It would have been nice to have a little more variety.
The side characters are extremely endearing filled with personality, even if a little cliché. But after their initial introduction, they barely get any extra personal touch and their problems don't get mentioned or resolved until the end of the game...
...which is rushed. And that's unfortunate, because it's VERY rushed. The game has a way of giving a good poetic feel when it comes to its plot. And certain things in this sort of fantasy setting aren't meant to make complete sense, but Child of Light still has it all structured. So it's pretty jarring when the game ends rather quickly, really quickly. It resolves everything, but it seems much more forced than everything you've been through so far. And certain plot twists and events don't get explained fully or at all at the end.
CONCLUSION -
Child of Light is really an amazing game and one of my favorites for 2014. It has everything put together so well and it’s just lovely. But the details are sometimes a little muddy.
Those issues didn't distract me enough though to not HIGHLY RECOMMEND this game to anyone.

Hyperdimension Neptunia, where to start...
Gameplay wise, it's your standard JRPG style turn-by-turn with a few minor tweaks.
Firstly, you can move around the circular border that surrounds your character and position your characters to where you want them to be to inflict damage to one or more enemies if you can get them to line up into your attack box. You get 3-Dimensional movement to where you want your characters to be, so I guess it's more immersive than your normal standard RPG.
Secondly, you are given 3 different types of attacks. Rush, Power and Break which are done in a succession of three times in any order of your choosing in addition to your initial strike. Depending on which one you choose, each type of attack does different things.
Rush is a low-power-high-combo style of attack that focuses more on building up a mechanic known as the "EXE Drive". The EXE Drive bar fills up gradually as you attack or are attacked and gives access to an additional rush/power/break attack, making it 5 attacks in a single turn. In addition to that, you are also given EXE drive skills, skills that not only do not require SP (This is the term for mana/mp used in this game) but are also extremely powerful, each having it's own cinematic.
Power does what its name implies, you hit hard and kill your enemies fast. Compared to rush attacks, this usually only comes in combos of 1-5 hits and does not charge the EXE fast even if it shares the same number of hits as a rush attack.
Break attacks are different from rush and power in the sense that it does not do as much damage as power but inflicts more damage on a mechanic known as the guard gauge. The guard gauge exists as the blue bar below the enemies' health and when it is reduced to zero, you trigger a status known as guard break where the enemies take more damage than normal and is usually done to allow EXE drive skills to reach a level of damage you can't achieve normally.
As for the story...
The cast of characters found in this game are rather entertaining to watch, although some of the jokes may sail past your head if you are not familliar with some of the popular game/anime(?) titles in Japan.
Our heroine Neptune is a pudding obsessed bundle of joy that somehow gains amnesia after being planted head first into the ground from Gameindustri's equivalent of Heaven also known as Celestia.
She is saved by Compa, a nurse in-training who then helps treat her injuries who also got her addicted to pudding. Shortly after, they team up with IF after bumping into each other in a dungeon... literally.
Together the three heroines will gather the four key fragments from across Gameindustri to free Histoire, a tome that holds all the power of Gameindustri and save the world.
The story itself is light, enjoyable and overall, just plain fun to watch the cast of characters interact with each other.
However, I do not recommend the game to buyers who are looking for a deep story because the game appeals more using it's art style and gameplay mechanics to appeal to the buyer rather than the story.
Overall, it's a game I'd term as moege, these types of games generally are typically only visually appealing without much of a story, if you like cute girls beating the living daylights out of monsters and you like JRPGs I'd recommend this this in a heartbeat
Watch out for the grind though...

Firstly, I must say I backed this on kickstarter so I naturally may have some biases towards my love of this game.
Grim Dawn is likely one of the best aRPG games I have played in recent years. To explore this I think I will break it down into several areas- World, Loot, Usablity and Progression.
World wise, the game runs a single continous map which only has loading screens when you either warp far away or enter a dungeon. Besides that you could technically run through every map- to every town- in one swoop. It feels very similar to Diablo 2 or Torchlight 2- but with the middle travel sections cut out. Each act has a significantly different terrain to explore with different colours and props. You move from a swamp, to a desert, to a farmland, to a ice world, to a cthulia-esque demon area, to a almost C&C tiberium style crystal world. Each section of the world seems fresh, vibrant and interesting because of this. There is a massive variety of monsters and some which are reused for good story reasons... There is just so much to love about this world. But one thing stands out most of all to me. It isn't always dark. With a game with a title like "Grim Dawn" I was expecting a ton of grim darkness- and while that certainly resonates in the theme and props of the world, the game sports a full day-night cycle which basically just makes the colours of the world come alive. I appreciate that SO much it isn't funny.
Loot wise... It has a nice progression, it has loot colour filters and it has a lot of different rarities. While the loot you receive may not be as crazy as say, torchlight 2, it is really smart about how it does the loot. Legendary items are always exciting to get- and they actually allow you to find "empowered" versions of the epics you found at lower levels. While there may not be as much variety as some games in the genre- they seem to constantly add more and use what they do have very competently.
Usability- this is where the game SHINES. Just when I thought the pet system of torchlight 2 couldn't be beaten- here comes grim dawn. In grim dawn you can freely make portals anywhere, any time. You are mid dungeon run? Teleport back to town and empty out- need to get from one town to another? Use a portal. Too lazy to warp back to the main portal to portal to another portal? Use a portal. They require no mana, no items, they just.. work. I couldn't have imagined just how valuable this ability was until I had a chance to experience it. But besides that there are so many other little features we have found that just make playing grim dawn a pleasure. Loot filters, point by point respec, massive expandable inventory and shared stash, likely many other things I have taken for granted and forgotten. Either way it plays really well.
Finally, Progression. Each level you gain stat and skill points- standard affair- up to level 85. Stat points are as you would expect, they provide broad boosts to various areas while also providing you with the points required to equip better and better items- cool. Skills- interesting. Because you can combo two of any class it is up to you to decide what you prefer. Do you like to summon creatures? Perhaps go for Occultist/Shaman? Want a bit more magical oomph? Try throwing an archanist in there instead. Each class has a sprinkling of both passive and active skills and toggle skills all of which may be upgraded over time. This allows people to really play how they want- when I as an occultist/shaman looked at my Nightblade/Solider friend we were shocked to see the differences. His tree was filled with passives and lots of active abilities- while mine had no passives, only a few actives and a massive amount of points to upgrade existing skills. Add in the "devotion" system you gain points for by fixing shrines and you have a lot of variety in what you can do. Even loot has intersting levels of progression, it often becomes a choice between higher stat boosts/other interesting effects and higher skills. It just requires a lot of tweaking and playing with, but you can really construct a nice character.
There is one more final point I wish to touch on here. Okay so when the game was "content complete" me and a friend powered through 50 hours of this game together and in doing so only reached around act 3? Months later we came back together and decided to keep on playing. Now, a lot had changed, but we were still able to pick up exactly where we left off and keep playing. It took us less then half an hour to get our bearings and come back to playing it. This may not sound like much, but honestly the ability to quickly start playing again is something which I really loved about the game. When we went to play torchlight 2 again for example, we kept starting new characters- it just- didn't work nearly as well for the runback. It may not be much, but I really feel that this trait is a very positive one.
Overall, I really loved this game. It is by far one of the best kickstarters I have EVER backed and I look forward to seeing what they do with it next. Promised free content upgrade in june sounds good- I know at least one paid expansion pack will be in the works thanks to my kickstarter pledge- but overall I really hope this game gets improved upon for years to come.

Grim Dawn is one of best ARPG with most various build choices.
In any APRG games, making a build is extremely important.
They represent you as a player, your style and personality.
Grim Dawn gives you 4 choices to complete the build
1. Class choice : You can choose A class or two
2. Skill choice : You can choose any of skills the way YOU want
3. Gear choice : There are so many variety of items from epic/empowered epic/legendary with many different purpose.
4. Constellation choice : You can choose constellation with 50 points of affinities to acquire special skills/passives/stats.
4 choices but within them, there are so many possible combinations that you will always find a way to make a build you want. You want to cast meteor shower, wielding duel sword, while having 2~3 pets? It is possible!
There are 4 difficulties for the game. Normal Veteran Elite and Ultimate.
Things will get harder at elite and deadly at Ultimate.
So for the end game, it boils down to the "Ultimate Build".
Can you beat Ultimate Loghorrean the Final Boss?!? Can you clear Ultimate Bastion of Chaos the Final Dungeon?
You are required to make a BUILD that can accomplish these to truely "beat the game".
I recommend this game for who loves to theory craft builds and loves to stand out among the others with unique build of your own.

I bought this game back when it first came out, hit level 35 (or whatever the level cap was then), and took about a year or so long break. I told myself I'd be back when they added multiplayer and increased the level cap, and well.. here I am, working on a Stormcaller and an Albrecht's Aether Ray build, and loving every second of it (the AAR grind is killing me softly).
In a lot of ways, it reminds me of Diablo 2, but I find the system they've implemented for character skills (being able to combine two character classes, and the importance of understanding how to proc abilities) differs greatly and actually makes the game more interesting. It also ups the replayability with all the different combinations, which is a plus in my books.
The only critique I can give is that unless you go looking for and read every single note, you'll probably end up missing out on some aspects of the story or the history of Cairn itself. If they'd expanded on some things - be it in conversations with NPCs or maybe even adding cutscenes similar to the opening one - it would have made following the story not only easier, but more enjoyable in my opinion.

A lot of things make sense after the final secrect route is complete whcih ties everything together.
The game is set in mid 1980's Russa just before the collapse of the soviet empire.  You wake up on a bus in front of a camp with no idea how you got there, only that you were on a bus headeding to a party at one moment, took a nap, and then your here.  As you play and attempt to find answers about the place you at (to no avil) you get choices and are able to choose which girl to persue, even if thats the last thing on your mind.
Each girl has a different ending, 3 of them (Alisa/Slavya/Ulyana) all have you wake back up in your pitaful apartment dazed and confused.  You finally go about life and start to make something of yourself (Alisa/Ulyana) and about one year later after you "woke up" you meet said older girl vertion.  Slavya rout you kinda just head back to normal routne and at long last meet her at the bus stop.
Lena Route will warm your heart as you do not leave that world, but instead live a full life With her as your Wife, having kids and all, and only ending when you reach (the long way around) the day you "left" your world.
Miku route is unlokced once you get at least one GOOD ending.  Its where your in an alternate world (surprise surprise) and your shooting a movie about the Pinoeer camp.  All the same people show up but wtih drastically different personalities then your used to if you have played through the other routes before this one, it is quite comical.  Route is quite sweet at the end, showing a life that could of been had he not chosen his carrier over having a family.
Semyon rout is YOUR route, and this is where things start to get strange, for one you do not get any of the girls (the cheevo is called Forever Alone lol).  However you do find out a lot about the world, and that there are multiple of "you" running through it with different outcomes.
The last Route you must have gotten all the Good endings and Miku's good ending. Yulya is a cat-girl that is a part of that world, and it is explained that all the other "you's" are all the other playthroughs/routs you just did.  That you get the girl, but then return to the camp not remembering anything about the last "run" and either are stuck in a forever loop or get a different girl.  At the very end you are faced with the choice of finally picking what girl you want to be waking up next to, for good this time.

Tactical RPGs are some of my favorite games and this one did not disappoint.
It had some unique battle mechanics such as the ability to break the opponent's armor, and the unit's strength serving as both HP and damage (so units who are hurt will deal less damage). Also turns always alternate between you and the enemy even if you have more troops than him and visa versa. This called for some unconventional strategies such as leaving certain opponents crippled rather than dead.
There is an economic element to the game where you have to spend renown (experience) to develop your characters, buy stats-increasing items and buy supplies for your caravan. Balancing between those three actions was quite challenging and interesting to do.
The story is reminiscent of the old Viking sagas (even the word Saga comes from the old Viking heroic tales) with tales of great heroism among a bleak and severe environment. It's you and your small party against an unforgiving world and bad things happen to you. Yet, there is great beauty and nobility in the actions of the characters who remain hopeful and honorable despite great adversity.
The graphics are gorgeous and the soundtrack complements the feel of the game quite nicely.
Overall this is a very solid, entertaining and engaging title. Looking forward to part 2!

The gameplay is akin to The Binding of Isaac, you collect items in shops to further inhance your character whilst exploring a randomly generated dungeon filled with monsters, the difference being that it's a cometitive multiplayer experience, where you your friends or even cpus (which play near identically to a human) are ghosts fighting over a single human body, by killing the player in the human body you gain control of it and can upgrade yourself (each player has their own seperate pool of items).
But how exactly do you kill the human as a ghost, well as a ghost you're able to temporarely control one of three monsters (the monsters you get depend on which god you pick), when you damage and get damaged by the human you gain blood which will turn into gold if you become human, if the human levels up you gain wrath which lets you make your monsters evolve after someone ends the floor, these mechanics allow someone to easily jump infront which leads to a constant intensity in the gameplay.
The end goal is to defeat the boss monster, the boss monster can only be fought by a level 10 human, the boss monster is controlled by your opponets, whoever defeats the boss monster wins, if you lose you are still a human (you just have very low health), however there are only 3 total attempts shared between all players, whoever loses on the final attempt is the loser and the game ends.
This game has beautiful pixel art graphics which invokes a feeling of arcade cabinets from the 90's, every sprite is well done and fits the same theme, while there are flashes that might pose a risk to someone who is prone to epileptic seizures.
The sound effects are very well done, all fitting the same theme.
The music is amazing, it's very energetic but not overly so which is very fitting for the gameplay.
A potato could run this game with no slow down, it's barely intensive.
This game will last you at least 3 action packed hours just by your self, you'll get an extra 1 or 2 hours from playing with friends, but if you play one run every now and then by yourself it will start to add up over time, I've got 13 hours just from playing this one or two runs and then setting it down, for $9.99 (usd) that's an amazing deal.

I don’t often write reviews, such is the way of an impatient creature. However, with this game I am compelled to. I’ve played a fair amount of VNs and Everlasting Summer is easily one of the best, if not the best, I’ve ever played. I picked it up because it was free and I figured why not? Little did I know, it’s a diamond in the rough that are free games. So here we go. And don’t worry, my review is
You play as Semyon, an ordinary anti-social guy in Russia who spends more time on his computer than doing anything else. However, he finds that he’s woken up in a strange pioneer camp in the old Soviet Union with no idea how he got there or how to get home. For the sake of not spoiling, I will simply say the story is full of mystery and emotion. At times the story will take you completely by surprise by going a direction you wouldn’t expect, or will present a situation so suspenseful that you can feel your heart pounding and wondering what the fate of our protagonist is. On the flipside, the story provides humor and romance and leaves you rooting for and laughing with the main character. Everlasting Summer is impeccably written.
The supporting characters are equally as interesting as Semyon. Olga Dmitrievna, the strict pioneer camp leader; Viola, the saucy camp nurse; Shurik and Electronik, the resident camp nerds fixated on their robotics club; Zhenya, the cranky camp librarian. And then there are the potential love interests. Responsible and friendly Slavya; quiet and timid Lena; aggressive and rebellious Alisa; childish and playful Ulyana; talkative and ditzy Miku; or mysterious Yulya. The characters are all well written and have their own quirks and personalities. However, they may not always be as they seem and they may even surprise you.
This game definitely has replayability, if not demands it. There are 13 possible endings and in each one you will learn something new to solve the mystery and figure out just what the hell is going on. And you definitely won’t know what’s really going on until you unlock the final possible endings. There are a lot of different choices to make that will give you new information, provide new interactions with characters, or simply give you more insight into Semyon’s mind. What makes all these choices manageable is the inclusion of a “Skip Read Text” option so you can play through all of the available routes without being forced to read the same dialogue over and over again. Additionally, there is a card game tournament to play at some point during your time in the camp. However, after playing through it the first time, you have the option to skip the tournament later and choose what the outcome is. If you decide you changed your mind or simply missed a line, you can either use the wheel on the mouse to scroll backward or simply hit the arrow to the left of the dialogue box, and move backward in the narration.
I definitely recommend playing this game, whether you like dating sims (there is a patch to put back in the explicit scenes), a good mystery, or simply well-written VNs. It blew my mind and sucked me into it’s world, itching to learn more and it didn’t disappoint and leave a bunch of loose ends. I cannot recommend Everlasting Summer enough.

It'd be an awesome game when judging the graphics, the gameplay, the soundtrack, the story, the characters or anything else except for the game's stability.
Yet, The Banner Saga is (currently) so horribly unstable, it doesn't make any fun playing it. The worst problems one can avoid by installing the beta version, but still it's just not acceptable that the game locks up regularly. Not that it'd crash or freeze completely, it just hangs and doesn't continue. For instance in battle often an enemy should end its turn, but never does. So, you have an NPC character that's out of possible actions blocking the initiative round. The UI is perfectly responsive, but your only option in that case is to exit the game, as you will never get control of any character on the battlefield.
Or in dialogues. Sometimes two dialogue options pop up simultaneously, and the game doesn't continue, no matter what you do. Same for information messages.
Ah, and there's a memory leak somewhere. The longer one plays, the more the animations stutter. Restarting the game helps.
All this brings me to the next point of critique: It's not possible to save manually. So, whenever one of the aforementioned bugs strikes (quite often), one has to reload the last autosave which might be half an hour old, or even older...
To summarize, I'd recommend this game, if it weren't so extremely buggy that playing it simply isn't fun.

I don't know what to say about this game, so here is a recipe for pancakes,
Ingredients:
4tbsp plain flour (about 100g)
1 large free range egg
½ pint semi-skimmed milk + water (about 300ml - ¾ milk ¼ water)
Pinch of salt
Butter for frying
How to make pancakes:
Sieve the flour and salt into a large bowl and make a well in the mixture.
Break in the egg and stir to make a breadcrumby mix.
In a jug add 1/3 of a pint of milk and top up with water to make 1/2 a pint (200ml milk, 100ml water) - this makes a lovely light batter.
Add the milk and the water mix bit by bit, beating constantly to avoid lumps.
Tip:*If you have a food processor just throw all the ingredients in and zap until smooth!
Pop a large frying pan over a medium heat.
Add a large knob of butter (roughly 50g) and melt.
Pour the excess butter into a small bowl and reserve it for later.
Using a ladle pour a spoonful of the pancake batter into the hot pan and swirl to get a full covering - cook for about 1 min each side (it's ready when it's easy to flip over).
Serve immediately with sugar and lemon or other exciting toppings. We love cheese and Marmite for an extra British twist! Delicious!!

I'll be straightforward: If you are not a really hardcore Game of Thrones fan, this game - as of now - is not for consideration. Don't bother.
I'll pass on what others have told of this game: There are no choices here except the illusion of choice. At some point, in my story, the plot itself didn't even make sense through the decisions I had made personally.
Don't get me wrong, this game has only delivered episode one so far, but the fact that there is only one defining ending to the story shows how this plot does not have multiple choices. The choices made by the playable characters in the game does not affect the story in any way whatsoever, which is greatly demotivating since I was expecting this to be the sort of game I wanted to play two or three times to get all the angles right.
I found myself attached in the first playthrough, but extremely shocked and frustrated by the fact that all the decisions made were undone in the end. To be frank, it was pointless. The inability of a story telling game to have multiple stories is kind of absurd. All I personally wanted was two variants of the story ending, or at least variants to the character's development, but it's not there - and I don't understand why.
It seems so cheap, and it's immensely disappointing to have so little influence on the story that's unfolding. At best the variations to be descripted are minor, and the team behind the game didn't bother having these choices influence the story in the bigger picture.
I was greatly into the first playthrough, and the plot and story is excellently voice-acted and nicely developed, but in the end, the lack of choice darkens the game too much and is too big a disappointment for me to actually recommend others to buy it in its current state.

Child of Light is so staggeringly beautiful that it’s not uncommon to find its presentation entirely overpowering that game underneath.
Pastel colors swirl lushly through the environments, soft details illuminating a world lost in darkness, as wondrously animated heroines fly onward curiously taking in places as foreign to them as the player. Elegant piano melodies accompany you in the background, often joined by your own flute before coming to crashing crescendos when a fight inevitably breaks out. It’s the sort of all encompassing grace and artistry that it’s easy to become so swept up in it that when the game itself comes into focus it almost feels unnecessary, maybe even somewhat annoying as it pulls you out of your marvelling as you're asked to take part in tasks rather a lot less captivating.
That game revealed itself to be a turn-based RPG, rather surprisingly large in scope yet scaled down so as to encompass a game far shorter than those it borrows elements from. There are quests to clear, huge skill trees to unlock, an ever growing party to manage, items to craft, and limitless enemies to take on. It’s ambitions are at once impressive, and a tad overwhelming, giving you so much to manage and consider that I was rather quickly lost in a sea of items and unlocks.
Child of Light is constantly giving you more stuff, but it doesn’t take long to see that much of it is superfluous, bogging the player down with perceived options while burying the ones you actually want. The intimidating skill tree quickly becomes much less so as the levels and skill points begin to roll in at a generous pace, but the reward you’re met with always feels intangible and minor. Points add upon points to stats that never feel important, informing you you’re apparently getting stronger but never feeling like you’ve actually grown.
The initially obscure crafting system spirals into inventory chaos, as you’re loaded down with materials that are more tedious to use than beneficial. Outfitting my party so as to broaden my elemental effect was only as useful as I was able to remember who was using what, in the continual swapping of materials as I attempted to build more useful items but inevitably ended up weakening someone in the process. The lack of any sort of guide as to the uses of different objects you can craft left me switching awkwardly between menus, testing loadouts before heading back in to actually make them. It’s convoluted and by the end I’d given up trying to make anything more from the system than I already had, hoping it was enough to get me through battles.
Combat is one of the few areas that’s more often than not actively engaging, utilizing an interesting turn system that’s more reliant on timing than just beating enemies down as hard as you can. The idea is if you position enemies on the timeline so as to attack them when they enter the last portion and are preparing to attack, you can beat them back and effectively skip their turn, which if done properly can see you continually attacking without the enemy ever getting a word in. It’s the sort of turn system that requires you always be engaging and anticipating the enemy, and when paired with the various moves of your different party members and differing enemy weaknesses can give you a lot to think about and be really satisfying to succeed with.
But as with all of Child of Light, you’re given far more than its systems can sustain, with enemies constantly pouncing you at every moment. After a point I began to run mostly on autopilot, so accustomed to an enemies patterns that they were no longer threats, but obstacles standing between me and what I hoped would be new things to fight if only I could get through to the next chapter. Even boss fights which are easily the most imaginative and interesting fights in the game, become agonizingly slow sets of attacks as you whittle away at an enormous invisible healthbar even as the boss becomes entirely helpless.
The only place Ubisoft shows an amount of restraint is in Child of Light’s simple, endearing narrative which blends its fairy tale bedtime story with that of a young girl’s coming of age and learning how to deal with the responsibilities newly put upon her. It’s intentionally cliche at times, though in a way that’s comfortingly familiar, while still subtly subverting its tropes to allow a refreshing portrayal of a story you already know before it’s even begun. The choice to writing it entirely in verse isn’t as consistently successful, changing stanzas so often that trying to follow its rhyming is a small challenge, and the necessity of rhyming causes lines to sometimes read sillily or feel forced.
Child of Light is an imperfect, exquisite creation, sometimes hard to love but yet difficult to pull yourself out of. I loved my time with it, even as I was becoming confused and annoyed at systems that often felt underdeveloped, finding trouble dismissing something so stunning and unexpectedly ambitious. It’s flaws are obvious and needing to be acknowledged, but I wanted so much not to, as my initial impression of unbelievably beauty continued to guide me through a game easily obscured by the creativity draped around it.

I'm not a big zombie game guy but nowadays it's hard to get around them.
This is one of the best out there though.  While Dead Island drew a lot of its inspiration from Borderlands, Dying Light drew the same amount of inspiration from Far Cry 3.
It's basically an open world zombie game with parkour type mechanics for traversal.  It does the parkour very well.  Possibly the best of any game I've played.  You have skill trees with some skills that aid your parkour and other skills that aid combat.
Combat starts off kind of difficult, then balances out, then becomes ridiculously easy.  I don't have an issue with this because the change is so gradual.  I felt like I achieved that power. Most of the quests are generic and NPCs all blend together, except for key story characters.  I don't really care about that, mainly because I played through the entire game in co-op.  The game was so fun to play for me, that repetitive quests were just another excuse for me to play in the sandbox.  But I imagine in single player it can get pretty tedious.
Overall I'd say that if you have a friend to co-op with, this is definitely worth playing.  If you're playing alone, I hope you're into zombie games or you may be disappointed.

Okay, straight facts first.
This game only has 11 levels, one of those being a tutorial and another being much shorter than the others.
Each level can be completed in under 10 minutes, and the entire game can be completed in about — or under — two hours.
Yet,
I've somehow managed to rack up over 100 hours in Mirror's Edge.
And I still plan on playing more.
That must speak volumes for itself.
Honestly, I don't quite know why I love this game so much. It might be the absolutely stunning views of the city from above and below. It might be the fantastic, complex but easy to learn gameplay. It might be the art style, which is very minimalistic yet bursting with color and character. It also might be the fact that I just want to strive to become better and better at a game which I love for all the reasons stated above. Whatever the reason is, I think this game is utterly fantastic, and if you've been considering a purchase, get this game. I know Catalyst is out already, but even if you have that, still get this game. It's a great experience, and even if you don't play it as much as I have, I almost guarantee that you'll still have loads of fun with it.
Also, another great but unintentional feature that makes this game great is its plethora of exploits. Yes, this game is very broken, yet in all the right ways. It allows you to, with practice, knowledge and skill, play the game faster than it was ever intended to be played. This leads to near-endless replayability as you find out new ways to complete the levels faster and faster. It gives you a great sense of progression when you remember back to yourself, before you knew that side-jumping and turning in the direction you jumped instantly gets you to your top speed, and realizing how slow you were back then. However, even though the game is broken, it's never unplayable. Every bug left in the game gives the player an advantage, and at no point in the game are you blocked from progressing due to something you didn't intend to do.
In conclusion, I absolutely love this game. Why?
No idea, Faithy. I just go there for the pretzels. ;)

Long story short: buy this game, it's an investment in quality over a very long time.
Long story long:
I've been playing this game since day 1, and it never bored me. Sure as hell it isn't perfect, but hey, what is? Let's see what's on the plate:
There is a real solid gameplay, an evolution of the already really fun KF1. It's really simple to understand yet very hard to master.
If you love realistic weapons here you will find all you want and need; and the same is true if you love over the top sci-fi weaponry: really, there's enough to satiate every palate, and every death instrument comes with top notch animations. Most AAA games don't get this level of quality.
If you love blood and gore then you shall go no further: you are home.
The really great part is that though: in a world where most online games have a very limited life span KF2 will be there for years, thanks to a really die hard comunity: sure, there will never be millions of players at once, but a few thousands of us will always be there. And there will always be updates, with new weapons, enemies, maps, gameplay mechanics and what-not: and the best part is that they will be free. No over-priced map packs, weapon packs, win packs. KF2 is still a newborn: I'm sure the best is yet to come.
And yes, there are micro transactions, but you know what? If you want to spend some money in vanities then go on; and if not then your game won't change the slightest bit.

Everlasting summer is a visual novel from developers Soviet Games aka Erogame Project released in 2013. It is currently available in Russian, English and Spanish.
Story:
The story revolves around our protagonist Semyon, in his mid-twenties, who seems to have given up on life. But one day he ventures to the 410th bus and boards it, only to wake up outside a pioneer camp. Now he must find a way out while living a week in the camp.
Most of them time the story feels like the usual slice of life/romance VN but it really shines when the main focus is on Semyon trying to find out why he is at that pioneer camp and how to get back home. The whole story, including the different paths and endings, is at a decent length with about 15-20 hours of playtime.
Writing (English version):
The writing is ok for the most part. There are some typos and grammatical errors but nothing too distracting, also the developers native language is not English so these mistakes can be forgiven.
Characters:
The characters are likeable and their interactions with each other is quite enjoyable. On the surface all the characters are quite generic stereotypes (energetic, shy, etc.) but they always seem intriguing and that there is more to them.
Art:
Is a mixed bag for me. I really like the backgrounds, sprites and overall character design. The problem I have with the art are the CGs. Some of them are just bad, some make the characters look different and just a few of them are really good.
Soundtrack:
Not much to say here. For me, there are no songs that stand out but on the other hand I wasn't annoyed of any of them either. Most of the time the songs match the scene nicely and that's what is most important.
Overall:
I'd recommend Everlasting Summer. Besides its flaws there is an intriguing story with likeable characters and a satisfactory ending.
And it's FREE, so why not give it a try?

What an amazing first episode. They have captured the impossible choices that makes Game of Thrones so watchable. Now you are the one torn between two bad decisions. The dialogue format suits the political machinations superbly well. While the art styles is well done, I wouldn't say it would win any awards... that said, the actual content of the game - the tremendously difficult decisions - will have you forgetting about the art style soon enough. Make no mistake, the art isn't terrible - far from it - I just wish it could have been more. The likenesses of familiar parts is however excellent. I cannot recommend this any more highly. I eagerly anticipate the next episode.
edit: played episode 2 and 3
I'm enjoying the narrative less and less, and it is becoming increasingly clear that player choice is an illusion. There is a specific sequence of events that must be told, and seemingly what you choose to do cannot stop or alter these events. You're on a railroad. It's fine when all options presented realisitcally follow on from the consequences of one's actions, but some outcomes actually end up feeling quite disjointed and jarring, as characters dialogue don't fit with the option you chose, but can be seen to have readily fit with one of the other options.
Its becoming a pet peeve of mine, were games promise roleplaying or meaningful choice and its all a facade. It's like a choose your own adventure, where at the bottom of the page there is only ever one page number to turn to. There may be minor paragraph selections on the page itself, but actualy plot... that has been written and its singular. Ultimately disappointing.
edit: episode 4
Back on track. Great dialogue. This is what I was expecting more from ep 2 and 3. Although still very railroady, it didnt bug me as much this episode. I'm now conflicted.

Not too far from Normal Mode, it brings an entirely new tier to the game. If you thought the game was difficult on Easy Mode without Advanced Edition, you will not want to go near Hard + Advanced. When it comes to scrap rewards, every bit of them are important for Hard Mode. You can get good weapons by finding them in abandoned beacons, in any sector. There are alternatives to getting items without purchasing them. The difficult part for some players is to maintain fuel surplus whilst hopping to as many beacons as possible before jumping to a new sector. On top of that, you can't do much against a ship with Advanced content and try to fend off without anything. If you have a ship attacking you with mind control, you can then either hack their mind control to disable it OR use mind control on your own mind-controlled player, it will cancel the two, without using a drone part to disable it.

So this is the 5th Divinity game, another prequel to
, but more connected to the world than
was. With OS the series changes genre again - this one is a pretty good party-based RPG. The general style is fairly
, with the story, dialogue, and NPC personalities being left weaker, but the actual gameplay even better. Mechanics are very strong, and exploration/combat is entertaining. The combat uses an action point system (like
) that works nicely. There's a reasonable number of attributes and skills, none of which seem useless. There's a nice elemental magic system where standing in water makes you vulnerable to lightning, getting hit by cold effects repeatedly might freeze you solid, which can be reversed by a fire effect, poison clouds can be detonated by fire, which is put down with water, etc. It results in sufficiently (rewardingly) tactical combat.
The game is also designed for two player co-op, with parts of the dialogue taking input from both. The choices have minor progression/stat effects, and disagreement is solved by rock-paper-scissors.
All in all, it's a good RPG and fun to play, but kind of light and lacks memorable characters or events. The plot is a bit w/e, and you won't meet a Minsc or an Irenicus, not to mention
levels of story. So it falls well short of brilliant. 8/10 yet easy to recommend.

Little Nightmares features everything I look for in a horror game: dark and atmospheric sciences, suspenseful stealth sequences, and intense and horrific chaces all wrapped up in a phenomenal score and topped of by incredible sound design. If you like cheap jumpscares then Little Nightmares is not the game for you. There's an overwhelming feeling of helplessness in the shear scale of everything against your own tiny size, compounded by the inability to defend yourself against the monstrosities inhabiting the Maw. From a game design standpoint, the art direction was astounding, the animation was gloriously unsettling, and the camera angles were perfection.
I, personally, found the keyboard controls to be awkward, and even after adjusting the key bindings to my prefered configuration found that I sometimes had significant difficulty controlling Six's movements, This was, however, only a minority of the time and I aknowledge that it may very well have been my own fault or the fault of my hardware - I haven't seen anyone else complain about the controls. At any rate, my struggles didn't detract from the game; rather, I found the more I failed and the more I replayed a section, the more intense it got and the more frightened I became.
All in all the game is fantastic, and ignoring my own problems with the controls I have absolutely no complaints. If I absolutely had to find a flaw then I suppose the final chapter could have been longer and more involved, but at that point it's just nitpicking as far as I'm concerned. I'm looking forward to playing the chapter part of the DLC as well as the parts to follow.

Okay, this is my first ever legit review, so bear with me.
First things first, you DON'T need to watch the anime in order to enjoy this game, or vice versa.
If you're like me and watched the show before playing this, that's not really a big deal. You'll just notice that some charaters are missing, but that doesn't matter since this is this is basically a prequel. (Except the 2 DLC characters; Plutia and Peashy.)
Second, this is an enhanced remake of the very first Hyperdimension Neptunia game for PS3 that utilizes the battle mechanic from Victory.
Third, please play this game in Japanese, not some bad English dub where they don't even say Japanese honorifics. There are several segments where the English voices simply fail to play leaving you with just dungeon BGM and subtitles with no voices.
-Characters - 8.5
Neptune (Purple Heart), the CPU of Planeptune (representing the Sega Neptune), which is depicted as a modern-futuristic city, with skyscrapers and various streets. Nep-Nep is probably one the best female JRPG leads ever. Constant fourth-wall-breaking, pudding loving, happy go-getter. The main protagonist in most games She has a childish personality and lots of energy, and likes to jump headfirst into danger. However, her personality completely changes once she transforms into Purple Heart, taking on a much more serious and mature character.
Noire (Black Heart), the CPU of Lastation (representing the PlayStation 3), a heavily industrialized steampunk-style city. Noire is the tsundere type character that wants to get things done. She has a very individual personality and likes to perform things by herself in her own time, yet is quite forgiving and fair. She initially has a strained relationship with Neptune, who acts as her rival.
Blanc (White Heart), the CPU of Lowee (representing the Wii), a frosty, forest style city covered with white snow. She tends to get very loud and angry quite easily despite her harmless appearance. Her short temper is matched by her foul mouth, which can easily be demonstrated in almost any conversation involving her. She is flat-chested, and easily gets frustrated when reminded so.
Vert (Green Heart), the CPU of Leanbox (representing the Xbox 360), a very rocky and mountainous area, with green grass at the base of the mountains. Vert, in some ways could be considered the most caring of the four, due to her gentle way of speaking and/or ways of helping. She is quite intelligent, but overestimates her strength, and is less informed about Arfoire's monsters compared to the others. She displays signs of arrogance, and has a rivalry with Blanc, partly due to Vert's large breast size. She is also a closet otaku and has a huge liking for videogames. Sometimes it is hinted that she is a lesbian because of the way she acts around IF (or Nepgear in the anime) but hasn't been confirmed.
-Gameplay - 7.5
The battle animation is very fluid and smooth being a huge step-up from the original game. As you level up a character, you unlock more powerful combos. Although some enemies may look similar to others from previous dungeons, level-wise, they are much more hardened. The tutorials may seems really annoying, but they really do help a lot, especially if you're new to turned-based JRPGs.
-Story - 8/10
It's your pretty generic and cliche "protagonist loses something (in this case, her memory) and must get it back in order to have world peace or save the world" or something story. But in addition to that, the main characters search for four things called Key Fragments (not from World of Warcraft) to release a tome called Histoire from her seal if she has any hope in remember who she really is. For the most part, it's pretty enjoyable, the character interactions make it that much better. The 8 chapters of the game are carefully planned out, so other than the battles, there's nothing really repeated.
Side Note
-It is stated several times about the importance of Shares. Share is a term describing the amount of influence a CPU and her formed nation has over a place. The amount of share is influenced by the amount of faith and belief people has over a CPU. In addition to influence, the CPU's powers depends on the amount of acquired share. CPUs can be incapacitated if they have insufficient shares, though this is proven wrong gameplay-wise. Although in this game, that's not the case. Pretty much, all you need shares for is to get the CPU Candidates as party members.
Nepgear - Planeptune: 30% Shares for plan / 50% for being able to craft said plan.
Uni - Lastation: 30% Shares for plan / 50% for being able to craft said plan.
Ram & Rom - Lowee: 30% Shares for plan / 50% for being able to craft said plan.
Leanbox doesn't give you anything which really sucks for Vert. :/
Cons
-There is a♥♥♥♥♥♥ton of grinding. Sometimes it takes hours of grinding to get to a decent level where you don't get immediately thrashed by starting the next story boss. So if you don't like grinding and crafting, you could either get a trainer, or just suck it up.
-Having 6 people in a party rather than 3 is sometimes pointless. When you're fighting a tough enemy, sometimes you can miscalculate their moves. This could probably mean a quick death for one of your front-line party members. Now if said party member dies, you're unable to swap out to the other pair (like Pokemon), thus severly handicapping the fight in your favor.
-There is no autosave so you have to save very often. So if your 3 party members die during a fight, that's Game Over. It's complete overkill, dragging you all the way back to the main menu signifying you seriously messed up in life.
-This is a console port so it has gamepad buttons where it should be keys (if you play on keyboard like this pleb) It will be confusing at first, but that doesn't mean this game is unplayable, just a tad bit more complicated.
I can't wait for Re;Birth 2 and Re;Birth 3 for later this year.

I first found out about this game through various let’s play channels on YouTube. It definitely gave me strong LIMBO and INSIDE vibes in terms of its gameplay and aesthetic, but I wouldn't consider it a 2D or 2.5D game in light of the fact that you can move in all 3 dimensions at any given time throughout the game.
Aesthetically, it's a beautifully grim world. In games like these, storytelling through the environment is a pretty integral part of the experience and Little Nightmares does it brilliantly. Even when the story remains abstract, the elements of the environment still feel eerily relevant to the unspoken script. Likewise, the sound design was excellent. Everything from ambience to warnings about how aware the enemies were of your presence and everything in between greatly enriched the experience.
It's also worth noting that it was very easy to distinguish the main character from the surroundings, but some of the interactive pieces within the environment needed better visual cues. There were a couple of areas where I got stuck simply because the way forward was nearly inconspicuous from the rest of the scenery.
Mechanically, the game felt a little clunky. I played using mouse and keyboard, but in retrospect it seemed clear that the game may have been designed for controllers first. Some of the deaths felt less than fair on account of misrepresented player-enemy collision. (i.e. I got teleported into death when it initially looked like I had avoided it.) Ultimately though, Little Nightmares is more of a puzzle-platformer than a precision platformer and the checkpoints aren’t too far apart, so these grievances can be easily forgiven. Eventually.
In regards to the story itself, there’s a degree of separation between the stages, as though the first and second halves of the game don’t quite fit together. It’s worth noting that at the time of writing this, I am only aware of one possible ending and I haven’t looked up any lore behind the game. As such, I’m drawing my own conclusions about what sort of messages the developers intended to portray, but at least I felt like the ending made a lot more sense than INSIDE’s.
Actually, I almost feel like I’d rather not know for sure what the intended message was! Much like LIMBO, I found that I was able to come up with a variety of conclusions that might be just as valid. Either way, it’s effectively gotten me thinking about the game long after I stopped playing.
I highly recommend Little Nightmares to anyone who enjoyed LIMBO and especially to those who enjoy a creepier style of horror.

South Park: The Stick of Truth is a turn-based combat adventure with a semi-simplistic weapon, ability, and stat upgrade system that has you running around an over-map based on the adult cartoon’s hometown. With its unique and stylised take on the genre you play through a bizarre story that takes you through many iconic locations and settings. You meet a huge cast of familiar and unfamiliar characters that are drawn from a huge variety of episodes.
I managed to stretch my playtime to well over 16 hours, completing most the side quests and befriending almost everyone I could find. With the multitude of achievements and four Combat Classes to pick from, replayability will come easily to those of us who wish to experience all this game has to offer. Through my first runthrough I only achieved roughly %70 of everything, but was satisfied enough with my experience to recommend this game to anyone who is a fan of the series and doesn’t mind a turn-based combat system.

The Banner Saga is a good idea that gets bogged down by execution. Bottom line is it’s only worth it if you get it on sale($5). The art is good…but IMO they could have given some more attention to detail. It definitely looks like an indie game in that it is a bit unpolished and there is next to no animation of the lovely art. Other good points of The Banner Saga are the story and music. The effort they put into both is apparent and it does pay off enough for the player to get a decent sense of the world they’re in. However, it was hard to care about any of the characters, races, or really the world itself(many are just dialogue+face). Seeing as there will be a Banner Saga 2(and assuming there will be another), I guess the story and world will be filled out more and the writing will improve. Unfortunately that just leaves the player feeling like the game is incomplete. I did, anyway. Essentially, the writing was complete in terms of the facets of the story, but each element was pretty shallow.
Gameplay was pretty fun at first, a lot like games such as Fire Emblem. I liked the idea of Strength as a combat mechanic a lot. Renown on the other hand, sucked. The RNG in the game sucked as well. I felt like many of my choices didn’t matter and I would be constantly supply-less or getting my people killed no matter what I did. The game has a lot of pointless stats and mechanics it tries to make seem meaningful, like your population, supplies, and morale. One final criticism is that the game was also super slow…a lot of time is spent staring at your caravan trod across the screen waiting for a pop-up event or place to rest.
Overall I still recommend it because I did have fun…it’s just a flawed game. The art and story were still good enough to have me  start up the game and play for 5 hours without even realizing. The first half was all charm–it was only in the second half of the game where all the issues really got to me. The Banner Saga 2 will be better hopefully.

Everlasting summer is a visual novel from developers Soviet Games aka Erogame Project released in 2013. It is currently available in Russian, English and Spanish.
Story:
The story revolves around our protagonist Semyon, in his mid-twenties, who seems to have given up on life. But one day he ventures to the 410th bus and boards it, only to wake up outside a pioneer camp. Now he must find a way out while living a week in the camp.
Most of them time the story feels like the usual slice of life/romance VN but it really shines when the main focus is on Semyon trying to find out why he is at that pioneer camp and how to get back home. The whole story, including the different paths and endings, is at a decent length with about 15-20 hours of playtime.
Writing (English version):
The writing is ok for the most part. There are some typos and grammatical errors but nothing too distracting, also the developers native language is not English so these mistakes can be forgiven.
Characters:
The characters are likeable and their interactions with each other is quite enjoyable. On the surface all the characters are quite generic stereotypes (energetic, shy, etc.) but they always seem intriguing and that there is more to them.
Art:
Is a mixed bag for me. I really like the backgrounds, sprites and overall character design. The problem I have with the art are the CGs. Some of them are just bad, some make the characters look different and just a few of them are really good.
Soundtrack:
Not much to say here. For me, there are no songs that stand out but on the other hand I wasn't annoyed of any of them either. Most of the time the songs match the scene nicely and that's what is most important.
Overall:
I'd recommend Everlasting Summer. Besides its flaws there is an intriguing story with likeable characters and a satisfactory ending.
And it's FREE, so why not give it a try?

15 minutes to learn, 1.5 years to master.
This game has crazy amounts of replayability before you even touch its glorious expansion: Enemy Within. It fulfills the power fantasy of being Commander-in-Chief beautifully, but its constantly-building suspense will still make you feel like you're fighting an uphill battle until you finally get your hands on those plasma weapons.
-Extensive unit customizability. You can alter just about every aspect of your squad, right down to their skin tone and nickname. I've fought off aliens with B. A. Barackus. I've rocket-punched aliens with Lex Luthor. I'm currently hunting down aliens with a team based on characters from Evolve.
-Great decision-making. XCOM begins as a game of making sacrifices, whether you let the aliens attack one city so you can go save another or you solemnly instruct a rookie to draw fire away from your veterans.
-Realistic permadeath. The best/worst feature of this game is perma-death: once your soldiers die, that's it. It makes everything you do
much more important, and makes the game seem more real. If that weren't bad enough, sometimes your soldiers will panic and put everyone at even
risk.
-Unique combat system. Because the game uses the "__% chance to hit" mechanic, it rakes fuller advantage of cover-based combat and lets the player know why they missed a shot.
-Meaningful DLC. Enemy Within adds
of worthwhile content to the game, and the other two each add their own spice.
-Great story. While much of the story is made up by the player as their soldiers form imaginary (but unbreakable) bonds, the player eventually becomes aware of the whole, fantastic, terrifying story.
Glitchy environment. Due to the sandbox-y nature of the game, bullets/guns will sometimes go through walls. This has no effect on gameplay but can be awkward to look at.
Limited late game: Once you research all the technologies, the last part of the game becomes a grind as you acquire enough resources to fully equip your super-squad.
Overall, this game is definitely a crown jewel in any steam collection. It's empowering, cerebral, and, without question, steals the "One More Turn" award from Civ.

Thoroughly enjoyed it. As a fan of GoT, telltale, adventure-esque games and fantasy, I was really pleased with this storywise and atmospherically. I thought the intro echoing the TV show was a nice touch.
There were however a few minor issues...
It feels slightly less polished than other telltale efforts, perhaps in part because it lacks the definitive styles of The Walking Dead and Wolf Among Us, so struggles aesthetically a little, but I'm sure it will grow as they build it up. Also every character seems to have the same shoulder pieces on their outfits regardless of who or where they are!
On that point a few things are jarring, character animations are a little rough and there were a few sound issues on mine where characters were talking and it slipped back so they said the same word twice.
Storywise as everyone else has pointed out, you can make minor changes to what happens, I could play through and make a few different choices but I feel like it would eventually end up the same way. I guess though, with a new series it needed a push and a little direction, so I'm sure as with everything the next episode will start to tell a bit more.
Accessibility to the story however could be a gripe for people unfamiliar. They will miss out on understanding the real gravitas of certain characters prescence as well as people who are only mentioned and discussed by name. As well as the general awareness of the Royal Wedding etc. Once you are past these though, I think next episode you probably have enough footing to know who is bad, who is good, who is a manipulator etc.
TL DR; If you are a telltale and GoT fan, definitely worth it. I can't wait for next episode.

This game gives the player the opportunity to explore and fight an unpredictible and dangerous space, racing against time to keep going forward and complete your quest. This game offers the possibility of developing a lot of strategies and builds with every ship available, and even more since the Advancce Edition update. This game mixes thrill real-time battles with exploration, limited resources management and constant risk-against-reward decisions. This game will introduce you into a hostile space in which you will have to survive and take one of the many paths that converge in the same ending, but since every run is different, each time you face the final boss you'll have to use whatever you got on your travel  in order to defeat it. This game is unforgettable, cheap for what is worth, and will probably frustrate you a couple of times, but the satisfaction of watching the Rebel Flagship being blown to smithereens will make up for every single bad time you had before. I promise.
+ Random world generation in every run. This makes the game unpredictable and fun.
+ Multiple strategies and builds for each ship. And there are lots of ships.
+ Secrets and fun events await out there to be discovered...
+ Hard achievements and multiple references in them.
+ Unforgiving game, even on "easy" mode. Every single error you make is going to be painful, but taking care of what you do will avoid more than one unpleasant situation. Keep that in mind.
+ Permadeath. Once you're dead, you're dead. This makes you focus on not dying.
- May be a little bit too linear and repetivite, even though it will take long to bore you...
- Some people will find easy to rage quit with this game. It IS a hard game, even in the lowest difficulty.
- Sometimes the Random World Generator just hates you. Just keep up until you blow up or heroically beat the run, then start over.
This game gets a 9 out of 10.
NOTE: I just nominated this game for "Test of Time" in the Steam Awards of 2016. Just tells you how ageless this game really is.

This game is based on one of the greatest non-serious movies I have ever seen and is also one of the greatest games I have ever played. Gameplay breaks down into two buttons; left mouse (or arrow) and right mouse (or arrow), even though it is so simplistic, the execution is perfect. All you are doing is killing Nazi's with your fists but it gets more complex as you play for example, the most common enemy is a Nazi wearing a gas mask, they die in one hit so they are easy to kill. Next up is a Nazi with blonde hair, they take two hits instead of one. After that you have Nazi women - and once they are in the mix,♥♥♥♥♥♥goes down - they take three hits to kill but, once you hit them they quickly teleport behind you meaning if you hit them from the right, they end up on your left ready to attack so, you must react quickly to hit them again by switching sides but, like I said before, they take three hits so, they will end up behind you again. After the women comes the Nazi Robots. They take four hits but, if you are not quick to destroy them, they will jump back and gang up with other enemies. There is no other strategy against them except to kill them as quickly as possible. The last enemy I have encountered is a Red Ninja and he is special because he is a robot and a woman combined meaning when you hit him, he will teleport behind you and on the second hit, he will jump back and gang up with other enemies.  The Red Ninja takes five hits and he kills me everytime I face him. In order to make this game more challenging, the developers added a health system for you, you have three hit points and no way to regenerate them (at least not from what I have seen). The entire point of this game is to get the highest score possible and it is a challenge to even get onto the leaderboard. If you like beat em ups with simple controls and want a challenge, buy this game now.

Simply one of the best RPGs I have ever played. As a veteran RPG player of almost 20 years it brings back a lot of memories, especially with games like Planescape Torment and Baldurs Gate, it's essentially an old school cRPG with updated graphics. While some people might be frustrated that not everything is clearly laid out as far as how to progress, it serves as a reminder of how much games hold our hands nowadays. Sure I did find myself looking up certain parts of quests to find where to go next but for the majority of my time playing I found the challenge  not only enjoyable, but balanced.
My only real complaint would be how the mid-late game Tenebrium skill interacts with your early game skill point choices, while not a huge deal it might be kind of a bummer for some depending on how many points they choose to put into regular weapon skills. I would suggest not putting more than 1-2 points in a given weapon skill, it will save you from potential disapointment.
The soundtrack was also excellent and I will probably have some of these tracks stuck in my head for the next couple of weeks. I already feel a sense of nostalgia for the game itself, similar to what I feel for games like FF7 and FF8 as far as what their respective soundtracks are able to invoke. The sense of longing for this game is strong, even though I just finished it. Like reading the final lines in an amazing book.. excuse me while I go play some Dragon Age: Origins to ease the pain.
If you're a fan of classic RPG style games, or even all types of RPGs in general, please do yourself a favor and give this game a chance, cheers.

I am an RPG veteran way back to the Wizardry days and played dozens of RPGs for the past 30 years.  This game lured me in from the metacritic score (what these critics saw in the game still boggles my mind) and screenshots... unfortunately it is a like a movie that shows you the good parts in the trailer but when you go to the theatre to watch it you're left with a feeling like you got duped as all the best scenes were in the trailer but the whole thing is a major letdown.
It is absolutely amazing to me how bad the quest system is and the map is as well.  You have no clue where to go to buy anything, repair anything or find any wares.  Quests are in a "journal" that doesn't do anything but log what people told you (which you already read).  Good quest systems (most RPGs) label quests, place progress notes in your quest log or journal, place visual marks on the map or on people when the quest is complete/progressed, etc.  You walk around aimlessly trying to figure out what the hell to do.  It is unbelievably infuriating!
There is also no tutorial or helpful initial guide to show you the game, combat, inventory, or certainly nothing about the quests.  There are some good elements which make me wish they had done the more important things correctly as described above so I could justify playing this game more.  At this rate I just can't and I am very unhappy I wasted $32 (yes it was on "sale").  I wish I could get my money back and buy a game that is enjoyable to play.  I don't need to be handheld through games but this product just makes you feel lost completely.  Whew unreal.

While the story of the game IS good, it would've been better served as a companion book or short film, rather than an interactive game where the player is supposed to be able to write their own fortunes.
Ultimately it seems, when you play the Game of Thrones, none of your choices matter!
TL:DR; not enough interactivity to be worth the money

Note that I played through this entire game in co-op.
I'm not a big zombie game guy but nowadays it's hard to get around them.
This is one of the best out there though.  While Dead Island drew a lot of its inspiration from Borderlands, Dying Light drew the same amount of inspiration from Far Cry 3.
It's basically an open world zombie game with parkour type mechanics for traversal.  It does the parkour very well.  Possibly the best of any game I've played.  You have skill trees with some skills that aid your parkour and other skills that aid combat.
Combat starts off kind of difficult, then balances out, then becomes ridiculously easy.  I don't have an issue with this because the change is so gradual.  I felt like I achieved that power.  Plus it's great to be able to fight back against certain zombies that you didn't stand a chance against earlier in the game.
Most of the quests are generic and NPCs all blend together, except for key story characters.  I don't really care about that, mainly because I played through the entire game in co-op.  The game was so fun to play for me, that repetitive quests were just another excuse for me to play in the sandbox.  But I imagine in single player it can get pretty tedious.
Overall I'd say that if you have a friend to co-op with, this is definitely worth playing.  If you're playing alone, I hope you're into zombie games or you may be disappointed.

This game revolutionizes 1v3 asymetrical gameplay by relying on an old game genre and reimagining it as a multiplayer experience. Basically, this game uses the dungeon crawler formula to pit one human or "hero" against 3 vengeful spirits. These teams are, however, not static. Ghosts can become monsters and control traps to attempt to defeat the human and steal his body for themselves.
At it's core, this is  not a dungeon crawler or an asymmetrical team game, but a cut-throat free for all game (often only really seen in boardgames or table-top games) where you must work together with your fellow players whilst plotting how you want to take them down at the same time. Thus, the race to salvation begins.
You need to reach lvl 10.
You need to defeat the boss.
You need to survive the pit.
But how can you defeat the hero without working together?
But are you able to defeat the boss with just the stats/equipment you have now?

Grim Dawn is an awesome arpg that takes place in a fictional world. The game provides fast and smooth gameplay with intriguing lore to uncover. The game looks dark and grim which I found very appealing compared to the cartoony look other games may have. There’s enough diversity in the different area’s to explore. Some areas are looking absolutely gorgeous. Most of the game is hand-crafted  with some randomization. There a plenty of different enemies to fight against providing enough verity and challenge. Sometimes you have to prioritize to kill a certain enemy otherwise things may get really tough. What You See Is What You Get (WYSIWYG), which means that an enemy could have an epic weapon or armor equipped that you can see him wearing. So kill him and he will drop that item, however if he might be tougher to fight against as the item can grant them more power than usual.
You can play this game single-player or multi-player with a party up to a max of 4 people.

There are currently 6 classes which are called masteries in the game. They each have their own unique skills. When you reach level 2 you can choose a mastery to start with and at level 10 you can choose a 2nd mastery if you want. This way it provides enough build diversity for your taste. Melee or ranged and a mix of both it’s all up to you to choose. You can use 1 handed weapons and shields, 2 handed weapons, dual wield, pistols, scepters, focus and pets (summons). So you are not bound to a few skills you can choose from. Items like armor, components , relics, etcetera could also grant extra skills to use. And let’s not forget about Devotion, thought out the game you can find Devotion Shrines to restore, which grants you loot and a Devotion point on which you can invest in the Devotion Window providing more stats and skills to customize your build. You can use any item you want just as long as you meet the required stats for it. You can reassign skill- and devotion points but not mastery- and attribute points.
There’s plenty of loot in this game which can be obtained from enemies, chest, bought at a vendor or you can craft items. Blueprints can be found to craft different items at the blacksmith.
I like the faction system on where you have hostile factions with increased negative reputation against them, brings increased enemy spawn additional monster spawns, increased Hero spawns and, upon reaching Nemesis status, Nemesis spawns. With friendly factions, increased reputation unlocks access to the bounty table. There you can do small quest for a gaining faster reputation with that faction and that unlocks more items at the faction vendor.
I love it  that certain quest can change the appearance a little bit of a refugee area. Bringing more survivors there and a cosmetic change. There are also quests that brings choice and consequence to your decisions. So the outcome for that quest could influence a small area.
The lore is great for those who are interested in that like me. You can find notes in the game that provide more information about certain events. But also by talking to npc’s and reading the description in the devotion windows.
There’s no magic arrow that points you into the right direction for a quest, only when your nearby you will see a star on the mini map that your close. Personally i think this is a big plus, i love to explore and find the area myself it’s way more immersive.
There are enough options in the game to change the camera angle zoom in and out. You can set the loot filter to only show magic items, so that your screen isn’t cluttered with loot.
Secret areas who doesn’t like them, i always have the urge to explore everything. Some secret areas are small others are larger. You can find them by breaking a wall or perhaps a hidden path to reach it. Explore and you shall be rewarded because there are plenty of secret areas to uncover.
Small things that matter like kicking in doors or at barrels, destructible objects like furniture walls that collapse. Weather changing effect that make the area darker with a bit or rain or just a sunny day. Enemies of different factions fighting each other.
Challenge dungeons  that provide a real challenge, where if you die you have to restart the game to start a new session. That means you have to redo the dungeon to get to the end. I play softcore so i won’t lose my character but still have the excitement of trying to survive and not to get killed.
Modding tools are released, so expect the community to create their own content, items, classes and even entire worlds.
The developers are very passionate about the making the game, since the Kickstarter the game has grown bigger and better with more features than they originally planned. There is even a free content update coming out soon!

*Take this review with a grain of salt*
Before I go through this review, please note that this game is not for everyone.
Alright, let's begin.
Story
The story was somewhat predictable, yet still good. It revolves around the main protagonist (Neptune), who has lost her memory and slowly brings the main cast together who at first hate each other, but later on become friends.
They then band together to fight an evil person thretening to destroy the world. Relatively cliche.
One thing you'll pick up straightaway is the reference to other games and anime. Oh god the references. Also there's fanservice.
Gameplay
The gameplay, in my opinion was solid. You don't need to excessively grind, so long as you know what you're doing and not avoid every monster. Strategic placement of your characters is a necessity for victory in the later stages. Great thing is, exp is shared with your entire party. For example, if you gain 5000 exp from a battle, EVERYONE gets 5000 exp, unlike some games which only give the most based on who does what. This significantly speeds up the levelling process. There is also the remake system which I'll go into further detail after.
Remake system
Alright, so basically when this game got remade from the original, they changed the storyline up a little and added this new feature called the REMAKE SYSTEM. Basicaly, what it allows you to do is add new dungeons, enemies for those dungeons, you can change the item pick ups, make new accessories and just create a load of stuff. Great addition to add variety to the game.
New Game+
One important feature of this game is NEW GAME+. Once you've finished the game, you can redo the game again and go for a second cycle. This is necessary to get all the added CPU candidates which you can create via the remake system. The good thing is, all your credits, experience, levels and items get rolled over, so you cna go for the achievements that you may have missed in the first run. The bad thing is that enemies dont get stronger at all, so if you're a high enough level, you have no challenge at all (aside from the colosseum).
DLC
Please note that DLC is not necessary to get all achievements, so its not a forced buy.
The DLC allows you to unlock 3 new characters:
-Histiore
-Peachy
-Plutia
And the additional packs give you 300 levels per pack and added dungeons and colosseum battles, so you can go back and have more fun.
All in all, you get 3 characters, 900 additional levels and new dungeons if you decide to purchase every DLC.
So to sum up
If you're an anime fan, like loli protagonists and have some money to throw at a screen, this is the game for you. As far as I'm concerned, it's worth the money and time that I invested in it and I don't regret one bit of it.
