This game is good. If anything the thousands of positive game reviews you already scrolled though by now makes that clear. But there’s one thing that’s hardly brought up that actually makes this game good. It cuts a lot of the BS that ARPG's tend to do and also adds a lot of quality of life features.
Here's some to list a few:
1) Loot grade filter. You only see the tier of loot you want to. If you want to change this it’s a simple button just left of your health bar. I’ve played a few ARPG's in my life and one of the worse things is the sea of useless grey items that flood the screen and block my view. No more, change the filter on the fly or even turn items off if you don't care.
2) Skill/Devotion point refund. In this game you get two classes and three skill points per level to put into skills that those classes have. While you need to hit a certain level in each classes mastery to get higher end skills (the bar at the bottom gets points that increase the base stats best associated with the class) the actual skill points spent on skills are refundable for a crazy cheap price in the first starting town. The skill points used in mastery are not refundable though, so be careful. Devotion points (points you get by activating shrines) are also able to be reset with a relatively small fee of one aether shard (a fairly common item). This is great of players figuring out the game as the risk of making major mistakes are diminished.
3) No identification/portal scroll middle men. You have the ability to make a personal portal that can travel to any main portal at any time. You can then travel back to that exact portal you made by using a main portal. No scrolls or spells needed. When you get an item you know exactly the stats that it gives and what you need to wear it. No scrolls to waste on times that have a high chance of not being in your build specs anyways. These changes make the game flow much more gracefully.
4) Constitution. Your health bar has a little transparent golden sheen overlaid on top of it. When you get out of combat and have missing health the bar will drain and fill your health. This might not seem like much with health potions being a thing but the system speeds up the game and makes the reliance on health regen and potions not so important in terms of general game play.
Now, this isn't to say this game is perfect. It’s not, but most of the problems stem from the ARPG game type and not so much the game itself. You kill mostly trash mobs, find mostly trash items, you sometimes get killed because the game decides to actually toss you a challenging enemy when you’re in trash mob mode. The game is incredibly grim just like all the popular ARPG's tend to be, so grim in fact that it almost borders parody. I don't think you see more than 60 or so friendly humans but you mow over thousands that want to kill you.  Theirs bones and bodies and pain and blood so much that you don't even mind it after a while.  Find items just for you is a pain with such a robust choice of builds. The quests are pretty paper thin, the characters are ok, but nothing to really write home about or get crazy attached too, the plots main antagonists get shafted, another threat comes and pretty much takes the spotlight. The ending is underwhelming, it kind of just spits you out into the world after killing a crazy big foe and the game hardly even pats you on the back.
But, all in all, grim dawn is pretty much your best choice for ARPG especially if you are new to them. While not perfect it will more than make up for the price of entry.

After just starting Ultimate difficulty (the highest of the 3 difficulties) and my counter saying I spend 76 hours on this game, I thought I might as well write a review.
Grim Dawn supports 6 classes: the soldier, demolitionist, occulist, nightblade, arcanist and shaman. While every class has a certain focus (e.g. a soldier is typically melee and an arcanist is usually a spellcaster), you can adapt pretty much any playstyle to any of the classes; it is mainly your equipment that will determine the effectiveness of your character. Also the game allows you to choose a second class later on, where every combination results in a different classname.
I play a Shaman/Arcanist (called a Druid), currently level 71 (out of 85), use 2 handed rifles/crossbows and mainly focus on dealing lightning damage. Every shot from my crossbow unleashes a chain lightning that jumps to pretty much everything on screen. Currently I am a full glass-cannon build which worked fine for most of the Elite difficulty (the 2nd difficulty) but now in Ultimate, where all your resistances are lowered by 50, I start to notice I really lack defence. Nothing a little gearing can't fix though.
A downside of the game I found is that the number of skills to choose from at the beginning of the game is quite overwhelming. Also the first time I opened the devotion skilltree I went like.. what the heck is this!?
You will quickly realise though that you can choose between about 5-6 active skills and the rest of the skilltree adds passive effects to the actived skill. I found this to be a bit of a let-down because it resulted in my character using the same skill for the entirety of the Normal difficulty because leveling up just added some more passive damage to single skill; once I reached Elite I started branching in my skilltree which opened up alot more abilities thus I enjoyed Elite alot more than Normal.
Another downside might be the lategame but since I haven't reached that yet I can't comment too much on it. 2 of my friends bought this game the same moment I did and they both reached max level quite some time ago; one of them quit pretty fast after reaching level 85 where the other started a new character and is still enjoying it quite alot.
Conclusion: Grim Dawn is a great game and for €25 (€22,50 for me in the early sale) you get quite a bang-for-buck.

A fairly good SRPG that makes you think about your actions rather than beat down your enemies with raw numbers. (such as Disgaea or Fire Emblem) In this game, your health is also your damage so getting hurt too much means you'll be able to do very little. For your enemies, this means it's often better to weaken them first rather than killing them one by one. Weakened enemies will have to pierce through your armor first to be able to more effectively damage your strength, whichs helps to keep your guys healhier longer.
Combat wise, the game gives you fairly insufficient information pre-combat to be able to make choices about party setup. You have to choose your party and what turn order they go in before you can even see the enemy lay out and what positions your characters will start in. During my first playthrough I wished I had a bit more information beforehand, because there were times where I would have used other units if I had known what I was getting into. Not a huge complaint, and since you can lose a battle and still continue with the game it's not a huge deal if you go into a battle at a slight disadvantage.
Aside from combat, this game is all about "choice", that is, choices you make in the story supposedly affect the outcome of it. I find though that it doesn't affect as much as I would have liked. Most choices have an impact immediately, and a few have an impact barely minutes after the choice was made. There's only one choice I can recall that you make early that impacts something later on, but aside from those choices causing you to lose a character permenately, nothing you do throughout the game will causing the ending to change dramatically (except for a choice, of course, at the end!) At the end of the day, the choices aren't as heavy as the game wants you to believe they are.
Overall, a good game, but it can be a bit overwhelming at times for a new player to the point of being frustrating. If you beat the game once though, you'll have a good idea of how the characters work, what choices to make/not to make and be able to more effectively fight battles.
It's worth noting that I bought this while it's on sale for $4.99, and I would only recommend this game on a sale. Seeing as it's fairly short, the game play, while fun, doesn't offer a whole lot, and the story sets itself up for a sequel with very little closure. $20 is just a bit too steep for what this game offers but still worth playing.

"X-COM: Enemy Unknown" is a shining example of game franchise reboot done right. Firaxis have seized and grasped the essence of the original games without being enslaved to their minutia, and taken it to a modern era of more streamlined gameplay and intuitive controls with much of its tactical depth untouched. The feat is more praiseworthy when we consider we're talking about a mid-high budget game with few or no recent genre models to imitate.
We could argue about details like the missions types and environments turning a bit repetitive after some time, the difficulty curve adjustment (somewhat irregular), and some arguable "minigame-like" additions like the spaceship interception feature, but none of those things ever tarnish an elegant final product that should be compelling for open-minded old fans and new players alike.

There's nothing like the feeling when a game which wasn't even on your radar comes along, completely blows you away and reminds you why you love this hobby very dearly. And that's paramount. Even the best of us lose our faith sometimes. Faster Than Light is one of those games that comes out of nowhere and makes you a believer again. It is a testament to the brilliance of design over budget and as such is a shining beacon of this medium.
In Faster Than Light, the player takes on the role of a starship captain whose singular goal is to defend the Federation from a rebel threat. The concept is simple, you have to make it through seven grueling sectors to face the mammoth rebel flagship which will mercilessly put your nerves and skill to the test. It employs tough but fair school of design in which you will dearly pay for every single mistake you make, no matter how small. You may not even realize your mistake until it is too late.
You start with a barebones crew and equipment which you'll want to heavily upgrade by the time you reach the end. You'll achieve that by travelling through the galaxy, doing quests, fighting or aiding other ships or just buying whatever you can afford. This is a roguelike so every playthrough is completely different with randomized quests and loot drops. Sometimes you may feel slighted by the item drops or the difficult situations you find yourself in, but almost every piece of equipment is useful in some way and there's almost always a way out of a sticky situation. Being a roguelike also means that if you die, you have to start all over again. The sense of urgency is further heightened by the oncoming rebel fleet which won't allow you to roam the galaxy however you wish. Absolutely everything in Faster Than Light is subject to careful forethought and planning, otherwise you might just back yourself into a corner.
As the ship's captain, it is your duty to take care of absolutely everything that goes on your ship, the design is meticulously detailed. You have absolute control over a variety of systems including engines, shields, weapons, medbay, oxygen supply, helm, sensors, even doors. You also control every single crewmember. There are different races in the game and each specializes in a certain trait (except for humans). For example, Engis repair damaged systems faster, the Rock are immune to fire whereas the Mantis are great for ship intruders.
This all might sound overwhelming and there's actually a lot more various nuances to talk about here, but the tutorial is fantastic and you'll get the hang of the game quickly. This is a classic case of easy to learn, difficult to master.
The universe in Faster Than Light is pretty basic, it borrows liberally from various other sci-fi sources. Nevertheless, it is expertly put together. It is a very believable universe in which you'll learn about what's going on mostly through direct gameplay when interacting with other races and factions.
The Advanced Edition adds more content to the game most notably a new race with a new ship, fantastic new weapons and new upgrades such as mind control, cloning bay and hacking. The completely free expansion fleshes out the universe even further, but much more importantly it adds a myriad of new combinations of tactics that are at your disposal.
Faster Than Light is an exceptional work of game design. Its biggest accomplishment, which so few games manage to pull off, is that it draws you in, hooks you and never lets go. It is extremely addictive, even when you lose horribly and quit the game, all it takes is a few seconds and you're thinking about what you could've done differently and what tactics you will use next time you fire it up. And then you click play. Again.

Divinity: Original Sin (D:OS) serves as a testament to counter the culture of modern gaming.  Larian allowed nothing to hinder their vision for their creation; their love for games and the players who enjoy them serves as the greatest foundation in the making of D:OS.  From gameplay, design philosophy, dedicated patches post-launch, Larian has such confidence in their product because they have faith that their players would appreciate their steadfast, dedicated approach than cave in to the poison of modern culture.
Whether you love or hate Divinity, one could not deny the amount of love, respect, and effort Larian put into this game.  It's an example that anyone should  be following in their daily lives.
As a result, D:OS performs marvelously on all fronts.
Graphics: It's a CRPG, so let's set the bar realistically.  Rivellon in D:OS is simply gorgeous.  The colours and art bring out the atmosphere of the locations.  Weather effects are sharp and clear.  Spell and weapon effects are a charm to behold.  The attention to detail and polish makes this play like a modern game.
Sound/Voice Acting/Writing: The sound effects are solid.  There is nothing I do in game where the sound effects were inappropriate or unconvincing, from combat to walking through different weather terrains.  Not all NPCs are voiced, but when they are it is definitely well written and acted out convincingly.  Voice acting was always a strength when it came to Larian's games and I really did wish that there were more of them in D:OS.
Writing is another one of Larian's strongest skills.  Taste in writing is subjective.  The two previous games share this trait and D:OS doesn't escape this formula.  Unlike them, most of the writing is read rather than voiced.  It doesn't make the writing any less effective, yet the voice acting in the previous games also displayed the skills of the voice actors and how Larian will not attempt at anything less than stellar.
Music: Although taste in music is subjective, you cannot accuse Larian for doing their soundtracks poorly.  The quality is excellent.
Story Progression: The beauty about how this game works is the content comes to you the more you talk to people.  The more people you talk to, the more quests you get, the more variety of solutions to solve quests open to you.  Character abilities could be enhanced through dialogue.  It also gives you the freedom to kill quest givers, emphasizing on the lack of hand holding in this game.  For those who complain about the main story progression is in reality linear and how it is pretending to be open world, I might need to remind you that Dragon Age: Origins was also linear in spite offering 5 factions to recruit.  In addition, in Fallout: New Vegas you were not advised to take the shortest path to get to Vegas from the beginning.  I loved both games and they both failed at attempting to make the main story feel non-linear.
Combat: Combat is turn based, and that is subjective.  The use of environment as a key addition to your tactics, however, is worthy of praise.  The game encourages you to make good use of all the elements at your disposal so you are capable of winning a battle you would not otherwise win by capitalizing the terrain.  If the terrain is not in your favour, the option of making your own environment is there.  The doors of variety are open, making every battle a different one.
DRM/Microtransactions: It has no reason to exist.
Free Companion DLC: This action is extremely pro-consumer and it speaks volumes of how Larian treats their players.  These two members give your party a good mix up and adds variety to the game.  Larian had no reason to do this for free, but they wanted players to have more experiences than less.
Kickstarter Success: Larian proved to us that they are very capable of not cheating money that came from good faith.  Given the amount of abuse and horror stories from many developers that failed to create a game to live up to the expectations or simply scammed the contributors, D:OS is a beacon of example.
All said and done, no doubt this is a 10/10, right?
No.  I adore the game and it's my favorite game of the year, but it's not a 10/10.  D:OS does so many things right so well that it's all the more glaring when it does something wrong.
Character Customization: Due to how the character progression is designed in D:OS, hybrids can easily become mediocre if points are allocated wrong.  This limits one's creativity and encourages pures to be made due to simplicity and efficiency.  Despite that, pure builds also have a problem from the inaccessibility to crucial spells.  The best example is the Two Handed Knight.  Both AoE attacks are very limited in the game.  One of them can only be selected through character creation.  The other one comes very scarcely.   Respec removes all abilities you have, thus you cannot make any errors on an AoE Knight.  How could handicapping a build and punishing trial and error exist here? Players won't know any of this information unless they read up all the info before hand.
RNG: Although it's a necessary system, this makes an already slow game even slower.  Players want all the legendary gear vendors sell and will reload the game over and over until they find the pieces they want.  Vendors reset their inventory every level and thus this happens with multiple vendors on every level up.  Any loot-able source that can drop legendaries will have the player reloading the game until a desired piece drops.
Crafting:  As wonderful it may be to see that there is little hand holding and the abundance of freedom, I wish the crafting wasn't so overwhelming.  It's annoying to be bombarded with so many different items and have little idea regarding how to use them.  I don't want the game to be simple, but it would've been great if there was something to point players towards the right direction.
What do all have in common?
Time Consumption: The above factors all contribute to many very time consuming activities in addition to the 80 to 100 hours it requires to finish the game.  The game is marvelous in its own right indeed, yet when it demands this much time from its players it's vital to make the experience as efficient as possible.  Let's face it, we all have a limited of time each day to play games due to real life commitments, and Larian needs to figure out how to make the most use of our time when we offer it.  It's frustrating to be engaged in a game for hours just to find yourself accomplishing little.
What's even more tragic is that Larian had no intention of doing this.  They embraced all the ideas they wanted in a great game, worked so diligently to create a masterpiece, and yet in oversight their creation caused a dilemma that would've easily destroyed games of lower caliber.  That proves just how powerful and brilliant D:OS is.  When you're doing stuff it feels like DA: Origins.  When it doesn't it leave you hungering more for what could have been if the pacing was more efficient.  I believe it could potentially surpass DA: Origins with the last stroke of polish.
Regardless of these flaws, due to my adoration to Divinity, I'll be giving all the time that's required of me to experience D:OS thoroughly.  However, not everyone will be compelled to give Larian such grace, and this notion hurts the presentation of the game.  No one can justify why there's little to no progress in a game after putting hours of their free time into it.
I pray that there are upcoming DLCs and detailed patches that could remedy the issues.  D:OS was ever so close to perfection.
Final Verdict: 8.7/10 (How I wish this was a 9/10)
This package of love, respect and care is only $40.  Support Larian for what they do and there will be hope that their next Divinity game will outperform Original Sin.  They are real risk takers, unafraid to make whatever they feel is fun, and have the integrity, talent, character and dignity to back it up.

I recommend this game but with a caveat.  Let's get the negative out of the way immediately.
Combat.
It is an interesting system that has more depth than anticipated and it works very very well for much of the game.  As the difficultly and story progresses you become handcuffed by it.  I believe this could be rectified by allowing for a third friendly combatant even if only for the second act.  Some party members are simply so specialized they are swapped in for one turn then back out but often times this simply serves to extend some of the more lengthy combat segments later in the game.  It nearly soured me on the entire title but the overwhelmingly positive experience in the rest of the game saves that.  Be warned of this, combat will become tedious and repetitive water beats fire, lightning beats water, rock paper scissors gameplay.  The debuff and buff mechanics tend to fall by the wayside do to the need to swap out characters when simply pouring out damage will suffice.  A missed opportunity.
Let me cover another aspect of this game that is (for me) a HUGE positive.  If you have small children as I do who constantly want to help and take part in your game time, the ability for a second player to control your firefly companion is amazing.  My kids LOVED lighting him up to heal my fighters or making bad guys duck.  They loved lighting him up to unlock the unfortunately simple puzzles found throughout.  This alone will make me revisit this game over and over in the future.
As so many reviewers have mentioned the art, music, and thematic elements are really superb.  It is incredibly easy to dive into this game and become enraptured by your surroundings and the surreal feel of playing through a daydream the game evokes.  That combined with overall solid gameplay and story save it from the somewhat troublesome combat issues mentioned.  It is truly a beautiful and memorable game.  It's style will stay with you for a long time.

Now, when it comes to games like these I find myself consistantly trying to find the thing that makes them memorable. In Little Nightmares' case, I'd most definetly give that to the atmosphere. But that's not the only thing that people will care too much about, is it? As you can see, I have but a measly 10 hours of playtime. I must clairify that this includes playing through the game multiple times (2 1/2 in total) and with this notion, it will more than likely steer players away from this game. If you are the kind of person who values their purchase to a reasonable extent, I would not entirely recommend this game, but with the games biggest flaw out of the way, the other aspects of this game are sure to catch an eye or two. The platforming is done decently well with a very incontrol feeling with the aspects of climbing and chase sequences, however in some situations the awkward placement of the camera angles feel like they were ment more for a cineric view rather than one that would make sense for the situation, resulting in some pretty fustrating deaths. Each one of the 5 chapters were very memorable and did a fantastic job at showing off the beauty of this twisted setting in it's own charming way thanks to Six's prospective of being much smaller than everything around her. While some areas are admitetly shorter than others, there's no doubt that they all provided a memorable experience throwout. With the game being how short it is (about 4 hours in 1 sitting), I was rather suprised by how fond I had been of this experience in the end. With all that being said, I would recommend this game to those who are fans of the platforming genre and enjoy interesting scenery.

Let's start with a note: Neptunia saga is not for all, that's a fact.
As far as you can try if you don't like these "breaking the fourth wall", other games references and the fact the characters (at least the main ones) are girls you are not going to enjoy it.
Now let's talk about the game:
HDNRB1 is not just a remake of HDN, infact much is changed between story and mechanics.
The game is a quite hard JRPG, at least at the begin, sadly later you will probably going to spam these EXE (super like moves) destroying everything in your path but still the game gives out quite a challenge.
There's not actuall grinding like other JRPGs but still you can't go around ignoring enemies or you'll be in trouble against these End chapter bosses.
Graphically the game is not that bad but not everyone like the "anime style".
Musics are good even if not that many.
Dungeons are... well there's many dungeons but not many types, you will find yourself unlocking many dungeons sure but in the same times many of them are just the same one with some differences and nothing more, same for the enemies, so be aware, if you want to see differences at every corner you are not going to like it.
As port is not perfect but still this is the very first port made by IFI and, in my opinion, they made a good job in the end.
Should you buy it then? Yes, you should.
Still, like i've said at the begin, this game is not for everyone but who knows, you may find yourself having more fun than you think.

And of course how long your index finger can still keep up.

My first review ever and English is not my native language so please bear with me.
Grim Dawn is an awesome arpg that takes place in a fictional world. The game provides fast and smooth gameplay with intriguing lore to uncover. The game looks dark and grim which I found very appealing compared to the cartoony look other games may have. There’s enough diversity in the different area’s to explore. Some areas are looking absolutely gorgeous. Most of the game is hand-crafted  with some randomization. There a plenty of different enemies to fight against providing enough verity and challenge. Sometimes you have to prioritize to kill a certain enemy otherwise things may get really tough. What You See Is What You Get (WYSIWYG), which means that an enemy could have an epic weapon or armor equipped that you can see him wearing. So kill him and he will drop that item, however if he might be tougher to fight against as the item can grant them more power than usual.
You can play this game single-player or multi-player with a party up to a max of 4 people.

There are currently 6 classes which are called masteries in the game. They each have their own unique skills. When you reach level 2 you can choose a mastery to start with and at level 10 you can choose a 2nd mastery if you want. This way it provides enough build diversity for your taste. Melee or ranged and a mix of both it’s all up to you to choose. You can use 1 handed weapons and shields, 2 handed weapons, dual wield, pistols, scepters, focus and pets (summons). So you are not bound to a few skills you can choose from. Items like armor, components , relics, etcetera could also grant extra skills to use. And let’s not forget about Devotion, thought out the game you can find Devotion Shrines to restore, which grants you loot and a Devotion point on which you can invest in the Devotion Window providing more stats and skills to customize your build. You can use any item you want just as long as you meet the required stats for it. You can reassign skill- and devotion points but not mastery- and attribute points.
There’s plenty of loot in this game which can be obtained from enemies, chest, bought at a vendor or you can craft items. Blueprints can be found to craft different items at the blacksmith.
I like the faction system on where you have hostile factions with increased negative reputation against them, brings increased enemy spawn additional monster spawns, increased Hero spawns and, upon reaching Nemesis status, Nemesis spawns. With friendly factions, increased reputation unlocks access to the bounty table. There you can do small quest for a gaining faster reputation with that faction and that unlocks more items at the faction vendor.
I love it  that certain quest can change the appearance a little bit of a refugee area. Bringing more survivors there and a cosmetic change. There are also quests that brings choice and consequence to your decisions. So the outcome for that quest could influence a small area.
The lore is great for those who are interested in that like me. You can find notes in the game that provide more information about certain events. But also by talking to npc’s and reading the description in the devotion windows.
There’s no magic arrow that points you into the right direction for a quest, only when your nearby you will see a star on the mini map that your close. Personally i think this is a big plus, i love to explore and find the area myself it’s way more immersive.
There are enough options in the game to change the camera angle zoom in and out. You can set the loot filter to only show magic items, so that your screen isn’t cluttered with loot.
Secret areas who doesn’t like them, i always have the urge to explore everything. Some secret areas are small others are larger. You can find them by breaking a wall or perhaps a hidden path to reach it. Explore and you shall be rewarded because there are plenty of secret areas to uncover.
Small things that matter like kicking in doors or at barrels, destructible objects like furniture walls that collapse. Weather changing effect that make the area darker with a bit or rain or just a sunny day. Enemies of different factions fighting each other.
Challenge dungeons  that provide a real challenge, where if you die you have to restart the game to start a new session. That means you have to redo the dungeon to get to the end. I play softcore so i won’t lose my character but still have the excitement of trying to survive and not to get killed.
Modding tools are released, so expect the community to create their own content, items, classes and even entire worlds.
The developers are very passionate about the making the game, since the Kickstarter the game has grown bigger and better with more features than they originally planned. There is even a free content update coming out soon!

To me the most important aspect of the game as a whole is the amazing concept that it embodies. I bought this game expecting a regular rougelike-ish dungeon crawler, I was, however, surprised to find it brought a whole new level to a already existing genre. Crawl assembles rougelike elements together with fast-paced and skillbased combat between the different players competing. Solo play is only possible against bot(s), but this is still a large amount of fun.

It's cool and all, but the controls aren't responsive and the fact that, counting glass, there's only like 5 colors in the whole game I was really just running in circles and jumping into windows like a confused bird. The command to jump backwards from a wall you're jumping at just rarely worked for me and I had to walk away often because the game wouldn't react to the proper input with anything but me falling to my death for the 15th time. Sometimes you jump towards a ledge that's within reach and you grab it, sometimes you don't grab it and you have to do the exact same motion to get a different result. There's a guide button that helps you if you're turned around but it points your character in the direction of where you're supposed to go, rather than in the direction of how to get there, so you pretty much end up running the wrong way and doubling back looking for something to jump at. I finally gave up at a section where you have to fight guys with assault rifles. I would get on a high ledge and jump kick them, and the game would shoot me 20 feet in the air at a slow speed and the enemies would shoot me to death before I landed.
Given it's age, I'm not all that disappointed, but I would recommend only buying if it's cheap and you're curious about how the first shaky steps of first person parkour games were like.

This game is good. If anything the thousands of positive game reviews you already scrolled though by now makes that clear. But there’s one thing that’s hardly brought up that actually makes this game good. It cuts a lot of the BS that ARPG's tend to do and also adds a lot of quality of life features.
Here's some to list a few:
1) Loot grade filter. You only see the tier of loot you want to. If you want to change this it’s a simple button just left of your health bar. I’ve played a few ARPG's in my life and one of the worse things is the sea of useless grey items that flood the screen and block my view. No more, change the filter on the fly or even turn items off if you don't care.
2) Skill/Devotion point refund. In this game you get two classes and three skill points per level to put into skills that those classes have. While you need to hit a certain level in each classes mastery to get higher end skills (the bar at the bottom gets points that increase the base stats best associated with the class) the actual skill points spent on skills are refundable for a crazy cheap price in the first starting town. The skill points used in mastery are not refundable though, so be careful. Devotion points (points you get by activating shrines) are also able to be reset with a relatively small fee of one aether shard (a fairly common item). This is great of players figuring out the game as the risk of making major mistakes are diminished.
3) No identification/portal scroll middle men. You have the ability to make a personal portal that can travel to any main portal at any time. You can then travel back to that exact portal you made by using a main portal. No scrolls or spells needed. When you get an item you know exactly the stats that it gives and what you need to wear it. No scrolls to waste on times that have a high chance of not being in your build specs anyways. These changes make the game flow much more gracefully.
4) Constitution. Your health bar has a little transparent golden sheen overlaid on top of it. When you get out of combat and have missing health the bar will drain and fill your health. This might not seem like much with health potions being a thing but the system speeds up the game and makes the reliance on health regen and potions not so important in terms of general game play.
Now, this isn't to say this game is perfect. It’s not, but most of the problems stem from the ARPG game type and not so much the game itself. You kill mostly trash mobs, find mostly trash items, you sometimes get killed because the game decides to actually toss you a challenging enemy when you’re in trash mob mode. The game is incredibly grim just like all the popular ARPG's tend to be, so grim in fact that it almost borders parody. I don't think you see more than 60 or so friendly humans but you mow over thousands that want to kill you.  Theirs bones and bodies and pain and blood so much that you don't even mind it after a while.  Find items just for you is a pain with such a robust choice of builds. The quests are pretty paper thin, the characters are ok, but nothing to really write home about or get crazy attached too, the plots main antagonists get shafted, another threat comes and pretty much takes the spotlight. The ending is underwhelming, it kind of just spits you out into the world after killing a crazy big foe and the game hardly even pats you on the back.
But, all in all, grim dawn is pretty much your best choice for ARPG especially if you are new to them. While not perfect it will more than make up for the price of entry.

After just starting Ultimate difficulty (the highest of the 3 difficulties) and my counter saying I spend 76 hours on this game, I thought I might as well write a review.
Grim Dawn supports 6 classes: the soldier, demolitionist, occulist, nightblade, arcanist and shaman. While every class has a certain focus (e.g. a soldier is typically melee and an arcanist is usually a spellcaster), you can adapt pretty much any playstyle to any of the classes; it is mainly your equipment that will determine the effectiveness of your character. Also the game allows you to choose a second class later on, where every combination results in a different classname.
I play a Shaman/Arcanist (called a Druid), currently level 71 (out of 85), use 2 handed rifles/crossbows and mainly focus on dealing lightning damage. Every shot from my crossbow unleashes a chain lightning that jumps to pretty much everything on screen. Currently I am a full glass-cannon build which worked fine for most of the Elite difficulty (the 2nd difficulty) but now in Ultimate, where all your resistances are lowered by 50, I start to notice I really lack defence. Nothing a little gearing can't fix though.
A downside of the game I found is that the number of skills to choose from at the beginning of the game is quite overwhelming. Also the first time I opened the devotion skilltree I went like.. what the heck is this!?
You will quickly realise though that you can choose between about 5-6 active skills and the rest of the skilltree adds passive effects to the actived skill. I found this to be a bit of a let-down because it resulted in my character using the same skill for the entirety of the Normal difficulty because leveling up just added some more passive damage to single skill; once I reached Elite I started branching in my skilltree which opened up alot more abilities thus I enjoyed Elite alot more than Normal.
Another downside might be the lategame but since I haven't reached that yet I can't comment too much on it. 2 of my friends bought this game the same moment I did and they both reached max level quite some time ago; one of them quit pretty fast after reaching level 85 where the other started a new character and is still enjoying it quite alot.
Conclusion: Grim Dawn is a great game and for €25 (€22,50 for me in the early sale) you get quite a bang-for-buck.

So after sinking about 5 hours into the game, give or take, I am now ready to review this Everlasting Summer. Initially when I saw this on the store, the art style prevented me from getting it, however the actual normal... sprites I guess? Are much better than the actual artwork in my opinion, so that's excusable. The characters follow pretty standard tropes for the most part, but being a game heavily influenced by anime, that's to be expected, and is forgivable. The main character is kind of an idiot sometimes, but I can't really argue due to the fact that I can't expect every character to be similar to myself, what really annoys me about him is he's given just enough time to be considered not a clean slate, but not enough to be an actual personality. My main problem with the game is it's obsession with Russia, don't get me wrong I have no problem with the place, and considering the setting it could have been a nice cultural dip into a type of life I normally wouldn't have looked at or read about, due to my hate of history. My issue is that it kind of attempts to shove it down your throat, the amount of.. information, to put it nicely, is over the top. In my eyes, the ideal setting of a VN is second to characters and story, both of which this game almost puts behind it's setting. I would like to see a more neutral setting in their newer game that has been announced, but who am I kidding, I'll probably play it either way.. Overall, so far this game has been fine. Being that it is free I can excuse a lot of it's flaws, but there are a few aspects of it that really annoy me. This review might seem really negative, but honestly I can't think of anything the game does... well, exceptionally that is worth mentioning, while it does have obvious flaws in my eyes. Don't let this deter you, if you want a visual novel that is both free and accessible, as I do, these flaws won't stop you. Overall I'd give this somewhere between a 6/10 and an 7.5/10, I really can't decide.

Absolutely LOVING this game! I got a little tired of Cyseal after my 3rd, and 4th restart.. Unfortunately, its one o fthe biggest zones.. I like how  can go in whichever direction i want, and do quests in the order i prefer, if at all.. The conversations are well done, and vast.. I played a shadowblade, which was effective, though i tended to lean more on my witchcraft, than my scoundrel abilities.. Since i used a dagger, i was able to backstab the hell out of targets when magic wasnt effective, or unecessary.. Summons for each character can make your party a bit OP however.. 3/4 f my characters on my recent playthrough could summon.
I had a hard time knowing which characters to take, with the burglar dlc, as i wanted to do the missions they came with.. I alway slike to switch it up, so i found myself constantly forcing yself to change up my group, just to experience them all.. If i didnt take the DLC i think i would not have done so, and i never tried the hirelings, so i cannot comment..
The crafting can be a bit difficult to figure out all the combinations too, but there are guides if you really want too.. You can cheese through the game with crafting, and blacksmithing, though i personally didnt, becaus ei like to "earn"  my victories.. Its a vast amount of ways to craft, and the sheer amount of different things that can be made is a minigame all its own.. Its really astonishing when you see all the little things that can be used.. That said, it makes inventory management a nightmare, as the inventory system is one of the worst kinds of drag n drop crao-shoots ive seen..
And now, for the real prize of this title.. The combat.. Turn based combat is fun all its own.. But the environmental element thrown in with this title really adds a layer of flavor that brings so much to each encounter.. Some people are compelled to min/max everything, and i submit that role playing the game without speccing specifically for max dmg/survivability in combat will really make the game shine from all angles.. Being able to shock a puddle, and stun an entire regiment is fun.. Likewise you can brn the puddle with fire, then shock the steam-cloud it made, for a similar effect.. Shoot poion on, or with fire, and make a toxic gas cloud, poisoning anyhting it encounters.. Freeze a puddle, and watch everyone slip and fall, effectively bypassing their turn altogether...Drop a barrel of oil, attack one, and llight it on fire to leave a trail of napalm accross the area, burning all who dare cross.. Leave the oil, and let enemy movemtn slowed, lessening their dmg, and defense.. All this ontop of what can already be done with the ton of fun in combat.. And no, you dont have to "happen upon" a puddle, or show, or poison to make use of the environmewnt.. You have items and spells to create rain/puddles, oil slicks, poison gas, steam clouds, etc..
Now, i have to say, the Rock/Paper/Scissor mechanic used to decide arguments really sucks.. It seems near impossible until you figure out the simple 3 turn algorythm used.. However, you can just switch characters, using  the [ ] keys and then spacebar to auto-win.. This is the method i suggest, as its poorly done.. You likely will not win, unless you invest heavily in a specific talent, and win 2 lucky rolls..
The artstyle isnt for everyone, as its less than realistic, but its color palet is vibrant, and beautiful, if you like that kind.. I prefer realism, and i loved the visuals.. Spells, effects, weather, environment, characters, etc.. Everything, really.. Just looks amazing!
Theres great music in this game.. The soundtrack never left you in silence, or annjoyed over hearing the same few second sountrack on repeat cycles!
The voice acting is well done, though its only tied to main quests.. (theres an Enhanced Edition being released soon, thats going to add alot more to the game, along with some tweaks to combat, story, placement, etc..Its going to be FREE to those of us who already own the PC version of thegame.. Big kudos to Larian for that)
I could go on, and on, but ill just stop there.. Any company who gives out a free Enhanced Edition upgrade, responds to player feedback, and shows obvious love for the game, the experience, and the community deserves your support!
Without a doubt_ Absolutely, positively Game of the Year!!!

It may be squalid and zombie-infested, but Dying Light's city of Harran isn't a depressing wasteland – it's a vibrant, ambitious, open-world playground. Here, buildings are for climbing, the undead are there to be destroyed in creative ways, and there's always something interesting to be discovered nearby. It takes a while for that to become clear, though; at first, you might even think Dying Light is really about running scared from mobs of seemingly unconquerable zombies, who can quickly drain your stamina and wear out your improvised weapons. Don't be fooled. Yes, it's a struggle to survive in Dying Light's early hours. Combat is initially clumsy, with the diverse and deadly zombies able to soak up a disturbing amount of punishment before they die for good. Jumping – which is unintuitively mapped to shoulder buttons on consoles – can take a while to get used to. Getting mobbed is usually a death sentence. So is attracting the attention of the much more dangerous things that come out when daytime dynamically gives way to night, at which point the focus shifts to tense stealth — or, if you’re discovered, an adrenaline-pumping sprint for the nearest safe point.
Before long, though, you'll build up a skill set that turns your rotting foes into objects of fun, letting you vault across their shoulders, quickly slice them apart with dramatic slow-motion kills, or trick them into gathering around explosives before blasting them all into the sky. Even nighttime becomes an opportunity to raise skills faster thanks to increased XP gain, rather than a period of sheer terror. It all feels great, too; once you adjust to the controls, Dying Light's first-person parkour becomes natural and fluid, and weaving high-speed paths through its decaying slums and picturesque old-world buildings is so much fun that I almost don't hate the lack of a fast-travel option.
Combat, meanwhile, gets increasingly satisfying, although it never quite loses its awkwardness. Even when expertly shredding zombies with elementally charged tools of death I built myself, strikes are still heavy and clumsy. And while the guns you'll find later can pop heads from a distance, their low rate of fire and zombie-attracting noise makes them more of an occasional quick fix than a game-changing weapon. To Dying Light's credit, though, your adversaries are surprisingly capable; while the rank-and-file Biters are dumb and fun to manipulate, more powerful enemies – like the quick, agile Virals – are formidable close-quarters opponents, ducking your strikes and sidestepping out of your reach while looking for an opening to attack. Hostile bandits are even deadlier, able to dodge and block at close quarters, throw knives from a distance, and use guns and group tactics to kill you if you get overconfident.
That Dying Light's world is so entertaining is important, because it's unexpectedly huge. Finishing the campaign took me more than 34 hours, with a 68 percent completion rate. The story is serviceable enough, focusing on an undercover agent who becomes a savior to infected survivors and a thorn in the side of a maniacal warlord, but the most surprising thing about it might be its lack of surprises. Similar games have primed me to expect shocks and betrayals that will yank the metaphorical rug out from beneath me, and yet apart from a few big twists early on, Dying Light plays it mostly straight, with little nuance and few hidden agendas from its interesting (but underdeveloped) characters and entertainingly cliché villains. In a way it's almost refreshing, even if the end result is nothing special.
A big chunk of my time, though, was spent on detours into side quests, which are where the storytelling really shines. Taking on one of the many requests from random survivors might lead to something ordinary, like a fetch quest – but more often than not, they're multi-part adventures with their own short storylines, which frequently start out as seemingly run-of-the-mill tasks and escalate into something much more lurid and creepy. A search for a missing person, for example, might turn into a hunt for progressively more unsettling clues in a seemingly abandoned apartment building, and a routine rescue mission might turn out to be a trap set by a conniving madman. These are some of Dying Light's most memorable moments, and they make exploring its world even more rewarding.
While it's entirely playable as a single-player game, Dying Light is – like most things – better with friends along. Up to three co-op partners can jump in at any time to help you carve up undead hordes, watch your back while you're picking locks, or pursue campaign missions, and while the online matchmaking is still fairly hit-or-miss on PS4, online sessions are smooth and stable once they get going.
It's also useful to have friends around if your game is invaded through the "Be the Zombie" mode, which lets a random player jump into your world as a super-powered monster with zipline tendrils and zombie-summoning spit. Playing as said monster is hugely enjoyable, especially after you’ve unlocked some of its grosser attacks, but it feels one-sided unless you're going up against at least two human players.
Other than moderately better visuals, the PC version's biggest leg up on its console counterparts is its customizable keyboard-and-mouse controls. Keeping track of the assorted key functions can be a little trying when things get frantic, but using the space bar to jump still feels more immediately natural than R1 or RB on PS4 or Xbox One. (Gamepads are, of course, supported.) Early on, there were reports that Dying Light would hang before dialogue or cutscenes, but these issues appear to have been patched, and the PC version now mostly runs smoothly for us, with only rare hitching while areas load. There is, however, an occasional issue with some textures popping in at low resolution and sticking that way. The PS4 version has a similar problem, but while it quickly corrects itself, textures that show up blurry on PC tend to stay that way.
Beginning as a furtive, desperate survival-horror experience, Dying Light gradually and gratifyingly evolves into a fast, hyper-violent celebration of vertical freedom and zombie destruction. Its main story is unspectacular, but the memorable side quests and sheer fun of exploring its world do a fantastic job of offsetting that, making Dying Light one of the most engrossing open-world games – zombie-infested or otherwise – I've played in a while

I absolutely loved the intro and the first few chapters.  The story was interesting and the characters compelling.  Unfortunately the turn based combat is uninspired and dare I say outright bad design.  This is a game I should have loved from top to bottom.  I love turn based games.  But the movement, lack of terrain and outright poor combat design principles just kill it dead.  Having your attack strenght directly tied to your hitpoints is one of the worst design ideas I have ever seen.  It completely eliminates any kind of come from behind strategy.  If you get behind in damage output you might as well restart the match because mathmatically you can't win.  Which brings me to the worst point.  Without any kind of cover or terrain the matches feel like math equations.  You put damage A+B against enemy C and your outcome is X.
Mid to late game you realize that spending renoun on anything other than upgrading your warriors is a complete waste of time.  Your people and troops are completely irrelevant and the later game enemies completely outclass your best warriors.  You will also extremely favor some warriors over other less useful characters to the point of completely ignoring them.  Since levelling is directly tied to defeating enemies there is no incentive to take less useful characters.
Bottom line, I bought this game for $5 and Card Hunter for $0.  Other than the story, I get way more enjoyment out of playing Card Hunters during the turn based battles.  I find this game to be highly over rated.  Maybe because its an indi game a lot of people give it a pass.  I wont be getting the sequels.

Incredible game. I fully recommend buying. And if you're off-put by the lack of online multiplayer, don't be. Because playing with the AIs is basically the same experience you'd get from online multiplayer, except no lag, no cheaters, and more consistantly fun to play with enemies.
The game is amazing about balance, and it makes it virtually impossible for one person to fall behind and end up not having a good time. Here's how it works:
There's always one person who plays as the "Hero", with the other three (or other two or other one) playing as "Ghosts" who summon and inhabit monsters, as well as using traps and throwing objects at the player. Whoever kills the current Hero becomes the Hero, with the dead one becoming a Ghost. When the Hero levels up, each of the Ghosts gains 5 wrath. At the end of each floor, players can spend wrath to level up the monsters that they summon during the level. So if you spent most of the last floor as a Hero, you'll be stronger in that aspect, whereas your monsters will be struggling (it's generally better to have a strong human though, as that's how you actually win the game). So even if you're doing terribly and haven't killed the Hero once, you still have a decent shot since you will have the strongest monsters in the game, and so the best chance of becoming the next Hero. Ghosts also gain gold passively through their interactions with the Hero (although the Hero gets more), so weak Heroes can still afford to upgrade their gear once they get to a shop.
Overall this game is just wonderfully balanced, both by the premise as a whole, and the amazing level of detail the developers have gone into to ensure that the scales never tip too far in one direction. You'll also never find a more attentive and responsive development team, just looking at their forums or their community page alone would be enough for me to buy this game, regardless of the amazing fun that it is.

I'm only a couple of hours in.
Firstly, this is not a "First Person Shooter".
The whole game (so far) seems to involve, pretty much running away, through scripted, time/checkpoint triggered areas, full of people shooting you.
Also, there is some lateral thinking and puzzle solving, but everything, is pretty much on rails. This is not "open world" exploration.
The movement, which take some time to get used to, is pretty good, and I admire what they have achieved, however, it lacks that final polish, and, as such, is still a little awkward.
The (very limted) combat, is a joke.
I kept waiting for the "intro chase scene" to end, and the real FPS game to start...but, it seems, this game, might be nothing but, one long chase sequence.
I bought in on special, so, not too fussed, but, after only a few hours, it's not drawing me back for more.
If I get around to giving it a further try, I might end up being surprised, but, I doubt it.

Divinity Original Sin is truly a shining diamond, a master-class in Old-School Top-Down RPG's. Taking inspiration from the likes of Baldur's Gate, D:OS shows that it isn't afraid to slap you in the face, kick you in the balls, cut you to pieces and make you get back up again for Round 2. It doesn't hold you're hand, it doesn't help you virtually at all... The tools are right in front of you, Divinity just expects you to learn and know how to use them, yourself.
The art-design is striking and gorgeous. The turn-based combat is rock-solid with great mechanics backing it. The story is great though I'll admit it could be a little better. The gameplay aside from the combat with the rock-paper scissors mini-games to accidentally starting a fight with a merchant when you misclick and throw a candle-stick at him lighting him on fire is just brilliant. I've never played an RPG as good as this one and I've played alot.
Call me a fanboy or whatever you want, but Divinity : Original Sin is one of those true gems, and a stellar masterpiece that roared out of its KickStarter funding. Thank you Larian for giving me an experience of a lifeitme.
10/10. Buy if you want your world and view on RPG's to be blown away. LOVE IT!

You already bought the game.  It says Game of Thrones, and so you shelled out the cash and already paid for it.  I'm not hardly trying to dissuade you or make you regret the descion, but here you are reading.  As a fan of the books, the handfull of comics, and of course the TV show, this is a black mark on the franchise and on Telltale.  It's not awful, but there sure is a lot of "bad" in it.
While some people complain about the "railroaded" plotline, that's not even my problem.  MY problem with the story is how it's presented.  In Walking Dead you control on character, in The Wolf Among Us you control one character.  In THIS you control 3 of them.  You barely get to spend any time with them before they toss another at you making them all feel dull.  The books do this, but for entire chapters, and you can see how they think.  The show does this, but there's still more content in the series than the game.    It's trying to hard to be like the other media for the franchise.
My biggest problem with the story is that it doesn't make sense.  You have to play it to see, but there are multiple scenes that simply don't follow any logic.
The animations are poor, but the character modeling is almost insulting.  First of all, when I saw Magaery Tyrell, I started laughing.  She looks hideous.  Secondly, to bring up Telltale's previous work again, WD had a small cast and only reuses zombie models.  TWAU does not reuse a single character model outside of completely faceless silouettes rarely even seen in the game and ALWAYS in the background.  GoT, on the other hand, reuses models constantly to the point where you start wondering if that guy with the pock-marked face you just ran from is the same guy who has a sword on you now and the same guy you run into an hour later.
Overall, it's not good.  If you're desperate for GoT, pick up some HBO box sets or (FOR GOD'S SAKE) read the books.  Otherwise play The Walking Dead (season 1), or The Wolf Among Us.

As a huge south park fan, the sheer number of show refferences are staggering. It feels like almost every epsiode has a callback somewhere, so it's hard not to love this as an extended piece of the South Park universe. The humor is a decent mix of new ideas and show callbacks, and though most of it isn't laugh-out-loud funny, it's enough to keep you smiling the whole time.
As a gamer, though, it fell a bit short. Some of your powers are poorly explained, and then don't get used often enough for you to really figure them out. Also, you end up unlocking new ways to progress through the game world, but other than the very first one they are barely used enough to warrant making them 5 or 6 different powers that you have to cycle through each time you need to use one. The game is also pretty short - it took about 18 hours to finish the whole story, and then one more to wrap up side missions. This is made worse by the fact that death has no real consequences, and over-leveling is easy if you're a gamer who is used to exploring all of the overworld before you move on with the story. And it's immensely frustrating that some of the collectibles you need to 100% the game are available only once and easily missable.
Get this game when it's super cheap on sale and play through it in a weekend, and you won't be dissapointed. But don't pay full price, and don't go in expecting more than a fun homage to the show.

A masterpiece of art, but just a average game as it is. This game draws from JRPGs such as Chrono Trigger and Grandia (or Grandia 2?), feels very Zeldaesque on some parts, looks a bit like Aquaria on other ones, and has western fairytales as a model on how the story unfolds.
This game has an epic Pan's Labyrinth feeling to it, looking like a dark fairytale as its story unfolds with magnificent visuals and a fitting soundtrack.
The story has a nice sense of progression, you feel the progress and feel rewarded as you play through the game.
It feels unique, the game seems handpainted all over it, including the 3D models, the movement and animations are perfect, you feel the innocence and the fragility of the character on the first instants of the game, you feel the weight of the sword on her hands and you feel like some dark places are really creepy and ominous.
The soundtrack that accompanies the game is pretty well executed, it's not the best around, but its still fitting through the entire game and adds to the fairytale feeling of the whole experience.
While the whole game feels astonishingly beautiful, what really inspired me to review it were the dialogues, all of them were written in prose, the whole narrative is driven by rhymes and poems sang by the characters while they venture Lemuria. Some simple lines are written so well that you'll be recalling them for days, and still feel glad to have experienced this game.
This game as a work of arts, visuals, sounds and story are 10/10. A masterpiece.
Now onto the "game" part of it, the mechanics are simple tight about JRPG that everyone knows well, feels a bit like the old Grandia 2 from PSX with a hint of Chrono Trigger on how you engage into fights, for the whole game you'll be going through simple Trine/Zelda puzzles while fighting (or not) mobs of the darkness, character customization comes from gems that you get while fighting mobs or finding treasures and through a simple skill system that looks a lot like Far Cry 3's. Too bad that some skills are almost mandatory for you to play through some parts of the game when playing on Hard, and that makes grinding a bit of a must if you chose the wrong skills early on. Fighting are simple enough to easily grasp onto them, but complex enough  so that if you want to play it well, you need to master every tiny bit of the fighting mechanics. The game is pretty linear as a whole, you don't get much to do on the side of the main story, and while all of the monsters are avoidable, fighting them is almost always a win-win on the grinding part, you level easily and fastly so that the whole grinding thing is less of a burden. As a game, without counting the masterfully done art, I'd rate it 7/10... It's just that nothing is really okay at all, but it's not bad, just feels flawed at times.
Final Verdict : Play it. It's really good.

Definitely treat this game with caution. I think a lot of the goodwill for this game is coming from a place of Nostalgia - Sure, it's great to see those old fashioned isometric games of old rendered in a modern game engine at a modern resolution - it really is quite lovely to behold in places, but the majority of the game's mechanics? Let's just say there's a reason we moved on. So many of the quests hinge upon inscrutably obscure and incoherent logic, the story is utter drivel and the crafting seems like a trial and error after-thought.
This game makes a very good first impression and I applaud many of the developers' decisions, but overall I think this game needed a bit more time in the oven, a bit more refinement and hell - a few hours less playtime. If this game had been a third of it's size and hung together a bit more coherently I'd probably be eagerly awaiting the next installment. As it is, I'm left trudging my way through the game with a walkthough, almost 100 hours in, dearly waiting for it to be over.
If I had as much time as I did for these games back when they were popular I might have had more patience for it - I can't recommend this to anyone but the most patient and time-rich gamers.

(disclaimer: I had heard that this game was easy so I played it on the harder difficulty, this may have underlined some of the faults and influenced my opinion)
The overworld and sub-quests are not bad, but I won't go into much detail, because plenty of people talk about them.
My complaint is with the interruption system in combat. If a character is attacked while preparing an action, they get knocked back on the timeline. The problem is that this is a feast or famine system; you're either obliterating the enemy or caught in an unwinnable situation.
In the second half of the game, there are enemy combinations who will caste haste on their entire team and slow on your team. Add to that, that there can be 3 enemies, but only 2 of you. This leads to battles where you're consistently getting knocked back or put into a situation where all you can do is block or try to heal (basically never being able to damage the enemies to give yourself a chance). Then, you try the fight again and get a bit luckier (or are better equiped) and win easily in 2-3 turns.
It really feels unbalanced, and I didn't enjoy it.

What to say, what to say... I was aware of the rabbit hole, yet I jumped into it. Don't repeat my mistake, I beg of you.
I'm familiar with the publisher, Playflock, and I've played their "Insanity" game when it was browser MMO. Soon I realized how many time and money I gotta spend to make progress in the original, so I dropped the issue quite soon. But, after some years passed, they came back for me, adapted their game to the clicker mechanics (almost the same at start as with Clicker Heroes and alike). And that hooked me for much longer. In the end, it's all the same: you can progress to some level, yeah, but there are no chances you'll finish the game fairly, even with making a bet with your very soul.
Now, what's interesting with the project?
First, the mechanic, it's not the 100% clone of any other clicker game, especially with the implementation of PvP fights in the process. However, as usual, it's badly calculated, making the gaming process not delightful, but very painful instead. Big gaps between levels of power, urge to do "reincarnating" every hour or so to make some progress later in the game... And those PvP battles in clicker game! The whole game is blasphemy, and those battles are really icing on this crud cake.
Talking about blasphemy, the second distinctive thing. The visuals, the arts of asylum goes total madhouse, all that horror pictures, which fans of the "Saw" movies are so fond of... I found it disgusting, but at least it's not another cartoon style blobs I'm so tired of in so many other clickers!
All in all, I'm strongly suggest you to keep away from "Insanity", Even if you're a clicker games true fan (which would be humiliating). The developers are so greedy, so wanted to milk you out of all your money, they deserved to be buried inside that madhouse they created. Mark 4/10 (style points).

Welcome to the HQ. You haven been given a handful of rookie soldiers, some contemporary firearms, a team of some of the best engineers and scientists available, and an almost unfallible alien menace encrouching on the planet.
Your move, commander.
---
The campaign begins after a tutorial mission with the XCOM HQ. Here as the game will show, you have various sub-sections. With engineering you fabricate items that can be used in combat and in your strategic, global operations and with the labs you research the technologies to create these new weapons, armour, equipment and designs. In the hangers you can allocate fighter aircraft around the world and modify their weapon loadouts. Likewise, in the barracks you can inspect your soldiers, change their loadouts, and provide them with promotions and medals when available to bolster their effectiveness.
The basic premises of combat is fairly simple. It is turn based, and your units have two action points per turn, which can involve moving, firing, reloading, etc. This can be split across two movements, but all other actions expend all action points in one go, although it still allows for a combination of one movement first and another action second. The map is laid out in a grid style, providing angular cover through the terrain that varies between half and full cover values. All attempts to fire will roll RNG, which is affected by the situation they are in. Units can move closer to gain an increased chance, but most notably can outflank others by moving to positions where the enemies cover is negligable. The closer the unit is to this, the greater their hit chance, and if outright flanking them, they also recieve a large boost to the chance to do critical damage. Equally, different equipment allows you to specialise soldiers where some like grenades and medikits must be selected to be used on a turn, while others like optical sights and protective vests provide passive effects. Explosives provide splash damage and can destroy cover, which gives the option of creatively outflanking and dealing with enemies through another means.
There are four main classes of soldier, being Assault, Support, Heavy and Sniper. All of these classes begin with unique functions and all soldiers recieve a new ability on every promotion, which allow for greater specialisation. Assault units are allowed shotguns and have various greater offensive capabilities like being able to use Flush to force enemies out of cover or Run and Gun to allow a full two movement and then a fire action on the turn. Support classes excel at providing buffs and using utility items, particularly as being medics, engineers, and using support grenades like smoke. Heavy classes have heavier MGs that allow for the use of suppressive fire but can also fire rockets. Sniper classes specialise in high DPS roles with the option to use the squadsight rule, firing from beyond their own sight. Later in the game you may find some of your soldiers hold the Gift - and with the Enemy Within expansion you can use the alien materials to enhance your soldiers in other ways, though that is for you to find out.
It is your job to disrupt the alien activity across the world. By constructing and launching satellites you can monitor UFO activity within specified areas, and send fighters to intercept them. Should a UFO land, be shot down, or begin an abduction mission, you are cleared to send in a squad to stop this. These three common missions simply require the death of all alien units to succeed, but missions that arrive later in the game will require specific goals. Further, the Council who provides the funding of XCOM will occasionally request help with a unique council mission, which could be anything from defusing a bomb to extracting a VIP, and several of these are pertinent to the development of the plot.
The funding nations are also subject to varying panic levels. Allow any nation to go out of control and it may withdraw funding and quit the XCOM project all together. If eight nations [half] decide to do this, the game will be lost. Abduction events will typically appear in threes, and force you to pick a single nation out of this three to defend. You can however reduce panic with Council missions and by deploying satellites over select nations. With the Enemy Within expansion you will also have to contend with an enemy within mankind itself which adds a further layer to the global strategy - but again, I will say no more.
The base also has a large building element. You have a large amount of building slots to work with, and effectively managing these can be key to the game - constructing more labs means you can keep pace with the technological developments of the aliens, more workshops helps to reduce costs to ensure the project can be fully supplied with new items, more satellite uplinks allows more satellites, and so on. These also require a steady source of power which necessitates building power plants, and more critically, large investments of money for each new building. Base building as such becomes a task stretched across the length of the campaign with the goal of creating the most efficient XCOM program possible.
-An immersive setting and a good plot
-Most of the maps have excellent atmospheric design which adds to the eeriness of the ambient music
-Addictive gameplay keeps you [or at least me] coming back for more
-The game difficulty scales as you advance, providing constant challenges to overcome
-The huge customisable aspect of the soldiers allows you to become invested in each
-Great replay value, particularly with the Second Wave rules to customise new playthroughs
-Although the weapons are somewhat blocky, it is regardless a pleasing art style that reflects on the original game
-There is also a multiplayer aspect with customisable skirmish decks
-Unlike the original, only one base and one Skyranger is allowed, although the game has been balanced around this
-The initial rookie soldiers can strain the immersion at times as they do not always reflect the elites they are meant to be in the background
-The combat is RNG based, which can lead to frustrating moments
---

Excellent game. I wish I hadn't put off playing it for so long because it provides a very interesting and original story.
The gameplay is innovative and requires quite a bit of strategic planning - you need to carefully consider each move and attack you make because just one mistake can result in your defeat. Because of this, almost every battle feels like a desperate struggle. You never feel too overpowered and your heroes are often downed during combat. Despite this, on medium, I personally didn't find the game to be overly challenging as some people are stating - so don't feel dissuaded. There were perhaps less than 5 battles in which I felt that I might lose (but in saying that, I only lost 2).  However, I also didn't find the game easy - it felt just right. I'm sure that the game would be very challenging on hard difficulty.
And as far as I could tell (becasue I've only played through once), your choices do matter throughout the game. The game definitely ends abruptly as others have said but this is just part 1 in a trilogy after all. The world and story appears to be very well fleshed-out and I'm eager to learn more about the lore and to find out what happens next in part 2.
If you enjoy good story telling, making choices that matter and turn-based strategy then this is a game for you. Think of a fantasy Viking era game by Telltale with strategy battles thrown in and you have The Banner Saga.

XCOM's focus is on single-player and in this day and age is a good thing! The long campaign is challenging enough on Normal, with a big leap in enemy threat and movement on Classic - both of which are enhanced immeasurably by Ironman mode, which removes the temptation to save-cheat. The last difficulty level, Impossible, rightly so, your soldiers will die, a lot! This game is a winner. So much craft has gone into its atmosphere, into small details that together add enormous depth and flavour to the world: the occasional conversations overheard while fiddling around in the base; the mission loading screen, which gives you a view of the troops inside the carrier, fidgeting and tapping their feet in transit; soldiers acquiring nicknames after a few missions; the memorial room for fallen warriors, with a cork board of photos on the wall, which records their names. Near the campaign's end, there's a direct tribute to the original game's designers, the Gollop brothers, accompanied by an achievement called 'On the Shoulders of Giants'. It's a beautiful touch, a nod from one development team to another across the generations. They have something in common now. In their own time and place, each made a fantastic game called XCOM.

Everlasting Summer is exactly what you would expect from a visual novel - a game that basically plays itself and lets you make a few (quite important) choices, depending on which your story progresses and eventually gets you to one of the 13 endings the game has to offer. Yep, 13. Quite impressive, right? If you're a fan of visual novels, what you've already read has probably got you hooked, but this game is something way more than just a visual novel.
First of all, this game is free. No micro transactions, no expensive DLC that actually holds 50% of the story. Absolutely free. It's even available on mobile devices, again, for free.
I'm not a huge fan of visual novels. I have barely even played any of the Telltale games, and I did approach Everlasting Summer with a bit of skepticism, considering the fact it was a FREE visual novel. But after just a couple of minutes in the game, I was hooked, I just could not get off, I could not stop playing. This game is an absolute masterpiece. Every dialogue, every scene, every possible outcome of the story is perfected. The story, in general, is amazing, It is original, fun, surprising and involves some beautiful plot twists at times. The atmosphere of the game is stunningly good, the music is always on point and so well made that it gave me the chills every other minute while playing the game and I still can't shake it off. I've been playing the game for 2 days and I've got 2 of the possible endings unlocked, but I look forward to getting each and every secret of that game unveiled, because it's definitely worth the time.
There is a reason this game is free - everyone should play it at some point of their life. Go now, Sovyonok awaits your arrival.

Nevertheless it is beautiful and truly emotional! I was very glad to hear that a secont installment is on it's way!
