Beat Hazard utilizes your own music library to generate unique waves of enemies and bosses. While gameplay isn't very deep (earn money to unlock new perks, no real campaign), the unique perk system adds some variation to the game[lay style. You have limited number of perks you can activate, resulting in loadouts that are designed to achieve high scores that sacrifice staying power, or heavy-hitting ones to get your through the harder difficulties without getting as high of a score.
Using your own personal music library with varying difficulty levels gives this game almost endless replay value. Different genres of music will affect how powerful your weapons are, making slow moving, quiet songs relaxing and amping up the pressure during fast, action-packed heavy metal or dubstep.
The only real issues I have with this game are the inability to redefine X-box controller keys (which are somehow different on Mac and Windows) and manually entering some custom settings in a text file in a certain location. Granted, some of those settings can purposefully reset your scores if you want, but some (like ConstVolume or ThanksButNoThanks) seem like they should be accessible through the in-game options menu.
Overall, this is a really fun game. It looks really amazing when playing in the dark and having your room light up like a rave, and online multi-player makes competition fun as well. I recommend it for people who enjoy twin-stick shooters and like listening to their own music while blowing up hordes of enemy ships.
PROS
+Gameplay varies based on what song is playing
+Online Multiplayer
+Re-bind keyboard controlls
+X-Box Controller Compatible
+Unique perks system
CONS
-Manual settings file
-Can't rebind X-box controller keys

FIRST AND FOREMOST: As the developers warn with their opening image, this game can deal with very sensitive issues at times. I highly urge the readers considering Everlasting Summer to approach this VN with that warning always in the back of their minds.
I've spent enough time to play through about 4 or 5 unique endings. These are my thoughts on Everlasting Summer.
This game could easily sell for $20. This opinion of mine stands on the justification that a single play through doesn't explain ANYTHING. It just creates more questions. Replaying the story itself to understand everything even has it's own explanation a specific ending. I've played Corpse Party so I have a pretty good idea at what the author(s) are communicating about the story of Camp Sovionok. After all, the protagonist is there for a reason and I look forward to finding out what that reason is.
The characters are decently written and getting a good ending is definitely satisfactory. The Miku ending though....oh....if you enjoy a messed up story and can't figure out how to get it, look it up online and go for this one. I had read the reviews saying not to do this one late at night. I did it IN A DARK ROOM IN THE MIDDLE OF THE NIGHT and it definitely did not disappoint. Though, Lena's ending has been the most satisfying ending for me to obtain on the grounds that she's a complex individual. Giving the reader more than a short bit of "ending" drivel followed by an image, like most older VNs, was a smart move and definitely expanded the ending to be well worth the trouble to pursue Lena.
The endings: While there is an "optimal" route, you do have a bit of leeway on your choices for getting that specific ending you want. Each choice impacts the way that the subtle things will play out. Some choices will even slightly alter the dialogue of a later event.
HOWEVER! As the developers warn with their opening image, this game can deal with very sensitive issues at times. This is especially true when it comes to the characters' views of life and death on certain endings.
Do I recommend this VN? YES!

Final Impressions (01/11/2015; 15.5 hours playtime; Story Complete)
If and when some unfortunate woman bears my child, I will do everything within my power to have that kid play this game. What a delightful synthesis of fairy tales, story-telling, and JRPG mechanics. This truly is a great coming-of-age story that was unfortunately ignored due to Ubisoft's many misteps in 2014. But I have the excellent meltotheany to thank for bringing it to my attention as I originally stated.
The art direction in the game is fantastic. It really does look and feel like a children's fairy tale is playing out on screen. Moreover, the landscapes are varied and colorful, ranging from caves, forests, fires, castles, villages, etc.
I found the rhyming dialogue charming. In addition, the dialogue really serves to bolster the characters' different personalities and backgrounds, whether they be brave warriors or merchants with a savvy eye on profit. Background characters aren't fleshed out as much in dialogue, often repeating the same two-line rhyming couplet. But this is forgiveable as they are background characters. A select few that give quests offers up for extensive dialogue that relates their personality so it's clear that it could've been done. But I will give Ubisoft the benefit of the doubt in that that didn't want to overencumber the game with too much irrelevant dialogue for the sake of word-building. There's just enough in there to give a generalized sense of the tribes and their cultues.
As far as battle mechanics go, this was pretty interesting to me. I've played a handful of JRPGs in my time and this echoes the turn-based model. However, it brings an interesting twist. The player can interrupt enemy attacks by timing their attacks to occur in a limited time window, and vice versa. This really put me on the defensive more than I otherwise would, often trying to decide whether I should gamble on getting an attack in before my characters are hit or whether I should buckle down and defend to mitigate damage. In addition, the use of Igniculus (a firefly companion that the player can control with the mouse) helps in the tide of battle by slowing enemies down, healing your character, or activating one of two or three troves of health and mana. Equipment management is largely tossed aside (which I think is actually a pretty good idea) with the exception of oculi. Oculi are gemstones you collect and craft throughout the game which can be placed in one of three slots for various combat perks. The crafting system is simple and easy to understand with the use of a small chart that is provided and the player is left to their own imagination as far as experimenting with different combinations.
The story of the game is also superb. On the one hand, it is somewhat traditional. On the other, being a sort of video fairy tale this is perfectly fine and there are a couple of twists to be enjoyed through the narrative. Ultimately, the game is a coming of age story as we watch Aurora deal with the new problems she has been presented with. Both the music and the narration butterfly perfectly with the narrative. This is especially true of the narrator, which chokes me up a little bit and brings me back to thoughts of listening to my mother tell me stories or read me books.
From what I've read and experienced, many of the chracters are optional and are not required. The genius part is that this drastically affects gameplay, making the lone wolf much enjoy a much more difficult experience and a slightly stripped down story.
All in all, this is an excellent, charming game with a sweet soul. It seems to me that a lot of love and attention went into its development and it really reflects in the experience. I encourage anyone to purchase it and give it a go. And THEN, after you beat it, do a little research on things mentioned in the game as there is a grain of truth at the heart of the story.
First Impressions (01/08/2015; 7 hours playtime)
Child of Light answers the question of, "What would've happened if fairy tales and video games were invented at the same time and co-evolved?" The music is beautiful. The art direction is fantastic. As it stands right now, this game is a diamond in the rough that hasn't received the attention it probably deserves. Hell, I wouldn't even have known about it if it weren't for my friend Melanie.
Only two minor complaints so far. First, you have to use Uplay. That's not such a bad thing. My other complaint, however, broke my immersion for a brief moment. Early on, I was getting a few chuckles out of a particular character's dialogue. Shortly after an achievement popped up that said "Comedy." Normally I don't notice these if I'm not looking specifically for them on Steam. However, Uplay's design pops them in a big black box in the upper right and it's hard not to notice. I have hopefully turned these notifications off for the future but I recommend doing this before you begin your first play session.

As a huge south park fan, the sheer number of show refferences are staggering. It feels like almost every epsiode has a callback somewhere, so it's hard not to love this as an extended piece of the South Park universe. The humor is a decent mix of new ideas and show callbacks, and though most of it isn't laugh-out-loud funny, it's enough to keep you smiling the whole time.
As a gamer, though, it fell a bit short. Some of your powers are poorly explained, and then don't get used often enough for you to really figure them out. Also, you end up unlocking new ways to progress through the game world, but other than the very first one they are barely used enough to warrant making them 5 or 6 different powers that you have to cycle through each time you need to use one. The game is also pretty short - it took about 18 hours to finish the whole story, and then one more to wrap up side missions. This is made worse by the fact that death has no real consequences, and over-leveling is easy if you're a gamer who is used to exploring all of the overworld before you move on with the story. And it's immensely frustrating that some of the collectibles you need to 100% the game are available only once and easily missable.
Get this game when it's super cheap on sale and play through it in a weekend, and you won't be dissapointed. But don't pay full price, and don't go in expecting more than a fun homage to the show.

I've found that the way the game steers you into doing what it wants you to do is by throwing larger and larger obstacles at you until it literally will place invisible mines that kill you when you walk on them. Other than that, the game is awesome and thoroughly engaging.

You are an agent send on a mission to recover a secret file for an agency in the infected town of Harran, Kyle Crane is the protagonist name and you will get to meet a lot of people and kill a lot of zombies while doing some pretty sweet parkour.
The idea of the game sounds pretty cool if you think about it and it is a pretty cool game to be honest, you get to parkour around town and kill wathever you want and at night you better brace yourself because it goes from 1 to 10 in a sec if you get detected by specials.
The gameplay:
The parkour mechanic are well made there are some times where you might find yourself wondering why you could've grab onto something or why you went on the rooftop while you wanted to enter by a window but overall it's an enjoyable experience, not a perfect one but pretty fun still.
The skills are divided in 3 aspects: survival, agility and power. Survival is about tweaks to help you go around like crafting, haggling, traps and more. Agility is around the parkour mostly, you can dodge, grapple, escape biters when they try to eat your face and more. Power is of course the combat, you get more health, power attack, throwing weapons and more. Each of these skill trees have independent experience level and will grow with different things, survival by doing quests and gathering air drops, agility by doing a lot of parkour and power by simply killing everything you can. It's different from so many games but it's actually an interesting way to approach things instead of having one experience bar you have 3 and it makes you do different things to raise your levels.
The combat system is really simple but fair enough, you hit or you kick mostly it doesn't really change agains specials either not until late game maybe where I had to actually make use of the shield to kill one kind of special. There are no real interesting bosses which is a bit sad it sort of feel like you're always fighting the same things over and over. Sometimes for some unknown reason they just like to take your inventory away because they don't seem to know how to balance things when you have your real gear on but it doesn't happend often. Also explosion are way too powerful in this game, the bombers appears out of nowhere most of the time and if you are in a narrow spot it's a good and fair instant death.
The crafting system is simple but efficient you gather resources from containers and fallen enemies, you can add effects to your weaponry and add up to 3 mods to either increase the durability, damage or/and attack speed. Sadly you can't mod your guns and guns don't scale with your levels at all so you might end up with a shotgun dealing less damage then your melee weapon at the end of the game. There are several tiers of weapons, the only difference between them is of course the color but also the number of repairs and sometimes the number of mods you can apply to the weapon. Yes, weapons have a limited number of time you can repair them after that it's only good to be salvaged sadly so don't get too attached to a weapon because you will have to trash it very quickly.
8/10
Story:
Not a lot to say about it here, it's really an average storyline but to be honest it's a zombie game they never had much stories in them. They want to survive and get the hell out of there and also find a cure, you have a dude, a girl and a vilain. Of course it can't be so simple as saying let's just go together out of this hell hole so they must blast each others face off for no logical reason until one win the war and credits. It's simply average I didn't find any characters to be interesting enough to care actually. Even the side quests were mostly average, some voice actors sound really ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ while I guess they shouldn't be.

Good lord that I hate those background noises, It drives me crazy! You get to hear zombies in the background 24/7, it always sound so stressful while most of the time nothing major is happening. I can clear an entire tunnel and I will still hear sounds like a war agains zombies is going on next door, so you don't know how to react 90% of the time they need to tone it down or at least have a damn setting for it like just for that background ambient sound kind of deal.

Although The Banner Saga is a tactical rpg, it is a distinct departure from other games with that label. The story is more linear, the composition of your party more limited, and the battle options less diverse. Nevertheless, it is an intriguing game.
The story focuses on the survival (rather than adventure and exploration) of two seperate groups traveling from one city to the next. Your caravan is composed of hundreds of npcs rather than just a party of a dozen or so like in many games and it is important to procure enough resources to feed them all. If you don't your clansmen and fighters begin to die off or abandon you. Likewise it is important to maintain good morale by resting during your travels, but doing so uses up a day's supplies without making any progress. It can be difficult to strike a balance especially since your resource for buying supplies is the same resource you use to level up your hero units and buy items to give them boosts.
Sometimes throughout the game you will engage in a War event in which you choose whether to attack aggressively, defend yourselves, or even run away. This decision determines how difficult your battle with the enemy will be and how many casualties your bulk forces will suffer. Additionally throughout the game random events will occur requiring you to make leadership decisions, like whether or not to aid the sick and injured, how to handle a drunkard, or whether or not to give in to bandits. These decisions are presumably meant to give you the sense that you truly are part of a large caravan of people, but you never have the option to talk with random clansmen on your own, or interact with them in any meaningful way. Essentially every clan interaction is a text box and a few options to choose from. Personally it fails to give me that immersive quality I was hoping for.
There is a vast map for the game world but you don't get to choose where to go or what route to take so the map hardly serves any purpose at all. Additionally it detracts from the beauty found in other areas of the game with it's childish scrawl and rough depiction. Similarly jarring are the many Godstones your caravan passes on it's travels. Each one is an opportunity to earn a special item but it is also a massive eyesore on the landscape and I hated having to see one each time. Otherwise the art was generally quite attractive with sweeping landscapes and beautiful splashes of color.
Battles employ an interesting mechanic in which your health and your attack are the same stat. As a character loses health they also less effectively. Characters also have an armor statistic that reduces damage they take from enemy attacks. So for most battles the goal is to reduce your opponent's armor until you are able to deal damage to their strength and kill them. While some strategy is involved essentially the game amounts to beating on your opponent until you win. What little variety in abilities and strategic options exists is hindered by the lack of characters to choose from who employ them. Each character, with few exceptions is unique, but it's impossible to level them all up so you generally end up choosing the strongest few and sticking with them. Completley ignoring the rest of your party.
I was also displeased to realize that if a character was equipped with one of my items when they left or were killed for story purposes, I lost the item forever. This made me paranoid about my party equipment and I would unequip everything from my characters after every fight, just in case.
Ultimately the rpg aspects of the game fell flat for me and the story didn't feel substantial enough, but the overall mood of the game and the unique battle system and story progressing were intriguing. It feels to me like an unfinished game in desperate need of polish and expanding. Nevertheless I do believe it is worth playing, even if it leaves you feeling a bit unsatisfied and wanting more.

Grim Dawn just seems to fill all of my ARGP desires and allows me to share them all with my friends, which nowdays co-op is a must for me.

•	More content (already coming in the next expansion)
•	Enhanced UI for crafting so I do not have to jump from item to item as much
•	More bank space . . . please for the love of god more.
•	The ability to respect your classes down to 1 point, meaning you cannot change classes.
•	Multiplayer questing overhaul

A brilliant strategic and tactical game with deep, challenging gameplay; despite being a little rough around the edges with small graphical glitches, it's an unforgettable experience and I whole-heartedly recommend playing it, as well as the Enemy Within expansion, which adds so much to the original game.
The combat is brutally unforgiving, and the out-of-combat decision making isn't for the faint-hearted, but there's no better feeling than overcoming impossibly stacked odds and taking the fight to the aliens. When I opened this game I didn't put it down for several hours, it just got me hooked from the get-go!
As well as having amazing gameplay, XCOM: EU is surprisingly emotional at times thanks to the permadeath aspect of the game - if your soldiers don't magically recover from bullet wounds. If they die, they're dead, and that brings a great deal of both immersion and attachment to the game. If a mission goes south for whatever reason and one of your veterans looks like they might get left behind, it's hard to just accept it and leave them to their fate - that's something that very few games can achieve with the basic footsoldiers.

More importantly is the fact that there is no replay value to be gained from a second playthrough, knowing that your actions have no consequence. The big example is when
I realise this is one of the constraints of choice-based games systems: being able to cleverly design the game into making you think your choice has a lasting effect on gameplay, or else be faced with the problem of having a complex cascade of events if too many choices are presented.

South Park: The Stick of Truth is fundamentally a well-paced, very extended, playable South Park episode. The Stick of Truth combines the best of the series' humor and jokes and pairs it with the gameplay of an old-school turn-based RPG. The two go together extremely well and both contribute to keeping the entire campaign fresh and without a dull moment. In typical South Park style things get more absurd and obscene every minute and the game caught more than one laugh-out-loud moments from me.
The combat does become a little too easy near the end of the game even on the highest difficulty, but that is a small complaint in an otherwise excellent game. If you're a fan of the show, do yourself a favor and pick this one up.

Child of Light comes off as a very, "strange" game at first. Once we enter the world of Lemuria, we are burdened with the task of finding the Stars, Moon, and Sun. We must traverse to the highest of the high and the lowest of the low, and some may ask, why? And just like any good old children's fairytale, we must do it in order to smite that which is evil, to see to it that justice will prevail. To smite the plague that is looming over Lemuria. And some of you at this point may ask, who are we? In our past lives we were a princess, a daughter of a king long past his time. And in our past lives, we were precarious and just like any loving daughter, we clung to our mother. So why is it that we must traverse the dangerous soils of Lemuria? To reclaim that which has been stolen? To prove to our predecessors that we can prevail the dark? Or is it because we are doing this solely for the sake of our own desires? To see our beloved father once again? As we traverse the lands of Lemuria, we are burdened with these questions, or at least some of you may be.  And, it's a good thing to ask these questions. To some, this may be a simple story of morality, a simple choice of good and evil, but one has to stop and ask; why are we doing all of this?
So, as you have guessed, that was my way of handing down the story from one person to another. In a way, a game like Child Of Light, is very much story based as it is combat based, so of course having a good story is very welcome.  Some may find it bland, but others, like myself, may find its simplicity perfect.  And it really is. The way I put it may have sugar coated some parts, and may have extended on some other meanings, but to boil it down, it really is just like a fairytale. It's something mystical and Child of Light is just that. A journey filled with mysticism.
Like I said, Child of Light is one part story, but also one part combat. The combat system is something akin to old style RPG's, in which, once your turn queue is up, you will be able to go through a number of options such as attacking, defending, or using an item.  But, Child of Light gives it a little twist. The combat system revolves mainly around a small time gauge at the bottom of your screen. Characters will have to move to the end of the gauge before they can initiate any moves. But if they are interpreted by enemies that are faster than them, then they will be kicked back on the gauge, and have their move cancelled. This mechanic can also work against enemies, effectively creating a way for players to strategically plan out their moves so that they can interrupt their enemies and keep up an onslaught of moves. Later on, things get more complicated as interrupting may actually work against you due to enemies possessing counter abilities , but that's for later in the game. To summarize, the core of the combat is pretty much a gauge based RPG.
With both of these elements converging and creating a package known as Child of Light, one may ask, haven't I forgotten a key aspect? And I have, and that is, music. The music at times, helped create a sense of tension, sadness, and excitement. In battle and story wise, each musical piece that was played was played in conjunction to what was happening on screen. Every piece helped add on to the mood, and every piece was very well made. In times of despair, all we really need, is for a calm and soothing tune to settle our dread. And with every triumph, there must have been an epic to follow. Child of Light brings these elements and many more to life with its well crafted music.
Over all, Child of Light is a well made game, and despite it not being perfect or majorly impressing me, I still had a ton of fun travelling Lemuria along with the companions that decided to join me.

UPDATE: Am I updating my review to get a new badge for 2017? You bet.
And it honestly goes without saying, but I'm still disappointed in Valve for letting their seminal series rot for the last ten years. Half-Life deserves better than this.
ORIGINAL: What's left to say about the game that brought most of us old-timers to Steam? Has it really been just over 12 years now? Will we ever see any proper sort of closure to the storyline in our lifetimes? It saddens me to say, but probably not, at least not at the rate Valve seems to be going these days. Is this any sort of revelation to anyone who's even halfway paying attention to things? Of course not. Am I posting a review now simply to satisfy a silly requirement for some silly badge? Most likely.
Anyway, if you have somehow managed to NOT play this game before now, then do yourself a favor: spend the measly $2 Valve asks for it when it's on sale, and just enjoy it. Sure, it's from a different time, and it doesn't feel like the AAA titles that kids are accustomed to these days-- but that's definitely a mark in its favor. If you've played it before, then do yourself a favor and play it again. Apart from a few things that really feel out of place these days (like the lack of iron sights for aiming), it has held up remarkably well. The vehicle sequences are just plain fun, as is the gravity gun. Oh, and Ravenholm? We don't go there anymore. But everyone remembers their first trip there.
I've lost count of the number of times I've played it over the years, starting from the original release in November '04 (long before Steam tracked your playtime), to the re-release as part of the Orange Box on consoles, and most recently as HL2: Update. It's one that I go back to every couple of years, and one that I enjoy every time that I do.

South Park : The Stick Of Truth is an outstanding RPG by visual, design, and sound in many ways. The game is based around the popular series, taking many of the nostalgic elements fans have loved about the show and throwing them into the game. Game is based around the events of Cartman, Stan, Kyle, Kenny, and friends, in a "fantasy game" involving the entire town. You play a new kid in town, who's only starting objective is to make friends. You find yourself helping Butters as your first friend, and he leads you to the group to start your journey.
Gameplay
Gameplay is very well done, taking elements of Paper Mario, and Final Fantasy, and mixing them in with catchy battle mechanics similar like games like Mario & Luigi, and Tomato Adventure. Your battles play out with a slight strategic element of planning your attacks wisely, and not attacking always head first.  The game, is designed as if you were playing a special whole season of the show, creating not only classic elements, but original new bosses and designs as well, making it a festive experience for fans of the show and newcomers alike.  The game is SHORT though. I played the PS3 version first, and can say it's only about 8-10 hours with searching for collectibles, which is very short in RPG standards.
Sound
The gangs all here. Matt Stone and Trey Parker resume their roles from the show, as well as the female cast members. Music is actually on point for its theme as well giving off very fitting Medieval sounds, and music, which is quite a delight to listen to. The jokes, and timing of gags are on point, and will give you laughs!
Controls.
Controls are ok; however, I did find at times the controls for certain battle mechanics, would stop working for one whole battle. For example on this, the game would tell me to rotate my L Analog stick, and the game wouldn't acknowledge it for the whole battle, so leaving me to use regular A button attacks. This happened maybe 3 times, so it's worth noting.
Overall, South Park : The Stick Of Truth is a very enjoyable game that everyone who's a fan of the show should try. If you're new to the show or game the game might be a little overwhelming with the amount of Easter Eggs and content you'd find around the game, so i'd recommend watching a few seasons to get the gears running first.   I HIGHLY RECOMMEND the game because it will leave a great impression; however, because of the length, i'd recommend waiting for a price drop.

Few video games in history have garnered as much critical praise and effusive adoration as Feminazi: The Triggering. When it came out in 2017 for the PC, Feminazi: The Triggering set a new standard for three-dimensional action and introduced gameplay mechanics that are still copied today. Though it has since appeared on the GameCube and the Wii Virtual Console, the new version for the PC marks the first time this classic has received a significant update. The completely overhauled visuals are the most striking improvement, and they infuse this 1-year-old game with a vibrant modern feel. The sharp motion controls and the video hint system are new additions that fit in well, but the real star is the original adventure. Though it shows its age, The quest is indeed a timeless one that is full of invigorating exploration, tricky puzzles, satisfying combat, memorable characters, and stirring music. Feminazi: The Triggering is a great way to experience this seminal adventure, and it's a shining example of how old can be made new again.

Prior to its release I had already logged a fair number hours in Banner Saga: Factions and I was pretty excited for Banner Saga to drop. There was so much that Stoic had done right with Factions: The artwork was beautiful, the setting and thematic design was origanal and refreshing, the combat engine was decent and the rudementary leveling system showed promise of creating a wide range of tactical options.
But the key here is that I enjoyed Factions because it did a good job of challenging me to think creatively about solving strategic and tactical problems. As I acquired new assets I got to play around with new and different approaches to certain classes of problems and as my opponents matured I had to constantly adapt to every new challenge they threw at me. Every time I logged in it was dynamic, it was fresh and it was fun.
I wish that this review didn't have to be a simple thumbs up/thumbs down. There is still so much good stuff that Stoic has brought to the table with this release. The world that they create is captivating and the artwork is exceptional. When it comes down to it though I just can't say that this game is the game I had hoped it would be... It just isn't fun.
There are too many constraints. The developers have over emphasized the story in this release and there just isn't any reason to pick this game up again after you've beaten it. Too often, when they stop to try to give you the illusion you have a choice there really is no choice: certain actions just don't pay off and too often there is always a right answer. In reality this isn't so much a game as it is a storybook.
I sincerely hope that the developers get back to what they had done right with Factions and develope that further. As far as I'm concerned I'm not interested in pursuing this series any further.

XCOM: Enemy Unknown is one of those sequels of old games, which sticks true to the original formula and delivers an authentic, but updated experience. XCOM: Enemy Unknown is a pleasant reboot to an aging game series which remained popular among fans. The original XCOM titles were unique themselves and many were skeptical that game developers might not be able to capture the same nostalgic feeling a niche market covets. XCOM: Enemy Unknown succeeds as a successor because it offers everything the old game did and more, with updated graphics, expanded content and a more modern feel.
The key components found in the previous XCOM titles involved building and developing a secret military base to track and counter alien activity. It is obvious the developers took extra care here, because the look and feel truly reminds one of XCOM. Not only is XCOM: Enemy Unknown a secret government facility simulator, but there are heart racing turn-based strategy components which pit your fragile squads of human secret agents against creators from other dimensions with weapons of other worldly power. After battles you can collect relics, weapons and corpses which can be studied at your research facility. Certain research merits greater rewards, such as capturing a live alien versus a corpse. Research is one of the most critical aspects of this game and proper use and prompt study will lead to a much more successful late game experience.
The game is surprisingly easy to learn in the begging and very fun to play and continue, but definitely can jump in difficulty if you fall behind in research or development of your troops. Missions can be failed and your entire squad can get lost by making fatal mistakes on even the most simple of assignments. As you progress through the game you encounter a whole slew of aliens, each different than the other. The aliens have unique powers and abilities each fitting to the type of alien seen.The more difficult aliens can pose a significant challenge if you are not properly prepared. In a way this game kind of forces you to fail but XCOM is one of those games that keeps you coming back for more until you can get that "perfect" run.
With XCOM: Enemy Unkown comes an expansion called XCOM: Enemy Within which adds a few new features and technology. The most notable addition is a new resource type, called meld. Meld fuels some of the new technologies, such as a new mechanized cyber exoskeleton. The expansion adds more stages and aliens as well but there is a focus on trans-human modification and most of the upgrades are seen to your units themselves. As you collect and research meld, you can use it to develop even more unique and complicated abilities for your squad mates.
XCOM: Enemy Unkown can be enjoyed by just about anyone and the title certainly stands as a staple of the series. The amount of time you spend playing the game quickly adds up as you are eager to begin the next stage, completing missions and unlocking research. The aliens are varied and interesting and the combined challenged presented by the base management aspect and the actual turn based stratedgy elements are highly enjoyable. Anyone interested in science fiction or solid and challenging turn based strategy mechanics should look into picking up XCOM: Enemy Unknown.

If you like or even dislike Dead Island get this game now even at full price it's definitely worth it. Ok here's my pro's and con's for the game:
Pro's
-Graphics are really great
-Parkour is amazing and very fun
-Night gameplay changes everything and it is very creepy to say the least
-The loot is one of the biggest factors in the game, you may spend hours looting and looking for things without doing one quest at all
-The sound quality is amazing
-There are 3 levels that you can max out, Survivor Rank, Agility Level and your Power Level
-Upgrading and modifying weapons is amazing too, it's a big step up from Dead Island's crafting and upgrade system
-The full game runs better than the demo so, if you're looking to play the demo to find out if you can run DL, don't
Now on to the Cons, which I really don't have many for this game actually:
-The game could use a little more optimiztion
That's all I have for this review for now, I'll update it as soon as I get fully leveled and play on NG+
So if you're a big zombie game fan or Dead Island fan, get this now either now or on sale, it's one of the best zombie games I've played in a long time, game of the decade IMO

Mirror's Edge is one of my favorite games. It has great graphics, especially for the year it came out in, and the action will really get the adrenaline going. Another amazing thing about this game is the music that plays during puzzles and action. During puzzles you will hear a nice Ambient electronic tune with a calming feel, while the tracks playing during action are more jungle and just overall action packed electronic tracks.
Of course, the game has some cons to it.
1. The game has PhysX support enabled on default. This setting is not intended for modern graphics cards and will make your 60 frames per second go to the single didgets in combat or when glass is breaking. Turning the setting off will fix the problem though.
2. The guns are weird to use. And no, I'm not talking about how you don't aim down the sights, because that sure isn't a problem, since wonderful shooter games like Half Life and Counter Strike don't have this option with a large majority of their weapons. However, those games made not aiming in feel so fluent while Mirror's Edge has a more inaccurate feel to it. And that's coming from someone who loves Half Life and Counter Strike.
3. The FOV slider is only available by editting the game's files to assign key bindings to it. While the default FOV in this game, which I assume is 90, is fine on its own, alot of gamers, including me prefer higher FOVs. Guided by a popular post on Mirror's Edge's steam community is a tutorial in which you have to add certain lines of code into the game's files to add hotkeys to change the FOV. While the edits are pretty simple, it's not something the average gamer would want to do.
That's all I really have to say about this game. It's a fun experience and you'll have a blast with the amount of general parkour and parkour puzzles, adrenaline fueled action scenes amazing scenary. I would recommend this game for sure!

Crawl has become, unexpectedly, one of my favorite games. As an indie game, it will be money well spent (privded you have people to play with for some fantastic couch co-op). Get it, its great.
I own a lot of shared/split-screen games. I tend to organize a bunch of team sports, and pre-drinking is mandatory. To this end, having simple to play, local co-op games is a must for some good rowdy entertainemt. Crawl is simple to play (moderately hard to master). There are only two buttons, attack and special but the hook is that it is dynamic 3v1 set up. A 'human' player competes against three 'ghosts' to gain enough levels to be the one that challenges the boss. Ghosts inhabit monsters to kill the 'human'. The one that lands the deadly blow becomes 'human'. As 'human' players level, ghosts get currency to in turn level up their mosters. Thus, if you can't get a kill on a human and everyone levels around you, you will have more to spen on leveling monsters, ergo a higher chance of getting the kill. As monsters do damage to humans they gain currency they can use if they become human in a shop to increase their effectiveness. Once someone reaches enough power to challenge a boss, the 3 ghots comibine to controll that boss to fight. Overall, the game design is solid, unique, and super fun. If there are no monsters to inhabit, ghost characters can controll various traps and jump into items to harrass the 'human'.
I've had this game for a long time and the developers are still providing updates with more monster evolutions, more items to purchas in the shop, and more trap dynamics. The only even remotely (possibly)negative thing is they have yet to add to the roster of end game bosses (currently there are only 2).
While the overall this is a simple game there is a slight learning curve (mainly what are the monster attack/specials, possible human specials). There is progression (unlocking monster evolves/items), but it is pretty quick. Super casual players may be turned off by this, but overall, whenever I bust this game out, response is always positive.

Hnnnnnng this GAME!
Everything about this game from the art design to the music to the rhyming dialogue is just so gosh darn charming. The battle system utilizes a "time bar" that determines when your characters and your enemies act. As each unit's turn bubble moves from left to right on the time bar, there are two thresholds that they pass through: first, one where they determine what action they are about to take, and second, one where they take said action. If a unit is attacked while in between these two thresholds their turn is delayed, making for some pretty strategic and challenging battles.
(Keep in mind I haven't beaten the game yet so the majority of the plot is still unknown to me) The story is about a little girl lost in a dream world and trying to find a way back home, but there seems to be an underlying story to it all that isn't told to us right away...! As your adventure unfolds you encounter several different party members to help you in battle, each one adding a different strategy and play style. These partners all have very distinct personalities and interact with each other outside of battle from time to time in fairly humorous exchanges. I have yet to find a character I DIDN'T like.
The environments are beautiful and so far for me have ranged from a lush forest to dark and dangerous looking mines to heated lava caverns. The map could be described as "linear" but honestly there are tons of hidden treasures and even some optional mini bosses that you could easily miss if you didn't look hard enough. Overall I feel the environments are very well put together and at no point have they bored me.
This game has scratched pretty much every itch that I have as a RPG lover: engaging battle system that makes me WANT to fight the next enemy, a beautifully told story that has just enough mystery to make me keep pushing forward, as well as a very likable and distinguished cast of characters. I could not recommend this game to other RPG lovers enough.

A beautiful game you should try. Don't compare it to classic JRPGs because you won't feel satisfied, try to judge it by it's own merits.

The music is great, it's very melancholic and fits the tone of the game just fine.
The combat system is entertaining and that's means a lot coming from someone who doesn't really like turn-based games that much. It's easy to understand and you have a great time planning your attacks on the go.
The story is quite interesting (even if very simple). By the end I was rushing trough the battles so I could see what happened next.
I spent 15 hours in this game and I really can't understand how some people beat it in much less time. I played it in Casual difficulty, I only lost like 3 battles and completed almost every sidequest, so it was a very regular play through and still it took me some time.
This game is an interesting experience, and if you are into this kind of game you're gonna love it. I hope this review helps you decide into buying this game, I know I'm not the only one who loved it.

A game like Kung Fury: Street Rage, really doesn't need an overlong review. To start with, this is a two-button game. No I don't mean two buttons like Super Mario Brothers, I mean two buttons: left-attack and right-attack. Enemies approach from both sides, and all you have to do is press the corresponding button to kill them. Your goal? Get a high score. The average game of Kung Fury lasts a minute or two, and it requires only a few seconds to figure out how everything works.
But you want to know something? Despite it's simplistic nature, this is a pretty good game. Kung Fury is all about getting into
and establishing a rhythm. You know about the
right? It's that place you go to where you feel untouchable. It's like gliding in-between billions of bullets, shredding innumerable enemy forces, or in the case of this game, landing dozens if not hundreds of attacks with perfect accuracy at a rapid pace. This is a very focused game, so the simplest mistake is costly. You're only allowed three hits before death and each hit rips into your precious multiplier bonus. Worst of all, taking a hit pulls you out of
. You're about to high-five zen and then suddenly...back to reality...and reality sucks hard.
Since there are only two buttons, your efforts should be focused entirely on your enemies. There are multiple types, each requiring a certain number of attacks before they're killed. There aren't really any recovery frames, so you're free to hit the attack button as much as you want. Of course, if you miss an enemy, you're left wide open (this also depletes your multiplier). This is part of what being in
is all about. You're constantly judging the effective distance of your attacks, the type of enemy, and keeping a mental count of the # of hits/button-presses required to dispatch them. Sometimes it helps to memorize specific button combinations, so you can pull them off immediately on particular enemies. Whatever the cases, this entire process must be handled at a constant rate, and you're given micro-seconds to breathe.
In my experience, this isn't a game that lends itself well to extended play. I usually play Kung Fury until I best my high-score, then move on to another game. While it sounds sensible to keep playing to further improve on that score, it's more effective to quit while I'm ahead. Due to the design of the game, there's a high chance I'll press one too many buttons, or slightly mis-judge the distance of that one enemy, and lose. Repeated failures will lead to burnout. My advice is that once you get that great run, stop, do a little fist pump, then play something else. This is a game you'll want to keep around, even if it's just to get that jolt of action to start your day off right.
It's fair to say that Kung Fury: Street Rage lacks in content, especially compared to the similarly-designed One Finger Death Punch. What you get for your 1.99 is a well-crafted action game with nice aesthetics. This is a quick-fix piece of disposable entertainment, with its long-term value hidden in acquiring high scores as well as giving your gaming-ability a serious workout. It's an altogether solid tie-in with the short movie (which is also entertaining, aside from a weak 2nd act).
Check it out sometime.

Well, with 50+ hours of playtime, having watched both endings, unlocked all secret characters, and almost completed all achievements, there is no way I'm going to give
a "Not Recommended" review, right?
Well, I'm going to skip a narration about what kind of games this is, since obviously you can read the description yourself :p
Soo, with that out of the way, here you go :
Pros :
-Fast paced turn based battle system, while also giving an extra layer of stategies in positioning your characters and deciding what kind of actions to use depending on the situations.
-Flashy special attacks, especially the finishers (called EXE Drive in the game), and even accompanied by a badass theme everytime it is performed.
-There are a lot of optional contents, like item crafting, quests, colosseum battles, and optional boss fights.
-The plan system, it is basically like your normal crafting system, but you can also alter the game by making enemies stronger / weaker, change the item you get in a dungeon, or even  summon optional bosses in a dungeon.
-Creative enemy designs, ranging from hilarious (Tetris block, Super Mario pipe, and even Visual Novel Window) to cool (your standard Dragon and Phoenix, also awesomely designed Robots)
-Very detailed character potraits & environments during cutscene.
-You can also customize how your characters look with costumes and accessories, though some costumes are quite hard to obtain.
-The dialogue, Oh man, the dialogue. I've lost count of how many times I laughed or at least grinned through the entire game. Being a parody of the console war, you are bound to see a lot of reference to other games and game consoles themselves, and this is done in a hilariously smart way.
Cons :
-Repeated dungeon designs. Saw a new dungeon? Well, be prepared to enter the same area (with slight alterations and different enemies) later in the game.
-Sometimes, you have to grind a few levels in order to win a boss fight, and maybe grind some more for the next boss. Granted, the battle system is fast and battles only took a while.
-The fanservice, this is mixed opinions, and it is not as bad as say, some animes out there, but I wouldn't mind if they toned it down a bit.
-The flashy attacks I mentioned before, apparently only applies to your party member, as most bosses doesn't have such flashy attacks.
All in all, I really enjoyed my time playing this game. Though it has is flaws (what game doesn't?), it can be easily overlooked. If you enjoyed turn based RPGs and doesn't mind a not-so-serious story, there is a great chance that you will love this game. I, myself, are looking forward to see the rest of this series to come to Steam.

Grim Dawn is set in the war torn world of Cairn and is easily one of the best arpgs I have seen in years having been developed by Crate Entertainment an indie company formed with some of the talented devs of Titan Quest. Crate was able to gain rights to the Titan Quest engine and began developing Grim Dawn which in my opinion is a worthy successor. While Grim Dawn does take inspiration from fan favorites such as the diablo series Torchlight series and Path of exile it introduces it's own unique ideas to these systems as well. Some of the things enjoy are.
Having been developed by some of the people that worked on Titan Quest one of the core features that i really enjoyed about Titan Quest makes a welcome return here in the dual class system. Upon entering the game you can create a Male or Female classless hero at level 2 you will have the ability to pick one of 6 class trees.
Solder
Demolitionist
shaman
archanist
nightblade
occultist
you can further flesh out your class at level 10 by combining a second of these trees. This combined with all the items that grant skills and augments to skills makes for some deep customization options which is one of the things i enjoy about rpgs in general.
while it is apparent that this system takes inspiration from Path of exile's massive skill tree the devotion system in Grim Dawn is quite unique in that you have to go exploring throughout the would to find shrines which need to be cleansed. once cleansed you will gain devotion points which can be spent in a constellation map to augment your skills.
Cairn  is a huge open world providing hours of fun content to delve into quests some with consequences /lore/Factions/Bounties/Dungeons there is allot to do in Grim Dawn and Crate have already confirmed they will be adding more content updates and full expansions
The component system works similar to the gem socket system present in other games in the genre. The difference here is that instead of having  gems and socketable items Grim Dawn has different components that can be added to any tier of item. Some of these components can really improve your build by having skills tied to them. For example I have a character that has a lodestone socketed into my offhand this item grants a lightning nova skill and to take that even further I have tied the lightning nova skill from the lodestone to the scorpion sting ability in the devotion system which adds an aoe poison to the lightning nova.There are tons of components for every gear type and you can combine these components to make more powerful ones. While I do enjoy this system it is not without it's flaws the biggest one being that if i want to modify or remove an item from a piece of gear I can do that  by way of the Inventor's apprentice however you can only keep one or the other the component item or the piece of gear. This can make the decision to salvage quite difficult if both items provide significant additions to a build.
Loot in Grim Dawn like other titles comes in different tier types Common/Magic/Rare/Epic and Legendary. What makes the loot different from other arpgs is the fact that like the component system some items can augment existing skills even after you have maxed them out on the skill tree or like the lodestone mentioned in the component section some loot can have specific skills tied to the item. This really makes for a unique customization experience.
While the inventory system is in many ways no different any other arpg out there there are a few things that are worth mentioning about the system in Grim Dawn such as quests that give bag upgrades for rewards a button that automatically combines components and my personal favorite and something that everyone has been asking for in several games of the genre. an AUTO SORT BUTTON!!! for those of us who hate playing inventory tetris. The stash system is also really well done as it has a character specific tab and an item transfer tab. The item transfer area can be upgraded to have more tabs within it as well so there really is no shortage of space.
Quests in Grim Dawn come in many forms. Some quests unlock vendors and crafting abilities some have choices and consequences. For example maybe there are 2 warring factions in the game if you choose to help one you will become enemies with the other. These kinds of choices make for a rich questing experience. while exploring the world you will find tons of pages and notes on the areas that you are exploring I have always been a fan of finding lore in these types of games and there is no shortage of that here.
Crafting in Grim Dawn borrows some of the ideas from Diablo 3's artisan system they have blueprints that you can find through out the world to increase the list of items available to craft. You can craft components and potions to give you extra damage or resistance fore specific monster type as well but the thing that stands out to me is the ability to craft relics these relics like other loot in the game can ultimately change your play style for example you might have a character such as the demolitionist that uses pistols but can't dual wield them no problem you can craft the gunslingers talisman equip it and you have your ability to dual wield pistols.
While exploring the world of Cairn you will encounter different factions and settlements that will have their own set of bounties and quests for you to do. These factions have quartermasters which are merchants that sell items specific to that faction depending on how high your friendly reputation is with them. As stated before in the quest section some factions are at war with each other so helping one faction may and in come cases will in definitely either damage or completely ruin your reputation with certain factions. If your reputation gets significantly low with a faction they will spawn more elites and nemesis monsters to hunt you down. This in my opinion makes for a very engaging exploration experience.
Grim Dawn features the ability to play your characters in both single and multiplayer modes. the multi player is easy to use the host options are quite good due to the fact that you can host a game for up to 4 players and because the game features a server browser rather than an account based system the player hosting the game  can easily customize the number of players allowed in the server weather there is instanced loot and even put a password on servers so that only friends can join this is somthing i wish all games like this had.
While I really Enjoy Grim Dawn I do have one minor complaint. I wold love for there to be more voice acting especially since there is literally tons of lore notes in the game and being a person that has some visual difficulties reading a whole bunch of text does tend to put allot of strain on my eyes so having audio to listen to is a big help but I also understand that they are an indie team and are only able to work with that they have and this grype aside they have made a fantastic rpg.
If your looking for a new action rpg title to dig into Than Grim Dawn will not disappoint. It has something for new comers and old veterans of the genre alike. It is a great value and well worth the asking price and i highly recommend this so i am going to give Grim Dawn a 9 out of 10.

XCOM: Enemy Unknown is one of those sequels of old games, which sticks true to the original formula and delivers an authentic, but updated experience. XCOM: Enemy Unknown is a pleasant reboot to an aging game series which remained popular among fans. The original XCOM titles were unique themselves and many were skeptical that game developers might not be able to capture the same nostalgic feeling a niche market covets. XCOM: Enemy Unknown succeeds as a successor because it offers everything the old game did and more, with updated graphics, expanded content and a more modern feel.
The key components found in the previous XCOM titles involved building and developing a secret military base to track and counter alien activity. It is obvious the developers took extra care here, because the look and feel truly reminds one of XCOM. Not only is XCOM: Enemy Unknown a secret government facility simulator, but there are heart racing turn-based strategy components which pit your fragile squads of human secret agents against creators from other dimensions with weapons of other worldly power. After battles you can collect relics, weapons and corpses which can be studied at your research facility. Certain research merits greater rewards, such as capturing a live alien versus a corpse. Research is one of the most critical aspects of this game and proper use and prompt study will lead to a much more successful late game experience.
The game is surprisingly easy to learn in the begging and very fun to play and continue, but definitely can jump in difficulty if you fall behind in research or development of your troops. Missions can be failed and your entire squad can get lost by making fatal mistakes on even the most simple of assignments. As you progress through the game you encounter a whole slew of aliens, each different than the other. The aliens have unique powers and abilities each fitting to the type of alien seen.The more difficult aliens can pose a significant challenge if you are not properly prepared. In a way this game kind of forces you to fail but XCOM is one of those games that keeps you coming back for more until you can get that "perfect" run.
With XCOM: Enemy Unkown comes an expansion called XCOM: Enemy Within which adds a few new features and technology. The most notable addition is a new resource type, called meld. Meld fuels some of the new technologies, such as a new mechanized cyber exoskeleton. The expansion adds more stages and aliens as well but there is a focus on trans-human modification and most of the upgrades are seen to your units themselves. As you collect and research meld, you can use it to develop even more unique and complicated abilities for your squad mates.
XCOM: Enemy Unkown can be enjoyed by just about anyone and the title certainly stands as a staple of the series. The amount of time you spend playing the game quickly adds up as you are eager to begin the next stage, completing missions and unlocking research. The aliens are varied and interesting and the combined challenged presented by the base management aspect and the actual turn based stratedgy elements are highly enjoyable. Anyone interested in science fiction or solid and challenging turn based strategy mechanics should look into picking up XCOM: Enemy Unknown.

I cannot possibly recommend this game enough. Tarsier Studios have done a stellar job with the games' atmosphere. The GFX, the sound design, the level design and aesthetic of the models, the story and it's implications...
The game is short, admittedly (finished it in 3 hours) but it is a rollercoaster of an experience and it certainly felt like longer. (Plus, DLC no. 1 just released, with more planned as I understand it, not that you need that to enjoy it)
The only faults I can find are that because the spaces and levels are in 3D but the camera is fixed, side-on perspective, it is difficult to judge the position/depth of some elements in the level, like holes in walls that are shown side-on, you need to crawl into, and during chase scenes, that can spell your death. And even though in general (not always) checkpoints are regular enough, sometimes you'll have to do a lot of things again after dying, which leads me to fault no. 2: doing a scene over and over due to death can make the horror feel and atmosphere peel off and ineffective. That, however, is true of all horror games with a degree of challenge. So, not entirely the game's fault.
If you are a fan of grotesque (but not necessarily gory) horror, great storytelling and environmental puzzles, do yourself the favour and get this game. It left me craving for more: more gameplay, more story, and answers to the story it already told me.
Fantastic job Tarsier Studios. You can be proud of this one.

The combat in this game is very slow and tedious, and to make matters worse there is a lot of it. The system uses some different stats that are sort of like a simplified version of an RPG ruleset. While the stat system is really unique it is also pretty boring. You basically just spend half the battle breaking armor and then the last few rounds killing everything. It's really repetitive. Also, the final boss is so easy it must be a joke, especially when compared to how crazy hard the rest of the game is.
Another flaw is the game's decision system. You will have to make choices about what your caravan should do. Sadly most of them are really boring because they adjust a few stat values in your caravan that ultimately don't matter too much. There is no emotional impact at all. Sometimes your choice will get a character killed for no apparent reason or by random chance. Seriously some random coincidence that has nothing to do with what's going on will come out of nowhere that gets characters killed. As if that's not dumb enough, if you didn't know they would die and invested all your points into them then your party becomes too weak and you have to savescum. Very frustrating.
One thing this game does have going for it is the story. It has a really neat story, some cool characters, and an original setting. It's essentially a viking RPG with some really unique lore. Sadly, there wasn't enough of this in the game. I would have liked to see more of that and more dialouge because those parts are what makes this game shine. However, the good stuff was so few and far between with the game mostly focusing on random encounters and combat.
You will notice the developers put a lot of effort and kickstart money into making special banners for backers and a really well fleshed out map. A map that has all kinds of lore info that is mostly irrelevant because your characters never visit those locations. They should have put the budget from that into fine tuning gameplay.
One last thing. I wouldn't call this is an RPG. It certainly has some RPG elements but it's more of a tactics game that mixes other genres in as well. It's one of these games that tries to appeal to every gamer instead of focusing on doing one thing really well.
That said, it's worth the sale price if you can catch it on sale. It's not a BAD game as there were certainly a lot of mildly entertaining moments. I just don't feel it's worth regular price.

I spent 40 hours playing before writing this; this a really good game in the fact that it compels you to come back & play repeatedly despite what some would call failure.
That being said I have had a great time replaying this in any difficulty, as should you, if you intend to make the most of this game. There are definitely more games out there that will make things much more brutal just for attempting it. The thrill is in the chase, hoping you can get enough power/resources to balance killing the Rebel Flagship in Sector 8.
The Good: Easy, casual playing with a desire to upgrade your ship while keeping ahead of the Rebel Fleet. Tutorial goes a long way to help the average FTL noob like myself. Once you get a foothold with ANY ship, you want to see it through to the end regardless of fail or pass. Even if you fail you feel compelled to retry, not something easily said of every game that makes you want to beat your head against a very hard surface. Advanced mode enhances this experience very much so with the new Clone Bay if nothing else.
The Bad: I hate to say it, the average person may look to play Normal, but I recommend Easy to start out. Why? Even Normal mode can be brutal & harsh to someone 1st starting out. Once you gain the learning curve, it becomes SOMEWHAT easier only to be offset by AI cheese. In the 1st sector you can often get ambushed a bit unfairly if inexperienced. Easy = Normal, Normal = Hard, Hard= Wanting to throw your monitor through the wall.
The Ugly: Graphics are not exactly great; don't look for extravagant, mind-boggling cutscenes/story as its more reminescent of 16/32 bit system. At the same time I retell of the AI toughness, it might turn-off/confuse some looking for something easy & casual without the burden of frustration.

For a while I avoided this game because I don't watch enough South Park to feel like I'd be able to get into it, and to an extent I do feel like I missed out on a ton of references, but it's generally pretty safe to go into this without much experience. It is still South Park so a lot of the jokes are just edgy shock humor (you can "look forward" to playing as a jew who can circumcise enemies as an attack,
, to name just a few of many examples), but there's also enough that's actually funny to make it worth trying. Gameplay-wise it's like Paper Mario for "adults", and while some things aren't explained that great (it tells you to just hit the block button whenever the circle appears under your character, for example, but the timing is actually a lot more specific than that and can be annoying on certain attacks) it's pretty fun, though the actual RPG mechanics are simple enough that if you're expecting anything like Obsidian's usual mechanics you'll probably be disappointed. It's also fairly short for an RPG, and even with doing all the sidequests it's unlikely that you'll break 20 hours, but I think given the combat system it probably would've outstayed its welcome if it was longer than that anyways.

Brought this game when it was on sale for a bargain, played it on Xbox 360/PS3 before hand, and after experiencing the game again on PC, I can honestly say its a game worth getting, whether your a South Park fan or not.
Rating for this is 8/10 overall.
Story is straight forward, your a new kid thats arrived in South Park, picking your character of either Warrior, Mage, Thief or Jew. First time playing I choose the Warrior class set up, as it seemed suited to do so for a first time round. You go on to fight for Cartmans side, but later on you get the option of which side you want to help either the Humans or Elf people, the ending is all the same, but this alternate choice only changes some dialog scenes, rather then affecting the overal experience.
The battle style is simple, easy to undertand. You can either use a melee weapon for close combat or a range weapon to target foes in the distance, giving you some advantage in battle. You also have a buddy with you which comes with there own abilities, the two buddies I found best to work with is Butters and Kyle.
Collectables in game can be annoying the first time round, as some items are only obtainable during certain story missions, this mostly occours to the Chimpokemon & Friend requests. So if your going for a 100% completion then you might want to do some research before hand or buy a guild book like I did for my second time round.
Overall I really liked this game, cant wait to play the Sequel in Fractured but Whole... but untill that day arrives I hope my review helped majority of you out.

At first glance, Child of Light looks like a children's nursry story with 2d platforming elements. However if you dig down a little bit further you find a story with a very dark tone to it, and a very rich battle system that will keep you engaged for hours. In fact, the battle system is the best part of the game.
I recorded on a video reviewing the games battle system in-depth:
It is very reminiscent of the battle system from the Grandia games. That battle system was my favorite of all jrpg's from the playstation 2 era. This game takes a unique twist on that system, and adds complexity through Oculi system.
The story itself is interesting, but the constant rhyming can get it a little boring. There isn't much for character customization other than choosing which branch of the different skill trees your characters go down.
Strategy Tip: Pick one branch of the skill tree for each character until you unlock all the major skills on that branch.
Oh and don't think you'll find your normal inns and shops in the locals you encournter along the way. There is none. All the items that you will get will either be from chests or enemy drops.
Nonetheless, it is the battle system that uplifts this game to a much higher rating than there would be without it.

I'd love to give this game a 10/10... I really would.  It's clear that the creators are true fans of old-school RPGs that required a large amount of strategy, planning, care, and investment in your characters.  In fact, I haven't even beat the game, and Ive only gotten to the second act.  Already, there are some nagging issues that impede quality of life for the player.  And I see where they are coming from.  The game is very "non-hand-holdy", and in a lot of senses it is great.  However, inventory management is a chore, so is crafting, so is lore-based equipment identifying, and these chores break up the gameply so heavily that it's hard to stay engaged without spending serious time doing menial tasks.  My opinion is that crafting should be done in a GW2 style, with crafting ingredients sent to a different "stash", and you can experiment with creating new recipies.  Items should be ID'ed upon pickup if you have the lore.  The fact that some items don't stack (dust?  of all things dust doesn't stack?) is both unusual and difficult to deal with.  These small things build and really impact my experience.  I'll review this again once I finish, but I think that small changes could make this game a 10/10 easy.

Grim Dawn is set in the war torn world of Cairn and is easily one of the best arpgs I have seen in years having been developed by Crate Entertainment an indie company formed with some of the talented devs of Titan Quest. Crate was able to gain rights to the Titan Quest engine and began developing Grim Dawn which in my opinion is a worthy successor. While Grim Dawn does take inspiration from fan favorites such as the diablo series Torchlight series and Path of exile it introduces it's own unique ideas to these systems as well. Some of the things enjoy are.
Having been developed by some of the people that worked on Titan Quest one of the core features that i really enjoyed about Titan Quest makes a welcome return here in the dual class system. Upon entering the game you can create a Male or Female classless hero at level 2 you will have the ability to pick one of 6 class trees.
Solder
Demolitionist
shaman
archanist
nightblade
occultist
you can further flesh out your class at level 10 by combining a second of these trees. This combined with all the items that grant skills and augments to skills makes for some deep customization options which is one of the things i enjoy about rpgs in general.
while it is apparent that this system takes inspiration from Path of exile's massive skill tree the devotion system in Grim Dawn is quite unique in that you have to go exploring throughout the would to find shrines which need to be cleansed. once cleansed you will gain devotion points which can be spent in a constellation map to augment your skills.
Cairn  is a huge open world providing hours of fun content to delve into quests some with consequences /lore/Factions/Bounties/Dungeons there is allot to do in Grim Dawn and Crate have already confirmed they will be adding more content updates and full expansions
The component system works similar to the gem socket system present in other games in the genre. The difference here is that instead of having  gems and socketable items Grim Dawn has different components that can be added to any tier of item. Some of these components can really improve your build by having skills tied to them. For example I have a character that has a lodestone socketed into my offhand this item grants a lightning nova skill and to take that even further I have tied the lightning nova skill from the lodestone to the scorpion sting ability in the devotion system which adds an aoe poison to the lightning nova.There are tons of components for every gear type and you can combine these components to make more powerful ones. While I do enjoy this system it is not without it's flaws the biggest one being that if i want to modify or remove an item from a piece of gear I can do that  by way of the Inventor's apprentice however you can only keep one or the other the component item or the piece of gear. This can make the decision to salvage quite difficult if both items provide significant additions to a build.
Loot in Grim Dawn like other titles comes in different tier types Common/Magic/Rare/Epic and Legendary. What makes the loot different from other arpgs is the fact that like the component system some items can augment existing skills even after you have maxed them out on the skill tree or like the lodestone mentioned in the component section some loot can have specific skills tied to the item. This really makes for a unique customization experience.
While the inventory system is in many ways no different any other arpg out there there are a few things that are worth mentioning about the system in Grim Dawn such as quests that give bag upgrades for rewards a button that automatically combines components and my personal favorite and something that everyone has been asking for in several games of the genre. an AUTO SORT BUTTON!!! for those of us who hate playing inventory tetris. The stash system is also really well done as it has a character specific tab and an item transfer tab. The item transfer area can be upgraded to have more tabs within it as well so there really is no shortage of space.
Quests in Grim Dawn come in many forms. Some quests unlock vendors and crafting abilities some have choices and consequences. For example maybe there are 2 warring factions in the game if you choose to help one you will become enemies with the other. These kinds of choices make for a rich questing experience. while exploring the world you will find tons of pages and notes on the areas that you are exploring I have always been a fan of finding lore in these types of games and there is no shortage of that here.
Crafting in Grim Dawn borrows some of the ideas from Diablo 3's artisan system they have blueprints that you can find through out the world to increase the list of items available to craft. You can craft components and potions to give you extra damage or resistance fore specific monster type as well but the thing that stands out to me is the ability to craft relics these relics like other loot in the game can ultimately change your play style for example you might have a character such as the demolitionist that uses pistols but can't dual wield them no problem you can craft the gunslingers talisman equip it and you have your ability to dual wield pistols.
While exploring the world of Cairn you will encounter different factions and settlements that will have their own set of bounties and quests for you to do. These factions have quartermasters which are merchants that sell items specific to that faction depending on how high your friendly reputation is with them. As stated before in the quest section some factions are at war with each other so helping one faction may and in come cases will in definitely either damage or completely ruin your reputation with certain factions. If your reputation gets significantly low with a faction they will spawn more elites and nemesis monsters to hunt you down. This in my opinion makes for a very engaging exploration experience.
Grim Dawn features the ability to play your characters in both single and multiplayer modes. the multi player is easy to use the host options are quite good due to the fact that you can host a game for up to 4 players and because the game features a server browser rather than an account based system the player hosting the game  can easily customize the number of players allowed in the server weather there is instanced loot and even put a password on servers so that only friends can join this is somthing i wish all games like this had.
While I really Enjoy Grim Dawn I do have one minor complaint. I wold love for there to be more voice acting especially since there is literally tons of lore notes in the game and being a person that has some visual difficulties reading a whole bunch of text does tend to put allot of strain on my eyes so having audio to listen to is a big help but I also understand that they are an indie team and are only able to work with that they have and this grype aside they have made a fantastic rpg.
If your looking for a new action rpg title to dig into Than Grim Dawn will not disappoint. It has something for new comers and old veterans of the genre alike. It is a great value and well worth the asking price and i highly recommend this so i am going to give Grim Dawn a 9 out of 10.
