The best adaptation of X -COM so far. Lots of innovations and good ideas, while retaining the atmosphere of the original and removing some unnecessary micromanagement: 100%
Strategic part of the game
This part of the game is vastly innovated in a good way. You have 1 base and are under a pressure to cover all of the world with satellites. The rules are fair and you can always see how close a country is to being lost, unlike in UFO or TFTD, where one undetected ship could infiltrate the country. Rewards are varied - they include scientists and technicians, whom you have to earn. Base building is also significantly refreshed - you have to consider the depth of your base and which facilities will neighbor each other. UFO fighter combat is also innovated, you can use bonuses made from alien corpses (which is hilarious by itself) in real time. Economics is also vastly improved. You can no longer manufacture goods to make endless money, instead you really have to care for your satellite coverage and make hard decisions about selling the fore mentioned corpses.
Tactical part of the game
This game remains true to the turn based concept. It makes extensive use of cover concept. The overall adaptation is very close to real-life infantry "fire team" tactics. Until you get used to this concept you will often end up in hopeless situations like Ripley did in Aliens along with her marines. Then your only way for salvation will be to turn the operations area into rubble using rockets and grenades. Hopefully along with the aliens .
Storyline and research
Streamlining is the direction of current gaming, so don´t expect to relive those memories of trying to actually figure out how to win UFO or TFTD (or determine that your game bugged out and you can´t win, AKA Tasoth commander problem). Despite this, the story is interesting and thrilling. The aliens mostly look as scary as their are dangerous, so when you see something that looks really baddass, you will indeed be in a world of pain if not prepared.
Notes
The difficulty curve is mostly well balanced and some additional challenges are provided. To get best out of the game (and all types of these games), use the ironman setting, even if it means dropping the difficulty level down a level or 2. You aren´t really playing the game, if the game has no chance of winning. Expert players should start on normal-ironman. I could beat that on my first attempt, classic-ironman took 12 attempts. Easy setting should be accessible to all players.
UFO enemy within DLC: mostly recommended, but dissapointing. improves AI, adds more missions and adds mech and mutant soldiers, which are fun. Disregard my disregard for DLC in general.
See also:
Ufo: Afterlight, Ufo: Aftershock, Ufo: Extraterrestrials, Ufo: aftermath, Battle isle 4: Incubation, Gorky 17, the authors if this game obviously researched these medium-cost remakes and took the best ideas from them

I can say with a relative degree of certainty that this is one of the most brilliant things I've ever had the pleasure of experiencing. It has a marvelous amout of content, extremely well drawn backgrounds and character designs, lovely music, well developed character personalities, a facinating story, and, I think above all, the ability to evoke profound feelings that I haven't had brought forth by many things, let alone visual novels. Also this particular VN gives its audience the ability to choose, and the choices are many and various.
Depending on your choices, you can influence the story, raise your reputation with various girls, and bring about your future, be it demise or happiness. It is quite immersive, and it's very easy to get absorbed into the enviroment and atmosphere. It is extremely fulfilling to win over a character by getting the good ending, though the bad endings are equally interesting. The story is sectioned off wonderfully, and if you want answers, you must first achieve the task of getting the good ending with all of the girls.
The only qualm I have with this VN is the occasional repetitiveness of beginning a new game after playing through once. I found myself skipping much of the text I'd already read the first time, which can something lighten the deep immersion I felt when first reading the intellectual speculations of Semyon, the protagonist, and the pleasant banter between characters.
Overall, I found Everlasting Summer to be an immensely satisfying and fulfulling experience, and I would recommend it to most anyone.
Plus, there's a catgirl, and who doesn't like those?

There seems to be an overarching narrative which your choices can't change - having said that, your characters really can (and will) die depending on the choices you make.  Some of the deaths are pretty devastating as well.
Altogether, I really enjoyed this game and would definitely buy the sequel.

Definitely a Great Game and will serve as a solid Benchmark for many ARPG's to come.
Pros:
- Extremely well balanced mechanics with very deep gameplay. No stat is a "dud" stat all have their advantages.
- Extreme Build Diversity, 5 classes, each with 20 skills, 15 class combinations and hundreds of passives through the devotion tree. There are literally 100's of viable builds.
- Fast Paced fun combat. I've been killing zombies for over 70 hours now and still enjoying every second!
- Great Developer Team. Remember how blizzard would only update their game every 6 monhs? Crate's already about to release it's next major update after less than a month. Many free content patches expected in the future - and still waiting for survival mode.
- Modding Tools. The community is going to create so many amazing mods that are truly going to push the limits of this game. Some people are still playing after 700 hours.
Cons:
- Multiplayer needs work. At its current state Grim Dawn is a single player game. This game is very easy to hack which means things like trading / random queues are just not a good idea. No economy is kind of a good thing though, you have to find your own gear.
- Lack of End Game content. Don't get me wrong, I've played 70 hours and I'm not even close to end game yet, my highest level is 58 (of 85). However I will reach the end game eventually and there are only basically 2 static dungeons to run (however 3 new ones are coming next update).
- No Random Dungeons. Due to the engine there are no random dungeons in this game which means there will never be things like rifts (diablo 3) or maps (PoE) which means we totally rely on the community and developer for new dungeons - can't just generate them!
The Developers have laid down an excellent foundation, easily the best RPG system of any of the ARPG's out there. If they keep supporting the game with expansions, and supporting community creations, there is no reason this game will not surpass Diablo 3 and PoE as king of the Hack and Slash.

This is one of the deepest RPGs available on PC. I've been playing RPGs for 20 years (yes, I'm getting old) and this game is definitely in my top 5 RPGs. Before I get into the review, I'll write a few bits of information that most people probably want to know:
1) 60+ hours for first play-through if you do some side quests. Probably closer to 50 for just the main story. 100 if you do everything. The community content and free game creation tools mean endless mods and added gameplay. It's easily worth full-price and then some.
2) This is not an action game. The combat is slow, strategic, but extremely fun. See review below for details.
3) The game has difficulty settings that make combat easier if you don't like strategy. Abilities interact with each other and the environment. You can combo for great success.
4) You can go almost everywhere right from the start. In fact, if you find a particular character in one of the end zones, you can get powerful equipment early on without having to fight anything (sneaking/invisibility helps get there). Exploration is rewarded with EXP and loot. Try it.
5) The CO-OP is *amazing* and so is the single-player.
The review:
The game world is full of amazing interactions, non-linear story and multiple routes to complete any given quest. Almost every NPC has their own story, and often quest. The people in the towns are not faceless and nameless robots that repeat the same 1-2 sentences and act as furniture like in other RPGs. They're people, with their own desires, actions, and stories. And, you can choose to interact with these stories and follow them to see what happens. Or, you can murder them and rob their dead bodies, their underwear drawers, and lie to their friends and families. It's up to you, really.
I don't believe any two players will have the same experience with this game given how much you can customize and how many different ways you can advance through the game. In this game you make real decisions - do you steal from, murder, help, ignore, or extort the people of Rivellon?
The combat system had me worried initially. I was hoping for an action-rpg type combat like the previous games in the series. I was so very, very wrong to want that. The depth of the combat in this game is extraordinary. It is entirely possible to finish the game on hard if you master the combat. If you don't bother learning how it works, even the easy difficulty may seem too difficult.  This is because the skills in the game interact with the environment, the characters, the enemy, and each other. Want to make an explosion? Set a fire field down then spray poison over top to blow it up. Want to make a mist cloud to provide cover? Water field + fire. Water + ice = frozen ground, which makes enemies slip. Oil slows, fire ignites it to burn.  This is just a small part of the combat. The AI is smart and will utilize these against you as well. You can also clear fields: E.g. Rain on a burning area/player and it extinguishes it. You can also just bring a bucket! I carried 3 buckets of water on me to create puddles that I could freeze, electrocute, or use to put out fire.
You can also charm, stun, knockdown, curse, slow, etc your opponents and summon minions. One time, I was exploring an area with just 1 character in stealth while the other 3 were waiting safely in town. I got discovered and had to face a large number of foes with a single thief that wasn't particularly skilled in damage abilities. It took some thinking, but with charm, blind, knockdown, stealth, a summoned skeleton, and some nearby oil barrels, I was able to dispatch the entire group of enemies. This was not a fight that I thought I could win, but I was rewarded for thinking outside the "Hulk smash" mentality.
If you like RPGs, this one will impress and leave you wanting more.

The best adaptation of X -COM so far. Lots of innovations and good ideas, while retaining the atmosphere of the original and removing some unnecessary micromanagement: 100%
Strategic part of the game
This part of the game is vastly innovated in a good way. You have 1 base and are under a pressure to cover all of the world with satellites. The rules are fair and you can always see how close a country is to being lost, unlike in UFO or TFTD, where one undetected ship could infiltrate the country. Rewards are varied - they include scientists and technicians, whom you have to earn. Base building is also significantly refreshed - you have to consider the depth of your base and which facilities will neighbor each other. UFO fighter combat is also innovated, you can use bonuses made from alien corpses (which is hilarious by itself) in real time. Economics is also vastly improved. You can no longer manufacture goods to make endless money, instead you really have to care for your satellite coverage and make hard decisions about selling the fore mentioned corpses.
Tactical part of the game
This game remains true to the turn based concept. It makes extensive use of cover concept. The overall adaptation is very close to real-life infantry "fire team" tactics. Until you get used to this concept you will often end up in hopeless situations like Ripley did in Aliens along with her marines. Then your only way for salvation will be to turn the operations area into rubble using rockets and grenades. Hopefully along with the aliens .
Storyline and research
Streamlining is the direction of current gaming, so don´t expect to relive those memories of trying to actually figure out how to win UFO or TFTD (or determine that your game bugged out and you can´t win, AKA Tasoth commander problem). Despite this, the story is interesting and thrilling. The aliens mostly look as scary as their are dangerous, so when you see something that looks really baddass, you will indeed be in a world of pain if not prepared.

The difficulty curve is mostly well balanced and some additional challenges are provided. Know what you're getting into before you purchase. Do you make decisions, tough decisions? Yes. Do those decisions "matter"? No, the story will go on very much the same way they will no matter what you do. Does that matter? Well, your mileage may vary. Personally I enjoyed Episode 1 very much, it was engaging, well written and it played with my emotions just like all good stories should. And that's just what this is, a story, a visual and interactive story but a story with pretty trappings and little else.
That said you WILL enjoy this infinitely more if you have seen the show and/or read the books as I have. Is it worth getting if you're not familiar with the material? That depends on how much you like Telltale's format. I found myself tailoring my decisions based on what I already knew was going to happen to the canonical characters, you may find this interesting or distracting, I found it a bit of both.
Visually it is pleasing enough. It has an "oil on canvas in motion" quality to it, but it isn't gorgeous and it isn't perfect. There isn't much action to be had and what little there is in Episode 1 centers around the squire, Gered. Honestly though, if you're getting into this for the visuals or flashy action sequences you're probably barking up the wrong tree. Like I said, this is a story and a damn good one.
My play time (2.6 as of the writing) is about what you can expect if you take your time, read everything, do everything and ruminate for a bit on the decisions that don't require you to make a snap judgement. If you blow through everything expect to clear it in half the time. But do you skim a good novel? No, you savor it, you may re-read a passage here or there. Personally, I can't wait for Episode 2 but know this isn't for everyone and read well about the mechanics of Game of Thrones before you pull the trigger.

This is a wonderful game.. actually it's an incredible game, here's why.
First off, the genuine quality of the game, as in the amount of bugs and errors are very little, and any at all barely even effect the game, actually one bug is on some customn maps Zeds get stuck, so that's mildy annoying, but is overwhelmed by the positves. The game is also very well polished, clean, and mechanics work well.
Another positive aspect I quite like, is the perk levelling system, it's quite an improvment over the first game, as it doesn't take weeks to get to top levels (not that i'd mind too much), which allows people to experience the games different difficulty levels and to try and become better at the game. Leading on to my next point about difficulty. The different levels of difficulty are quite nice, as you've got the normal mode, for people who recently got the game, or if you want to try out a low level perk with other players, then you got hard for general players who are decent at the game and then Suicidal and Hell On Earth, which I personally have difficulty doing (barely do suicidal on a select amount of maps), but I still love playing these, of course only with other people who are also of a similar skill, cause HoE is as it would be, very very hard. And the difficulty allows you to try different perks to see what you are a good at and what not, thus giving you practice in all perks.
Another incredible positive, is the continual support and updates for the game. Like it's predecessor KF1, the game has had continuous updates since it's intial development and early access, which is common, but what makes it different with KF2, is that it's still being updated, Tripwire still give it the content that we consume for it, I mean, look at KF1, that games was being updated for years, showing that Tripwire care about the games, and what people think about it. So this gives the game not only consistant new content, but also a sense of understanding between the community and the company (most of the time), and props to Tripwire for constant updates to this game whilst also managing another game with the same kind of care.
Here's a negative. There are very few negative, but there is a large negative, The graphics. Now I don't mean the enitre graphics, but, I do mean the lack of support for Integrated GPUs (meaning the CPU is running the Graphics), as there are a heap of people (don't know what percentage of players) that are running off of a laptop, that have to deal with parts of maps, or in some cases, the entire map, being completely pitch black, with no possible way of playing effectively. Also ♥♥♥♥ sirens (not a negtive part, I just ♥♥♥♥ing hate them)\
So all in all, a very well polished game that runs well on
computers. I'll give it 9.49 outta 10, .50 for the graphics issue, and .01 for the ♥♥♥♥ing sirens

Based on a playthrough of the first episode:-
Another excellent entry from Telltale games, i would recommend it to everyone if it wasn't specifically aimed at fans of the HBO show and the A Song of Ice & Fire Books, it's hard to get into it if you aren't one of those two .. but still if you liked previous Telltale games and like gritty fantasy trying this game might get you to watch the HBO show and/or read the Novels by George R.R Martin.
Now to the game itself, it starts at a critical point in the story and integrates the new family/house very well into the main story line of Game of Thrones ... there are many tense moments and tough choices, and the game does a great job luring you in with false promises of hope then smacks you in the face with harsh cold truths, and smacks you hard it does, specially in the finale of the episode which reflects and captures the intensity of many similar moments in the show and books so well.
The graphics might be a little rough around the edges but the painted textures with visible brush strokes looks lovely and fits well with the atmosphere of the story and fantasy themes .. the tapestry specifically you see early on is a lovely work of art.
As for the voice acting, many actors from the show reprise their roles in the game and to fantastic results and engrossing voice acting, even the non-show characters done a damn fine job.
Choices here might not feel very impactful but from previous experiences in Telltale games i can tell you that many of those choices will come back in later episodes to bite you in the back .. logically if the game forks so early on it would be so daunting to cover all the different variations of the story in later episodes .. don't take the "{X} will remember that" exclamations lightly XD
All in all excellent experience specially for the fans of the show and the books who would like to see the GoT universe expanded and need something to chew on until season 5 or the next book comes out.

A lot seem to enjoy the simple game play but it's too simple and forces the game to lack any depth whatsoever.  Too much time was spent on presentation with the lack of trying to make a decent game.  Instead of going with a tried and true formula, the game goes with a 2 button masher for moving left/right w/attacking at the same time. Overall, stunning visuals, grand storytelling, easy-to-learn and smooth gameplay, and immersive audio. 10/10 for sure.

Crafting isn't much better.  The base system is OK but the constant exceptions to how the crafting interface works make it very frustrating to learn.  Recipies are stored as bizarre text descriptions intead of listing the actual recipie  ingrediants and results and so are quite useless unless you need another puzzle.

Game is strictly for those who like to do puzzle-box/adventure games.  If you like to leave town and actually adventure, do it somewhere else.

Grim Dawn is, appropriately enough, a dark fantasy action-RPG, a Diablo-like from the makers of Titan Quest and its expansion, Immortal Throne. It exchanges the sword-and-sandal world of Greek, Egyptian and Chinese myth of its predecessor for a world of iron, blood and gunpowder where humanity sees itself trapped in a post-apocalypse wrought by two mighty armies as despicable as they are really damn old: the body-snatching Aetherials and the blood-happy Cthonians. You are a rare survivor of an Aetherial possession- the creature was driven from your body and you are yourself again- only you have no memory of who you are or how you got the ability to surf the Aether via conveniently placed rifts scattered throughout the world. You begin the game combating your bog-standard undead and quickly move up to more threatening foes as you progress. Along the way you meet a handful of NPCs and pick up a lot of notes that gradually piece together the gruesome fall of the once-mighty empire of Erulan, now beset on all sides by beasts, zombies, bandits, and extra-planar nightmares.
Grim Dawn plays much like Titan Quest, but with a wealth of quality-of-life improvements that make it a much more enjoyable experience overall. It notably features a reusable portal spell in the vein of Diablo 3 that allows you to access any unlocked Rift in the world, as well as none of that stupid item durability business, so you never need to repair your gear (read: suffer an arbitrary drain on your wallet). The most you lose on death is a small amount of experience, which can be retrieved from the headstone that marks where you last died. However, I have only played on normal mode so far and this may change later, I do know that you suffer a 25% penalty to your elemental resistances on elite, and a whopping 50% on ultimate. In addition, there is an NPC in the very first town that you can purchase skill point refunds from for a flat price that quickly becomes inconsequential, at least on normal. However, you cannot refund points spent on your mastery level itself (more on that in a moment), which increases your base stats and unlocks new skills at certain thresholds. Grim Dawn also generally feels friendlier to play then Titan Quest or Diablo 2, and at least on normal I felt like I was not punished for experimenting with new skills, and I was consistently dealing very high damage to all enemies as early as a third of the way into the game, to the point of one-shotting most enemies at the endgame. However, the same is also true of normal difficulty in Path of Exile, which quickly kicks you in the balls on higher difficulties if you do not have a "good" build- but I'll enjoy it while it lasts.
Grim Dawn retains Titan Quest's unique class system. You begin the game with no class at all, but are quickly given a choice of skill trees the first time you level. You are then able to pick a second tree not long thereafter, combining any two skill trees to create the hybrid class you want. I went with Demolitionist first, a primarily ranged tree dealing with explosives, flames, “thorns”-style defenses that burn attackers, and a bit of lightning, with a few points in the Soldier tree for defense, creating what the game calls a Commando. My basic attack was quickly replaced by the ever-useful Flame Strike, which in addition to adding massive fire damage to my attacks, can also be augmented with splash damage, lightning damage and ultimately bursts of magma shards for even more fun. The tree also includes grenades, molotovs, cluster bombs, mortars and mines- a respectable arsenal. Other trees include the spell-blasting Arcanist, demon-summoning Occultist, poisonous, sneaky Nightblade, and lightning-hurling Shaman trees. There is also a special "Devotion" skill web represented by constellations, which you put points into earned from reactivating special shrines found throughout the world. These devotion points earn you minor stat buffs useful to most builds, as well as special skills that can be attached to your normal abilities to enhance their effects. I got a skill called Twin Fang that added a chance for a life-stealing attack to my basic attack, for example. However, I do not currently know a way to respec Devotion points, and you cannot switch your choice of basic skill tree.
As with any Diablolike, you can expect to find a large amount of magically-enhanced gear with a range of stats- including guns, proving once again that all you really need to take out a legion of extra-dimensional horrors is a little firepower and a lot of explosions. The flavor of the gear is very Warhammer Fantasy, especially in the witch hunter-style occultist hats, with lots of dark leather and scratched, pitted metal for the heavy stuff, sharply contrasting the tunics and Corinthian helms of Titan Quest, the colorful and often steampunkish gear of Torchlight or the shiny, pointy and delightfully over-designed armors of Diablo 3.  Notably, the highest tier of gear (color-coded purple, oddly enough) does not start dropping until your reach level 50, which will probably not happen until near the end of the game, even if you make a point of doing all the side quests and exploring optional dungeons. However, I got a nice pair of purple-rank gloves almost immediately upon reaching 50, so don't worry about it too much. Make sure to check out the two big side dungeons, the Steps of Torment and the Bastion of Chaos. Note that you need to craft a key to get into these dungeons, but hey.
I would be remiss not to mention a feature of Grim Dawn I don't particularly enjoy, borrowed from MMOs: factions and reputation grinding. There are handful of groups you can impress in the game by killing their enemies, doing story or side quests for their NPCs, doing their faction-specific sidequests (some of which don't unlock until you're at a certain reputation level) and doing bounties, which are repeatable small side-quests obtainable from a bounty table found in each major settlement. You are forced at one point to chose between two groups, and allying with one permanently puts you in negative rep with the other, locking your current character out of their quests and reputation rewards for that entire run, though this in no way impedes your progress in the story. Some quests also have choices that may have unintended consequences later on, and you aren't going to like some of them. If you're concerned, just look up what does what on the wiki like I did: No sense going into anything unprepared here. You can also lose rep with the enemy groups, and reaching a new rank of hate results in nastier elite enemy spawns and more of them, which is probably beneficial in the long run.
Grim Dawn is respectably long and content-dense, especially for the price. I clocked in over thirty hours, and like most Diablolikes, you spend most of that knee-deep in the bad guys, and it never really gets old- the hallmark of a good game in a genre known for its repetitiveness. Sure, it's a little rough around the edges- the graphics aren't anything special, the voice acting is iffy, and the music, though good, is largely atmospheric, but its mechanically very solid. Crate Entertainment has created an excellent ARPG with much potential replay value that is well worth your time. If you've played any other ARPG before, Grim Dawn will be right up your alley, and even if you haven't, it's a fine place to start.

I do not recommend this game for the casual player.
In my opinion, the devs have taken the RPG elements of this game too far. Only play this game if you are cool with the following:
1. Health does not regenerate over time. Normally you would rely on health potions, however they are very scare and expensive to buy. You could steal all the food in the town to eat or all the items in the town to eat, but you wreck your playing environment to do so. Generally the only solution is to have a mage on your crew to cast heeling spells, otherwise you have to find a bed after each battle and heal your characters.
2. Dead characters don’t respawn after battle. If you loss a character after battle, you only have a finite number of resurrection scrolls to revive them. So losing one character is a big deal and losing more is problematic for the following reason.
3. The inventory system is terrible. Each character has its own bag, which means it’s a high level of micro managing to ensure that each character has what it needs before each battle. if the character if the resurrection scrolls dies, well you cannot save them because you lose their items! Secondly, characters don’t share money, so you need to always share the money smog characters to enable them to buy things.
4. You pick up loot, but you cannot use it until it is identified. There is a skill called 'identifying'. Every piece of loot needs to be identified before it can be used. This means you need to send all loot to the character with that skill to identify the items, before you distribute the loot to the relevant characters. I have never seen this mechanic in a game before and it is really annoying.
5. You can steal nearly veering you see! Like elders scrolls, you can easily steal everything you see in the game world. It might be fun at first.... until you realized your town is rather dull and now empty.
6. There is real no combat in this game until 6ish hour in. However, the peaceful mission is rather fun. I have stopped playing this game after experiencing the combat for the reasons above. The combat is very challenging and fun. But the lack of health potions and not auto resurrection mechanics kills the game for me.
7. Crafting potions is a joke. You require empty flask to craft health potions. However you cannot really buy them or easily find them into he game world. So health potions are a luxury and not a throw away thing like other games. This is a good thing, but not a casual gamer how just wants to charge into combat, takes hits, lose a few people and heal up after. Nope, the game is not built for that kind of play.
I want to have fun in my games and not role play doing boring tasks like finding a bed to rest or hunting or ingredients

Saints Row 4 is one of the most stupidly fun games that I've ever played. You are President of the United States. An alien invasion terrorizes Earth, and it's up to the Saints to stop them. Armed with a bevy of superpowers, you battle Aliens (as well as a few familiar foes) in order to rid the alien menace led by Zinyak.
The gameplay is great, but I felt that the addition of superpowers made the game a bit too easy. Still, it's rather fun jumping, flying, and plowing through the city. Some of the battles can get pretty crazy as well. The customization is pretty similar to SR3 in the way of cars, characters, and weapons. One negative I have is that the enemies feel like bullet sponges a lot of the time, and that can be frustrating before the later levels kick in.
The story is insane, but easy enough to follow. It's also hilarious at times. The voice acting is top notch, and a cameo by Keith David doesn't hurt matters. There will be lots of surprises along the way (including a stage recreating one of the best scenes in Sci-Fi history), and new characters to find along the way. It's a real treat for long time fans of the SR franchise.
The soundtrack is really good, but not as varied as I would've liked. Pretty much all of the songs that most people will know is on one station, and the other stations just don't match up. This is something I would like expanded on in SR5.
Overall, it's a very solid game. It's not as polished as something like GTA is, but it doesn't need to be. This game doesn't take itself seriously in any aspect and doesn't expect you to either. So sit back, relax, and enjoy the awesomeness that Saints Row 4 delivers.

When it comes to good old shooters, this is a must have. As old as it is, there are still very few shooters which I enjoy more than this one - brilliant campaigns with decent AI, brilliant mutliplayer (as long as the host is decent) and great all-round gameplay.
Having first owned the PSP version, I was amazed at how much better the PC version was. The controls and feel of the game feel natural, with aiming and shooting being easy to learn but difficult to master - making it all the way to General with legendary on all of the medals is a real acheivement.
The AI is decent - offering a challenge when on elite difficulty - but not so much that the game feels impossible. The reall test comes in multiplayer - it's easy enough to outwit and outgun a few AI, but with a human player on the other team the game becomes a lot more interesting.
I'd better not forget to mention the gamemode available - conquest, space assault, Jedi Vs Sith Assault (sadly only on one map) and many more - including the epic XL gamemode which sees massive numbers of AI and players pitted against each other - quite a sight to behold.
I only have three greivences about this game:
1) That acheivements, stats etc. from multiplayer are not carried over to your singleplayer stats. This is an understandable feature, as it stops online from skewing their stats in online play - I'm probably just a bit annoyed aboutit because I mainly play multiplayer (more fun, in my opinion).
2) Hitboxes. Again, for the time the game was made it was brilliant, but some of the hitboxes of the map objects are slightly off, making it difficult to shoot over pieces of debris as the invisible hitboxes block your shots. It happens on some maps more than others, but only really affects you if you're sniping over odd parts of the map.
3) Lack of Maps for Jedi Vs Sith Assault and XL Gamemodes. These gamemodes have got to be the most fun out of all of the gamemodes, and it seems a shame that so few maps were included for them - only one for Jedi Vs Sith and a handful for XL. It feels as if the devs put these gamemodes in at the last minute for the fun of it, not really giving them the attention they deserved. The gamemodes are brilliant fun, it just feels like more should have been done with them!
All in all, this game is a classic; brilliant fun with a group of friends and even decent when playing alone. COD ain't got nothing on this.

The menu button designs are boring, not really matching the theme to the rest of the game, and the robots themselves look awkward. The game could stand a few design improvements, however, the overall mechanics of the game work just fine. Perhaps some design ideas could be inspired from Rocket League?
Also, the controls for a controller are absurdly weird and awkward, good thing I prefer to use a keyboard and mouse over a controller.
But overall, very fun game. I would recommend this to friends, so long as the game continues to be improved. I think this could be a diamond-in-the-rough game.

I really enjoyed the turn-based combat in The Banner Saga.  Individual units felt unique and the customization available to those units added another layer to your strategic options.  Multiplayer was especially fun and challenging. The single-player campaign has a good story and sets up the mythology just fine, but there are moments where arbitrary events force you to make decisions that may cost you veteran units.  Hours spent leveling units to veteran status in the turn-based battles feel wasted when you lose them in a text dialogue.  The final balle also pulls a bit of a stunt I personally don't think much of (NO SPOILER), but it's not uncommon to see this type of dragging things out in final boss fights so I'll leave that up to the individual.
A very unique turn-based strategy game with reat multi-player if you can get it and a variable single-player campaign.  Worth picking up at a good price.

Banner Saga is a member of the very old, almost protogenic style of adventures where you move from random event to random event, each time making choices á la "you meet an old bum at a crossroad - will you feed him/kill him/steal his shoes?". The crux of the genre has always been the unpredictable nature of the outcome of your decision (stealing his shoes might be the best choice since they're a magic item your party can use, but of course you don't get that info until after the fact) and Banner Saga does nothing to make that less of an issue. Instead they simply prettied up the concept with nice visuals and an interesting combat system.
Ultimately, if the presentation and the setting doesn't appeal to you, there isn't much left to reel you in. The actual gametime is short, it's very linear unless you care about minute changes and thus barely replayable and, worst of all, ends abruptely in a cliffhanger.
If you have a weak spot for stringent adventures of its kind regardless, and can heed the caveat that you should really only pick it up for 5 bucks during a sale, a single walkthrough to see what the fuzz is about is still worth a recommendation. You probably won't touch it ever again after that, but despite all its flaws it manages to be quite enjoyable to play through once.

This game has the best parkour in any game I've played, and is a truly unique and pleasant gaming experience in my opinion. I especially like the way that the game forces you to RUN by setting enemies with guns on you most levels. This element of danger and the need to keep moving makes the parkour much more fun - you can't often plan your route carefully, you just have to see an opening and hope you're skilled enough to make the jump. In other levels there are more complicated puzzle rooms that you may have to take longer to figure out, which creates a nice balance.
My only problem with the game is the combat focused levels, which become more common later on. When the game forces you to fight your way through an area rather than parkour around the enemies, it can become frustrating. The combat is quite clunky and while I don't mind taking out the occasional lone guard or even stealing his gun and sniping his buddies, a whole room of machine gun wielding maniacs who instakill you whenever you try to stop and take one out is a bit much for a parkour game. These few levels where this becomes overwhelming detract from the other parts of the game, where the simple combat system is useful and fun but isn't the focus of the whole level.
That said, the game is still really fun for the most part, and it's worth buying if it's on sale - it is quite short, I finished it in about 6 hours, so take that into account in the price you're willing to pay.
P.S. I had some technical issues with screen tearing when I turned the game on, this is a common problem and can usually be fixed by either forcing Vsync on through the graphics driver, or updating/reinstalling your drivers, which for some reason fixed it for me.

Little Nightmares is a very short, polished foray into allegorical storytelling.  The game is aesthetically gorgeous but a tough value sell due to its short length.  The game itself can be finished within 4 hours, moving at a reasonably slow pace. I myself replayed several areas, listened to the music for a bit and was AFK having lunch for a few hours.  The game's graphics, courtesy of Unreal Engine 4, are absolutely stunning, with lighting, reflective and texture assets showcasing a vibrant, yet creepy world motif.  The character designs, animations and personalities all convey extreme amounts of charisma.  As odd as it is to affirm, Little Nightmares is probably one of the top 20 best-looking games on Steam both technically and by design.  The game's plot is an ambiguous, yet disturbingly unsettling tale with no real closure.  Voice acting is non-existent.  Sound effects and music are absolutely fantastic, however, and most puzzles are reasonably easy but satisfying.
While the game is gorgeous, wonderfully orchestrated, atmospheric as all get-out and genuinely tense at times, Little Nightmares is not without some key flaws.  While the story of abandoned Six is dark and compelling, it is ulimately weak due to the staggering lack of clarification concerning the game's ending.  I myself have some theories and have included them after the spoiler symbols below.  Additionally, while the side-scrolling mechanics are often clever and sometimes well-realized, the controls are sufficiently lacking that death can result from an imprecise or a poorly-translated key press.  In fact, expect a good 30% of your playthrough to be comprised of trial-and-error replays as you struggle with the often unintuitive control scheme to execute the correct action that you already figured out...four deaths ago.  The game lacks co-op and multiplayer, and can be buggy at times, as the game crashed to desktop twice for me.
Still, as a whole, the art design, technical prowess and amazing atmosphere in Little Nightmares, as well as some truly vicious plot twists are sure to justify a steam sale purchase.  The game can still be picked up for 15 dollars and that price may be viable for many.  The game is definitely worth a price of 10 dollars and you should absolutely pick it up then.  It is, after all, a truly tense, creepy and enjoyable experience.

It is my belief that the Maw is a representation of a resort for satisfactions and pleasures of the flesh.  As such, it's possible that the Maw is in fact a brothel.  The Lady, Six' archenemy and patron of the Maw, is actually Six' mother, who abandoned and cast her daughter out for a variety of reasons.  Six, cast out after the apparent suicide of her father (the hanging man in chapter one of Little Nightmares), threatened both The Lady's inherent vanity, since she is the only thin and beautifully-framed adult in Little Nightmares, as well as reminding the mother of her of her own sinful preoccupations.  The brothel-like Maw offers visitors a never-ending source of gluttony and lust, represented in the form of cannibalistic consumption and, in turn, the patronage by the visitors fed The Lady's inherent need for "life force" which can be construed as money, wealth, status, security and 'eternal vitality' (attractiveness).
The gnomes and, indeed the children theselves throughout the ship, were subject to the predations of the Visitors.  It is therefore, possible to interpret the gnomes as the empty, broken vessels of indentured children that were trapped within the Maw.  Six' own metamorphosis into a monster of vicious vindication represents wrath at her mother's sinfulness and desire to escape the Maw at any cost.  Her final slaying of the Maw 's inhabitants, as well as The Lady promoted the idea that the brothel was ultimately destroyed by Six' unwillingness to die or capitulate to the predations of the visitors.  As such, she becomes every bit the monster that her mother is and, ultimately, the game does not represent a series of nightmarish vignettes but, instead, Six' transformation *INTO* the "Little Nightmare".
At least that's the way I interpreted it.  Ymmv.

Graphics: 9/10
Overall very good, and hold up extremely well. Good animations, crisp, detailed textures and decent lighting.
Optimization: 9/10
I would give this a 10/10, because most of it runs flawlessly on max settings on my Gtx 970m. The parts that don't are when there's a big shootout going on, with lots of glass flying everywhere, but only with physics enabled. Turn that off and you shouldn't have any optimization issues at all.
Gameplay: 8/10
The gameplay is what this game is most well known for, and it's one of the founding fathers of the First Person Parkour type genre. You feel pretty awesome when you're zooming along the top of a sky scraper, chasing after some guy in a mask (you'll understand later). HOWEVER, occasionally the controls don't really do what you want to them do, and trying to perform a jump or land roll can be a bit clunky. There can be quite a bit of trial and error at certain parts as well, but if you have enough patience you shouldn't really mind.
Story: 6.3/10
I am not giving it a low score because it is bad. It's not bad at all, it's just it's all stuff that has been done before, and there's really only one plot twist that most people won't see coming. So really, it's not that it's bad or not well thought out; it's just that it's not super original, either. The voice acting is pretty good for the major characters, and laughable for some of the police people. So overall, voice acting is pretty good.
Replay value: 9/10
This game includes time trials, which are extremely fun to play, and are a great way to kill some time if you are bored. The campaign is also very replay friendly, as you can skip literally every cutscene, and just get on with the pure gameplay.
Atmosphere: 9/10
Ok, I admit, I am a little biased about this one. You see, my all time favorite setting in a video game is futuristic city, and this game is exactly that.
Soundtrack: 10/10
A pretty fantastic soundtrack that's very slightly similar to Portal 2, and fits the setting perfectly. Except the song at the last 30 seconds. That didn't fit in at all. But beside that, fantastic.
So overall, it's a decent looking, orinal, fun game with a decent story and fantastic soundtrack, with a fair price tag (although I suggest buying it on sale).
Alright, time for some ranting
A lot of people really seem to hate the combat system. I admit, it's pretty difficult at the beginning, but when you have enough experience it's actually not all that bad. The shooting is mediocre, and the hand to hand combat requires fast reaction time and knowledge of how the enemy is going to react. Some people have a problem with this fast reaction time requirement (although combat is not at all shoved down your throat, you can pretty much run away from any conflict), namely people that also happen to enjoy older, skill base games *cough cough Gggmanlives cough*.
So overall, if I had to give this game a rating I'd probably go with a solid 8.5/10. It's a memorable experience that will stick with you.

Think of the old-school isometric approach of Baldur's Gate carried forward into a contemporary 3D engine. Now, throw on a unique and flexible "class-less" skill system, solid turn-based combat mechanics, and a clever personality trait idea. Finally, make spells react to the environment. The result is one of the most entertaining RPG experiences I've ever had - and I've been playing them for over 30 years.
At some point, the developers behind "Divine Divinity" and the early sequels (we'll refrain from talking about how silly the name is) were camping outside during a company off-site and got hit by tiny meteors, infusing their brains with large amounts of radiation, turning them into super-game-creating heroes. Having been blessed by The Gods, they returned to the studio and created one of the coolest RPGs of all time. Or something like that.
If you enjoyed the prior Divinity titles (as I did), keep in mind this is a complete departure mechanically. The others (more Diablo-esque) were fun in their own right. This one goes down the "Pillars of Eternity" path, giving people who've been looking for a modern Baldur's Gate experience something to spend untold, gleeful hours playing. Pillars, I'm calling you out - you have a very high bar to traverse now.
I'm not going to take the time to go into each detail of the mechanics. Suffice it to say, if you are reading this review you may be considering purchasing the game. Do it. You will not be disappointed.

Ultimately I recommend this game, but not without mixed feelings.
First and foremost, I adored Titan Quest.  And if you loved Titan Quest, you'll love Grim Dawn, full stop.  It takes the formula, and it just adds so much more.  I especially appreciate the devotion system, which is a sort of parallel leveling system that comes from exploration and discovering shrines.
That being said, it suffers from some of Titan Quest's problems as well.  It's a grindy game.  It's a slow game at times.  It's the sort of game you mindlessly click through while you have a podcast on in the background.
That aside, I love it.  Seems like the developers went through quite the struggle to make this happen, but I'm glad they did.

I gotta say, this is one of the best games i've ever played, and i've played alot. The free movement is absolutely the best out of any game, to the point that I really hope other developers take notes on what level of character control is possible. The weapons have a natural progression that are all very fun to use, with no one way being overpowered or completely useless. The side missions are unique, atleast to the point that I had no problem doing every single one of them. And most of all, the games challenging. I played through only on hard, and i died, alot. Sometimes its because I turn a corner and there's a god damn exploding guy, other times its because of a fricken zombie gorilla who can take corners way too god damn tight while charging. While I do think that the character leveling could use a bit more tweaking, I still throughly enjoyed the "Survivor, Agility, Power" concept and trees. All and all, if you are looking for a game that can and honestly will show you what a real open world game is capable of, this is it.

+ Top-shelf voice-acting (what little there is, unfortunately)
+ Gorgeous environmental visuals; backdrops have clearly been painstakingly created
+ Spectacular toon-inspired animations; work well in practice, & contrast well with the somber tone of the game
+ Soundtrack is quite moving, & is implemented perfectly
+ Rich in lore; the world map is a great place to read up on different regions and their history
+ The need for balance of supplies outside of battle adds significant planning & depth to the meta game
+ When the caravan is moving, the player is confronted with myriad choices (similar to Oregon Trail), most of which are difficult; one's decisions often have large ripples that deeply affect the course of the narrative
+ Combat system is superb; simple & easy to learn, but rife with nuance that makes for a satisfying experience (& encourages practice & experimentation)
+ Competent & well-delivered narrative; dialogue is uniformly well-written
+ Does well to showcase adult themes & the gravity of difficult decisions
+ The 'War' mechanic is well-handled, & adds another layer of depth & challenge to enemy encounters; choices made here will affect the enemy strength that you encounter, as well as casualties along your entire caravan
+ Balance of morale & willpower, on & off the battlefield, will keep one on one's toes
- Occasional, momentary drops in framerate during caravan marches

The concept of a parkour based game is great, and it's not done often at all, but Mirror's Edge is just a broken mess. The game is incredibly picky about how you interact with things to do parkour tricks with them. Often times I'll do what's basically the exact same jump towards a pole that you can grab only for it to not grab the pole, even though I've done it before. You also get stuck on tons of stuff that looks like simple enviornment objects. Sometimes you can just move backwards to free yourself, sometimes if softlocks the game and requires you to quit to the main menu. The story is incredibly average. The characters are very one-dimentional, and the voice acting's also incredibly average. The music's not bad, though it's mostly atmospheric, and during action sequences it's drowned out by other sound effects and character speech. The graphics could have been really good, and at times are, but are ruined by the over-saturated colors and bloom effects. Every rooftop is pure white and it makes it very difficult to even see what you're looking at, and you spend a lot of time on rooftops. Also, there's no option for windowed mode, or FOV slider, though a mod fixes that.
There's a lot of potential for a great game, and some parts are actually fun, but it generally is just frustrating as you'll often be redoing the same thing trying to get a jump right so you grab onto a pole, or something like that.

Spectacular!! In the same vein as other recent platformers like Limbo and Inside, Little Nightmares is full of atmosphere in it's haunting environments, gross creatures (that you observe going about their oddly mundane daily chores) and masterfully ups the stakes in a well-paced, tightly designed adventure.
The game is brief, but is never frustrating or overstay its welcome, always introducing new elements and scenarios even while keeping the core platforming puzzle solving and hide & seek mechanics stay fairly simple but effective throughout.
The animation and visual design is truly outstanding. The creatures in particular are incredibly well-realized with their unnervingly stiff, awkward but graceful motion that needs to be seen to be believed  (especially an encounter from early on.) The environments are very detailed and tell a subtle story without exposition, with the environments caked in fantaatic shadows and lighting design. Clearly a lot of passion has gone into this title that can be felt in every small, sinister detail.
There are some very memorable standout moments, especially in the late game, that will keep your interest even if you aren't into horror or stealth mechanics. It's a shame this hasn't gotten more exposure, because this is a brilliant little experience from start to finish, and I couldn't recommend it enough!

Quick Review
Pros
- Very pretty 2D style that is a big departure for the team of FarCry 3
- There are an appropriate amount of sidescroller elements and they largely help immerse the player into the different environments of Lemuria
- I enjoyed the tons of chests and secret bosses/areas to discover
- The combat system is fairly simple but required the player to be on their toes throughout a fight
Slag
- I wish the party could expand past 2 active fighters
- The rhyming dialogue eventually grates on the player (and by eventually, I mean pretty quickly)
- It could use a couple more side quests
- The inability to change your  party anywhere but in a battle gets frustrating
- Before I played the game I liked that the main character was from relatively unused location and time period, 1895 Austria, but it ended up not really adding anything.
Verdict
Though the Ghibli-esc art style, Lemurian legend, rhyming dialogue, Austrian stuff, and fairy tale-like setting combine into a somewhat scattered experience, I still very much enjoyed the game and would recommend it to any JRPG fan.

A quirky 2D-artillery game.
Your dude jogs to a spot which is then overrun by nasties.
Your objective is to kill those wierdos by throwing your speer, using mostly angle-mastery as well as some minor special powers managment to fend them off.
Repeat this a couple of times and one of about a dozen levels is over.
Depending on how well your spear chuckery went, you get more or less shekels to spend on unlocking a few extras that function as a form of loadout.
There are boss monsters. And they are surprisingly well-made.
Rare enough, these days.
General game-depth is okay. Perfecting shots and playthrough speed will take some time. There's not a whole of loadouts, however.
You should definitely like the genre or the idea of chasing the perfect shot, over and over.
Graphics are fine, music is passable, if unremarkable.
The difficulty is medium high, so you will die but it's rather fair.
One aspect stinks mightily, however. The last two levels feature obstacles that obstruct your view needlessly. It's hard to determine what's actually going on. A few times this is unintended, like when a disco lightshow tries to give you epilepsy with an Umlaut- bad enough. Later, this is even part of the design - very questionable for a game that relies on perfect angles and split seconds. Strike one, Lichtspeer!
The game passes nontheless,
It's simply uncomplicated fun for the most part without much ballast.

Hello and welcome to my review of Hyperdimension Neptunia Re;Birth1, first off I'm gunna put out that this review may include some spoilers so if you're not into that, then you might wanna look else where.
After completeing this game several times, unlocked every dungeon, collected every Achievement, Top Processor Units, Characters, DLC, Colisium, Best Defense and Offensive Equipment for every Character, All Characters at top level (999) and Defeating the most toughest of battles the game has to offer. I can come to the conclusion that just like it's predecessors it's very, very good. I enjoyed every moment in the game with some minor setbacks that could be overlooked but I will get to that later.
First off the game is basically a remake of the First game released on PS3 known as Hyperdimension Neptunia with some minor changes so that the game can be tied together with the others known as MK2 and Victory. The game takes place in Gamindustri during the console war between Goddess which are personifications of the earlier game consoles.
*CPU Black Heart of Lastation, the Land Of Black Regality = Playstation 3
*CPU White Heart of Lowee, The land of White Serenity  = Wii
*CPU Green Heart of Leanbox, the land of Green Pastures = Xbox 360
*CPU Purple Heart of Planetune, the land of Purple Progress = Based on the canceled Sega system, Sega Neptune
The Goddess come to the conclussion they can't win and the fight comes to a stand still, they believe if they axe someone off somehow that'll end thier problems of power or something? Anyway they choose Neptune and so gang up on her, after defeating her she is exiled from Celestia and thrown to the world below... why they didn't just finish her off and kill her I don't know but we wouldn't have a game if that happened would we? Neptune falls to the world below and and crashes hard, causing her to lose her memory. She is found by Compa a nurse in training who takes her home and patches her wounds in a CG scene. Just like in the previous games they like to give the players abit of fan service now and then just to spice things up and make sure you're still paying attention. With Compa and other friends and CPU's across the land they must unite and say the Tome Of the World called Histoire from the Evil Clutches of the Ex Goddess Arfoire, who plans to copy or even steal the goddess power to become all powerful and destroy Gaminidustry... so your generic evil Villian.
The game used to be for PS Vita so you couldn't play it unless you had a Vita, so I'm overjoyed that they brought over to the PC. I bought it for a discount of £11 and wouldn't work, it crashed over and over again at the startup before the intro movie. Then if you somehow got it to work it would crash after a fight during the results. 5 days later a patch was introduced so it should be fine now, but I got it working from messing with a few startup folders around the 3rd day. This left the game at a very bad first impression.
Now I'm going to spilt stuff up into Catergoreys and give my opinion on them respectively.
Voice
----------
I played the game throughout on English, I like the voice actresses in this game and grown too attached to them. The Japanese are fine and dare say better but I still stuck with English. For the first 30 mins the characters voices are down right bad! They were horrible, they had no emotion, most of the insults and things said were no where as good as the original and felt like they were just reading off a script. After a while you get used to it and even gets better. In this game Compa sounds very cute and even more funnier then before. however I can not Look over CPU Black Hearts voice in this game, I personally Hate It. It's just seems too regal, and snobby and out of place from the normal form Noire and what she used to sound like that I just end up hating it. To think the most popular character in the game would have such a downgrade is abit of a stumble into the lion enclosure but still. If you don't like "Moe" or "adorable" voices then you will hate the voices in this game as they can come off as annoying.
An annoying thing in this game to note is that not every scene has voices, important ones do and then the rest are just text... ok I can dig it, not every bit of dialouge has to be read to me. But sometimes I noticed 3 times that characters will say something else what the text said and sometimes nothing happens at all. for example "...." For english the audio makes a weird sound like it's turning somethign on and off again, but in the japanese voices they actually say something. It sometimes comes off as annoying and even lazy on the english part.
Side Characters/ NPCs
-------------------------
Unlike the previous games where they were just silouutes, in this game not only do they have a voice but also a portraint to give a face to a voice. Which is a nice addition if it wern't for the fact 80% of the voices are borderline had and sound thrown in. The only good ones of the top of my head are Ganache and Yvoire. The portraints are really dazzling but are a nice addition. The big brother and younger brother voices as well as thier character are just BAD! I hope I never see or hear them again, they were annoying, stupid, one sided and not funny in the slightest. They added nothing to the game just irratation for the player and other characters.
Main Characters
----------------------
Every character that is playable is very memerable and all have thier own unique personalty... kinda. In this game pertaining to Neptune she isn't as good as she used to be. Her obsession for pudding in this game is just pathetic to try get a cheap laugh but comes off as uncomfortable and annoying. She may be the Main Character but she doesn't have to be our main character. Noire also seems abit downgraded from previous games, she acts more like a child and trys to come off as more cute in this one but sacrifices her usual Tsundere nature which made her likeable in the first place. That god her voice actress is the same and didn't do away like her transformed form. The awesome part about this game is that all the Human Characters are based on certain games and companys involved.
*IF = Idea Factory
*Compa = Compile Heart
*Tekken = ....Tekken
*CyberConnect2 = Take a guess
ect, ect
It's nice little addition to the game which I like.
The only issue I have in this game is where's Red and Cave? They were in the previous game but not this one? I beleive they'll be in Re;Birth2 but still seems odd.
A nice addition and also a connection to the next game is that you have the chance at the end of the game to get the CPU Candidates.
*Uni = PSP
*Nepgear = another cancelled device.
*Rom & Ram = based on the blue and pink Nintendo DS
Gameplay
------------
Most of the stages, music and the actual fighting system is taken from Victory, but then again if it's not broken don't change it and Victory was perfect. MK2 was horrible but Victory brought it make and made it so much better. Basically you attack an enemy with either Rush attacks that build EXE to use finishing moves that do a ton of damage, Power which is your main damage dealer and Break which as it says, it breaks enemies guard so you can inflict even more damage. *Genre: aRPG, hack & slash
*Avg length: ~25 hours (1 playthrough on normal)
*Developer: Crate Entertainment
*Publisher: Crate Entertainment
*Release date: February 25th 2016
*Platform: pc
+ Indepth (but not overly complex) character building
+ Ability to (partially) respec
+ Exploration is greatly rewarded
+ 3 difficulties to play through
+ Faction system
+ Appropriate atmosphere
+ Multiplayer available
+ Multiple little features to make life easier
+ Insanely replayable
+ Aesthetically, the game is gorgeous, but
- Graphics seem a little outdated in certain places
- The soundtrack is good, however repetitive at times
It is almost a miracle. After about 6 years of development, Crate Entertainment's
has finally been released. A game that had been in early access on Steam for so long due to the developers experiencing some personal difficulties. Not only that, they also greatly expanded on the game's original content due to fantastic support by fans along the way. The result is a superb aRPG that is currently among the very best. Having owned and closely followed the game for about 2 years, looking at the (finally) complete game is a pure joy. Hold on tight aRPG lovers, because you're in for a most wonderful ride with this one.
Enter Cairn, a dark and mysterious world that was once a great empire, but now on the brink of extinction. At fault are the overly curious arcanists who brought Aetherials into their world. These spiritual beings seek to use humans as hosts and consequently turn them into powerful, yet abhorrent creatures. If that wasn't already enough, survivors also have to battle the Chthonians: they have the malicious intent of offering as much blood as they can to their almighty god. You, the player, awaken at the worst time possible: a grim dawn. For a little while, you yourself were possessed by an aetherial and thus have no memory of your former life. This possession almost cost you your life. However, those aetherial remains dwelling inside your body seem to grant you odd, yet useful powers ...
is an aRPG like there are quite a few others in the genre:
While each game differs and has its uniqueness, they all have the same core gameplay: run around, kill monsters, find loot. And all of that in an isometric perspective. Even though a bit repetitive in gameplay (which is no problem if you're a fan of the genre), they have great replay value, mostly due to their theorycrafting: how to create and finetune the 'perfect' build(s). In trying to do so comes a lot of experimentation and farming, which can take quite long.
Unlike certain other aRPG's,
does not force you into a specific class. Mages don't necessarily have to wield wands and warriors don't have to wear heavy armour and shields. Every character has access to all gear. However, you are required to invest in specific attributes in order to wear different equipment. Another feature that is quite welcome, which was present in
also, is how the game lets you combine any of the 6 available masteries to create your personalized class (= 2 masteries combined). A first mastery can be chosen at level 2 and the second at level 10. There are so many skills that one can choose to build around, that even within the same mastery, there is a lot of room for variety. This allows for an insane amount of experimentation and theorycrafting, which is sometimes even more fun than actually playing the game!
One day, Crate decided that character customization wasn't deep enough already, so they released the devotion system. What is this system exactly? It is basically another (yet smaller) layer of customization where players have a total of 50 points to invest in certain passives (e.g. +10% piercing dmg, +20% elemental resistances etc) or actives that enhance your main skills. Those actives can be bound to certain skills and will proc under various circumstances (e.g. 100% to occur when critically hitting). Devotion points can be acquired by restoring old shrines that are spread throughout the whole world and between the 3 difficulties (normal -> elite -> ultimate).
Seeing the amount of customization, being able to (partially) respec is a relief. Reallocating is done by visiting the spirit guide in one of the major cities and can be done at any given time, granted you have the currency for it. It starts out pretty cheap, but can get extremely expensive for those who experiment endlessly. Both skill and devotion points can be reallocated; mastery and attribute points can not. This allows for decent experimentation, but also reminds you to choose carefully when needed.
Cairn is a place full of mystery and secrets and is not afraid to reward players who feel like exploring everything. Exploration is rewarded by various things: one-time chests containing extra rare loot, hidden devotion shrines and notes. More loot is always good to have (this is an aRPG after all), devotion shrines keep your character's customization up to date and lore notes inform you of the story - which was better than expected - of Cairn.
Besides the deep character customization and satisfying exploration, Grim Dawn offers other features that may interest you. The first thing that comes to mind is the 'fast travel' system. Your character can use rift portals anywhere, anytime (except in certain challenging rogue-like dungeons), which sets the game at a good pace. Don't worry about picking everything up, as you can sell it right away by teleporting back and forth. Another feature that is a nice 'extra' is the faction system: by killing certain enemies and completing certain quests, you gain reputation. This reputation allows you to buy certain goods and complete certain objectives. A last feature that is definitely more than welcome is the ability to play with up to 3 other people. There are no dedicated servers though, since the game is more single player focused. But the fact that it is there, is what counts.
Like many other aRPG's, actions are mostly executed via the mouse: killing enemies, opening doors, speaking to npc's ... everything's done with the mouse, with the exception of using your skills. They are activated by pressing the corresponding keys. All keys are rebindable if desired.
Graphically, the game seemed a little outdated in certain places, however, it is not too bothersome. Aesthetically on the other hand, the game is very well made and really brings that atmosphere of eeriness and desperation to life. Most animations are ok.
The soundtrack was enjoyable to listen to for the first x amount of hours and certainly added to the atmosphere. However, certain tracks get replayed over and over again in way too many areas. A little bit more variation certainly wouldn't harm the game. Tracks that are most excellent are the boss tracks. They sound exciting and make the fights more epic.
is one of the finest aRPG's I have played in the last couple of years - if not my favourite of all time.

can be overly complex. This game brings the best of two worlds together: being indepth enough without being overly complex. Therefore it is recommended to all aRPG lovers for 100%, but even regular rpg/hack & slash fans might enjoy this one, if just for 1 playthrough.

I've spent countless hours on a variety of RPGs over the years so I figured I'd give this one a try but I sadly regret doing so...
I spent 20 hours trying to like this game, but I just can't get into it.
The Banner Saga is a rather unique square grid turn based RPG with good music and sound effects (though lacking a volume slider for some reason), good controls, and it features a very unique art style.
That's all that's good in my opinion.
This game offers you very little control, as you move along automatically on a linear path, stopping here and there as the story takes you from places of interest and battles. You are constantly asked to answer multiple choice questions that affect various events and cause battles to trigger. When you get in a battle you move a single character, your opponent moves a single character, and this process continues until the end.
You will generally be fighting the same enemies and slightly different versions of them throughout at least the first 20 hours of the game.
Personally, When I play an RPG I desire the ability to explore the world but this game does not allow this.
I don't find it fun to have the gameplay consist of watching a parade move from location to location, answering various multiple choice questions, and fighting robot enemies I've seen a hundred times.
The battle system is another problem. Strength and HP are the same basically, and breaking defense before HP results in better hits on HP. All the characters get maybe a single special move which is kind of lacking in my opinion. There are no magic spells or trinkets to use, it's just simple attack and a single special. You can't even defend.
Another problem is that you can't grind in this game. There are no opportunities (in the first 20 hours anyway), to replay battles or trigger random battles to help build your team. The characters are all rather weak (especially the humans), so an opportunity to grind would be nice.
The currency in this world is called renown, and it's used to rank up your characters (levelling), buy things in the market (!?), and it's also used to buy supplies for your journey. It's overused for everything and it's easy to run out of it as you start collecting a lot of party members and market items.Yes that's another problem, for some reason we have resource management here to feed all those people in your parade. This is not fun.
That's a lot of negatives, this game is really underwhelming.
There are many better RPGs out there, (let me suggest some great titles such as Grandia 2, the Final Fantasy Series, Shining Force Series, Phantasy Star Series)  and while this game has some unique features and some very nice graphics, the gameplay is simply not fun.
Skip this one.

I'll admit that I originally started The Banner Saga months ago, lost interest, and then picked it up again later and finished it in a day. The first bit of the game throws a lot of names and lore at the player very quickly without much contextualization. Also, even though I've played everything from Jagged Alliance to the new XCOM and Shadowrun - and the battle system of this game is in those traditions - I felt very overwhelmed initially. Even though the system is not very deep at all. I think it was because the "tutorial" made it seem like a deeper system than it really was.
Once the story got going, though....Even though there are only two endings there are several side stories and vignettes that build upon the world and your interactions with it that you will only encounter if you play the game in a certain way. I've played a lot of games where "your choices matter" but it was always really obvious when you were making a choice, and, once you become used to that style of game what the "good character" choice is. This is quite an interesting and enjoyable game. It's set in a world ,heavily influenced by Norse mythology, which is populated by humans, a race of horned giants called Varl, and a race called the Dredge who are the games villains and are invading the human and varl lands. The gameplay is a mix of boardgame style tactical combat and sequences where your characters are travelling to escape the dredge where managing supplies and pop up events where you have to make choices, choices which can have a real impact like you characters getting killed.
Good points:
- this game is beautifully animated as well as featuring a great soundtrack
-the story is quite good and features a large number of characters most of which can join your group though they always arent well fleshed out or feature heavily in the game
- I liked the way the choices you make can have an impact. For example i made a decision to let one character join my group only for him to turn on my hours later killing one of my other characters in the process. Other choices you make can gain or lose you supplies or gain you new characters for your group for example and they fit quite well into the games story.
Bad points:
- while the combat isnt too bad its not very deep either. You can choose two types of basic attack ,one to wear down an opponents armour or an attack that wears down health. You normally need to wear down armour first to do more damage to health and most battles just revolve around this with not a lot of variation.
Overall this is a pretty great game that will appeal to people who like a game with a good story and decisions that have a real impact of its outcome.

Dying Light is a first person action game that involves parkour, melee combat, some guns, and other fun features. The game takes place in a developing country that is hit with a zombie outbreak. You (Kyle Crane) are sent in to get a file for the company you work for but things kinda go downhill the second you get in.
Pros
-Interesting Story
-Lots to do
-Tons of weapon customization
-Very large map
-Tons to explore
-Lots of sidequests
-Fun and challanging multiplayer
-Parkour!
Cons
-Short main story if you only do that
-Controls take a lot of getting used to
-Parkour in first person doesn't exactly work how you want it to sometimes
-Guns come in about 2/3 the way through, and can only do so much
-Final boss is a quick time event
The start of the game is kinda slow at first. Your parkour is clunkey, your weapons suck, you die quickly, etc. But things pick up the more you run around and chop things up. Your parkour will go faster, you can craft better weapons, and escape from hoards with ease. Just be patient and be willing to explore nearly every nook and cranny for those spare parts.
Parkour in the first person perspective barely works. Problem is you can't see your feet or your hands without looking up or down. Not to mention that when I reached for something above me, I wouldn't grab it unless I looked slightly down or upward. Can't tell you how many times that got me killed. But with a lot of practice you will get the hang of things, and running atop the roof and buildings becomes wicked fun.
The story and dialougue is well down, and at times downright hilarious. There were moments where I had to pause the game because I was laughing at what Crane had said. The story can be done rather quickly if it is all you focus on. I did it with a mix of sidequests and finished it in around 15 hours. If I did the story alone, I think I could do it in around 7 hours. Mix it up and do sidequests to make it more fun and last longer.
The controls take a lot of getting used to. I used a controller for most of the game, despite it being in first person. You can go and change them to how you like, but I stuck with the default settings. Jump was on R1. That took a LONG time to get used to. My hands also got tired after a while because I was pressing a lot of things to do parkour and stay alive at the same time.
Overall, the game is awesome and worth full price ONLY if you plan to do everything there is to offer in the game. I got it on sale for $20 during the Holiday sale, and know it was completely worth it.
