Child of Light is a very artistic roleplaying adventure game that is unique in a lot of ways.  With impressive hand-drawn graphics in the background, unique looking characters and monsters, and excellent lighting, this game at first impression looks fantastic.  Throw in an interesting storyline written in poetic prose that makes dialogue feel fun and alive, a beautiful soundtrack, and flowing gameplay, and that makes Child of Light more than worth getting.
As far as gameplay goes, you control Aurora, the main character--a female protagonist--and journey through the lands of Lemuria, running, jumping, and flying.  Along the way, you find interesting and unique NPCs that will join your party, and more importantly, a firefly named Igniculus, that becomes a major part of the player's mouse controls.  With Igniculus, you slow down monsters, pick up items out of reach, heal your characters, and perform many other functions in and out of combat.
The combat system is very different, with a feel of turn-based roleplaying games with a time-delay system.  Timing attacks, usage of items, using Igniculus to slow down monsters, and swapping party members in and out, is all a vital part of succeeding in this somewhat difficult game.  Once fights are completed, you are rewarded with experience and items, where you can build each of your characters through certain skill paths.
Child of Light isn't without its flaws, however.  The fact that you can only use two party members at a time, without exchanging during combat, leaves the player unable to use all of his or her characters.  I found myself throughout the entire game using mainly only Aurora (being the main character) and one other character, because he just simply felt better than the others.  On top of that, while the combat system is well-designed, it can lead to very time-consuming battles, where it feels like you simply get nowhere, as you are constantly pressured, overwhelmed, and interrupted, which moves characters back down the timeline to perform an attack.  Also, because of this, most items appear to be pretty worthless, because attacks are so important to deliver successfully and quickly; there simply isn't enough time to use most items in the game.
All in all, Child of Light is a very beautiful, inspiring, well-crafted game with a lot of added humor and fun for all ages.  I can't rate this as high as other reviews because the downsides really killed the game for me after a while, but I do recommend this game nontheless.  I rate it a 7.3 out of 10.

I haven't even beat this game yet and it's one of the best games I've ever had the chance of playing. Bought it for 5.99 during the Winter Sale and can honestly say, one of the best purchases I've ever made.
Seriously. Read on for more.
Gameplay wise, you can fly around and do pretty much everything. It kind of reminds  me of Dust -An Elysian Tail in how the map works, but combat is turn based instead of hack and slash. Speaking of gameplay-  i LOVE LOVE LOVE LOVE how the characters interact with each other! Everyone speaks in a rhyming meter and its PERFECT for the type of game they were going for! The story is rich and the characters are amazing.
Speaking of the combat system - it's something I havent seen in a while. Basically you have a "Wait" period, then a "cast" period. If you get hit while you're casting an attack, then you get interrupted and set back on the wait period. It's really quite interesting - you have to time your attacks properly so that you can intterupt your enemies.
You get loads of party members (as I'm writing this, I have had a total of 5 different members, excluding Aurora). You can only have one person helping you per battle, but you can switch them out mid battle without any penalty. Every party member is slightly different - you have a healer/jester character, a mage, an archer, a swordsman, and a tank (as far as I've seen). I will update this further if I get more party members. You also get a firefly, Igniculus, who talks to you and gives you advice, as well as being usable to light up dark passages and interact with puzzles throughout the world map. In addition he is crucial for battles, where you can shine light on your enemies and slow their speed in a battle, which is crucial to winning.
The augment system with the Oculi crystals is pretty simple to get the hang of. It actually reminds me a lot of the Rune Combiner in League of Legends. You have your basic crystals, ruby, sapphire, and emerald, and you can make combinations to create different gems and upgrade existing ones (ex. 3x rough ruby goes into tumbled ruby, 3x tumbled --> faceted, 3x faceted --> brilliant.) Each oculi gives a unique stat bonus depending on whether you put it on attack, defense, or time.
Overall I give this game a 10/10. Buy this game!

It is almost a miracle. After about 6 years of development, Crate Entertainment's
has finally been released. A game that had been in early access on Steam for so long due to the developers experiencing some personal difficulties. Not only that, they also greatly expanded on the game's original content due to fantastic support by fans along the way. The result is a superb aRPG that is currently among the very best. Having owned and closely followed the game for about 2 years, looking at the (finally) complete game is a pure joy. Hold on tight aRPG lovers, because you're in for a most wonderful ride with this one.
Enter Cairn, a dark and mysterious world that was once a great empire, but now on the brink of extinction. At fault are the overly curious arcanists who brought Aetherials into their world. These spiritual beings seek to use humans as hosts and consequently turn them into powerful, yet abhorrent creatures. If that wasn't already enough, survivors also have to battle the Chthonians: they have the malicious intent of offering as much blood as they can to their almighty god. You, the player, awaken at the worst time possible: a grim dawn. For a little while, you yourself were possessed by an aetherial and thus have no memory of your former life. This possession almost cost you your life. However, those aetherial remains dwelling inside your body seem to grant you odd, yet useful powers ...
is an aRPG like there are quite a few others in the genre:
While each game differs and has its uniqueness, they all have the same core gameplay: run around, kill monsters, find loot. And all of that in an isometric perspective. Even though a bit repetitive in gameplay (which is no problem if you're a fan of the genre), they have great replay value, mostly due to their theorycrafting: how to create and finetune the 'perfect' build(s). In trying to do so comes a lot of experimentation and farming, which can take quite long.
Unlike certain other aRPG's,
does not force you into a specific class. Mages don't necessarily have to wield wands and warriors don't have to wear heavy armour and shields. Every character has access to all gear. However, you are required to invest in specific attributes in order to wear different equipment. Another feature that is quite welcome, which was present in
also, is how the game lets you combine any of the 6 available masteries to create your personalized class (= 2 masteries combined). A first mastery can be chosen at level 2 and the second at level 10. There are so many skills that one can choose to build around, that even within the same mastery, there is a lot of room for variety. This allows for an insane amount of experimentation and theorycrafting, which is sometimes even more fun than actually playing the game!
One day, Crate decided that character customization wasn't deep enough already, so they released the devotion system. What is this system exactly? It is basically another (yet smaller) layer of customization where players have a total of 50 points to invest in certain passives (e.g. +10% piercing dmg, +20% elemental resistances etc) or actives that enhance your main skills. Those actives can be bound to certain skills and will proc under various circumstances (e.g. 100% to occur when critically hitting). Devotion points can be acquired by restoring old shrines that are spread throughout the whole world and between the 3 difficulties (normal -> elite -> ultimate).
Seeing the amount of customization, being able to (partially) respec is a relief. Reallocating is done by visiting the spirit guide in one of the major cities and can be done at any given time, granted you have the currency for it. It starts out pretty cheap, but can get extremely expensive for those who experiment endlessly. Both skill and devotion points can be reallocated; mastery and attribute points can not. This allows for decent experimentation, but also reminds you to choose carefully when needed.
Cairn is a place full of mystery and secrets and is not afraid to reward players who feel like exploring everything. Exploration is rewarded by various things: one-time chests containing extra rare loot, hidden devotion shrines and notes. More loot is always good to have (this is an aRPG after all), devotion shrines keep your character's customization up to date and lore notes inform you of the story - which was better than expected - of Cairn.
Besides the deep character customization and satisfying exploration, Grim Dawn offers other features that may interest you. The first thing that comes to mind is the 'fast travel' system. Your character can use rift portals anywhere, anytime (except in certain challenging rogue-like dungeons), which sets the game at a good pace. Don't worry about picking everything up, as you can sell it right away by teleporting back and forth. Another feature that is a nice 'extra' is the faction system: by killing certain enemies and completing certain quests, you gain reputation. This reputation allows you to buy certain goods and complete certain objectives. A last feature that is definitely more than welcome is the ability to play with up to 3 other people. There are no dedicated servers though, since the game is more single player focused. But the fact that it is there, is what counts.
Like many other aRPG's, actions are mostly executed via the mouse: killing enemies, opening doors, speaking to npc's ... everything's done with the mouse, with the exception of using your skills. They are activated by pressing the corresponding keys. All keys are rebindable if desired.
Graphically, the game seemed a little outdated in certain places, however, it is not too bothersome. Aesthetically on the other hand, the game is very well made and really brings that atmosphere of eeriness and desperation to life. Most animations are ok.
The soundtrack was enjoyable to listen to for the first x amount of hours and certainly added to the atmosphere. However, certain tracks get replayed over and over again in way too many areas. A little bit more variation certainly wouldn't harm the game. Tracks that are most excellent are the boss tracks. They sound exciting and make the fights more epic.

I've tried Diablo 3, Torchlight 2 and some others and all of them don't keep me interested unlike Grim Dawn. Usually I play them for a few hours then get bored however I've played Grim Dawn for 44 hours and have owned it for about a week.
It has good graphics with a
art-style with most dungeons being really dark.
The controls are good with bindable keys. You can also change your skills on the hotbar (mouse, 1 to 8 and then 9 & 0).
The character progression in the game in terms of points is skill points (your points for active skills or passives for your class (also this game lets you choose 2 classes for 1 character) and you gain 3 of these points every time you level up.
There are attribute points that you get from leveling up and you get 1 per time to go into either of the 3 primary stats; Physique, cunning or spirit.
The last is devotion points which you get from finding
in the world. To get the point you either need a certain item, activate it's trap (basically kill a few enemies and maybe a hero) or just get it anyway. These points go into the devotion tab that grants mostly small passives with some bigger ones and active skills.
In the world you find rift-gates which allow you to teleport there at any time, which are usually found in / near the cities or in some dungeons.
You've got the loot system that has an armour stat, and with how common they are (common, magic, legendary, epic, ect) which give extra and greater stats.
The game allows you to do the quests in basically any order you want and you're not required to do them at all, you could just find loot and kill things if you wanted to.
This game features multiplayer too. It's mostly a single player game but the multiplayer works really well and I play online most of the time I'm on.
Overall I rate Grim Dawn 9/10.
There is also mod support coming out soon and there is at least 1 DLC expansion promised to be added.

First off, I really didn't expect to be writing a negative review for this game when I started playing it.
However, now after reaching chapter 3, I can barely bring myself to play on...
By games with more caracter depth, or all the high rated visual novels I play, but
the game, to me, seems horribly bad designed.
1.) Game mechanics
The game is heavily overloaded with features that actually do nothing.
For example the item search and jump functions, when exploring dungeons
seem to exist only in order to give the buttons that didn't have a function one.
I end up permanently spamming the item search button, since there is no way
to know where a hidden item might be.
There are so many different skills that do absolutely nothing...
Having 10 different combo skills I can assign (only outside of battle mind you),
all doing about the same damage is pretty useles for me...
HDD-Mode, the ability for some of the characters to change into a stronger form.
Since there is practically no disadvantage to changing forms, and it doesn't even cost
a turn to do so, there really is no reason EVER to not change into HDD form,...
other than the animation you don't want to see for the 2000th time.
Also the fights are not really hard, but incredibly repetitious.
If an enemy has 150k HP and I do 1k damage per round, yet the enemy is unable to KO any of my
characters due to the healer always being able to compensate the enemy damage, the fight will
last half an hour with me doing exactly the same actions in an infinity loop until the enemy suddelny starts
using stronger attacks when he's down to 10% hp, KOing all of my characters, and therefore having me repeat
the whole 30min fight just because my tank got critically hit or something like that...
80% Of the items and dungeons are unlocked by collecting items, which means defeating 1000 enemies that can't
actually damage you at all anymore, making the whole process even more repetitious.
The item discription most of the time just tells you how the item is named... which is not really helpfull, since
there is no way to know whether you even want to unlock them.
2.) Story
The story seems horribly inconsistent, with 2/3 of all cutscenes having nothing to do with the story at all.
Yea, I get it, it's super funny if someone can't pronounce someone elses name, please, I long for another
20 scenes where this is made obvious.
3.) Translation
The translation is horrible, half of the time there is stuff in the english text that was never said in the
Japanese version, the other half of the time there are half sentences missing in the translation...
I also don't really undertand why in the english version the term "Goddess" is constantly replaced by "CPU",
which is as far as I remember never mentioned in the Jap. version.
Also a lot of jokes are plainly replaced by totally different jokes, that don't even really fit the situation they're used in.
All in all I think the game is okay for 10$, but certainly not worth 30$.

The game started out fantastically. For about the first half of the game, you can tell the developers really put as much effort as possible into creating their game. At the midway point, however, you can start to see the game fall apart. Quest lines become convoluted and impossible to follow. The writing falls off, and the story becomes one of the most disappointing I've ever experienced in a fantasy game. They couldn't even bother to come up with their own story, instead they forced the stories of Pandora's box and the biblical fall of man to make a baby and give birth to a convoluted, nonsensical ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ child.
The game got difficult toward the end, but for the wrong reasons. The puzzles didn't become challenging yet rewarding (a la Portal). Instead, they became difficult because there was absolutely no method to the developer's madness. "Difficult" does not equal "fun" unless it's rewarding, and 90% of all puzzles had nothing to do with critical thinking. Instead, it's pretty much clicking randomly until your journal becomes updated or praying that your character's perception is high enough to spot the stupid little ♥♥♥♥ing switch on the wall because otherwise you'll run around like a chicken with its head cut off for 2 extra hours.
The endgame was laughably disappointing. The final boss, the biggest baddest enemy you'll ever face, has NO DEATH ANIMATION. It literally just disappears from the screen with a poof, and you're greeted with a dialogue-free slideshow to suffice as the game's epilogue. I don't know if it was a lack of budget, or time constraint, but this game was easily the worst ending I've ever experienced, and I say this having suffered through Mass Effect 3.
Long story short, this game, while amazingly fun and promising at first, ends up a complete waste of time. If you just want solid RPG-style combat and fun random little sidequests, then maybe you would like this game. But if you want an immersive storyline containing depth and complexity, and puzzles that actually require critical thinking, you need to look elsewhere.

From a gameplay perspective, Little Nightmares is slightly lacking. The level design of each chapter loosely follows the same pattern: introduction to enemy, stealth, puzzle, difficulty ramp-up, puzzle, final confrontation, and variation comes from the enemy's abilities. This means that at times gameplay is repetitive, but not enough so that you would become bored of it - in fact, the biggest offenders are the 'chase' scenes that occurs at least once per chapter, and these are more often than not the most thrilling moments of the game. I was almost upset that the final boss fight /wasn't/ a chase... The least enjoyable moments are when Six gets hungry.
And that's the only jab I can take at Little Nightmares. I love the character designs, the atmosphere, the soundtrack, and most of all I love the subtle way a story is told with nothing but imagery. Depending on what's in the DLC, Little Nightmares might end up being my favourite game.
Look out for "one more turn" syndrome.

This is a really outstanding combination of survival horror, light puzzling, and side-scrolling adventure platforming, featuring some outstanding gross-out animations and beautiful-looking (in a gloomy and forbidding kind of a way) levels. No shooting or fighting here: you are playing as a kid with only a cigarette lighter and your wits. I say it's light puzzling because I am terrible at puzzles and I managed to get through this with maybe only one hint needed right at the end. If you've played other platformers you'll find it very intuitive: I played on an xb1 controller and rarely had too much difficulty in pulling off the moves needed to progress. It's not a terribly long game and it's extremely linear, but the art is unique and the environments wonderfully creative. Not by coincidence, the people who made this also worked on the Little Big Planet games for the Playstation (which were some of the best reasons to own a PS3) and although this is very different in tone, much of the same approach is in evidence. Highly recommended; when they've finished releasing the DLC for the expansion, I am definitely coming back to this one.

If Tim Burton and Roald Dahl teamed up to remake Inside, I think they'd end up with something pretty close to Little Nightmares. Like Inside, LN is a 2.5D surreal-horror game about a little kid trying to escape from a perverted version of reality and probably dying horribly more than a few times along the way. Also like Inside, it's a game that very much thrives on a sense of surprise, so beyond saying that LN is more reliant on stealth and orders of magnitude more tense, I'm not going to ruin anything about the world. I will say that, although there's nothing in LN that's quite as shocking as parts of Inside, (and you know exactly which parts I'm talking about if you've played it), it's the clear winner for me in terms of moment-to-moment gameplay. It's only three hours long, but there's almost nothing about the design of those three hours that I'd criticize.
Unfortunately, I have to specifically say "design" because there are serious issues with the controls: Jumping, running, and grabbing are all mapped to your right hand on a DS4 and frequently have to be done in quick succession, which makes transitions between any two of them awkward. Some objects are grabbable but not climbable or movable, and the logic behind which is which is often unclear beyond "this one is necessary for progress." Grabbing or throwing objects while near a wall can be frustratingly inconsistent. Most critically, the game sometimes does fancy camera angles without remapping the analog axes while the character is walking along narrow ledges. Predictably, this leads to accidentally walking off said platform and dying.
Still, if you can look past those issues, this is a fantastic game. Highly recommended.

Little Nightmares' art style and beautifully understated soundtrack can't conceal its numerous problems.
- Artsy camera angles, leading to many frustrating accidental deaths
- Broken AI, meaning that no matter how careful you are, enemies will often be able to detect you anyway
- Puzzles so simplistic that one can't help but wonder if they were added to pad the game's length
- Scripted events so contrived that any tension is lost
- A late plot twist which is rendered meaningless by the game's lack of a plot or any significant payoff
- Boring final boss
- Unskippable ending credits (a petty gripe, but I'm feeling particuarly malicious today)
- A short runtime and zero replay value
I know I'm in the minority here, so who knows? Maybe you'll play Little Nightmares and be able to see through its horrid design choices. Although, if you're on the fence about buying this and haven't played Inside yet, you should get Inside instead. It's like this but good.

First off, I really didn't expect to be writing a negative review for this game when I started playing it.
However, now after reaching chapter 3, I can barely bring myself to play on...
By games with more caracter depth, or all the high rated visual novels I play, but
the game, to me, seems horribly bad designed.
1.) Game mechanics
The game is heavily overloaded with features that actually do nothing.
For example the item search and jump functions, when exploring dungeons
seem to exist only in order to give the buttons that didn't have a function one.
I end up permanently spamming the item search button, since there is no way
to know where a hidden item might be.
There are so many different skills that do absolutely nothing...
Having 10 different combo skills I can assign (only outside of battle mind you),
all doing about the same damage is pretty useles for me...
HDD-Mode, the ability for some of the characters to change into a stronger form.
Since there is practically no disadvantage to changing forms, and it doesn't even cost
a turn to do so, there really is no reason EVER to not change into HDD form,...
other than the animation you don't want to see for the 2000th time.
Also the fights are not really hard, but incredibly repetitious.
If an enemy has 150k HP and I do 1k damage per round, yet the enemy is unable to KO any of my
characters due to the healer always being able to compensate the enemy damage, the fight will
last half an hour with me doing exactly the same actions in an infinity loop until the enemy suddelny starts
using stronger attacks when he's down to 10% hp, KOing all of my characters, and therefore having me repeat
the whole 30min fight just because my tank got critically hit or something like that...
80% Of the items and dungeons are unlocked by collecting items, which means defeating 1000 enemies that can't
actually damage you at all anymore, making the whole process even more repetitious.
The item discription most of the time just tells you how the item is named... which is not really helpfull, since
there is no way to know whether you even want to unlock them.
2.) Story
The story seems horribly inconsistent, with 2/3 of all cutscenes having nothing to do with the story at all.
Yea, I get it, it's super funny if someone can't pronounce someone elses name, please, I long for another
20 scenes where this is made obvious.
3.) Translation
The translation is horrible, half of the time there is stuff in the english text that was never said in the
Japanese version, the other half of the time there are half sentences missing in the translation...
I also don't really undertand why in the english version the term "Goddess" is constantly replaced by "CPU",
which is as far as I remember never mentioned in the Jap. version.
Also a lot of jokes are plainly replaced by totally different jokes, that don't even really fit the situation they're used in.
All in all I think the game is okay for 10$, but certainly not worth 30$.

Short Version:
Do you love ARPG's in the 'classical' sense?  Do you giggle in delight while hordes of the undead and other vile creatures explode like piñatas into delightfully colored piles of loot? Do you thrill at the thought of digging through those piles to determine how to pump out an extra 5% of acid damage while maintaining your max resists?  Do you not give a patoot about your position on some ladder populated by automated bots and those fortunate(?) enough to earn a living playing video games?  If you answered yes to the questions above - buy the game now and let your work know you'll be taking the rest of the week off. If your answers were no, this game is not for you.
Or, if you love PvP and find your satisfaction with a game is derived directly from the number of keys needed to be pressed in order to win, you will most likely not enjoy Grim Dawn.
Want Specifics?
Grim Dawn is an Action Role Playing Game in the tradition of Diablo and is created by the team who developed Titan Quest, a game which is also held in high regard in the genre.  During your adventures, you will first select a starting class which determines your overall play style. For example, if you want to be the guy/gal with a huge hammer you may select the Soldier (but, really, you can make *any* build work for normal difficulty).  After you hit level 10 you'll be able to select another class to either compliment or hybridize your build. So, going back to the Soldier with a huge hammer, maybe you'll pick the Demolitionist and add some explosive fire based AOE's to help deal with crowds. Or, maybe you choose the Arcanist and shroud yourself in a protective bubble to help mitigate damage.  The choice is yours and it really helps with replayability.
Your build is equally impacted by your gear selection - and hear GD really shines.  There are multiple tiers of loot, from Vanilla White with no buffs or enhancements to Royal Purple with heaps of added effects that make you the rival of gods.  That same loot will also come with extra skills and buffs.  With so much coming from your gear, you will often times find yourself in the predicament of either upgrading your gear and losing a skill or keeping the skill and suffering from an overall lower armor/resist rating.  Personally I find those choices thrilling, and it really draws me into the game. however, if the thought of having the same weapon for (potentially) a dozen levels or more (due to an amazing skill it grants for example) turns you off, you may have some issues with the game.
After gear comes modifications - you'll find a lot of crafting components in Grim Dawn, and soon your stash is going to resemble your grandmothers medicine cabinet.  A lot of those components can be combined themselves into even stronger iterations.  Those combined components can then be used to craft even more advanced items and those can be used to craft some of the most powerful items in the game. So, if you abhor the idea of hunting for crafting materials - this may not be the game for you.  That said, keeping track of it all really isn't difficult, and within your stash you'll be able to combine everything that is possible to be combined with one button press.
Graphics/aesthetics:
Grim Dawn is a dark and moody game, an environment awash in deep greens and blues for a majority of your play-through. However there are far more vibrantly colored desert areas as well as otherworldly zones bathed in red and crimson.  The overall graphic fidelity is great, but not at the same level as it's triple A cousin Diablo 3.  Likewise the combat animations are not as detailed or complex as D3.  However the combat is visceral in GD with the impacts of swords, clubs and fireballs all feeling weighty and satisfying as the denizens of evil are burnt to a crisp or beaten into gelatinous puddles.
Stability:
Overall the game runs fine, with some mild stuttering as you traverse the game world.  However, a wide spread issue is known regarding the game crashing (and locking the system) when you attempt to exit the game.  Currently, this is the most urgent issue that needs to be addressed with the game and I expect it will be in future patches, but for the moment choose to play the game in full-screened windowed mode to avoid any complications.
Thanks for reading! I hope you choose to experience the wonderful game that Crate has created.

Going into this after Saints Row 3, I had no idea what to expect except for what I had heard from reviews and videos talking about the game. Right off the bat, the writing and over-the-top humor got me laughing more than SR3 ever could, and the intro itself was very well done. At first, the game does go a bit slow after you finish the first third of the opening missions prior to entering Steelport. Things do pick up right after the opening, however, when you get your first set of superpowers. A lot of people complained that the superpowers made things too easy. Personally, the game is still difficult with the powers, though I recommend setting the difficulty to hardcore for some real challenge. The interaction between you and your homies is funny to listen to, as well as their interactions with Zinyak, the alien leader.
The music choice is awesome. What is Love, The Touch and How We Do It are great tracks to listen to while beating up aliens, and it further increases the fun when you can listen to the music on foot (unlike SR3 where you had to be in a vehicle).
There are a few problems with the game, though. A majority of the extra missions get repetitive, almost always being a destruction-based minigame, followed by a clear the area segment and then returning to the ship to claim your reward. Some of the rewards are saitisfying, like the Dubstep Gun, but the missions get too repititive to want to do them all consistantly. The use of powers make vehicles a bit useless unless you're one to cause old-style mayhem ala SR3. Unless you have Superpowered homies, it even makes the use of calling homies useless, as you are a one-man powerhouse from the get-go. It's a shame because you get alot more in homie selection and vehicle customization.
Aside from that, the game has MANY more pros than cons, and I recommend this game in every way possible. If you want to play an open-world superhero game with great humor, this is the game for you

This review will include an XCOM: Enemy Within expansion review.
I'm reposting some of my old reviews because I adopted an easier to read format (and because for some reason I can't edit my old reviews)
XCOM: Enemy Unknown is an isometric turn-based strategy game and a remake, or rather, reimagining of the classic UFO and X-COM games.  The 2012 version aims to bring back the turn-based genre into the mainstream market by introducing the series to modern day graphics, mechanics, and a streamlined and revamped gameplay but still maintaining its tactical stratigic depth.
The player assumes the role of the XCOM Commander who is tasked to lead an elite team of soldiers, scientists and engineers from all across the globe in an effort to thwart a massive alien invasion.  You are Earth's first and last line of defense.
XCOM: Enemy Unknown (BASE GAME)
+ High Replayability with multiple interchanging missions.
+ Very challenging difficulty.
+ Streamlined Gameplay Mechanic: This remake of the series streamlined the gameplay in a way that it is easier to learn but very difficult to master.
+ Good voice acting and cut scenes.
+ Tense and action-packed gameplay.
+ Customization options for your base, air force and soldiers.
+ Good enemy variety which forces players to adapt.
+ Well Optimized for the PC.
XCOM: Enemy Within (EXPANSION)
+ New 'Mechtrooper' Class is fun to play and a great addition to the roster of soldiers.
+ New 'Meld' resource forces players on a more aggressive and fast-paced play style.
+ New 'Soldier Augmentations' using the Meld substance will provide soldiers with alien-like abilities which is fun to use.
+ Localized Voices: The expansion now gives the option to use the localized version of the game and make their soldiers speak in their native tongue (not all countries though).
+ New missions such as Infiltration with Extraction Missions and Base Defense.

First off, let's look at the world of Dying Light; it's small. Everything together, you've got a few square kilometers. And these aren't even really unique kilometers; many of the rooms and buildings are exact copies of each other. There is precious little reason to go exploring except to find random junk for crafting, which I should mention refills when you turn the game off (so you can just loot the same area over and over for randomly-generated items), useless collectibles that are just there, and blueprints for crafting, which are not useless but nowhere near worth systematically searching the whole city. With SO many zombies around, and the game's penchant for spawning new ones, sometimes literally feet away from you, it's certainly not worth going through the floors on the ground or any one a shambler could walk to. Really, the size and openness of the world is not a feature, it's a problem in this game, just a bunch of nothing you are forced to traverse over and over and over again. Don't expect to see many other people or to witness anything interesting; it's just drab and repetitive. And there is a day-night cycle, just to be more annoying. See, at night, a few things happen; first off, the game goes ridiculously dark. I had to literally up the gamma so high that when it was daytime again, everything was a blur. Great. But really, the "nightmares" come out; fast zombies who can climb buildings like spiders, take you out in a single tackle attack, can spit toxic loogies at you, etc. And not just a few, oh no, these things spawn every few hundred feet and will chase you for miles. Only high level players can deal with these things; everyone else has to hit them with the UV flashlight (which drains in a few seconds) and run. These things make night play simply impossible for the most part, so you just never go out at night and have to watch th time and go sleep when it gets late, another irritating delay to the game. And FYI, even the regular zombies get tougher and faster at night, just to add another headache.
Then there's the parkour. And...well, there is only slightly more parkour in this game than one finds in Far Cry 4 or Shadows of Morder, and that's only because of the more packed city-scape map. It's not Mirror's Edge. You mostly just run, jump, and pull yourself up ledges, hardly breaking new ground and most games wouldn't even presume to call that parkour. The only two things that might justify such a title is the ability to jump up and then leap off of the head of an enemy, which is fun, and the grappling hook, when you eventually get it. That might still sound okay, but this is where the game starts gimping itself; in order to force in an RPG-style progression system, you have to unlock these special abilities...and also unlock the ability to run more than 50 feet without getting tired and having to stop and rest. And you do this by leveling up agility, which is mostly only done by, well, running and jumping. For hours and hours. Yippee.
So what about combat? Well, first off, guns are generally out of the question. They exist, but they are not common, nor are they that great, but the real problem is that shooting summons zombies, fast ones who can chase you down. As a method of removing opposition, it leaves something to be desired, outside of a few story missions maybe. Same story for home-made explosives; only useful if you are already in substantial danger and it's worth signaling to enemies to come eat you in order to gain breathing room. You can safely ignore both of these, almost all the time. Predominately, you rely on melee combat. Now, this wouldn't be too bad, but again, the game gimps you; first off, all weapons break down with use, and can only be repaired a limited number of times. With the right skills and high-level weapons, this isn't too bad, but for a long time you are going to be frustrated at how many weapons you have to carry as you chew through them. Early on, it'll take several strikes with any given weapon to kill even the weakes zombies, so taking out a single group will likely deplete your little armory. Tougher enemies like Goons will take entire weapons by themselves. Furthermore, our protagonist, again, gets tired easily, and just a few swings will leave him winded, so you have to use hit-and-run tactics or try to get to a convenient purch where you can kneel down and hopefully whack zombie heads. What could have been a fun first-person hand-and-slash experience become a boring, tedious exercise. Oh, and that's just for zombies, you do have to fight regular people sometimes too, and you'll love this; our hero, who is a soldier, not only gets tired far easier than regular people and somehow manages to wear down a steel pipe by hitting soft flesh, but is also simply incapable of going toe-to-toe with civilians. Civies can block your attacks, or duck under them (since you only ever swing horizonally), and you can't. At all. No such button exists. Your only means of avoiding an incoming attack is to side-step or back-step several feet. This works, but makes it very difficult to try and counter attack, as you are far out of range, but your enemies will easily parry your blows and then cave your skull in. I can't believe the designers though this was a good idea. Oh, lastly, you do also get throwing weapons, like knives, and can even through regular melee weapons if you want, but humans and some zombies will simply dodge these unless it's a sneak attack.
As for the crafting system, yeah, it's pretty disappointing. You can't experiment or modify plans; all you can do is follow blueprints to the letter. Most items you can make completely out of parts are very meh. The weapon upgrades you can do are slightly more useful, but still not amazing. For one thing, like I said, weapons break down, so spending resources for tiny upgrades that you'll just throw away isn't really compelling. For another, though, equipment power increases exponentially in this game; even common end-game weapons are dozens of times as powerful as early ones. So what seems like a strong weapon now will, after gaining just one level, become average, unless it's exceptional. This really disincentivizes even spending the time to try to upgrade things, unless they are of legendary rarity and likely to remain useful for at least a few hours. This is assuming you even have plans for a given weapon; most plans are limited to one or a few specific weapons. Why can't I use a plan on a kukri or machete that's designed for a short or long knife? No idea, but I can't. Considering the plans are basically things like "smack a battery and power cord on a stick", it seems asinine to tell me only one kind of stick will do, but that's how it works. I frequently found that my best weapons were only craftable with the more generic upgrades that give smaller bonuses.
I could continue, but I think the point is made; the game isn't really fun from any angle. It's not a shooter, it's not a hack-and-slash, it's not an RPG, it's not a sandbox, and it's certainly not a story-oriented experience. The protagonist is dull and lifeless, and the whole world is just repetitive and bland. It seems as though the game was designed to be more of an action game, but then they decided to make it an RPG and so nerfed your hero six ways from Sunday so you'd have something to unlock. The most fun I had with this game was after I used a trainer to max out my levels and turn off weapon durability, because then I could go to town on zombie heads. But that got boring quickly. Just, don't bother with this game; absolutely nothing about it is unique, memorable, or engaging, it's all mediocre at best.

I started the Killing Floor franchise with Killing Floor 1. I stumbled upon the game through one of my best friends. At first, I wasn’t impressed at all. Another zombie horde shooter? I wasn’t a fan of Left 4 Dead, this one doesn’t look any different. Boy was I wrong. Fast forward to a couple of days later and my friend and I were both up the whole night playing this game co-op. Fast forward a few years later when I built my own PC and my friend gets me Killing Floor 1. So many hours have I sunk into that game. It easily holds some of my best gaming experiences. Now we are in 2017.
Killing Floor 2 officially came out a little more than a year ago. I was following this game like crazy ever since it was announced and released into Early Access. Hearing about some questionable updates and the inclusion of microtransactions in Early Access, I lost a good chunk of hope, but I still wanted to give this game a try. I bought Killing Floor 2 when it officially released out of Early Access and it has been my go to game ever since.
So, what is Killing Floor 2? To put it in simple terms, Killing Floor 2 is a post-apocalyptic co-op survival horror shooter. There is an offline mode where you can play by yourself, but the game truly shines when you play with other people. Up to 6 players must survive increasingly difficult number of waves and in the end, kill the boss. After each wave is when players can stock up on weapons and ammo they bought with money from killing Zeds (the enemies in the game) Everything about this game just shows you have much time and care the developers have put into it. From the good visuals, to the fantastic weapon animations and sounds, Tripwire puts an insane amount of detail in their games.
But who cares about all the small details if the gameplay isn’t good? I can say without hesitation that this is not only one of the most fun games I have ever played, but also one of the most satisfying games I have ever played. Performance has also been great. Numerous number of settings to customize to your playstyle and I have heard that the game scales well in hardware. From the numerous number of maps, enemy varieties, weapons and customization options, this game is packed with dozens of hours of entertainment.
Now not everything is perfect though. Ever since the official release there have been a few changes the community does not agree with regarding gameplay and with how some weapons are not satisfying to use. The microtransactions, although I am not a big fan of them in any game, are completely cosmetic and have been ever since they were first introduced.
So why am I reviewing this game after almost a year? It’s because Tripwire is passionate about the long-term health of all their games. Killing Floor 2 has gotten many updated since it first released, and it has added a ton of new gameplay features and services to keep the players coming back. From the bug fixes and an in-game currency all the way to their fantastic seasonal events, Tripwire listens to the community and I have no doubt that they will update this game, adding in more content for years to come. Oh yeah and all the updates are free. No locked weapons or maps, everyone gets everything. More developers and publishers need to take note.
All in all, Killing Floor 2 has come a long way since the original Killing Floor released back in 2009. From the upgraded graphics, top-notch weapon animations and sound, tight gameplay, great performance and free updates, I believe Killing Floor 2 will only get better and better. I recommend this game for anyone who is looking for a satisfying first-person shooter, a co-op game or for someone (like me) who enjoys the Call of Duty zombie’s mode or Left 4 Dead games and wants something with more depth and customization. Killing Floor 2 as of right now, is the best co-op game I have ever played, and I won’t stop playing anytime soon.

TL:DR
Ultimately this is a game with a ton of potential but falls short on many of its core aspects. The best and greatest part of the game is the sole purpose it gets a thumbs-up, and that is its asthetic value. Wonderous at first and increadibly pretty, but after its inital wonder the game becomes more frusterating then enjoyable.
Visuals:
The visual asthetic of the game is beautiful and is one of the best in recent memory. From the music, the animation (hand-drawn), the backgrounds, and just the overall theme of the game is wonderful. Full marks. It pulls of the Norse/Viking  theme amazingly, which is pretty under represented in games it seems (Not so much anymore. Thanks TV for that I guess.) The world it creates is one I would love to see fleshed out so I can learn more about it. The music is good enough that it is worth listing to on its own outside of the game and it only enriches every aspect of the game. So very good.
However, after the initial awe of the game, these aspects get over-shadowed by what the game lacks. Genuinely compelling gameplay. From the combat, to the player choices, and to the overall story; they all start to fall flat once you learn a bit about the games mechanics and inner working design. It is these bits that are lacking that makes the experience go from one of wonder to one of being more tedious then enjoyable. So I will go through each of these aspects and detail why I think so.
Combat:
The combat is a turn-based, strategic affair that has become all the rage in many games lately; laid out across a field of squares. While the base mechanics are solid in The Banner Saga they are just that. Basic. After the first few battles they quickly all become the same fights, on the same board, using the same tactics. A sludge of tired mechanics over and over with little complexity and even fewer variations. I found that many of the character abilities were irrelevant most of the time and that (very dissapointingly) archers are all but useless.

(Hint: Their range is the same as the enemies movement, making it all but impossible to be able to use them in combat effectively. Even more so due to the next bit.)
Perhaps the most frusterating part of the combat is that the core mechanic of it is very counter-intuitive. This is that all characters and monsters get weaker the lower life they have. What you must learn is that it is more beneficial to leave enemies alive in a very weak state then it is to kill them. (It took me a many frustrated amount of tries to figure this out. Most likly due to this being wrong in almost all other similar tactical games.)
The problem is if you kill enemies right away the stronger enemies get mulitple turns due to the turn order. The mechanic here is that in every battle the turn order always goes one friendly, one enemy, one friendly, one enemy; repeat, repeat. Very simple and basic. If there are fewer enemies left on the board the remaining ones go more often. So if you leave a few strong enemies on the board they go more often and destroy your friendly characters who are weakned by combat.
The last problem with this scenario is that the 1st hit in combat is by far the most important as it will significantly weaken the opponent. So almost all combat is simply jockying for position so you can hit the enemy first. Due to the lack of variation mentioned previously, all battles quickly become repetitious and all so similiar to one another.
Player Choice:
The Banner Saga is advertised as a player-choice driven game and it is, sort of.
Throughout the game the player will be forced to make choices in a variety of different scenarios, usually being able to pick from a handfull of options. The biggest problem here are the consequences of these choices seem almost random, giving the player absolutely no input. These choices can range from small boons, small annoyances, or even permamnent death of a main character. This is a real problem as this can severely cripple your party for the rest of the game (even ending it), and with no input into the decisions, this process is beyond frusterating. GG, start over.
Which leads into the next problem of this design: after multiple restarts you will quickly realize that these choices are not randomly generated during your travels (as the game at first seems), but all of them are hard-coded and linear for when and how they occur during the story. Given the first problem, all this leads to is blindly fumbling through the story trying to find the best "choices" (or more accurately; just trying not to get screwed over by them). Thus, forcing you to replay the same linear story over and over or save scumming to find the proper decisions, which only trial and error can solve. (Or look up guides)
Both of these problems are compounded by the fact that you cannot save the game manually. The game only auto-saves at certain points. Meaning if you do have to reload due to losing a character you spent most of your resources leveling while also losing your best items that they had equipped, you have to replay a large section of the game over.
Lastly, since the choices and options are all set and the story is linear, replay of the game is very limited and not really worth the time it takes to go through again and again from the start. Thus, making guides all the more attractive to use.
Story:
So overall the story pretty good, and for the most part I was drawn in. The game does an admirable job of creating a suspenceful and compelling story. As your resources dwindle you must choose between getting food for followers, leveling them up, or pushing farther in your travels. Seeing your fellow clansmen die of starvation is a pity, and at first adds a real gritty emotional attachment to the story.
The problem here is that once you learn the mechanics of the game, you quickly realize that there is no reason not to have people starve and to only save your resources for leveling your heroes up. The heroes of the game are independant of the other non-warrior tribes people, who for all purposes seem to have no effect on the game other than achievements. Once this mechanic, or lack there-of, is figured out the game becomes less compelling and more tedious as you are simply left with a basic, boring, single resource management game, where the choices you make to gain those resources is largely trial and error as described above.
Final: 60/100
So overall The Banner Saga is a game of almosts. With a bit more time in the cooker and a little more designing it could have been Grade A every way around. Instead, I am left with a game that is so beautiful, yet so very dissapointing. The love that went into it is very apparent, which makes me want to like it even more.
So in my humble opinion I say while it is worth spending the 10ish hours to play it, save your money for a sale and your time for when you just wanna light non-commitment game. I also recommend after your first few tries to look up a guide. Bypass the annoying gameplay and just focus on the story and visuals. I give it 60/100 where 50 is average.  If possbile I would give it more of a side-thumbs then thumbs-up, but that unfortunately is not an option.

The second and much bigger problem are the boss fights. They remove all your powers and make you learn a series of attacks to get through them. This usually ends up cycling between modes of attack, and getting reset aaaaall the way back to the start of the boss if you die. This is INCREDIBLY frustrating as they ramp up the bosses to more and more ridiculous heights, to the stupidity of the DJ fight, where you literally have to launch a spear at the exact right second and angle to get between obstacles... just to not die and have a chance at causing the boss some damage.
Because you don't get your powers you can't use zuper time to bullet time it perfectly. I get why the damaging powers shouldn't be allowed, but other ways to make them achievable would have been good.
Overall I would vote mixed on this if I could, the early game and late game outside the bosses is pretty good

Lichtspeer starts off as a whole lot of fun.  If you're willing to spend an hour, maybe an hour and a half, on it then buy it, play it, move on.  You'll not regret it.
To start you'll be a licht throwing god.  Three, five, seven headhost combos.  You'll be rattling off spears like lightning and feel like the god of thunder.  It's a complete blast and chasing those high scores couldn't have been more fun.
However if you play up to the Zoculus (I forget it's name) then things start turning sour.  The number of you're-dead-if-you-miss situations multiply and the stages get longer.  The gameplay becomes shallow and repetitive and replaying stages becomes a chore.
And the controls are (intentionally?) broken.  You aim with the mouse cursor but the cursor is invisible.  Turning around consitently is a pain because you can't tell at what point the cursor will move over the character and cause them to flip.  It's no longer skill-based hard, it's a random death slog.  I think the same problem exists when throwing spears near the ceiling.  Sometimes aiming is quick (when the cursor is near the character); but sometimes the aim trajectory barely moves at all making the tricky dead-if-you miss shots frustrating beyond words.
By the time I'd gotten to the Executive Golem I wasn't enjoying myself at all.
Which brings me to the problem with all the boss fights.  Your special powers are taken away.  I can't see that they would have made boss fights easy but they would have removed the frustration of one small slip being insta-death.  Those special powers need quite a lot of grinding to get and taking them away when they'd be most needed really twists the knife in your wasted time.
I've also got a couple of small gripes around the character's death.  Either the character's hitbox is bigger than I expected or there is some sort of lag before death.  Many times I've felt I've activated a shield or thrown a spear but nothing happens, time passes, then the player dies.  A slight nuisance compounded by the very lackluste death sequence: generally a wurst zombie standing quietly next to your fallen body as the muzak keeps playing.  Meh.
My biggest issue - and what prompted this review - is Lichtspeer's achievments.  One in particular.  Play for 100 hours.  That's not an achievement, that's just leaving the process running and making me do marketing for free for Lichthund.  If I did this my then not only would Lichtspeer turn up as one of my most played games, it would also intrigue my friends into wondering why I was in-game so much.  Both would be false impressions.
And the time based achievements don't work anway so it would all be for nothing.
Lichtspeer ultimately feels like a flash game that has overstayed it's welcome.  The more I play the more deficient it feels.  Get it on sale or on a mobile device (if the aiming is easier) but be warned it's rage inducing and not in a Dark Souls way.

So, this is now one of the few games I played for a long time and I am still not done with it.
In the beginning this game is quite tough and exciting (because it is quite tough). You think about every step you take, every fight you take, every item you buy and sell and every quest you take. And the good thing about the quests is that you will never find a giant golden question mark hovering over an NPCs head to really make sure you see the quest. If you do not explore or try stuff out, you will not find certain quests. This is very motivating because it drags you into the story. The game does not remind you all the time that it is a game. Unofrtunately, this is also one of the major disadvantages of the game. Sometimes you (almost) miss an interesting quest, because you do not see a tiny button on the wall or because you forget to loot a corpse. Sometimes, especially if you want to get all achievements or just finish all quests, this forces you to look up a walkthrough guide in the internet. Another downside, but this is more personal, is the crafting system. It is easy and intuitive but it also needs you to be motivated to just try it out and put stuff in your inventory unto other stuff in your inventory.
The quests are interesting and very funny. Most of the story is in text and the story, when time passes, gets quite branchy but I never thought I lost the plot (which I do quite often). This is a very important pro aspect of the game.
The characters gain a certain depth because you can play them differently. This is probably even more fun when you play with a friend but even in single player I sometimes chuckle because of the funny dialogues both characters have.
My biggest negative point, however, is the following: I play with two magic characters and until now I haven't found a single proper rare staff or robe. Why is that? That gets me really frustrated because I find good stuff all the time for my ranger and melee, never for the two mages though.
Game is awesome.

Going into this after Saints Row 3, I had no idea what to expect except for what I had heard from reviews and videos talking about the game. Right off the bat, the writing and over-the-top humor got me laughing more than SR3 ever could, and the intro itself was very well done. At first, the game does go a bit slow after you finish the first third of the opening missions prior to entering Steelport. Things do pick up right after the opening, however, when you get your first set of superpowers. A lot of people complained that the superpowers made things too easy. Personally, the game is still difficult with the powers, though I recommend setting the difficulty to hardcore for some real challenge. The interaction between you and your homies is funny to listen to, as well as their interactions with Zinyak, the alien leader.
The music choice is awesome. What is Love, The Touch and How We Do It are great tracks to listen to while beating up aliens, and it further increases the fun when you can listen to the music on foot (unlike SR3 where you had to be in a vehicle).
There are a few problems with the game, though. A majority of the extra missions get repetitive, almost always being a destruction-based minigame, followed by a clear the area segment and then returning to the ship to claim your reward. Some of the rewards are saitisfying, like the Dubstep Gun, but the missions get too repititive to want to do them all consistantly. The use of powers make vehicles a bit useless unless you're one to cause old-style mayhem ala SR3. Unless you have Superpowered homies, it even makes the use of calling homies useless, as you are a one-man powerhouse from the get-go. It's a shame because you get alot more in homie selection and vehicle customization.
Aside from that, the game has MANY more pros than cons, and I recommend this game in every way possible. If you want to play an open-world superhero game with great humor, this is the game for you

Allow me to take a few valuable moments of my time to write my first product review I've ever written for anything ever.
This is the RPG I've been waiting my whole life to play, I just didnt know it.
I'll try to be as factual as possible while describing it. I don't want you to purchase this game because of my enthusiasm for it. I'll write the details, you can decide for yourself if it is something you would enjoy.
CHARACTER CREATION/LEVELING
The game starts with you selecting one of several classic RPG types, fighter, wizard, rogue, etc. The game is nowhere near as constricting in regards to classes as other RPGs though. Your character is set up thusly. You have your attributes: STR, CON, DEX, etc. which inherently reflect your ability to do their respective skills. You are given skill points. Spending these skill points allows you to learn what I know as "feats" under those specific skills. Spending a point in pyromancer unlocks the ability to learn and cast fire spells. Spending a point in man-at-arms gives you the ability to learn bullrushes, etc.  Unlike other games of the genre, there is nothing to inhibit your character from spending points in any category. Your fighter can learn fire spells, and your mage can learn swordplay. That being said, you can have a very specific character who is very good at one or two select things, or have a jack-of-all trades type character who is mediocre but useful in every category. They also allow you to select talents, which do exactly what you are thinking.
COMBAT
Combat is turn based with action points. The battlefield has no hex or grid, certain weapons require base-to-base contact. Battles are won with brain of the player rather than brawn of your characters. The environment is your ally or enemy. Throw a cask of oil on a baddie and then light him up with a fire spell, or throw a candle on him, cast a electricity spell on a puddle rather than an enemy and get every monster in the wet. Rainstorms augment your electric spells, and diminish your fire. The combat system takes the good from BG2 and the older Fallout games, throws in a modern twist and makes something beautiful
GRAPHICS
3d isometric, and stunning. It's a colorful, bright game when it needs to be and sets the mood with darkness to keep you tense when te timing is right. It leaves nothing to be desired.
SOUND
A wide range of music keeps the game moving. Voice acting is limited, but the amount of dialogue they'd have to cover would double the data of the game.
STORYLINE
so far so good. A good balance of "go to x, kill y, get z" quests and quests of a little more substance.
OTHER
you start with two characters. Traps, side quests, treasure opportunities are based on your perception skill, not whether you are a thief, or looking far and wide for every opportunity. Tons to explore.
SUMMARY
D:OS is a back to basics RPG with a modern twist. Players of Fallout and BG, NVN and Icewind Dale, will rejoice in playing what feels like a classic game with so many modern touches.

This review will include an XCOM: Enemy Within expansion review.
I'm reposting some of my old reviews because I adopted an easier to read format (and because for some reason I can't edit my old reviews)
XCOM: Enemy Unknown is an isometric turn-based strategy game and a remake, or rather, reimagining of the classic UFO and X-COM games.  The 2012 version aims to bring back the turn-based genre into the mainstream market by introducing the series to modern day graphics, mechanics, and a streamlined and revamped gameplay but still maintaining its tactical stratigic depth.
The player assumes the role of the XCOM Commander who is tasked to lead an elite team of soldiers, scientists and engineers from all across the globe in an effort to thwart a massive alien invasion.  You are Earth's first and last line of defense.
XCOM: Enemy Unknown (BASE GAME)
+ High Replayability with multiple interchanging missions.
+ Very challenging difficulty.
+ Streamlined Gameplay Mechanic: This remake of the series streamlined the gameplay in a way that it is easier to learn but very difficult to master.
+ Good voice acting and cut scenes.
+ Tense and action-packed gameplay.
+ Customization options for your base, air force and soldiers.
+ Good enemy variety which forces players to adapt.
+ Well Optimized for the PC.
XCOM: Enemy Within (EXPANSION)
+ New 'Mechtrooper' Class is fun to play and a great addition to the roster of soldiers.
+ New 'Meld' resource forces players on a more aggressive and fast-paced play style.
+ New 'Soldier Augmentations' using the Meld substance will provide soldiers with alien-like abilities which is fun to use.
+ Localized Voices: The expansion now gives the option to use the localized version of the game and make their soldiers speak in their native tongue (not all countries though).
+ New missions such as Infiltration with Extraction Missions and Base Defense.
+ XCOM: Long War Mod is available and easy to install to give the game a fresh new life.
- Bugs: Updated, patched plus an expansion, but still having some of the day one bugs lingering around.
- Graphic and Camera glitches.
- No Co-op challenges or missions.
- Not enough special missions.
- Interceptor Jets have limited upgrades and customization (can't even change the name of the pilot).
- Late game is a bit too easy and may become boring when everyone in your team is fully upgraded.
- No mid-battle or mid-mission inventory change.
- Some maps repeat if your campaign drags on too long (ex. If you enable the Second Wave 'Marathon' Option).
GREAT GAME and HIGHLY RECOMMENDED.  X-COM: Enemy Unknown / Within, is an excellent remake with a revamped game mechanic that is easy to learn yet hard to master.  It has updated graphics and visuals that bring the world alive.  The combat is tense and action-packed that keeps you at the edge of your seat. Plus, it has lots of missions that have good variety which provides a very challenging difficulty.  And above all, it provides a very fun experience for both fans of the series and new players alike.
Well worth its full price. I never had the pleasure of playing the original X-COM games and I know that some of the hardcore fans might have been put off by the streamlining of the series.  As for me however, the 2012 remake is a game that delivered one of my best experience on any turn-based strategy game in a long time.

First off, let's look at the world of Dying Light; it's small. Everything together, you've got a few square kilometers. And these aren't even really unique kilometers; many of the rooms and buildings are exact copies of each other. There is precious little reason to go exploring except to find random junk for crafting, which I should mention refills when you turn the game off (so you can just loot the same area over and over for randomly-generated items), useless collectibles that are just there, and blueprints for crafting, which are not useless but nowhere near worth systematically searching the whole city. With SO many zombies around, and the game's penchant for spawning new ones, sometimes literally feet away from you, it's certainly not worth going through the floors on the ground or any one a shambler could walk to. Really, the size and openness of the world is not a feature, it's a problem in this game, just a bunch of nothing you are forced to traverse over and over and over again. Don't expect to see many other people or to witness anything interesting; it's just drab and repetitive. And there is a day-night cycle, just to be more annoying. See, at night, a few things happen; first off, the game goes ridiculously dark. I had to literally up the gamma so high that when it was daytime again, everything was a blur. Great. But really, the "nightmares" come out; fast zombies who can climb buildings like spiders, take you out in a single tackle attack, can spit toxic loogies at you, etc. And not just a few, oh no, these things spawn every few hundred feet and will chase you for miles. Only high level players can deal with these things; everyone else has to hit them with the UV flashlight (which drains in a few seconds) and run. These things make night play simply impossible for the most part, so you just never go out at night and have to watch th time and go sleep when it gets late, another irritating delay to the game. And FYI, even the regular zombies get tougher and faster at night, just to add another headache.
Then there's the parkour. And...well, there is only slightly more parkour in this game than one finds in Far Cry 4 or Shadows of Morder, and that's only because of the more packed city-scape map. It's not Mirror's Edge. You mostly just run, jump, and pull yourself up ledges, hardly breaking new ground and most games wouldn't even presume to call that parkour. The only two things that might justify such a title is the ability to jump up and then leap off of the head of an enemy, which is fun, and the grappling hook, when you eventually get it. That might still sound okay, but this is where the game starts gimping itself; in order to force in an RPG-style progression system, you have to unlock these special abilities...and also unlock the ability to run more than 50 feet without getting tired and having to stop and rest. And you do this by leveling up agility, which is mostly only done by, well, running and jumping. For hours and hours. Yippee.
So what about combat? Well, first off, guns are generally out of the question. They exist, but they are not common, nor are they that great, but the real problem is that shooting summons zombies, fast ones who can chase you down. As a method of removing opposition, it leaves something to be desired, outside of a few story missions maybe. Same story for home-made explosives; only useful if you are already in substantial danger and it's worth signaling to enemies to come eat you in order to gain breathing room. You can safely ignore both of these, almost all the time. Predominately, you rely on melee combat. Now, this wouldn't be too bad, but again, the game gimps you; first off, all weapons break down with use, and can only be repaired a limited number of times. With the right skills and high-level weapons, this isn't too bad, but for a long time you are going to be frustrated at how many weapons you have to carry as you chew through them. Early on, it'll take several strikes with any given weapon to kill even the weakes zombies, so taking out a single group will likely deplete your little armory. Tougher enemies like Goons will take entire weapons by themselves. Furthermore, our protagonist, again, gets tired easily, and just a few swings will leave him winded, so you have to use hit-and-run tactics or try to get to a convenient purch where you can kneel down and hopefully whack zombie heads. What could have been a fun first-person hand-and-slash experience become a boring, tedious exercise. Oh, and that's just for zombies, you do have to fight regular people sometimes too, and you'll love this; our hero, who is a soldier, not only gets tired far easier than regular people and somehow manages to wear down a steel pipe by hitting soft flesh, but is also simply incapable of going toe-to-toe with civilians. Civies can block your attacks, or duck under them (since you only ever swing horizonally), and you can't. At all. No such button exists. Your only means of avoiding an incoming attack is to side-step or back-step several feet. This works, but makes it very difficult to try and counter attack, as you are far out of range, but your enemies will easily parry your blows and then cave your skull in. I can't believe the designers though this was a good idea. Oh, lastly, you do also get throwing weapons, like knives, and can even through regular melee weapons if you want, but humans and some zombies will simply dodge these unless it's a sneak attack.
As for the crafting system, yeah, it's pretty disappointing. You can't experiment or modify plans; all you can do is follow blueprints to the letter. Most items you can make completely out of parts are very meh. The weapon upgrades you can do are slightly more useful, but still not amazing. For one thing, like I said, weapons break down, so spending resources for tiny upgrades that you'll just throw away isn't really compelling. For another, though, equipment power increases exponentially in this game; even common end-game weapons are dozens of times as powerful as early ones. So what seems like a strong weapon now will, after gaining just one level, become average, unless it's exceptional. This really disincentivizes even spending the time to try to upgrade things, unless they are of legendary rarity and likely to remain useful for at least a few hours. This is assuming you even have plans for a given weapon; most plans are limited to one or a few specific weapons. Why can't I use a plan on a kukri or machete that's designed for a short or long knife? No idea, but I can't. Considering the plans are basically things like "smack a battery and power cord on a stick", it seems asinine to tell me only one kind of stick will do, but that's how it works. I frequently found that my best weapons were only craftable with the more generic upgrades that give smaller bonuses.
I could continue, but I think the point is made; the game isn't really fun from any angle. It's not a shooter, it's not a hack-and-slash, it's not an RPG, it's not a sandbox, and it's certainly not a story-oriented experience. The protagonist is dull and lifeless, and the whole world is just repetitive and bland. BBQ Pitmasters is an American reality television series which follows barbecue cooks as they compete for cash and prizes in barbecue cooking competitions.
The series premiered on TLC on December 3, 2009. The eight-episode first season was filmed in a docu-reality format as it followed several competing BBQ teams around the country to various BBQ contests.
Season two premiered on August 12, 2010 at 10 pm EDT featuring a completely new competition game show-based format. Each week, four teams competed against each other. Challenges included common protein and more exotic meat. Weekly winners faced off against each other in the second season finale as they vied for $100,000 and the Kingsford Cup. The judges for the second season were Myron Mixon, Art Smith, and Warren Sapp. Kevin Roberts served as host.
On January 29, 2012, Myron Mixon confirmed on his Facebook account for Jack's Old South that filming for Season 3 would start in March. On April 4, 2012, it was announced that Season 3 would air on Destination America, which is a rebranded version of the Planet Green channel that launched on May 26, 2012.
On May 26, 2014, Destination America debuted a preview of their new TV series named BBQ Pit Wars. The episode first aired in May 31, 2014. This new reality show uses the old docu-reality format of BBQ Pitmasters season 1 (many viewers had voiced their preference for this format on the channel's website), in which Myron Mixon is one of the team competitors rather than a BBQ judge. Along with Stump McDowell of Stump’s BBQ, Moe Cason of Ponderosa BBQ, and Michael Character of Character BBQ, the four teams compete in regional BBQ championships around the nation, for prizes, and bragging rights to be named the master of BBQ.

This has got the be the one of the best RPGs of all time.
I don't mean RPG in the distorted sense of the definition, where anything with stats and levels might qualify as an RPG; this game seamlessly blends true role-playing aspects into fun and meaningful game mechanics. The game allows you to sculpt your character through gameplay and dialogue options, and it's a first time I've ended up thinking about who I want my character to be, rather than what dialogue options I want to choose to maximize my stats.
The game's roleplaying/gameplay mechanic is not shallow like Mass Effect's paragon/renegade system. Is your character bold? well then, you'll get +1 to initiative. Cautious? +1 to sneak then. There are a dozen or so character traits paired up with each other as opposites, with equivalent rewards at each end that make sense in the context of your character's personality and skills.
The way the game handles co-op is brilliant and unique as well. Each of the two main characters have a say in major conversations, and thus allow you and your partner to develop your characters' personalities differently. If there's a story decision that you and your partner disagree on, the game resolves it with a rock-paper-scissors mechanic that gets influenced by your character's charisma. This mechanic also appears when you're trying to influence NPCs as well, but there's additional factors that come into play depending on the context of the situation. (You're probably not going to have much success intimidating a giant ogre, for example).
There's also always multiple ways to solve quests too.  You can pickpocket and steal your way through quests, charm the pants off people, or bash people's heads in. The quests are written in a way that it feels like you're truly exploring; they don't force you to go through a series of predetermined checkpoints. The game doesn't stop you from stumbling onto a quest item in the process of rummaging through a random person's house, before you get guided there by the storyline. (Smelly panties, what?). In general, the game does very little handholding, which is perfect for this genre.
Lastly, the game's writing is excellent. It strikes a good balance between seriousness and humor, and the storyline progresses well from small-town tasks to the expected grandeur, world-changing quests, as you would expect from a properly developed RPG storyline. After all, if you reveal the end-game objective too soon, then it feels like you're spoiling the discovery element of the game. At the same time however, the game does do enough to keep you moving towards a greater goal, something I felt Skyrim could've used as I wandered aimlessly from town to town.

Child of Light is a heartwarming RPG that pulls you into the world of Lemuria through its wonderful artwork and completely completely (yes two completely's) outstanding soundtrack.
It can be slow at times, but this is not a game you want to rush through. This is a game you really want to experience. The watercolor and wonderful tone of art complements the beautiful sound track playing in the background. Be it the ambient piano playing in the background while exploring the 2D world of Lemuria, or the intense choir belting it out during boss fights, you'll never be left without feeling immersed in the game. The combat system may seem a little odd and hard to grasp at first, but it soons starts making sense and is quite interesting to experiment with with the multiple characters you can play with.
Overall, if you just want something relaxing and beautiful to play, you will definitely not want to pass up on this game.
