XCOM: Enemy Unknown, the fast paced strategy game about protecting the Earth from a full blown alien invasion.
XCOM: Enemy Unknown has quickly become a favorite of mine, and I find myself revisiting it every few months. Here's why:
As an impatient fan of strategy games, XCOM has the only turn based combat I would describe as 'gripping' and 'exciting'. Watching your soldiers fight it out in mini cutscenes where the timing is fast paced makes the game feel like an action movie makes for a very engaging strategy game. I can sit and play without getting bogged down in numbers, tedious bulk unit movement, grand strategies, or overly complex mechanics - but it still feels like I've got hard choices, clear tradeoffs, and new strategies to learn.
You can fail, without losing and having to restart. In most games, you've got only yourself. If you die, that's it. In XCOM you control a couple of small teams. I love the risk and attachment you get to your soldiers, each of whom may die forever from but a single mistake or really unlucky shot. You can lose a good soldier, but still win a key battle. You can even fail a mission, with 6 of your best soldiers who you have had for the last 4 hours - all die - and still beat the game without needing to reload. If you like to live with your mistakes, play on Ironman mode, which prevents any save-scumming.
XCOM tells you a story. Most strategy games have a story you will follow, with you mostly watching it play out, and having to win all the battles for the characters. The best strategy games, like XCOM, make you feel like you're running the show. XCOM walks you through the stages of a full blown alien invasion of Earth, and you play the leader of the clandestine military organization tasked with protecting our pale blue dot. Between the musings of your advisors, the discoveries and reports they make to you, and the insights into your own soldiers' operations as you push on towards victory or defeat - you play out the story, one hard fought victory at a time. Its fantastic and much needed fluff for a successor to the old Microprose XCOM.
Lastly, XCOM makes you tell stories. Everyone I've talked to who has played this game has a couple stories. Its not about the crunch, or min-maxing to win - everyone has a story about their team, who did some crazy thing and won the day, or whom died tragically in the line of duty. You get attached to all the random soldiers as they grow, taking on nicknames and new skills. They seem to take on a personality all their own with you attributing the random chance of the game to their own ability. I hear stories about that sniper who always hits his mark, no matter the odds, or the heavy weapons girl who just refuses to die. Sometimes its about how the old veteran blew himself and a horrible alien to smithereens to save the team. Whatever the story, it is amazing to hear all the different things that can and have happened throught a dozen different playthroughs.

The Banna saga is a beautiful Stylized game that takes turn based mechanics from other influential games and puts its own unique spin on them.
Visuals/Graphics
The Style of graphics that this game uses are very beautiful with cut scenes that really showcase their full potential and gameplay that integrates them nicely. The style of these graphics (Coupled with the gameplay) should make this game easy to run on most PCs whilst still being quite amazing.
Sound/Atmosphere
The music that strikes up sometimes when the wagon is trundling across the countryside is beautiful with a nordic feel to it that adds immensly to the games atmosphere. The gameplay sounds are also very sharp which complements the combat.
Gameplay
I enjoyed the turnbased gameplay in the Banner Saga as it is an interesting take on turnbased combat but i also felt that more could have been added to it because it can get repetitive and easy to master quite quickly (I am going to do a Hard difficulty walkthrough and see how this changes things). The parts of the game that revolve around the characters which includes levelling up abilities and buying items is interesting and gives the game somewhat more longevity but it would also benefit by being fleshed out further.
Story
The Story in this game is amazing with decisions actually changing some parts of the game such as who lives or dies and even the ending quiet drastically. This is exciting as in your first playthrough you come to learn that most characters could be killed and this lends the story some intrigue. This mechanic can also be seen as annoying as you can spend time levelling characters up and investing resources into them only to have them killed suddenly and this has been an issue for many people playing the game.
My time in The Banner Saga was enjoyable and i felt engrossed in the story and character development ! This game costs 20USD as of now and i would not reccommend picking this game up unless it is on sale as it is relatively short (My own playthrough was just over 7 hours). I can reccomend this game as a solid title that will be enjoyed by people interested in turn based games or strong story driven games.

Fans of the "tactics" genre will love this game, which is set in a world inspired by Norse myth. You're sucked in immediately by the gorgeous art and design. Then you stay for the intricate combat and for the Oregon Trail-style survival game between fights. Make no mistake about the "survival" part: all games are hardcore mode (no rolling back to old saves, except at the very end of the game), bad things happen a lot, and story decisions usually have to be made on the spot, with no option to go back or put them off till later. That said, this adds a compelling immersion and gravity to the gameplay, which you really don't find in a lot of RPGs. (If minmaxing is your idea of "role-playing," you won't like this game.) Another interesting feature is that no matter what you choose, the game constantly progresses forward -- there is no way to "lose" the game, there are just different consequences.
This is not a beginner's game (unless the beginner has thick skin) -- the difficulty curve is steep, and the game doesn't give you a lot in the way of tutorials or handholding. It's also a little on the short side, which may be a pro or a con depending on whether you like replays.

Beat Hazard is a fun twin stick shooter where you select a track from your music library as your level selection.  While playing, you'll hear the track you selected and the enemy waves will be generated based on what you're hearing.  It happens in such a way that a given track will always play the same, allowing you to learn and get better at a specific track.
The graphics are great, and the gamepad controls are perfect.  If you don't have a gamepad, you can attempt to make due with mouse and keyboard controls.
Beat Hazard is also the only game I'm aware of that has in-game rewards for crafting its Steam badge.  You unlock a ship skin with the level 1 badge, the level 5 badge, and the foil badge.  These ship skins are purely aesthetic changes, though the width of the firing pattern does vary slightly between them.
DLC:
Beat Hazard Ultra completely transforms the game and makes it better in every way, adding more enemies, more bosses, and a perk system, as well as making enemy waves far less predictable.  Highly recommended.
iTunes and m4a support is only necessary if you have music in these formats that you want to play.  Otherwise, you can ignore this DLC entirely.
Shadow Operations Unit adds extra ships to the game with different stats and their own separate leaderboards, and Steam Workshop support for creating and sharing your own ships.  Each ship also has a set of missions (read: challenges) to complete.  Highly recommended.

I've got a very mixed feeling about Mirror's Edge. On the side of the positives you've got the simple fun of running and jumping across buildings and the beautiful visuals, on the other side you've got several annoyances that constantly break the flow of gameplay and generally just left me confused.
First the positives: The most obvious strength of Mirror's Edge is the gorgeous depiction of its near-future dystopian cityscape. The combination of bright, solid colors together with pure white gives everything a slightly futuristic, sparkling clean feel while also making it easier to navigate the levels by removing unnecessary visual clutter. Since each area has its own color (in addition to the ever-present white), you can see the progress you're making in the levels and the game in general by just observing the changing colors around you, which I feel is a very cool thing. There was also never an area that felt out of place, everything seemed distinctive through its layout and coloring, but also obviously familiar and connected. The textures aren't great, but since most surfaces are only seen in passing or from afar, the concept still works very well and overall I have nothing bad to say about the graphics.
The running and jumping are at the best moments really fun and engaging, at the worst moments frustrating. Most of the time though the simple controls do their job fine and after a very short learning phase you'll be chaining runs, jumps, wallruns and slides together like it's nothing. Since there is no sprint-button and you instead build up speed by staying in motion, the game is most rewarding when the way forward is more or less clear and you can concentrate on how to most efficiently move to your goal without having to stop and look around. Every once in a while however, Faith decides that she'd rather not grab that ledge that's right in front of her, which often ends in death through a fall or gunfire or just a frustrating waste of time.
This leads me into the negatives, the most glaring one to me being the integration of combat sections into nearly every level. Every combat section works the same in that there is a goal you have to reach but with the addition of security personnel shooting at you. You don't actually have to fight at all, but in my experience engaging enemies in combat instead of out-running them seems to be the lesser of the two evils, especially towards the end of the game. The punching, kicking and disarming is workable, but not especially interesting and if you decide to pick up a dropped gun and use it, you'll see that the gunplay is rather anemic. "With good reason" you might say, since this isn't a first-person shooter, but trying to dodge enemies and climbing around the place with multiple enemies constantly shooting at you from every which way, forcing you into cover and shutting down your momentum was just unbearably painful to me, so I took up arms and made do with the blandness of it, knowing that I'm  at least not getting pummelled with bullets while trying to nail this next wallrun. Considering how weak I think these sections are I cannot understand why they happen so often.
The second negative in my book is the level design in the later stages. This one is relatively minor and the smallest of my three main problems with this game, but it did in a few spots hamper my enjoyment. The issue here are the overly cramped, slightly puzzle-ish areas towards the end where I had to stop and look around the place to find my way. It was manageable, but seemed to me to break the flow of movement too much, it felt less like running and jumping and more like a slow climb and crawl.
The third and final negative is the story and its presentation. The basic gist of it (without spoilers) is that you're a Runner, delivering messages and packages in the city away from the watchful eye of the local government.  Between chapters the story is told using short animated cutscenes that explain some of the backgrounds of the characters and tie together the chapters. Although the plot is quite obviously not supposed to be some kind of masterpiece in storytelling, it still has to be mentioned just how trite and paper-thin the narrative is. The characters are completely one-dimensional and uninteresting and stay that way to the end, never moving out of the realm of overused B-movie clichés. The government and security agencies provide nothing more than human obstacles, liberally strewn across the levels, and stay just as faceless and impersonal as the masked goons they send to fight you.
To top it all off, the dialogue (both the writing and the voice-acting) is for the most part really mediocre with the occasional dip into shockingly bad. Smaller immersion-breakers like the unimaginably awful aim of supposedly trained police men and the extremely convenient presence of enemy forces wherever you go pale in the face of Merc, your info-guy that's constantly connnected via earpiece, robotically relaying information of variable usefulness to you. The only thing about Merc I found truly believable was his perplexion upon infroming you that the police have somehow managed to track you down once again, because I don't believe even the writers knew how or why that was supposed to make any sense apart from "we need a combat section right now."
On the whole I would definitely give this game a 'mixed' rating, it's a prime candidate for something like a two or two-and-a-half star rating. The visuals are fantastic and the gameplay is for the most part really quite enjoyable, but I can honestly say that, in light of its numerous shortcomings, I found the rather short playtime of four to five hours to be merciful rather than disappointing since I felt my interest rapidly waning towards the end. It's not a waste of time, but it is in my opinion safely skippable.

If I were to look at this game purely from an objective stand point, I'd probably go as far to say that this is not a good game. In a lot of ways it's a fairly bad game. The areas are incredibly repetitive going from Forest area to Snow area to Factory area pretty much exclusively bar the last dungeon, and not only are these dungeons very repetitive, they are also incredibly short 90% of the time and very linear 100% of the time. They are not randomly generated meaning you get one short floor and this gets tiring very fast as this can be, at times, an absolute grind fest of a game, especially early on, not so much in the late game. The music is incredibly forgettable and doesn't stand out at all and the voice acting (in English) ranges from pretty decent (Sam Reigal and Cristina Vee) to pretty awful (Almost everyone else). The story is very generic with the entire story being 'Evil Witch wants world domination' and the characters are also fairly one note receiving only small amounts development throughout.
That being said, when I look back at the time I had with this game, I had a good time. The game has it's charm, it's certainly not a bad looking game, the art style and direction is very nice with the characters design being good between all the different characters. The combat system implemented is very fun and active, going for a slight twist on Turn Based Combat, allowing characters to freely roam the arena and positions playing a role in combat. It reminded me of Ni No Kuni's combat, which I also enjoyed. There is a variety of different moves that are unlocked throughout the game that are all very well animated and are fun to watch (Even if that fun is diminished somewhat the 100th time you've used them) and there are a ton of characters to unlock on use which all play quite differently. The regular moves that you do in battle are also quite customisable, as you are allotted a certain amount of points to allocate to Guard Break, Power or Rush moves, and you can customise the moves to suite your play style. As well as combat customisability, there are also a variety of different costumes to change the appearance of all the characters if you're into that kind of thing (and if you're they type of guy to play this game, chances are you are) as well as accessories which change appearance as well. The game can also be quite funny at times, depending on your sense of humour.
Would I recommend this game? That is entirely dependent on what kind of games you like. If you were put off by anything that I said in that first paragraph, this game probably isn't for you and if you're not really into self aware humour, then avoid it like the plague. While this game certainly isn't a masterpiece, I had my fun with it and I would recommend it any of the stuff in the second paragraph sounded appealing. I don't think I'd pay full price for it (I bought it at 50% off) but for the price I paid, I definitely think I got my money's worth.
Final Playtime: 34 hours 54 minutes.

Good game. There are many things to do (Research, Air Force, Engineering, Building, Gray Market, Barracks, etc) and you have to plan your game well. You can't just rush in without some rudimentary planning as there are consequences for every action and these things help to make the game fun.
Note : There is a lot of DLC for this game.
PROS
1. Story
Interesting, lots to listen to in the Temple Ship. It's not an epic and you can see the similarities it has with HALO.
2. Aliens
Aliens are varied and attack you in different ways. E.g. Thin Man poisons you and shoots, Berserker rushes you and melees, Chryssalid melees and creates zombies that become another Chryssalid.
I like the Chryssalid the most. It is the most memorable monster I have seen.
3. Headquarters
I like the look and design of the HQ. It looks like a little ant farm where you can see how your troops/ants live. It would have been better if the base came alive like the Sims.
4. Combat
Exploding objects, destructible walls, elevation, cover, etc. It adds a lot of tactics to the game.
5. Additional Objectives
Do you want to stun or kill? Do you want to use explosives or kill normally? All these things affect the rewards you get and influences the research.
6. Simulation?
Going into an Engineering Bay or a Research Lab really gives a different feel compared to opening up a standard template. Either Starcraft II borrowed from X-Com or vice versa, but I love the way you have to allocate resources between manufacturing and research. I do feel the Foundry is the same as the Research Lab though.
CONS
1. Line of Sight
Extremely horrible for curved surfaces and elevation. There was a bug where the Sectopod spawned on the curved corner of a building. Couldn't even trace a LOS to hit it. I had to walk up to it and shoot it point blank.
Sometimes, you are guessing if you the space you are moving to, is able to attack any alien. The game would be a lot better if there was a system to let you know if the space you are moving to will give you LOS to the alien.
2. Bugs
Crashes, doorway glitches.
3. Move/Attack
You can't move the moment you attack. This is most ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. You actually have to learn a skill (Bullet Swarm) with the Heavy in order to prevent pauses.
4. AI
The Sectoid actually wasted an action to mind control its own ally to attack you, it is not 2 attacks. Although, it could have been because my difficulty was on Easy.
5. Linearity
Bullets -> Lasers - > Plasma. Brown, red, green. It is most boring to see that Plasma is the obviously stronger choice as it has the highest statistics for accuracy, damage and critical damage. I would have loved to see the weapons vary according to playstyle. E.g. Laser could have been high accuracy, low damage with pierce. Plasma could have been high damage with a status effect.
Other examples include Floater to Heavy Floater and Muton to Muton Elite.
6. Aircraft Combat
Very bland. It stands out a lot as it's the only part of the game that is wireframe and you just try to down UFOs. Also, you can't send multiple planes to attack a UFO, which is ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. You could have built 10 planes and you can only ever send one.
7. Slow Motion
The game always slows in a Sniper reaction shot. It is very anti-climactic to slow the game just to see a miss.
8. DLC
Most distasteful. X-COM Enemy Within has to be bought if you want to play with all the fineries.
9. Multiplayer
Very boring. 120 seconds per turn is a yawn-fest.
10. Height Levels
1st storey, 2nd storey, 3rd storey does not work well in this game. It is not very clear where you looking at.
11. Movement
Units will move along a single path. They will take the most exposed route even if there was a route around lots of cover. I think this could be solved.
Suggestions
1. Secrets
I was hoping to have secrets in the game when I found the Alien Entertainment (there was a voiceover when I found it). I thought we could capture and convert aliens to our side.
2. New Game Plus
I actually wanted to keep expanding the base to make a mega fortress. Something for the developers to think about.

Beat Hazard is a fun twin stick shooter where you select a track from your music library as your level selection.  While playing, you'll hear the track you selected and the enemy waves will be generated based on what you're hearing.  It happens in such a way that a given track will always play the same, allowing you to learn and get better at a specific track.
The graphics are great, and the gamepad controls are perfect.  If you don't have a gamepad, you can attempt to make due with mouse and keyboard controls.
Beat Hazard is also the only game I'm aware of that has in-game rewards for crafting its Steam badge.  You unlock a ship skin with the level 1 badge, the level 5 badge, and the foil badge.  These ship skins are purely aesthetic changes, though the width of the firing pattern does vary slightly between them.
DLC:
Beat Hazard Ultra completely transforms the game and makes it better in every way, adding more enemies, more bosses, and a perk system, as well as making enemy waves far less predictable.  Highly recommended.
iTunes and m4a support is only necessary if you have music in these formats that you want to play.  Otherwise, you can ignore this DLC entirely.
Shadow Operations Unit adds extra ships to the game with different stats and their own separate leaderboards, and Steam Workshop support for creating and sharing your own ships.  Each ship also has a set of missions (read: challenges) to complete.  Highly recommended.

It really is like oregon trail mixed with fire emblem with a viking aesthetic. If you don't like any of that, then this game isn't for you. Plain and simple. On your journey, you will encounter various scripted events and battles. Your moral judgment will be tested. Depending on how you answer events, the course of the story is slightly altered; but I'd imagine the majority of the game remains the same.
There are some flaws here. The game feels rigid and half baked at points. You'll fight two major types of enemies, in two variations; ranged and melee. This bothered me a little throughout my time playing. You'd travel the world, but you'd fight the same enemies. As the game progresses, you get to fight slightly stronger versions of these enemies. Sometimes they might be palette swapped, but honestly if you've fought one raider you've fought them all.
The story is one of the strongest parts of this game. I don't think I would've finished the game if the plot didn't suck me in like it did. I cared about these characters; especially after you got to investing so much into them to make them effective fighters. It makes the plot that much more interesting. On top of that, the gameplay is pretty solid. You're given an assortment of tools, and its up to you to make it work.
It's all a matter of taste. If what I've described sounds interesting, then this game is more or less worth a buy. There's definite room for improvement, and I have some minor gripes with the game; but overall I'm pleased.

Good, pure, zombie killing fun. The core gameplay is simple: "Kill ever more difficult waves of zombies with friends. Then kill a boss." But it's been polished to a mirror sheen. The guns look and "feel" amazing. The sound effects are amazing. The enemies are varied and interesting. The kills are visceral and satisfying. And there's a lot of little touches that feel cool, like how if you press reload when your gun is fully loaded, you instead perform one of a couple different "gun check" animations.
It's a simple game, well executed. And it's co-op.
Note, if you're familiar with the first game, it's faster paced. As a consequence it becomes a little more twitchy. In KF1 you could often see a wipe coming from a mile away. Here the danger of a wipe always feels a little closer, but also more escapable with some clutch play. YMMV

With graphics that look like they have come fresh from a high-budget animated film, this game is best described as an interactive novel with combat. There is almost no voice acting, but you just end up imagining voices and accents in your head, like we all did back when we read books. The characters are compelling, the story gripping and the moral dilemmas you must answer maddening. Is it better for you to lose a few soldiers for some of your civilians to get away, or for you to lose some civilians so you can hit the enemy harder later on? The story mostly focuses on the return of a terrifying race called the Dredge, who are slaughtering their way through both Humans and a race of giants called the Varl. All this is set in a world that obviously recalls Scandinavia - a world in which the Sun shines perpetually after having just mysteriously stopped in the sky one day. There is a haunting soundtrack that perfectly captures the whole atmosphere of desperation and impending doom that accompanies the travels of your caravan across half a continent, and the world itself is packed full of lore for those who like that sort of thing. The only downside that occurs to me is that the combat can get very repetetive. But that really is a tiny thing in an otherwise brilliant game.
PROS:
-Excellent, long story
-Excellent graphics
-Plenty of lore
-Good soundtrack
CONS:
-Lack of voice acting
-Slightly repetetive gameplay

If you played and enjoyed Titan Quest, don't bother reading anymore and just buy this!
If you like dungeon crawlers with class customization and a challenge, don't bother reading anymore and just buy this!
If you're still not convinced, I'll point out a few of the great features in this game:
Positives:
1) You have a main class and a sub class (just like in Titan Quest), allowing for an almost unlimited variety of ways to create and customize your character. There's really no wrong way to build your character, and almost all choices can be undone to experiment with other combinations.
2) Devotion Trees allow for an even deeper ability to customize how your character plays, and really helps fill any voids you might have from the class selections you've made. It takes some time to really dig through the tree to know what will fit your character the best, but it's worth it!
3) The game is actually challenging! Your first playthrough you can choose from playing on normal or veteran. I'd suggest that anyone with any bit of experience in these types of games choose veteran (or up it to veteran once you have the basics down). The other difficulties past veteran start to make you have to play smarter and focus your gear selection for survival. There was never a point that I felt it became TOO hard, but I almost always felt challenged to get better. This is sadly rare in most games in recent memory.
4) Theorycrafting! If you like trying to pick the best possible combination of skills and gear, you will love the theorycrafting this game provides. Like I mentioned before, there's almost an endless amount of ways to make your character. Probably 5-10 hours of my play time on this game has probably been spent theorycrafting. Looking at trees, changing points, swapping gear to see how things change. Even if theory crafting isn't for you, just pick a way you want to build your character and stick with it! You can make almost anything work.
Negatives:
1) NO COMBAT LOGS! There is nothing more frustrating than dying to something and you have NO idea what the hell just happened. I wish there were combat logs so you could see where the damage was coming from and what type of damage it is. Yes, you can eventually learn what types of enemies do certain types of damage, but when you're in a cluster ♥♥♥♥ of 20+ enemies with one or two elite monsters thrown into the mix, good luck knowing what was actually killing you!
2) Bugs! The game is complete and doesn't feel empty in any kind of way, but there is still a lot of bug fixing that needs to happen. I'm sure they'll get it down eventually, and the bugs aren't big enough to make me want to stop playing. A funny bug that I've found is for some reason when you put on a new item and you've met a large number of requirements for the bug to happen, you'll randomly start doing burst damage to EVERYTHING around you, be it enemy or ally (and maybe even yourself). It's happened to me twice in over 190 hours of play time, so not a common bug but it will surprise the hell out of you when you (or your friends) randomly die while in town.
Overall a great game. I can't wait for expansions and additional classes!

Child of Light is a fantastically well done game. Every detail has been refined to its best, and what few issues I had with it are so simplistic, it doesn't take away one speck of the value the game has!
The Story: It is incredibly well done; even if you don't like rhymes, it's worth it to go through and follow along. It seems very predictable and a little cliche, but feels and plays as the exact opposite. They did a wonderful job in keeping the player's interest peaked for the entirety of the play-through, and it concludes rather nicely. The game usually revolves around the story, so it's hard to step away from it without feeling the need to go forward.
The World and Characters: Also both well done. The world is enriched by the splendid art style and captivating music, and the characters each have their own personality and differ from each other, so nothing congeals together. Each party member is unique in his or her own way as well, allowing you to play the game as you wish. Despite the overall fantasy-feel of it, it remains unique, straying from what has been overused in order to carve its own path.
The Gameplay: I usually am not one for turn-based combat, yet I found myself enjoying it in this game! They turned away the inevitable-moments-of-doom usually found in turn-based if you make a wrong decision, by allowing you to turn the tables in the time it takes for the enemy to attack. It makes combat much more bearable, even desired!
The animations are smooth, and the transfer from exploring to an event or a battle is not interruptive at all, so afterward you can easily resume your previous task. I haven't encountered any odd clipping errors or hesitance in the controls, and the maps are linear enough that if you don't want to explore, you can just go with the plotline. Everything is smooth, simple, and easy to get into, and if you do decide to invest more time into the game by exploring, you are well-rewarded! The simple dialog sequences also bring you closer to the characters, and is a clever way to avoid odd animations the player would have to watch from a distance. Overall, the gameplay allows you to enjoy the game more, instead of hindering it in any way.
The Art and Sound: The artwork and the soundtracks of games are like icing for a cake, and this is some delicious frosting! The artwork is colorful and unique, and has that fantasy-rpg feel to it to really suck you in. Despite some of the characters having models, instead of being animated images, they are almost impossible to tell apart, allowing the more complex works to fit well inside the world, instead of being an obvious difference that makes you wonder why the developers didn't just go one way or the other. The soundtracks are spectacular, immersing you into Lemuria with the rich symphony it conducts. I have yet to meet someone who didn't like orchestral music, and this music is so well done, it's art within itself! If you like this game, I recommend buying the soundtrack as well!
UPlay and being a Port: I had doubts with UPlay, but other reviews made me reconsider. I, for one, do not like installing other programs, just to interface with another program so I can play one game. Child of Light will most likely be the only game in my UPlay account for a long time. But it's well worth it, even if it seems tedious! (Which it kind of is... But that might have something to do with the fact that Child of Light is also on PS4). After playing the game, the only thing that would ever turn me away is UPlay. And I don't care about it that much to let it hinder me.
Though since Child of Light is on PS4, I'm guessing the PC version is a port, which would explain the only other issue I've had in the game. Sometimes at intersections it's hard to go down the path you want to go, instead of the other one which the game thinks you want to go. I imagine it's easier to avoid on console, but on PC it can get frustrating. Luckily, there is a key that allows Aurora to jump down from something if possible, so most of those instances are simply fixed.
Child of Light kept me entertained for hours, and even though it doesn't have much replay on one profile, it tempts you to start up a new game and play all over again! The DLC spice it up even more-It's well worth any game investment, and should be in any rpg-lover's library!

I enjoyed almost everything about this game. It is a platformer/puzzle/turn-based RPG game in which all three would fall in the "casual" category. The music, art, gameplay was all very good. Nothing about this game was complicated and the battle system was not intricate.
Your gear was combining/upgrading gems that give different abilities or effects and it can be unequipped or changed without penalty. A lot of party members, to choose from but you can only use 2 at a time. You can switch them mid battle without penalty or losing a turn incase one is about to get knocked out. Each character has their own pro/cons. Other than that, it is a stright forward turned based battle system with a bar that lets you know who might be going next (stronger abilites take longer time to get ready).
Some things in the story was never explained (i.e. *Spoiler Alert* *Spoiler Alert* the flooding I assumed was caused by the main villain, but it never stopped even after her defeat).
The "confessions" which are hidden notes you find that pieces together a story was never explained. I have no idea who those people are that is mentioned in the confessions or what significane they play in the game at all. (None i guess since I beat the game and still don't know who they were.)
The ending of the game seemed very rushed and a little online research suggests content was removed before release. *Spoiler Alert**Spoiler Alert* After I got my♥♥♥♥♥whooped and was revived and powered up I was excited to go through another dungeon etc etc fight the villain etc, but nothing.♥♥♥♥♥whooped - power up cut-scene and final boss. The end.
I did enjoy the overall game though despite that end.
--------------

I estimated i spent $4.50 for this game.
Light-hearted platformer, puzzle and rpg game with some exploring.
Great visuals, music, story (for the most part).
Straight forward turn based combat system.
Lots of party members but only 2 can be active at a time.

This review was written after I had completed my first playthrough of Little Nightmares.
The Positives:
- Compelling and creepy artstyle that remains consistant and enchanting.
- Superb audio design, appropriatly aiding the player through clear audio cues
- A cryptic and bizzare narrative that silently encorages the player to deconstruct its story
The Mixed:
- The game is shorter than I expected. However its short length did not leave me bored at any point
- Full 3D movement. While the game mostly does a fine job of utilising an enjoyable 3D enviroment to play in, there are some scenes in the game whereby distance and perspective are hard to judge, causing for some miscalculations and frustrations.
The Negatives:
- A lacking tutorial. There were some puzzles in the beginning of the game whereby I couldn't progress because I was not taught about a certain game mechanic. However a tutorial prompt does show up after some time or if the player previously died attempting to solve the puzzle.

- Too story heavy: You can debate this one but i got through this game pretty quickly reason being is i felt like i needed to play the story to keep interested in playing the game which isn't a bad thing per say (The story line despite being completely bonkers is pretty good and entertaining i mean you are president of the United States who gets kidnapped by Aliens and you have to fight your way out of a virtual world and save the real world!)...But i dunno the rest of the virtual world seemed empty and lifeless and boring. Yea you have the minigames and some other small things but nothing that will make you go 'WOW' in fact the only one i enjoyed and had a laugh at was 'Insurance Fraud' (There is something amusing about hitting a car and flying half way across the map). Just not enough to keep you interested and lacks replayability.
- Enemies: Or maybe it's because there is no challenge in the enemies and despite the fact this sounds stupid the further in the game you get the easier it is due to the overpowered superpowers. Not do say i didn't die i died a fair few times but i think thats because i was messing about but anyway back to the enemies...'sigh'.. they are soo painfully boring when in a game you already have blown completely out of context compared to the other Saints Row games why go so linear with the enemies? Basically you have normal aliens with guns (And grenades which disable your powers..Which is cool wish they used them more) who use portals to always find you, a alien car (Yea a car) with a turret, aliens on hover bikes (Bit more interesting) the Vtol (Alien edition) and alien tanks (Generic and boring)... (Which by the way all vehicles have no cool characteristics apart from they float...Little effort went into that) and 2 more interesting enemies which are a ball thing that rolls around and unfolds into this turret which trys to shoot you..it's quite laughable it's easy to dodge as once it begins to charge to fire it can't aim anywhere else so simply move out of the way and you will be fine and then when you hit maximum wanted level if you like a warden shows up which is this fowl beast of Zinyaks which is a cool concept but fails quickly as it's not hard whatsoever to kill and when you do kill it with a quick time event all your wanted level is
So no more gunfights where you would use every bullet and every ounce of health to survive the endless police force pounding you down?..i think that was the best part of the whole game myself.
Not so say this game isn't fun to play. You can enjoy this game and i did for the most part the storyline is good and the leader of the aliens Zinyak is so likable as an enemy you will find yourself laughing as he is a complete♥♥♥♥♥♥but a funny one. The game has lots of throwback to the other Saint's Row games, there is plently of collectables to find if you enjoy that, the level up system is rewarding although i don't like the unlimited ammo myself. The scenery is amazing and has a good computer simulation feel to it, The Superpowers despite ruining the game for me is admittingly fun to use and when you have your homies suited up with super powers too it's quite amusing to watch yourself become untouchable,There is a surprise return i won't ruin for you ;), still have all the awesome customization for yourself, weapon's and cars....The inflatoray is so amusing xD. Do i regret buying this game for $40....Yes unfortunately i should of waited for a sale but i got drawn in by the hype. Should you pick it up on sale your decision! ....Think i would rather jump back to Saints row 3 though it's more fun in my opinion.

If you are looking for that competitive, fast-paced type of game to have some good times (alone and with friends), then this may be just what you were looking for. Although the base of the game is dodgeball with unicicle robots, instead of sticking to that, the developers went ahead and squeezed as much as they could from that idea resulting in varied and fun (with "fun" being, of course, relative) matches.
What you may like:
-The game is extremely competitive with the concept being of the "easy to learn but hard to master" type.
-The variety of game modes and maps complemented with Workshop support for BOTH things
-The online multiplayer is cleverly designed as you jump from a randomized match to another, wasting as little time as possible
-You also get to customize you robot with several items, some of which can be bought on the market or instead, crafted with items you get from random drops. But fear not! These items are purely cosmetic, holding no effect on the gameplay at all.
What may put you off:
-There is no splitscreen mode which is a shame even for PC. It would be awesome to be able to connect you machine to a bigger screen and play with 2 to 4 people.
-The current player count is a bit low. I never had any problems connecting to servers (living in the UTC), but I often find myself playing with mostly bots whenever I connect to a server.
-As this is dodgeball, the relatively slow nature of the ball throw, although being part of the fun learning how to predict the opponent's movement, having that combined with the fast movement, makes this what I can only describe as "Lucky Shot Simulator" in many cases.

First of all, if you have not yet seen the movie "Kung Fury", do so (it's available on videostreaming sites).
Secondly, if you grew up in the late 80s, early 90s, or simply like retro games you will recognize the look of the game.
Ok.. Review..
This game is simple, complex, challenging and addictive. It's simple because you only have two buttons, "attack left" and "attack right". It's complex because different enemies will take different combinations using those two buttons to kill. It's challenging because the different types of enemies will swarm you at an increasing speed. It's addictive because you'll keep trying to beat your highscore or those of your friends.
If you liked the movie, if you like the retro style of the game and if you don't mind spending the price of peeing in a public restroom on a game you might like this.

Good game. There are many things to do (Research, Air Force, Engineering, Building, Gray Market, Barracks, etc) and you have to plan your game well. You can't just rush in without some rudimentary planning as there are consequences for every action and these things help to make the game fun.
Note : There is a lot of DLC for this game.
PROS
1. Story
Interesting, lots to listen to in the Temple Ship. It's not an epic and you can see the similarities it has with HALO.
2. Aliens
Aliens are varied and attack you in different ways. E.g. Thin Man poisons you and shoots, Berserker rushes you and melees, Chryssalid melees and creates zombies that become another Chryssalid.
I like the Chryssalid the most. It is the most memorable monster I have seen.
3. Headquarters
I like the look and design of the HQ. It looks like a little ant farm where you can see how your troops/ants live. It would have been better if the base came alive like the Sims.
4. Combat
Exploding objects, destructible walls, elevation, cover, etc. It adds a lot of tactics to the game.
5. Additional Objectives
Do you want to stun or kill? Do you want to use explosives or kill normally? All these things affect the rewards you get and influences the research.
6. Simulation?
Going into an Engineering Bay or a Research Lab really gives a different feel compared to opening up a standard template. Either Starcraft II borrowed from X-Com or vice versa, but I love the way you have to allocate resources between manufacturing and research. I do feel the Foundry is the same as the Research Lab though.
CONS
1. Line of Sight
Extremely horrible for curved surfaces and elevation. There was a bug where the Sectopod spawned on the curved corner of a building. Couldn't even trace a LOS to hit it. I had to walk up to it and shoot it point blank.
Sometimes, you are guessing if you the space you are moving to, is able to attack any alien. The game would be a lot better if there was a system to let you know if the space you are moving to will give you LOS to the alien.
2. Bugs
Crashes, doorway glitches.
3. Move/Attack
You can't move the moment you attack. This is most ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. You actually have to learn a skill (Bullet Swarm) with the Heavy in order to prevent pauses.
4. AI
The Sectoid actually wasted an action to mind control its own ally to attack you, it is not 2 attacks. Although, it could have been because my difficulty was on Easy.
5. Linearity
Bullets -> Lasers - > Plasma. Brown, red, green. It is most boring to see that Plasma is the obviously stronger choice as it has the highest statistics for accuracy, damage and critical damage. I would have loved to see the weapons vary according to playstyle. E.g. Laser could have been high accuracy, low damage with pierce. Plasma could have been high damage with a status effect.
Other examples include Floater to Heavy Floater and Muton to Muton Elite.
6. Aircraft Combat
Very bland. It stands out a lot as it's the only part of the game that is wireframe and you just try to down UFOs. Also, you can't send multiple planes to attack a UFO, which is ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. You could have built 10 planes and you can only ever send one.
7. Slow Motion
The game always slows in a Sniper reaction shot. It is very anti-climactic to slow the game just to see a miss.
8. DLC
Most distasteful. X-COM Enemy Within has to be bought if you want to play with all the fineries.
9. Multiplayer
Very boring. 120 seconds per turn is a yawn-fest.
10. Height Levels
1st storey, 2nd storey, 3rd storey does not work well in this game. It is not very clear where you looking at.
11. Movement
Units will move along a single path. They will take the most exposed route even if there was a route around lots of cover. I think this could be solved.
Suggestions
1. Secrets
I was hoping to have secrets in the game when I found the Alien Entertainment (there was a voiceover when I found it). I thought we could capture and convert aliens to our side.
2. New Game Plus
I actually wanted to keep expanding the base to make a mega fortress. Something for the developers to think about.

This is a neat little title that pays tribute to the film of the same name, as well as 80's arcade games in general.
Its a painfully simple game but hard to master. You have two attacks - left and right. That's it. No movement, no special power ups. Just manage your attacks as best you can until your three lives run out, and hope you can make a dent on the High Score list.
The aesthetic is awesome - the game plays as if it were on an older arcade cabinet, complete with scanlines and slowdown. The music is nothing too great, but they did include a 16-bit version of one of the songs from the movie (the game's trailer plays it about 12 seconds in - its a good track!)
There's not much else here. Sadly its a shallow game at its core, but overall its a fun time-waster that will push you to reach first place, which is no easy feat. A great homage to games of past, and definitely a great way to spend a couple of bucks to support those who graced us with the Kung Fury movie.
Here's to hoping for more games in the Kung Fury series. Well, I need to head back to the office. Looks like it's gonna be a hell of a lot of paperwork.

This game is a classic example of what not to do when making an RPG. The game starts fairly well, introducing you to the basics of combat and movement and giving you a good amount of time to get to grips with these mechanics. The game falls down when it reaches the first populated area however; after an initial conversation I found myself trapped in a fairly small city surrounded by largely useless NPCs who just info-dumped me with useless dialogue.
The main problem I had with the city area was the complete lack of any guidance, it was almost as if the developers had forgotten to explain the majority of their game. Dialogue is hugely important, as are the various traits your character recieves  by making important decisions during said dialogues, this was not emphasised at all. No information was given about bargaining, buying/selling items or even where to find skillbooks (necessary to gain new abilities) and I found myself having to resort to outside sources and guides far too often.
The sudden difference in gameplay is also jarring, as the "tutorial" segment of the game gives no impression of the boring dialogue fest to come. The game was, in my opinion, poorly designed in this aspect as there is practically no combat available till level 4 (which takes longer to get to then you might think) and the game kills you constantly to remind you not to have too much fun. The quests early on were incredibly dull and most took ages to complete, giving me the impression I wasn't making any progress.
The combat after the tutorial is often very misleading, on several occasions my party was wiped almost instantly by enemies of the same (or even lower) level as my party. I don't really see the point of having the levels clearly visable on an enemy if the strength of a creature is often far greater than a character with the same level. This grew particularly annoying after I realised that enemies did not respawn, meaning I quickly cleared all the fights possible to do and was left with the boring quests in the city (these quests often led me to areas that vastly out-leveled me).
The game seems to have no reasonable way to gauge the player character's strength, as skeleton opponents casually waltzed through my abilties and backstabs before planting an axe firmly in my face. Whilst I am aware that my character (an assassin) was not a tank character, I feel that being two-hit killed by a brainless zombie was fairly ridiculous, especially when I planned my attacks well and had a clear advantage (invisibility+backstab).
The game seemed intent on stamping out any brief enjoyment I had with the mechanics, dragging out boring sections and explaining none of the important mechanics other than combat, which was practically non-existant until level 5 due to the enemy level increase. A poorly thought out game with huge amounts of content but no guidance to accessing most of it, I would not recommend this at all.

A game this good and expensive shouldn't be filled with bugs and some very flawed game mechanics. Sometimes it freezes, sometimes the line-of-sight is erroneous, sometimes enemies spawn in your midst, and the list goes on. It's a great game, but that only makes the frustration that much worse. The challenge of harder difficulties and development of your skill is unsatisfying because of the problems it has. If you think it's still worth it and you have the money to spend, get it, and remember that your survival depends more on an understanding of the games problems than a mastery of its tactical options.

One of the best RPGs I've played in a long time! Original Sin gives the player a modern take on classical RPGs; meaning no spoonfeeding mechanics and handholding. This game utilises the freedom its predecessors had; meaning the story's flow could be changed substantially by the player's actions as opposed to being locked onto a linear grid, and its use of elements which can be fun to experiment with as one uses their environment to their advantage. This game isn't like most popular modern RPGS. It takes more thought to go through than just mindlessly bashing skulls from point A to point B. It won't be a game that everyone would like but I am glad that this genre of RPG is still alive and well; even in today's gaming standards. Larian really outdid themselves with Original Sin. 8.5/10.

Oregon Trail meets Final Fantasy Tactics!
-Overview-
Seriously this game is very fun and has a way of drawing you in. The neatest part that will also be the most frustrating is that you cannot create save slots. So if you are at a juncture and someone dies, they stay dead in your game. Don't worry, characters that fall in combat will only be injured for an amount of days equal to how badly they got gibbed in battle (at least on normal difficulty). But sometimes people will die as a result of your actions and then they are just dead. The story is well done with some twists along the way. The setting is the real powerhouse though - it's the end of the world and you are trying to eke out some survival. It's reminiscent to zombie apocalypse games because the dredge you fight seem rather mindless. What saves it is the nordic fantasy theme and the varls. The varls are apparently a cross between human and ox, but they live for hundreds of years and are basically giants. Also they cannot reproduce anymore so the amount left is finite.
-Gameplay-
There are 2 main screens in the game, the traveling screen which tracks how many people, varls, and supplies you have as you trek across the landscape and the grid battle view where you fight tactical combats. Overall both of these systems work very well. I was frustrated at first by how frequently my archers and other squishies died. Now I treat them like fragile objects and play very carefully with them. It isn't worth it to run halfway across the map for a kill only to get swarmed and killed. Send the tanks in first, create a wall, then pepper them with your long-range units. Instead of getting gold and experience you acquire Renown which functions as a currency for everything in the game. Want to buy an item? Spend renown. Want to buy food supplies? Spend renown. Want to level up your army? Spend renown. Obviously you don't get enough to do it all, so you balance losing women and children with wanting to have a stronger army to fight through and save the rest of the caravan. Lots of little decisions come back later in the game too, which shows you that your choices do matter. Overall it's very fun and addicting, with a "One More Turn Style" gameplay.
-Story-
It just throws you into this lord of the rings inspired setting, but instead of dwarves, elves, and orcs, you get human, varl, and dredge. Along the way you start piecing together the history and relationships of the world, but rather than show a setting where the fantasy races are leaving or dying off, everything is dying off. The sun has literally stopped in the sky and people are constantly asking you what to do because its the end of the world. While this might make the whole thing seem pointless, you do get sucked into the characters and their struggle to survive through some good characterization and lots of poignant moments with your own personal choices driving the narrative.
-Music-
A bit halting here and there, sometimes there will be silence for a long time and then suddenly music begins! The quality of the tracks is very high though, I am usually glad when the music does come on. It's also voice-acted but I can't tell you to what extent because I prefer reading walls of texts.
-Verdict-
Great tactical game. If you like tactical combat and reminisce for Oregon Trail style random stuff happening then this is for you. The whole thing plods along and is very slow, so take your time with it and you will be richly rewarded. I've sat at a key decision juncture for 5 or 10 minutes trying to deduce how things will play out. Since I can't just reload and find out, it may actually get a replay out of me too. The combat is unforgiving but once you learn some tricks you'll feel unstoppable.

Some people I have talked to have wanted to play Mirror's Edge for a variety of parkour options through which to traverse an environment, but that is simply not what this game is about. Mirror's Edge is as much a puzzle game as a parkour game - it's all about finding the best path to go by through trial and error. This may sound tedious, but this game is so fast paced that the process is seamless, and once you get going on the right path, you get the most thrilling feeling.
Mirror's Edge is all about what you can do, and what your limitations as a character and as a player are. You must always figure out 1. whether Faith (the protagonist) has a long enough jump to clear that gap and 2. whether you, the player, have enough skill and experience with the controls to clear that gap efficiently, for a better time or to stay ahead of the police.

Imagine a chose-your-own-adventure book where none of your choices matter.  This game is a story being told under the thin veneer of interactivity, but after multiple playthroughs it is clear that your “choices” are all superficial and utterly without consequence.
The gameplay itself is nothing but quicktime events or choosing from some dialogue options.  The combat is handled through quicktime events, but don’t worry, there is no penalty for dying; you get as many mulligans as you need.  The truth is that this barely feels like a game at all.  90% of this game is spent passively watching people have conversations, and then your character says something (or remains silent, since none of your choices matter anyway silence is a real in-game option) and then the game can go back to playing itself.
Even despite these problems it’s almost worth it.  Almost.  The story IS interesting and well told.  If you want to be told a story that is pretending to be a game maybe you should buy this, you may enjoy it.  Unfortunately for me at least, the fact that none of your choices matter killed any interest I had in the game.  None of your decisions make any difference. Let me be very clear on one thing: Saints Row IV isn't really a GTA clone. It's taken an entirely different direction than its predecessors (SR2 and SR:TT as the ones on Steam) and as such really isn't comparable. It doesn't even have actual gangs this time. And you have super powers.
While it's good that the game has stepped away from its roots, if you're a fan of GTA/SR1/SR2 and you're not super fond of completely over the top ridiculousness, SRIV will probably lose you. If you're skeptical the game goes on sale pretty often and honestly, even if you don't enjoy it as much as the previously mentioned titles, you'll probably get enough fun out of it for the $10 you spend on it.
Anyway, I've been a fan of the Saints Row series for a while now, and I can say with complete honesty that this game ties with Saints Row 2 as my favorite of the bunch. While Saints Row: The Third tended to flip flop tones and was overall unfocused and nonsensical (even for the world it established), Saints Row IV starts off completely over the top and stays that way. There aren't any jarring 'Ho Boat'-esque tones because, well, the entire game is that. Despite that, though, it feels more grounded than SR:TT simply due to the fact that it knows what it is and it's not going to pretend it's anything but that.
The story is as follows: You are the President of the United States after taking out a group of terrorists and disarming a nuke (all in the opening tutorials). As you're heading for a press conference an alien emporer named Zinyak attacks Earth and takes you and your gang hostage. You wake up in a virtual reality with one goal: kick Zinyak's♥♥♥♥♥
It's a paper thin plot, really, but it's done well. The characters are as likeable and well acted as always and Zinyak is an enjoyable villain. Despite the silliness of the game it also briefly touches on some deep character moments involving Shaundi and a certain returning character, which was welcome as a chance to breathe. Even when the game gets heavy, though, it's never to the point where you stop having fun or you stop laughing. It doesn't make fun of the issues it's presenting but instead works with the tone while keeping the weight that such issues deserve.
The gameplay is fun, but unbalanced. You get super powers basically a half hour - hour into the game (during the second set of tutorial missions) and that renders cars completely obsolete (which is a shame since they added in new customization options and an easier way to access the garage). Guns are also only needed every so often, with the most effective way to take down enemies usually just meleeing them to death. It's not as though the AI is really smart enough to present any challenge to this tactic, especially since you can learn a talent that allowed you to regenerate health when you're knocked back or do damage.
In order to spice things up the game throws in a few super powered enemies. These can range from somewhat challenging and fun to annoyingly frustrating. A few will just do constant knockbacks which will help you regain your health (if you invest in the previously mentioned talent), but you have a very limited amount of time in which you can damage them. They also tend to jump around which adds challenge at first, but soon becomes tedious as all of the enemies share the same movesets.
Some scenarios in the game take your powers away, which is a little bit annoying but understandable. I honestly never had an issue with it but I figured it would be good to bring up.
Your homies are also basically useless and the main characters can sometimes even be a hazard to have around. There's been multiple times where I've gone in to charge an enemy but was immediately knocked back by Kinzie either stomping or using telekinesis. The only reason to have them around at all is to hear their idle chatter, which is as enjoyable as always.
The DLC in SRIV is a bit... lacking. Compared to the three or four hour to two hour missions and activities Saints Row: The Third got, SRIV is disappointing in terms of length and price. Both Enter the Dominatrix and How the Saints Saved Christmas are fun, enjoyable missions but ultimately only clock in at about two hours total (there are multiple achievements and collectibles that increase replay value slightly). I'd suggest getting the Season Pass when it's on sale, but otherwise just waiting.
Overall Saints Row IV is a fun time, even without a co-op partner. I'm still not even close to one hundred percenting it, but even with about 70 hours in I'm still finding new things and enjoying the activities and city takeover. If you're uncertain, I'd suggest waiting for a sale (which it's frequently on) and trying it out.

The perfect Xcom game. The old classics are hugely outdated, therefore the loving rip-off Xenonauts is too in its painful, archaic turn-based combat. With this they kept all the classic components of an isometric xcom strategy game and updated it, not just with slick graphics and a perfect and atmospheric soundtrack by Michael McCann but with fluid combat as well, without just streamlining it.
I love the overall story arch, especially with the core missions added by Enemy Within. The focus on psionic powers and hidden knowledge is an intriguing plotline. I feel the ending was rather quick and anticlimactic, but there's still plenty of replay value with this game.
Researching weapons and tech is a lot of fun, regarding specialising I guess that depends on personal strategy and on how long you delay core missions for, especially if you become quite reliant on the technology introduced in enemy within at an early stage (this happened with me this play through and I got into the psionic abilities quite late into the game, or rather quite late into overall development).
Voice acting is good, especially in EW with the options for different languages. As said the music is perfect, very reminiscent of deus ex human revolution, which McCann also scored.
Overall a great variety of missions, with a specific strategy you have to get used to for each, what took me the longest was the chryssalid missions. Hate those things.
Can't recommend the enemy within expansion highly enough, it adds so much to the game, and probably worth getting for the base defence mission alone.

Crafting in this game ends up being very simple and easy to learn. I LOVE THE PARKOUR SO MUCH AGGGHH. The parkour is for the most part realistic but that's not what RAELLY matters. The parkour is really fun and adds so much to the game and the very in depth map. The map is very open and you're always discovering something new. The leveling systen is really unique as I have NEVER seen anything like it in any other games I've played. You level up as you use any abilities under whichever category they branched from. The story is really good and you can easily get attached to the characters. With all this being said, let's review:
Good story-Very detailed characters that you learn to either love or hate
Good quests-Quests are fun, unique, and never ogrewhelming
Graphics-Game looks stunningly good, even on the lowest settings.
Performance-One of the few things I don't like so far. I don't know how this performs on anything NVIDIA, but it plays like absolute garbage on anything AMD. My computer is more than capable of running this on high settings without lag, yet my frames range from 20-30 when on high settings.
Combat-Very entertaining. Slo mos of zombies getting their heads split open and ribcages cracking is so satisfying to hear and see. Always an original way to take down the zombies. One bad thing about this that i forgot to say at the top. The weapons and their durabilities are quite annoying. For almost all weapons, you need metal parts to repair them. At the beginning of the game metal parts seemed kind of hard to find, but after about 2 hours you have 30-40 metal parts in your inventory. The only problem is that weapons only have so many repairs, and it's really annoying to have a broken weapon after taking out about 30 zombies. Weapons can be hard to find and really expensive when bought. You end up feeling bad breaking a well modded weapon because it's horrid durability.
Crafting-Slightly confusing at first glance, but becomes very interesting to do and simple after a few minutes of testing things out.
Parkour-One of the bests parts to this game. Very addicting parkour. The parkour adds so much diversity to the game that it's amazing. (The only bad part is that it doesn't seem right when other games DON'T have parkour in them)
Map-Very exploritive and fun to play on. This map has a lot of cool stuff to explore and gives you a lot to look at. The map is very open and in my opinion perfect for this game type.
In conclusion: Very very fun game. I R8 9/10

I have finished the game, and decided to write a review afterwords so I can give you my one hundred percent honest review of this game, especially since I can recall every about it since I've just finished it.
STORY
The Banner Saga is one of those games that you see it, and say, "That looks epic." And it really is. The story of the game is lengthy, and it took me eight hours to beat it (however, I played it on Easy which I highly recommend you play for your first playthrough, since this game is VERY unforgiving in combat later on). You switch from two groups in the game who are trying to survive in this world, which is inspired by Viking mythology and design. However, the game focuses on one after the first three or four chapters. The group that isn't the main group is about a group of varl (giant humans who have horns sticking out of their heads) trying to deliver the prince of the humans back to his home, while also having their soon to be varl with them. The main group is about a man, named Rook, trying to escape from the Dredge (stone-like golems that seem to want nothing more than death and destruction, and the end of the world) while protecting his daughter.
You play as Rook most of the game, while you sometimes go to the varl group as you see their story unfold. In the end, their paths will intertwine. That is all I can give about the story without giving spoilers, but I will say it's one of the greatest stories I've ever seen in a videogame. And the game had even surprised me many times with emotional moments, which I didn't expect in a game like this.
GAMEPLAY
The gameplay of the game is very simple. Outside of combat, you make choices by clicking on one of the options of what to do. And I will say, there is no voice acting in this game. Some voice acting comes up when they talk about a town, since you must travel from town-to-town while managing supplies and morale (like Oregon Trail, but easier). Conversations should the characters speak to one another, but you merely read the words. To me, it felt like reading a visual novel, but yet it was so well done. In combat, you also use the mouse. The combat is turn-based RPG, where units have armor and strength (health). If you damage armor, you can basically kill enemies in one hit by hitting their strength afterwards. However, you get numbers of how much your unit will take off, and it's very nice and clean. The combat animations are slick, and characters look fantastic in the art design the game has done. Combat can take up to five minutes, or twenty depending on how good you are at strategy, which you don't have to worry as much in Easy mode. The battles at first are simple and easy, but later on you will get your♥♥♥♥♥♥kicked, because the Dredge are powerful and sometimes unfair on higher difficulties. So, if you're playing the game for the first time, play it on Easy. You will enjoy it a lot more.
DESIGN
As I've stated, the game looks gorgeous with it's hand-drawn graphics that are breath-taking at moments. Everything fits together, and everybody looks different in the game, despite on character who you don't get more then ten minutes, so it's fine. Every character looks like they could be real, and the game actually makes you care about these characters,  So if you make a choice that kills one, or one just dies in battle, you really do feel the emotional impacts. You have the characters you love, and the characters that annoy you, and the characters you hate. It really does feel like a visual novel in a way, but with choices and some fighting including some RPG elements, but it does a fine job of making worth playing.
VERDICT
The Banner Saga is one of the games that you can't wait for the sequel to come out (especially since the only thing that stunk was that it ended suddenly, and will pick off in the game with your choices, so we can only hope the next game[s] are as good as this one) and truly surpirsed me. It shows that RPG turn-based combat works really well for an amazing story that this game has. You feel connected to the characters, and when one dies, you feel that emotional impact as you can even cry sometimes. Sure, it doesn't have fancy cutscenes and has a lot of reading, but it's one of the best RPG games out there, and I will be waiting for when the next game comes out, and probably praise that game too.  9/10

From then on you realize the primary purpose of this game is to make you feel safe then immediately cause you to♥♥♥♥♥♥in your pants.  The moment you feel like you have a handle on the game and can easily bound around the open areas, the game informs you that you are wrong.  From zombies that seem to have spawned directly behind you the instant you look away to the butt-clenching moments when you try to parkour away from a raging horde only to miss the ledge and fall to a pit of grasping hands and gnashing teeth you never get fully used to the game.  Once I made the mistake of laughing at the zombies below and farming them from a rooftop with my shiny new gun.  Once.  There is also a ton of content in the game.  Many of the games missions make you feel like you're really trying to help the locals survive, and many of the missions force you to check your current stock of clean underwear.  Need me to go out at night and grab some stuff for you?  Sure, I can do that...until I hear a weird noise behind me then NOPE ENGINES ACTIVATED!  Suddenly my heart is racing, I am running, and clicking wildly as I become a whirlwind of melee weapons and whatever the hell else I have on me to attack with.  Also, there is a grappling hook.  As soon as I got the grappling hook I thought "Weeee!  I am Spoderman!" until I hooked the side of a building that you cannot climb up and fell into the things that stir in the night.  I found a small spot where you can seriously farm at night safely and decided to farm night zombies with grenades.  Apparently one landed too close to me and blew me off the rooftop and into my demise below.  The game's main story line is also pretty cool, and it gets F'ed up pretty quickly.  It keeps things interesting.  There is one mission in particular that is part of the story that seems pretty normal and actiony...until the music kicks in.  Once I heard the music I tried to tell the game to stop trying to scare me, but it wouldn't.  Have you ever seen the look on a cat's face the instant it turns around and notices a cucumber on the floor?  That was my face for the entire mission.

Complexity. It’s an old RPG trait largely forgotten by a lot of gamers and ignored by most developers. If you like your RPG’s action-oriented and filled with commodities such as quest markers, move right along. Divinity: Original Sin from Belgian developer Larian assumes you’re prepared to actually figure out quite a bit all on your own. It provides a large game world and simply lets you wander around in it. Areas aren’t closed off, all quests can be finished in at least two different ways and you won’t be punished for playing your own way. It brings about the kind of design philosophy that really should exist in every RPG, regardless of its style, combat system or any other differentiating feature.
The story follows two main protagonists who start out as Source Hunters trying to figure out a local murder mystery. Naturally, soon they find themselves involved in something much bigger including an orc invasion, undead uprising, mad kings in a frozen land inhabited by elementals and they’ll even visit other dimensions and take to the heavens. Unfortunately, this is the weakest part of the game as the writing isn’t particularly compelling and the characterization is awfully shallow, especially regarding the playable characters. Speaking of which, apart from the two main characters, you’ll be able to recruit more people along the way. However, you’ll only be able to keep up to four in your party. Any others will await for your call in a place called the Hall of Heroes if you get the urge to switch them up a bit.
The only real reason to switch characters is to try out different classes and tactics. The character upgrade system is extremely deep and customizable, each class is extremely different with a load of unique traits, abilities and spells. And it’s extremely flexible as well. Just because you committed to a certain class at the beginning doesn’t mean you’re stuck with it if you change your mind. On the contrary, you can mix things up and create something like a rogue specialized in fire spells. You can customize all characters further with weapons and equipment you find along the way. And there’s a ton of loot in this game. Upgrading and customizing your character as well as constantly finding new loot is a huge source of addiction and probably the biggest motivation to continue playing.
Original Sin has a turn-based combat system which is awesome because it’s not an under-the-hood system with pause, but with actual turns akin to a regular turn-based strategy game. Apart from being able to witness the myriad of different combat styles, the combat shines thanks to its fantastic convergence of elemental powers. For example, summoning rain will create puddles on the ground and will make your enemies wet. Throwing a lightning bolt onto one enemy will fry him, but will also zap anyone standing in a puddle nearby. Then you can throw a fireball which will dry out the puddles and create mist that will cause enemies to have limited sight. Frozen surfaces will make characters slip and fall, spilled poison can be ignited for additional damage, the possibilities are nearly endless. Naturally, considering that everything you cast on the battlefield will affect your party as well, you have to be careful what you’re doing at all times. It’s just a superb system that never gets old.
Divinity: Original Sin is a fantastic looking game, however the art style isn’t particularly distinctive and falls under usual fantasy tropes a bit too often. The same can be said about the soundtrack, it’s definitely pleasing and appropriate, but just doesn’t really stand out in any way. My biggest complaint about the game is that it can be incredibly obtuse at times, particularly regarding the puzzle design. You will actually get hints from books and other sources, but I honestly don’t know what frame of mind you have to be in to figure some of this stuff out. This can get especially frustrating due to how big the world is and considering that a lot of quests span across multiple huge areas.
Divinity: Original Sin is one of the big Kickstarter success stories – a rewarding, addictive and unapologetic hardcore RPG brimming with complexity, gameplay depth and content breadth. If only it had a more motivating story, more interesting characters and a more unique game world, it would have been a masterpiece. Still, a few design quibbles aside, this is a great game that will delight anyone looking for a true RPG that brings back cherished genre values and wraps them up in a modern package.
8 OUT OF 10 (GREAT)
