Killing Floor 2 is a solo/co-op FPS with up to 6 players. Each player takes the role mercenary fighting creatures technically called “specimines” but are commonly referred to as “zeds”. Zeds were biological experiments by the Horzine Biotech, and are made with human DNA, but they are far from human now. All have been altered in some way and some have weapons or special abilities. And it’s not just a few of these zeds, there are 20, 30 and more of them. The weaker ones can grab the player and hold them in place allowing bigger more powerful zeds to get close and kill them. Some zeds can launch fireballs, others are nearly invisible until they attack and one has a sonic attack. The most powerful zeds are extremely tough, fast and can quickly kill a player with melee attacks.
After surviving a wave of zed attacks, the players are given a short break to buy improved weapons, more ammo and armor before a new wave of zeds attack. The players gain money from what the kill and from helping others. After fighting through the waves of zeds a Boss shows up. The bosses are powerful, fast and equipped with advanced weapons.
The players are far from helpless though. A large arsenal of weapons is available, many based on real weapons, but a few are beyond cutting edge. The players have 9 classed to choose from, each with their own special abilities. Unlike many games of this type experience in a class is carried over from game to game and the players can raise up to 25 levels. As the player increases in levels they get bonuses for such things as reload speed and increased. As well as special abilities such as seeing invisible enemies, extra damage from headshots, damage resistance or increased speed. There is also something known as “Zed Time”. While in Zed time is in effect everything slows down allowing the players to target with great accuracy. Zed Time can occur whenever a Zed dies and is random.
The weapons in the game ave very well modeled and a great deal of effort was put into seemingly simple things such as the reloading animations. Combat is VERY fast paced with player movement being very important. Staying in place is likely to get the player killed as they get swarmed by zeds. Players must keep on their toes, work with each other and stay together. I don’t play online much preferring solo play, but the battles are always intense. sm

Having thought about this for awhile.
Initially I was quite excited about this game, it is awesome in many ways, and beats Diablo3 and Math of Exile on several areas.
The excitment lasted until I had finished my first play through and realized there was no servers, and the grind which has a pretty high focus in Grim Dawn, is utterly pointless when you can just download a single savefile and get everything instantly. Still I thought, well that shouldn't ruin it for me, I can just play by myself and ignore all multiplayer - But I am afraid I can't ignore it... I have fired up the game every day for two weeks now, but I can't find the will to play knowing it is pointless.
The final nail in the coffin was when I further investigated this, and found out the devs are very firm on never having servers. Since having servers, for me are the single most important feature of an arpg, and despite how great the game is, I can't recommend it.
If you don't care about cheats and being able to jump straight to the end of a game with everything maxxed and all gear, or don't play with other players, then Grim Dawn is an excellent high quality game.

Not for experienced rogue-like RPG players.
Yes, it has lovely pastel visuals. Yes, the dialogues rhyme. Yes, it actually has a pleasantly optimized battle system.
It is also extremely EASY. I started the game on "Casual" and immediately switched to "Expert" because "Casual" played more like a peaceful demo than an RPG ("Casual", - the name says it all).
I mean, I can see why this game would be geared towards people like me - those who enjoy having a strong story, nice visuals, and simpler, easier battle that can just serve the story instead of presenting an additional and parallel challenge.
I know we're not in Dark Souls territory here, but I like earning my victories and the Expert mode is barely making me work for it. If it's too easy for me, it's probably too easy for 90% of players out there.
This would be a must-have game for youngsters (14-18 year olds) interested in getting into rogue-like RPGs. It's gentle enough, eases you into the battle and has an engrossing story.
For experienced players though, the game would get old fast and the characters seem very over-powered for a real challenge to eventually develop.
Now, if the previous warning hasn't changed your mind, here are all the wonderful things that this game has to offer.
SPOILER WARNINGS (perhaps)
In combat there is a time-dependent turn system that allows the player to skip ahead of enemies' turns if the right casts and potions are used. Each actor's time to next action can vary, sometimes spectacularly (you thought you were behind an enemy, but suddenly he is interrupted by your teammate and his TTNA is lengthened). This adds a level of interesting unpredictability to combat gameplay.
Another useful bit of info that nobody else has mentioned: during battle the firefly glims generated when Igniculus "shakes" the light bushes are worth about twice Igniculus' light meter. For optimal utilization of the glims, always try to capture about half of the glims, then let the rest float around until the light meter is running low again. Otherwise, once the meter is full, any additional glims are going to waste.
Ubisoft made the welcome change here of shifting cleric-type casts like healing and enemy debuffs outside of the turn system and onto the Igniculus character.
This enables a more offensive dynamic to develop with PCs and focuses on matching attacks to enemies, timing offense and defense (NB: when enemy and player character are within the timer's "red zone" the preferred action should be defense), and generally making your party more proactive and less micro-managed.
I personally spend most of battle with the Igniculus trigger enabled on one of the enemies, according to each of their turns in the battle sequence and their action speed.
Party members start out "pre-typed" so to speak - Aurora is clearly a mage-type build, despite the big MFKN sword she receives at the beginning. The skill tree however, offers an opportunity to shift the character type more towards a melee fighter with strength and HP boosts. If that is your intention, I would recommend to either grind a bit at the beginning to earn Uplay credits that you can redeem for HP and strength bonuses, or maybe to wait for the right party member to join gameplay and mould it into the fighter that you want to have up-front and in the face of your enemies.
Sadly there is no cover system, no grid and no distinction between melee and ranged fighting - a mage cast is equivalent to a physical attack, and each character has a primary physical attack. Honestly at my current level my characters are so OP that I can't tell if it makes a difference or not. The only noticeable thing is that my fighter character has MP that she never uses unless there's a major crisis like HP drastically low while Igniculus' meter is empty - in which case she can heal any party member (as a turn-based action). This permits for the fighter character to occasionally squeeze out a buff for the entire party at the beginning of a battle and just sit on the rest of the MP until needed at a later time.
The gem upgrade system was also nice (called "oculi" in-game) with a no-nonsense elemental interdependence (fire, water, lightning) that allows you to have ridiculously unfair advantages against enemies. A typical attack makes almost triple the damage if the correct oculus (can I decline it that way?) is applied to the weapon.
One thing that bothered me at the beginning was that when Aurora walked, the feet were misaligned with the path on which she was walking (it looked pretty half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥for all the effort that was put into creating the backgrounds in the first place), but after the first boss-battle where the additional ability of flight is unlocked, and implicitly moving speed increases, that is no longer an issue.
That being said, it's a nice game that's difficult to put down. If I had kids, I'd let them play this.
Will update my review if my opinion changes before I beat the game.

First of all I would like to clear it out that this was a birthday gift from my friend this year, that I really liked.
I liked Child of Light mainly for the art when I saw this over at an Australian gaming show called Good Game (you can find their YouTube easy peasy!), where the hosts made a review of this game.
I was pretty astonished by art, as the obvious fact here and it was also because I loved watercolour art/paint and I thought it was an interesting medium itself more than oil paintings. I really loved the watercolour art feel of this one as it feels rather unique to be seen on a game. It is not often you see an art like this. Did I mention that I loved Auriora's har? Her hair reminded me of Ariel, somehow, but that probably didn't come in as a surprise. I just really loved the flowing hair animation coming from her. It's just so beautiful to look at.
Besides that, I also loved the story behind it. The story was just sad and learning how to redeem yourself/make yourself worthy of the position. i liked how she isn't your typical princess (ahem.. Princess Peach!) and how she was a generous person who'd like to help everyone, I liked how her character develops in the entire game, from this scared little princess to the queen worthy to take place of her father and mother's reign. I liked how she proved herself, it shows a great deal and strength of the character.
Aside from my love of Aurora, the combat system is where I liked it the most. It shines a lot of new things to a genre that the genre needs (pun intended). I liked how it included a timeline and a real-time strategy element to the game so the players will know when to attack and when to defend themselves from enemies. I liked how you have to use your party to defend and attack a lot of monsters instead of just sticking to one most of the time to uncover the enemies' vulnerabilities. Though I ended up using one for most parts because of their abilities and their resourcefulness.
However, it falls flat on some places. I don't know if you're an autosave person or manual save person like me, but sometimes, I liked having manual saves and I usually miss those. I literally miss saving my own file before anything comes up. Also, Tristis and Rubella's story wasn't that interesting as they just became less used than everyone else in the game. It was more likely a long wait to find themselves together again. And I can't stress it enough of how awkward and awful is the writing. It just seems wrong and just awful to read. It was awkward how every end has to rhyme and how everything should be in sing-song/rhyming.
Along with my pet peeves of this game, I wasn't much of a fan of the forced UPlay integration. I reallly don't feel like it was needed but I think it was more of their jab at online game industry, I liked my Steam as much as any other users here, but we don't really liked being forced to do things such as this.
but my overall thoughs: great game if you like Real Time combat system, free flowing hair of Aurora's and are sick of any other games that contained "Dark" or "Light" matters, try this game. It is worth it despite of its shortcomings.

Very fun game. Not too far into the campaign but so far it's had all original and fun quests. None of the quests seem boring, annoying, or repetative like they are in a lot of games. Each quest has it's own level of originality. The game looks very very good. It looks good, but at the same time performs like GARBAGE on AMD devices. I have an AMD FX 6300 ogreclocked to 4.3 Ghz and an R9 280X and with everything turned down all the way I get 80 frames at the very max. When I turn everything up all the way it just becomes a mess. I get around 20-30 frames on highest settings. The combat is very fun and unique. Every level up gives you acess to a brand new badass ability. The combat never feels boring or dry. You constantly have different ways to take down the zombies. Whether it be a powerful dropkick or an explosive fire bomb, there's always new ways to fight. Crafting to me seemed very confusing at first. But after looking at it for a few minutes you realize that it's so easy it's not even funny. Crafting in this game ends up being very simple and easy to learn. Crafting is an important part of this game and is easy to pick up on and isn't frustratingly difficult like in a lot of other games I've played. The parkour in this game is addictingly fun. I LOVE THE PARKOUR SO MUCH AGGGHH. The parkour is for the most part realistic but that's not what RAELLY matters. The parkour is really fun and adds so much to the game and the very in depth map. The map is very open and you're always discovering something new. The leveling systen is really unique as I have NEVER seen anything like it in any other games I've played. You level up as you use any abilities under whichever category they branched from. The story is really good and you can easily get attached to the characters. With all this being said, let's review:
Good story-Very detailed characters that you learn to either love or hate
Good quests-Quests are fun, unique, and never ogrewhelming
Graphics-Game looks stunningly good, even on the lowest settings.
Performance-One of the few things I don't like so far. I don't know how this performs on anything NVIDIA, but it plays like absolute garbage on anything AMD. My computer is more than capable of running this on high settings without lag, yet my frames range from 20-30 when on high settings.
Combat-Very entertaining. Slo mos of zombies getting their heads split open and ribcages cracking is so satisfying to hear and see. Always an original way to take down the zombies. One bad thing about this that i forgot to say at the top. The weapons and their durabilities are quite annoying. For almost all weapons, you need metal parts to repair them. At the beginning of the game metal parts seemed kind of hard to find, but after about 2 hours you have 30-40 metal parts in your inventory. The only problem is that weapons only have so many repairs, and it's really annoying to have a broken weapon after taking out about 30 zombies. Weapons can be hard to find and really expensive when bought. You end up feeling bad breaking a well modded weapon because it's horrid durability.
Crafting-Slightly confusing at first glance, but becomes very interesting to do and simple after a few minutes of testing things out.
Parkour-One of the bests parts to this game. Very addicting parkour. The parkour adds so much diversity to the game that it's amazing. (The only bad part is that it doesn't seem right when other games DON'T have parkour in them)
Map-Very exploritive and fun to play on. This map has a lot of cool stuff to explore and gives you a lot to look at. The map is very open and in my opinion perfect for this game type.
In conclusion: Very very fun game. I R8 9/10

Have you ever played Dead Island and/or Mirror's Edge? If you haven't played either one, let me tell you. This game is what happens when you put parkour into a zombie apocalype.
The story/plot of the game is not bad but pretty predictable which is kind of unfortunate but the gameplay is a different story. You can craft weapons, upgrade you weapons and craft more items as you level up and encounter survivors that aid you as you play, for example, using firecrackers to lure them away or using traps set around the city to stop their pursuit or simply run as fast as far as whatever you can to get away in style. The best thing to do, however, would be dropkicking every single zombie you see and send them flying. Literally.
Overall I would give the game a 8/10 but I'll give it a 9/10 simply because of how much fun I had with dropkicks.
I would recommend this game for players who enjoy zombie survival games and and parkour freely around the place.

After playing SR3, and having a good time with it, I was eagerly awaiting the next installment in the serie... Boy, was I dissapointed? Sure was!
First of all, this use the very same game engine and map as the third. The vehicles are mostly the same too. What they did change however is the core mechanics of the game: Think "Matrix" here. You are basically and overpowered "Neo" that can run faster than a car, jump higher than an helicopter and hit harder than a tank. So, what is the problem you ask?
Well, this renders the vehicles AND guns pretty pointless. In fact, you would do best not to use any vehicles at all since running pretty much is faster and easier. Same goes for weapons. You can hit and throw the opposition with so much power that a rifles becomes unnecessary. After about halfway thru the game, it became clear to me that being OP is not fun! And the game setting, a computer simulation, allow the DEV team to take the easy way out when it comes to what is realistic and what is not. Example: When you throw someone out of a vehicle, it just warp outside it without animation.
If you played the third game, then I would suggest you stick with it or go look somewhere else. If you did not play SR3, pick it before you pick this one. I assure you, 3 is bigger than 4 in this case!

If you're a fan of either music games or twitch arcade shooters you'll probably love Beat Hazard.
The mechanics are esentially a homage to the classic arcade Asteroids... except made completely insane by more visual stimuli than the human eye can probably process. The real hook of the game though is that every level is generated by whatever music track you've selected. It's easy to zone out as you steer your little ship through bullet hell while jamming along to whatever it is you fill your iDevice with.
Bottom line is that the game is fun as hell. And it's replay value is roughly whatever the size of your music collection is (although the included tracks are actually quite good). Just be aware of the photosensitive warning at the game's start. This game isn't messing aorund. There will be colors flying everywhere constantly.
And did I mention this game was made by just one man? Indie game win.

Wow, this is seriously a great game.  It starts of feeling like a fairly normal action game until your first real mission to investigate part of the first area.  From then on you realize the primary purpose of this game is to make you feel safe then immediately cause you to♥♥♥♥♥♥in your pants.  The moment you feel like you have a handle on the game and can easily bound around the open areas, the game informs you that you are wrong.  From zombies that seem to have spawned directly behind you the instant you look away to the butt-clenching moments when you try to parkour away from a raging horde only to miss the ledge and fall to a pit of grasping hands and gnashing teeth you never get fully used to the game.  Once I made the mistake of laughing at the zombies below and farming them from a rooftop with my shiny new gun.  Once.  There is also a ton of content in the game.  Many of the games missions make you feel like you're really trying to help the locals survive, and many of the missions force you to check your current stock of clean underwear.  Need me to go out at night and grab some stuff for you?  Sure, I can do that...until I hear a weird noise behind me then NOPE ENGINES ACTIVATED!  Suddenly my heart is racing, I am running, and clicking wildly as I become a whirlwind of melee weapons and whatever the hell else I have on me to attack with.  Also, there is a grappling hook.  As soon as I got the grappling hook I thought "Weeee!  I am Spoderman!" until I hooked the side of a building that you cannot climb up and fell into the things that stir in the night.  I found a small spot where you can seriously farm at night safely and decided to farm night zombies with grenades.  Apparently one landed too close to me and blew me off the rooftop and into my demise below.  The game's main story line is also pretty cool, and it gets F'ed up pretty quickly.  It keeps things interesting.  There is one mission in particular that is part of the story that seems pretty normal and actiony...until the music kicks in.  Once I heard the music I tried to tell the game to stop trying to scare me, but it wouldn't.  Have you ever seen the look on a cat's face the instant it turns around and notices a cucumber on the floor?  That was my face for the entire mission.
TL;DR This game is a 9.5/10 in my opinion.  There is apparently some new content coming in February and honestly my body is ready.

A very enjoyable and amusing game for any South Park fan.
PROS
+ Filled with call backs and references to many iconic moments and characters from the series
+ Feels like you're playing through a South Park movie
+ Combat abilities are unique and clever
+ Quests feel well integrated and not tedious
+ Turn based combat is straight forward and enjoyable
+ Replay value with several different companion characters and achievements
CONS
- Many side quests and areas are impossible to complete until you further yourself down the main storyline. There is no warning or dialogue to tell you this so there are several frustrating moments where you hit a dead end on a quest until you go complete something else
- Some tutorial moments get stuck in a loop if you are unable to grasp what is being asked of you
- Several times was forced to look at walkthrough guides because artwork or layout of a level made it difficult to realize there was a ramp, door or walkway to the next area
- Equipment management was deep but tedious to switch every item between outfits for various scenarios and enemies. A simple couple "saved outfit" options for full switching would've solved this easily.
CONCLUSION
If you are a fan of South Park, this is a unique playable movie with plenty of laughs and fun gameplay that can be completed in a casual 20 hours. Looking forward to the next game!

The lore and story is pretty good. Some very funny moments in there as well.
Somehow it feels "just right". It's not too level-grindey nor is it too fast-paced.
Due to the fact that you can progress your own way without a set path, some story elements can break and you are often left wondering, "Did I leave something out?"
I find it is a bit disappointing that you cannot craft items with legendary stats and some item crafting combinations do not really make sense when you think about it. Overall, it feels quite dodgy and forced. Some item combinations that you would expect to work just don't, (e.g., Mysterious Dye, adding elemental damage to some weapons)
These two cons aside, this is a very good CRPG.

Captain's Edition Review
I had finally maxed out my sheilds and this was finally looking like it might be my winning run. Oh how wrong was I, I came across some aliens in need of help so I did, their reward, a fancy new weapon, sadly though my ship had taken some damage from the ordeal but no matter I thought. Then fate had it that a store would pop up, go back and waste precious feul, (yes I realise you can buy feul at stores but i was low on funds) or move on. I moved on, second Jump in the new sector I came across a Rebel scout drone, it had an Ion Blast (Something that can disable your systems) and a pair of drones. Feeling confident with my four sheilds and kickass weapon I went on the offensive.
Before I say what happens next I would like to say that I am in my opinion very experienced at this game but by no means close to mastering it.
Anyway, I decided to save my missles thinking I could buy more later, so I didn't even charge them, but then it happened, their Ion Blast must've been something out of ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t Landia because it rapid fires three blasts disabling my sheilds then its drones hammered away at my weapons while my sheilds struggled to come back online. Now I was in trouble, my weapons wounded I ordered every man onboard to fix them while I waited desperately for my missle to charge (Missles only need one power.) Finally my weapons were online but my sheilds were still down, I fired missle after missle while a volly of lasers tried to pierce the sheilds tried to take out the Ion Blast. I needed one of my six remaining missles to hit their drone control system or I was dead. I used every last missle and they all missed, unbelievable, I was about to die a terrible death, my crew hopefully would die from lack of oxygen (those sick ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s took out my O2 system too) before they were blown to pieces.
This is yet another wild and fun moment that can happen in FTL, the new release of FTL Captain's Edition adds more random events and some new features along with a brand spanking new alien race. For those who aren't aware of the awesomeness that is FTL I will explain, if you are already well aware please skip this paragraph. Now FTL is a game based around the Star Trek era rather than the Star Wars. You are Captain Kirk, or for Star Wars fans I guess Han Solo would compare, and you are the commander of an all mighty spacecraft, you have a section of usable power and then many systems to balance them between. You can decide to draft - or buy - more crewman who you find anywhere from stores to dark caves, and they range from humans to giant rock people each better at something than others. Speaking of buying things stores pop up here and there that you can buy from, at least one per sector anyway. Oh yeah and the evil federation is on your butt so you better move it because if they catch you you're in for some scary battles.
Now the newly released free DLC is in a word awesome, the indie developer added one of my personal favourite features, a system where you could save wherever you crew was, say one person manning the weapons, another engines and the last at the helm, and then you could move them wherever then press a button that returns them to their saved positions. This is especially helpful considering that your crew gets better at whatever they do and I would often have to name my charaters, Engine, Helm and Weapons. Along with this feature you can also see when you enter the Jump map (to see where you want to go next) it shows you where you can Jump from that position. I remember a time when I was low on feul and I Jumped over to a store thinking I could easily make it from their to the exit of the sector when I realised I couldn't Jump that far, I was forced to backtrack into enemy territory and I was low on feul, my story didn't end well.
Every now and then in the game you'll Jump somewhere and you have to make a decision, for example you come up to a cave, it looks abandoned your choices: Search through it, or leave. Usually upon your choice either something good - you find someone living inside and they join your crew, or bad - a wild madman hiding inside kills one of you crew. Cool I guess but the fourth time I saved giant mutant spiders the nerd in me had gotten bored, but no more! Now theres a whole bunch more of these guilty pleasure stories.
Another old feature that I really need to mention is the ability to pause the game, I do believe it's some new technology I've never seen it before. But seriously pausing FTL doesn't just give you a second to grab a bite but to also tell your crew where to go, what to fix and what things to target. Heck you can even teleport into the enemy ship, blow up a sub-system then teleport back to saftety!
All in all this is a spectacular game, and for only $15 it will give you hours of enjoyment along with a whole bunch of mods to keep you up long past midnight.

Hipster name, but the game works. Simple dodgeball simulator, with robots.
It weights little, the gameplay is easy to get into: you pick a ball, load the shot, shoot it, if it hits, you get a frag.
You also can do a (small) jump, and a (small) sprint.
Has powerups, such as returning ball (more useful than it sounds), jetpack, longer sprint, bigger ball, and similar. Not game changing, but can spice up the gameplay.
As far as I played, there was no situation of some player hogging up a cool powerup and winning the match this way: death is the great equalizer.
Everyone gets destroyed and often, the respawn time is almost null, maps are tight. This provides for frenetic action.
Small hiccup would be the movement, it's not fluid, but clunky.
Your jumps are really small, you can't run really fast, sometimes you keep going even though you're not pressing anything: for all intents and purposes you're controlling a vehicle.
Robot on wheels to be exact, not an fps character, so forget bunnyjumping, crouching or covers, you've got a limited set of movements and you're expected to make the best out of them.
Flaw or feature, that's for you to decide, but it's still something you'll have to get used to if you plan on plaiyng properly.
There's a leveling up system, and you get drops that you can use to craft better skins for your character, a way to keep interest going after you've played all the maps and tried all the modes.
Speaking of that, the game doesn't really offer lots of diversity: regardless of the variations, you're still throwing balls at robots in a symmetrical arena with colors flashing to disco music.
I'd compare this game to ratz:instagib or rocket league, it's a fast arena game, that will prove really amusing for the 10 to 20 minutes you'll be playing it. But gets dry if you try to dedicate more to it. Not that you can't, and the game encourages you to, but you've already seen all it has to offer. "been there, done that".
When it's on sale for 5$ or less, it's worth it, as a 5$ title.
15$ wouldn't really recommend, unless you desperately have a vehicular dodgeball arena simulator itch you need to scratch.

Saints Row IV is an open world action-adventure game developed by Volition, the developing team behind the Red Faction and Saints Row series of video games, and published by Deep Silver, who have published a variety of other series, such as Metro, Dead Island, Risen, Homefront, and of course, Saints Row. The game was released in August 2013 for Microsoft Windows, PlayStation 3 and Xbox 360. It is the fourth installment in the Saints Row series following Saints Row: The Third in 2011.
The game takes place five years after the events of its predecessor, in a virtual reality based on the fictional city of Steelport, in which the protagonist must fight an alien invasion as well as simulations of the gangs and enemies from their past. As in previous titles in the series, the player controls the leader of the Third Street Saints, who has now become the president of the United States. Throughout the main course of the game, your mission is to overthrow the alien warlord Zinyak, who has taken over the world and put every human being into a matrix-like stasis where they can remain as a living energy source in their hypnotic submission. Over the course of the game, you'll find yourself participating in a variety of activities in order to further break down Zinyaks virtual reality while fighting a variety of alien soldiers who attempt to stop you from busting out of the simulation. While most games simulating virtual reality often attempt to recreate the most convincing virtual world possible, Saints Row IV takes this in stride, as you'll often find visual glitches in the game that serve to convince you that the Steelport you're in isn't real, along with the various superpowers you gain over the course of the game that serve to drive home the point that everything you experience in the game is only a fictional recreation of reality. This question of real versus unreal serves as a comedic subject for the game, as the writers made it a point to make a joke of this as much as possible (shocking for a Saints Row title, I know). However, the writing is nearly overshadowed by the sheer ridiculousness of various other elements of the game, such as the weapon loadouts available to your character, like a duel set of Han Solo's Blasters, or the Dub-Step Gun, or even the Tentacle Sword. Furthermore, the character customization in Saints Row IV gives you a huge variety of options to make your character as unique as you are, and, along with the DLC provided with the game (often free of charge on the day of release), will give you many more options than you will ever even care to experiment with. Finally, Saints Row IV presents the most polished cooperative play out of any Saints Row Title, and only becomes more fun with another player. Personally, I played through the entire game with a friend, and I'm proud to say that Saints Row IV offers one of the best co-op experiences on Steam. The campaign is never hindered by the presence of a Player Two, and if you're anything like me, when you play alone, you'll only find yourself wishing that there was somebody playing with you to share the laughs.
While the plot may be ludicrous, the world may be fake, and the jokes may be cheesy, Saints Row IV is still an absolute blast to play, and is a title you should be sure to catch (during a Steam Sale, of course).

The field of vision is a little messed up, sometimes I've found myself wondering why my sniper can't get a shot on "ET" when my support soldier next to them can. All in all, it is a tough game that requires a lot of forethought before making moves and when crafting/researching/building. Because money is so limited, and time is precious, it is very important that you calculate how you want everything to go by the END of the game, rather than considering the here and now. It is all about planning to prevent future bottlenecks. You know when a game has an actual ending for a "losing" scenario, that the roads are about to get really bumpy.

Two words. Seed generator.
You've heard of the RNG, right? No. Not until you know what 'seed generator' means can you understand. At the start of every mission, the game rolls a bunch of magical virtua-dice. Fantastic, you say, this is only good, yay, dice. Nope. This is bad.
So lets say the dice come up... oh, what, 1, 2, 3, 99, 100, 99 etc, and so on. You, as the player, are not told or shown any of these numbers. This is expected.
So you start the mission, you spot some alien dudes, and you rush your shotgunner crew of 3 walks up to the enemies. You pull out them shotties point blank. 99% chance to hit. Or 100%. Whatever. Fire, fire, fire. All 3 aliens take 0 damage, and are completely unaffected in any way.
Next turn, they all have a go and crit your team one at a time, murdering all of them. GG.
This is an unlikely scenario, but I am trying to prove a point. Any percentages you are shown matter almost not at all. If the game says you are gonna hit, you are gonna hit. If the game has deemed at the start of the encounter that if you fire on this turn you will miss, then you WILL miss, and no matter how high the percent is, you are boned, you will never hit no matter what you do.
Another thing in this game is the 'capturing' of alien scum.
So say you get lucky. There's one last super powerful enemy left, and you want his heavy plasma real bad. You've got him down to 1 health point, and you pull up your entire team of 5 or whatever. Every single one of your crew uses their stun guns, at... what, 80-90% or whatever, and, every single stun fails. Why? Because the seed generator rolled super low.
Now, as opposed to simple 'dumb luck' or pseudo-random distribution, seed generation is in my opinion disgusting. Because, sometimes I like save scumming it, such as in the case above, where I really badly want to stun a few ape dudes or whatever. The problem is that this option isn't open to me. Yes! Sure. I can simply annihilate every enemy on the board, no probs. But that's not the point. Sometimes I don't want to. I want to grab their equipment so's I can stockpile it just in case I lose someone.
The seed generator does it's thing at the moment you lock yourself into a mission. It is all predetermined. And for this reason, I can't recommend this game personally. I mean, hell, look at all the other reviews out there, the people who don't care about this crap. I do. You may not. If you feel like, hey, whatever, I can deal with a little bit of bulldust, go for it. Aside from the seed generation, this game really is fantastic. It's great. I just can't stand not being able to 'cheat'. At least have it an option, or something, I mean, really.
There's also the... less than fantastic controls. I just had some problems with the interface during combat, but mostly it's because I'm used to having perfectly responsive buttons that don't result questioned actions constantly. I just wish there was like, a Disgaea type queue for actions.

Very fun game. Not too far into the campaign but so far it's had all original and fun quests. None of the quests seem boring, annoying, or repetative like they are in a lot of games. Each quest has it's own level of originality. The game looks very very good. It looks good, but at the same time performs like GARBAGE on AMD devices. I have an AMD FX 6300 ogreclocked to 4.3 Ghz and an R9 280X and with everything turned down all the way I get 80 frames at the very max. When I turn everything up all the way it just becomes a mess. I get around 20-30 frames on highest settings. The combat is very fun and unique. Every level up gives you acess to a brand new badass ability. The combat never feels boring or dry. You constantly have different ways to take down the zombies. Whether it be a powerful dropkick or an explosive fire bomb, there's always new ways to fight. Crafting to me seemed very confusing at first. But after looking at it for a few minutes you realize that it's so easy it's not even funny. Crafting in this game ends up being very simple and easy to learn. Crafting is an important part of this game and is easy to pick up on and isn't frustratingly difficult like in a lot of other games I've played. The parkour in this game is addictingly fun. I LOVE THE PARKOUR SO MUCH AGGGHH. The parkour is for the most part realistic but that's not what RAELLY matters. The parkour is really fun and adds so much to the game and the very in depth map. The map is very open and you're always discovering something new. The leveling systen is really unique as I have NEVER seen anything like it in any other games I've played. You level up as you use any abilities under whichever category they branched from. The story is really good and you can easily get attached to the characters. With all this being said, let's review:
Good story-Very detailed characters that you learn to either love or hate
Good quests-Quests are fun, unique, and never ogrewhelming
Graphics-Game looks stunningly good, even on the lowest settings.
Performance-One of the few things I don't like so far. I don't know how this performs on anything NVIDIA, but it plays like absolute garbage on anything AMD. My computer is more than capable of running this on high settings without lag, yet my frames range from 20-30 when on high settings.
Combat-Very entertaining. Slo mos of zombies getting their heads split open and ribcages cracking is so satisfying to hear and see. Always an original way to take down the zombies. One bad thing about this that i forgot to say at the top. The weapons and their durabilities are quite annoying. For almost all weapons, you need metal parts to repair them. At the beginning of the game metal parts seemed kind of hard to find, but after about 2 hours you have 30-40 metal parts in your inventory. The only problem is that weapons only have so many repairs, and it's really annoying to have a broken weapon after taking out about 30 zombies. Weapons can be hard to find and really expensive when bought. You end up feeling bad breaking a well modded weapon because it's horrid durability.
Crafting-Slightly confusing at first glance, but becomes very interesting to do and simple after a few minutes of testing things out.
Parkour-One of the bests parts to this game. Very addicting parkour. The parkour adds so much diversity to the game that it's amazing. (The only bad part is that it doesn't seem right when other games DON'T have parkour in them)
Map-Very exploritive and fun to play on. This map has a lot of cool stuff to explore and gives you a lot to look at. The map is very open and in my opinion perfect for this game type.
In conclusion: Very very fun game. I R8 9/10

While the game has lots of flavour, a diverse soundtrack and a decent enough story, it unfortuneately is hampered by a strange combat mechanic that has completely turned me off The Banner Saga.
In normal turn based strategy/rpg games, everyone rotates through their turns, going one after another. However in Banner Saga, it is one faction then the other faction, regardless of how many soldiers/characters are left. What this equals out to is that fights are brutally rough when trying to take out single tough enemies. More that that it feels so utterly non-sensical that if you fought well, and had all four/five/six characters, and your enemy has one left, that one will get to act four/five/six times more often then anyone of your characters.
The whole concept is confusing if you think about it too much, but more than that, characters you like to use, are used less often in relation to the enemy in most fights, and they are more likely to die, if they catch a lone opponents ire, because that enemy can attack your one character four/five/six times before you can get them out of danger.

I can't recommend this game highly enough.  Baldur's Gate II is probably my favorite game of all time.  After playing through the 100+ hours more than ten times though, I've been stuck looking for a game that scratches the same itch.  Neverwinter Nights and Dragon Age were both disappointing (with DA2 signalling the death of Bioware quality and old-school RPGs.)  I had sort of accepted that the old Black Isle-style RPG was a thing of the past.
When I saw this game described as a return to that style of gaming, I was interested.  Though it had piqued my interest, I was reluctant to buy it at full price.  When it didn't show up on the Halloween sale, I bit the bullet and grabbed it.  I couldn't be more pleased.   THIS is what a modern-day BG2 should feel like.  The combat is deep and complex, the storyline is engaging, and the world is huge and open.  Larian said their two biggest influences were Ultima 7 and Baldur's gate - that works for me!
There are minor quibbles.  The characters aren't particularly memorable and I wish there were more unique items and lore (BG2 style.)  Also, if you're a fan of games that hold your hand, this is NOT the title for you.  It can be pretty obtuse at the beginning, but for some of us, that's half the fun.  These issues don't detract from what is a spectacularly engaging experience.    If you're even a little bit interested in this type of game, grab it.  You won't regret it.  Highly highly recommended.

Absolutely fantastic game! The writing is rough but its charm will win you over before you even realize it. So, so many different endings each satisfying and worth pursuing. I also like the overall story here, it's a bit of a deconstruction of the typical Visual Novel. We see our protagonist in a bad state (Yes, a typical anime shut-in) but believe me you begin rooting for our character (and its worth noting that in all my experiences with novels there's only been a few times where I agreed completely with every action of the hero- and this is one of them. In other words its no Sakura Spirit haha). But by the end there is a serious change that's honestly inspiring.
For a free, a FREE ♥♥♥♥ing game, I was completely blown away by the quality. Now, don't set your expectations too high. A large factor of my enjoyment of this game is because I went in with rock bottom expectations but if you're looking for a review to just win you over enough- play it. It has a lot of heavy russian culture and names, the pacing is rough, I can see a few endings being completely horrendous for a first playthrough (i.e. Lela bad end and any of the non-girl endings). And I'd say if the charm of nostalgia, summer camps, cute girls, and living life to the fullest doesn't win you over you might have some problems with the rough writing as well- it's not bad at all but there were one or two moments.
Overall, for having rock bottom expectations: I was completely blown away. But if you read this then it's an above average visual novel with a very inspiring dynamic main character, several endings that range from sweet- to brutal- to loving- to sci fi wonders, and a certain charm that drew me in completely. So without my rock bottom expectations being blown away I'd honestly give it a high recommendation (very high for fans of VN's)- I don't do that score♥♥♥♥♥♥br>

The Banner Saga is an amazing story wrapped into a punishing combat system. The two stat combat , and you go I go turn system take some getting used to. But, once you become familiar with it the game rewards you with getting to see your Varl wade into your enemies while your archer pour arrows into the Dredge.
But it's not the combat that this game does best, it's the story. There are moments in this game where my jaw literally dropped, and that's a rare feeling for me. There are realizations that come up in this game that you will talk with your friends about for days after. While some of the random speech encounters can be a bit annoying (you never know what will happen, or who will die, without consulting a wiki) this broad story is what makes this a great game.
I very much hope that the story will continue soon with either an expansion (hopefully with some gameplay/mechanic improvements) or a whole new game. Either way I will be buying it because I want to continue the story and see what will happen next.

Team work is essential in this game.  This will teach you to take up roles and communicate effectively in a team survival cooperation.  You have to kill all the specimen that spawn in a wave to advance.  You earn money for every kill you get.  Once they're all dead you get a minute to spend your money on better weapons or ammo.  If you die you only respawn at the end of the wave.  The more players you have in a game, the more enemies spawn per wave and the tougher they are.  The gore is extremely advanced.  Limbs can be severed at multiple points, heads can be chipped away, intestines can spill.  If you have a powerful computer you can have dynamic blood fluid render in real time for realistic spraying and pooling blood effects.  But most importantly be prepared to die.  This game is brutal on the higher difficulties and unforgiving for inexperienced players.  You'll go from feeling like you have everything under control to dying in a few seconds.  But most of the time you'll have a pretty good idea of how you could have prevented your death.

No but srsly in the recent years of degrading game depth/skill ceiling, increasing focus on pretty graphics and simply catering to the average person, this game is what you and your group of competitive gaming oldones need. It's easy to pick up, since its basically only two action buttons, but the sheer amount of movement, item and monster mechanics allow it to be played in uncountable ways.
To cut to the point: This piece of software right here is pretty much a top-down twin-stick rpg/shooter versus/co-op game, currently only supporting local multiplayer. Controls are basically L-stick to move/aim, A to shoot/slash, B to dodge/special move.
The goal for every player is the same, kill the boss after reaching lvl10 in human form, to be released from the dungeon. A sudden-death at the start determines the first ''runner'' to enter the dungeon in human form, your slaughtered companions souls steadily haunting your every step to kill you and take away your humanity for themselves i.e. their try at defeating the dungeon. The dungeon in itself is harmless, but every trap and contraption can be used by the ghosts of the other players to make your run a living bullethell. Furthermore each room contains a differing amount of pentagrams which can be used as a ghost to spawn into a monster, each with its own unique moveset. These creeps can be lvled after every floor, levels in human form of enemy player determine your evolution points. Human Form spends picked up cash to get new weapons, artifacts, moves etc. each weapon with its own moveset, each ability with its own uses. After a human form hits lvl 10 they can enter the boss portal on every floor to have one of the three tries at defeating the boss, problem is, the boss is also controlled by the enemy players, making this whole game a really competitive experience best enjoyed if all players have the gitgud mentality.
Soundtrack is amazing, fits the game perfect, really raw dark 8bit sounds whose rhythm still keeps you looped into the game.
Graphics can be seen on screens.
Only missing feature is online-multiplayer, in other aspects this is a game I support in every way and would buy again just to support development and show my gratitude for creating this piece of art.
Definitely worth more than 10bucks.
p.s. gitgud, dodge moves only, abuse the MoI, take the bow, crush the boss

12 hours of this game, and I've made it to the flagship 3 times, and he killed me every single time.  You'd think the difficulty would ramp up reasonably, but it's easy, and then you get to the boss and are blown apart in no time. Not to mention every playthrough is a gamble.  It makes it ridiculously hard (with the amount of luck, I'd say it's impossible) to actually get good at the game.  You can learn the mechanics and what everything does, but you can have a ship with the most badass guns, get boarded or get into a node with an environmental effect and the game can be over just like that.  I read a lot of people saying that's what they love about this game, but for me it's money wasted.  It's fun and worth it for a while, but when you make it to the flagship one playthrough and then the other you get boarded or shot to hell in the second sector it just gets old.  Especially after more than 5 hours of it.

Looking throught the reviews prior to purchase I saw so many comparisons between Diablo (2 and 3) and Path of Exile with Grim Dawn.  Not that I minded, I loved Diablo 2, enjoyed Diablo 3 and Path of Exile.
There are noticible things from D3 all over the place.  The lands to the west of Devils Crossing look very very similar to the lands west of New Tristram in D3.  Even the background music is almost carbon copy in some places.  Some of the sound effects and atmosperics will be very familiar to D3 players too
At first it's not a point I minded until I realized that it is Grim Dawn just trying to win over the Diablo fans (and they've succeded to a large degree - just look at the positive reviews).  Then I thought it's a shame, because Crate certainly have the talent to step out of the Blizzard shadow and should have made their own game from scratch.  Grim Dawn often feels like the developers looked at D3, dissected it, took the things they liked, replicated them and redid the bits they didn't like.
Mirroring someone elses vision  inevitably made the game OK to Good overall.
There are too many annoyances for it to be great.
The amount on screen is a bit lacking and while you can zoom in and out,  you can't really zoom out quite enough.  Because of this NPCs can shoot at you, cast spells and all sorts of other ranged shenanigans while they are way way off screen and GD does not allow you to blind fire in the direction the spell came from; you end up shooting the ground where your cursor is.
It's often not possible to see enemies behind the scenery too.  Where the elaborate tree canopies or walls disappear when the player is standing behind them, this doesn't happen for NPCs so half the time you're asking yourself who the **** just shot me???
Finding where your current objective is often just guesswork (objective markers don't show up until you're really close) and this is to the game's detriment.  There may be a few tasks to do in an area of the map, but because you've been wandering aimlessly killing everything everywhere to find your objective, only one of the tasks you do is meaningful, the rest are just wander back through the areas you just cleared out.
The map is no help either.  GD gives quick access to areas through rifts (not unlike the waypoints in D3).  Look on the world map and the rifts are roughly situated.  Switch to the detailed map to see which rift is closest your objective and you can't... the rifts don't show on the detailed map.  You will find yourself going to the wrong area because you weren't sure which rift to use.
This is not a game where you can say ''I'll have a quick 20 minutes in Grim Dawn'', because it takes that long to find anything.
The devotion points are a good idea but the celestial bodies screen where you asign your points is a mess.  Figuring out the best way to spend your points involves hovering over all of the stars to see what is on offer.
The game is too short.  The whole game feels about the size of 2 acts of Diablo 2.
All of that said Grim Dawn is still just enough fun to give it a recommendation.  Worth it on sale.

Captain's Edition Review
I had finally maxed out my sheilds and this was finally looking like it might be my winning run. Oh how wrong was I, I came across some aliens in need of help so I did, their reward, a fancy new weapon, sadly though my ship had taken some damage from the ordeal but no matter I thought. Then fate had it that a store would pop up, go back and waste precious feul, (yes I realise you can buy feul at stores but i was low on funds) or move on. I moved on, second Jump in the new sector I came across a Rebel scout drone, it had an Ion Blast (Something that can disable your systems) and a pair of drones. Feeling confident with my four sheilds and kickass weapon I went on the offensive.
Before I say what happens next I would like to say that I am in my opinion very experienced at this game but by no means close to mastering it.
Anyway, I decided to save my missles thinking I could buy more later, so I didn't even charge them, but then it happened, their Ion Blast must've been something out of ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t Landia because it rapid fires three blasts disabling my sheilds then its drones hammered away at my weapons while my sheilds struggled to come back online. Now I was in trouble, my weapons wounded I ordered every man onboard to fix them while I waited desperately for my missle to charge (Missles only need one power.) Finally my weapons were online but my sheilds were still down, I fired missle after missle while a volly of lasers tried to pierce the sheilds tried to take out the Ion Blast. I needed one of my six remaining missles to hit their drone control system or I was dead. I used every last missle and they all missed, unbelievable, I was about to die a terrible death, my crew hopefully would die from lack of oxygen (those sick ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s took out my O2 system too) before they were blown to pieces.
This is yet another wild and fun moment that can happen in FTL, the new release of FTL Captain's Edition adds more random events and some new features along with a brand spanking new alien race. For those who aren't aware of the awesomeness that is FTL I will explain, if you are already well aware please skip this paragraph. Now FTL is a game based around the Star Trek era rather than the Star Wars. You are Captain Kirk, or for Star Wars fans I guess Han Solo would compare, and you are the commander of an all mighty spacecraft, you have a section of usable power and then many systems to balance them between. You can decide to draft - or buy - more crewman who you find anywhere from stores to dark caves, and they range from humans to giant rock people each better at something than others. Speaking of buying things stores pop up here and there that you can buy from, at least one per sector anyway. Oh yeah and the evil federation is on your butt so you better move it because if they catch you you're in for some scary battles.
Now the newly released free DLC is in a word awesome, the indie developer added one of my personal favourite features, a system where you could save wherever you crew was, say one person manning the weapons, another engines and the last at the helm, and then you could move them wherever then press a button that returns them to their saved positions. This is especially helpful considering that your crew gets better at whatever they do and I would often have to name my charaters, Engine, Helm and Weapons. Along with this feature you can also see when you enter the Jump map (to see where you want to go next) it shows you where you can Jump from that position. I remember a time when I was low on feul and I Jumped over to a store thinking I could easily make it from their to the exit of the sector when I realised I couldn't Jump that far, I was forced to backtrack into enemy territory and I was low on feul, my story didn't end well.
Every now and then in the game you'll Jump somewhere and you have to make a decision, for example you come up to a cave, it looks abandoned your choices: Search through it, or leave. Usually upon your choice either something good - you find someone living inside and they join your crew, or bad - a wild madman hiding inside kills one of you crew. Cool I guess but the fourth time I saved giant mutant spiders the nerd in me had gotten bored, but no more! Now theres a whole bunch more of these guilty pleasure stories.
Another old feature that I really need to mention is the ability to pause the game, I do believe it's some new technology I've never seen it before. But seriously pausing FTL doesn't just give you a second to grab a bite but to also tell your crew where to go, what to fix and what things to target. Heck you can even teleport into the enemy ship, blow up a sub-system then teleport back to saftety!
All in all this is a spectacular game, and for only $15 it will give you hours of enjoyment along with a whole bunch of mods to keep you up long past midnight.

If I had to define FTL to you, I would be forced to say that it's an RPG Rouge-like Simulation game, and that makes it sound like♥♥♥♥♥♥ so ignore that bit. To do it justice: FTL is a game where you must go from your little wimpy ship at the beginning of comfortable space all the way to hell where you must battle the grand daddy of all ships... because of something or someone... the storyline is something I oft forget because this game is just so god damn good and intense with its gameplay that I don't worry about the story line.
Yes, this game at its core looks nothing more than controlling your cursor and clicking a couple enemy ships -- I thought the same exact thing when I saw trailers and looked the other way -- but this game is much more than that: it's going at the long journey to the Flagship again and again and again until you've earned the experience and knowledge to accomplish beating this game; it's experimenting with all sorts of different ships, weapon combos, and crews until you find one that resonates with you; it's feeling a sense of absolute redemption once you see that mother♥♥♥♥ing Flagship explode into a million, beautiful pieces after all that work. And as you experience all this, you'll realize quickly that there's a lot of deep management that goes into this game, management that goes way beyond a couple cursor clicks.
The replay value is very high, I assure you. A Rogue-like, if you are unfamiliar, is a perma-death game in which you must progress through levels in which everything down to your very character is randomly generated, as a result the game is fairly short to save being tedious, and makes each run a vastly different experience. FTL is such a game; the only things saved after a run-through are your scores/achievements, your unlocked ships, and your real-life brain. You're playing to get better, suffice to say, and I promise that is more than enough to keep me and its fanbase to continue playing FTL again and again.
Both the audio and aesthetic in this game are superb. The music resonates so very well with every quiet lurking in a nebula and every frantic battle, that the only way to do it justice is to experience it yourself. As for graphics, I hope you didn't expect too much from an Indie game with pixel art. Despite that, the aesthetic does a great job of blending in with everything in the game, and sometimes I forget I'm playing anything graphically inferior to Skyrim with 200+ mods.
Now for the downside: since this game thrives on repeated trial-and-error runs, that inevitably opens itself to lots and lots of keyboard smashing, monitor punching, rage eatings at the local In-N-Out, and lots more fun anger stuff. Although the learning curve is smoothed out very quickly -- one or two runs after the tutorial should make you fully comfortable with the game -- FTL, to this day for me, never fails to be infuriatingly difficult at times. There's not much getting around it: know that there is stress to playing this game.
To end, FTL is absolutely superb and shines especially in its gameplay. As long as you can stomach getting kicked in the balls repeatedly by the RNG (Fire Emblem fans will know what I'm talking about), you're in for one of the most fantastic Indie games available here on Steam. Just remember: nobody likes Stealth Ship B.

This game has the best parkour in any game I've played, and is a truly unique and pleasant gaming experience in my opinion. I especially like the way that the game forces you to RUN by setting enemies with guns on you most levels. This element of danger and the need to keep moving makes the parkour much more fun - you can't often plan your route carefully, you just have to see an opening and hope you're skilled enough to make the jump. In other levels there are more complicated puzzle rooms that you may have to take longer to figure out, which creates a nice balance.
My only problem with the game is the combat focused levels, which become more common later on. When the game forces you to fight your way through an area rather than parkour around the enemies, it can become frustrating. The combat is quite clunky and while I don't mind taking out the occasional lone guard or even stealing his gun and sniping his buddies, a whole room of machine gun wielding maniacs who instakill you whenever you try to stop and take one out is a bit much for a parkour game. These few levels where this becomes overwhelming detract from the other parts of the game, where the simple combat system is useful and fun but isn't the focus of the whole level.
That said, the game is still really fun for the most part, and it's worth buying if it's on sale - it is quite short, I finished it in about 6 hours, so take that into account in the price you're willing to pay.
P.S. I had some technical issues with screen tearing when I turned the game on, this is a common problem and can usually be fixed by either forcing Vsync on through the graphics driver, or updating/reinstalling your drivers, which for some reason fixed it for me.

Great game.
Its essentially UFO Defense with some beefed up FX, streamlined combat system, and enhanced storyline.
The soldiers are split up into classes now, and each class has skills that you can choose as you level them up.
Double edged sword really, on one hand the soldiers become ultra badass.. On the other hand, you'll be reloading your game when one dies because they are so much stronger than a new recruit- especially late game.
Base mechanics are very similar to older installments, being 2D with an ant-farm view of all your structures. Of course, theres some new types of buildings to make but a lot of it will be similar stuff that was in previous games.
(Living quarters, labs, alien containment, hangers, radar, etc.. )
Economy is also very similar to older installments, you get funding but most of your paydirt comes from selling alien tech and producing wares in your foundries.
Research is an area that really shines in this game- a lot of new gear/tech is available, and your autopsies/live-research provide more than just lore. Theres buffs you can unlock, helpful info on combating aliens, and more.
Combat is the main overhaul of this game. Moving and shooting are streamlined and theres no longer a need to do time-unit math. The maps are also more tactical. Soldiers can utilize cover more effectively, crash through windows, or even zipline to the top of structures. Flanking an enemy gives huge bonuses and forming a parameter is a big deal.
Overall, the graphics are amusingly fun and most of the changes are good ones. If you liked the first X-Com, its safe to say you'll hit the ground running and enjoy this all the way to the very end. There may be a few small caveats but I feel those are mostly debateable and would vary from player to player. I haven't gotten the DLC, so my experience is solely from the vanilla game- which I enjoyed very much. At 70+ hours, this game is worth the full cost.

In a gaming world full of handholding, uninspired battle systems, and just sheer crap, Divinity is a shining diamond in the rough.
Graphics - 9/10:
Loot-based, dungeon-crawling RPGs are never known for their graphics so I will rate it on a level equivalent to similar games like Torchlight 2 and Diablo 3.  I'm going to put this simply - Divinity is ****ing gorgeous.  The art direction is spot on, the colors are bright and bring the world to life, and the character designs are great too.  You won't feel like you're trudging through the same damn dungeon or cave for the 50th time in a row.  Everywhere feels unique.  You'll traverse vast forests of green, blistering cold mountain tops, firey fields of skeletons and so much more.  It's a well-imagined world that makes the game worth of a 9/10 score in the graphics department.
Sound - 8/10:
So don't expect full voice overs or anything like that.  There will be spoken dialogue from time to time- particularly from your main characters, but for the most part NPCs' dialogue is all written (but very well written mind you).  So why am I giving it an 8 for sound?  Because the music is some of the best I've heard in a video game...EVER!
Story - 8/10:
You're a Source Hunter (yeah I know...just another cliche name for a hero that's received his title and known for aboloshing evil magic and foes from the land).  But don't let that make you overlook what's an otherwise pretty good story as far as loot-based RPGs go.  You start out by coming to town to solve a murder.  I think this mystery-style beginning really helps drive the games gameplay.  Divinity: OS expects you to listen to NPCs, pick up on subtle hints found in text and side character dialogue, and really just discover, discover, discover to unravel the story and new missions.
It's worth noting that some may as a result get really frustrated by this lack of handholding; I on the other hand think it's great and really helps add to the game's charm.
Gameplay - 11/10:
This is where the game shines.  All aspects of this game are fun.  As stated earlier, the clue-finding and unravelling of the story are fun.  You'll be posed with hints, clues, and puzzles which will lead to scratching your head, yet always persistant on unlocking the next series of quests.
Beyond this, the interactions amongst your party's characters and NPCs is fun.  Divinity includes a rock-paper-scissors style mini-game to determine the outcome of conversations.  I know it sounds weird, but it's actually really fun.  If an NPC is not particularly interested in giving up information to you, then you can try to beat him at a game of RPS.
Where this game truly shines though is in the battle system.  Everything is action point and turn-based driven.  Depending on speed and initiative, an order to character turns will be determined at the beginning of the fight (similar to FFX).  Character's can obviously use special skills and spells to influence their turn postions.  You also have action points for each turn which again is stat-driven based on a characters constitution among other things.  Obviously different skills and spells take different amount of points to cast depending on their power and your overall skill level.
So far I'm sure this sounds like a pretty standard turn-based battle system.  BUT WAIT - THERE's MORE.  Truly the best part about Divinity is the unique use of elemental environments.  Characters can cast spells, blow up barrles, and manipulate the environment in all sorts of ways to overcome foes.
Group of enemies standing in a puddle of water?  Shoot an electric bolt to make them all stunned for 3 turns.  No puddle of water?  No problem- cast a rain spell first across the battlefield to create your own puddles then shock it.
Of course that's a simplistic approach that you'll learn how to do in the first 10 minutes of the game.  I won't mention the other awesome environmental elements you can manipulate 'cause I think Divinity is one of those games where part or if its spirit is the unknown.  There's A LOT to learn in this game.  There is, for instance, both crafting and blacksmithing skills in the game, that is so deep and complex, that after 40 hours of playing, I haven't even begun to scratch the surface yet.
Overall 10/10:  It's one of the best RPGs I've ever played - hands down.  You're really not doing yourself any favors by passing on this game.  In fact, I'd call you a fool if you did.  This game should be played by every and any person that considers themselves a gamer.

I don't want to comment on this game as a game because only the first episode has been released as of this writing.
I will say that if you're not familiar with the Game of Thrones story, this game will be utterly incomprehensible to you. It's not like Walking Dead, where you can pick up what's happening right away. You will be lost.
Also, there seems to be an audio issue where when you pause, the game will pause on the sound and play static.
edit:
Okay, the game is done now.
I'd still say it's incomprehensible if you're not familiar with the Game of Thrones story. The impact of interacting with characters from the main story will be lost on you.
As for the game itself, the ending will likely leave you feeling ambiguous. On the one hand, it very much fits the theme and tone of Game of Thrones. On the other hand, it ends very "cliffhanger"-ish and it feels like they will need a sequel just to finish the story. It is not a real resolution to the story and therefore doesn't feel like a satisfactory conclusion. (Unlike the TWD and WAU games, which felt like they had good conclusions while also leaving the possibility for sequels.)
If you're a fan of the books or the show and the prospect of interacting with Tyrion Lannister, Jon Snow, and Daenerys Targaryen excites you, by all means, get the game. (Though, you'll have to interact with Ramsay Bolton too.)
If you're looking for a good story as a story itself and you're not crazy about GoT, you may want to hold off.

Yes. Definitely yes.
Full disclosure: I'm a huge fan of ASOIAF, have watched every episode, read every book (even #4 and #5, and boy were they a hard slog!), so this is from somebody who already knows the canon inside and out. If you're completely new to the ASOIAF world, your experience will most likely vary, but I can't "unlearn" what I've learned of Westeros. Maybe the game could use more exposition, I don't know and can't now, as I'm not approaching it from the angle of somebody who'd need it.
I like TellTale's graphics style, even though there are some, in my opinion, unnecessary instances of blurred outlines and pixellation. But not enough to bother me, and they're certainly good enough to set the stage and provide atmosphere. And the modeling of the known (from the show) characters is awesome. TellTale nails every one of them. You don't need to be told who you're facing, because you'll know instantly. Voice acting is superb, but that's to be expected when they're using the original actors. Still, it's important, because to me it would have been extremely jarring if I'd had to listen to the game's Lord Tyrion using anybody but Peter Dinklage's voice now that I've watched the show. If I'd only read the books, it wouldn't matter, obviously.
The episode itself is too short, way too short, but that's not because I feel that I've been "cheated", it's because it's done so well that I can't wait for the next episode. There are six of them, after all, so if it keeps its current pace I'll get a total of 12-15 hours out of the whole thing, which is not at all bad value. The reason I'm saying it's too short is because I love it so much, and that's really a compliment, isn't it?
I can't say that I feel that my choices have that much of an effect, but maybe a bunch of additional playthroughs will change that. It really doesn't matter all that much anyway to me, as I just wanted to be "in the show", and this game certainly gave me a lot of that.
"I'm really talking to Tyrion! Me! Squee!" Yes, I know I'm a hopeless fanboi, but that's what I was hoping for and that's what I got, so I am well satisfied, even if it turns out I can't really change the story that much. As a matter of fact, maybe me *not* being The Most Important Character In The Game is really what I like about it. After all, most games place you in exactly that role, and it's quite refreshing to, for once, be somebody who's caught up in something bigger than him or herself, just trying desperately to survive, rather than The Knight In Shining Armor Here To Save The World, a setting that I also quite enjoy, witness the God knows how many hours I've spent in games like Skyrim, all of which I've enjoyed, but it's also interesting to be an insignificant underdog for once, being acted upon rather than acting upon everybody and everything else.
TL;DR If you're a fan of Game of Thrones/ASOIAF, you could do a lot worse than this. It's true to canon, hits all the right notes and has a bunch of your favorite characters and a believable storyline. If you're not, I really don't know. If you just enjoy a good story, I think you'll like it regardless.

Let me share my INCREDIBLE first few hours of dying light:
At first the game was a struggle, it took me a while to even be able to freerun through the tutorial course xD
Once I got the hang of it, the gameplay seemed slightly dull and mediocre.... until I got through my first night.
My first night run in Dying Light was THE best experience Ive ever had playing a video game.
Seeking a challenge I had my settings on the highest difficulty with Zombie Invasion on Always.
This was a mistake.
Following the end of the cutscene of your first volatile encounter I ran into three volatiles within 30 seconds of running. Panicking, I ran into the heart of the city.
This was also a mistake.
There was no light Whatsoever and I walked into a steet, FILLED with infected, their figures could only be seen as eerie silouettes in the moonlight. I took to the roofs as quickly as possible, so as to use the moonlight to plot a path, My heart pounding in my chest as I could hear the volatiles snarling behind me barely missing me as I scrambled onto the roofs. There must have been 5+ volatiles chasing me, I had one medkit left, and I didnt pack any diapers.
I ran like never before.
Addrenaline coursing through me, I ran at top speed, never missing a step. I could almost feel the cool night air running through my hair. But the volatiles are relentless. I could hear their snarling and breathing getting louder and louder as they slowly caught up to me.
I missed a precision jump (mechanics for which are done perfectly in the game ) and plummeted into the dark abyss of the streets below.
I kept running, it was all I could do, taking sharp turns in alleyways and vaulting the smaller obstacles, as packs of zombies clawed at me, tugging my shirt, slowing me down and damaging me where they could. Despite slowing down to use my final medkit I was gaining ground. Laughing at the insanity that is night running.
Until I hit a dead end.
In a moment of brilliance, I remembered the Light. The UV flashlight, Spikes words echoing in my mind "If you run into one of those volatiles give them a blast of UV light".  I spun around and shined the light directly in the face of a volatile, making full eye contact with one of the grotesque husks of a being that had been chasing me, before it recoiled from the light. The sight of it still haunts me to this day. I was not bothered by its rotting flesh or jagged teeth, but rather the look in its bloodshot eyes. It almost looked ...not happy, but content as if it somehow knew my situation was hopeless.
Time seemed to slow down as I kicked the creature in its exposed ribcage, frantically searching for a way out. There it was. A single perfect ramp angling toward an adjacent roof. Without hesitation I pushed past the creature as 2 more arrived to seal the alleyway, each hitting me in turn. With 17HP I somehow slipped between them,  ran up the ramp and back onto the moonlit rooftops. I could hear my own panting in tune with Kranes as we ran towards the MASSIVE suspension bridge.
There must have been hundreds of zombies on that bridge.
I ran, jumping car to car, knowing that with one wrong step, I would surely perish. I kept running, night blind. My path barely visible in the low flames of wrecked cars. I tripped and scrambled, screamed and prayed, desperately trying to get off that god forsaken bridge. I ran and ran until I reached the center of the bridge, which had been destroyed, presumably in order to quarantine the area. There was no way out, in front there was nothing but a hole in the bridge, looming what seemed like a thousand meters over pitch black water. To my rear the volatiles had caught up with me, now within 20 meters. I took one last look at the murky black water and jumped.
I saw the distant UV lights of a settlement when I finally surfaced and began the long swim back.
I managed to get back to the tower that night, counting my blessings. For I  doubt many others could've survived that run.
