Great game.
Its essentially UFO Defense with some beefed up FX, streamlined combat system, and enhanced storyline.
The soldiers are split up into classes now, and each class has skills that you can choose as you level them up.
Double edged sword really, on one hand the soldiers become ultra badass.. On the other hand, you'll be reloading your game when one dies because they are so much stronger than a new recruit- especially late game.
Base mechanics are very similar to older installments, being 2D with an ant-farm view of all your structures. Of course, theres some new types of buildings to make but a lot of it will be similar stuff that was in previous games.
(Living quarters, labs, alien containment, hangers, radar, etc.. )
Economy is also very similar to older installments, you get funding but most of your paydirt comes from selling alien tech and producing wares in your foundries.
Research is an area that really shines in this game- a lot of new gear/tech is available, and your autopsies/live-research provide more than just lore. Theres buffs you can unlock, helpful info on combating aliens, and more.
Combat is the main overhaul of this game. Moving and shooting are streamlined and theres no longer a need to do time-unit math. The maps are also more tactical. Soldiers can utilize cover more effectively, crash through windows, or even zipline to the top of structures. Flanking an enemy gives huge bonuses and forming a parameter is a big deal.
Overall, the graphics are amusingly fun and most of the changes are good ones. If you liked the first X-Com, its safe to say you'll hit the ground running and enjoy this all the way to the very end. There may be a few small caveats but I feel those are mostly debateable and would vary from player to player. I haven't gotten the DLC, so my experience is solely from the vanilla game- which I enjoyed very much. At 70+ hours, this game is worth the full cost.

I don't write reviews often, but i just had to with this game. Everlasting Summer was recently translated to English and in my opinion is very overlooked and underrated, more people definitely need to find this amazing gem of a visual novel.
This was my first time playing a visual novel and i probably won't ever forget it, the Story is absolutely amazing and very interesting at that with a total of 13 endings and different choices and routes to take (i highly recommend getting all endings to get the whole story of the game). You can easily find spoiler free Guides or Walkthroughs on how to get certain endings if you want, which is what i ended up doing. You can automatically fast forward through all the scenes which you've already seen and the game will automatically stop when it reaches words or scenes you haven't read or seen.
The music in Everlasting Summer is fantastic and probably one of the best parts of the game, trust me, it will get stuck in your head for a while.
The art was overall pretty good, although certain scenes were drawn and had slight quirks, it can be easily overlooked and actually adds a certain charm to it and you get used to it, the background CGs more than make up for it.
On average the game should take about 15-20 hours to get all endings and the game is free + it also has free DLC! The game is about 800 MB and is definitely worth installing and trying out.
Steam however has the game censored, but you can go to the official website of Everlasting Summer
and get a simple drag & drop patch to restore the censored scenes if you wish.
TL;DR Amazing free visual novel with lots of endings, fantastic music, great CGs and an amazing story. Give it a try!

Hoo, boy!  This game is brutal!  But it's also one of the most fun I've had the pleasure of playing.  Every run is different and you'll likely die a lot more than you succeed.  One run you may find yourself swimming in powerful weapons to use and tons of scrap you can use to buy and upgrade stuff.  Another run you'll have to be a miser, conserving what little scrap resources you have and usually just barely surviving battles that on a more successful, lucky run would be a cakewalk.  It's that allure of great success that keeps you fighting through the failures, and it works amazingly well.
The game looks and plays well with a great UI and the ships and backgrounds look great.  You can pause in the middle of combat to plan your moves, so it's not like most RTS games where you need to go crazy with hotkeys; you can actually take your time and make the most of your attacks, which is very welcome in a game as hard as this.  The game is randomly generated, meaning every playthrough will have different encounters, places, ect.  The random events will always keep you on your toes, with life-or-death situations being mere occupational hazards in most cases (of course, you want to keep your crew alive and well, so don't take too many unneccessary risks).  Expect to die, but always strive to win.  Oh, and make sure you get a teleporter and a cloaking device for the end.  Well, a teleporter if nothing else.
The final boss fight actually my only big criticism (as well as a particularly annoying weapon added in the Advanced Edition Update/Expansion, the flak cannon).  Of course, once you've played through the game once, you'll know what to expect, but to go from running away from the enormous enemy fleet to confronting it head-on, it feels like they were going for giving the player a feeling of "Oh yeah, it's payback time," but it comes across as unfair, especially the first time you get there.  Again, it almost requires you to have a teleporter, but yeah, you'll see when you get there...or IF you get there (muahahaha).
So yeah, if you have $10 (or your regional equivalent) to spare, get this game.  I also recommend spending an extra $4 so you can buy the exquisite soundtrack by Ben Prunty.  Seriously, there's great stuff all over this game, so buy it NAOW...unless you want to get it on discount.  Yeah, that's always nice, too.

This game is simple, awesome, fun, and dangerously addicting. There's literally two buttons, and those are used to attack on either side of you when enemies get in your range. The more attacks you do without missing or getting hit, the more delicious points you rack up. Simple stuff.
Except not really.
Enemies start off hilariously easy. You'll be punching through time travelling nazi skulls like cake at the beginning. Soon enough one punch won't take down certain enemies. Then certain enemies will teleport on the other side of you, so you'll need to respond with a sweet roundhouse, then punch them again when they teleport once more. Then you'll fight robots that take a ton of hits. Then you'll fight kung fu masters who teleport like four times! It just adds onto the insanity that is Kung Fury.
Soon enough you'll start being a kung fu master. You'll learn the combos to take down each enemy, executing them in half-second and you watch yourself tear through each enemy. You'll be so aware on what's on both sides of you you'll grow a third eye just to watch your character punch, kick, shoot, and deliver justice to each and every last enemy.
Once you take your three hits, you start over and try to beat your scores. I keep coming back for mor justice delivering each time.
TL;DR: It's like One Finger Death Punch but with better style and a super rad soundtrack.

I can't even begin to describe how GORGEOUS this game is! It's like you're literally inside a watercolor masterpiece world! I would put this on the same level as Okami for aesthetic value :) Yes, the rhyming does feel forced (because it is) especially during the dialogue, but that just adds to the quirky-ness of the Lemurian world.
I found the battle system interesting. It took me a while to get used to because I'd never played a game with this timer-turn-based strategy system (though I'm sure it's not the first of its kind). But once I got the hang of how it worked, I was surprised, and elated, by how thoughtful your moves need to be, particularly in boss battles, to be successful and effective. However, you could certainly get through this game by simply throwing your most powerful moves at the monsters, you just won't be nearly as efficient. Some may consider that a downside to the game, but I think it is an upside: you can progress through and enjoy the story whether you want to play strategically or not, allowing more skill levels to be able to enjoy the game.
There is also a significant amount of exploring you can do to find bonuses, which I simply loved. This game exceeded my expectations in every way, and I would highly recommend it to anyone! As of this review (about 16 hours of gameplay), I have completed the main plot and all of the side quests (that I have found anyway), but I still have a bit more exploration to do to find the remaining hidden items in all the areas.
I did experience a few glitches, such as Aurora's hair disappearing during battles and visual stutters near the end of the game, but nothing that effected gameplay.

Long version
I saw this game when it first came out , and i said oh well lets fly the jolly roger. Then after i finished it , i just went and bought it . My experience was so good and felt those weird thingies called emotions that actually i shed a tear (meaning i had to literally wipe my eyes.. those onion-cutting ninjas). The selling points of this game are the atmosphere and the plot. But i will explain all of it below
Child of Light is tagged as a RPG , but offers you no choices in the plot element. But (and it is a big but) offers character customization (talents and occuli) and the most important thing character development . For me RPGs should be like that. You see as the time passes that Aurora and her companions grow up emotionally and stand up to the task .
The thing that made me play this game was the atmosphere . Graphics , dialogues , music are all so immersive that after 12 hours of playing i realized it was morning and i should tuck myself in bed and let the game and complete it later.
arent realistic . Instead they follow a fantasy and are dreamlike , but that doesnt stop them for being stunning and once in a while you stop to enjoy the view .
is a nice background which not only doesnt bother you but you like to hear it .. i cant find the words how well the soundtrack accompanies the game.
are in verse , meaning they are poems. They are fun , yet you understand the characters and their motivations and you want to help em .  I always like the dialogeus and read them through but at times speaking in verse can be overwhelming .
Before  saying anything about the story i must say that this is a game which a child of 8 years can play . There is no blood , no cursing , a little jump scaring (you can always scout with the firefly) , and a simple plot(thougt simple doesnt mean not beautiful)
. You are a princess of Austria and somehow you wake up in the middle of a dark scary forest away from your papa . Also you mist find the moon and the stars and defeat the evil queen umbra. How the hell a little child will do this ? . Of course with the help of the forest lady , Indignicus , and your companions ! each one has his/her own story and motivation and flaws . As the game goes on Aurora will grow up (changing her model) and finally will be an adult. Aurora is not either a warrior or a wizard... she is just a princess ... how you play is up to you. And that is another thing i love about this game.

Well things are simple... you see the timebar , you see when everyone is going to take action and how fast they are gonna do it. Every character ( Aurora included) has strenghs and weaknesses , same goes for enemies. You can change chars by swapping them in battle. You dont get punished for changing a character . After a while you can indentify the enemies and know what to do . What should be mentioned is that you can avoid all battles except bosses . Also you can run from them.
Go see the screenshots . you fly up and high and the wind brushes your hair and you are free. You are almost always airbound (at least i did it) , and everything is within reach either by you or the shiny blue ball.
Overall if you like fairy tales this game is just for you . Even if you dont, i think you can find a place in your heart for Lemuria and Aurora . This game is a piece or art in which you can actually play . the only bad thing i find is that the game is short and has little to no replay value .

Generally this game is OK, but some of you can be suprised by a high difficulty level on the beginning, which is just a result of a bad character creation choices and choosing wrong paths of exploration.
- Tactics demanding turn-based combat. Running blindly toward your enemies almost always ends with loading the game.
- Full impact on your team actions and development.
- Interesting system of magic (besides of magic being a bit OP)
- Maybe a bit 'mocky' but there's an illusory feel of freedom of choice - i didn't tested yet if theres a chance to finish this game while killing every NPC in it, but i have (at least)  feeling that it's possible.
- Lots of good loot, game is rewarding checking out every drawer and barrel (not as Skyrim)
- Convenient inventory and crafting system
- Perks and Traits like in Fallout series
- Low graphic requirements
- No need of mana and ammo for bows/crossbows
- Nice item and skills designs. Couple of really nice locations too.
- Climate and game environment. You keep discovering it after a while, like in a Dungeon Siege series, there's a lot of trivia going on around here.
- Dellicate humour here and there.
- Knowing the fact that from pigs bowels and block of wood you can make a great bow.
- Game mechanics is too much about spilling stuff on the ground. It's a nice addition to have but it shouldnt suppose to be the main aspect of every combat. 9 out of 10 cases you will have to watch the steps of your characters and choose their walking paths carefully. Devs should reduce the damage inflicted by ground modifiers because now its too much 'ground is lava' game.
- Craftings is artificially suppressed by cost of buying skills and slow leveling. It's another RPG where crafted items never gonna be used as main weapons if you're not invested every precious skill points in smithing.
- Balancing of powers. Magic is way OP to might. At least at the beginning. I may be wrong because I didn't tested Rogue character and backstabing. But when I started to play this game with Warrior and Archer it was hard to defeat anybody. Every skeleton was a challenge.
- Minimal voice acting, and lack of distinctive NPC's. It's hard to tell in the game who is who and where he was. Especially if you have no good memory for names. The main quest characters at least suppose to be originally voice acted, and portraits should be bigger and more unique (every person looks the same on it)
- Map in this game is basically useless, there's no tags of main NPC's and places. you can always put your own tags but 'aint nobody got time for that.'
- Journey Quest Log is way too laconic, and mostly useless.
- Game is maybe not linear but it force you to stick with the main story. All attempts of doing something in wrong order ends with brutal death of your company. Maybe not directly but the monsters level are dependent to the game main quest.
For example: at the beginning i unintentionally let one zombie into the city. He killed all of the city guards by himself (over 30 men) and spilled his green goo over all the area, every run through the city ended with dead by poison. (->1 con)
- For the gamers like myself (natural born betatesters - chaotic good) - those who like to go 'not-with-the-line-of-scenario' game creates sometimes weird unpredicted consequences and unsolvable quests (lack of good QA i guess), you have to always have some spare older save files, do not quick save the game on a same slot whole time.
- Didn't tested Multi because I don't have friends. At least friends who invest 60 bucks in a video game, lol.
8/10
It's a good game, but it would be great if it had online multiplayer.

I'm not sure if I'm missing something, but I just didn't love this game. Once you get past the lol factor of playing a communist dating game, there's really not much to it.
I didn't find any of the characters new or relatable, least of all the protagonist, whose 'completely average in every way' schtick has been totally played out by essentially every other media form on planet earth, yet everyone likes him for whatever reason. Folks, we got us a bona-fide Gary Sue. He's unsocible and awkward to a fault, this much is establshed within the first 10 minutes, but he somehow gets along swimmingly in a camp full of girls. The fact that he isn't actually given a face in the art is a testament to how little work was put into him.
All of the romance options are based on overused cliches: you have the tsundere girl, the mischevious girl, the shy girl, the wholesome girl, to name a few. You name an anime trope, it's there. And Hatsune Miku is there, in Soviet Russia, for whatever reason? That probably broke a copyright law or ten. The fact that they're all based on anime cliches is jarring, considering its set in the Soviet Union.
The character art is also, like, really bad. The backgrounds are nice, but are overshadowed by the poorly done characters. The character designs themselves look incredibly forced- it seems like the designers were trying incredibly hard to make them look like anime/manga characters (see: Hatsune Miku) and totally missed the mark. Spiky bangs, unnatural hair colors, eyes the size of saucers, etc. work in anime, but this isn't anime, and they are clearly SUPPOSED to look like anime. Just incredibly forced.
This game was also clearly designed by men, for men; the character designs of all the romance options are blatant fanservice. There are a lot of clearly fanservice moments, too, such as spying on one girl in the shower, walking in on a girl changing, and watching two other girls (one literally like 12 years old, wtf) fight in the showers. Hatsune Miku's opening scene is a shameless crotch/panty shot (again, where did she come from?), and the girls spend like 30% of their time in beachwear (in Russia???). Like if that's something you're interested in, go for it, but the pedophilia options freak me out (and should freak you out too. I hope like hell that they freak you out too) and the fanservice isn't even well done. Everything looks like it was drawn by a 13 year old boy with the help of a 'How to Draw Manga' book he bought on sale at a craft store. Like, if you're going to do fanservice, do it well.
Gameplay itself is incredibly slow. You only get to make a few choices a day, and between those choices is what seems like an eternity of Semyon musing to himself- and oh, how he muses. His thoughts are full of psuedo-intellectual angst and are painful to read. The dialogue itself (Semyon actually interacts once or twice with other people when he gets tired of his whiny inner monologue) is fairly uninteresting. I'd chalk some of that up to being lost in translation, as I did the English version, but the rest must have been plain unoriginality. Part of what slows the game down so much is, I think, that every action is described by our friend Semyon, who is way, way too thorough.
The creators didn't seem to be able to make up their mind: is this game driven by romance or mystery? They get in the way of each other in Everlasting Summer. They tried to fit too much into one game and the focus seems scattered. One or the other needed to take the back burner, but instead, they were forced to coexist as equals, muddling the gameplay. If this was a mystery with a romance subplot or a romance with a mystery subplot, it would've played out more smoothly.
TLDR; The plotline isn't terrible, but it's not great. It's CERTAINLY not good enough to make up for how flat, uninventive, and crudely drawn the characters are. That being said, it's fun to laugh at the communist propoganda and the game's ridiculous enough to kill a few hours, and the music isn't awful. I played it through once, had some laughs, no harm no foul. I mean it's free, so  why not?

So I decided to uninstall this clicker game a few days ago after hoping that some features would be fixed so they'd actually work.
As there does not seem to be an update with fixes to the major problems I'll assume they have not been fixed yet;
Items: So once you hit floor level 100-101 you have a CHANCE to gain an item and a supposed guaranteed item.
The items themself aren't even working properly. The affixes on these items, such as "reduces cooldown by x%" do not work at all once you cap (75%) the Illness that does the same thing.
Certain other affixes are not working properly either and in fact do the opposite of what they're supposed to do.
Then there's the "crafting". Basically you need a certain amount of "parts" to reroll the stats on a certain item with a chance for it to either get a better version or get a worse version, fair enough I guess and that's not the issue with it; besides having to get the parts (you need a higher amount to reroll higher quality items, which is ridiculous due to the sheer lack of items you'll be getting) you also need CRYSTALS. Now these crystals can either be obtained by BUYING them or have a chance to come out of briefcases that spawn from time to time.
This is a major design flaw. It appears they want you to buy crystals to then wasted it on some RNG thing which has a chance of screwing you over that also needs a high amount of another currency (parts).
The devs bring out new "sets" (note: no set bonuses) of items while neglecting to fix broken affixes and now they're even throwing in a "DLC pack" of €20 with items (of which the affixes frequently don't even work as intended or at all).
I've rebirthed (Amnesia'd, whatever) a bunch of times only to slowly progress on to a few additional floors after taking forever to get there again and while they state they "raised the chance to gain an item at higher levels" I have not seen anything of the sort. In fact it's actually the opposite.
My last 2 rebirths, after passing floor 101, I did NOT get ANY item whatsoever.
Moving on to the actual unlockable monsters/heroes; Eventually you'll get slammed into a ceiling as you'll need a substantial number of teeth to unlock the next monster which'll take forever to get (and a heap of rebirths) and once you unlock it you'll get slammed against a few more ceilings all the way until the last monster.
Then when you unlock the last monster, it supposedly trashes everything for you and you can basically sit afk and level it up until you hit "MAX" on damage, teeth and whatnot.
The floor level limit is 4825. Been there, done that and after rebirthing the game stopped giving me items.
So, for those that are reading this game's reviews and are wondering "should I play this?" My advice to you: Unless you don't like your life and wouldn't mind going full retard, stay away from this game and play another clicker instead. Feels more like a cashgrab thing (you need 200 crystals to gain a certain amount of souls. Then when you're 1000+ floors higher than where you were when you spent those 200 crystals you'll noticed that you can now gain 5-10 times more souls from the same amount of crystals and the pace you gain them from briefcases, due to "chance to" is way too slow) without much needed fixes to certain features of this game.

There aren't many games that have made me shed tears. The only games that have been able to get to me on an emotional level are Metal Gear Solid 3 and 4 and The Walking Dead game. Ever since the release of SimGirls many years ago, I've been a fan of Dating Sims, and while Katawa Shoujo had very deep and emotional moments, never surprised me in such a way as Everlasting Summer.
I've never been, (and probably won't ever be), one to actually buy a Dating Sim. I've enjoyed many, but never enough to put more than a few dollars into. When I saw that this game was free, I knew I would have to give it a chance; especially since the game was about the Soviet Union.
I booted up the game, and about twenty minutes through, encountered a jump-scare. Usually, I find them to be cheesy instead of scary, but with the otherwise cheerful atmosphere, it surprised me greatly. The first character I went for was Ulyana, which, instead of focusing on the romantic side of their relationship, focused purely on the friendship between the two characters. The good ending with her touched me very very deeply, leaving several questions, but a very satisfying answer as well.
On the game itself, it plays just like you'd think it would. The background images are simply perfect, and while the characters themselves don't look nearly as good as the areas they live in, are still very well-drawn.
What surprised me the most, however, was the Miku ending, which is absolutely insane. Comparing the other girls' good endings with that insanity makes you question whether the two are from the same game. Miku's ending is downright horrifying at times, and is well worth a replay just to see it.
What makes this game even better is the amount endings: 13 in all. While some endings are better than others, all are beautifully-written and have satisfying conclusions for our protagonist, INCLUDING Lena's bad ending, which is incredibly sad.
If this game had a pricetag on it, I'd probably highly recommend it. Since it's free, however, I demand that anyone who enjoys Dating Sims to pick this up; you won't be disappointed.

This game is exactly what it says it is! A trippy, fast-paced, sci-fi sports game where funky robots throw balls at each other. Sounds simple, right? Honestly, it sounds like it might be
simple, or even boring, but trust me - it's not.
Ah, yes. This game reminds me of the days when games were built for fun, when small studios would think of a good idea and
with it, without worrying about whether or not it fit current market trends. This game is surprisingly original as a result; I can't think of any other game like it. It scratches an itch that most other games simply don't.
I was pleasantly surprised by how robust this game is. The map designs are highly varied, there are a ton of powerups to grant your robot different abilities (flaming balls, homing balls, giant balls, and boomerang balls to name a few), your robot will "level up" and unlock new cosmetics, and there is a crafting system. There are a plethora of different game modes to keep you adapting to new styles of play. There's just so much here to keep a person entertained, but for some reason, none of this came across to me when I watched trailers for it. Truly, this is a game that you have to play for yourself in order to understand how awesome it is.
To try and describe it though, this game is all about skill. Learning how to react quickly and precisely is the key to victory. The matches are fast and furious, but at times feel like a ballet - occasionally your robot will drift, skid, or soar through the air, and you will find that it takes some careful tactics in order to avoid becoming exposed and killed. You will also find, occasionally, that you will be in the "zone" and, as if in a trance, start to rack up massive amounts of kills while jamming to the beat of the killer soundtrack.
Speaking of which, this game has some of the best music I've heard in recent memory. Finally, I've found a game where I don't have to turn the music off! If you like electronic music at all, I can promise you that you will fall in love with the soundtrack immediately. To make things even better, the psychedelic arenas
and change colour when the songs turn over, which only serves to enhance the whole experience. "Stimulating" is the word I would use to describe the fusion of sights and sound, and it is a stroke of pure brilliance on the developers' parts.
I really can't think of enough good things to say about this game, but with that said, there are a few downsides that I feel I should mention:
Firstly, the community seems to be very small. This can lead to a deficit of viable servers, or servers that are crowded with bots. It's easy enough to use the server browser to find out where the human players are at, but if you elect to use the "quick match" feature, you will be thrown into the ring with bots every time.
Secondly, if your ping is higher than 100, you will quickly find that you are at a marked disadvantage against people who have, say, 30-50 ping. Joining the right server is crucial for this reason, but it's a bit disappointing that the netcode doesn't do anything to compensate for this.
Thirdly, you will encounter the occasional hacker. It seems that the community is largely hacker-free, but this unfortunate element does seem to exist to some degree. Thankfully, the game has a votekick feature so that troublemakers can be dealt with swiftly.
Lastly, I feel like the game needs a teensy, tiny bit of polish. The UI and menus are a bit ugly. While the arenas do look great, there are some rough edges on a few of the maps. These are small gripes, but they are gripes nonetheless.
Minor issues aside, I am already hooked on
despite having played very little of it. This game "grabbed" me right away and refuses to let go, and that is an impressive feat to be said for any game. I am planning to play a lot more of it, and I hope you will take the plunge and do the same!

This is easily one of my favorite JRPG games. I've beat this game to completion on the Vita, and am currently 100%ing it on PC.
PROS:
NEP NEP IS ON PC WOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOO
Pretty casual battle elements
Solid, and enjoyable story
Decent amount of replayability
CONS:
It's a pretty iffy (heh) console port, so crashes can and will happen
Codec packs can screw with the ingame cutscenes
A battle early on has a pretty solid chance of crashing it
Grinding is sometimes the only way to progress through a certain part if you weren't murdering every living thing on the map
It's a pretty casual game, the battles themselves are nothing incredibly difficult, except for a few early game fights (A fair amount of grinding is required to beat these early on). If you're having trouble, you can always activate a 'plan' (gameplay modifiers and the way that you unlock weapons/costumes/consumables) that makes the enemies easier to defeat. Somewhere around an 8.5/10 for gameplay.
The story is freakin great. The characters are pretty well written (NOIRE IS BEST), most of the dialog is spattered with references to other games and the fourth wall is nigh-inexistant. Overall an 9/10 for story and characters.
Replayability is pretty solid. A single run of the game, if you listen to all the dialog, is easily about 15 hours. There's 2 ending-related achievements so if you're looking to get both endings, it's about 20-25 hours. If you're looking to get all the achievements (DAMN THAT MILLIONARE ACHIEVEMENT) you're looking at a solid 40-50 hours. Plus you can unlock the candidates, which are the main CPU's little sisters (UNI IS BEST). Something around a 7.5/10 for replayability.
Overall, this game is a solid 9/10 if you're into cute moe vidya-gaem console grills.

Detour is an odd game. First off, it’s based around multiplayer, but unless you have played through the first couple of single player missions, you have no idea what’s going on. Another thing I noticed right off was the framerate. On a computer with a Core i5 processor, 16 GB of RAM, and a GPU with 2 GB of RAM of its own, I was getting 16 frames per second. On a computer that’s about 4 times the system requirements! However, once the game started, it didn’t disappoint. While the graphics aren’t the best, especially running at 16 frames per second on the lowest settings, the gameplay was fantastic.
The goal of the game is to get a certain number of trucks from your factory to the other side of the map using roads and tunnels. However, your opponent can try to stop you through many methods. One of these is by bribing the police to stop your trucks. After getting sufficiently angry, retaliation can be had by bombing your fellow opponent off of the face of the earth. Mad at the fog of war? No problem! Just run a scan! Don’t want to be scanned? Jam the signal! Don’t want your opponents getting across wetlands? Just fund the local conservation foundation! The fun in this game truly lies in the simplicity of the gameplay, but the complexity the game can take on when played by two skilled players.
After all this, I give this game a thumbs up. It may not be the most visually appealing, but it’s all it set out to be: a good RTS based around semi trucks. I never thought I’d ever type that last sentence, but there it is. Anything can happen.

Preliminary note:  Child of Light requires UPlay to... well, play.  I personally haven't had issues with this, but if you don't like the idea of handing over your personal data to yet another steam knock-off, well, you've been warned then.
Aside from that, Child of Light is a really well-done game, easily one of my personal contenders for Game of the Year.  I've played through it twice, completing both the normal game and the game+ variant.  I'm even considering playing it through a third time because I continue to find new details each time I play through it.  Not to mention, the music is just wonderful.  If anything, this masterpiece is worth it just for the soundtrack alone.
To understand why this game is good, understand that every detail in this game feels like it was put there with a purpose.  Everything from the background music, to the shades in the landscape, to the characters you meet, to the art of the landscapes themselves, all feel well-placed with regards to the story.  Everything follows the story arch beautifully.  There's very little backtracking involved (unless you want to look for extra treasures), so it feels as though the story progresses at a nice pace.  It may sound like the game is narrow, but it doesn't feel that way at all as there are a lot of optional areas you can explore.
Even the combat, which one would suspect could most easily fall victim to redundancy, is very well done.  Almost every chapter, you are introduced to new combat styles and enemies, so it never really gets old.
My only criticism of the game is that the end of the last chapter feels a tad rushed, and apparently it is because there was a section between the end of the previous chapter and the final boss that was omitted, per the creative director in a reddit Q&A.  And it is a real shame too, because I just want more!
If you like fairy tales, JRPGs, normal RPGs, story-driven games, or even just Coeur du Pirate, you should play this game.  Nowadays, I rarely spend more than $15 on any base game given the frequency of steam sales, but this game was worth every cent and then some.

Based on the lack of price tag and inconsistent art style, you may be tempted to pass up Everlasting Summer out of hand. Don't. While there are certainly aspects of this visual novel you could take issue with or just plain dislike, Everlasting Summer is an obvious labor of love on the part of the developers, one that for the most part paid off.
The story opens with a day in the life of Semyeon, a Russian man who seems to be in his late twenties or perhaps early thirties. Semyeon doesn't do much with his life. In fact, he's the Russian equivalent of the Japanese Hikkikomori: he leaves his apartment solely for the sake of things like buying food before returning to his computer to♥♥♥♥♥♥around on Russian imageboards. Only one thing separates his life from an ordinary, if reclusive, existence: Semyeon has a recurring dream of life at a form of summer camp that has not existed since the fall of the USSR, designed to make "ideal citizens" of its campers.
That is the surreal premise of Everlasting Summer: Semyeon living in a time and place that seems entirely real, with no idea how or why he got there or if it is even possible to leave. If you're expecting a full-on psychological horror premise, don't. While there are unsettling elements to the whole thing and Semyeon never stops being concerned about the fantastic nature of his situation, the focus is mostly on romance. In the dream world, Semyeon is physically but not mentally his 17-year old self. Through interacting with the (mostly female) other campers, Semyeon grows as a person from his initially aimless self in a way that depends on the individual route.
Given the premise, it would be easy to fall back on simple character archetypes that are a dime a dozen in visual novels and dating sims. To its credit, Everlasting Summer never does that. While initially you might expect every character to be a simple, unaltered form of the archetype they initially appear to be... That would be incorrect, to say the least. Every one of the girls has a decent amount of depth, and none are entirely what they present themselves as.
The only real faults of Everlasting Summer are highly subjective. If you wanted the horror you might initially expect from the premise, that is fairly limited outside of a few routes designed around it. If you are simply uninterested in visual novels with dating sim tendencies, Everlasting Summer isn't likely to change your mind. If you expect entirely professional and consistent artwork, you won't find that here. If you expect to get through all the routes and endings without occasionally looking at a guide, good luck with that.
Yet despite or because of its flaws, I truly loved my time with Everlasting Summer and felt compelled to go through as many routes and endings as I could manage. What this visual novel occasionally lacks in proffesionalism given its amateur development team it more that makes up for in heart. Give it a shot.

In a city that’s gotten rid of crime, one group rises up against the authorities, because reasons. … Mirror’s Edge (2008) is supposed to be set in a dystopian future where a totalitarian regime and corrupt politicians pull a big brother on the inhabitants, but there really are too many unexplained plot elements for players to feel immersed in. Additionally, the characters are somewhat inconsistent.
For example, Kate Connors, the sister of the protagonist, Faith Connors, is a police officer working for the City Protection Force and her superior, Miller, reveals himself to be a kind of frenemy to Faith as the story unfolds. Yet the heroine has no qualms shooting cops left and right. Naturally, players would assume that these (albeit optional) killing sprees would unsettle her sister or Miller, but they don’t. Murdering blues has absolutely no impact on the story whatsoever. What’s more, Faith herself is a member of the so-called Runners, a group of parkourists who deliver secretive packages from A to B within the City and are opposed to the forces that be. Unfortunately, the game doesn’t really explain what exactly makes the system so inherently evil that it requires annihilation rather than reform and players also never learn what these packages are for, so that the only reason why anyone would identify with Faith is because she is the playable character. Even so, while a good story is always nice to have, the main focus of action-filled video games is the gameplay, of which Mirror’s Edge has quite a bit to show of.
In fact, the ideas within this production are quite fascinating and definitely what gave it its cult status amongst gamers. Mirror’s Edge is a first person parkour simulation that essentially switches back and forth between three gameplay designs. The first will see the player run and jump across linear paths on top of the rooftops of the City. In what basically is a fast-paced obstacle course, one will not only have to build up momentum, but also string together different maneuvers to maintain it and get to the goal. The second transforms the game into a calm puzzle platformer. Here, the music as well as settings are toned down, and players will find themselves in closed environments where they will have to slowly but surely reach their destination.
Finally, the third component is one many players detest about the game: The combat sections. Though mostly optional, when confronted with the blues, Faith can either punch, disarm, or shoot them using their own firearms. The downside here is that she can only take about two direct hits from her rivals before dying, while they take about five and are armed. So, the best way for Faith to get through enemy encounters is really just by running away. Disarming the hostiles then is the second best option, though in order to strip the guns from the goons, players will have to pretty much perform frame perfect button inputs, which require quite a bit of practice to pull off consistently. Once a firearm is then picked up, Mirror’s Edge magically transforms into a standard first person shooter, at least until Faith runs out of ammunition, at which point it’s back to normal.
In short, while the combat is nothing to write home about, the first and second design elements definitely carry the game, which is why it’s sad to see them haunted by some shortcomings. For one, the field of view is quite narrow and not customizable by default, causing players to often not see where they could go next or not notice when enemies are nearby. The other worriment is Mirror’s Edge‘s terrible sign posting. Often times, uninitiated players will find themselves wondering where they are supposed to go to, which isn’t a problem during the puzzle platforming sections, where they have all the time in the world to progress, but becomes an issue during the fast-paced roof top segments, where the police insistently shoots at Faith.
The game tries to alleviate the confusion by having certain key items light up in bright red when Faith is near them to show that this is where she needs to go, however, the way they pop up is somewhat inconsistent. Sometimes, areas won’t have any red elements at all – like in Chapter 1: Flight – Checkpoint B, after Faith has talked to her sister, Kate – other times, objects that aren’t part of the route are still highlighted in red – like the bright, red, massive, crane during Prologue: The Edge – Checkpoint D – then other times again – like in the Chapter 6: Pirandello Kruger – Checkpoint C – everything is in either red or a shade of orange that is very close to it, so that players can’t really tell where the protagonist is supposed to be headed towards.
As it seems that the developers themselves are aware of how problematic their directions might be to newer players, they decided to include a button prompt that will have Faith immediately face towards the goal, but since I completely forgot about its existence, I had finished most of the game without it. Due to these issues, I found the platforming to be quite a mixed bag overall. The puzzle platforming sections – like climbing up the yellow interior of the New Eden shopping mall in the Chapter 8: Kate – Section C – were definitely well-made and enjoyable, but the fast-paced areas were held back by the troublesome directions. Clueless gamers will therefore see Faith either be shot to death by the police every other minute or fall into the onslaught of instant deaths that rob the game of any tension that could have been had.
The insta-deaths also aren’t just the result of lack of orientation, but feel as if they have something to do with unresponsive controls as well. Of course, Mirror’s Edge let’s players switch freely between their gamepad and the PC typical keyboard & mouse combination (the latter certainly being the superior option, if only for better camera manipulation and because the keyboard layout is customizable; unlike the gamepad’s). However, the game seems to randomly refuse to accept inputs, and so Faith sometimes just won’t jump when she needs to. Quite the bother. It is unlikely though that this stands in connection to the game’s perfomance as Mirror’s Edge does run at around 30 – 40 frames per seconds (fps) on the computer I was playing it on, a 32-bit Windows Vista Home Premium desktop PC with an Intel Core 2 CPU, 3070 MB RAM, DirectX 11, and a GeForce 9500 GT graphics card, and it can even run with up to 62 fps on stronger setups. Nevertheless, those with a Radeon Graphic Processing Unit (GPUs) might consider turning off the game’s PhysX as that will drop the framerate down to about 4 fps.
Is Mirror’s Edge fun? No, not really. It can be fun to players who already know what to do and have experience with the mechanics, but that’s certainly no metric to go by and getting to that skill level certainly isn’t any kind of fun. It also takes about 10 hours to finish the game including finding all collectibles, which is why, in the end, Mirror’s Edge is merely a very stylized tech demo with great ideas, but little beyond that. The platforming has some satisfying moments, but these are sadly overshadowed by the lack of directions, shaky camera, occasionally unresponsive controls, as well as the awful, awful combat. Any tension the game tries to build up is also for naught with a story that is barely there and the player character dying for the umpteenth time at the same spot. All in all, Mirror’s Edge has a vision of a first person parkour game, but isn’t quite there yet.

I want to warn anyone that has plans on seeing Game of Thrones to avoid this game at all cost. It spoils a few major scenes that were revealed in the show. The Forrester’s have been loyal banner men to the Starks for years. However, things have changed now that the head of the family has been slain during a betrayal of the Starks. The Forrester family has now been targeted by the Warden of the North, Roose Bolton, who sends his son Ramsey Snow to obtain Fealty from the new Lord. Something simple turns into a big deal when the squire returns to the Forrester’s with a message from the slain Father of the House.
What we liked
Interweaving story line – For the first time in a Telltale game, we get to play as multiple characters. In typical Game of Thrones fashion the tale weaves between three people in the lives of the Forrester’s House. Gared, the squire to the former Lord of the Forrester House. Ethan, the second son of House Forrester and the new Lord, and Mira, the eldest daughter of the Forrester’s and the Handmaiden to Margaery Tyrell.
Each of these characters have their own reasons for protecting House Forrester. A squire that just wants to protect his lord, a son that wishes to live up to the legacy of his father, and a daughter trapped in a foreign place forced to trust a nest full of vipers. Much like Game of Thrones, you never know what to expect from new people you encounter. However, when you encounter characters you’ve read about or watched on a show… you’ll try to use your knowledge to sway their favor or stay their hand.
Without a doubt the adventure game genre is the best avenue for Game of Thrones. Drama and reaction is a mainstay of the books and the show. We all know that combat goes down in Game of Thrones, but the best kills are those that happen when least expected. Game of Thrones - A Telltale Games Series weighs heavy dialogue and characters making choices that may or may not lead to their death. Think of the tale of Robb Stark and you’ll understand what the game is accomplishing here.
Unlike games like The Walking Dead or The Wolf Among Us. We’re not exactly stuck with a character who can make bad choices and reach the end of the game unscathed. I never feared for Lee or Clementine losing their lives or precious body parts. That is not the case in Game of Thrones, you are faced with choices over a long period of time that could call a trickle-down effect. You may have saved one character with your actions, but the next character could suffer for that mistake. It’s the hard life you’d expect out of this series, and Telltale has done a great job at bringing us into that world.
What we didn't like
Art Problems – The interactive storytelling is always the best part of a Telltale game, the art on the other hand is hit or miss. The Wolf Among Us looked to be pushing a new art direction for the company. The characters in this title manage to provide of us with gratifying likenesses of Peter Dinklage, Lena Headey, Iwan Rheon and Natalie Dorner. It even creates some convincing new characters for us to lose. It’s the scenery that lacks polish and looks completely out of place with the world they are trying to convey.
The backdrops feature a weird blur during dialogue cutscenes, the blur can be spotted at the edge of the actors faces. It tries to hide the badly textured environments with an oil painting style that completely fails to do so.
I don’t want to talk too much about this game, it doesn’t deserve to be spoiled in the least. A Telltale game has not impacted me this way since the first The Walking Dead. I’m a big fan of the books and the show, but I wasn’t particularly hyped about this game. Now I’m itching for the second episode, and will try to play the game multiple times for different endings. Even though the art style isn’t that great, this is a must for fans of the series.
*This title was provided to us by the Publisher*

Let me share my INCREDIBLE first few hours of dying light:
At first the game was a struggle, it took me a while to even be able to freerun through the tutorial course xD
Once I got the hang of it, the gameplay seemed slightly dull and mediocre.... until I got through my first night.
My first night run in Dying Light was THE best experience Ive ever had playing a video game.
Seeking a challenge I had my settings on the highest difficulty with Zombie Invasion on Always.
This was a mistake.
Following the end of the cutscene of your first volatile encounter I ran into three volatiles within 30 seconds of running. Panicking, I ran into the heart of the city.
This was also a mistake.
There was no light Whatsoever and I walked into a steet, FILLED with infected, their figures could only be seen as eerie silouettes in the moonlight. I took to the roofs as quickly as possible, so as to use the moonlight to plot a path, My heart pounding in my chest as I could hear the volatiles snarling behind me barely missing me as I scrambled onto the roofs. There must have been 5+ volatiles chasing me, I had one medkit left, and I didnt pack any diapers.
I ran like never before.
Addrenaline coursing through me, I ran at top speed, never missing a step. I could almost feel the cool night air running through my hair. But the volatiles are relentless. I could hear their snarling and breathing getting louder and louder as they slowly caught up to me.
I missed a precision jump (mechanics for which are done perfectly in the game ) and plummeted into the dark abyss of the streets below.
I kept running, it was all I could do, taking sharp turns in alleyways and vaulting the smaller obstacles, as packs of zombies clawed at me, tugging my shirt, slowing me down and damaging me where they could. Despite slowing down to use my final medkit I was gaining ground. Laughing at the insanity that is night running.
Until I hit a dead end.
In a moment of brilliance, I remembered the Light. The UV flashlight, Spikes words echoing in my mind "If you run into one of those volatiles give them a blast of UV light".  I spun around and shined the light directly in the face of a volatile, making full eye contact with one of the grotesque husks of a being that had been chasing me, before it recoiled from the light. The sight of it still haunts me to this day. I was not bothered by its rotting flesh or jagged teeth, but rather the look in its bloodshot eyes. It almost looked ...not happy, but content as if it somehow knew my situation was hopeless.
Time seemed to slow down as I kicked the creature in its exposed ribcage, frantically searching for a way out. There it was. A single perfect ramp angling toward an adjacent roof. Without hesitation I pushed past the creature as 2 more arrived to seal the alleyway, each hitting me in turn. With 17HP I somehow slipped between them,  ran up the ramp and back onto the moonlit rooftops. I could hear my own panting in tune with Kranes as we ran towards the MASSIVE suspension bridge.
There must have been hundreds of zombies on that bridge.
I ran, jumping car to car, knowing that with one wrong step, I would surely perish. I kept running, night blind. My path barely visible in the low flames of wrecked cars. I tripped and scrambled, screamed and prayed, desperately trying to get off that god forsaken bridge. I ran and ran until I reached the center of the bridge, which had been destroyed, presumably in order to quarantine the area. There was no way out, in front there was nothing but a hole in the bridge, looming what seemed like a thousand meters over pitch black water. To my rear the volatiles had caught up with me, now within 20 meters. I took one last look at the murky black water and jumped.
I saw the distant UV lights of a settlement when I finally surfaced and began the long swim back.
I managed to get back to the tower that night, counting my blessings. For I  doubt many others could've survived that run.

Aside from that, Child of Light is a really well-done game, easily one of my personal contenders for Game of the Year.  I've played through it twice, completing both the normal game and the game+ variant.  I'm even considering playing it through a third time because I continue to find new details each time I play through it.  Not to mention, the music is just wonderful.  If anything, this masterpiece is worth it just for the soundtrack alone.
To understand why this game is good, understand that every detail in this game feels like it was put there with a purpose.  Everything from the background music, to the shades in the landscape, to the characters you meet, to the art of the landscapes themselves, all feel well-placed with regards to the story.  Everything follows the story arch beautifully.  There's very little backtracking involved (unless you want to look for extra treasures), so it feels as though the story progresses at a nice pace.  It may sound like the game is narrow, but it doesn't feel that way at all as there are a lot of optional areas you can explore.
Even the combat, which one would suspect could most easily fall victim to redundancy, is very well done.  Almost every chapter, you are introduced to new combat styles and enemies, so it never really gets old.
My only criticism of the game is that the end of the last chapter feels a tad rushed, and apparently it is because there was a section between the end of the previous chapter and the final boss that was omitted, per the creative director in a reddit Q&A.  And it is a real shame too, because I just want more!
If you like fairy tales, JRPGs, normal RPGs, story-driven games, or even just Coeur du Pirate, you should play this game.  Nowadays, I rarely spend more than $15 on any base game given the frequency of steam sales, but this game was worth every cent and then some.

I didn't know much about this game prior to playing, beyond knowing it involved parkour. I picked it up on sale expecting a fun action/adventure romp around a city, but the game is so much more than that. The game is essentially a puzzle game relying on skills over creativity, wrapped in a sleek parkour, gunfighting adventure. Until it sunk in that it was a puzzle game that required patience and thinking, the gameplay had me furious with my frequent deaths. I beat the story in 5-6 hours on normal difficulty, but it could be done much faster. It reminded me a lot of Portal, with its quick but enjoyable gameplay, unique, mildly dystopian worldbuilding, and creative puzzle elements. Where Portal is go-at-your-own-pace and humourous, Mirror's Edge is fast paced and thrilling.
PROS:
-Fun and exciting gameplay
-Unique worldbuilding
-Interesting (and IMO gorgeous) artwork
-Flows well, hardly any load times
-Surprisingly well crafted and enjoyable shoot outs
-Solid storyline
CONS:
-Can be incredibly frustrating
-Some areas require precision, adding to the frustration/confusion of certain levels
-Minor lag/loading towards end of story, nothing brutal
Tl;dr:
It's a well crafted game, short but sweet, don't get too frustrated

I recommend Child of Light, but not without reservations. I bought it for the graphic design and the badass little girl heroine, and in those respects I was certainly not disappointed. Here is a breakdown of what worked and didn't work for me.
Pros:
- Aurora is a great little heroine. She's brave and capable, and though she's polite to other characters, she doesn't take any bull. If I had small children, I would feel good about letting them play this game and this character. But I enjoy her plenty as an adult, too.
- The artwork is lush. If you're drawn to this game for the artistic style, just go ahead and get it, because it's worth it just for that.
- The gameplay itself is more engaging than I expected. It's not particularly challenging, but it remains interesting mainly for the exploration of the beautiful world and a few pleasant navigation puzzles.
Cons:
- The other characters tend towards the overly cutesy. Their dialogue rhymes, which is annoying.
- Though you can technically have a second person "playing" the little firefly, it isn't necessary and it would be boring for that person. I would not call this a co-op game.
- Level-ups happen so frequently -- and you eventually have half a dozen characters in your party to level up -- that it feels tedious. Similarly, the crafting of "oculi" can get tedious as well, although I do appreciate that there is no guide to making them, and you need to figure recipes out on your own.
I'm pleased to have this game; I mostly enjoyed playing it and certainly felt it was worth what I paid for it. If I play again, I'll select the mode with less narration in the hope of avoiding the forced-sounding rhymed dialogue. I won't likely play it more than one more time through, though, if that.

I bought this with a lot of hesitation, because I wasn't a fan of the original title. I liked the idea of creating a parody of the whole console wars. The story begins with 4 sister goddesses who were born from one original one (possibly the Atari?). However, for long as they can remember, the 4 goddesses engage in a long battle and eventually, Neptune gets knocked out and sent flying to the land below. She loses her memory like a stereotypical JRPG character and begins finding a way to regain her memories, only to eventually unite all 4 goddesses together to fight the main enemy.
The story overall was mediocre. Despite all of the cracks about consoles and poking fun of various game/anime stereotypes, (the characters are all a form of one) the game itself was ironically still one. However, it's all about the characters and they're all unique in their own way. Of course, there's a lot of fanfare and random breast physics. Like how IF has jiggle physics is beyond me..But it's there. There's no real "movie" sequences in the game, but only still pictures that only use those jiggle "physics" to compliment the sequences. However, although there's a bit of fanfare, the game doesn't focus TOO much on breast jokes. There's a bit more game jokes as the game centers around the idea of poking fun of console wars. The idea of having flash cards like the R4 as enemies made me laugh.
The music makes you feel as if you're in a digital Japanese setting. Though I'm not a fan of JPOP, I kind of enjoyed the music in the fields and for some characters which were all more instrumental. The opening and ending sequences made me groan.
What helps this game shine is the battle system. It's turn based, but it's fast paced and flashy. You choose sequences of attacks, or a special move to either break the enemy defense, or simply deplete the health. By breaking the enemy shield, your attacks will do a lot more damage. You also build an EXE meter which allows you to unleash devastating attacks to enemies.
The difficulty of the game bounces back and forth from ridiculously easy to managably hard. There was never one time where I felt like I had to adjust my strategy to make the battle easier. You'll just need to grind some levels to make sure the enemies can be defeated.
There's a huge cast of characters in this game, most of which will join your team. Like any fanfare game, there's also a number of costumes and accessories for your characters. You want the swimsuit? Well, yeah, that's there. There's also costumes that are inspired by certain characters of various anime/games as well. Most of the items are created through plans where you have to grind out materials for. The materials aren't tough to get either. You won't have to grind out the same monster several times before getting one piece you need.
It was pretty easy to reach 100% achievements for this game. Maxing out your level doesn't feel like much of a grind, especially since there's some enemies that give a ridiculous amount of experience. Overall, I was happy to give this game another chance and it managed to get me excited enough to play the second one when it releases on Steam.

Edit (since people actually took the time to read this)
I play this game along with my girlfriend in co-op mode. While i wouldn't consider myself new to this type of games, i was soon reminded of how hard RPGs can be.
For people that are new to the genre, this game can prove to be quite frightening, especially at the beginning, even in normal difficulty. The lack of direction given, or... the freedom of choice you have... makes the game quite confusing at first, which is why its highly recommended to always read the dialogue carefully. The game even gives you the option to read again the whole conversation through the conversation log tab.
Co-op mode adds to the fun of the game. The fact that you can play the entire game along with a friend makes it the more enjoyable to go through. While people can argue that co-op can make any game look better, Divinity: Original Sin, gives a further meaning to play with your friend, having the NPCs actually acknowledging your companion and not just simply having it there for the sake of having someone around. You can get to talk with your allies at any time, getting to know them more. At certain times, depending on your actions, you will even get short interactions with whoever is in your party that can boost certain traits based on the answer given. There is a meaning for your friend to be there, is not like other games where your co-op companion is just another clone of yourself.
The gameplay is fun. Turn-base combat system based on AP (Action points) is self explanatory, the more AP's you have, the more actions you can make in your turn. Each character has its own APs that are boosted by their attributes and gear.
You are given several classes to pick from though you are not prohibit from learning other classes abiilties. For example, my knight can use water-based skills which are the ones that can grant healing spells along with other water/ice abilities. As for character appearance customization, its not really deep, in fact, i believe it might be one weak point of the game.
Overall, the game is incredibly addicting and fun. While the early levels might discourage newcomers, this game sure is one big reminder that classic-style RPGs are not dead and can show up at any time to surprise us and remind just how fun and frustrating they used to be. I was lucky enough to encounter no bugs so far, which is something i am grateful for seeing how i read some bugs around that can make progress quite more painful than what it should.
I would hate myself if i had to give a real numeric value to the game, so i will say this: "If you are curious about the game, buy it, you will simply not regret it"
One last thing, save often. F5 will be one of your strongest allies. (Not kidding, really, save often)

Grim Dawn is a great game if you are a fan of Diablo II or Titan Quest -Immortal Throne. The gameplay is like a hybrid of the best elements of both. You get to have a dual class character and there are a lot of skills you can spec as you level up.
For my first character I chose the Shaman/Soldier combo, which I unfortunately regret adding Soldier to. I prefer the two-handed skill tree of the Shaman and his ability to have a pet. Many of the soldier's skills are shield based, so it wasn't the wisest choice by me to combine the two. For my game I leveled the mess out of the Shaman tree and found my character to be very powerful in the early levels, almost too much so at the normal difficulty. I played it solo and having the pet was a huge boon because many times several enemies will swarm you at once. They are also very aggressive in their pursuit if you try to run.
The map reveals itself as you explore and there are portals at various places to travel around or you can cast a portal. Which leads me to one of my minor problems with Grim Dawn. If you need to quit the game, but you are halfway through a dungeon, for example, or not near a standing portal, you can't save where you're at. Even if you cast a portal for yourself. When you log back in it is gone and your character is sent back to one of the "starting" towns. As a family man, I find myself having to pause the game for very long periods of time to do things so I wont lose my place and so I don't have to replay the same area, or say to my wife "I just need to find a portal to link to so I can save my progress!". Making your way to various places can take awhile and I find that my playing sessions are very long. Good for such an enjoyable game, but bad if your playing time is limited.
Nevertheless, I was very impressed by Grim Dawn and found it to be a very good bargain (I got it on a minor sale, but it is  worth full price for sure.)  In fact I plan to buy 3 additional copies so the whole family can play. If you're on the fence, but like point and click dungeon crawlers  this is a must buy for your game library.

I've never played the XCOM franchise before this game so I cannot compare this one to it's predecesors and neither can I judge the franchise as a whole, but I WILL tell you that this is an amazingly fun strategy game. As you can see from the store page; you are the leader of a worldwide anti-alien organisation and it's up to YOU to keep your troops alive and save the planet from their invasion.
IN SHORT:
GOOD
+ The gameplay starts of quite simple but get's more complex and incredibly hard later on, especially on higher difficulties! Great game to just step into without any prior information. No manual needed.
+ First playthrough took me over 40 hours to beat.
+ Simple but engaging story. Aliens invade earth and you're going to stop them. Characters are a bit stereotypical, but the voice acting and music make it all very endearing and fun.
+ Atmosphere is incredible for a top-down turn based game. You really feel the pressure of surviving and trying to complete your objective with little to no casualties. Every decision feels heavy and important; they really nailed that feeling here.
+ Mission variation. There is not a whole lot of it, but the many different maps, scenario's and objectives make it a fun experience for most of the playthrough. Might get a bit repetitive later on if you're trying to max out everything in your base though, expect to do some grinding for that.
+ Overal Quality. It's a very polished game with good graphics and great interface. The tutorial is short but sufficient and the rest speaks for itself.
+ Creating and customizing your own team is SUPER FUN. There arent a billion options to choose from but it's fleshed out enough to make you spend some time trying to recreate you best friends as supersoldiers!
+ The Enemy Within DLC is actually worth buying. It's not as great of an expension as say the Elder Scrolls games. But still a bunch of extra content worthy to give the game another playthrough or two.
+ The aliens are cool and unique. They all have their own strengths and weaknesses and figuring out how to deal with them best while doing scientific research about their bioligy feels as if you're really fighting an unknown enemy that you're slowly starting to understand better.
+ Quite long. Quite hard. Expect to spend a lot of time on this one.
NOT SO GOOD
- Since this is a turn-based strategy game where your chance to hit is a roll of the dice, expect to get frustrated sometimes when your sniper with 95% accuracy misses 2 shots in a row. Can feel unfair, especially on higher difficulties.
- After all aliens and weapons are introduced the game goes on for quite a while. More unlocks or enemies would make it feel less bland and repetitive near the end.
- Though there's quite a lot of dialogue in the game, expect your collegues to repeat themselves a bit too much through the course of the game.
- Though there is some variation in the missions, there are basically only 3 kinds: Exterminate all forces, save civilians or disarm the bomb. It's enough variation for the beginning of the game but can get really bland if you're playing too long in one sitting. I suggest taking breaks from this game so it feels more stimulating.
- Story begins and ends rather abrubtly with little to no explenation to motives or origin of the aliens.
- Even though I said earlier that the Enemy Within DLC is fun, it's also kinda bland without it. All the most awesome stuff like Mechs and and Geneticly-Enhanced soldiers are within the DLC so buying this game without it seems like a waste and you'll never want to replay the vanilla game again without it.
- Even though Multiplayer let's you take control of aliens as well, there's not much reason to stick around after you've finished the single player campaign. I know some people LOVE the multiplayer though, so this is just my personal opinion.
And that's it for XCOM, I hope this review helped you out! If you have any questions be sure to leave a comment!

There are not many games that can boast being remotely as beautiful, challenging, and atmospheric as The Banner Saga.
The Banner Saga is, at its core, a turn-based RPG. The turn-based combat is conducted on a "game board" with square spaces for your units to occupy. Truthfully, The Banner Saga's combat works well enough, but it's not anything special - there's nothing innovative or exceptional about it. It serves its purpose well enough, is fun, and offers some challenge. What makes The Banner Saga so wonderful is just about everything else about it.
It's difficult to summarize all of the aspects The Banner Saga does really well. Right off the bat however, you'll probably notice both the art and audio of the game are fantastic.
It's rare to find a game that creates a unique artistic vision and implements it so well, while still managing to include a great, effective soundtrack. It's probably fair to say a lot of games struggle with nailing either one of these, let alone both. But, The Banner Saga creates a beautiful, deeply atmospheric experience with its classically inspired animation visuals and moving soundtrack. Of course, this could be all for nothing if it's being used to prop-up a weak story; fortunately, it isn't.
If I'm being honest, I don't think I could name another game that comes close to creating such an oppressive story and atmosphere. The pacing of The Banner Saga is excellent; there's a true feeling of dread and desperation constantly building from chapter to chapter as you try to make (what you think are) the best decisions for your caravan, while fighting through seemingly impossible odds. This is a game full of choices - who to accept into your caravan, who to help, when and where to camp, who to take with you into battle - there are many, often tough, decisions that you'll have to make. All of these decisions are presented well, and all of them have consequences, some dire. This makes each playthrough potentially unique.
In The Banner Saga, the world is crashing down around you, and you're left facing insurmountable odds. It will be up to you to lead men, women, and varl. You'll make many decisions, some of which you may come to regret. The world of The Banner Saga is bleak and grim. It's hard not to look at this game with a sense of both wonder and despair, and for that it's impossible for me not to recommend it.

I never can enjoy games that don't make logical sense. As such, I simply could no longer stand to play XCOM Enemy Unknown.
The graphics are good, the gameplay is pretty good and there is plenty of content as well. Not to mention that each playthrough will be different.
But, this game just doesn't make sense, here are just a few issues that simply do not make sense:
1) So you are the commander of an organization that is tasked with protecting the entire world from an alien invasion, yet somehow this organization receives very little funding, despite the fact that every country in the world is helping fund it. I mean, just wtf... this organization receives less funding than the US army does and it is only funded by one country and not the entire world.
2) Walls, they do nothing. While the actual cover you are in will be counted as a physical object, other walls and such will not. This means you can shoot through your allies to kill enemies or in other cases shoot straight through walls to kill an enemy. Yes, that totally makes sense. While other times an enemy is completely in the open and will be missed by your military at less than 10 meters away.
3) Alien versus human accuracy; apparently in the future when we become invaded by aliens, humans will forget how to aim. Even with a 80 percent hit chance my characters missed so often to enemies, even ones in the open. While the aliens can often shoot from far away and hit my characters who are in cover! Where is the logic?!

I didn't know much about this game prior to playing, beyond knowing it involved parkour. I picked it up on sale expecting a fun action/adventure romp around a city, but the game is so much more than that. The game is essentially a puzzle game relying on skills over creativity, wrapped in a sleek parkour, gunfighting adventure. Until it sunk in that it was a puzzle game that required patience and thinking, the gameplay had me furious with my frequent deaths. I beat the story in 5-6 hours on normal difficulty, but it could be done much faster. It reminded me a lot of Portal, with its quick but enjoyable gameplay, unique, mildly dystopian worldbuilding, and creative puzzle elements. Where Portal is go-at-your-own-pace and humourous, Mirror's Edge is fast paced and thrilling.
PROS:
-Fun and exciting gameplay
-Unique worldbuilding
-Interesting (and IMO gorgeous) artwork
-Flows well, hardly any load times
-Surprisingly well crafted and enjoyable shoot outs
-Solid storyline
CONS:
-Can be incredibly frustrating
-Some areas require precision, adding to the frustration/confusion of certain levels
-Minor lag/loading towards end of story, nothing brutal
Tl;dr:
It's a well crafted game, short but sweet, don't get too frustrated
